text: Hormozi identifies three drivers of business value: expanding the customer base, increasing each customer's value, and sustaining those results. He regards branding as the most economical long-term means he knows of addressing all three.

Hormozi argues branding can reduce acquisition costs through better advertising conversion, support prices 2x, 5x, or 10x competitors' prices for identical offerings, and reduce risk by encouraging repeat purchases without comparison shopping.
Hormozi defines learning as responding differently when the same situation recurs; consuming educational material counts as learning only if behavior changes.
Branding connects at least two things. Hormozi calls an association good when most intended customers like it, bad when most dislike it, and absent when exposure leaves behavior unchanged.
Advertising creates awareness of an offering; branding determines the associations communicated through that exposure, identifying the particular seller.
section: What’s the difference between branding and advertising?

text: Reach measures how many people know about an offering. Hormozi treats this advertising output as a prerequisite for having a brand.

Influence measures the likelihood that brand exposure alters behavior; direction measures whether that response approaches or avoids the brand. Direction depends on the audience, so strong influence can accompany either attraction or rejection.

For business owners, Hormozi evaluates branding through financial outcomes: favorable branding produces liking and purchases among intended customers; unfavorable branding produces dislike and nonpurchase.

Hormozi argues that unfavorable publicity can still generate more sales than obscurity because almost no association repels everyone, while favorable publicity offers better sales prospects than unfavorable publicity.
section: Author Note: “There’s no such thing as bad publicity.”

text: Hormozi rejects deliberate polarization as necessary for brand strength. He recommends fulfilling promises that benefit a broad audience and concentrating on purchases, arguing that intentionally provoking division interferes with business.
section: Author Note: “You Have To Be Polarizing”

text: Customers may pay a premium for an otherwise ordinary product because its brand connects them to an identity or outcome they desire.
Branding produces a financial gain when the additional profit earned through premium prices exceeds the expense of creating favorable associations.
Hormozi argues that branding can support higher prices without higher product costs, improve advertising results, and encourage subsequent purchases without additional acquisition spending.

Four-Step Brand Building covers starting, expanding, or redirecting a brand: select the customer, identify their preferences, connect the brand with those preferences, and refine the associations for maximum profit.
section: How to Start, Grow, then Pivot Your Own Brand

text: Four-Step Brand Building, step 1: Narrow the intended audience to increase value delivered per customer. Favor a growing market whose buyers can afford the offer, can be reached readily, and strongly need the solution.
section: Step 1) Figure Out Who Your Ideal Customer Is

text: Four-Step Brand Building, step 2: Identify what the selected customers want and which problems they need resolved; use their specific priorities to determine desirable brand associations.
section: Step 2) Figure Out What They Like

text: Four-Step Brand Building, step 3: Create useful content for the chosen audience, distribute it, and revise it using their responses. Give the material away so customers connect the business with improvements they value.
section: Step 3) Associate Your Brand With Relevant Things They Like

text: Levels of Authority ranks three influences from weakest to strongest: the business’s own messaging, other people’s assessments, and the customer’s direct experience. Personal experience shapes subsequent recommendations and the lasting influence of advertising.
section: Levels Of Authority: The Branding Cycle

text: Advertising can secure an initial purchase despite poor delivery. Unfulfilled promises then create negative associations, deter repeat buying, and encourage unfavorable recommendations, making future customer acquisition harder.
section: Levels Of Authority: The Branding Cycle

text: Brand perceptions affect purchases, while product experiences reshape perceptions of both the brand and its recommenders. Recommenders also shape product perceptions. Advertising matters more initially; product experience has greater influence over time.

Four-Step Brand Building, step 4: Adapt associations to the intended audience. The five market directions are larger buyers, smaller buyers, neighboring segments, a whole category, or a more specific segment.
section: Step 4) Optimizing Your Associations For Max Profit

text: Brand Bouquet describes a brand as a combination of associations with products, values, experiences, and people. Their selection, sources, and relative amounts determine the resulting brand.
Hormozi evaluates a brand pivot by its net audience change: additions should exceed departures. Some existing followers may leave even when the change succeeds overall.
section: Brand Pivots: All About Net Changes in Audience

text: Increasing the volume, quality, and distribution of proven work offers a more reliable growth path. Brand changes involve greater risk and potentially greater rewards; the incoming audience should also care about the products being sold.
section: Brand Pivots: All About Net Changes in Audience

text: A single harmful association can damage perceptions of the entire brand. Hormozi recommends recovery through repeated associations customers favor, reducing the harmful association’s relative importance rather than attempting to erase what happened.

Hormozi argues that branding outperforms direct response advertising over longer periods, although an aggressive offer may earn more immediately. Reputation develops through delivery, others’ commentary, and fulfilled commitments.

Brand communication requires ongoing repetition because newcomers continually encounter the business without knowing its identity. Hormozi recommends continuing to serve these newcomers as attentively as early followers.
The branding checklist favors a target market that is expanding, has pressing problems, can pay for the offering, and is readily reachable.
Hormozi’s branding checklist prescribes five years of persistence without quitting.
Hormozi treats available cash as essential to survival: it allows a business to withstand mistakes, while running out threatens even an otherwise strong business.

Fast Cash Plays are deadline-bound promotions for current buyers, former buyers, and engaged prospects who permit marketing contact. Hormozi recommends quarterly offers that generate purchases beyond customers’ existing spending.
Fast Cash Plays combine restricted availability, intensive personal service, premium pricing, and a purchase deadline to collect money quickly from likely buyers, usually existing customers.

The 10x the 10% rule proposes doubling revenue when 10% of customers purchase an additional offer at ten times the usual price. Hormozi attributes the added profit to acquisition already being paid for, with delivery costs still deducted.
Hormozi recommends preparing cash-generating promotions before unforeseen expenses arise and scheduling them even without an immediate cash shortage.
For premium Fast Cash offers, Hormozi recommends valuable services that resist scaling, such as direct expert attention, customization, greater convenience, or faster service.

Build the offer around one to three primary components plus three bonuses. Introduce bonuses separately to strengthen perceived value, but give every bonus to every buyer, including those who purchased before its announcement.

Initially limit purchases to a quantity likely to sell out, roughly 5–10% of customers. With 1,000 or more customers, delivery capacity may require a lower cap. Hormozi argues that selling out strengthens demand for subsequent promotions.
Hormozi recommends pricing a Fast Cash offer at 10–50 times the usual transaction amount, with exceptional value and greater service effort to match.
After selling out, Hormozi recommends waitlisting people who attempted to purchase and obtaining permission to notify and charge them if capacity becomes available.

When constructing an exceptionally expensive offer, retain services that are difficult to scale; Hormozi says these often justify the premium price. Separate bonuses so they can be introduced during promotion.
Hormozi says an annual prepayment offer to existing customers typically needs little beyond added bonuses to obtain acceptance from 10% of them.
section: Recurring Max Cash Offer - Price: Monthly Price x 12

text: Consider excluding leads who have received no communication for at least six months, and reengage them for a later promotion. For the current offer, Hormozi recommends existing customers and former customers whose relationships remain positive.

For automated checkout, build anticipation before buyers compete for limited availability. For consultation sales, open access immediately and schedule every sales appointment within the seven-day promotion.
Hormozi recommends running Fast Cash offers quarterly, allowing time between promotions to fulfill commitments and prepare again.
section: 5 Reasons To Run Fast Cash Offers Every 90 Days

text: Hormozi reports achieving gross margins of at least 90% on his Fast Cash promotions and recommends that readers target the same threshold.

Hormozi recommends emphasizing value that is difficult to scale and choosing a matching price; his checklist specifies 10–50 times for maximum cash, without identifying the comparison price on this page.
For consultation sales, accept purchases immediately and schedule calls before the deadline. For automated checkout, generate anticipation first, then use a brief purchasing window.
Hormozi expects a strong offer to sell out by campaign day 3 or 4. If sales have not reached a substantial share of capacity, he suggests adding value before sending the remaining messages.

Hormozi uses seven days for consultation campaigns: longer campaigns weaken urgency, while shorter ones leave insufficient time to capture sales. He aims to complete meetings and close purchases before the deadline.
Send a sold-out announcement only after the offer has actually sold out.
Hormozi argues that an apparent market ceiling can reflect inadequate ad quality: stronger creative can persuade a wider audience, and producing more ads is his route to improving quality.

The awareness framework attributed to Eugene Schwartz distinguishes buyers awaiting an offer, evaluating a familiar product, seeking a known outcome, recognizing only a problem, or recognizing neither problem nor need.
section: Why Ads Hit A Wall And How To Scale Past It

text: Hormozi treats awareness as a continuum rather than rigid categories. He argues that hook strength, the offer, and its presenter influence how unfamiliar an audience an ad can profitably convert.
section: Why Ads Hit A Wall And How To Scale Past It

text: The Ad Assembly Process combines separately produced components: 50 hooks, 3–5 body scripts, and 1–3 calls to action yield 150–750 possible ads each week.

Hormozi assigns 90% of advertising work to preparation. Within preparation, he allocates 80% to hooks, 20% to the body, and approximately 0% to calls to action, because viewers must pass the opening before anything else matters.
Hook development has two tracks: weekly variations built from previous successes and experimental openings intended to reach new markets.

Hormozi sources hooks from successful ads and unpaid content, both his own and others’. He consults platform ad libraries last because visible ads provide inspiration without reliably revealing which ones perform well.
section: Writing Hooks For Immediate Results From Previous Winners

text: When additional spending stops being profitable, Hormozi suggests refreshing creative. If that has already been tried, hooks may need to address a broader audience.
section: Writing Expansion Hooks To Enter New Markets

text: Awareness-Level Hooks: For people already familiar with the business and its products, emphasize the offer. For people familiar with the product category but unaware the business sells it, emphasize evidence of results and experience.
Awareness-Level Hooks: When people recognize both their problem and available solution types, lead with a promised outcome. Specific results and timing can strengthen that promise.
Awareness-Level Hooks: When people recognize their problem but do not know available solutions, lead with the pain they already experience.
Awareness-Level Hooks: When people do not recognize a problem, use curiosity about an unnoticed cost or issue to introduce it.
Hormozi recommends testing memes that reflect the intended audience's culture as a way to expose more people to an ad.
section: Pro Tip: The Widest Hooks Possible

text: Hormozi reviews previous winners and drafts roughly 50 hooks across awareness categories. If 90% address only the most aware audience, he recommends diversifying; broader hooks can also reach less familiar prospects.
section: Pro Tip: The Widest Hooks Possible

text: The ad body should deliver on the hook, which should fit the audience's awareness. Hormozi groups bodies into five formats: demonstrations, testimonials, education, stories, and faceless creative; formats can be combined.
Hormozi gives ad bodies 20% of his attention and usually records three to five per weekly session. He replaces them less frequently because fewer viewers reach that part of an ad.
Demonstration ads can show a product being used, people's reactions, package openings, or comparisons of conditions before and after use. Elaborately produced hero ads also belong to this format.
Testimonial ads accommodate customer-created recordings, polished or informal endorsements, podcast excerpts, group appearances, street interviews, influencer collaborations, and lifecycle material.
Education ads can explain a subject, teach practical actions through a list, or repurpose organic content that has already performed well.
Story ads can use narratives about lifestyles, risks, or opportunities, along with documentary treatments, acted scenes, and statements of brand convictions.
Faceless ads can use captured customer messages, written copy alone, sequences of slides, animated material, cartoons, or visual effects.
An interested viewer's motivation may fade quickly. Give an explicit instruction for the next action and demonstrate the response process so the experience matches what the viewer expects.
Urgency, scarcity, guarantees, and bonuses can strengthen a call to action and encourage more responses.

A CTA should identify the requested action, explain its execution and timing, and state the benefit. Explaining the following stage is optional but matters more for lead magnets and sales processes involving multiple steps.
section: Make One To Three CTAs Per Recording Session

text: Create one to three CTAs per recording session. To compare them, run three ads with identical hooks, bodies, and audiences, changing only the CTA. Hormozi generally retains one or two effective versions.
section: Make One To Three CTAs Per Recording Session

text: Begin with many ad variations to reach different market segments and discover strong performers. Then concentrate on winners and reuse their hooks; new market entrants may still be seeing familiar creative for the first time.
Hormozi’s ad-production checklist specifies writing 50 hooks, 3–5 main ad segments, and 1–3 calls to action, then repeating the process to seek another winning ad.
A hook should emphasize what matters to the audience rather than the featured person's importance.
The opening of an email, post, advertisement, webinar, or training should persuade people to continue consuming it and shape how they receive the remaining material.
Hormozi describes hooks as having two components: a call-out that signals relevance to the intended audience and a condition for receiving value.
Hormozi recommends spending the first eight of ten available advertising hours developing hooks.
A hook can communicate its value promise explicitly or implicitly. People consume when they expect the benefit to exceed the cost of consuming.
Hooks can attract attention through sounds and visuals as well as language; Hormozi recommends combining verbal and nonverbal elements when the platform supports them.
section: Types Of Hooks: Verbal And Nonverbal

text: The 70-20-10 Hook Rule assigns 70% of effort to hooks already shown to work in Hormozi’s content or other creators’ content.
The 70-20-10 Hook Rule assigns 20% of effort to promising but less established approaches, including adapting concepts that perform well in another niche.
The 70-20-10 Hook Rule reserves 10% of effort for entirely new experiments. Record failures to avoid repeating them; move successes into the 70% allocation and retain them until surpassed.
For advertising, Hormozi records approximately 10 different hooks per piece of ad content.
For long-form content, Hormozi records 3–4 opening alternatives; his team selects the one they expect to perform best during editing.

Beginners should publish content to establish performance data, then apply 70-20-10. Make more hooks resembling those in their own top 10% and fewer resembling those in their bottom 10%, repeating the comparison.
section: Author Note: Let The Data Do The Teaching

text: Hormozi argues that stronger hooks improve click volume and quality, reduce customer acquisition costs, and make additional markets and colder audiences profitable to reach.
section: Why You Should Actually Take The Time To Improve Your Hooks

text: For subsequent ad batches, identify the best-performing 10% (five hooks): allocate 70% to those winners, 20% to visual or verbal variations, and 10% to entirely different hooks sourced through the initial research approach.
A good hook combines an attention-catching callout with an implied benefit from consuming the material.
Hook variety can come from asking a question, directing the viewer to act, making an assertion, presenting numbered guidance, or opening a narrative.
Scarcity can be expressed through the number of units or places still available; urgency can be expressed through a deadline.
A continuity offer can use a valuable product or service provided free at enrollment as an incentive to join.
The Value Equation multiplies the desired outcome by perceived probability of success, then divides by the product of waiting time and required effort or sacrifice.
section: FIRST DRAFT OF THE VALUE EQUATION

text: The gap between value and price represents customer surplus; the gap between price and cost represents business surplus.
section: FIRST CONCEPT OF THE PRICE TO VALUE DISCREPANCY

text: The pricing-cycle sketch associates higher prices with greater perceived value, better results, more fulfillment revenue per customer, higher service levels, and stronger sales-team conviction; lower prices reverse those directions.
section: FIRST DRAFT OF THE VICIOUS VS. VIRTUOUS CYCLE OF PRICE

text: Offer design includes duration, payment timing, deliverables, assurance of delivery, incentives for immediate action, and actions required from the buyer.
section: FIRST DRAFT OF THE SALES TO FULFILLMENT CONTINUUM

text: The sales-to-fulfillment continuum contrasts offers that are easier to sell but harder to deliver with offers that are harder to sell but easier to deliver.
section: FIRST DRAFT OF THE SALES TO FULFILLMENT CONTINUUM

text: Offer development moves from the desired result to customer obstacles and possible solutions, then evaluates components by value and cost to assemble a valuable, profitable package.
section: FIRST DRAFT OF THE 6 STEPS TO CREATE YOUR GRAND SLAM OFFER

text: The headline framework is flexible: an offer name does not need to include every component.
section: FIRST DRAFTS OF THE MAGIC HEADLINE FORMULA

text: MAGIC structures offer names around a compelling reason, the intended audience, a desired result, a time span, and a word identifying the package format.
section: FIRST DRAFTS OF THE MAGIC HEADLINE FORMULA

text: An offer can receive a different name and presentation while retaining the same underlying bundle.
section: FIRST DRAFTS OF THE MAGIC HEADLINE FORMULA

text: Guarantee design starts by identifying customers' greatest perceived risks and reversing them, including risks involving time, emotions, and outside expenses. Greater specificity helps a guarantee stand out.
section: FIRST DRAFT OF THE GUARANTEES INGREDIENT

text: A guarantee can tie its remedy to a specified result and deadline, with optional customer requirements. Remedies can include refunds, additional service, expense reimbursement, or postponed billing.
section: FIRST DRAFT OF THE GUARANTEES INGREDIENT

text: The lead-generation outline treats customers, partners, employees, affiliates, and resellers as potential targets, and pairs multiple offers with multiple pipelines.
section: FIGURING OUT THE TABLE OF CONTENTS (DRAWINGS BELOW)

text: The draft evaluation stage considers cost, operational burden, and reliability before deciding whether to improve or scale an acquisition approach.
section: FIGURING OUT THE TABLE OF CONTENTS (DRAWINGS BELOW)

text: A promotion can be analyzed as an offer communicated through a medium on a platform.
An activity plan specifies its target, action, channel, timing, responsible person, process, measurement, quantity, and duration.
Avatar selection considers beliefs, eligibility requirements, aspirations, and demographic characteristics.
Lead refinement is depicted as filtering an existing population to identify suitable prospects, rather than creating those prospects.
The lead-source sketch distinguishes paid, earned, and owned attention alongside outbound contact, affiliates, and referrals.
The media matrix classifies material along two dimensions: reading, watching, or listening, and short, medium, or long duration.
The advertising-cycle diagram links the offer, intended customer, medium, acquisition channel, platform, and audience with engaged leads.
The scaling sketch moves from personal advertising toward others advertising, from an existing audience toward additional audiences, and from one platform toward similar platforms.
Advertising leverage includes having employees, affiliates, customers, or machines perform messaging and publishing activities.
The acquisition diagram tracks prospects through five states: not yet contacted, contacted, engaged, qualified, and sold.
The Core Four matrix combines two distinctions: whether people already know the advertiser and whether communication is private to one person or public to many.
Partner arrangements can connect one business's offer with another's upsell and divide revenue from the initial sale, lifetime sales, or sales during a specified period.
Lead-magnet sketches include uncovering a problem and providing one free step from a larger process.
Lead magnets can take the form of informational material, a service, or a physical product.
Warm outreach addresses someone who already knows the sender; illustrated contact methods include email, telephone, direct messaging, text messaging, and voicemail.
Content publication is depicted as delivering value to an audience that can grow.
Media choices extend beyond format and length to whether delivery is live or recorded and whether participation is virtual or in person.
Hormozi advocates repeatedly giving value until the audience initiates a request.
Each word in content should justify its inclusion.
Both short and long content need to attract attention, sustain it, and provide a payoff.
A content unit combines a hook, retention, and reward; longer content can integrate multiple such units into one piece.
The content-unit structure can operate at nested scales within writing, including an entire book, its chapters, and individual paragraphs.
A single piece of content can contain several hooks and several rewards.
The three identified retention structures organize material as a list, a sequence of steps, or a story.
Cold outreach addresses strangers through channels illustrated as email, telephone, direct messaging, text messaging, and voicemail.
Prospect contacts can be sourced through software extraction, purchased from brokers, or found through manual searching.
Outreach execution can vary between manual and automated activity and between live and recorded communication.
The paid-advertising diagram shows free value being presented to people who do not know the advertiser.
The expansion sketch ranks trying new placements as easier than trying new platforms, with trying another Core Four method harder still.
Lifetime gross profit is calculated by multiplying gross profit per month by the number of months the customer remains.
The LTGP-to-CAC ratio compares lifetime gross profit with customer acquisition cost; lifetime gross profit of 30 and acquisition cost of 10 produce a 3:1 ratio.
The What-Who-When Framework combines outcome dimensions, the perspective of oneself or relevant other people, and a past, present, or future time frame.
Lead volume can increase through greater advertising expenditure, more content, more outreach, or activity on additional channels and platforms.
Better leads means a larger proportion of leads become customers; the diagram links this to a more concentrated channel.
A business's visible competitors on one channel do not establish its share of the entire market; that view covers only one method, platform, and medium.
The broader acquisition landscape includes warm and cold outreach, publishing content, paid advertising, referrals, and affiliates.
Lead getters are other parties who spread awareness of the business's offerings, including customers, affiliate partners, staff, and agencies.
Leverage concerns the relationship between the input someone contributes and the output they receive.
Instead of personally producing every lead, a business owner can acquire lead getters who repeatedly produce leads, then acquire additional lead getters.
A recruiter adds another layer of delegation by finding lead getters who then generate leads.
Referrals can multiply across successive generations of customers, producing exponential growth.
Goodwill occupies the gap between customer value and price, while profit occupies the gap between price and the business's cost.
Set expectations below what the business delivers, rather than promising more than it delivers.
Improve customer outcomes by increasing the proportion of customers who achieve success.
Bring customer wins forward in time.
The Golden Ratio divides referred customers by customers lost to churn; the accompanying growth equation subtracts monthly customer losses from monthly referral gains.
Four customer milestones cover activation, giving a testimonial, making a referral, and moving to a further purchase; their order can vary.
Sales and customer success should coordinate the customer transition, connecting activation, continuing value, and ascension.
Hormozi presents purchasing the product and understanding it as prerequisites for ethically selling it as an affiliate.
Whisper, Tease, Shout organizes launch promotion into three successive stages.
Acquiring affiliates creates a structure in which those partners acquire customers.
Moving from personal execution toward leadership involves accepting that other people can perform the work better than the owner.
The Dual Advertising Funnel pairs a customer funnel that converts leads into buyers with an employee funnel that converts leads into hires.
The Internal Core Four applies recruiting through existing contacts, cold outreach, posts to one's network, and paid promotion of job postings.
Internal lead getters include employee referrals, community owners, in-house recruiters, and recruiting or staffing agencies.
The Performance Diamond places performance among four factors: communication, training, motivation, and circumstances.
The Rule of 100 prescribes 100 daily outreach attempts, 100 minutes of content work, or 100 dollars in paid advertising, sustained for 100 days.
An additional version of the Rule of 100 applies the daily commitment to more than one Core Four method.
The advertising sequence selects customers, affiliates, or employees as the target; chooses daily Rule of 100 actions; completes the advertising checklist; then applies More, Better, New.
For sales that depend on an appointment, a prospect must attend before a purchase can happen.
Schedule rate measures bookings as a share of engaged leads; show rate measures attendance as a share of scheduled leads; throughput measures attendance as a share of engaged leads.
Hormozi reports that shorter delays between booking and appointments, more follow-up attempts, and more frequent lead replies correlate with higher attendance rates.

This playbook addresses medium-term nurturing between initial interest and purchase, specifically improving appointment attendance within 30 days; ongoing content and long-term follow-up fall outside its scope.
section: Next Up: The Four Pillars of Lead Nurture

text: The Four Pillars of Lead Nurture are availability, meaning open appointment capacity; speed to contact, covering response delay and booking distance; personalization, meaning relevant, useful communication; and volume, meaning outreach attempts before stopping.

Availability combines appointment capacity with how far ahead bookings are permitted. Hormozi reports that days offered, daily hours, and slots per hour collectively were the strongest predictor of throughput, with diminishing returns as availability increased.

When available appointments conflict with a lead’s schedule, the lead may avoid booking or accept an inconvenient time. Hormozi warns that inconvenient bookings invite missed appointments, reduce purchase likelihood, and occupy slots others could use.
Hormozi recommends accepting appointments on more days each week, including all seven days, to create more opportunities to sell.
section: 1) Take Appointments More Days Per Week:

text: For businesses selling across the United States, Hormozi reports that 6 am–6 pm PST captured the greatest share of sales relative to hours offered.
section: 2) Take Appointments More Hours Per Day:

text: Offer appointment starts every 15 minutes instead of every 30 or 60 minutes while retaining existing appointment lengths. Hormozi notes that this can create gaps between appointments and may require additional salespeople.
section: 3) Give Leads More Flexible Appointment Times:

text: Scheduling pages should identify the intended audience, explain the next action and its purpose, display available slots immediately on desktop and mobile, and remove unnecessary steps or requests for information already supplied.

When too many unsuitable appointments fill the calendar, Hormozi recommends adding booking barriers through preparatory content, visible pricing, or delayed scheduler access to reduce bookings while improving their quality.
section: Author Note: Solution For Too Many Bad Appointments

text: Hormozi distinguishes three dimensions of speed: initial outreach, getting to the first appointment, and answering subsequent messages.
section: How To Increase Speed To Contact

text: Hormozi sets a target of contacting every lead within five minutes; he says faster initial outreach reduces the number of contact attempts needed before purchase.

Hormozi recommends restricting bookings to the next three days, or 72 hours, because shorter waits improve attendance. Five days is an acceptable fallback; monitor attendance rates to determine the best window for the business.

After handling fresh leads, use available time to call people who booked themselves and bring their appointments earlier, preferably today; if a qualified lead is available immediately, proceed with the sale or transfer to an available closer.
When another closer will conduct the appointment, introduce the lead and closer in a shared text conversation and explain the closer’s relevant experience and results.
Use message and call timestamps to investigate response delays when appointment attendance declines, particularly when the decline concerns one representative.
Hormozi recommends initiating contact through several channels, then prioritizing whichever channel the lead answers; moving to phone, video, or an in-person conversation can happen later.
section: 1) Use The Lead’s Preferred Communication Method

text: Use pre-call applications to assess fit, cancel appointments with unsuitable prospects, and devote more sales time to promising leads.

Build qualification questions from top customers’ behaviors and demographics, collect answers before appointments, assign scores using 1–5 or red/yellow/green categories, and direct the strongest prospects to the strongest closers.
section: 3) Send The Best Leads To The Best Closers

text: Create separate email and text sequences for lead categories identified through qualification questions, tailoring content to each category’s particular problems.

Push incentives provide benefits before attendance to encourage reciprocity; pull incentives provide benefits upon arrival to motivate attendance. An advance gift remains the lead’s even if they miss the appointment.
An A/B attendance incentive should satisfy three conditions: the prospect wants it, its connection to the eventual offer is apparent, and preparing it costs the business something real.

Match customer evidence to the prospect’s characteristics. Send it before scheduled appointments, between calls one and two, and every 90 days after disengagement; for disengaged leads, feature customers who joined around the time contact stopped.
Hormozi recommends selecting testimonials and case studies that reflect a lead’s demographics to build enthusiasm for attending.
Scheduling Appointments, step 1: Telephone new leads within five minutes after they opt in.

Hormozi’s opening-day cadence uses an immediate second call after an unanswered first call, then voicemail and text if unanswered. Repeat paired calls plus text twice more that day, spacing attempts several hours apart; comply with local laws.

After day one, Hormozi recommends two calls daily for two days, one earlier and one later, texting after the latter. Follow with one daily call and text for four days; these durations are adjustable, subject to local laws.

Hormozi recommends clearly identified automated messages: an immediate booking confirmation with appointment date, time, caller number, and representative, followed by reminders 24, 12, and 3 hours beforehand. Express times in the lead’s local zone.
BAMFAM means arranging the subsequent meeting during the current one. Hormozi treats reluctance to commit to another appointment as an objection to address during that conversation.
section: 3) Book Their Next Appointment At The Current Appointment

text: Hormozi recommends personalized manual reminders sent using an actual mobile phone the preceding evening, on the appointment morning, and one hour before the meeting.

Hormozi defines organizational culture through its rules about acceptable and unacceptable conduct. An execution culture reinforces availability, quick responses, personalization, and persistence while discouraging their opposites.
Hormozi recommends an attendance-related commission supplement, usually 5–30% of the salesperson’s earnings from one sale, with the amount depending on the sale price.

Hormozi ranks representatives by attendance rate, closing rate, and overall call-to-sale conversion. He recommends accounting for both nurturing and closing when determining compensation and team recognition.
Hormozi recommends offering appointments seven days weekly, aiming for 9 a.m.–9 p.m. EST and four booking options hourly, spaced 15 minutes apart.

Hormozi recommends staffing for initial lead contact within five minutes, ideally under 60 seconds; appointments should fall on the inquiry day or either of the following two days, moving earlier when possible.
His outreach schedule pairs double-dialing with texting: three times on day one, twice daily on days two and three, then once daily for another one to four days.

Hormozi schedules automated reminders 24, 12, and three hours beforehand, identifying the name, appointment date and time, and caller number or area code. Manual reminders from an actual phone occur the preceding evening, that morning, and 60 minutes beforehand.
Hormozi uses free or steeply discounted introductory offers in new markets to allow refinement, obtain testimonials, strengthen his selling confidence, and encourage referrals.
section: Why I Use Free & Discount Promotions

text: Hormozi prioritizes creating demand before increasing monetization and purchase barriers. When later upsells support the business, he keeps the introductory price low to sustain incoming leads.
section: Get Flow. Monetize Flow. Then Add Friction.

text: Promotions should increase the existing offer's appeal rather than alter its substance; unfamiliar audiences need a clear personal benefit to become interested.
section: Get Flow. Monetize Flow. Then Add Friction.

text: Premium offers require both substantial customer value and a sales process capable of communicating that value.
section: Section A: Premium Promotions: Presenting Your Grand Slam Offer On Its Own

text: Hormozi advises newcomers to attract customers with free or discounted offers, establish results, then transition to premium pricing. A premium follow-on offer depends on having shown value through the initial free offer.
section: If I lost Everything And Had To Start Over . . .

text: A premium offer aims to sell the option most likely to produce the customer's best attainable result; Hormozi does not rank this approach above other offer types.
Hormozi says premium offers generally attract more qualified customers, reducing customer screening and operational burden, while requiring higher acquisition spending for those buyers.
Premium promotions make each sales opportunity expensive, increasing the cash needed for volume and reducing tolerance for mistakes while learning the sales process.
section: #1 Most Expensive Cost Per Lead/Can Take More Time To Break Even

text: Before leading with a premium offer, have either a demonstrated sales process suited to the target customer or enough cash to develop one.
section: #3 Must be good at sales because this is a good old fashioned sale

text: An unsuccessful free promotion can indicate an unwanted or poorly described giveaway, insufficient credibility, or targeting that fails to reach the appropriate audience.
For the same paid audience exposure, a higher response rate reduces cost per lead; Hormozi presents free promotions as producing the greatest response volume and lowest lead cost.
Use participation requirements to balance free-offer volume against lead quality and operational capacity. Additional steps reduce participation and can also eliminate otherwise suitable prospects.
section: #1 Volume Can Be A Double-Edged Sword

text: Requiring prospects to consume sales material improves lead quality while reducing volume. Hormozi recommends this when audiences are large and exposure is inexpensive; smaller volumes may not justify the filter.
Compare qualified-lead totals at a given advertising spend rather than qualification rates alone; keep the giveaway valuable without exceeding delivery capacity or resources.

Hormozi reports 4 independent gym tests, each covering 10 representative markets: free and premium promotions matched on closing rate and average purchase amount; switching to free usually cut lead costs by a factor of at least 5.
Hormozi favors discounts of at least 50% for attracting otherwise unresponsive prospects; he considers 5–25% reductions insufficient to change behavior and costly to margins.
Revenue from a discounted introductory purchase can offset some acquisition spending, but Hormozi cautions against relying on that payment to finance marketing.
Hormozi estimates attendance at 85–90% or higher when people have paid, presenting discounted entry purchases as a way to reduce missed appointments in a two-step sale.
section: #4 The Two-Step Sale (Probably the Biggest Benefit)

text: Use a heavily discounted purchase outside the core offer to obtain payment details, deliver initial value, and facilitate a more expensive sale; an existing card on file reduces payment friction during the upsell.
section: #5 Discount Offers Make Upsells Smoothe As Buttaaa

text: Repeated reductions on the main offering can teach buyers to wait for sales. Hormozi recommends discounting a small component for customer acquisition instead of routinely reducing the whole offering.
Treat introductory discount buyers as qualified prospects for the core service. Hormozi attributes bargain-only buying partly to offers that fail to qualify people for the main purchase.
Hormozi finds introductory discounts more effective for familiar services whose normal price ranges buyers understand; unfamiliar offerings lack the comparison buyers need to appreciate the savings.

Hormozi orders acquisition development as attracting responses, making those responses profitable, then adding barriers. He usually establishes an initial performance baseline with a free or deeply discounted offer.
Making money requires an offer, prospective customers, and a sales process that converts those prospects into buyers.
Hormozi initially describes leads as potential customers who have a problem to address and money available to spend, while acknowledging that definitions vary.
Advertising means making an offering known to people unfamiliar with it. Hormozi presents increased awareness as a way to generate more sales.
Hormozi attributes insufficient leads to insufficient advertising: prospective buyers remain unaware the business exists, limiting incoming revenue.
Hormozi identifies two routes to business growth: increase the number of customers or increase each customer's value to the business.
Hormozi identifies four lead acquisition priorities: greater volume, higher quality, lower cost, and dependable supply through multiple sources.
Hormozi proposes that doubling lead volume doubles the business, provided all other factors stay constant.
A lead is someone reachable through a means of contact; demonstrated buying interest is not required for this definition.
Engaged leads are reachable people who demonstrate interest in what a business sells. Hormozi identifies these interested contacts as advertising’s intended result.
Generating engagement requires offering something the intended audience wants.

Hormozi recommends first advertising the main paid offer directly; a preliminary offer may attract more engagement when prospective customers need additional understanding before buying, particularly for expensive purchases.
A lead magnet fully addresses a limited problem, usually free or inexpensively, while exposing a subsequent need that the main paid offer addresses.
A lead magnet should have enough standalone value to justify a price while increasing interest in the business's further offerings.
Seven Steps To Creating an Effective Lead Magnet, step 1: Choose the intended audience and the specific problem the introductory offer will address.
section: Step 1: Figure out the problem you want to solve and who to solve it for

text: The Problem-Solution cycle describes how resolving an issue exposes further issues, with smaller cycles nested within broader ones.
section: Step 1: Figure out the problem you want to solve and who to solve it for

text: Choose a limited problem whose resolution exposes a subsequent problem that the main paid offer can address.
section: Step 1: Figure out the problem you want to solve and who to solve it for

text: Diagnostic lead magnets uncover problems the audience has not recognized; Hormozi particularly recommends them for issues that deteriorate with delay.
Sample or trial lead magnets provide complete access briefly, restricting usage, duration, or both. Hormozi recommends this approach when the paid offer repeatedly addresses a recurring need.
A partial-process lead magnet provides one useful stage without charge and sells the remaining stages. Hormozi recommends this approach for paid offers addressing complex problems.
Seven Steps To Creating an Effective Lead Magnet, step 3: Select delivery through a digital tool, educational material, work performed for the prospect, or a tangible item.
section: Step 3: Figure out how to deliver it

text: Combining 3 solution types with 4 delivery methods yields up to 12 lead magnet variants for one limited problem.
section: Step 3: Figure out how to deliver it

text: Seven Steps To Creating an Effective Lead Magnet, step 4: Test the headline first, visuals second, and supporting headline third. If only one element can be tested, prioritize the headline.
section: Step 4: Test What To Name It

text: Hormozi distinguishes generating leads from selling: this book targets expressions of interest from unfamiliar people, with the purchase occurring later.

Test packaging with audience polls, posts requesting a choice, or direct messages. A small response count can indicate direction; unsolicited requests for availability provide an additional positive signal.
Seven Steps To Creating an Effective Lead Magnet, step 5: Reduce access and usage effort through device compatibility, varied media formats, and broader service hours and communication options.
section: Step 5: Make it easy for them to consume

text: Hormozi says simplifying consumption can increase uptake and actual use by 2x, 3x, or 4x and beyond.
section: Step 5: Make it easy for them to consume

text: Offering a lead magnet in several formats can attract additional engaged leads by accommodating different ways people prefer to consume it.
Lead magnet creation, step 6: Make the free material sufficiently valuable that prospects receive more value before purchasing than the core offer costs.
section: Give Away The Secrets, Sell The Implementation

text: Lead magnet creation, step 7: After prospects consume it, provide a call to action specifying their next action and reasons to take it immediately, using straightforward language.
section: Step 7: Make it easy for them to tell you they want more

text: Scarcity means restricted supply, particularly relative to demand. Hormozi recommends advertising genuine operational limits, such as onboarding capacity or inventory, to create an ethical reason for acting now.
Urgency comes from limiting the time available to act, even when supply is unlimited. Deadlines on purchases, discounts, or bonuses can prompt faster responses.
The Fraternity Party Planner approach supplies a reason to act even without scarcity or urgency. Hormozi argues that an arbitrary reason can outperform giving none.
section: c) Fraternity Party Planner (my favorite) - Make Up A Reason.

text: Allocating money to lead magnet delivery can increase its value relative to competitors, encouraging more strangers to engage and more recipients to buy.
section: c) Fraternity Party Planner (my favorite) - Make Up A Reason.

text: Hormozi evaluates lead magnets by whether they attract suitable prospects, generate greater engagement than the main offer alone, deliver enough value to be consumed, and increase purchase likelihood among suitable buyers.
A warm audience consists of people who have permitted contact, including existing relationships, followers, and customers.
section: Two Types of Audiences: Warm and Cold

text: A cold audience consists of people who have not permitted contact. Hormozi includes strangers reached through acquired contact lists or paid access to platforms.
section: Two Types of Audiences: Warm and Cold

text: Private communication delivers messages individually; public communication can reach many recipients simultaneously. Automation does not change this classification: sending email to 10,000 recipients remains individual communication performed rapidly by machines.
section: Two Ways To Communicate: One to One (Private), One to Many (Public)

text: The Core Four crosses audience type with communication format: warm outreach addresses warm contacts individually; posting content addresses them publicly; cold outreach addresses strangers individually; paid ads address strangers publicly.
Hormozi attributes insufficient lead generation to inadequate proficiency or activity volume in the Core Four.
Warm outreach means contacting people who already know you individually. The communication can introduce either a free lead magnet or the main paid offering.
Hormozi describes warm outreach as applicable to audiences of 100 or 1,000,000 contacts; employees and automation can increase efficiency as the business grows.
Hormozi recommends warm outreach for acquiring the first five customers of a new offering, reconnecting with previous contacts, and introducing additional product lines.
section: How To Do Warm Reach Outs in 10 Steps

text: Warm Outreach, step 1: Gather and count contacts across your phone, past email accounts, and social platforms to establish an initial prospect list.
section: (Step 1) “But I don’t have any leads…” → Everyone Has A List

text: Warm Outreach, step 2: Begin on whichever platform contains your largest number of contacts; the remaining platforms can follow.
section: (Step 2) “But I don’t know where to start…” → Pick A Platform

text: Warm Outreach, step 4: Contact 100 people daily with individually tailored messages.
section: (Step 4) “Now what?” → Reach. Out. To. One. Hundred. People. Every. Day.

text: Limit outreach to three attempts per contact, stopping when they reply. Space attempts one day apart over three days, or one week apart for physical mail.
section: (Step 4) “Now what?” → Reach. Out. To. One. Hundred. People. Every. Day.

text: The A-C-A framework begins by paraphrasing the person's response to demonstrate listening, then offering a compliment, preferably connected to a positive personal quality.
section: (Step 5): “What do I say when they respond?” → Act like a human.

text: The final element of A-C-A is a further question that moves the discussion toward a subject relevant to the offer while learning about the other person.
section: (Step 5): “What do I say when they respond?” → Act like a human.

text: Warm Outreach, step 6: Present an offer to test interest after roughly 3–4 conversational exchanges by phone or messaging, or 3–4 minutes of conversation in person.
section: (Step 6) “How do I know if they’re interested?” → Make them an offer.

text: The Value Equation weighs four elements: the desired result, confidence in attaining it, the expected wait, and required effort or sacrifices. Increase the first two while reducing the latter two.
section: (Step 6) “How do I know if they’re interested?” → Make them an offer.

text: Support confidence in an offer with customer outcomes, reviews, awards, endorsements, credentials, other outside validation, and guarantees.
section: (Step 6) “How do I know if they’re interested?” → Make them an offer.

text: Approach the ideal of a certain, rapid result requiring minimal effort or sacrifice without making false or exaggerated claims.
section: (Step 6) “How do I know if they’re interested?” → Make them an offer.

text: Ask contacts whether they know a suitable prospect instead of directly requesting a purchase. This can produce personal interest, referrals, or both.
section: (Step 6) “How do I know if they’re interested?” → Make them an offer.

text: Use evidence from customers with circumstances and difficulties resembling the contact's own to strengthen their confidence that they could achieve the result.
section: (Step 6) “How do I know if they’re interested?” → Make them an offer.

text: Warm Outreach, step 7: Remove the price to make accepting the offer easier.
section: (Step 7) “How do I get them to say yes?” → Make it easy for them to say yes. Make it free.

text: For an initial free offer, Hormozi recommends setting expectations that participants use the offering, provide feedback, and review it positively only if they believe it merits that assessment.

For a new product or service, Hormozi recommends serving the first five customers free. The precise count is secondary to practicing offers, learning delivery, and receiving greater tolerance for early mistakes.
Customers served free can generate revenue by later purchasing, referring buyers, or supplying testimonials that attract buyers.

Rejection of a free offer can indicate an unwanted outcome, insufficient confidence in results, or excessive demands on the customer's time and effort. Removing the price does not remove these other costs.
After a rejection, ask what would need to change for participation to become worthwhile. The answer can reveal an obstacle the seller can address.
Warm Outreach, step 8: After exhausting contacts on one platform, move to the platform with the next-largest pool of contacts, continuing in that order.
section: (Step 8) “What Do I Do Once I’ve Reached Out To Everyone?” → Start Back At The Top

text: Warm Outreach, step 9: Begin charging when customers start referring others. Offer successive groups of five discounts of 80%, 60%, then 40%, continuing to reduce discounts. Actual price increases create urgency.
section: (Step 9) “But I can’t work for free forever…” → Start Charging.

text: Warm Outreach, step 10: Keep contacts receptive by regularly sharing useful material through channels such as email and social media.
section: (Step 10) “But what do I do from here?” →Keep your list warm.

text: After providing value or observing interest, send a plain question checking whether contacts still want a particular outcome. Omit images and links; prioritize respondents for subsequent warm outreach.
section: (Step 10) “But what do I do from here?” →Keep your list warm.

text: Hormozi's illustrative warm-outreach funnel yields approximately 20 replies per 100 contacts, four free-offer acceptances, and one eventual paid customer. Results depend on the offer's value and recipients' trust.
section: Benchmarks: How well am I doing?

text: At a 1% purchase rate and $400 per sale, 500 weekly outreach attempts produce five customers and $2,000 weekly revenue, totaling $104,000 over 52 weeks.
section: Benchmarks: How well am I doing?

text: For someone starting out, Hormozi recommends making customer acquisition the first daily activity, allocating at least four hours per day, and continuing until the goal is reached.
Warm outreach is constrained by available time and the number of people who already know the seller. Publishing free content is the next Core Four activity introduced to expand that audience.
Hormozi treats the audience as the asset that accumulates through content creation: individual posts can fade while the audience continues growing.
section: How To Build An Audience To Get Engaged Leads

text: Hormozi recommends looking for what higher-earning people do better in business and learning from it, rather than explaining their success in ways that offer no path to improvement.
section: How To Build An Audience To Get Engaged Leads

text: Paying to learn from another person's experience can reduce the time needed to work things out independently.
section: How To Build An Audience To Get Engaged Leads

text: Free content lets one message reach multiple people. Those who value it can join the warm audience and introduce others through sharing; occasional valuable offers give that audience opportunities to buy.
section: How Building An Audience Works - You Post Great Free Content

text: Public content sacrifices personalization, faces competition from other creators, and attracts imitators when successful. Hormozi identifies continued innovation as necessary when others copy the content.
section: How Building An Audience Works - You Post Great Free Content

text: A content unit is the minimum material needed to attract attention, sustain consumption, and deliver the satisfaction that motivated consumption. Its three functions can occur simultaneously, even within a single sentence or image.

Hook effectiveness is the percentage of people who begin consuming the content. Hormozi identifies subject interest, a compelling headline, and familiar presentation as ways to improve that percentage.

Hormozi organizes content subjects into five sources: distant experiences, recent experiences, ideas arising now, currently popular subjects, and deliberately created experiences. Personal experience provides differentiation because others have not lived the same life.
Capture ideas when they arise. Hormozi also publishes ideas as an interest test: when a post outperforms his usual results, he creates additional content about that subject.
Creating an experience specifically for content requires more time and effort than drawing on existing experiences, but Hormozi says it can produce the greatest returns.

Hormozi recommends trying to combine at least two attention drivers in a headline. Drivers introduced here include freshness, personal significance, prominent individuals, geographic closeness, and clashes between people or ideas.
Headline interest can also come from departures from the ordinary or events whose outcomes are still unfolding. The headline action step recommends including one or more attention drivers.
Adapt content presentation to the platform before refining it for the intended audience. Use successful content serving that market on that platform as the reference.
Hormozi sustains attention by creating unanswered questions, either directly or by implication. His preferred structures for generating that curiosity are lists, steps, and stories.
For list content, keep entries connected by a theme and announce the item count in the headline or opening seconds. Hormozi reports that setting this expectation helps retain attention longer.

Steps require a particular action sequence to achieve an outcome, giving them a clearer payoff but less flexibility. Lists permit varied entries and ordering, making them more flexible but their payoff less explicit.
Lists, sequential instructions, and narratives can sustain curiosity, separately or in combination, by leaving the audience wanting answers.
Rewarding content meets or surpasses the expectations that attracted its intended audience. Hormozi treats audience growth as evidence that the content delivers this reward.
A content unit is the minimum material needed to attract attention, sustain it, and deliver a payoff. Longer pieces connect more units, requiring greater skill to keep delivering worthwhile payoffs.

Hormozi cites television’s approximately 3.5:1 content-to-advertising ratio and Facebook’s roughly 4:1 ratio as monetization benchmarks. He recommends substantially fewer asks relative to useful content when audience growth is the priority.
Give Until They Ask means publishing useful material publicly and making offers privately when audience members initiate interest in buying.

Integrated offers place promotions inside otherwise useful content. Hormozi says every piece can contain a promotion if helpful material sufficiently outweighs requests to buy; excessive promotion can shrink the audience.
section: How To Make Money From Content: Ask

text: Begin placing calls to action immediately following useful material or at the conclusion. Check whether audience growth slows before adding another placement.
section: How To Make Money From Content: Ask

text: Intermittent offers alternate numerous entirely helpful content pieces with occasional pieces devoted to promotion.
section: How To Make Money From Content: Ask

text: Hormozi generally favors separate promotional posts for short-form platforms and promotions embedded within content for long-form platforms.
section: How To Make Money From Content: Ask

text: Content promotions can direct people either to the main paid offer or to a lead magnet. When uncertain, Hormozi recommends the lead magnet as the lower-risk choice.
section: How To Make Money From Content: Ask

text: Depth-Then-Width develops one relevant platform to its full content quality and volume before adding another, preserving output on established platforms. Hormozi presents this approach as requiring fewer resources.
section: Depth then width: Maximize a platform, then move onto the next platform.

text: When maximizing platform output, Hormozi suggests short-form publishing may sometimes reach ten posts daily per platform, while long-form publishing may need to reach five days weekly.
section: Depth then width: Maximize a platform, then move onto the next platform.

text: Concentrating on one platform initially creates dependence on that channel. Platform changes or bans can threaten the business when that channel supplies its only route to customers.
section: Depth then width: Maximize a platform, then move onto the next platform.

text: Width-Then-Depth establishes regular publishing across relevant platforms before maximizing them together. Its advantages include reaching a wider audience sooner and adapting existing content for multiple platforms with relatively little additional work.
section: Width then depth: Get on every platform early, then maximize them together.

text: Hormozi argues that audience-relevant free content helps people discover and share a business, nurtures potential buyers, and improves returns from other advertising methods even when its contribution is difficult to measure.
section: Why You Should Make Content (even if it’s not your primary advertising strategy)

text: Especially when starting, describe personal experience and preferences instead of prescribing universal solutions. Hormozi recommends this framing to share useful knowledge without sounding arrogant or preachy.
section: 7 Lessons I’ve Learned From Making Content

text: Puddles, Ponds, Lakes, Oceans: begin with narrowly focused content about the work and location where credibility is strongest, then broaden the subject area over time.
section: 7 Lessons I’ve Learned From Making Content

text: Build a library of effective content, labeled by the issue each piece addresses and its benefit. Salespeople can send relevant pieces around sales calls, especially to address recurring prospect concerns.
section: 7 Lessons I’ve Learned From Making Content

text: Paying customers incorporate free content into their assessment of purchase value. Useful content can strengthen loyalty, while poor content can reduce their opinion of the paid product.
section: 7 Lessons I’ve Learned From Making Content

text: Hormozi reports better performance from manually published posts than scheduled ones. He attributes this to the immediate feedback encouraging a final quality improvement and recommends having someone publish each post manually.
section: 7 Lessons I’ve Learned From Making Content

text: Track follower totals and reach monthly, including absolute increases and percentage growth. Calculate percentage growth by dividing the increase during the month by the starting total.
section: Benchmarks - How Well Am I Doing?

text: Output measurements become useful when activity stays consistent. Choose a publishing frequency and a separate frequency for invitations that turn audience members into interested leads on each platform, then maintain both.
section: Benchmarks - How Well Am I Doing?

text: An initial post can include an invitation to buy or engage because the author may already have helped others. If it produces no interested lead, provide value for a while before asking again.
Add free content alongside warm outreach. Content is less predictable but produces interested leads directly and enlarges the familiar audience available for subsequent outreach.
section: So What Do I Do Right Now?

text: Cold outreach means contacting strangers to generate engaged leads.

Cold outreach means contacting people unfamiliar with the business through private, individual communication. It extends outreach beyond existing relationships and can support faster growth or more predictable lead flow.
Unlike familiar contacts, strangers lack trust in the sender. Cold outreach must overcome missing contact details, ignored messages, and lack of interest even after gaining attention.

Hormozi orders cold outreach preparation and execution as finding contact routes, developing the message, then persisting until prospects can pay attention. He pairs repeated contact across channels with substantial value before asking prospects to advance.
Hormozi recommends compensating for cold outreach's lower response rates with more attempts and a wider range of contact methods.
Cold outreach lets a business select prospects using precise eligibility criteria instead of relying on whoever its existing audience supplies.
section: Problem #1: “But how do I contact them?” →Build a List

text: Cold Outreach list building, step 1: Search multiple lead tools using audience criteria. Test representative samples of a few hundred contacts per tool for accurate details, responsiveness, and targeting fit before obtaining larger lists.

Cold Outreach list building, step 2: If software cannot locate suitable prospects, request audience-specific samples from several list brokers. Test each sample and continue with providers whose lists perform well.

Cold Outreach list building, step 3: If brokers also fail, locate qualified prospects in relevant communities and collect available contact details. Manual sourcing takes longer, but these prospects may have received fewer competing solicitations than searchable database contacts.
Hormozi sets an initial list-building target of 1,000 names. When time is more available than money, he suggests starting with manual sourcing.

Cold messages should combine personalization with substantial, quickly delivered value because strangers neither recognize nor trust the sender, and outreach has only seconds to address both barriers.
section: Problem #2: “I have my list, but what do I say to them?” →Personalize, Then Give Big Fast Value

text: Personalize outreach using one to three researched details about the prospect that an acquaintance might know.
section: a) They Don’t Know Us→Personalize (Act Like You Know Them).

text: Research prospects in batches before contacting them, then use those notes to personalize the opening. Hormozi suggests doing the research personally, hiring help, or using software.

For cold prospects, demonstrate substantial value immediately through an offer or lead magnet. Hormozi recommends giving away something buyers already spend money on, rather than something merely judged worth paying for.
section: b) They Don’t Trust Us→Big Fast Value.

text: Before revising an initial outreach script, Hormozi recommends completing 100 conversations or sending 10,000 emails, then adjusting based on experience.
section: b) They Don’t Trust Us→Big Fast Value.

text: Automating message delivery can increase engaged leads per unit of time even when the percentage of recipients who engage declines.
Manual delivery requires someone to convey each message individually; automated delivery reuses a prepared message. Distribution is the separate task of sending that message to prospects.
Automation generally trades personalization for reach. Personalized outreach earns higher response rates, so Hormozi recommends less automation when the pool of suitable prospects is small.
Devote 10–20% of outreach effort to testing unfamiliar technology, comparing its performance with the tools already in use.
Follow up repeatedly through different channels because prospects respond differently to each. For higher-priced sales to strangers, Hormozi advises beginners to expect two to three conversations.
section: c) Follow up. More times. More ways.

text: After several contact attempts across channels, revisit the list following a three-to-six-month interval. Earlier messages may have gone unseen, arrived at inconvenient moments, or preceded a change in need.
section: c) Follow up. More times. More ways.

text: Hormozi sets a cold-outreach performance floor of customer lifetime profit reaching at least three times customer acquisition cost.
For email outreach, Hormozi suggests targeting engaged leads equal to 3% of the contacted list, while noting that actual results vary.
Use the A-C-A framework introduced for warm outreach to qualify direct-message respondents for a call.
Cold outreach costs are predominantly labor. When calculating advertising returns, include labor and software expenses across the outreach process.
Hormozi warns that people substantially underestimate both the outreach volume required and the time needed to make the channel work.
Cold outreach becomes forecastable when the relationship between contact volume and customer acquisition is known; work backward from the customer target to determine outreach volume and staffing.
An established outreach team can increase a business's saleability and value by allowing customer acquisition to continue without its owner's public presence.
Cold outreach systems are difficult to imitate because competitors cannot readily observe their list sourcing, personalization, distribution tools, or team operations.

Paid advertising purchases access to someone else's audience to reach many unfamiliar prospects at once. It buys exposure without requiring the advertiser to build an audience first, but does not assure a financial return.
Hormozi's paid advertising process selects a platform, narrows its audience through targeting, uses the advertisement to discourage unsuitable prospects, and asks the remaining prospects to act.

After achieving profitability with a narrow audience, expand while remaining profitable. Broader audiences can reduce returns relative to spending while increasing total profit and the amount of money at risk.
Paid Ads, step 1: Evaluate platforms for personal familiarity as a consumer, access to relevant prospects through targeting, and knowledge of the platform's advertising formats.
section: Step 1: “But where do I advertise?” → Find a platform where these four things are true

text: Paid Ads, step 1: The fourth platform requirement is being able to afford its minimum advertising spend. Begin with one qualifying platform and study the advertisements appearing there.
section: Step 1: “But where do I advertise?” → Find a platform where these four things are true

text: A lookalike audience is a larger group a platform identifies as resembling an advertiser's supplied contact list. Creating one requires meeting the platform's minimum list size.
section: Step #2: “But how do I get the right people to see it?” → Target them

text: Paid Ads, step 2: Seed lookalike targeting with existing and former customers. If that list falls below the platform minimum, supplement it with warm outreach contacts, then cold outreach leads if necessary.
section: Step #2: “But how do I get the right people to see it?” → Target them

text: Additional targeting filters can improve advertising efficiency but exhaust a smaller audience sooner. Hormozi recommends using early gains from specific audiences to fund expansion into broader ones.
section: Step #2: “But how do I get the right people to see it?” → Target them

text: Paid Ads, step 2: Where supported, combine lookalike audiences with additional filters. If lookalike targeting is unavailable, begin with interest targeting.
section: Step #2: “But how do I get the right people to see it?” → Target them

text: Paid Ads, step 3: Build the advertisement around a callout that attracts intended customers, a presentation of value that develops interest, and a call to action directing their next move.
section: Step #3 “But what should my ad say?” → Call Out + Value + Call to Action (CTA)

text: A callout attracts audience attention. Hormozi recommends balancing precision about whom it addresses with enough breadth to reach many suitable prospects.
Hormozi prioritizes testing the opening of an ad and allocating most creative effort to its first five seconds, because attention must come before the remaining message can work.

Verbal callouts can identify an audience group, ask a qualifying question, connect a condition to a benefit, or highlight an unusually desirable result. Identity labels work when intended customers recognize themselves in them.
Nonverbal callouts can attract attention through sensory contrast or recognizable audience characteristics. When the medium permits, combine these with verbal attention cues.
Match spokesperson variety to audience breadth: represent multiple demographic groups for a broad market, and use people resembling the intended customers for a narrow market.
An ad builds interest by making an offer’s benefits appear large relative to its costs. That perceived value motivates prospects to exchange payment or contact details for the offer or lead magnet.
The What-Who-When Framework develops ad angles from benefits and avoided costs, the people whose perspectives reveal those effects, and the time periods in which they occur.

To increase confidence in success, ads can address previous failures, demonstrate results among similar customers, and offer authoritative reassurance or guarantees. They can also explain the risks of continuing without change.
The Who lens distinguishes customers receiving status from people whose treatment confers it. Advertising can explain how the offer changes those relationships, making additional benefits visible.
Apply each relevant observer’s perspective to each value driver to generate additional advertising angles and reveal benefits missed when considering only the buyer’s own experience.
The What-Who-When Framework combines desired benefits and avoided problems with personal and social perspectives across past, present, and future consequences to explain why an offer matters.
Adapt ad length to the platform by changing how many persuasive angles appear, while retaining the same opening callout and call to action.
Tell interested viewers precisely which action to take, and reduce the effort required through obvious controls and short, memorable contact destinations.
section: 3) CTA - Tell Them What To Do Next

text: Run Paid Ads, step 4: Obtain contact details after the viewer responds. Hormozi favors a simple landing page, emphasizing its wording and image because simplicity makes testing easier.
section: Step #4 “How do I get their info?” → Get Permission To Contact Them

text: Preserve the ad’s visual presentation, language, and promised benefit on its landing page so the visitor experiences continuity throughout the buying journey.
section: Step #4 “How do I get their info?” → Get Permission To Contact Them

text: When requesting contact details, connect that request to the action the visitor just completed. Hormozi draws on Cialdini’s consistency principle to encourage completion of the next step.
section: Step #4 “How do I get their info?” → Get Permission To Contact Them

text: Hormozi organizes ads around three functions: a callout attracts attention, value elements establish motivation, and a call to action provides the next move.
section: Run Paid Ads Part I Conclusion

text: Judge paid advertising primarily by financial efficiency. Hormozi prioritizes returns sufficient for scaling over perfecting creative execution.
section: #4 Run Paid Ads Part II: Money Stuff

text: Three Phases of Scaling Paid Ads, step 1: Establish accurate return tracking before spending on ads, enabling spending decisions to follow what earns money and what loses it.

Three Phases of Scaling Paid Ads, step 2: Expect testing losses, contain spending on unsuccessful ads, and expand spending on successful ones. The size of gains and losses matters more than their frequency.
Hormozi allows a new ad up to twice a customer’s first 30 days of collected cash in test spending if leads arrive. With no leads, he stops before spending once that amount.

Three Phases of Scaling Paid Ads, step 3: Once ads reach break-even or better, calculate spending from desired or serviceable customer volume multiplied by acquisition cost. Hormozi typically adds 20% to allow for declining efficiency at larger scale.
Hormozi works backward from his lead acquisition target to set a daily advertising budget, then commits to that spending.
Lifetime gross profit equals everything a customer spends over the relationship minus the costs of delivering those purchases.
section: I Measure LTGP Instead of “Lifetime Value” or “LTV”

text: LTGP:CAC compares a customer's lifetime gross profit with their acquisition cost. Advertising produces a positive return when LTGP exceeds CAC and a loss when CAC exceeds LTGP.
section: I Measure LTGP Instead of “Lifetime Value” or “LTV”

text: Hormozi observed scaling difficulties in his investments below a 3:1 LTGP:CAC ratio and growth after exceeding 3:1. He explicitly presents this as a personal observation rather than a universal rule.
section: I Measure LTGP Instead of “Lifetime Value” or “LTV”

text: Increasing lifetime gross profit through a stronger business model is another way to improve acquisition economics; Hormozi favors combining this with lower acquisition costs.
section: I Measure LTGP Instead of “Lifetime Value” or “LTV”

text: Hormozi's diagnostic: research average CAC in the industry. Below three times that average, prioritize improving LTGP through the business model; above three times that average, prioritize improving advertising to reduce CAC.
section: I Measure LTGP Instead of “Lifetime Value” or “LTV”

text: Once acquisition costs are sufficiently low, Hormozi shifts attention toward earning more per customer: costs have a zero floor, while customer earnings have more room to grow.
section: I Measure LTGP Instead of “Lifetime Value” or “LTV”

text: Client Financed Acquisition means collecting enough customer revenue within 30 days to cover acquisition and fulfillment costs, making those funds available for acquiring additional customers.
section: “My ads aren’t profitable, how do I fix it?” → Client Financed Acquisition

text: An early upsell can raise average gross profit per acquired customer enough to recover CAC within 30 days, allowing acquisition funds to be reused while later purchases continue generating profit.
section: “My ads aren’t profitable, how do I fix it?” → Client Financed Acquisition

text: When engaged leads have both the problem the business solves and sufficient money but do not buy, Hormozi diagnoses a sales problem rather than an advertising problem.

Use strong organic content as potential advertising material. Hormozi recommends systematically encouraging customer reviews and testimonials, publishing them organically, and considering successful posts for paid ads.
For initial paid advertising practice, Hormozi recommends finding platform instructions and placing a $100 ad. Then set a monthly amount affordable to lose and treat early spending as learning.
Hormozi recommends learning paid advertising after the other three core methods because their skills transfer and their earnings can fund advertising practice.
