Reaching $1M–$3M in annual revenue through one platform does not establish market saturation; Hormozi warns against treating that stage of growth as proof that further customer acquisition is exhausted.
section: Core Four On Steroids: More Better New

text: More, Better, New identifies three routes to additional engaged leads: increase existing advertising activity, improve its effectiveness, or expand where it happens.
The Rule of 100 prescribes 100 primary advertising actions daily for 100 consecutive days.
section: Here’s how I do more: The Rule of 100

text: For content, the Rule of 100 uses 100 daily creation minutes and at least one daily publication on a platform; publishing frequency should increase as capability improves.
section: Here’s how I do more: The Rule of 100

text: For paid advertising, the Rule of 100 calls for 100 daily minutes creating ads and 100 consecutive days running them, using the budget established in the paid-ads chapter and targeting Client Financed Acquisition.
section: Here’s how I do more: The Rule of 100

text: Hormozi identifies the conversion stage with the greatest proportional loss of leads as the constraint and prioritizes testing there, where small improvements can produce the largest overall gains.
Hormozi tests one change per platform each week. Changing several things together obscures which change worked and how a change at one stage affected later stages.
Hormozi starts a split test on each platform every Monday. The following Monday, his team selects winners, records outcomes in a cumulative log, and designs a challenger to the strongest version.
If four attempts, or one month, fail to improve the current version, Hormozi shifts testing to another constraint. His typical one-week test duration reflects his team's size and advertising spend.
The Size Of The Pie Fallacy is mistaking the narrow audience reached through one advertising activity, platform, and execution for the entire available market.
Try a new advertising placement or method when its expected return exceeds the return available from increasing or improving existing advertising.

Choose expansion opportunities by expected leads per unit of effort. Hormozi says this favors additional placements, then additional platforms, then another Core Four activity in nine out of ten cases.

Increase effective advertising until a bottleneck appears, then maintain that volume while improving the bottleneck. Asking what prevents a tenfold increase helps distinguish a need for more activity from a need for improvement.
After using warm outreach to establish customers, Hormozi chooses content when time exceeds money, and cold outreach or paid advertising when money exceeds time.
One Core Four activity can generate engaged leads. Mastering it creates money, systems, and experience that help with the next activity; combining activities can strengthen their results.
Lead getters are people who generate additional leads for a business, extending its advertising capacity through other people's efforts.
Lead getters are other people who use the core four to attract prospects for a business, reducing the owner's work per engaged lead.
Recruiting someone who recruits additional lead getters creates more leverage than personally recruiting each one: lead generation can keep expanding after the owner's initial recruitment effort.
The core four operates at successive levels: a business uses it to recruit lead getters, who use it to attract engaged leads and can recruit further lead getters.
Customers become lead getters by recommending what they bought; employees generate leads from inside the business.
Agencies supply lead generation as a service; affiliates promote a business's offerings to their own audiences.
Hormozi argues that outstanding products make customers a source of leads; copying a company's advertising assets alone does not reproduce that advantage.
A referral occurs when someone directs an engaged lead to a business. Anyone can make one, but Hormozi regards customers as the strongest source.
Hormozi attributes higher lifetime gross profit from referred customers to their purchasing higher-priced offerings and buying more frequently.
When an existing customer brings another customer simply because they like the offering, the referred customer's acquisition costs nothing, lowering acquisition cost.

Referral-driven customer growth equals incoming referred customers minus departing customers. More arrivals mean growth without other advertising; equal flows require other advertising for growth; fewer arrivals require advertising just to maintain customer numbers.

When the monthly referral percentage exceeds the monthly customer departure percentage, the customer base compounds. Successive customers generating further referrals can produce exponential growth, unlike the roughly proportional relationship between core-four activity and leads.
Hormozi identifies two main obstacles to referrals: owners overestimate their product's quality, and businesses fail to request referrals.
section: Two Reasons Most Businesses Don’t Get Referrals

text: For businesses selling directly to consumers, Hormozi treats customers' failure to bring additional customers as evidence that the product needs improvement.
section: Problem #1: The Product Isn’t Good Enough

text: Hormozi defines goodwill as the gap between the value customers receive and the price they pay. He favors increasing value over cutting prices because price reductions have financial limits.
section: Six Ways To Get More Referrals By Giving More Value

text: His six goodwill levers are customer fit, manageable expectations, stronger customer outcomes, quicker results, reduced customer burdens, and guidance toward another purchase.
section: Six Ways To Get More Referrals By Giving More Value

text: Identify shared traits among your most successful customers, use those traits to define targeting criteria, and restrict sales to prospects meeting those criteria.
Gradually reduce offer promises while preserving delivery quality; stop reducing them when closing rates decline. This creates more room to exceed expectations without continuing to sacrifice sales.

Survey for top performers, interview them, identify shared behaviors, require those behaviors from new customers, and measure changes in outcome quality and speed. Tie guarantee eligibility to the behaviors associated with success.
section: 3. Increase Perceived Likelihood of Achievement → Get More People Better Results:

text: Concentrate positive experiences within 48 hours of purchase. Keep the next contact clear; BAMFAM means scheduling the following meeting during the current one.
Hormozi adds 50% to his delivery estimates to create room for early completion. His delivery rule permits being early but rejects being late.

Each month, identify the most common product problem through support data, surveys, and reviews. Learn from customers who overcame it, test improvements with a small struggling group, expand successful fixes, revise unsuccessful ones, then address the next problem.
section: 5. Decrease Effort & Sacrifice → Keep Making Your Stuff Better:

text: After each major customer success, prompt another purchase. Offer either additional quantities or a different product, and make the subsequent offer more attractive than the initial one.
section: 6.Call To Action→ Tell Them What To Buy Next:

text: Treat a referral request as an offer: explain the benefit the customer receives for introducing friends.
A referral program has three design choices: the method of delivering an incentive, the reward itself, and the way the referral request is made.
section: Seven Ways To Ask For Referrals

text: For a one-sided referral incentive, pay either the referring customer or the referred friend an amount equal to your average customer acquisition cost.
Hormozi’s two-sided referral incentive divides the customer acquisition cost equally: the referrer receives cash or credit, and the incoming customer receives credit.
Ask buyers for prospective companions’ contact details at checkout or on the sales agreement, explaining how participating together can improve their results.
section: 3)Ask For A Referral Right When They Buy:

text: Use introductions as something a buyer provides in exchange for a discount; Hormozi treats the resulting price difference as justified by different sale terms.
Referral events generally run for 1–4 weeks and reward customers for bringing friends. Support the promotion with internal or external evidence of the benefits of participating together.
An ongoing referral program repeatedly promotes the advantages of participating with others through content, outreach, and advertising, rather than limiting promotion to a temporary event.
Make additional benefits available to customers who provide referrals and testimonials. Noncash rewards can benefit both participants while costing the business less than cash payouts.
Customers put their relationships at risk when recommending a business. Hormozi argues that reliable delivery reduces that perceived risk, while incentives increase the personal benefit of referring.
Establish baseline referral and churn percentages, apply the six customer-value practices, then use at least one of the seven referral-request methods.

Lead-getting employees work inside the business and learn its advertising activities, including ads, content, and outreach, increasing lead-generation capacity while reducing the owner’s direct execution work.
Delegation still requires management, but Hormozi argues that managing employees takes less time than personally performing all their work; hiring managers can further reduce the owner’s workload.
A business whose earnings depend on its owner is less attractive to buyers. Having other people operate it returns the owner’s time and makes the business a more valuable asset.

Hormozi rejects the belief that only the owner can perform essential work. He recommends replacing the owner's operational contribution as early as possible, potentially through several people or technology.
The Internal Core Four applies customer acquisition channels to hiring: contact existing connections, recruit through cold contact, publish vacancies, and pay to distribute those vacancies.
section: How To Get Employee Leads: The Internal Core Four

text: Document, Demonstrate, Duplicate, step 1: Capture the actual task sequence in a checklist. Observers or recordings can document execution without interrupting the person performing it.
Document, Demonstrate, Duplicate, step 2: Perform the task while the employee watches, explaining each checklist item. Revise instructions wherever the employee needs clarification.
Document, Demonstrate, Duplicate, step 3: Observe the employee executing the checklist. Correct flaws in the instructions, then continue employee practice until execution is correct.

Distinguish understanding from execution skill: an employee who understands the task but performs poorly may need practice rather than revised instructions. Confusion or repeated explanations instead indicate that the checklist needs improvement.

During training, reinforce correct execution and avoid penalties for mistakes. Give one correction per practice cycle, let employees retry instead of taking over, and revise faulty instructions even when employees followed them correctly.

For payroll-based lead generation, divide payroll by engaged leads to find unit lead cost; multiply by leads required per customer to calculate CAC. Divide customer lifetime gross profit by CAC to assess the return ratio.
section: How to Calculate Returns From Lead-Getting Employees

text: Hormozi treats CAC no higher than three times the industry average as adequate for shifting attention toward increasing customer lifetime gross profit.
section: How To Know Which Employees to Focus On To Maximize Returns

text: When CAC exceeds three times the industry average, check whether leads need the solution and can afford it. Unqualified leads or insufficient buyers indicate advertising issues; qualified nonbuyers indicate sales issues. Direct employee interventions accordingly.
section: How To Know Which Employees to Focus On To Maximize Returns

text: Advertising agencies sell lead-generation services through advertising, prospect outreach, or content preparation and distribution.
section: How Agencies Want You To Think They Work

text: Hormozi describes a recurring agency problem: senior staff initially produce results, then junior staff inherit the account and performance declines; occasional senior intervention fails to restore results.
section: How Agencies Want You To Think They Work

text: Without funds for a capable agency, learn through experimentation. With sufficient funds, Hormozi recommends agencies for acquiring unfamiliar advertising methods or learning unfamiliar platforms.
section: Hiring An Agency Versus Doing It Yourself

text: Hormozi proposes an explicit six-month learning engagement: pay extra for explanations of agency decisions, train an internal team, then move to cheaper consulting once the team can perform adequately. Negotiate this purpose upfront.
section: How I Use Agencies Now. And How You Can Too.

text: Hormozi recommends learning platform fundamentals from a competent agency, then hiring a more advanced agency to learn how to improve performance further.
section: How I Use Agencies Now. And How You Can Too.

text: Compare internal team performance against the agency. Once the team outperforms it, end the agency engagement and redirect that spending toward expanding the newly learned activity.
section: How I Use Agencies Now. And How You Can Too.

text: Hormozi treats successful work for personal contacts, results for recognizable businesses, and demand exceeding capacity as favorable agency-selection signals.
section: How to Pick The Right Agency

text: Evaluate agencies for realistic expectations, durable strategy, explicit delivery timelines, defined client responsibilities, recurring progress meetings, understandable reporting, and measurement that connects spending with outcomes.
section: How to Pick The Right Agency

text: Assess an agency offer by whether its promised result matches the goal, its success with comparable clients, expected waiting time, and the work and sacrifices required from the client.
section: How to Pick The Right Agency

text: Hormozi considers high prices characteristic of good agencies, but warns that an expensive agency is not necessarily good.
section: How to Pick The Right Agency

text: Even after an agency accepts the proposed arrangement, interview additional candidates and compare them against the selection criteria before choosing.
section: How to Pick The Right Agency

text: Budget for a substantial overlap during which both the agency and internal staff perform the work. This allows agency delivery, learning, and team training to happen concurrently.

Set a deadline for learning an agency's skills. Run internal and agency teams together until the internal team consistently performs better, then retain discounted consulting until its teaching value is exhausted.
An affiliate operates an independent business, conducts its own marketing, and promotes your products to its engaged audience in return for payment, products, or both.
Recruit affiliates through advertising and offers, as with customers, but sell the opportunity to earn commissions quickly and easily by promoting the product.
Each recruited affiliate can supply an additional source of prospects and buyers; recruiting, activating, and integrating affiliates expands those sources.
section: Why You Want An Affiliate Army

text: Affiliate Army has six stages: identify suitable partners, pitch participation, establish eligibility, design compensation, initiate promotion, and sustain promotion.
section: How To Build An Affiliate Army in Six Steps

text: Affiliate Army, step 1: List businesses with established, receptive audiences resembling your customers.
Find potential affiliates by identifying businesses connected to customers' purchases, destinations, and activities. For consumer products, their employers may also be suitable partners.
Affiliate Army, step 2: Offer businesses an additional earning opportunity, using an audience-specific opening, a value proposition, and an explicit next action.
Position affiliate value through increased earnings and leads, existing customer demand, relief from product creation and fulfillment responsibilities, and a short wait before selling.
Affiliate Army, step 3: Secure agreement to participation terms and require investment of time, money, or product ownership to encourage an early win. Hormozi prefers combining these commitments.
One affiliate qualification method requires purchasing the product to retain eligibility; Hormozi also prefers affiliates to use it themselves.
Another qualification method charges affiliates for onboarding and product-expert certification. Their qualifying product purchase can count toward the certification fee.

Hormozi recommends onboarding and training fees equal to 10–20% of an average active affiliate's earnings during their first 12 months. He reports this range maximized the number becoming active affiliates.

Reduce the required affiliate commitment when too few begin; increase it when too few follow through. For a new program without physical products, test higher minimum investments after every 5 signups.
Choose affiliate rewards around desired behavior. Hormozi pays for first-time and returning buyers; sufficiently reliable tracking can justify paying for earlier actions known to produce sales.
Base affiliate payment amounts on the maximum customer acquisition cost the business can afford.
Affiliate Payout Tiers allocate 25% of maximum allowable CAC to affiliates meeting entry terms, 50% after activation, and 100% after sustained performance.

Reserving the maximum commission for top affiliates keeps average payouts below the acquisition ceiling; the difference can fund contests, affiliate recruitment, emerging performers, or retained profit.
Affiliate Army, step 5: Activate affiliates with a launch. They attract interested prospects before purchasing opens, then offer the product to those prospects when it becomes available.
Whisper, Tease, Shout, step 1: Build curiosity through brief hints and glimpses of development while withholding the product reveal. Showing the work over time can increase its perceived value.
Schedule whispers every 4–6 weeks until 60 days before launch, then every 2–3 weeks until 30 days before launch; switch to teasing at that point.
Whisper, Tease, Shout, step 2: Disclose the product and launch date, explaining its value through What-Who-When. Tease weekly until 14 days remain, then twice weekly until 3 days remain.
Whisper, Tease, Shout, step 3: Specify the actions audiences should take at launch, emphasizing bonuses, limited availability, deadlines, and guarantees associated with buying early.
Begin shouting at least twice daily 3 days before launch. On launch day, communicate every few hours until 2 hours remain, then every 30 minutes until release.

Affiliate Army, step 6: Sustain promotion by embedding your product in affiliates' offers. In increasing difficulty, affiliates can distribute your lead magnet free, sell that lead magnet, or sell your main offer.

Including your lead magnet with an affiliate's purchase should strengthen their offer. Your business then sells to the resulting leads; the affiliate can use the added value to attract leads and support higher prices.
section: 1) Affiliates Give Your Lead Magnet Away When Somebody Buys Their Stuff.

text: Affiliates can retain all revenue from a lead magnet you deliver. Your return comes from subsequent main-offer sales exceeding fulfillment costs; this arrangement need not include commissions on the main offer.

For direct affiliate sales, revenue sharing can cover the initial payment, a specified duration, or the customer's lifetime. Hormozi favors lifetime commissions without payout caps to keep affiliates motivated to retain customers.
When affiliates sell the main offer directly, they receive a larger share of lifetime gross profit, while your business handles delivery.
Evaluate affiliate acquisition by comparing recruitment cost with the gross profit generated by all customers that affiliate brings, accounting for product costs and affiliate compensation.
Hormozi treats a 3:1 affiliate lifetime gross profit to acquisition cost ratio as a minimum for a viable business, while preferring 5:1, 10:1, or higher.

When affiliate LTGP:CAC falls below 3:1, improve recruitment advertising, offers, and selling to reduce acquisition costs; activate more affiliates through launches; and improve ongoing integration to increase their lifetime value.
Affiliates are partners who promote a business for mutual benefit, rather than a separate advertising channel. Recruit them through the Core Four and serve them as customers.

An affiliate relationship should deliver value exceeding the partner's costs, including hidden costs. A stronger offer, greater profits, or both should let the partner spend more acquiring customers while supplying the business with engaged leads.
Recruit 10–20 affiliates first. Use their outcomes and feedback to refine the offer, terms, launch, and integration; then turn those outcomes into lead magnets for recruiting more affiliates.
The Core Four can attract either prospective customers or people who generate leads. Hormozi identifies four groups of lead generators: referring customers, employees, agencies, and affiliates.
section: Section IV Conclusion: Get Lead Getters

text: Referrals offer the greatest potential for inexpensive exponential growth; employees operate under direct influence; agencies teach skills transferable to an internal team; established affiliates can function independently.
section: Section IV Conclusion: Get Lead Getters

text: Hormozi expects developing a new lead source to take 3–6 months despite his experience. Early failures are normal and should not automatically trigger abandoning or changing methods.
section: Section IV Conclusion: Get Lead Getters

text: The speaker describes allocating a portion of revenue to experiments with campaigns, channels, pages, and unconventional ideas, treating what each test teaches as a worthwhile return on that spending.
Reserve a portion of advertising spending for experiments without requiring a financial return; suggested allocations are 1%, 5%, or 10%. Treat this spending as education.
Keep experimenting until an approach succeeds, concentrate effort on it until it stops working, then resume testing for the next successful approach.
Advertising can fail because the activity volume is insufficient even when the activity itself is appropriate; low inputs produce few, inconsistent engaged leads.
section: Advertising in Real Life: Open To Goal

text: Open to Goal replaces a fixed activity count with a specified outcome target: continue working until that target is reached, however many repetitions it requires.
section: Rule of 100 on Steroids–Open To Goal

text: Hormozi protects uninterrupted work immediately after sleep and sets daily targets based on his expected capacity. He attributes the benefit to sustained focus rather than an inherently superior waking time.
section: How I Make Open To Goal Work For Myself

text: One Page Advertising Checklist, step 1: Select the lead category to pursue: prospective customers, affiliate partners, employees, or agencies.
One Page Advertising Checklist, step 2: Choose between the Rule of 100 and Open to Goal, then commit to daily advertising activity.
One Page Advertising Checklist, step 4: Continue the chosen activity each day until the business can afford to hire someone to perform it.
One Page Advertising Checklist, step 5: Return to the first step with employees as the lead target. Repeat steps 1–4 until sufficient help is available, then expand again.
Advertising Roadmap, level 1: Begin with a single offer aimed at a single customer avatar through a single platform. Warm outreach is the primary activity.
section: The Roadmap - Putting it All Together

text: Advertising Roadmap, level 2: Know the activity inputs needed to produce an engaged lead and increase them to generate customers consistently. Maximize sustainable personal effort in warm outreach and free content.
section: The Roadmap - Putting it All Together

text: Advertising Roadmap, level 4: Product quality supports steady referrals. Continue earning goodwill and aim for referrals to supply at least 25% of customers; further advertising expansion requires greater attention to team hiring.
section: The Roadmap - Putting it All Together

text: Prioritize product improvement until referrals become dependable; then resume expanding advertising with a larger team. Hormozi warns that neglecting product quality can leave the business unable to recover.
Advertising Roadmap, step 6: Put seasoned executives and department leaders in charge of additional advertising activities and channels, selecting people with experience directly suited to the work.
Finding effective audiences, lead magnets, advertising methods, and platforms requires varied experiments sustained long enough to judge their results.
In Hormozi’s envisioned business exceeding $100 million in annual revenue, one-third of customers generate additional customers, while executives direct growth independently of the owner.

Hormozi estimates that building the envisioned $100 million-plus annual-revenue operation takes five to ten years for owners who already know what to do; larger ambitions require longer time horizons.
Lead generation should pursue engaged prospects, rather than merely collecting leads; offers and lead magnets help create that engagement.
The Core Four classifies advertising into contacting existing connections, publishing public content, contacting strangers, and buying advertising.
To expand advertising, identify what prevents tenfold activity. Test changes against the current constraint, then increase volume until another constraint appears.

The four categories of lead getters are customers, employees, agencies, and affiliates; they contribute through referrals, delegated advertising, teaching new capabilities, and affiliate partnerships respectively.

The Many-Sided Die illustrates Hormozi’s belief that repeated advertising attempts reveal what works and make later success more likely; observing another advertiser’s results does not reveal their starting ability or accumulated attempts.
An additional product for existing customers can cushion revenue when new customer acquisition slows and increase revenue when acquisition remains strong.
A follow-on offer should address customers’ next problem and stay connected to what they already value about the initial product, rather than reflect only the founders’ interests.
Hormozi defines LTV, also called LTGP or CLV, as the total gross profit a customer generates throughout the relationship: their payments minus delivery costs.
How To Calculate LTV, step 1: Determine revenue remaining after fulfillment expenses. This gross profit differs from net profit, which accounts for all expenses.

How To Calculate LTV, step 2: Estimate purchases per customer by averaging transaction counts in historical customer records. For recurring businesses, calculate churn by dividing departing customers by the customer count at the period’s start.

How To Calculate LTV, step 3: For transactional businesses, multiply average gross profit per purchase by average lifetime purchases. For recurring businesses, divide gross profit per customer per period by that period’s churn rate.
New customer signups do not change churn for the starting customer group; measure departures from that original group regardless of how many customers join.

The Crazy Eight covers higher prices, cheaper fulfillment, repeat purchases, larger purchases, premium upgrades, smaller purchases instead of no sale, cheaper alternatives instead of no sale, and additional purchases of different products.

Evaluate prices using conversion rate multiplied by LTGP. Calculate the conversion threshold needed to match the previous price’s profitability, measure actual conversion, and continue testing until the product of conversion and LTGP declines. Hormozi tests quarterly.
After confirming demand and getting delivery working, Hormozi recommends raising prices roughly 20% after every 10 sales until sales fall sharply, then returning to the best-performing price.
section: Pro Tip: Start Low Then Go Up.

text: Serve customers with similar problems so fulfillment can use shared templates and automation instead of individually customized solutions; Hormozi presents this as a way to improve delivery speed, consistency, and profitability.
Hormozi identifies three routes to more repeat purchases: introduce recurring billing, reduce cancellations, or make follow-up offers regularly.
For recurring offers, Hormozi calculates lifetime revenue as price divided by churn. He states that reducing monthly churn from 10% to 5% doubles LTV.
Hormozi favors quarterly promotions for long-term reactivation, providing useful material between promotions to balance requests with giving and remain familiar until prospects are ready to purchase.
A cross-sell offers a complementary product. Its expected contribution to LTV equals the proportion of customers accepting it multiplied by its gross profit, added to existing LTV.
Choose cross-sells that fit existing capabilities and resources without substantially changing the customer served or daily operations; extra revenue should not disrupt the business.

Quantity upsells increase the amount committed to in one purchase through bulk buying, more frequent service, or a larger unit. Hormozi recommends presenting these before offering the standard package as a fallback.
Hormozi distinguishes two quality upgrades that command higher prices: a newer edition and a premium edition with improved inputs or service.

Present a quality upgrade before the standard offer, or revisit customers after their initial purchase to propose upgrading. Hormozi reports routinely seeing increases of 20% or more in both upfront collections and overall LTV.
Quantity downsells reduce unit count, unit size, or delivery frequency. Hormozi argues they can improve revenue when the alternative is no purchase, so pricing decisions must account for conversion.
Restrict downsells to buyers who do not qualify for the main offers. Allowing customers who would have purchased the main offer to choose a cheaper alternative sacrifices revenue.
A quality downsell preserves the intended customer result while reducing the experience's value, potentially requiring more time, accepting greater risk, or tolerating additional inconvenience.
Earning more from an equivalent customer allows a business to spend more to acquire that customer than competitors can.
For prospects who do not qualify, develop and offer downsells with either a smaller quantity or a lower-grade version.
Dependence on the founder's appearance in advertising can make a business acquisition conditional on the founder remaining involved.
To enable growth without the founder, inventory the founder's responsibilities and build systems that perform those functions independently.
Existing customer interactions can supply advertising material: recordings of sales, onboarding, and upsell conversations can be edited to show a customer's progression.
Gather customer testimonials during events, request customer videos, and offer prizes for submissions suitable for advertising.
Hormozi argues that reducing a company's dependence on its founder lowers investment risk; customer-generated advertising can help remove the founder from customer acquisition.
The Marketing Machine is a checklist of repeatable sources of customer videos, images, and written material that can support advertising, outreach, content, and sales presentations.

Lifecycle Ads document a customer's progression using recorded interactions: sales conversations establish the starting situation, support conversations show progress, and upgrade or award conversations capture outcomes.

For businesses with physical delivery, capture customers' immediate reactions to the reveal. Use those reactions in the opening 3–5 seconds of individual ads or combine them into reaction compilations.

Hormozi obtains contractual consent for recording and advertising use, then separately checks whether customers are comfortable having their stories advertised; he respects refusals despite the signed permission.

Make lifecycle footage retrievable by retaining call recordings, disabling automatic deletion, naming calendar entries after customers, matching recordings against event names and dates, and labeling extracted clips consistently.

Give customers a profile or community hashtag to tag, then schedule collection of tagged media across platforms. Prioritize stories that disappear within 24 hours and save assets with searchable identifiers.

Separate social assets that outperform ordinary posts and pair the strongest visuals with advertising copy that already works. Hormozi says strong organic performance correlates closely with advertising and outbound performance.
Capture stage photos and brief footage with a celebrating audience to demonstrate event scale. Hormozi recommends the end of the first day or just before lunch on the second day.

For event testimonials, preselect customers and obtain written confirmation, prepare a nearby recording space, assign the stronger camera crew to testimonials, and test multiple microphones and cameras to avoid losing an event's recordings.

The Six-Point Testimonial Script covers prior emotional difficulties, measurable starting conditions, purchase doubts, the reason for proceeding, measurable results, and resulting improvements in the customer's life.

Hormozi treats the testimonial opening as its most important component. Record several alternative hooks for comparison and have participants identify themselves at the start so footage can later be matched to names.

For brief event interviews, prepare 10 questions and collect at least 10 answers per question. Compile responses around a shared outcome; alternatively, assemble testimonial-script segments using answers from at least 5 people.
For event interviews, Hormozi recommends rapidly asking each participant all six testimonial questions; the interview can take under two minutes.
section: Six-Point Testimonial Script and Event Capture

text: Systematize support-message collection with scheduled keyword searches, date-sorted screenshots, and a shared folder. Managers should track contributions and recognize contributors to sustain participation.

Review collection requires an inventory of review platforms, scheduled checks for recent favorable reviews, screenshot storage, and managerial recognition. Collected evidence must actually appear in advertising to help acquire customers.
Bonus unlocks exchange a separately priced benefit for a customer testimonial. Request a video shorter than five minutes covering six prompts, plus a community post containing the video and results.

An award can produce four evidence formats: a community results post, an emailed testimonial video, an unboxing recording, and footage of public recognition. Use a personalized mailed award and a separate generic presentation version.
Testimonial competitions should run no more than once or twice annually because participants tire of them. Judge submissions by conversions generated when used as ads over 30 days.
Promote a testimonial competition through internal communication channels, count down toward its deadline, and personally invite and repeatedly follow up with roughly 50 priority customers.

Hormozi prioritizes competitions for an initial material influx, then existing chat, community, review, and social evidence requiring little editing. Bonuses and awards follow because incentives must be created; events and lifecycle ads come last.
Hormozi places lifecycle ads last in his implementation sequence because they require the greatest editing capacity; he describes them as distinctive but time-consuming.
For community evidence, a screen recording can show the wins category or keyword-filtered search results; filtering helps assemble a more relevant selection of posts.
Create a lifecycle video by combining footage of customers receiving awards, reaching milestones, or moving to a higher offering.
A Money Model consists of offers arranged in an intentional order, each addressing a customer problem the business identifies.
Hormozi places no fixed limit on the number of offers when each offer matches a need at the moment the customer recognizes it.

When acquiring a buyer costs more than the purchase generates in profit, acquisition loses money. Hormozi warns this can force advertising cuts and reliance on personal funds, borrowing, or selling ownership to sustain operations.
section: Beware: Bad Money Models Kill Businesses

text: Recovering acquisition costs gradually from customer profits constrains cash available for advertising. Hormozi says businesses with substantial funds, including investor backing, can afford this delay.
section: Beware: Bad Money Models Kill Businesses

text: A customer can be profitable overall while taking so long to repay acquisition spending that the business exhausts its cash.
Hormozi targets recovering customer acquisition costs through profit within 30 days, allowing the acquisition funding to be reused.
section: Author Note: Make Enough Profit To Cover Your Costs In 30 Days Or Less

text: A Money Model arranges offers into a sequence; deciding the next offer requires understanding which problem it addresses.
Attraction Offers acquire customers; Upsell Offers increase spending; Downsell Offers secure purchases from people otherwise declining; Continuity Offers encourage ongoing purchases.
Money Models need adaptation to the business: some fit particular businesses better, and copying another business's approach without designing for one's own can disappoint.

Offer legality depends on the applicable setting and rules. Hormozi recommends consulting lawyers before using an offer, particularly because advertising restrictions involving free promotions can change.
Offers can operate independently or appear in different orders and at different times; the business must still produce a profit.
Attraction Offers use free or reduced-price products to generate leads and acquire customers. Hormozi treats free, $1, and other discounted prices as interchangeable variations of the approach.
Free incentives can generate revenue when receiving them requires a purchase.
section: So How Do You Make Money By Offering Free Stuff?

text: Win Your Money Back collects payment upfront and offers reimbursement in cash or store credit when customers satisfy specified conditions. Qualifying behavior and outcomes must be easy to measure.
Win Your Money Back can qualify customers solely through an achieved outcome, regardless of behavior, or solely through required behavior, regardless of outcome.
Win Your Money Back can also require both prescribed behavior and an achieved outcome. In this version, customers rely on following the instructions and on those instructions producing the outcome.
Hormozi reports that roughly 10% of customers request reimbursement in data collected across thousands of gyms; he advises using Win Your Money Back only if the seller can accept making refunds.
section: Only Offer “Win Your Money Back” If You Feel Ok With Giving Money Back!

text: Win Your Money Back requirements should be straightforward to verify, encourage behaviors that produce the customer's desired outcome, and include activities that promote the business.
section: How To Create Your Win Your Money Back Criteria.

text: For earned store credit, Hormozi recommends first proposing an extended arrangement or bulk purchase priced above the credit amount.

Around the program's midpoint, Hormozi recommends offering credit toward a subsequent program regardless of whether the customer ultimately achieves the initial goal, to reduce failure anxiety and improve retention.
Hormozi recommends using Win Your Money Back only with an existing refund rate under 5%; otherwise, improve the product first to avoid excessive reimbursements.
The giveaway chapter warns that incorrectly structured promotions can constitute illegal lotteries and instructs readers to comply with applicable local advertising laws.

A Giveaway Offer exchanges a chance at a major prize for contact details and potentially other requirements; after selecting the winner, the business offers the remaining entrants that product at a reduced price.
Giveaway Offer, step 1: Choose the product customers should ultimately purchase as the main prize, and state its monetary value to establish a price reference.
Giveaway Offer, step 5: Set a drawing deadline, preferably 3–7 days after promotion begins. Update entrants daily with the remaining time, prize benefits, and evidence from customers.
section: Put The Giveaway On A Deadline To Add Urgency.

text: Giveaway Offer, step 6: Publicly identify the main winner, then privately contact other entrants who fit the core product and invite them to book a call about the promotional offer they qualify for.
section: Announce The Grand Prize Winner And Start Contacting Everyone Else.

text: Hormozi’s guideline is to size the core-offer discount at 10%–30% of gross margins, then compare the resulting price with the offer’s value.
section: Explain The Cost-To-Value Using Their Discount.

text: Giveaway entry questions can reveal why an offer matters to each prospect. Requiring more effort to enter reduces participation but increases qualification.
section: Eligibility Criteria Get More Customers To Buy Your Core Offer.

text: To encourage giveaway referrals, offer a second grand prize to whoever referred the winner. Hormozi says this can double leads or more and gives referrers a stake in their referrals’ success.
section: Give Away Two Prizes For Twice The Leads.

text: Cap a giveaway by duration, entry count, or both. Hormozi prefers both and limits entrants to the number his team can contact within seven days.

Giveaways need deadlines for entering, claiming, and using prizes. Where feasible, schedule claim calls that day or the next. Hormozi prefers redemption windows measured in hours but has allowed up to five days.
For recurring businesses, distribute the giveaway discount across the longest period the customer accepts, then have monthly billing automatically return to regular rates.
section: If You Have A Recurring Revenue Business.

text: A Decoy Offer attracts prospects with a free or reduced-price option, then introduces a premium alternative with additional value. Comparing them highlights the premium choice; customers choosing the basic version remain potential upgrades.
Decoy Offer, step 2: After prospects respond, present both choices while giving the premium option greater emphasis.
Build a decoy by reducing components or personalization, using older models, and excluding guarantees. Its immediate job is to generate prospect engagement.
section: How To Make Your Decoy Offer.

text: In Hormozi’s experience, free offers attract more leads, while discounted offers attract fewer but achieve better appointment attendance. He suggests testing a discount when attendance is poor, particularly when missed appointments are costly.
section: Discount Offers Have Higher Show-Up Rates Than Free Offers.

text: A Decoy Offer draws interest with a free or reduced-price option, then introduces a premium alternative with greater value.
For customers choosing the decoy, he suggests optionally adding inexpensive or costless premium features as an unexpected benefit to build goodwill and improve later upsell prospects.
Keep the decoy reasonably minimal and strengthen the premium alternative’s value. If the offer does not produce money quickly, Hormozi recommends widening the difference between the options.
Buy X Get Y Free attaches free extras to a purchase. Bundling several items allows a business to present the same total price through free extras instead of individual prices or discounts.
Before using free extras to attract customers, genuinely increase prices enough to preserve profitability; the higher prices must be real rather than invented for the promotion.
section: Raise Prices Before Giving Stuff Away To Preserve Profits.

text: Hormozi recommends making the quantity of free items exceed the quantity customers pay for, adjusting prices so the bundle remains financially workable.
section: Buy X Get Y Free Works Better If You Have More Free Stuff Than Paid Stuff.

text: At the same giveaway cost, test several inexpensive extras against a smaller quantity of expensive extras; customers may respond better to the greater item count.
section: More Free Cheaper Things Can Work Better Than Fewer Free Expensive Things.

text: When collecting long-term payments in advance, budget enough to fulfill the entire service agreement. Upfront receipts must remain available for the promised delivery.
section: Do Not Make Offers Like This If You Can’t Manage Money.

text: For quick cash in an existing recurring business, offer current customers a prepayment bundle, but restrict participation to 10% of customers to preserve recurring cash flow.
section: Make This Offer To Existing Customers For Fast Cash.

text: When customers are likely to purchase only once, aim for a larger transaction and provide enough value to justify its size.
section: If Customers Only Buy Once, Make Them Buy Big.

text: Service bundles can extend customer duration beyond the usual stay, creating additional opportunities to deliver value and make further offers.

Pay Less Now or Pay More Later pairs deferred full-price billing with a satisfaction guarantee and an alternative discounted immediate purchase. Customers choosing deferred billing supply payment details and can cancel before being charged.
After a customer accepts deferred billing, Hormozi recommends offering immediate payment at a 20–50% discount with additional bonuses.
The promised outcome should have an unambiguous pass-or-fail measure and be achievable within the stated period. Clear measurement helps prevent unnecessary cancellations.
Eligibility to cancel deferred billing should depend on tracked participation requirements. Choose requirements that help customers obtain value from the product.

If more than 10% of deferred-payment customers cancel, Hormozi identifies three possible problems: an excessive promise, insufficient guarantee requirements, or excessive pricing. Some cancellations remain unavoidable and should be included in business costs.
For recurring purchases, offer a higher ongoing price beginning 30 days later or a lower price paid today that remains available permanently, with bonuses added to the immediate-payment option.
Customers choosing immediate payment exchange the guarantee for the discount and bonuses.

Attraction Offers aim to convert strangers into buyers while collecting upfront cash, ideally covering acquisition and fulfillment costs several times over so the business can recover its spending and acquire another customer.
Hormozi defines an upsell as whichever offer follows the current purchase. Upsell Offers aim to maximize profit within 30 days.

An upsell addresses a problem exposed by the preceding offer, and an upsell can itself reveal another selling opportunity. Hormozi says these subsequent purchases often generate most of a money model’s profit.
The initial purchase or highest-volume product need not generate the most profit; subsequent offers can supply it.
Upsells can fail because the product is unwanted or unrelated to the customer's problem, the offer precedes awareness of that problem, or the presentation lacks credibility.
The Classic Upsell addresses a new problem produced by the core purchase, offering its solution as soon as the customer recognizes the need.
When choosing between two upsell products with different profits, Hormozi presents the more profitable product first.
A hyper buying cycle is a brief period of enthusiasm and concentrated spending when customers begin something new. Hormozi recommends continuing to offer relevant upsells during that window.
Combine multiple upsell items into one named package, organized around a customer category or desired outcome. Individual components can subsequently be removed to create a downsell.
BAMFAM means arranging the following appointment before the current one ends, agreeing on both its purpose and timing to create further upsell opportunities.

Narrow the price gap above the size customers commonly buy to encourage an upgrade: small buyers toward medium, or medium buyers toward large. If many customers already choose large, Hormozi recommends increasing every size's price.
section: How To Upsell More Of The Same Thing

text: Hormozi proposes selling guarantees, warranties, or insurance as optional additions instead of including them free, with an extra charge of 5–50% of the product price.
section: How To Upsell More Of The Same Thing

text: The A/B Upsell asks customers to select their preferred product option instead of asking whether they want to purchase the product.
For an upsell purchase, ask whether the customer wants to pay with their stored card instead of requesting that they produce a card again.

A Menu Upsell can combine four tactics: eliminate unsuitable choices through Unselling, recommend suitable purchases through Prescription Upselling, elicit preferences through A/B Upselling, and simplify payment through Card On File.

Prescription Upselling suits situations where offering choices is inconvenient and only one product solves the problem. Explain its relationship to previous purchases and provide personalized, detailed usage guidance as though the customer already owns it.
A/B Upselling suits multiple offers addressing the same problem. Ask customers to choose their preferred option rather than decide whether to purchase; either selection produces an upsell.
When customers lack experience with the available products or services, accompany an A/B choice with a brief recommendation to help them decide.
For unavailable inventory, consider accepting payment, ordering the product, and establishing its expected arrival. Hormozi says this enabled a wider selection without stocking everything.
To encourage purchasing two products together, present each separately alongside a bundle priced equal to the costlier individual option. Set prices that maintain margins.
section: If You Have Two Options And Want People To Buy Both

text: Menu Upsell, step 4: Simplify completing the purchase by asking whether the customer wants to pay with their stored card.

An Anchor Upsell presents a premium version costing 5–10 times the main offer before introducing the main offer. If the premium price meets resistance, the cheaper alternative benefits from the comparison.
Anchor Upsells are most effective when the less expensive alternative retains the premium option’s essential functions.
Anchor Upsell presents a premium option first, anticipates price resistance, asks whether its premium distinctions matter, introduces the core option, and requests payment.
An anchor must be a genuine offer the seller wants to deliver. Hormozi advises selling it seriously and waiting for hesitation or a request for an alternative before introducing the next option.
Hormozi recommends pricing the premium anchor at 5–10 times the core offer for the strongest anchoring effect.

The core and premium offers should preserve their main features while differing in secondary attributes. After anchoring, providing those main features at one-fifth the price makes the core option appear attractive.
A Rollover Upsell applies credit from part or all of earlier purchases toward a subsequent offer. Its design requires choosing the customer, the next offer, and the credit arrangement.

Rollover credit can fund more of the existing purchase, an upgraded option, or a different product. Hormozi advises directing it toward a higher-priced offer and applying the discount immediately or distributing it over time.
Before issuing a refund, Hormozi recommends offering purchase credit toward repeating poorly delivered work or toward a different product the customer wants.
Hormozi aims to price the subsequent offer at least four times the rollover credit, limiting the discount to 25%. Profit must remain after applying the credit.
Hormozi recommends making rollover credit available only once per customer, optionally requiring acceptance when presented; customers who decline can purchase later at the regular price.
A Rollover Upsell applies credit from an earlier purchase to a subsequent offer; the credit can cover all or part of the earlier payment and be applied immediately or in installments.
Hormozi recommends pricing the next offer at least four times the rollover credit, limiting the resulting discount to 25% or less.
A downsell is an offer following a refusal. It seeks a fit within the customer's budget by changing payment timing or changing the quantity, quality, or kind of product offered.
Lowering the price of an unchanged offer after rejection can damage confidence in the seller's other prices. Hormozi recommends offering something different when charging less.
section: How Not To Downsell—AReal Story FromAFriend.

text: Plan price experiments in advance, specifying both the price and how many prospects receive it. Improvised discounts to rescue individual sales can upset customers who discover unequal prices for identical purchases.

Payment plans earn more when additional buyers finish paying, but lose money when cancellations precede profitability. Hormozi identifies the greatest loss when buyers who would have prepaid instead choose installments and cancel early.
A Payment Plan Downsell retains the product while dividing its cost between an initial payment and scheduled later payments.
Hormozi's Payment Plan Downsell process has up to seven steps, progressively shifting collection from upfront payment toward later payments. Stop the sequence once the customer buys.

Payment Plan Downsell, step 1: Include the financing premium in the presented price, then offer a reduction for full prepayment. Hormozi uses this framing to anchor the price and present prepayment as a benefit.
section: Step 1) Reward For Paying In Full Rather Than Punish For Paying Over Time.

text: Payment Plan Downsell, step 2: Offer external financing or card payment so the seller collects now while customers repay elsewhere; alternatively, offer layaway, withholding delivery until the customer completes payment.
section: Step 2) Offer 3rd-Party Financing, Credit Card, and Layaway Options.

text: Payment Plan Downsell, step 4: Ask customers to rate their desire from 1–10. At 8 or higher, continue exploring payment arrangements; at 7 or lower, investigate what is missing and offer a different product.
section: Step 4) Check To See If They Still Want The Thing.

text: Payment Plan Downsell, step 5: For prospects rating their desire 8–10, reduce half upfront to one third, collecting the remaining thirds on their next two paydays or over the following two months.
section: Step 5) Offer To Split Into Three Payments.

text: Payment Plan Downsell, step 6: If three installments remain unaffordable, divide the price into equal payments throughout the remaining service period.

Payment plans should increase total sales while preserving the percentage of sales appointments producing full upfront payment. A decline in full-payment buyers indicates installment plans are replacing purchases that would have generated immediate cash.
section: How To Make Sure Payment Plans Make You Money.

text: Hormozi cites Profitwell data covering 14,000 businesses: monthly cancellation rates were 10.7% with monthly billing, 5% with quarterly billing, and 2% with annual billing. He uses this to support presenting larger, less frequent payments first.
section: Another Reason To Start High Before Working Your Way Down.

text: A Payment Plan Downsell collects part of the price initially and schedules the remainder. Its growth benefit depends on adding buyers who actually complete their payments.

Trial With Penalty makes trial access free when customers satisfy specified requirements; unmet requirements trigger payment. Hormozi recommends requirements that develop desirable customer behaviors, using fee avoidance as the incentive.

Hormozi generally prefers separate penalties for individual missed requirements over charging the entire fee for the first failure. When one missed requirement substantially undermines success, he says the penalty should reflect that importance.
section: Breaking Up Fees vs. One Lump Fee.

text: Hormozi requires a credit card for trial enrollment and declines prospects unwilling to provide one or perform the required work; he reports that these prospects complain more and convert less.

Before granting a trial, Hormozi seeks agreement that the prospect will remain a paying customer if the program produces results. He considers a trial pointless when the prospect rejects that conditional commitment.

Hormozi recommends explaining penalties after collecting card details, claiming this reduces resistance. Customers must still consent to the charges; he requires separate initials beside fee provisions to ensure salespeople explain them.
section: Explain the fees after getting their card.

text: Hormozi makes trial check-ins compulsory, explaining each meeting's benefit and the charges for absence. These meetings also provide opportunities to sell additional services.

For weak trial uptake, reduce obligations or penalties. For poor participation, explain the fees' purpose and require sales appointments. For weak paid retention, improve delivery, communicate ongoing value, and align the subsequent offer with the trial.
section: Tweak Your Trial To Get The Most Customers.

text: Hormozi uses Pay Less Now or Pay More Later for physical goods or single services, and Trial With Penalty for recurring purchases. He reports success only where achieving results requires customer effort.
section: Pay Less Now or Pay More Later vs. Trial With Penalty.

text: Trial With Penalty provides free access conditional on meeting requirements. Setup includes collecting payment details, securing agreement, specifying participation and meeting obligations, and explaining charges for noncompliance.
Feature Downsells reduce the total price by reducing quantity, quality, or included components, or by substituting a cheaper alternative. Unlike a discount, the customer receives a different offer.

Removing a highly valued feature for relatively little savings can make the original offer appear preferable. Hormozi recommends removing features in descending order of customer value to encourage reconsideration of higher-priced options.
After a prospect rejects every service downsell, offer a do-it-yourself product addressing the same problem.

Hormozi advises against reducing the price for unchanged deliverables: use a payment plan when customers need a smaller immediate payment, and a feature downsell when they need a smaller total purchase.
After two rejected downsells, ask for purchase desire on a 1–10 scale. At 8 or higher, offer payment plans; at 7 or lower, ask what would merit 10 and adjust the feature combination accordingly.
section: If They Say 8 Or Above, Start Payment Plan Downselling.

text: Include guarantee removal among feature downsell options. Hormozi says losing that protection often reveals its value to prospects and leads them to accept the original offer.
Hormozi sometimes trades a discount for customer promotion, including reviews, testimonials, public progress updates, and introductions to prospective customers.
section: Barter With Reviews, Testimonials, And Referrals.

text: A Feature Downsell reduces the price by reducing what the buyer receives. Removing unwanted elements with a substantial price reduction favors the downsell; removing valued elements for a small saving favors the original offer.
After repeated downsell rejections, check whether the prospect still wants the product. If the feature combination appeals but its price does not, switch to payment-plan downselling.
Continuity Offers exchange continuing value for recurring payments that persist until cancellation.

A lower-priced continuity offer can attract more buyers while collecting less money immediately. Hormozi therefore prefers placing continuity after attraction, upsell, and downsell offers, though it can also serve acquisition, expansion, or reactivation.

Repeated payments toward a finite purchase constitute a payment plan. Continuing payments fit continuing value; Hormozi cautions against accepting one payment in exchange for providing a service indefinitely.
A Continuity Bonus Offer provides a joining incentive for enrolling immediately. The incentive typically exceeds the first recurring payment in perceived value.

Hormozi first makes offers that collect substantial cash, then sells continuity, then offers new monthly buyers a discount for prepaying additional months. He uses this sequence to support 30-day profit goals and advertising while building recurring revenue.
Membership bonuses should relate to the main purchase; unrelated incentives can attract customers who are unsuitable for the core offer.
section: Keep Your Bonuses Related To Your Core Offer.

text: Use existing assets or work already required for delivery as membership bonuses. Hormozi recommends assigning value to these resources instead of overlooking them because they are already available.
section: Make Bonuses Things You Already Have And Do.

text: Bonus valuations must be believable. Exaggerated figures undermine trust and fail to establish a useful price reference; previously sold products provide actual prices that can support the claimed value.
Present the bonus benefits and establish their value before explaining the membership. Then offer the bonus through enrollment, optionally alongside a separately priced purchase option.
section: When Making Your Continuity Offer, Anchor The Bonuses.

text: Hormozi uses the price gap between standalone purchases and subscriptions to influence customer choice: a relatively cheaper standalone option attracts more standalone buyers; a relatively costlier one shifts buyers toward subscriptions.
section: Pricing For Continuity vs. Up Front Cash.

text: Restricting bonuses to customers committing for 3, 6, 12, or more months sacrifices some month-to-month signups in exchange for stronger commitments.
section: If You Want Commitments—Prepare To Make A Trade.

text: A Continuity Discount Offer supplies free goods or services in exchange for a commitment to future purchases. Designing it requires choosing when the discount applies and establishing cancellation terms.

Giving the discount before paid service begins postpones cash collection. Hormozi favors this arrangement where contracts have historically been enforceable and advises businesses with high churn to choose another discount schedule.

A subscription discount can be divided across payments throughout the commitment. Hormozi also suggests allowing customers who pay punctually throughout that term to retain the reduced rate permanently.

At an unchanged charge per billing cycle, four-week billing produces 13 charges rather than 12 monthly charges annually, increasing revenue approximately 8.3%. Hormozi estimates a 41% profit increase for a business initially earning a 20% margin.
section: Highest Value Per Word Note In This Book

text: Hormozi offers to remove a 3% processing surcharge when customers provide a backup payment method, addressing failed collections caused by expired or changed payment details, exhausted credit, or insufficient balances.
Advertise a permanent price reduction that customers earn by remaining subscribed beyond the usual cancellation point; remind them of the approaching reduction as they near eligibility.
section: Try Lifetime Discount At Your Most Common Churn Point.

text: For customers receiving discounts in exchange for a commitment, Hormozi prefers a cancellation charge matching the agreed discount amount, allowing them to end the commitment by repaying that amount.
section: You Need To Have A Cancellation Policy Figured Out Ahead Of Time.

text: Hormozi suggests exchanging a cancellation fee waiver for an exit interview, then addressing the problem or proposing a better-fitting offer. He reports retaining roughly one-third of customers who agree to these interviews.
section: Use Cancellation Fees To The Customer’s Advantage.

text: Hormozi suggests letting customers qualify for a permanent lower price during the month with the highest churn, encouraging them to remain through that period.

When customers request cancellation, offer to remove the cancellation charge in exchange for an exit interview. Hormozi uses these conversations to retain customers, sell additional services, or learn why they want to leave.

A Waived Fee Offer pairs flexible monthly enrollment with a startup charge, typically 3–5 times the monthly price. A longer commitment removes that charge; cancellation before completing the term makes it payable.
Investigate when more than 5% of customers want to end their commitments early. Hormozi warns that pricing incentives cannot compensate for a poor product and should not trap dissatisfied customers.
For greater initial cash receipts, Hormozi suggests a setup charge of 1.5–3 times the monthly price: smaller charges encourage flexible monthly enrollment, while larger charges encourage commitments.
Hormozi recommends commitments lasting at least one year for Waived Fee Offers. Once customers complete the agreed term, the waived charge no longer applies.

Hormozi places continuity after profitable attraction, upsell, and downsell offers. After acceptance, he offers discounted bulk time or product, with recurring billing beginning once that purchase is consumed.

A Money Model deliberately sequences offers, their timing, and presentation to accelerate revenue. Hormozi's ideal is collecting enough from one customer within fewer than 30 days to acquire and serve at least two additional customers.

Hormozi divides Money Models into three stages: attraction reduces customer acquisition expense; upsells and downsells increase near-term receipts; continuity increases total customer spending. He cautions bootstrapped solo founders against launching with all stages fully developed.

Make Your Own Money Model, step 1: Choose an Attraction Offer, decide its presentation, and advertise it to acquire paying customers while covering costs. Hormozi allows up to a year to discover what works best.

Make Your Own Money Model, step 2: Choose an Upsell Offer addressing a problem created by the initial purchase. Present it when need peaks, aiming for 30-day profits substantially above acquisition and delivery costs.
Develop one offer within the current stage until results are dependable and execution becomes automatic before advancing. Hormozi recommends judging progress over quarters rather than weeks.
section: Perfect One Offer At A Time.

text: Introduce offers at low prices to encourage purchases and gather improvement feedback. Once dependable, increase prices progressively until additional revenue per buyer no longer compensates for lost purchases and total revenue falls.
An initial Attraction Offer can become a Continuity Offer by automatically transitioning customers into a subscription when the initial purchase period ends.
section: Turn Attraction Offers Into Continuity Offers With Automatic Renewal.

text: A Money Model arranges offers to increase customer count, spending per customer, and payment speed.
Hormozi's minimum standard for a good Money Model is customer profit within the first 30 days exceeding the expense of acquiring and serving that customer.

Hormozi defines a $100M Money Model as generating enough profit from one customer within the first 30 days to exceed acquisition and service costs for multiple customers, removing cash as a growth constraint.
An Anchor Upsell presents the highest-priced option first, then introduces a substantially cheaper acceptable alternative if the customer resists.
A Rollover Upsell applies credit from part or all of a customer's earlier purchases toward a subsequent offer.

Develop a Money Model sequentially: establish reliable customer acquisition, ensure customers cover their acquisition costs, then fund acquisition of additional customers, and finally maximize each customer's long-term value.
Hormozi argues that confidence comes from accumulating evidence through action that supports one's self-image, rather than repeating affirmations.
Hormozi recommends shifting acquisition effort away from channels producing less valuable customers and toward channels producing customers who spend more and remain longer.

Best Customer Avatar, step 1: Survey existing customers about their characteristics, business performance, goals, and purchase journey. Collect responses through a form or live conversation; make a benefit conditional on completion to encourage participation.

Best Customer Avatar, steps 2–3: Select the top 20% using customer preference, spending, and relationship duration. Identify the smallest shared set of qualifying characteristics, typically three to five.

Best Customer Avatar, step 4: Enforce the chosen eligibility criteria, expand effort in channels supplying suitable customers, and deliberately recreate the purchase journey observed among the best customers.

Hormozi reports that whenever his business removed qualification requirements, it generated more leads but earned less money. He recommends choosing the number of acquisition steps according to long-term advertising returns.

Hormozi combined marketing and sales into a single acquisition department to resolve their competing complaints about lead supply and closing performance, giving both teams a shared focus on winning valuable customers.
Narrowing customer eligibility can initially reduce the number served and may lower revenue during the transition. Hormozi argues that the longer-term benefits are better retention and profitability.
Hormozi argues that developing business skills can change the probability of success in an entrepreneur’s favor.
An offer specifies what a customer receives for their payment and provides the starting point for discussing a transaction.
Hormozi calls a coordinated approach to price, customer value, guarantees, and offer naming a Grand Slam Offer, designed to make advertising profitable.
Failed offers are part of developing marketing skill; Hormozi presents practice and learning from failure as necessary even for accomplished marketers.
Hormozi recommends reading a book while listening to its audio edition, claiming this improves reading speed and retention.
section: Pro Tip: Faster, Deeper Learning By Reading & Listening At Same Time

text: Hormozi's approach to selling emphasizes making the proposed purchase compelling enough that customers readily accept it, reducing reliance on the seller's skill.

Expertise in the work that motivates someone to start a business does not establish competence at running it profitably; commercial success requires persuading prospects to pay for what the business provides.
An offer specifies the products or services being provided, the payment arrangements, and the transaction's terms. It initiates the exchange between a business and its customer.
Cutting prices to attract customers can leave a business with a full workload but insufficient profit because each sale contributes too little margin.
section: The Two Main Problems Most Entrepreneurs Face and How This Book Solves Them

text: Hormozi treats growth as necessary to maintain relative position: using his stated stock-market growth rate of 9% annually, a business growing more slowly falls behind that benchmark.
In an expanding market, Hormozi says a business may need annual growth of 20–30% merely to maintain its position.
Three Ways to Grow identifies three revenue levers: expand the customer base, raise average spending per transaction, and increase repeat purchasing.
Hormozi defines gross profit as sales revenue less the direct expense of serving an additional customer. Net profit instead deducts every business expense.

Hormozi’s lifetime value measures cumulative customer gross profit: gross profit per purchase multiplied by expected lifetime purchases. It excludes indirect expenses such as administration, software, and rent; other definitions may measure revenue instead.
Hormozi defines a commodity as an offering obtainable from many sellers. When buyers regard alternatives as equivalent, lower prices determine preference, and competition compresses sellers’ margins.

A Grand Slam Offer differentiates an offering so buyers evaluate its value instead of primarily comparing prices. Hormozi connects this differentiation to acquiring additional customers, securing higher payments, and encouraging repeat purchases.

A Grand Slam Offer combines compelling promotion, distinctive value, premium pricing, a strong guarantee, and payment terms intended to fund customer acquisition, making direct comparisons with alternatives difficult.
section: But What Does A Grand Slam Offer Do?

text: Hormozi identifies three benefits of a Grand Slam Offer: more advertising responses, a greater share of respondents buying, and higher selling prices.
section: But What Does A Grand Slam Offer Do?

text: Changing the offer can shift a purchase from price comparison to value assessment even when the underlying fulfillment work stays the same.
section: But What Does A Grand Slam Offer Do?

text: When customers see competing services as interchangeable, cheaper alternatives pressure providers to lower prices to retain business, eroding margins.
section: Old Commoditized Way (Price-Driven) — Race to the bottom

text: When acquisition generates enough upfront cash, delivery capacity can replace cash flow and customer acquisition as the business's limiting factor.
section: New Grand Slam Offer Way (Differentiated, Incomparable) (Value-Driven)

text: A Grand Slam Offer can fail when presented to an unsuitable audience; selecting the market is a prerequisite to applying the pricing approach.
Strong demand for a solution can support sales despite weak offers, limited persuasion skills, and mediocre business execution.
section: PRICING: FINDING THE RIGHT MARKET -- A STARVING CROWD

text: Market contraction can defeat strong products, favorable offers, and effective selling; entrepreneurial persistence does not remove the market's influence on results.

The book assumes existing demand and at least a normal market: one matching overall marketplace growth, with unmet needs involving health, wealth, or relationships. Its approach directs demand rather than creating it.
The first of Hormozi's four market-selection indicators is intense customer pain: buyers should urgently need the proposed solution, beyond merely wanting it.
Hormozi links the intensity of a buyer's problem to the price a solution can command; accurately describing that problem helps the buyer feel understood.
section: Pricing: Finding the Right Market — A Starving Crowd

text: A viable target audience must possess, or be able to obtain, enough money to purchase at the price that makes serving it worthwhile.
Evaluate whether prospective buyers can actually be reached through identifiable gathering places or channels; even an excellent offer needs promotion that reaches its intended audience.
Prefer expanding markets: contraction can undermine a business even when buyers have substantial problems, sufficient money, and are easy to reach.

Hormozi ranks market demand first, offer quality second, and persuasive ability third. Exceptional demand can compensate for weaknesses in both other factors; in an ordinary market, an exceptional offer can compensate for weak selling skills.
section: Order of Importance: Three Levers on Success

text: An unsuccessful initial offer does not establish that a market is unsuitable. Commit to one viable niche long enough to experiment; repeatedly changing audiences forces learning to restart.

Hormozi generally recommends narrowing the audience below $10M in annual revenue. Beyond that, expansion may require serving additional audiences, depending on the total addressable market available within the existing niche.
section: Author Note - When To Broaden (Advice For Most People)

text: Applying a product to a narrowly defined buyer and tailoring its messaging can make it more compelling and valuable, supporting higher prices even when its underlying content remains similar.
Hormozi recommends avoiding poor markets, accepting ordinary ones, and persisting in a chosen market while refining offers rather than treating an unsuccessful offer as personal failure.
Hormozi evaluates markets through customer pain, purchasing resources, ease of targeting, and growth.
Customers buy when they believe the benefits exceed the price; they stop purchasing when what they receive becomes worth less than their payment.
Hormozi advises against competing through low prices unless a business can radically reduce its costs to one-tenth of competitors’ costs.
A Grand Slam Offer aims to increase purchases at a higher price by first adding enough value to widen the customer's advantage over the amount paid.
Copying competitors while offering slightly more at a slightly lower price drives the market toward margins that barely sustain operators.
section: Why You Should Charge So Much It Hurts

text: In the Virtuous Cycle of Price, lower prices weaken customers’ emotional commitment and their assessment of service quality.
Hormozi argues that higher prices strengthen customer commitment and perceived value, improving results and attracting customers who are easier to satisfy and less costly to serve.
Premium pricing supplies margin for better systems, capable staff, customer experience, and expansion; low pricing can remove the funds needed to deliver exceptional service.
Hormozi argues that a sufficiently large price premium can lead buyers to perceive an offering as fundamentally different, creating a category of one.
For services requiring customers to take action to obtain results, Hormozi argues that greater customer commitment increases their likelihood of success.
Hormozi argues that a purchase demanding meaningful financial commitment increases customer attention and follow-through, which can improve results and the value delivered.
Confidence in charging premium fees should come from repeated successful delivery; the product must produce results rather than rely on pricing alone.
Premium pricing can fund greater customer support and success while remaining attractive when the value customers receive substantially exceeds their payment.
Hormozi asserts that 99 percent of businesses should increase prices to grow, because profit finances expansion and greater reach.

Hormozi advocates pricing below the value delivered but substantially above fulfillment cost, suggesting up to 100 times cost rather than merely two or three times, provided the buyer still receives strong value.
