The Value Equation identifies four levers: increase the desired result and perceived chance of attaining it; reduce the perceived wait for that result and the work or sacrifices required.
Reducing waiting and customer effort offers stronger competitive differentiation than escalating promises about outcomes or success, because promises are easier for competitors to make.
The Value Equation’s hypothetical ideal is an outcome delivered immediately upon purchase with zero customer effort or sacrifice; Hormozi presents this as unlimited value to strive toward.

An offer gains perceived value only when prospects recognize its better chances of success, shorter wait, or lower demands on them; improving delivery without their awareness does not establish that value.
Hormozi recommends exploring psychological solutions when obvious logical fixes have already been tried; changing how customers experience a problem can offer another way to address it.
section: Pro Tip: Logical vs Psychological Solutions

text: Dream outcome means the feelings and experiences a prospect imagines attaining. An offer should reflect that desired future and explain a route to it, directing existing desire rather than attempting to manufacture it.

Hormozi argues that prospects generally assign greater value to outcomes that most directly improve their social standing. Status depends on the comparison group, so messaging should reflect what the prospect believes raises their standing.

Perceived likelihood of achievement is the buyer's confidence that purchasing will deliver their intended result. Greater confidence increases perceived value, even when the underlying service is unchanged.
Time delay measures the interval from purchase to the promised benefit. Shortening that interval increases value; intermediate benefits help customers persist until the longer-term result arrives.

Build early wins into delivery so customers can recognize progress and feel reassured about their purchase. Make benefits apparent quickly to support continued participation toward the ultimate result.
When competing with free alternatives, emphasize speed: customers may pay to obtain a result sooner even when a slower option costs nothing.
Effort and sacrifice encompass additional tangible and intangible costs customers incur while pursuing the result.

Hormozi attributes the generally higher prices of done-for-you services to reduced customer effort and sacrifice, plus greater confidence that an expert will achieve the result than customers would on their own.
When products promise similar outcomes, lower perceived demands on the customer's time and effort can make one seem more valuable.
Convergent problem solving derives one answer from known variables under fixed conditions.
Divergent problem solving generates multiple possible answers amid changing conditions and both known and unknown variables; several answers may work, with some substantially better than others.
The Brick Exercise trains divergent thinking by allowing 120 seconds to generate as many useful applications for a brick as possible.
Changing assumptions about an object's dimensions, material, or shape can reveal additional uses.
Offer design applies divergent thinking to combine offer components in multiple easy ways that create value for a customer's particular desire.
Offer Creation Process, step 1: Identify the customer's desired end result and experience, rather than treating the service purchased as the goal.
Offer Creation Process, step 2: Enumerate customer difficulties and limiting beliefs, including obstacles immediately before and after using the product or service.
Build the obstacle inventory from the prospect's viewpoint, following the order in which difficulties arise and recording detailed points of friction.

Use four value dimensions to uncover objections: whether the result justifies its cost, whether personal success seems achievable, whether required effort feels tolerable, and whether the time demands or wait for results seem acceptable.
The four objection categories are prompts for discovering problems, not boundaries that should exclude other customer obstacles.

Offer Creation Process, step 3: Convert each obstacle into a solution and give that solution a name. Determine what the customer needs to be shown, then express the obstacle as something the solution enables.
The solution inventory becomes a checklist of customer problems the offer must address; deciding how to deliver those solutions comes afterward.

Customer objections repeatedly reflect the four value drivers. Hormozi warns that leaving even one need unanswered can prevent a purchase, so the problem inventory should be extensive before problems are converted into solutions.

For an initial Grand Slam Offer, Hormozi recommends delivering unusually substantial value, making sales, and then improving convenience for customers. A high price can still seem inexpensive relative to the value received.
section: VALUE OFFER: CREATING YOUR GRAND SLAM OFFER PART II: TRIM & STACK

text: The Sales to Fulfillment Continuum describes a tradeoff: reducing delivery work makes selling harder, while providing more makes selling easier but demands more delivery time. The target is an offer that sells readily and is manageable to fulfill.

Hormozi first establishes demand, then secures purchases, and only afterward increases marketing friction or reduces what the same price includes. Without incoming demand, he lacks evidence for judging the offer.

Initially, deliver enough value to generate cash, then fund operational improvements with that cash. Systems can preserve customer value while reducing the resources needed to deliver it, potentially without changing the offer.

Offer Creation Process, step 4: Generate possible delivery methods for every identified problem. Include possibilities beyond what he would currently agree to provide; exploring them can reveal alternatives to his habitual solution.
section: Step #4 Create Your Solutions Delivery Vehicles (“The How”)

text: Generate delivery alternatives for perceived customer problems across the entire experience, including what happens before service, during delivery, and afterward.
section: Step #4 Create Your Solutions Delivery Vehicles (“The How”)

text: Delivery design variables include individual versus group attention; customer execution, guided execution, or provider execution; live communication channel; recorded content format; and support availability and response speed.
To expand delivery ideas, consider what he would provide at 10 times the price or $100,000. Then consider charging one-tenth the price while making the product more valuable than its current version.
Generate delivery options for each customer problem separately; working through one problem can suggest solutions for others.

An unresolved obstacle the buyer anticipates can prevent a purchase. Hormozi recommends addressing every perceived obstacle to maximize conversion, rather than insisting customers accept the seller’s preferred method.
section: Anecdote: Why We Must Solve Every Perceived Problem

text: Offer Creation Process, step 5a: Eliminate expensive options that contribute little value, then inexpensive options that contribute little value. Retain valuable options whether their delivery costs are low or high.
Assess an offer component by its financial worth to the buyer, its effect on confidence in success, and how much it reduces required effort, sacrifice, and time.

Solutions delivered to many customers can require substantial initial development while adding very little work per additional customer. Hormozi favors these reusable assets for their potential to generate sustained high margins.
Reserve costly individual or small-group delivery for substantial value contributions. If a cheaper delivery method provides equivalent value, use it.
Offer Creation Process, step 5b: Assemble the selected solution bundles into the complete deliverable.
Structure each bundle around a customer problem, describe the solution, give the bundle an appealing name, and specify the actual services or materials provided.
A complete bundle should address buyers’ perceived obstacles, strengthen the seller’s conviction that the offer is distinctive, and prevent easy comparison with competing offers.
Hormozi’s objective in offer creation is differentiation that resists direct comparison, allowing prospects to judge the offer by its value rather than commodity pricing.

Hormozi recommends increasing demand while reducing perceived availability to support higher prices and greater sales over time. He excludes businesses seeking mass market penetration for another strategic purpose.
From his service-selling experience, Hormozi estimates that 20 percent of prospects may accept a price at least five times higher, describing willingness to pay as uneven rather than linear.
When excluded prospects see admitted customers enjoying an offer, Hormozi argues their unmet interest can grow, making them quicker to purchase and more willing to pay at the next opening.
Hormozi Law links a longer wait before requesting a purchase with the ability to request a larger amount.

Providing nothing produces no revenue and can eventually alienate prospects; serving everyone can exhaust accumulated demand. Hormozi recommends keeping availability below the demand the business can create.
Hormozi distinguishes scarcity, which restricts availability to support prices and exclusivity, from urgency, which makes prospects more ready to act and thereby increases demand.

Bonuses strengthen demand and perceived exclusivity; guarantees strengthen demand by shifting risk away from buyers; offer names renew interest and help more intended buyers become aware of the offer.
Authorities and celebrities benefit from assumed demand: buyers infer that many people want their limited time and therefore expect high prices.

Expertise commands greater value when suitable providers are rare and the solution delivers substantial benefits. Hormozi treats provider rarity and the value delivered as mutually reinforcing sources of profit.
Clients pay specialized consultants for accumulated expertise that helps them avoid costly mistakes and reach results sooner, at less expense than discovering the solution independently.
Scarcity means restricting purchase availability through quantity limits. Hormozi distinguishes limits on service places, limits on bonuses, and offers that will not return.

For limited product releases, Hormozi recommends quantities that consistently sell out and announcing each sellout. He identifies roughly monthly releases as effective for most businesses he knows using this approach regularly.

A total business cap limits the active client base or a particular service tier and uses a waiting list. Hormozi suggests periodically expanding capacity by 10–20% before reinstating the limit, particularly for premium tiers.
A growth rate cap restricts recurring new-client intake according to onboarding capacity; prospects learn how many openings remain. A cohort cap instead restricts enrollment for each scheduled group.

Honest scarcity starts by setting the number of clients the business is willing to accept within a period and communicating how close it is to that limit. Filled capacity also signals that others have already purchased.

Hormozi recommends a very expensive service tier with very few places providing direct personal access. Delivery should use a communication medium the provider finds acceptable, even though the arrangement does not scale.
For a capped service, permanently excluding departing members from rejoining can discourage cancellation. Hormozi says this works best in small groups and becomes less effective as groups grow.
section: Pro Tip - Once You’re Out, You Can Never Come Back

text: Urgency restricts the time available to purchase or enroll, whereas scarcity restricts quantity. The two mechanisms can operate together.

Cohort-based rolling urgency ties enrollment to scheduled start dates: delaying enrollment means waiting for another group, even without a capacity limit. Hormozi says longer intervals between starts strengthen this effect.

Promotional countdowns and enrollment deadlines must be genuine; fabricated ones damage credibility. Hormozi recommends making promotion dates prominent on landing pages and throughout promotional copy.
For local businesses, Hormozi recommends refreshing the same service with seasonal promotion names and end dates to introduce novelty and urgency.
Businesses selling throughout the year can attach deadlines to discounts or bonuses without falsely claiming that the underlying service will become unavailable.
Before a genuine price increase, notify undecided prospects so they can purchase at the existing price; Hormozi recommends doing this with every increase.
section: Pro Tip - Clean Your Pipeline With Every Price Change:

text: An exploding opportunity creates urgency because its potential rewards decline over time. When that decline is real, emphasize what delaying action costs the prospect.
Hormozi argues that presenting an offer's components separately as bonuses increases perceived value compared with presenting the same contents as one undifferentiated package.
When closing a sale, Hormozi recommends adding bonuses rather than reducing the core price, because discounting teaches customers that the price can be negotiated.
section: Pro Tip: Add Bonuses Instead of Discounting Whenever Possible on Core Offers

text: In individual sales, disclose bonuses after an accepted purchase to reinforce the decision. If the initial request fails, introduce a bonus addressing the prospect's obstacle and ask for the purchase again.
Hormozi favors tools and checklists over extra training as bonuses because they require less customer time and effort.
Choose bonuses that resolve a specific perceived barrier to success or meet a need the customer will encounter next.
Noncompeting businesses may provide bonus products or services without charge in exchange for exposure to existing customers, increasing the offer's value without acquisition costs for those bonuses.
section: Advanced Level Bonuses - Other People’s Products and Services

text: Negotiate customer discounts alongside referral commissions with bonus partners; these arrangements can both help sell the original offer and generate revenue from referred purchases.
section: Advanced Level Bonuses - Other People’s Products and Services

text: Hormozi recommends accumulating reusable bonus assets, including recorded events, and negotiating customer discounts and referral payments with complementary businesses serving customers’ subsequent needs.
Separate distinctive, nearly standalone components from the main package as bonuses so their value receives attention; brief, useful resources can otherwise disappear among everything included.
section: What should be a bonus vs part of the core offer if I am the one fulfilling it?

text: Customers persuaded solely by a guarantee may be unwilling to do the work needed for success; Hormozi cautions that stronger sales appeal can attract difficult customers.
For expensive-to-deliver offerings, Hormozi favors conditional guarantees or final-sale policies because a refund can leave the seller bearing both repayment and fulfillment costs.
section: Pro Tip: High Cost Services Warning

text: A strong guarantee specifies an outcome, a deadline, and the remedy if the outcome is missed. A promise without an explicit remedy is weaker.

Conditional guarantees attach eligibility requirements to a remedy. Hormozi recommends requirements reflecting actions necessary for customer success and a remedy whose perceived value exceeds a refund.

Anti-guarantees explicitly make purchases nonrefundable and explain the seller’s exposure. Hormozi particularly associates them with consumable offerings or items that lose substantial value upon delivery.
Performance-dependent compensation requires visible, measurable outcomes and either confidence that payment will follow successful delivery or control over collecting that payment.
Guarantees can be combined: an unconditional refund policy can accompany a conditional remedy, or multiple conditional promises can cover separate outcomes or successive milestones.
An unconditional guarantee makes the seller responsible even when failure is outside the seller’s control. Adding eligibility restrictions progressively reduces its persuasive strength.

An Outsized Refund Guarantee promises double or triple the purchase price, or another substantially larger payment. Hormozi recommends it for high-margin products, with eligibility tied to required customer actions.

A Service Guarantee promises continued work without additional charges until the customer achieves the specified outcome. It leaves the completion date open and can require customer actions associated with success.

A Modified Service Guarantee provides a fixed additional period of free service or access instead of an indefinite extension. Hormozi recommends an extension lasting at least twice the original duration.

A Personal Service Guarantee promises individual help at no extra charge until the customer reaches a specified result. Hormozi advises attaching participation requirements, such as responding within 24 hours and using prescribed products.

A Delayed Second Payment Guarantee postpones further billing until the customer achieves an initial outcome. Hormozi recommends it when a repeatable process produces that result and a known activation indicator predicts longer retention.

An anti-guarantee makes purchases nonrefundable, explaining that valuable information or capabilities cannot be withdrawn after access. Hormozi says this positioning requires a compelling rationale and becomes stronger when the seller demonstrates actual exposure.

Performance fees, revenue sharing, and profit sharing function as implied guarantees: compensation depends on results under terms agreed beforehand. Hormozi favors their alignment of provider and customer interests.
section: Implied Guarantees: Performance Models, Revshares, and Profit-Sharing

text: Design a guarantee by identifying what customers fear losing or experiencing after purchase, then addressing those fears specifically. Consider their time, emotional investment, and expenses beyond the purchase price.
Guarantees strengthen an offer but cannot compensate for a weak product or sales team. Hormozi warns that using guarantees to conceal these weaknesses leads to substantial refunds.
An offer's name should make intended prospects interested enough to act; a strong underlying offer still needs to attract their attention.
One audience exposure does not establish offer fatigue. Hormozi recommends refreshing advertising around an unchanged offer and describes eventual fatigue on a timescale of years rather than months.

MAGIC combines a promotional reason, intended customer, desired result, timeframe, and bundle descriptor. Hormozi generally recommends three to five components, balancing specificity against length and testing candidate names.

MAGIC Naming Formula, step 2: Identify the intended customer precisely enough to distinguish suitable clients from unsuitable ones. For local businesses, Hormozi recommends naming the smaller service area rather than the broader city.
MAGIC Naming Formula, step 3: Name the result prospects want, favoring something concrete and specific. The desired result can concern an event, emotion, experience, or achievement.
Hormozi warns that pairing a measurable result with a deadline can imply a guarantee and violate advertising platform policies. Use that combination only where the platform permits it.
MAGIC Naming Formula, step 5: Add a descriptor that presents the offer's components as a unified system, making straightforward comparison with commodity alternatives harder.
MAGIC components can appear in any order. Test two to three promising names in advertising, identify the strongest performer, and make it the baseline against which subsequent names compete.
Apply MAGIC naming to individual bundle components and bonuses; Hormozi argues that names aligned with prospect interests increase perceived value.
section: Pro Tip - Name Sub Items & Bonuses

text: For fatigue, refresh advertising visuals first, then body text, offer headline, duration, and free or discounted incentive; alter the offer sequence and associated prices last. Earlier changes usually suffice and can be repeated.

Exhaust marketing adjustments before operational changes, which can create inefficiency. Once an offer earns money, Hormozi favors preserving its structure; rotating successful offers is an option when doing so adds little operational burden.
Proper product naming signals to target avatars that an offering was specifically designed for them, delivers meaningful value, and resolves their core issues.
section: Free Gift # 10 BONUS: Create The Perfect Name For Your Product

text: True financial milestone security is measured by personal cash reserves unencumbered by business liabilities, unexpected operational emergencies, or debt obligations, rather than top-line revenue or retained business earnings.
A single validated, high-margin grand slam offer should generate enough demand and pricing power to carry an entrepreneur to their initial $100,000 in wealth.
Entrepreneurial progress requires identifying and developing deficits across one's skills, mindset, and character attributes through direct trial and error or high-quality education.
Societal improvement depends on entrepreneurs creating solutions through commercial innovation rather than waiting for external rescue.
Hormozi argues that businesses need not wait for financial distress before increasing prices to improve profits.
Hormozi warns that a poorly executed price increase can threaten a business’s survival, while a well-executed increase can improve profitability.

Higher prices increase client emotional investment, perceived value, and results while reducing client demandingness, enabling businesses to generate higher profit per customer and reinvest into superior service delivery.
section: Why Raising Prices Is A Good Idea

text: Businesses should avoid grandfathered pricing and lifetime deals unless fulfillment costs zero, because long-term service obligations outlast upfront payments and eventually exhaust the collected revenue.

Firms should implement price increases at least annually by roughly ten percent, mirroring Warren Buffett's management of See's Candies, which averaged ten percent yearly increases and reached seventeen percent in select years.
Owners planning price increases exceeding fifty percent should schedule direct individual conversations with affected clients to present the elevated value and protect retention.

Doubling price with a twenty percent conversion decline and steady churn yields sixty percent higher total revenue, proving that price hikes do not need full customer retention to dramatically expand profitability.
Entrepreneurs should pilot updated rates on new buyers first to evaluate conversion and churn metrics safely before rolling out adjustments across the existing client base.
RAISE Price Increase Letter, step 1: Remind clients of their historical results, deliverables used, calls attended, and financial improvements achieved since becoming a customer.
section: Section #1 - R: Remind them of the value you provided them already.

text: RAISE Price Increase Letter, step 2: State the price increase directly in a single, unambiguous sentence without delaying or padding the announcement.
section: Section #2 - A. Address the price change directly.

text: RAISE Price Increase Letter, step 3: Detail business investments scheduled over the coming year and explain how each upgrade increases value, delivery speed, ease, or customer security.
section: Section #3 - I: Invest in their future.

text: Warning: Never introduce new operating expenses simply to rationalize a price hike, as added overhead cancels out the expanded profit margin.
section: Section #3 - I: Invest in their future.

text: RAISE Price Increase Letter, step 4: Announce the new rate immediately while granting existing buyers an expiring discount for three to six months to delay their cost increase as a loyalty reward.
section: Section #4 - S: Soften the news with a loyalty reward.

text: RAISE Price Increase Letter, step 5: Add a direct personal postscript inviting clients facing severe financial hardship to reply so leadership can provide custom relief, such as an extended discount.
section: Section #5 - E: Explain away their concerns.

text: Price hikes typically trigger higher churn in month one, below-average churn in month two, and normal churn by month three, because customers intending to leave soon simply accelerate their departure.
section: Section #5 - E: Explain away their concerns.

text: Tactic: Manage substantial price adjustments by stepping up costs across one to three periods, gradually reducing credits every few months or quarters to soften customer transition.
Principle: Charge incoming customers the higher rate immediately without hesitation, as new buyers lack prior pricing expectations.
section: What To Do About Incoming Customers

text: Address price increase inquiries exclusively through private, direct communication, banning public forum discussions to stop rumors from spreading among clients.
Higher pricing creates a compounding advantage by generating margin to improve product quality, fund expensive acquisition channels, and pay premium wages to retain top talent.
section: Why You Should Actually Do This

text: Businesses should re-evaluate and raise pricing at least annually to outpace inflation and cover expanding operating expenses.
section: Why You Should Actually Do This

text: When implementing a price increase of 50% or greater, deliver notifications through individual one-on-one outreach if team volume allows.
For large price hikes, phase out grandfathered discounts in six-month intervals, because customers adapt to expiring discounts more readily than abrupt rate jumps.
The price increase notification should frame continuing existing rates as an expiring loyalty discount or credit for three to six months before charging the higher price.

text: Conclude the price increase notice with a postscript encouraging clients facing severe financial hardship to reach out directly to arrange custom accommodation.

text: Hormozi asserts that profit never happens naturally in business and must be intentionally forced into existence.
A business can double potential top-line revenue through three core levers: doubling new customer acquisition, doubling prices, or doubling purchase frequency.
section: Pricing To Make The Most Money

text: Dividing monthly new customer volume by the monthly churn percentage yields the total customer plateau where a subscription business stabilizes.
section: Option #1: Double Your # of New Customers Per Month (aka - cut cost to acquire a customer in half)

text: Doubling customer acquisition by cutting acquisition expense in half yields a 3.5x profit increase, because marketing savings flow directly into net earnings rather than just doubling ordinary margins.
section: Option #1: Double Your # of New Customers Per Month (aka - cut cost to acquire a customer in half)

text: In recurring revenue models, total active customer capacity equals monthly new customer acquisitions divided by the monthly churn rate.
section: Option #2: Double The Number of Purchases (aka - how many times they buy from you)

text: Doubling prices while keeping customer count and fixed costs constant can produce a sixfold increase in net profit, as all incremental revenue flows directly to the bottom line.
section: Option #3: Double Your Prices (aka - how much you charge for the same thing)

text: ProfitWell data shows that a 1% price optimization improves profit approximately twice as efficiently as improving customer retention and nearly four times as efficiently as improving customer acquisition.
section: Case Study: 512 Companies’ Data in Three Important Graphs

text: Cost-plus pricing marks up delivery expenses with an arbitrary margin, failing to capture value from customers with higher willingness to pay while leaving the seller vulnerable to unpredictable cost fluctuations.

Competitor-based pricing sets fees according to prevailing market averages, forcing a business to copy rival operations rather than aligning prices with its own unique cost structure and customer value.

Value-based pricing sets rates according to customer willingness to pay rather than competitor benchmarks, incentivizing continuous product enhancements so the business can charge multiple times standard market rates.
The optimal price point is whichever rate maximizes total lifetime gross profit across all transactions and churn behavior, rather than the price that attracts the largest total volume of buyers.
section: Three Metrics To Determine Value-Driven Pricing

text: Raising prices increases overall business profits through two concurrent mechanisms: generating greater gross margin per buyer and lowering delivery overhead by serving fewer total clients.
Consistently closing more than 50% of sales opportunities or reaching full operational capacity indicates that prices are set too low to maximize earnings.

Businesses typically serve two to three customer avatars, with one segment frequently willing to spend five to ten times more than another; companies should provide distinct service levels titled after aspirational identities.

Hormozi warns that owners often abandon price hikes because facing more rejections is uncomfortable, forgetting that earning more profit from fewer buyers inevitably requires hearing no more frequently.

Under the Lookback Window of Value, clients measure return on investment solely against their latest billing period rather than the cumulative engagement; extending billing cycles prevents cancellation by giving service providers more time to deliver results.
section: Author Note: The Lookback Window of Value.

text: Because standard small companies generate 7% to 10% net profit margins, a 10% price bump doubles bottom-line profit; implementing minor pricing adjustments totaling 26.8% to 63.8% can multiply total profit four to six times over.

The Instant Profit Pricing Playbook consists of ten rapid pricing adjustments that collectively yield a 26.8% to 63.8% revenue increase with minimal operational risk or negative impact on customer conversion rates.
section: The *Instant Profit* Pricing Playbook: Here’s what we’re going to cover:

text: Transitioning subscriptions from calendar-month to 28-day cycles yields 13 billing intervals annually instead of 12, generating an automatic 8.3% revenue increase with identical conversion; for a company with 20% margins, bottom-line profit rises by 41.5%.
section: Pricing Play #1: Monthly to 28 Day Billing Cycles

text: To minimize perceived price while avoiding customer pause requests, display rates on a weekly basis but charge clients every four or twelve weeks, capturing extra annual cycles without the administrative friction of frequent billing.
section: Pricing Play #1: Monthly to 28 Day Billing Cycles

text: After closing a sale, apply a 3.99% credit card processing fee; if the buyer hesitates, offer to waive the surcharge if they provide a backup payment method to protect against monthly card declines.
section: Pricing Play #2: Processing Fees & Second Form of Payment

text: Involuntary payment failures cause 1.2% to 1.7% monthly churn, representing 24% to 34% of cancellations for businesses with 5% monthly attrition; securing a secondary payment method prevents this loss, boosting customer lifetime value by 31% to 51%.
section: Pricing Play #2: Processing Fees & Second Form of Payment

text: Absorbing sales tax directly harms profitability because it is levied on gross revenue; paying a 5% sales tax on a 20% profit margin forfeits 25% of the business's net profit.
A business cannot legally collect sales tax from customers unless the business itself is legally required to pay those taxes.
section: Pro Tip: You Cannot Charge Taxes You Do Not Pay

text: A business earning a 20% profit margin that keeps prices unchanged for seven years loses its entire profit due to standard wage and goods inflation.

Incorporate automatic annual rate increases of 5% to 15% pegged to the consumer price index into contracts, introducing the clause during customer onboarding paperwork rather than during sales conversations.

Billing annually lowers monthly churn to 2% and multiplies customer lifetime value by 5.35 compared to monthly billing at 10.7% churn, demonstrating that churn drops significantly as billing frequency decreases.
To offset conversion drops from higher upfront costs, sell an initial six-to-twelve-week service to build trust, then upgrade clients into prepaid annual agreements.
section: Pro Tip: High Conversions and Annual Billing?

text: Offering a 16% discount for annual prepayment achieves 10% to 15% adoption on checkout pages, 30% when selected as the default choice, and 35% to 40% when sold over the phone.
section: Pro Tip: High Conversions and Annual Billing?

text: Anchor price negotiations by stating the full undiscounted annualized sum first, framing upfront annual or quarterly prepayment as a cost-saving discount rather than monthly billing as an added penalty.
section: Pro Tip: Always Start With Highest Price

text: Rounding price endings up from 7 to 9 across recurring tiers increases annualized revenue by 4% to 7% without triggering customer pushback or cancellations.

Luxury goods should end in round figures like zero or five because luxury buyers seek exclusivity rather than bargains. In non-luxury markets, ending prices in 99 cents or replacing sevens with nines lifts margins without harming conversion.
section: Pro Tip: When NOT To Add .99 or change 7s to 9s

text: Premium products reflect the inherent value of the underlying solution, whereas luxury items derive their value strictly from high price tags. Consequently, sellers can safely use 99-cent and nine endings on premium offers without degrading prestige.

Consumers focus heavily on immediate monthly charges rather than annualized commitments. Bolting a yearly renewal fee onto monthly memberships increases effective monthly income significantly while preserving the conversion advantages of an advertised low monthly figure.
section: Pricing Play #7: Annual Renewal Fee On Top of Monthly

text: In price-sensitive markets where charging a full annual fee upfront hurts conversion, businesses should combine monthly billing with an annual renewal fee to maximize annual customer value without depressing sales volume.
section: Author Note: Conflict With Billing Annually?

text: Establishing both an onboarding fee and an annual renewal fee provides closing flexibility, allowing sellers to waive one charge as an incentive to secure agreement on the other.
section: Pro Tip: Have A Setup Fee And An Annual Renewal Fee

text: Annual Renewal Fee, step 1: Set the renewal charge between one and three times the normal monthly fee, generating an 8.3% to 24.9% increase in top-line revenue without expanding operational fulfillment.
Automatic continuity is a retention model where customers commit upfront to rolling into a low-cost, minimal-fulfillment subscription once their initial service period or course access expires.

Setting recurring maintenance pricing between 5% and 20% of the primary product price leverages sunk cost psychology: customers pay a small fee to avoid abandoning previous progress or losing access to assets.

Continuity billing must be transparently disclosed and accepted during initial checkout rather than hidden. Surreptitious or forced billing damages customer trust, whereas upfront transparency provides reassurance about future affordability.
section: Pro Tip: Don’t Be A Sneak

text: Automatic Continuity, step 4: Attach the recurring maintenance tier to initial sales contracts, stipulating that clients only unlock the discounted rate after completing their primary program, reinforcing retention.

Introducing a flagship offering priced at ten times or more of the standard offer re-anchors buyer expectations, making the core tier appear substantially more affordable and lifting overall conversions.
Ultra High Ticket Anchor, step 1: Pitch the most comprehensive, premium tier first to set a high anchor; if the prospect declines, transition downward to the better-fitting core offer.
If delivering a premium high-ticket package creates stress or resentment, Hormozi advises continuing to increase its price until the compensation makes fulfilling the service genuinely enjoyable.
After securing an agreement to buy, offer a guarantee or warranty priced at 5% to 30% of the product, or match replacement cost of goods so fulfillment never produces a net loss.
If half of customers accept a 10% warranty upsell, the business recovers 5% of total revenue, offsetting roughly half of a standard 10% sales team commission.
A 4% rise in top-line revenue can produce a 20% or greater increase in profit.
Price optimization boosts business profits roughly fourfold compared to acquiring new buyers, and twofold compared to retaining existing clients.
section: DO YOU WANT TO SCALE YOUR BUSINESS?

text: Implementing all ten tactics in the Instant Profit Pricing Playbook provides a cumulative price and revenue increase between 26.8% and 63.8%.

At a 15% monthly churn rate, a subscription business loses 83% of its customer base annually, requiring constant replacement volume merely to remain flat and risking business failure if acquisition dips slightly.

The 5 Horsemen of Retention framework curbs cancellations through five core operational tactics: monitoring attendance, reaching out twice weekly, sending personal handwritten milestone notes, hosting events every 21 to 63 days, and conducting structured exit interviews.

Gym members attending three or more weekly sessions consistently stay, while attending fewer than two predicts cancellation; reaching out as soon as weekly attendance drops to two sessions enables operators to save the client.

Executing systematic retention procedures initially spikes cancellations by roughly 50% as inactive billing accounts surface, followed by consecutive 50% month-over-month churn reductions as active client engagement stabilizes.
Reducing monthly churn from 9% down to 3% multiplies customer lifetime value by 3.3 times, and sustaining sub-3% churn consistently signals a highly lucrative business.
Churn measures the percentage of an existing customer pool that departs over a defined period, unaffected by any new customers acquired during that same interval.
To identify retention priorities, invert the core problem by cataloging every action that would cause complete customer defection, then systematically implement the exact opposite practices.

The ideal product price maximizes total sales volume multiplied by lifetime value rather than minimizing churn, meaning higher price points can tolerate lower conversion rates and higher cancellations.
Customer overwhelm represents the leading driver of cancellations; companies should maximize perceived value per second by deleting nonessential deliverables rather than expanding decent offerings.
section: Provide On-Going Value To Get On-Going Customers

text: Reducing customer churn from ten percent to three percent increases customer lifetime value by 3.3 times, stretching average retention duration from ten months to thirty-three months.
section: Why Is Reducing Churn So Important?

text: Acquiring a new customer costs between five and twenty-five times more than retaining an existing one, making a retention budget equivalent to twenty percent of acquisition cost highly profitable.
section: Why Is Reducing Churn So Important?

text: A business achieves compounding organic growth whenever the rate of incoming customer referrals exceeds the rate of customer churn.
section: Why Is Reducing Churn So Important?

text: The Churn Checklist outlines nine sequential retention plays: finding activation points, customer onboarding, activation incentives, community linking, pruning bad customers, annual pricing, cancellation interviews, regular surveying, and mapping the customer journey.
Activation points are leading indicators of customer retention defined by specific actions completed or results achieved that correlate with longer customer lifespans.
section: Churn Checklist #1: Figure Out Your Activation Points

text: To identify activation points, analyze churned clients who lasted at least three months, isolate the top revenue-producing twenty percent, and identify five common usage or service patterns.
section: Churn Checklist #1: Figure Out Your Activation Points

text: The Fast Cash Play drives new clients to fully recoup their initial investment within thirty days of onboarding, rapidly cutting cancellation rates.

Onboarding produces the best retention when tailored individually, conducted live rather than recorded, and encouraged through positive incentives rather than penalties, though providing any onboarding whatsoever is vastly superior to offering none.

Offering desirable rewards and unlockable bonuses immediately past historical churn drop-off periods preserves at-risk subscribers who would otherwise abandon the service at those specific milestones.

Usage churn defines a scenario where a subscriber continues paying but stops utilizing the service, functioning as a vital early warning of upcoming cancellation unless the company immediately intervenes to re-engage them.

Facilitating relationships between peers rather than tethering members exclusively to the company founder strengthens retention, because customers readily abandon an impersonal commercial membership but hesitate to walk away from genuine friendships.

Pinning the top one or two member posts daily signals behavioral expectations and provides immediate value, while strictly enforcing a three-strike eviction policy against low-quality contributors prevents community degradation.

If average customer retention is under twelve months, price annual plans higher than cumulative average monthly earnings; if retention exceeds twelve months, price annual subscriptions at ten months of recurring fees to convert ten to twenty percent of buyers.
section: Churn Checklist #6: Add Annual Payment Options

text: He believes people often have substantially more capacity for effort than their initial sense of reaching their limit suggests.

text: His father's experience of losing family assets during Iran's revolution shaped his emphasis on education: acquired knowledge remained valuable even when possessions could be confiscated.
title: Life Changing 'Dad Advice'' for Father’s Day

text: Being responsible for an outcome does not require having caused the problem. He argues that accepting responsibility encourages advance planning and restores a sense of control despite external circumstances.

text: Choosing a direction requires accepting that other paths will remain unexplored. Trying to satisfy everyone or cover every possibility can prevent someone from committing where they are needed.

text: He thinks a person's interpretation helps determine how difficult an experience feels. Familiarity with a recurring inconvenience can make it less upsetting, even when the circumstance remains unchanged.
title: Life Changing 'Dad Advice'' for Father’s Day

text: When offering help, deliver substantially beyond expectations rather than treating unpaid work as permission for poor quality. He says consistently doing this builds an association between the person and excellent work.
title: Life Changing 'Dad Advice'' for Father’s Day

text: He believes longtime acquaintances may resist someone's growth because they continue relating to an earlier version of that person. He frames this resistance as an expected part of becoming more successful.
title: Life Changing 'Dad Advice'' for Father’s Day

text: Some opportunities disappear before complete information becomes available. Taking them requires tolerating uncertainty rather than waiting until a decision can feel perfect.
title: Life Changing 'Dad Advice'' for Father’s Day

text: For major decisions, he favors being rested, fed, and ideally somewhere different from the usual environment. He thinks these conditions provide perspective and support longer-term judgment.

title: Life Changing 'Dad Advice'' for Father’s Day

text: He finds observable behavior more useful than stated intentions or self-descriptions when deciding what to believe about people.

text: He views TikTok Shop as a hot arbitrage opportunity that will not last forever, and thinks returns in three years are unlikely to match today's.
title: \"How Do I Know Which Business to Go All In On?\"

text: When the target is only a certain revenue figure, like 12 million, it filters nothing, since almost any business can hit it. A much bigger goal, like 100 million, forces harder choices.
title: \"How Do I Know Which Business to Go All In On?\"

text: Instead of investing in client brands, he thinks taking a revenue share is easier and cleaner, since most such brands never sell and the cash is what they produce.
title: \"How Do I Know Which Business to Go All In On?\"

text: Fear of missing out is, in his view, the worst drive for an entrepreneur. He says he lost it last year after many years of feeling it.
title: \"How Do I Know Which Business to Go All In On?\"

text: There will always be more opportunities than anyone can pursue, and greater skill brings more good ones to decline. Doing one thing well for life gets big; splitting attention makes neither big.
title: \"How Do I Know Which Business to Go All In On?\"

text: Customers who ask whether you can make them big are the wrong avatar. They churn, and you become the villain the moment results stall after being their savior.
title: \"How Do I Know Which Business to Go All In On?\"

text: When a business has more demand than it can serve and is fully staffed, Hormozi's first answers are to sell more, do more, and raise prices, since the constraint is supply rather than demand.
title: The Cobbler’s Shoes Problem Killing Your Agency Growth

text: Hormozi says that if a price increase lost some clients, the downside is small: it frees capacity, while the upside is more money, cash flow and growth.
title: The Cobbler’s Shoes Problem Killing Your Agency Growth

text: A business built purely on getting people into roles can be a good business. The whole recruiting and placement industry does this, and some such companies are worth billions.
title: “I Own a Recruiting Company. What Do I Sell After I Get Someone a Job?”

text: Most recruiting and placement companies niche down to one type of role, such as engineers, sales, customer success or legal, and over time build a large network of that kind of candidate.
title: “I Own a Recruiting Company. What Do I Sell After I Get Someone a Job?”

text: For an ongoing offer after placement, he suggests something like a professional association at a small fraction of the original price, focused on career advancement and continued education. This works only with one specific niche.
title: “I Own a Recruiting Company. What Do I Sell After I Get Someone a Job?”

text: Once someone lands the role, their next problem is upward trajectory: raises, upskilling to earn more, negotiating annual raises, and using outside offers to move up at other companies.
title: “I Own a Recruiting Company. What Do I Sell After I Get Someone a Job?”

text: If the front-end offer only sells getting a foot in the door, retention is short. Painting a larger vision, a career with a five-year playbook, lets you keep people much longer.
title: “I Own a Recruiting Company. What Do I Sell After I Get Someone a Job?”

text: Engineer example: after a foot-in-the-door program, walk them through learning the three highest-paying, highest-demand languages over 12 months, then run another job cycle with the new resume and skills, bidding it out.
title: “I Own a Recruiting Company. What Do I Sell After I Get Someone a Job?”

text: Bidding out upleveled skills has two good outcomes: a job they like, or an offer they can take to their current employer and ask them to match, yielding a raise in place.
title: “I Own a Recruiting Company. What Do I Sell After I Get Someone a Job?”

text: The same career-ladder approach works in other fields, such as legal, where specialties like tax law are worth more than generic law. It depends on the skills you can teach.
title: “I Own a Recruiting Company. What Do I Sell After I Get Someone a Job?”

text: All of this depends on niching down enough to know the specific avatar's problems and deliver very high-value solutions.
title: “I Own a Recruiting Company. What Do I Sell After I Get Someone a Job?”

text: Hormozi says not to scale ad spend until churn is fixed, because extra customers just leak out the back. First identify the activation event that makes customers stay, then make it happen faster.
title: I built an app and no one's using it

text: Total churn that includes trial cancellations distorts your numbers, especially for a smaller company. He says to work out churn after conversion, meaning among people who actually became paying customers.
title: I built an app and no one's using it

text: A free trial with a penalty is the smallest operational change to improve a trial. It can serve as a front-end offer: free only if the user does a required action, so there is a cost to not using it.
title: I built an app and no one's using it

text: For a subscription business to work well, he says annual retention should be 80 percent or higher, meaning monthly churn under 2 percent and ideally closer to 1 percent.
title: I built an app and no one's using it

text: Skip the churn number on the front end. Track trial conversion rate first, then measure churn only among customers after they have converted.
title: I built an app and no one's using it

text: Charging upfront and offering hands-on onboarding help makes customers more likely to commit. All effort and incentive should go toward activation, since once that works the rest of the machine follows.
title: I built an app and no one's using it

text: Hormozi thinks your environment affects how efficient your behavior is, meaning how much output you get per hour.
title: Focus on Winning, Not the People Beating You

text: No matter what you are struggling with, someone else has already faced the same struggle and solved it.
title: Focus on Winning, Not the People Beating You

text: When someone lists around six separate problems in their business, Hormozi's read is that the real issue is a lack of people to help, so he treats it as a hiring need rather than six separate problems.
title: “Why Is My Business So Hard to Run?”

text: Hormozi says what people call fear of failing is often fear of what a specific person will think. He notes that if he could fail in complete privacy, he would not care.
title: Nobody Is Thinking About You as Much as You Think

text: He argues that if you fail publicly, other people mostly think nothing about you at all, because they are not thinking about you.
title: Nobody Is Thinking About You as Much as You Think

text: Hormozi says that since everyone is insecure, you might as well use your insecurity to get something out of it, in line with his entrepreneurship idea of using what you have.
title: Nobody Is Thinking About You as Much as You Think

text: He says waiting for perfect conditions before starting is a mistake; the perfect condition is the one you are in, since your existing assets are the cards you were dealt and you just play the hand.
title: Nobody Is Thinking About You as Much as You Think

text: Having nothing to lose makes you dangerous. Hormozi adds that every position, in business and probably elsewhere, carries both an advantage and a disadvantage.
title: Nobody Is Thinking About You as Much as You Think

text: Hormozi recalls telling younger competitors in gym licensing that they held the bigger advantage: personal attention versus his large firm's process. He says most people study rivals' advantages instead of asking which one they themselves have.
title: Nobody Is Thinking About You as Much as You Think

text: He thinks cynicism is popular online because never trying means never feeling the pain of failure.
title: Nobody Is Thinking About You as Much as You Think

text: Hormozi compares avoiding failure to investing: fearing losses, yet the only investment guaranteed not to work is never investing. People pick a long failure over a short one.
title: Nobody Is Thinking About You as Much as You Think

text: He lists reasons not to fear judgment: the judges will die, you will die, they will not care even if you succeed, and they will not think of you if you do nothing.
title: Nobody Is Thinking About You as Much as You Think

text: Hormozi describes having lunch with his 90-year-old grandfather three times a week in Baltimore and seeing how painful it is to watch someone with regrets and no options left.
title: Nobody Is Thinking About You as Much as You Think

text: His grandfather, who fled Germans in World War II, repeatedly told him he had two hands and one brain and should use them. Hormozi says this made his own problems feel smaller.
title: Nobody Is Thinking About You as Much as You Think

text: Hormozi says hearing how his grandfather raised his mother helped him forgive her. He cites Pascal that to understand is to forgive, and says it is hard to hate someone up close.
title: Nobody Is Thinking About You as Much as You Think

text: He argues that without understanding, we assume people are evil, but most act as they do because past behavior was reinforced or punished. Taking a longer time horizon helped him extend grace to his mother.
title: Nobody Is Thinking About You as Much as You Think

text: After acquiring a teeth whitening chain he is invested in, they stopped waiting for repeat customers and sold whitening plans so everyone returned. He says this quadrupled lifetime value, which is what allows a business to scale.
title: $15 in, $550 out. Why aren't you scaling this?

text: If people come in for one thing, let them, then sell everything else to raise lifetime value. Give them what they want so you can give them what they need, via a sales motion and education toward the next purchase.
title: $15 in, $550 out. Why aren't you scaling this?

text: When the sale must happen in person, he suggests installing a check-in and check-out process that seeds the sale, and asking every arriving customer whether they are here for a specific offer, even knowing they are not.
title: $15 in, $550 out. Why aren't you scaling this?

text: Using the Buddha's two arrows story, he says the first arrow is life and cannot be avoided, while the second arrow is self-inflicted and can be avoided.
title: A Great Rule to Live By: Only Suffer Once

text: He treats suffering as a fixed cost of life: everyone will face downsides, bad seasons, bad moments and bad days.
title: A Great Rule to Live By: Only Suffer Once

text: He thinks a great rule to live by is to only suffer once: allow a bad event to hurt one time and do not replay it repeatedly.
title: A Great Rule to Live By: Only Suffer Once

text: He likes short personal mottos to recall in the moment; his is to not judge himself for failing to behave as he wished, which he calls an endless loop of self-criticism.
title: A Great Rule to Live By: Only Suffer Once

text: He wants memory dividends rather than memory liabilities, meaning past moments should benefit him instead of weighing on him.
title: A Great Rule to Live By: Only Suffer Once

text: Every business is limited by demand, either for customers or for talent. Most problems can be solved with advertising; the real question is whether you are advertising to customers or to potential hires.
title: Most problems can be solved with advertising

text: Top players are found the same way as customers. For leaders or top talent, the main method is outreach, although A-level talent can also be found other ways.
title: Most problems can be solved with advertising

text: Many people burn their effort on a short challenge or competition and then stop. Hormozi says that sustained effort over a long stretch is how business is actually done, and it is what makes someone a champion.
title: Missionaries vs Mercenaries: Who Makes More Money

text: Hormozi thinks people quit after winning because they were working to win rather than to help a community. If you truly believe in your mission, you keep going because it is not just for you.
title: Missionaries vs Mercenaries: Who Makes More Money

text: In his opinion, missionaries make more money than mercenaries over the long haul. A mercenary's personal goals are easy to satisfy, while a mission bigger than one person keeps founders pushing past their own needs. Wealth is an outcome.
title: Missionaries vs Mercenaries: Who Makes More Money

text: He cites Bezos, building a store that delivers conveniently for everyone, and Elon as missionaries who built bigger things because their drive was larger than personal wealth.
title: Missionaries vs Mercenaries: Who Makes More Money

text: Self-check for people who won in past challenges and then eased off: if you took your foot off the gas, remember that sustained effort is what defines a champion.
title: Missionaries vs Mercenaries: Who Makes More Money

text: To keep effort going, ask how to keep the same input continuing. If an input produced a given amount of recurring revenue, have someone else take two-thirds of your tasks while the input stays the same.
title: Missionaries vs Mercenaries: Who Makes More Money

text: Judge inputs from a macro perspective, meaning total team output, not only your own work ethic. He claims his team does more than his audience does, though he personally does less.
title: Missionaries vs Mercenaries: Who Makes More Money

text: The work is two steps: first learn the skill, then transfer it so someone else does it just as well. Many people never reach step two and say they cannot keep this up, because they do several people's work.
title: Missionaries vs Mercenaries: Who Makes More Money

text: It is fine if replacing you takes two or three people to match the output of one person's work.
title: Missionaries vs Mercenaries: Who Makes More Money

text: Hormozi recalls Munger inverting success by listing ways to guarantee failure, with inconsistency among them. Munger's point, as he tells it, is that a consistent person with none of the other flaws will still likely succeed.
title: The Bar For Excellence Is Embarrassingly Low

text: He believes consistency is among the hardest virtues for people because humans are drawn to novelty.
title: The Bar For Excellence Is Embarrassingly Low

text: When he ran gyms, asking clients if they followed the meal plan got a yes. Asking how many of the 21 planned meals they ate exactly as written exposed the truth; many said about half, as if that were success.
title: The Bar For Excellence Is Embarrassingly Low

text: The meal plan example applies to any plan, such as content, arriving at work on time, or side hustle hours. He says the one muscle to flex is doing the same thing repeatedly.
title: The Bar For Excellence Is Embarrassingly Low

text: He uses a cheap twist kitchen timer on his desk: set it to a predicted duration when starting work, and stop it whenever a phone call or Slack interrupts. This improves his time predictions and shows real time on task.
title: The Bar For Excellence Is Embarrassingly Low

text: He says his time on task is usually well below what he assumes, and early on he sat at a computer a long time with few minutes actually working.
title: The Bar For Excellence Is Embarrassingly Low

text: He thinks most things are easier than people believe because people do not know how to try hard. In his view, the harder you try, the easier it gets, so learn to love how trying hard feels.
title: The Bar For Excellence Is Embarrassingly Low

text: To become unreasonably good, ask what actions someone would have to have done, regardless of outcome, to be a top 1% salesperson or creator. Then do those actions; he says you find it is not that hard because others' effort is so low.
title: The Bar For Excellence Is Embarrassingly Low

text: Hormozi bets that doubling everything currently done for acquisition will work; data attribution matters afterward for improving efficiency, not as a prerequisite for scaling.
title: Helping a Real Estate Consulting Firm Get to $100M

text: A simple step before full forensic attribution is directional, qualitative attribution: ask customers where they first heard of you. It gives at least some indication of where people originally come from.
title: Helping a Real Estate Consulting Firm Get to $100M

text: Last-touch attribution sits closest to the conversion but skews everything toward direct response. Scientific attribution blends the two: last touch if the conversion is within 30 days, first touch if it is longer.
title: Helping a Real Estate Consulting Firm Get to $100M

text: Survey customers about their first touch. Where most say they began should guide reinvestment for disproportionate return, while keeping other brand touches since they likely nudge or convert, especially for complex, higher-touch services with long conversion times.
title: Helping a Real Estate Consulting Firm Get to $100M

text: Everything is teachable and most sales skills can be taught within a couple of weeks. Identify what top performers do differently, make it the standard, and see whether the rest of the team improves.
title: Helping a Real Estate Consulting Firm Get to $100M

text: If team members fail to follow the new standards, the issue may be adherence or work ethic, which are skills but probably not worth training.
title: Helping a Real Estate Consulting Firm Get to $100M

text: Hormozi treats a funding problem like closing deals. When volume is too low, such as applying to three or four grants, he asks how to reach 300, and what it would take to make failure impossible.
title: Apply to 300 Grants, Not 3

text: He always looks for the highest likelihood path, then does so much volume on it that failing becomes unreasonable. If you already know how to win grants, multiply the volume tenfold.
title: Apply to 300 Grants, Not 3

text: When a known method already works, he prefers to pursue it ruthlessly rather than spend time hunting for a different strategy, comparing it to sticking with an existing sales funnel instead of building a new one.
title: Apply to 300 Grants, Not 3

text: Most people who call themselves perfectionists are actually procrastinating, since they are doing nothing. He says a true perfectionist works constantly on the thing and can show progress toward finishing it.
title: Be a Perfectionist

text: Planning, thinking about, or getting angry at people who already did the thing does not count as doing the thing.
title: Be a Perfectionist

text: Someone with high standards must pick their battles. Holding perfection everywhere slows the velocity needed for progress, so find the highest-contribution areas and refuse to compromise there.
title: Be a Perfectionist

text: He reframes perfectionism in content as being about volume. Since nobody can predict which content goes viral, making more pieces offsets that ignorance; ten pieces reach more people than one polished piece.
title: Be a Perfectionist

text: In the pottery class story, the group graded on quantity of pots made both more pots and better ones than the group graded on producing one perfect pot.
title: Be a Perfectionist

text: He calls the biggest lesson of his life that volume negates luck: rather than trying to pick the one perfect thing, do so much work that you brute force your way to figuring it out.
title: Be a Perfectionist

text: A newcomer told to make one perfect podcast lacks data to judge what is good. Doing a thousand gives the perspective to make the best one around number 1,000.
title: Be a Perfectionist

text: He says he does this with over half the businesses he buys and considers it one of the biggest value unlocks: study your best customers, the top 10-20%, and find what they share that others lack.
title: How to Find Your Ideal Customer (Most Businesses Miss This)

text: Aim to pick one to four characteristics that make top customers distinct. He promises that if you look, you will find them, by testing filters like demographics, psychographics (beliefs), geographics and past activities.
title: How to Find Your Ideal Customer (Most Businesses Miss This)

text: The informal shortcut is to list the clients you love and help most, identify what they have in common, and be willing to turn away people who do not fit.
title: How to Find Your Ideal Customer (Most Businesses Miss This)

text: Knowing your ideal customer lets you be specific and niche down your messaging. He states that a narrower message lets you raise prices and also improves conversion rates.
title: How to Find Your Ideal Customer (Most Businesses Miss This)

text: Hormozi believes an AI automation community is currently one of the top communities on school, and that people definitely buy it. He suggests selling it as an annual membership.
title: How do I make money teaching AI automation?

text: If you lack confidence in a new annual membership price, Hormozi says to start around 3k a year and raise it to 5 or 6k later.
title: How do I make money teaching AI automation?

text: To be more efficient selling a community, Hormozi advises driving people to a sales call funnel instead of straight to a purchase page, showing them the community on the call, and having them buy during the call.
title: How do I make money teaching AI automation?

text: Hormozi notes that an automation community attracts both business owners who want automations for themselves and freelancers who want to do it for others, and either group works.
title: How do I make money teaching AI automation?

text: He shares the usual entrepreneur complaint of wanting things to happen faster, but he tries to reset his expectations, and he notes that progress often happens faster than originally expected.
title: \"Is there anything you're unhappy about?\"

text: He says he genuinely likes his life. He has put lots of effort into building an environment of people and activities he enjoys, and he likes his daily work partly because he feels he is good at it.
title: \"Is there anything you're unhappy about?\"

text: He once wore a sleep-tracking ring around age 22 and became competitive about beating his prior night's score. He stayed still to avoid waking the ring, slept worse, and found the ring's verdict on his day was silly.
title: \"Is there anything you're unhappy about?\"

text: He cites a friend, Dr. Kashif, who defines a scam as something whose removal makes your functioning worse than baseline. He treats such things as crutches, like needing green juice just to feel normal.
title: \"Is there anything you're unhappy about?\"

text: He tries not to be superstitious about anything so he keeps as many controllable factors under his own control as possible. He likes competing against people with many crutches, since knocking out one can derail them.
title: \"Is there anything you're unhappy about?\"

text: He sleeps shorter or longer depending on the night, as long as he can, and says he works fine after short nights rather than needing a fixed eight hours.
title: \"Is there anything you're unhappy about?\"

text: Alongside the investor's circle of competence, he says creators have a content circle of competence: if a topic falls outside it, he shouldn't talk about it, simply because he doesn't know it.
title: Only Talk About What You've Actually Done

text: He says material added from outside your experience is usually a generalization heard from someone else, which makes it their opinion rather than yours.
title: Only Talk About What You've Actually Done

text: He wants first-principles, first-experience content, described as N equals one or one-of-zero content. His litmus test is whether it is something he knows from experience.
title: Only Talk About What You've Actually Done

text: He shared a plan for reaching 100 million a month, labeling it his current plan since he hasn't been there yet. He says he only speaks about things he has already done.
title: Only Talk About What You've Actually Done

text: He believes speaking only about what he has done lets him avoid suffering from criticism. If someone denies that Gym Launch was a company, it is like denying he had oatmeal for breakfast; he knows he did.
title: Only Talk About What You've Actually Done

text: Hormozi thinks a human appointment setter role will be short-lived, maybe twelve months at most, because AI appointment setting is rapidly taking hold, especially in well-understood fields like medical.
title: Hormozi's AI Just Out-Coached Him on an Invisalign Offer

text: For hiring a phone-based appointment setter, he says young, hungry 20-year-olds tend to work great.
title: Hormozi's AI Just Out-Coached Him on an Invisalign Offer

text: Collect a card over the phone when booking a discounted front-end offer. That lets you charge a no-show fee, and billing up front dramatically lowers no-shows, in his view.
title: Hormozi's AI Just Out-Coached Him on an Invisalign Offer

text: When the customer arrives, use roughly half of a menu upsell: show several outcome options from imaging, ask which they prefer, recommend one, and charge the card already on file to keep the sale smooth.
title: Hormozi's AI Just Out-Coached Him on an Invisalign Offer

text: He says the whitening sales process his company designed for its teeth whitening chain more than doubled LTV.
title: Hormozi's AI Just Out-Coached Him on an Invisalign Offer

text: Hormozi says his tweets are written by him alone, as single sentences, and he uses no AI tools such as ChatGPT for them.
title: My Writing Process

text: He argues you should either sell something very expensive to a select few or something very cheap to everyone, because the middle is where businesses die.
title: My Writing Process

text: For people in their 20s who want to stand out, he says to do what you promised even when nobody is watching, and to outwork everyone through early arrival, research, using names, following up quickly and doing more than your share.
title: My Writing Process

text: He states that work ethic is a universal currency of respect that costs nothing but can give you everything.
title: My Writing Process

text: He says greatness requires first being misunderstood.
title: My Writing Process

text: His recipe for winning: accept that nobody is coming to rescue you, take responsibility for where you are, and be ready to sacrifice who you are now for who you want to become.
title: My Writing Process

text: He says the quickest route to confidence is building evidence: a stack of undeniable proof, made through so much volume that you stop doubting whether you can do it.
title: My Writing Process

text: When a paid channel is working and getting easier, that is the time to push harder. He suggests scaling it until something breaks rather than holding back.
title: Helping a $7M Foundation Company Pick Its Lane

text: With a 30 percent close rate, he says that is fine. Rather than working to push closing to 50 percent, increasing lead volume from 10 to 20 is the simpler lever, though both can be done.
title: Helping a $7M Foundation Company Pick Its Lane

text: He would build demand on the strong side of the business so it creates a supply constraint, letting him backfill it with good staff from the shrinking line instead of laying people off.
title: Helping a $7M Foundation Company Pick Its Lane

text: Beyond closing the same buyers, look at whether they could be closed at a bigger price or in a different combination, which he finds more exciting.
title: Helping a $7M Foundation Company Pick Its Lane

text: If every buyer told at least one other person about the product, advertising would never be needed again, so he argues you should put heavy emphasis on making the product good enough that customers refer others.
title: How to Get More Customers Without Ever Spending More on Advertising

text: He says people over-invest in logo, colors and website when the bigger return comes from making the product so good that people want it and tell friends after consuming it.
title: How to Get More Customers Without Ever Spending More on Advertising

text: He values brand because you build it once and use it many times. He cites early work on Alpha Brain that still pays dividends as a high-leverage activity.
title: How to Get More Customers Without Ever Spending More on Advertising

text: He says the rush to make money tomorrow kills most people. As much as possible, balance short-term needs with solving a problem for good so you can move on rather than fighting monthly.
title: How to Get More Customers Without Ever Spending More on Advertising

text: Only four things let others know about your stuff: reach out to friends one-on-one, reach out to strangers one-on-one, post content publicly, or run paid ads. If you do none, you will not make more money.
title: How to Get More Customers Without Ever Spending More on Advertising

text: More leverage comes from getting others to do the Core Four for you. First option: customers tell friends, strangers and their audience through posts, reviews and testimonials.
title: How to Get More Customers Without Ever Spending More on Advertising

text: Employees can do the Core Four for you, for example handling outreach or editing and distributing videos you record, so you get more output for the same input.
title: How to Get More Customers Without Ever Spending More on Advertising

text: You can hire an agency to make content, run ads, or do cold outbound on your behalf.
title: How to Get More Customers Without Ever Spending More on Advertising

text: Affiliates are businesses or influencers who already hold your customers' attention. Make a sensible deal with them, and treat a friend with a following as a stranger; if the deal still works, both benefit.
title: How to Get More Customers Without Ever Spending More on Advertising

text: Use the Core Four to recruit employees, affiliates, agencies and customers; those customers then use the Core Four to bring more customers, forming a repeating cycle.
title: How to Get More Customers Without Ever Spending More on Advertising

text: Start a fresh chat for each new unrelated topic rather than one endless conversation.
title: Get RICH in the A.I. Revolution (2026)

text: Providing more iterations and feedback within one chat makes later outputs better; the fourth answer in a string will beat the first, because context builds up.
title: Get RICH in the A.I. Revolution (2026)

text: Double-check numbers and cited studies in AI outputs, since hallucinations are minimized but not eliminated.
title: Get RICH in the A.I. Revolution (2026)

text: Decision-making stays with you; you cannot outsource thinking. Use AI to outsource the typing, since judgment and taste still get rewarded.
title: Get RICH in the A.I. Revolution (2026)

text: The idea is still the alpha: for content, sales messages or offers, the highest returns come from the idea, not the collateral that executes it.
title: Get RICH in the A.I. Revolution (2026)

text: A prompt is the same as an SOP, a standard operating procedure for getting an output. Most people's prompts are too short, like handing an employee work with one sentence.
title: Get RICH in the A.I. Revolution (2026)

text: Create standardized prompts for repeated work in a dedicated SOP prompts folder. If unsure what repeats, run a time study using 15-minute slots across a week.
title: Get RICH in the A.I. Revolution (2026)

text: Store prompts in a master doc with tabs or folders, often one tab per task in a role. Solo workers can embed the prompt in a repeating calendar block.
title: Get RICH in the A.I. Revolution (2026)

text: Train the team on specific SOP prompts instead of telling them to just use AI. Prompts are SOPs 2.0, and if you do a task repeatedly, do it right once and replicate.
title: Get RICH in the A.I. Revolution (2026)

text: Update a prompt when it stops producing good outputs.
title: Get RICH in the A.I. Revolution (2026)

text: Past work is data. Build a data sources folder organized by function, such as exported tweets, so AI can create more work like what you already did.
title: Get RICH in the A.I. Revolution (2026)

text: AI sounds like a melting pot of the internet, or like us with no personality. Give it your past work and tell it to sound like that, and it pattern matches.
title: Get RICH in the A.I. Revolution (2026)

text: Three things produce strong outputs: complete business context, high-quality curated data showing what right looks like, and clear detailed instructions. Higher quality sources yield better pattern matching.
title: Get RICH in the A.I. Revolution (2026)

text: He uses AI for structure and ideation, having it prompt him with interesting things to respond to rather than telling him what to say. Memos went from about four hours to about one.
title: Get RICH in the A.I. Revolution (2026)

text: Paste transcripts of about ten successful sales calls for the same offer and use a prompt to extract one unified script from what moves the sale forward.
title: Get RICH in the A.I. Revolution (2026)

text: Good prompts have four parts: role, task, rules and output format. For newsletters, analyze past winners, build a template, then generate new ones from a new topic idea you supply.
title: Get RICH in the A.I. Revolution (2026)

text: Upload failed sales transcripts and have AI identify primary and secondary objections, write short handling lines, and build a top-10 objection playbook with root causes.
title: Get RICH in the A.I. Revolution (2026)

text: He uses several LLMs, and prefers one for business strategy, offers, pricing and sales process questions because he thinks it draws on more business-relevant context.
title: Get RICH in the A.I. Revolution (2026)

text: Copy two or three YouTube transcripts from the see transcript button, separate them with clear delimiters, and have AI build a script template from videos you like.
title: Get RICH in the A.I. Revolution (2026)

text: Feed transcripts and existing assets into a prompt to build a lead magnet using the tone and structure of content you like, with new original content.
title: Get RICH in the A.I. Revolution (2026)

text: An offer architect prompt analyzes your current offer (promise, mechanism, pricing, guarantees, bonuses) then builds a more irresistible version with pricing architecture and optional upsells and downsells.
title: Get RICH in the A.I. Revolution (2026)

text: Hormozi says nearly every franchising problem can be solved by focusing on one North Star metric: unit economics. The restaurant itself has to be fixed first.
title: How to Sell More Franchises (Without Selling Them)

text: He says that if a franchise offer showed a low opening cost and very high first-year profit, selling franchises would not be a problem. Weak sales suggest the offer is not compelling.
title: How to Sell More Franchises (Without Selling Them)
