text: The longer the prompt, the shorter and more precise the output; short prompts get long answers because the AI lacks context and hedges. Give more context to narrow it.
title: How to use AI to grow your business

text: Chain prompts by pasting one output as the next input: offer architect output feeds sales page copy, then call script, then VSL, letting you build a whole marketing set.
title: How to use AI to grow your business

text: Three wheels make AI work better: full business context, strong prompts with clear instructions, and a data source to pull from.
title: How to use AI to grow your business

text: Everyone should be able to 10x output while keeping quality. Use AI as a workhorse, not to make decisions; the value is in idea, story and experience, so document what you do.
title: How to use AI to grow your business

text: There is no single universal step-by-step path from 1 million to 10 million, because every business is different and the thing that limits growth varies, for example software versus a restaurant, home services or a gym.
title: The only way to grow your business

text: Businesses grow only by getting more customers or by making each customer worth more: sell more units, or make the units worth more. So the key question is why the company cannot do that yet.
title: The only way to grow your business

text: The constraint differs by business type. A restaurant may be capped by its physical space unless it adds locations, a home services company may need more trucks, and a gym may need more marketing.
title: The only way to grow your business

text: Revenue level matters much less than the constraint. His scaling roadmaps use generalized buckets, but mostly the question is what stops the company from doing the growth activity.
title: The only way to grow your business

text: Human limits at points like growing from 10 to 100 people are predictable, and he thinks AI, by giving much more return per unit of human capital, will make operational scaling concerns mostly fade.
title: The only way to grow your business

text: To go from 10 million to 100 million, identify your constraint, focus on it, and ignore everything that is not the constraint.
title: The only way to grow your business

text: He says a good financing partner typically brings around a 30% revenue lift, across the board, especially in high-ticket offers, and health businesses have many lenders to choose from.
title: We raised prices 4 times and still can't grow

text: He argues that selling packages above 2K with no VSL and no financing in place likely means there is still room to raise prices.
title: We raised prices 4 times and still can't grow

text: He argues that a 95% close rate, with buyers in acute pain and sales systems not fully built, likely means the business could at least double its price.
title: We raised prices 4 times and still can't grow

text: A decoy offer works by pricing a premium short program high, then giving it free to anyone who joins a membership. Buyers can pay upfront or get it free with continuity, and he says goodwill on it is strong.
title: We raised prices 4 times and still can't grow

text: His testing found a 50/50 split between one-time buyers and members when the one-time price sits about 30% above the recurring price. Raise the gap in 10% steps to push more people into membership.
title: We raised prices 4 times and still can't grow

text: He suggests pairing the decoy-plus-membership offer with a waived fee: if a member cancels before a set period, they owe the fee.
title: We raised prices 4 times and still can't grow

text: Gym ownership can make money only if you love small business ownership and are truly in love with the product and experience. He calls it a limited opportunity vehicle, though it teaches you to do everything.
title: How I Scaled My First Gyms

text: He thinks fitness is a strong place to learn selling, because you talk to 10 to 20 people a day and get repetition after repetition.
title: How I Scaled My First Gyms

text: Gyms are all-service businesses, so they carry lots of headcount for very low revenue.
title: How I Scaled My First Gyms

text: With the turnkey sales model, he had a third of the employees while making four times the revenue compared with the same headcount before.
title: How I Scaled My First Gyms

text: Moving from turnkey to the licensing model, he went from eight employees to about 30 in the first year, doing about 7 million, then 26 million the next year.
title: How I Scaled My First Gyms

text: Turnkey meant the gym owners did nothing: he flew out, ran the marketing, spent the ad money, worked the leads and did the sales, then handed them customers.
title: How I Scaled My First Gyms

text: In the turnkey arrangement, owners paid him nothing upfront or as a percentage. He kept 100% of the cash he collected, while the owners kept the recurring revenue.
title: How I Scaled My First Gyms

text: He believes an audience has an endless appetite for value and almost none for fluff or waste, so content should be packed with value.
title: You need to post more

text: Each post reaches only about 1 to 2% of an audience, so publishing more posts gives you more separate 1 to 2% slices who see your content.
title: You need to post more

text: Posts with a direct call to action get their reach hammered compared with pure value posts, so the visible audience shrinks sharply.
title: You need to post more

text: A CTA is not fatal; what matters is how long it is relative to the length of the post. A six-second CTA he called long.
title: You need to post more

text: Rotate the lead magnets in your CTAs constantly, because people who already grabbed an offer have no reason to respond to it again.
title: You need to post more

text: Hormozi says the bar for excellence is very low because most competitors quit at the first sign of difficulty, having never experienced what hard feels like. If something is hard for you, it is hard for everyone, so simply trying beats most people.
title: The #1 Thing That Separates You From 99% of Your Competition

text: He notes that successful people mostly share consistency, and it cannot be seen in a snapshot, sound bite or reel. He thinks such lessons need large amounts of exposure to absorb, and trying is one of them.
title: The #1 Thing That Separates You From 99% of Your Competition

text: People who now work near him often tell him they had not grasped how much he works and that he does not stop.
title: The #1 Thing That Separates You From 99% of Your Competition

text: A mentor asked his partner whether she was settling or moving mountains over a house they failed to get. For Hormozi it became a vivid test of whether you truly tried or did everything possible to make it happen.
title: The #1 Thing That Separates You From 99% of Your Competition

text: He argues that people limit their idea of effort because they never considered trading far more for a goal. Occasional searches and a few hours of videos weekly are not trying; if you cannot count your repetitions in the hundreds, it is not trying.
title: The #1 Thing That Separates You From 99% of Your Competition

text: Trades you refuse to make mean you choose not to move that mountain, which he says is perfectly acceptable. Imagining extreme options for the house, like offering an extra $20 million, showed him his own limits.
title: The #1 Thing That Separates You From 99% of Your Competition

text: Hormozi defines learning as new behavior under the same condition. If you face the same situation and keep acting the same way, and get the same result, you have not learned anything.
title: What is Learning?

text: He defines intelligence as rate of learning, meaning how fast someone changes behavior. A person who stays in the same conditions and does not change behavior is not that smart, however smart others think they are.
title: What is Learning?

text: If you keep losing to the same challenge and do not change your approach, he says the fault lies with you, not the game or the challenge.
title: What is Learning?

text: When he asks entrepreneur audiences who works all day and who has been stuck at the same revenue for six months or more, mostly the same hands stay up. His verdict is they are doing the wrong things.
title: What is Learning?

text: If you put in all your inputs and outputs have not changed, you have the same condition and behavior, so you learned nothing. Moving up in career or business should show as changed behavior.
title: What is Learning?

text: Exposure to information is not learning. Whatever you are struggling with, someone else has already faced and solved it.
title: What is Learning?

text: He is investing heavily in media, and the building will hold many studios and sets so his team can produce content at higher quality and higher frequency.
title: Why I Bought the UFC Headquarters

text: His public brand has grown from only about half a day of filming every week or two; the rest is a team that cuts, distributes and repurposes content. He now wants to put more input into that machine.
title: Why I Bought the UFC Headquarters

text: He finds it notable that Dave Ramsey sells courses, coaching, events and an app, the typical guru mix, yet avoids being seen as a scam and runs a business of about 300 million dollars a year.
title: Why I Bought the UFC Headquarters

text: His first Ramsey takeaway: the promise is believable and hard to dispute, because spending less leaves more money over, unlike typical promises to help people earn extra money.
title: Why I Bought the UFC Headquarters

text: His second Ramsey takeaway: Ramsey puts brand and reputation first. Media is his largest revenue slice, reportedly about 10 million a month, since he builds goodwill instead of hammering the audience with hard sells.
title: Why I Bought the UFC Headquarters

text: Bonus lessons: Ramsey's company runs an event every week, and Ramsey spends about 20 hours a week making content, as PBD reportedly also does. Hormozi's own hours are significantly lower, which inspired him to do more.
title: Why I Bought the UFC Headquarters

text: Having worked remotely most of his career, he believes teaching, upskilling the team and influencing culture at scale are much faster in person, and he expects faster execution.
title: Why I Bought the UFC Headquarters

text: His office aim is an environment so rewarding that people choose to come often, without rules on hours or days, since the company was remote before.
title: Why I Bought the UFC Headquarters

text: He is now strongly pro-office and expects to record content while working out at the new gym, giving him extra reasons to train.
title: Why I Bought the UFC Headquarters

text: His mission is to document and share best practices for building wonderful businesses. He says the wealth he accumulates is irrelevant once he dies, and he regrets that figures like Elon, Bezos and Buffett wrote no books.
title: The Mission for My Life

text: He treats his businesses as support for his books and lessons: they give credibility and real stories to drive fundamental truths home, and they let him discover those truths as he goes.
title: The Mission for My Life

text: He is horrified by some things he said five years ago and believed true. He still shares what he currently thinks is least wrong, because the only alternative is silence, and he expects to refine it later.
title: The Mission for My Life

text: After selling his company, he took a year off with nightly five-star dinners for seven months, a temporary move to Vegas and lots of travel. It felt pretty empty, though the rest felt good.
title: The Mission for My Life

text: The first six months after the sale he needed to decompress. About a year after selling, he says he is ready for war again.
title: The Mission for My Life

text: He thinks people need breaks from being in the trenches. He suggests framing a break as a shift in thinking, from dirt to clouds, which he still sees as high-leverage output of a different type.
title: The Mission for My Life

text: He thinks in entrepreneurial seasons of roughly five years each and is in his fourth. He estimates about three years to see something through and two more to transition, realize or monetize it.
title: The Mission for My Life

text: If you already follow the basics, such as calling leads immediately and repeatedly, and show rates still do not improve, the cause is usually something that happens before scheduling.
title: Our Close Rate Is Insane But Nobody Shows Up

text: Removing too much friction makes booking so easy that total shows fall. Booking counts are a vanity metric; only who shows up matters, so it can be worth paying more per booking to raise show rate.
title: Our Close Rate Is Insane But Nobody Shows Up

text: Example math he gives: if cost per booking doubles but show rate goes from 20% to 60%, shows triple, so cost per show rises only about 50%.
title: Our Close Rate Is Insane But Nobody Shows Up

text: A VSL should run roughly five to seven minutes and open with promise, plan and proof. Then it walks through four beliefs, each with what they believe, why it is wrong, what is right, and proof, giving 16 pieces, then a call to action.
title: Our Close Rate Is Insane But Nobody Shows Up

text: When a prospect responds to the call to action, personalize the roadmap you show them so they see you did work in advance. This makes the question of whether they will show up fade.
title: Our Close Rate Is Insane But Nobody Shows Up

text: Hormozi recalls his grandfather, who was very close to him and died ten years earlier, telling him that a person has two hands and one brain and should use them.
title: \"Can You Outrun Your Problems by Working?\"

text: Hormozi says that if you are not putting your hands and brain to work, you are probably living in someone else's game rather than your own.
title: \"Can You Outrun Your Problems by Working?\"

text: Cheap early customer acquisition can mislead. Only after a while do you learn whether that customer type is a headache with poor lifetime value, so wait for LTV to CAC data before judging a new market.
title: Why You Can't Run Two Businesses at Once

text: If the new business's lifetime value turns out similar to the existing one, it may make sense to sunset the old business, stop selling to those customers, and move fully to the new one.
title: Why You Can't Run Two Businesses at Once

text: He thinks it is unwise to serve two entirely different avatars in one business.
title: Why You Can't Run Two Businesses at Once

text: Reaching a much bigger revenue goal requires paying a price: giving up much of the small business you have today. If you are willing to pay it, the decision is easy.
title: Why You Can't Run Two Businesses at Once

text: He favors a blend: charge more upfront as a one-time setup fee, while keeping ownership of the client relationship and earning recurring monthly revenue on the backend through continuity.
title: Charge 6K Upfront, Then $1K Forever (Here's How)

text: He suggests selling to businesses that already have something working, so the pitch is helping them make more, rather than helping them go from zero to one.
title: Charge 6K Upfront, Then $1K Forever (Here's How)

text: When unsure what to say in marketing, describe the offer in the simplest possible terms: what exactly you will do for the customer.
title: Charge 6K Upfront, Then $1K Forever (Here's How)

text: He would pair ad copy with a replacement promise, plus a set of around twenty real customers who used the service, as proof.
title: Charge 6K Upfront, Then $1K Forever (Here's How)

text: Set a regular promotion cadence with community owners, such as twice a year, and show each group results only from members of that same group, since those testimonials are most relevant and convert strongly.
title: Charge 6K Upfront, Then $1K Forever (Here's How)

text: Two levels of testimonials are needed: proof that other community owners earned money from partnering, to win partners, and proof of delivered work for each partner's customers.
title: Charge 6K Upfront, Then $1K Forever (Here's How)

text: For outreach to community owners, warm or mutual introductions are significantly more effective than cold contact, and giving the introducer a slice of the deal is fine when recurring revenue matters more than upfront.
title: Charge 6K Upfront, Then $1K Forever (Here's How)

text: After sequencing capacity work first, he stresses volume of outreach and not changing the offer repeatedly; stick with what you are already doing.
title: Charge 6K Upfront, Then $1K Forever (Here's How)

text: When staff keep leaving, Hormozi says to trace the problem back: low pay comes from low prices, and low prices come from a weak sales process, so fix sales first.
title: Scale Any Business With These 3 Levers

text: He notes that inbound lead conversion can be improved to around 50 percent, even though a 30 percent close rate was fine for the discussion.
title: Scale Any Business With These 3 Levers

text: Gyms with strong returns on ad spend often spent only enough to cover fixed costs and never got profitable, playing business on defense instead of offense. Hormozi says this is a classic mistake.
title: Scale Any Business With These 3 Levers

text: If first-30-day gross profit on a new customer exceeds what it cost to acquire them, the acquisition pays for itself, so you can keep spending more on ads without needing outside cash.
title: Scale Any Business With These 3 Levers

text: Pay a trainer a bonus for getting a new hire road-ready faster, and make the trainer certify the trainee's work for the following month, fixing errors unpaid.
title: Scale Any Business With These 3 Levers

text: When a business is small and unknown, the core problem is irrelevance: nobody knows it exists. The fix is simply to advertise more, and he says this is the whole leads playbook from A to Z.
title: You're Spending Zero Hours Advertising. That's Why You're Broke.

text: He counts content creation as advertising and asks owners how many hours per day they spend on it; he implies that one reel a day does not amount to three or four hours of real advertising effort.
title: You're Spending Zero Hours Advertising. That's Why You're Broke.

text: First level of advertising advice: post everything cross-platform, so each reel also goes to TikTok, YouTube Shorts, Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn video and X, since he says video is growing on those.
title: You're Spending Zero Hours Advertising. That's Why You're Broke.

text: Being genuinely excellent at any task makes a person interesting, because learning someone is a top performer in a field changes how others see them. His advice: get really good, then keep improving.
title: You Need to Be Exceptional

text: Standing out usually comes from combining several distinct traits rather than one. A strong track record becomes more compelling when paired with a unique story, limited working hours, and a humble, student-minded attitude.
title: You Need to Be Exceptional

text: Being warm, humble and curious about others, even when you are outperforming them, is a big reason people like you. He treats this as the biggest factor on top of a strong track record.
title: You Need to Be Exceptional

text: When an e-commerce owner already has supply sorted, what remains is mostly media buying and brand building. With the right person, he says a business can grow from three million to six in about 60 days.
title: How to Scale a $3M Sports Memorabilia Business to $10M

text: He says e-commerce scales easily, which is why many people like it, but the issue that then appears is cash flow.
title: How to Scale a $3M Sports Memorabilia Business to $10M

text: If you lack media buying skill, either learn it yourself or bring in a strong media buyer, possibly giving up a few points of equity so you do not hand over the whole margin.
title: How to Scale a $3M Sports Memorabilia Business to $10M

text: Sequence for an e-commerce owner strong on product: first get a media person to drive sales and revenue, then learn branding to become a household name in the niche.
title: How to Scale a $3M Sports Memorabilia Business to $10M

text: In a cleaning business, winning and keeping customers is not the hard part. Delivering the work, meaning the talent side, is the real constraint.
title: Most Cleaning Businesses Fail Because of This

text: One model that has worked for cleaning: show staff a career path with many levels, alternating a new title and a pay raise at each step, with new skills required to unlock each one.
title: Most Cleaning Businesses Fail Because of This

text: He saw a nail salon chain with about eight levels that took high school dropouts who could not read up to roughly 70,000 dollars a year.
title: Most Cleaning Businesses Fail Because of This

text: If pay is a percentage of revenue, start people low and let them unlock about 5% at a time, tied to keeping their customers, possibly with quotas.
title: Most Cleaning Businesses Fail Because of This

text: Another model he liked was fully centralized: the company handled all sales and paid cleaners a flat amount per clean, with a free redo if the customer called back over a poor job.
title: Most Cleaning Businesses Fail Because of This

text: In that centralized model, cleaners were paid about 50 dollars for a job billed near 200, and team output reportedly tripled because they worked faster to earn per clean.
title: Most Cleaning Businesses Fail Because of This

text: Simple tasks needing little skill can improve hugely when incentives are set right, similar to UPS and FedEx.
title: Most Cleaning Businesses Fail Because of This

text: If you change nothing else, make the rev share tiered. Once people hear a maximum earning figure, they assume they will reach it and will work for years toward it, as in network marketing or investment banking.
title: Most Cleaning Businesses Fail Because of This

text: Hormozi says a business with a recurring product, like extensions that customers rebuy every several weeks, is not necessarily unsellable. In his view the main need is simply more customers.
title: “I’m in E-Commerce. Should I Build a Software Product?”

text: He warns that hitting a problem you cannot solve and then looking for a greener pasture in another business is a trap. The new field will have its own, often bigger, problems.
title: “I’m in E-Commerce. Should I Build a Software Product?”

text: Hormozi argues an existing business is usually calmer and far more cash flow positive than a software venture, which he says may bring no profit for many years, if ever.
title: “I’m in E-Commerce. Should I Build a Software Product?”

text: Hormozi says the biggest solar sales businesses are really recruiting businesses, so the business you are actually in is recruiting people to sell.
title: You're Not in the Business You Think You're In

text: He suggests tracking cost of acquiring talent against lifetime gross profit per employee. For a sales rep, treat the rep like a recurring customer who becomes a revenue-generating node for the company.
title: You're Not in the Business You Think You're In

text: New sales hires drop off heavily in the first week or two, then again around day 30. Those who get past day 90 tend to stay long term, so he frames retention around those milestones.
title: You're Not in the Business You Think You're In

text: To fill a recruiting-limited sales team, he says you need many more people entering at the front end, described as kissing more toads.
title: You're Not in the Business You Think You're In

text: He argues sales training should be reduced to concrete behaviors, such as what you do with arms, mouth and head, because salespeople lean on mysticism and make-believe when they train.
title: You're Not in the Business You Think You're In

text: Role plays should simulate the real selling environment, such as actually knocking on doors, as closely as possible.
title: You're Not in the Business You Think You're In

text: Hormozi says a business is limited by its ability to attract talent.
title: “My Best Store Is Dying and My Team Blames the Economy”

text: The longer he has been in business, the lower his tolerance for weak performance has become and the higher his bar for excellence. He feels the best talent is always still ahead of him.
title: “My Best Store Is Dying and My Team Blames the Economy”

text: Looking back, he finds his team from three years earlier was always weaker than his current team, and he expects to feel the same about today's team three years from now.
title: “My Best Store Is Dying and My Team Blames the Economy”

text: He says the hiring bar should only move one direction, and he suggests that accepting mediocrity may be what limits a business.
title: “My Best Store Is Dying and My Team Blames the Economy”

text: Even in a store selling mostly products, the store's culture is set by its leader, meaning whatever effort that person treats as good enough.
title: “My Best Store Is Dying and My Team Blames the Economy”

text: When hiring now, he wants to feel pulled toward a candidate, not driven by pain. He keeps a reminder on his computer to want the person, not merely relief from lacking someone.
title: “My Best Store Is Dying and My Team Blames the Economy”

text: Rewards work best when they arrive quickly. Speed of payoff drives habit more than size. He compares phone addiction to fast feedback, and suggests paying a small amount right at the end of the session instead of one monthly bonus.
title: Why Your Team Isn't Doing What You Ask

text: Once the behavior takes hold with immediate rewards, you can stretch reinforcement out by paying every other time, which is how he says addiction works.
title: Why Your Team Isn't Doing What You Ask

text: When staff avoid a task, he guesses there is a social cost. The fix is to make the task easier for them instead of demanding they push through it.
title: Why Your Team Isn't Doing What You Ask

text: He prefers building a required task into the standard process, with steps that must be checked off before a customer can be signed out, rather than relying on extra incentives.
title: Why Your Team Isn't Doing What You Ask

text: To make a bonus tied to work actually motivate, tell the team the money will go to a new hire if the work isn't done, giving 30 days to fix it. Make it collective: if one person fails, nobody gets it.
title: Why Your Team Isn't Doing What You Ask

text: Qualities that make someone a fantastic operator in business and career can be counterproductive at home, at the kitchen table. He summarizes it as being praised publicly and paying privately.
title: The Hidden Cost of Being a Great Operator

text: He thinks monomaniacal people often get much further because they avoid the mental cost of constantly managing trade-offs between competing priorities.
title: The Hidden Cost of Being a Great Operator

text: He thinks it is almost impossible to make big progress without going all-out on one thing for an extended period, which he puts at about 10 years. How extreme depends on the phase you are in.
title: The Hidden Cost of Being a Great Operator

text: Half measures do not produce half results; they produce nothing. Many people split effort across four domains, work constantly, and get no outcome in any of them.
title: The Hidden Cost of Being a Great Operator

text: You must be willing to admit you want one thing more than another and sacrifice something, not forever but for now, rather than compromise on everything.
title: The Hidden Cost of Being a Great Operator

text: People believe inaction is free, but it has a cost, usually a higher one. He cites the idea that wealth loves speed and poverty loves indecision.
title: The Hidden Cost of Being a Great Operator

text: Most outcomes people truly want arrive after a delay, which makes them worth wanting but also hard to get. He frames daily behavior as voting for the outcome you want.
title: The Hidden Cost of Being a Great Operator

text: On most days he spends roughly 5am to 1pm on his own projects, then holds meetings from about 1pm to 4:30pm, and finishes with the gym and eating.
title: My Actual Daily Schedule

text: He believes in simply starting and letting the way forward become clear as you go. His early videos were rough because he began without a media team.
title: My Actual Daily Schedule

text: Early on he simply recorded videos and dropped them in a shared folder for others to upload. He kept that routine for around 6 to 9 months before hiring someone to film properly.
title: My Actual Daily Schedule

text: Better audio, better video and more happening on screen have made his newer videos perform better by objective measures, and the extra help did not cost him more time.
title: My Actual Daily Schedule

text: His aim is to make his content available to everyone, including people with short attention spans, so he adapts the format instead of complaining that attention spans have shrunk.
title: My Actual Daily Schedule

text: He argues that a lot can be covered in 60 seconds if you truly know your subject.
title: My Actual Daily Schedule

text: He describes people who do M&A as a core competency: they take a platform company, leave its business largely alone, add five to ten tuck-in acquisitions, and their operational skill is mainly integrating those businesses.
title: \"Should I Buy Growth or Build It?\"

text: He says Acquisition.com drives above-baseline results almost entirely through organic growth rather than acquisition.
title: \"Should I Buy Growth or Build It?\"

text: For a strategic choice, he suggests asking which problem you would rather have. Spelling out the problems each path brings helps you pay down ignorance tax, so play each option out.
title: \"Should I Buy Growth or Build It?\"

text: Growing by acquisition brings problems: finding deal flow, finding motivated sellers willing to accept your price, raising capital through credit relationships or a fund, or sharing a holding company with many owners.
title: \"Should I Buy Growth or Build It?\"

text: Organic growth has its own problems, such as regional caps on local market size, solved by expanding to a new market with a team or lead gen, and improving operational efficiency for more EBITDA per revenue dollar.
title: \"Should I Buy Growth or Build It?\"

text: His rule for choosing a path: list the problems of each option, then pick the path whose problems you feel best equipped to solve with your skills and resources.
title: \"Should I Buy Growth or Build It?\"

text: He thinks work-life balance depends on the season of life, and he holds no shoulds: people can do whatever they want.
title: How I Think About Work Life Balance

text: He frames income percentiles as a room of people: a top 1% income in the US, around $600,000 a year, means being number one among 100 people. Top 0.1%, a few million a year, means beating 1,000.
title: How I Think About Work Life Balance

text: Earning around $10 million a year means being the best among roughly 11,000 people, about a third of a stadium. He asks whether it makes sense to behave and spend time like everyone else at that level.
title: How I Think About Work Life Balance

text: He observed that people criticized him for working so hard when he had no money, and criticized him for it again after he had money.
title: How I Think About Work Life Balance

text: Outbound is among the hardest channels to scale because it targets the most valuable attention and that attention is the most protected. The most effective methods are legally restricted, so outreach is deliberately handicapped.
title: How to Scale Your Outbound System

text: In outbound, the goal is only to approximate a real person reaching out to someone. Achieving that takes a lot of technology and legal skirting, just to get an offer texted to someone and read.
title: How to Scale Your Outbound System

text: Timing for outbound has no specific revenue band. It follows the same logic as scaling anything: pick the channel with the highest risk-adjusted return on the resources put in, whether outbound, ads, content or affiliates.
title: How to Scale Your Outbound System

text: He estimates risk-adjusted return using three variables: what could happen, his confidence level in that outcome, and the resources required. He then puts attention on whatever yields the highest result.
title: How to Scale Your Outbound System

text: When choosing a vendor or path, someone who has repeatedly taken clients from a similar starting point to the desired goal earns higher confidence. He will pay more for that confidence because the risk-adjusted return can still be higher.
title: How to Scale Your Outbound System

text: For B2B sellers, price can be reframed: the question is not whether you cost more or less but the risk-adjusted return. A cheaper provider is less likely to help hit the goal, making it the riskier choice.
title: How to Scale Your Outbound System

text: If a service is cheap enough that a third party covers the bill, he considers it wildly underpriced, especially when the client earns the fee back through the margin on the extra sales it produces.
title: He's Charging $7K. I'd Charge $22K

text: To get clients who ignore your guidance to actually do the work, he suggests charging them. He implies that a fee of a few thousand is so small it feels free, so payment itself starts the commitment.
title: He's Charging $7K. I'd Charge $22K

text: He says an avatar that gets credit easily and is used to borrowing for things that do not pay back right away is a strong fit for high prices.
title: He's Charging $7K. I'd Charge $22K

text: Hormozi says a weak close rate calls for building a sales motion: a VSL, a set qualification, a pre-frame before the close call, and a training cadence so the sales team follows the process.
title: Helping a Marketing Agency Get to $20M/Year

text: He says testing the VSL parts lets you iterate on the process, shortening sales cycles and raising close rates. Pulling calls forward means fewer calls on the back end, which raises sales team utilization.
title: Helping a Marketing Agency Get to $20M/Year

text: He says fewer salespeople closing more deals lets you attract even better salespeople, making a virtuous loop instead of a vicious one.
title: Helping a Marketing Agency Get to $20M/Year

text: If you want more legitimate investors, he thinks it is largely a branding and messaging issue: speaking in language that sounds less legit attracts less legit people, so talk like a fund.
title: Helping a Fund Manager Attract Real Investors

text: To check whether your brand looks legitimate, review your site, Instagram, Facebook and YouTube, and compare them with the content other fund managers in your space put out.
title: Helping a Fund Manager Attract Real Investors

text: He strongly recommends X and LinkedIn for reaching accredited investors, calling them a goldmine for quality of people, with money Twitter packed.
title: Helping a Fund Manager Attract Real Investors

text: A show rate near 1% among people who bought suggests something in the funnel is disjointed. He names possible causes: the wrong people are buying, or the offer does not match what the call is about.
title: They'll Pay You and Still Not Show Up

text: He rejects the idea that a niche is too busy to attend calls. He says every entrepreneur is busy, and that an avatar is not special in that way.
title: They'll Pay You and Still Not Show Up

text: Whatever a customer just bought, the scheduling page should match it as closely as possible. The new product can be introduced on the sales call itself.
title: They'll Pay You and Still Not Show Up

text: Customers who already bought should show up better than cold leads. If a company gets very low attendance from buyers, he suspects missing reminders, integration failures or time zone errors.
title: They'll Pay You and Still Not Show Up

text: Outbound dialing buyers can replace the scheduler: when they pick up the phone, that call is the meeting. He suggests offering to set them up with a specialist at a time that suits them.
title: They'll Pay You and Still Not Show Up

text: He says he studied a company doing the same thing as the caller, and it had normal metrics. So restaurant owners are not the problem; the funnel is what is broken.
title: They'll Pay You and Still Not Show Up

text: Keep doing whatever filled the free community, on a regular schedule. Block the first two to four hours of each day for promotion, then use the back half of the day for delivering.
title: When to Launch a Paid Community After Going Free First

text: Before opening a paid community, he would announce something coming in four to six weeks, share value meanwhile, and use that window to talk to members and learn what they want.
title: When to Launch a Paid Community After Going Free First

text: Use the research period to identify the two or three core deliverables, such as a newsletter and a weekly call, that members would find clearly worth paying for, and put those in the paid offer.
title: When to Launch a Paid Community After Going Free First

text: Practice the whisper to shout method in weekly webinars, add one extra post per week as the launch nears, and follow the book's countdown timer for raising frequency before opening the valve to sell.
title: When to Launch a Paid Community After Going Free First

text: After the paid community launches, use four conversion points: lead magnet into free group, then a weekly webinar, an onboarding call for everyone, and a module with a call to action, plus DMs and engagement.
title: When to Launch a Paid Community After Going Free First

text: Branding often pays off slowly. He made content for 3 years while asking nothing from people, and his brand became valuable, even though he considers himself still early.
title: Helping an E-Com Business Build a Brand

text: He was able to invest in brand for years because he had money coming in from elsewhere. Without that, he says it would have been much harder and would have cost him other opportunities.
title: Helping an E-Com Business Build a Brand

text: A business with an economic engine can fund a brand-building project. If the spending does not lead to more people discovering and buying, then the brand investment is not working.
title: Helping an E-Com Business Build a Brand

text: He points to Amazon's product page as the highest converting on the internet, built from a few images, a video, reviews and a handful of bullets, plus cross-sells. He cites roughly 4% conversion versus about 1 to 2% for typical e-commerce stores.
title: Your Sales Page Is Too Complicated

text: He says one-click purchase lifts conversion for Skool communities. If about 30% of community traffic comes from Skool itself, that share converts far better, which pulls the overall rate up and compounds as the platform grows.
title: Your Sales Page Is Too Complicated

text: Simple pages like Airbnb's let people decide quickly. Over time the platform earns more trust than any individual on it. His advice is to simplify the offer and run many tests until it converts, rather than building long landing pages.
title: Your Sales Page Is Too Complicated

text: In a short test he offered all three of his books physical for 15 dollars total, five per book. The page converted at 32% on click to purchase, across about 20,000 purchases, showing a killer offer still matters.
title: Your Sales Page Is Too Complicated

text: Each added bullet or bonus costs the prospect mental real estate to read, so it must be worth it. He believes buyers are single-issue buyers who read the page and then buy.
title: Your Sales Page Is Too Complicated

text: His razor for bullets: each one should, for the right buyer, be worth the whole price times two or three. Other things can be included in the community but not take up space in the pitch.
title: Your Sales Page Is Too Complicated

text: At a launch, each playbook, though 30 to 40 pages long, was shown with only three bullets. He values concision of words and, more so, of ideas: fewer bullets, each one made perfect.
title: Your Sales Page Is Too Complicated

text: Hormozi says the same work will be paid roughly ten times more if you sell to businesses in richer countries such as the UK, US or Australia, so sell outside your own zip code and out of their wallet, not yours.
title: You Don't Have to Be an Expert, Just Be a Facilitator

text: He says the original meaning of a mastermind was a round table where everyone is equal and shares what is working for them, and that internet marketing has distorted the term.
title: You Don't Have to Be an Expert, Just Be a Facilitator

text: He says if you are not an expert, do not pretend to be one; position yourself as a facilitator who asks the members what is working and what they struggle with, so they share and get to know each other.
title: You Don't Have to Be an Expert, Just Be a Facilitator

text: He thinks a facilitated call about once every other week would probably provide value, with the group chat available in between for members to talk to each other.
title: You Don't Have to Be an Expert, Just Be a Facilitator

text: He says a simple pitch is easy to understand: a group, two calls a month, and you set up their pages. Three things, and no need to overcomplicate it.
title: You Don't Have to Be an Expert, Just Be a Facilitator

text: When a business has a clear goal, he suggests narrowing to one question: how to get ten times the leads currently received, and ignoring everything else until that is answered.
title: Helping a Pilot Scale His Aviation Safety Business

text: He says that if the same result is delivered more conveniently, faster and on demand, a group format can be sold like a one-on-one, since the vehicle matters little to the buyer.
title: Helping a Pilot Scale His Aviation Safety Business

text: He states that when one-on-one delivery is maxed out, the fix is to change the delivery ratio and then advertise more; finding a supply constraint early makes the whole process quick.
title: Helping a Pilot Scale His Aviation Safety Business

text: Some entrepreneurial questions have no universal answer because they are entirely personal: how much risk to take, how much to invest versus spend now, and how long to push before pivoting.
title: The Framework I Use to Never Regret a Decision

text: For a decision like this, he likes the regret minimization approach: imagine yourself at 85 looking back, and ask whether you could accept failing and losing the working business just to say you took a shot.
title: The Framework I Use to Never Regret a Decision

text: Judge a risky bet by its worst-case outcome, not the best case, since the upside always sounds good. If you can live with the worst case, take the swing; if not, do not.
title: The Framework I Use to Never Regret a Decision

text: Using other people's money instead of your own does not remove the main risk of a second venture: you split your focus and likely damage the business that already works.
title: The Framework I Use to Never Regret a Decision

text: If you pursue the risky new venture, he says commit fully and accept giving up your comfortable lifestyle, because he thinks a split effort has a low chance of making it work.
title: The Framework I Use to Never Regret a Decision

text: Chasing an extreme growth jump in a very short window can backfire: every strategy tried fails because of the deadline, whereas the same target over ten years would almost surely be reached.
title: Your expectation of growth is stopping you from success

text: A sale has two parts: getting the yes and actually collecting the money. Closing a deal is not finished until payment is collected.
title: Your expectation of growth is stopping you from success

text: Industry-standard payment terms are not fixed. Being better than competitors can include offering different terms, and a buyer choosing between two contractors may pick the one they prefer even with slightly different terms.
title: Your expectation of growth is stopping you from success

text: He thinks that if you see your service as a commodity, you are missing the point; you should show how you differ from everyone else.
title: Your expectation of growth is stopping you from success

text: He believes cash flow problems from payment terms are mostly a sales issue rather than something else.
title: Your expectation of growth is stopping you from success

text: During a multi-day selling event, Hormozi says to sell the expensive option rather than the recurring one, even if you fear losing people who would have taken the smaller recurring plan.
title: The Real Math Behind a $27/Month Membership

text: Run two cart closes: first make the annual offer with its bonuses the only one available, then after it closes run a mop-up campaign for the monthly plan carrying fewer or none of those bonuses.
title: The Real Math Behind a $27/Month Membership

text: When people request monthly during the annual-only window, you can say monthly options exist but without the bonuses. Do not lie, but you may make the option you prefer they skip less convenient to buy.
title: The Real Math Behind a $27/Month Membership

text: He calculates true lifetime value by dividing the monthly price by the churn rate, for example $27 divided by 7% monthly churn.
title: The Real Math Behind a $27/Month Membership

text: Content algorithms still come down to people and what humans find interesting. If a content concept works in one country, you can build the local version of that same concept for another market.
title: I Worked 12-Hour Days for 2 Years and Made $30K

text: Being early in your business is the best time for a major change, because a business far along is much heavier to change. So aim big and get it right the first time.
title: I Worked 12-Hour Days for 2 Years and Made $30K

text: Two different avatars mean two different offerings, customers and businesses. You do not need two; pick the one you prefer to serve and there is plenty of demand within it.
title: I Worked 12-Hour Days for 2 Years and Made $30K

text: The real answer for organic growth is a very large amount of content, produced for an unending period of time. He calls it a gross, disgusting volume.
title: The Answer to Organic Growth Is Disgusting Volume

text: His learning loop: make about 100 pieces, review which did well, identify what set them apart, then add two points to the checklist for the next 100 videos. That is how his team keeps improving its content.
title: The Answer to Organic Growth Is Disgusting Volume

text: Creators commonly cycle between better and more: make many, notice a hit, spend more time on fewer pieces, get good at that, scale back up to more, and repeat. He calls this a normal cadence.
title: The Answer to Organic Growth Is Disgusting Volume

text: He says the belief that Instagram or TikTok cap useful posts per day is mythology, and advises not worrying about it. As an example, he cites a huge Bollywood account posting a hundred times a day and getting nine billion monthly views.
title: The Answer to Organic Growth Is Disgusting Volume

text: He used to space posts out carefully, but now says it does not matter. Platforms want to distribute content people find valuable, so the advice is to give them more to distribute and go heavy on input.
title: The Answer to Organic Growth Is Disgusting Volume

text: When explaining anything, he recommends using analogy only. It is imprecise, but it gets people to understand far better than technical or scientific explanations, which he says nobody cares about.
title: How to Communicate Clearly

text: Good content is declarative rather than procedural: talk about what is possible or what is wrong with an existing option, not the step-by-step of how to do something. Once content gets granular, you lose most of the audience, so stay conceptual.
title: How to Communicate Clearly

text: In training, teaching pattern matching is much faster than explaining how something works, and just as effective. Staff can run the playbook in the roughly 95% of cases that fit the pattern.
title: How to Communicate Clearly

text: For the roughly 5% of cases that break the pattern, people escalate to you, and you then create a new pattern and train them on it. Most of the time they need the protocol, not the underlying mechanism.
title: How to Communicate Clearly

text: Whoever stands behind the camera while you record tends to become the person you actually talk to, rather than your real audience. He says a crew of different ages and backgrounds would have made his content different.
title: Don’t Make This Mistake When You Record Content

text: He admits one mistake was speaking mostly to his own team and choosing examples relevant to them, because he wanted to help them and could see them nodding and taking notes.
title: Don’t Make This Mistake When You Record Content

text: He asks his team to react visibly while he films, since their faces give him a signal about what is interesting. Because his content is prompt driven rather than heavily scripted, those reactions steer where it goes.
title: Don’t Make This Mistake When You Record Content

text: He now does live streams to diversify his audience and see chat in real time, giving him a broader sense of who he is really addressing instead of the people in the room.
title: Don’t Make This Mistake When You Record Content

text: His earlier content was hardcore because he was effectively scolding his team through the camera, hoping they would listen, rather than speaking to them directly.
title: Don’t Make This Mistake When You Record Content

text: Podcast hosts saw his hardcore content and defined him by it, asking questions that assumed that persona. His answers then matched, creating a self-fulfilling loop that reinforced the image.
title: Don’t Make This Mistake When You Record Content

text: He expects to choose future podcasts that lean less toward red-pill masculinity themes. He says he is not in that world but sits near its edge, and thinks that image misrepresents him.
title: Don’t Make This Mistake When You Record Content

text: Hormozi generally prefers interruption-based advertising (such as Meta, YouTube, TikTok) over pay-per-click search advertising.
title: Helping a Solar Company Lower Its Customer Acquisition Cost

text: A benefit of PPC is that it needs little creative: once one high-converting search ad works, it can keep running unchanged, since new people with intent search for that solution every month.
title: Helping a Solar Company Lower Its Customer Acquisition Cost

text: A downside of PPC is that you compete with everyone else paying for the same search terms, so it becomes a lifetime value battle where whoever can spend more owns those terms.
title: Helping a Solar Company Lower Its Customer Acquisition Cost

text: Revenue can grow by converting more of the people who already know you, such as adding a phone sales team and raising price. This does not add awareness, so it stays capped by how many people know you.
title: \"I'm stuck at $3M/year in my coaching business.\"

text: The other route to more revenue is making better content that widens the pool of people aware of you, so a larger share of a bigger audience gets monetized.
title: \"I'm stuck at $3M/year in my coaching business.\"

text: Of a given follower count, only a small slice sees any post, and an even tinier slice sees the call to action, especially when the ask is harder and retention drops.
title: \"I'm stuck at $3M/year in my coaching business.\"

text: Paid ads reach people who consume your content through their interest graph without following you. They know who you are and might respond to an ad.
title: \"I'm stuck at $3M/year in my coaching business.\"

text: Ads, a sales team and price increases are one-time levers, pulled once. He says they might take a business from 3M to 10M, but at 10M the same growth problem returns.
title: \"I'm stuck at $3M/year in my coaching business.\"

text: After pulling those levers, the next question is whether to scale into colder traffic instead of retargeting the existing warm audience, whether to grow the warm audience, or both.
title: \"I'm stuck at $3M/year in my coaching business.\"

text: Starting a business always means taking on debt. The real choice is which kind: financial, management (hiring people underskilled for the opportunity), or technical (lacking infrastructure). He advises taking the kind that is easiest to repay fastest.
title: You Always Have Debt

text: If your goal is around 100,000, 500,000 or a million dollars a year, he thinks you can mostly do it owning all the equity and just developing skills.
title: You Always Have Debt

text: Below a million in revenue, everything comes down to marketing and sales, and product matters much less because you are too small for word of mouth to make a dent. He says this from a realist view.
title: You Always Have Debt

text: Over the longest time horizon, only the product matters: how good is what you give in exchange for money, and whether people feel they got the better end of the deal.
title: You Always Have Debt

text: He went from caring only about sales, to loving one-to-many marketing, to realizing it is a hamster wheel because nothing stacks.
title: You Always Have Debt

text: To build something big you need to be paid today for work done years ago. That requires a product past customers still use or speak well of; otherwise you hunt for revenue every month.
title: You Always Have Debt

text: His companies now hold off on marketing and sales spend until customers love the product and refer others every month. Only then do they add marketing and sales on top to build something really big.
title: You Always Have Debt

text: Start by reverse-engineering what the math must look like. He breaks a goal into days: a million a year is about 20,000 a week, roughly three grand a day.
title: You Always Have Debt

text: He invests using the simplest formula: units sold multiplied by lifetime value. To grow, either sell more units or make each customer worth more.
title: You Always Have Debt

text: Early on, review your calendar. Anything that does not bring more customers or make them worth more should stop. If working every hour isn't earning more, you are working on the wrong things.
title: You Always Have Debt

text: There are eight ways to let people know about your stuff, at any size. Four you do yourself and four use other people. The cheapest is telling people you know and asking whether they know anyone interested.
title: You Always Have Debt

text: Build one contact list from your phone contacts, old sent emails, and social followers and DM contacts. He says most people can reach at least a thousand people.
title: You Always Have Debt

text: He favors a violent approach to action: reach out to 100 people a day, taking about five hours. Being broke means time is your main asset to spend.
title: You Always Have Debt

text: The founder's job at the start is promotion, since nobody knows the business exists. He did his outreach around four or five in the morning, finishing near ten before starting his day.
title: You Always Have Debt

text: Hormozi separates deciding from committing. Committing only happens when you remove your other options; until then there is always an escape hatch, so many people who say they decided to quit or end something are not truly committed.
title: Have the Hard Conversation...

text: He finds that what stops him from deciding is usually fear of one particular person's judgment. Naming that person turns vague society-wide judgment into something concrete and easier to question.
title: Have the Hard Conversation...

text: At 19 he realized that blaming his parents handed them control over his life. Being disgusted that people he resented held that power pushed him to flip his narrative and take control.
title: Have the Hard Conversation...

text: He calls the time lost to an unmade decision its anxiety cost, similar to opportunity cost. Every moment spent thinking about it could be recovered by simply deciding, which he offers as a reason to do hard tasks early.
title: Have the Hard Conversation...

text: Using four decisions as an example, someone taking a week each needs a month, while someone deciding one per day finishes in four days. He says fast decision making explains how young people achieve so much.
title: Have the Hard Conversation...

text: Before leaving Baltimore he was much like the average person in risk tolerance, fear of failure and insecurity. He thinks he may have had more insecurity than most, and it drove him to do well because he cared what others thought.
title: Have the Hard Conversation...

text: He generally dislikes seed and idea-stage investing. He notes creators tend to be big idea people, so ideas are not their constraint; execution and business acumen are what they lack.
title: How I Scale Companies I Invest In

text: In a traditional creator deal he would probably not get majority control or ownership, which he thinks makes it very high risk, so he likely would not take that kind of deal.
title: How I Scale Companies I Invest In

text: He would consider an incubation deal where the creator owns about 20% and his side owns 80% and funds everything, but only if it proved to add more alpha than his existing deal flow, which he doubts.
title: How I Scale Companies I Invest In

text: He says investing in a large established creator company is not really investing; he describes it as a joint venture.
title: How I Scale Companies I Invest In

text: A skill gap only matters if it relates to the current constraint. A company with no advertising skill isn't hurt by it unless it is demand constrained; if it isn't, the gap is irrelevant for now.
title: The 3 Core Roles Every Company Needs

text: Start by asking whether the business is supply or demand constrained. For the most part it is only one of the two, so everything on the other side can be ignored until the constraint changes.
title: The 3 Core Roles Every Company Needs

text: Once demand is cracked enough that supply becomes the limit, fix supply and ignore demand. Growth follows a rhythm of alternating between the two sides over time.
title: The 3 Core Roles Every Company Needs

text: He and his partner Leila alternate: one of them is always working hard on their side while the other coasts, never both at once. He fills the calendars, then she builds delivery capacity to expand availability.
title: The 3 Core Roles Every Company Needs

text: Acquisition.com began as a cash-flow-based family office run by him and Leila. It was the most relaxed period of his life, though he was also extremely bored.
title: The Chillest Season of My Life

text: After roughly 24 deals in 24 months, real purchases and not VC-style bets, only about three companies turned out to be really good, consistent with portfolio theory.
title: The Chillest Season of My Life

text: As his brand grew, he recalculated resources: the brand was becoming as valuable as, or more than, the cash they could invest from their own money.
title: The Chillest Season of My Life

text: The advisory practice started in January 2024 and produced about 36 million in EBITDA in year one, from that single unit.
title: The Chillest Season of My Life

text: They stopped doing deals where they were only passive investors. Now the model is brand plus capital plus work, and he prefers fewer bets with huge outsized returns.
title: The Chillest Season of My Life

text: School, also started January 2024, now has about 30 million users and over a billion in GMV, making it a very large platform.
title: The Chillest Season of My Life

text: When you have a standout asset, focus on running it rather than spreading effort across side ventures. He notes big founders did not run side hustles alongside their main company.
title: The Chillest Season of My Life

text: He says all marketing works. When a channel fails, the cause is either that the ad or offer is not reaching the right people, or that what is shown is not what they want.
title: Helping a Tax Firm Get More Leads

text: He advises choosing one growth channel and committing fully to it rather than spreading effort, noting that several different channels can all work.
title: Helping a Tax Firm Get More Leads

text: He argues that if you can at least break even on the first transaction and customers return to buy again, the customer becomes a compounding asset, so a first-sale breakeven is an acceptable worst case.
title: Helping a Tax Firm Get More Leads

text: He says his own outbound took about a year to reach where he wanted, so he suggests a channel that has produced some sales may just need more months of iteration.
title: Helping a Tax Firm Get More Leads

text: He states that the rule of 100 for outbound means 100 outreach attempts a day, not a single batch of 100.
title: Helping a Tax Firm Get More Leads

text: Hormozi thinks the CPA-partner strategy was right; the problem is having only three or four partners, which makes you dependent. He suggests building toward 30 or 40 so no single partner has leverage over you.
title: Helping a Real Estate Developer Scale

text: When a business has been flat for six months and nothing changes, Hormozi told this person something has to change. He said to go get good at the underlying skill, and that the old door stays open since the skills remain.
title: Helping a Real Estate Developer Scale

text: Some of the best returns in a business come from comparing what it costs to acquire talent against the lifetime gross profit each employee generates. He saw a 5:1 return in this example.
title: Helping a Home Services Company Build a Sales Team

text: He frames a hiring investment against an alternative like the S&P: putting the same money into a hiring machine that yields a million in gross profit, which at an 8x enterprise value multiple is worth far more than the amount invested.
title: Helping a Home Services Company Build a Sales Team

text: He observes that when a very small acquired business is stuck, the founder is usually the problem, and the business stays limited by that person.
title: He Buys Businesses but Can't Make Them Grow

text: He says good founders instinctively focus on the one thing that could make the business 10x, while mediocre and bad founders get pulled into daily fires and stay mediocre for a long time.
title: He Buys Businesses but Can't Make Them Grow

text: Between 2020 and 2023 he did 24 acquisitions and later sold or gave back his shares in 19 of them because they were not worth it; the founders were not winners.
title: He Buys Businesses but Can't Make Them Grow

text: He says real winners will either win or die rather than accept staying flat for a third year, and he now spends a larger share of his time looking for such people.
title: He Buys Businesses but Can't Make Them Grow

text: For a buy-and-hold approach, he says one of the best signs of a strong founder is a bigger business, since someone reaching 20 million in ARR is probably better than someone capping at three million and selling.
title: He Buys Businesses but Can't Make Them Grow

text: He thinks founders who only needed to make 20 or 30 million dollars are hard to motivate; once they hit it, they want to keep the team cared for rather than push from three to thirty.
title: He Buys Businesses but Can't Make Them Grow

text: His nuanced answer is that the acquired founders probably are not driven enough, so buy bigger businesses that already have the right talent.
title: He Buys Businesses but Can't Make Them Grow

text: He says investors each reinvent the wheel, himself included: buying small and flipping big looks easy, but you end up building the whole business, and then understand why people buy bigger companies.
title: He Buys Businesses but Can't Make Them Grow

text: When people list brands in a category, they often name the people who stand for those brands. Hormozi says a founder lacking that personal association is missing something important.
title: $250M CEO Explains How to Build A Brand in 2026

text: He says a few premium brand associations can be enough to cover a brand, and that a brand cannot be driven by discounts.
title: $250M CEO Explains How to Build A Brand in 2026

text: Selling only a product with paid traffic is arbitrage: buy clicks at one price, sell them at another, and keep the spread. He compares it to the e-commerce version of an info business.
title: $250M CEO Explains How to Build A Brand in 2026

text: Some brands are better off starting fresh than repairing a damaged one. If people react with surprise that the new brand is the old company, that reaction suggests the old one was bad.
title: $250M CEO Explains How to Build A Brand in 2026

text: Affiliates and AI influencers should each represent one specific avatar, not everyone. Otherwise the brand looks like AI slop, and everything must stay on message and on brand.
title: $250M CEO Explains How to Build A Brand in 2026

text: A larger brand can gain from a person's association over years of visible use, until the brand can run its own ads without him. Get the best product, then the coolest person to talk about it.
title: $250M CEO Explains How to Build A Brand in 2026

text: If premium people you approach think you are a scammer, you probably need to rebrand. If they accept and like the product, the brand is likely fine and will shift.
title: $250M CEO Explains How to Build A Brand in 2026

text: Until you have good products, building a business around them is pointless. He wants the owner to truly love the products first.
title: $250M CEO Explains How to Build A Brand in 2026

text: Well-run e-commerce gets about half of revenue from email. This needs flows for each decision path, such as abandoned cart, plus two to three value emails per week.
title: $250M CEO Explains How to Build A Brand in 2026

text: He once thought sales was beneath him, seeing himself as an academic and consultant. Paying rent on a gym lease made him realize he needed customers paying him, which forced him to learn selling.
title: \"How did you learn how to sell?\"

text: In 2013 he paid $3,000 for a weekend workshop on Facebook ads, then ran ads for his gym. He signed 27 people in two weeks at $300 each, on roughly $1,000 of ad spend.
title: \"How did you learn how to sell?\"

text: He believes he opened the gym too quickly, thinking opening was when money started. In hindsight he thinks he should have run a long pre-sale and collected cash the whole time.
title: \"How did you learn how to sell?\"

text: His launch offer was a six-week challenge at $300: lose 20 pounds in six weeks and get your money back. He wanted customers to have skin in the game. Success rate was just under 80%.
title: \"How did you learn how to sell?\"

text: He describes three buckets in the challenge: people who miss the goal and are unhappy, people who hit it and keep going with the new habit (the vast majority), and people who take the refund.
title: \"How did you learn how to sell?\"

text: For refund-seekers he offered to credit the $300 toward a year at the gym, framing it around keeping the new habit and momentum. Some people committed to the year before the challenge ended.
title: \"How did you learn how to sell?\"

text: Halfway through the challenge he would check in, point out progress such as ten pounds down, and ask how much more weight they wanted to lose, since nobody has a perfect body and there is always more to work on.
title: \"How did you learn how to sell?\"

text: People with no big successes still have smaller ones, like getting dressed or sitting down at the computer. He holds that this is enough evidence to claim you can do the thing, and repeating it builds a stronger claim.
title: Outwork Your Self-Doubt

text: Big outcomes come from many constrained tiny impulses, where you win small victories by saying no to small temptations. Each one adds another piece of proof that you do what you say you can do.
title: Outwork Your Self-Doubt

text: Fighting a crowd of competitors to divide small amounts of money many ways is a weak approach. If you want to make money, go to the place where the money already is.
title: Sell to the Rich (The Top 1% Has More Than the Bottom 90%)

text: Whatever problem you are struggling with, someone else has already faced it and solved it, so you can look to them rather than starting from nothing.
title: Sell to the Rich (The Top 1% Has More Than the Bottom 90%)

text: Private equity firms typically keep finance as an in-house, centralized function, or replace the finance team after an acquisition, rather than relying on outside providers.
title: Most Entrepreneurs Stay Distracted Because They Can't Say No to Bad Customers

text: To find your ideal customer, take your top group of customers, for example the best 10 to 16 out of 80, and pick those you like most, who pay most and stay longest. Then refine messaging and offer and advertise only to that type.
title: Most Entrepreneurs Stay Distracted Because They Can't Say No to Bad Customers

text: A Vista Private Equity pricing head described their playbook: learn the customer base better than the owners, identify the most profitable customers and their source channels, stop low-ROI channels, and multiply the channel with the best LTV to CAC ratio fivefold.
title: Most Entrepreneurs Stay Distracted Because They Can't Say No to Bad Customers

text: Because the business can already serve the current customer count, replacing weaker customers with the best type adds almost no infrastructure. He says this typically doubles or triples profitability over five years.
title: Most Entrepreneurs Stay Distracted Because They Can't Say No to Bad Customers

text: One of the first steps he takes with any company is reviewing customer data to find the most valuable customers, their channels and the offers they respond to, then reorganizing acquisition to attract them.
title: Most Entrepreneurs Stay Distracted Because They Can't Say No to Bad Customers

text: He argues most people fail to do this because they cannot say no, which is why entrepreneurs stay distracted and poor.
title: Most Entrepreneurs Stay Distracted Because They Can't Say No to Bad Customers

text: Seasonal swings are normal in some businesses and do not by themselves mean the business is flawed. The job is to earn strongly in the busy season so it covers the slow one.
title: \"How Do I Go From Word of Mouth to a Real Marketing System\"

text: Some owners impose an artificial constraint, claiming a particular month is always bad, and this can become a self-fulfilling prophecy. He asks whether capturing all local demand in that month would make it a top month.
title: \"How Do I Go From Word of Mouth to a Real Marketing System\"

text: Outmarketing competitors can smooth out a demand curve. He argues that what looks like volatility is often just a shortage of leads, which better marketing fixes.
title: \"How Do I Go From Word of Mouth to a Real Marketing System\"

text: For a catering business he thinks paid ads such as Meta would work fine, but he would start with PPC because high-intent searchers make the warmest leads, then move on to Meta.
title: \"How Do I Go From Word of Mouth to a Real Marketing System\"

text: Moving from word of mouth to paid leads requires a process: a landing page, lead nurture, scheduling, and a short VSL before the call to frame expectations, so the leads can then be closed.
title: \"How Do I Go From Word of Mouth to a Real Marketing System\"

text: Hormozi says paying a recruiter a large fee per hire is worth it when each hire generates far more profit than the fee. Businesses treat stock investments this way but rarely treat hiring the same way.
title: You Need to Pay More to Get Better Talent

text: Hormozi expects that for the next few years the cost of acquiring and paying good tradespeople will rise, since it is a supply-constrained market where workers hold the upper hand. He thinks a compression and steep drop may follow later.
title: You Need to Pay More to Get Better Talent

text: Hormozi notes many people in the trades are not strong at business and so will not reason about talent costs this way, which leaves an opening for owners who do the math.
title: You Need to Pay More to Get Better Talent

text: Hormozi defines LTGPE, lifetime gross profit per employee, compared against CAT, the cost of acquiring talent. It mirrors LTGP to CAC on the customer side: how much you will pay to get talent versus what that talent earns you.
title: You Need to Pay More to Get Better Talent

text: Example math: if an employee stays six years, a 20 thousand recruiter fee plus 150 thousand yearly pay totals about a million dollars, while the employee generates 200 thousand gross profit yearly, so the cost is recovered.
title: You Need to Pay More to Get Better Talent

text: Hormozi thinks that once posting volume is adequate, the thing to tighten is content quality, including the research put into hooks and scripting, rather than simply posting more.
title: The Future of Ads: Content and Ads Are Merging

text: Hormozi suggests putting your biggest accomplishment front and center and repeating it when you introduce yourself in every video, so that you build authority before delivering content.
title: The Future of Ads: Content and Ads Are Merging

text: AI depends on data, so a data layer must come first. Frontier models learn from freely available information, so an edge over them requires proprietary data sets they cannot access or replicate.
title: You Can't Win at AI Without Your Own Data

text: A unique data set only gives an edge if it produces outcomes different from other data sets. If a different data set creates the same outcomes, the edge is not the same.
title: You Can't Win at AI Without Your Own Data

text: He thinks 95 to 99 percent of businesses only use AI internally rather than selling an AI product, so for them the goal is getting more from the tools, not owning unique training data.
title: You Can't Win at AI Without Your Own Data

text: Training an employee requires documenting the steps of the right behaviors, and that documentation is data. More documentation of business processes means more to feed AI tools.
title: You Can't Win at AI Without Your Own Data

text: Document each process as inputs, step-by-step manufacturing into outputs, and a way to judge outputs as good or bad. He calls that judging reinforcement training, which works for humans and machines.
title: You Can't Win at AI Without Your Own Data

text: Hormozi holds that identity is simply the aggregate of everything a person does. Describing someone, such as a carpenter or a podcaster, means listing their behaviors, so the idea of being something adds confusion for many people.
title: Why You Shouldn't Put Your Actions on a Pedestal

text: Treating any single behavior as sacred makes it feel meaningful, but he says fundamentally it is only a behavior. Seeing yourself as a list of roughly a thousand behaviors makes it easier to consider changing one.
title: Why You Shouldn't Put Your Actions on a Pedestal

text: To decide whether to change a behavior for someone, ask whether the effort of changing it matters more to you than the relationship. If not, change it, especially when the cost to you is near zero and the benefit to them is significant.
title: Why You Shouldn't Put Your Actions on a Pedestal

text: When you see yourself as a person who simply does various things, he says there is much less emotional rigidity around change.
title: Why You Shouldn't Put Your Actions on a Pedestal

text: Hormozi thinks leaders must be people worth admiring. The leader should admire some part of you, and you should admire parts of them, otherwise they should not lead. He says you get to hire your mentors.
title: How to Build Company Culture

text: If you are always the best person in the room, the company will never grow beyond you. Hiring someone better than you is hard, and he jokes that they often do not know they are better.
title: How to Build Company Culture

text: His preference is to start the second location only once the first runs and grows without you and you are bored. Sending someone out to launch while the first still needs you usually pulls attention off it and things slip.
title: How to Build Company Culture

text: Any business, even one not truly brick and mortar, works the same way: nail it, then scale it. He calls this scale zero, meaning getting your current business to need none of your time, then replicating using those zero-founder economics.
title: How to Build Company Culture

text: Having someone run your main location and eat some margin gives less risk and faster feedback loops to train them, so they know how to do the next one because you already fixed problems at the first.
title: How to Build Company Culture

text: To duplicate culture, codify everything that creates it and apply those to the conditions where culture occurs. Leaders then need faster reinforcement loops: check-ins, performance monitoring, and real-time feedback like salespeople get.
title: How to Build Company Culture

text: Roleplay leadership conversations the way you roleplay sales conversations. He notes a leadership conversation is a sales conversation, just more numerous and more varied, so it relies on question-based frameworks rather than scripts.
title: How to Build Company Culture

text: Equity bundles four things: risk, decision-making control, profit sharing, and sale value. Asking which ones the person really wants usually shows they want profits and sale proceeds, not risk or control, so you can solve for just those.
title: What to Do When People Ask for Equity

text: Handing someone equity outright forces a company valuation and creates a tax bill on something they got without receiving cash, which they probably do not want.
title: What to Do When People Ask for Equity

text: For an LLC, a profits interest can stand in for equity value. It is structured as a sale bonus equal to the percentage the person holds at the moment of sale, earned at 0.25% per year up to 1%.
title: What to Do When People Ask for Equity

text: If the person is let go, the profits interest returns to the pool. It pays out only if the company sells while they still work there, so they do not leave with a piece of the company.
title: What to Do When People Ask for Equity

text: A profits interest can optionally include profit share equal to its percentage, such as 1% of profits on top, with both sides agreeing to it.
title: What to Do When People Ask for Equity

text: You cannot simply give people equity. They must buy it by writing a check, or receive it free and pay tax on the gift.
title: What to Do When People Ask for Equity

text: Profits interest upside: the person pays nothing. Downsides: it is taxed as ordinary income at sale, around 37% instead of about 20% capital gains, and it is lost if they are let go.
title: What to Do When People Ask for Equity

text: A smart employee might negotiate a tail on the interest to guard against being fired just before a deal closes. He thinks that fear is unrealistic, since buyers would not like a company that fired its sales leaders.
title: What to Do When People Ask for Equity
