text: He is fine using vendors but wants no vendor to own how the business works. He treats track, convert and deliver as the three core elements of a business that should never be outsourced.
title: The 3 Things You Should Never Outsource

text: Vendors can help with specific tasks inside those core areas, but if they leave, the owner should still know how to do the work. Otherwise one of three legs of the stool is missing and the founder cannot grow it.
title: The 3 Things You Should Never Outsource

text: He says paid-ad leads are among the better lead types. His ranking puts referrals best, then content, then paid ads, with Google display network leads being the true worst.
title: The 3 Things You Should Never Outsource

text: Marketing comes down to finding the sweet spot of friction. A bare price with a buy button fails for most people, and forcing 100 forms is too much friction as well.
title: The 3 Things You Should Never Outsource

text: If leads are real potential buyers but quality is weak, add the right amount of selling between them and the purchase. Targeting a higher-end customer means adding more friction.
title: The 3 Things You Should Never Outsource

text: When serving a good 20% and a weaker 80%, businesses price in the middle. He says the good customers may be underpriced by about 2x, and the right price would repel the wrong buyers.
title: The 3 Things You Should Never Outsource

text: Moving to the right avatar requires changing the product offering, price and sales motion, and expecting cost per lead to rise two or three times. Doubling price might lift gross margin about five times.
title: The 3 Things You Should Never Outsource

text: He says most business owners will not make the jump to higher pricing, which is why most people stay poor.
title: The 3 Things You Should Never Outsource

text: When choosing between quitting a job to run the business yourself or hiring someone to do your role, he argues hiring can be the riskier path, since a capable replacement may consume most of the profit.
title: \"When Should I Quit My Day Job?\"

text: He frames the decision as choosing which risk you prefer: paying someone and keeping the burden, or losing lower job income while gaining hours to earn it back in the business.
title: \"When Should I Quit My Day Job?\"

text: Service businesses, especially B2B, tend to see prices rise over time: a good reputation creates more demand than supply, higher prices let you afford better talent, which lifts reputation and demand again.
title: “I Build Sales Teams. How Do I Scale?”

text: Talent cost climbs alongside price in services: you move from paying people around $100,000 a year to $250,000, then $1,000,000, and eventually multi-million-dollar earners.
title: “I Build Sales Teams. How Do I Scale?”

text: Within a service team's workload, some activities likely correlate with retention, some have no effect, and some may even hurt it. Identify which are which and prune the ones that do not help.
title: “I Build Sales Teams. How Do I Scale?”

text: When you charge a percentage of a client's top line, the fix is usually bottom-up: get clients where each rep earns more, meaning bigger companies with more zeros, rather than just raising the percentage.
title: “I Build Sales Teams. How Do I Scale?”

text: Work out profitability per customer, use it to define the ideal customer profile, then change messaging to target that customer type.
title: “I Build Sales Teams. How Do I Scale?”

text: A percentage-of-revenue model can pay well only if the clients are large. Taking 25% of a client's top line works with very big clients, not with small ones like cheap gym memberships.
title: “I Build Sales Teams. How Do I Scale?”

text: Serving one specific avatar allows more efficiency, templatized service levels and automation, which he says should let margins expand over time or at least hold steady as you scale.
title: “I Build Sales Teams. How Do I Scale?”

text: When selling to senior executives in enterprise sales, Hormozi says they mainly want the data, rather than the training or solution that a lower-level buyer might care about.
title: “What Do High-Level Buyers Actually Want?”

text: When customers can easily compare your offer with competitors, or it is hard for them to, you should win on at least one of three vectors: be faster, be less risky, or be easier for the customer.
title: How to Make Better Offers and Lead Magnets

text: He says every industry, including remodeling, roofing and concrete, has some way to be faster, lower risk, or easier for customers.
title: How to Make Better Offers and Lead Magnets

text: If you worry you cannot afford to improve speed, risk or ease, raise prices to reflect the premium. You are no longer a commodity, and he says people will pay for it.
title: How to Make Better Offers and Lead Magnets

text: To improve your offer, actually answer this question: what would it take to deliver the same outcome to a customer in one-third the time?
title: How to Make Better Offers and Lead Magnets

text: He prefers insane discounts, around 80 or 90 percent, over 10 or 20 percent ones, because a discount must be big enough to change behavior. It works when the discounted item costs you very little.
title: How to Make Better Offers and Lead Magnets

text: The cheap discounted item exists so you can build an upsell process from it into your main offer.
title: How to Make Better Offers and Lead Magnets

text: Weak offers explain why many people cannot get cheap leads: they promise nothing on speed or ease and do nothing to reverse risk. You need not do all three; pick one and execute it hard.
title: How to Make Better Offers and Lead Magnets

text: His favorite lead magnet approach is giving away something other people normally charge for. The more real it is and the more it truly costs you, the more likely it works.
title: How to Make Better Offers and Lead Magnets

text: Hormozi says his hard season came not from long hours, which he enjoys and treats as baseline, but from the kind of tasks filling that time: necessary non-work chores that let him return to work he likes.
title: Why Life Feels Difficult

text: He notes that overhead becomes a problem when it takes a disproportionate share of your time. At every entrepreneurship level he sees periods where overhead keeps growing until he fixes it.
title: Why Life Feels Difficult

text: He describes thinking a loved one had cancer, then learning it was a mistake. He uses it as a vivid example of gratitude: a lesser problem feels good once a worse one is removed.
title: Why Life Feels Difficult

text: A printing error made a whole run of his upcoming book unusable, so he destroyed it. He decided readers would only remember receiving a flawed book, so spinning it was not an option.
title: Why Life Feels Difficult

text: After the setbacks he concluded that continuing his current path means facing more such problems, so he built a legal team. He is unsure whether he gained gratitude or solved the problem.
title: Why Life Feels Difficult

text: His HRV averaged about 32 with many low-20s days. After deciding to stop calling the year bad, it rose about 15 points from May 1st with no change in diet or training.
title: Why Life Feels Difficult

text: For gym clients, his team ran a daily morning session for trainers and front desk staff, using group role-play on whichever script section they struggled with, run like a sales manager meeting, sold as an add-on.
title: How We Trained Sales Teams Across Thousands of Gyms

text: In gyms, he taught owners the one skill of running local ads, then licensed them fresh creative monthly since that was their recurring need. This avoided needing many account reps, because owners ran their own ads to pre-tested pages.
title: How We Trained Sales Teams Across Thousands of Gyms

text: If clients who get activated tend to stay, the effort should go into activating them faster. One lever is selling only to the better-performing avatars, segmented by demographics and quantifiable traits like business size.
title: How We Trained Sales Teams Across Thousands of Gyms

text: Restricting sales to higher-converting avatars will raise your CAC, but he says it fixes the problem of clients not sticking.
title: How We Trained Sales Teams Across Thousands of Gyms

text: His advice to creators: do not try to solve churn on products people naturally leave, like gym memberships. Instead find products people already do not cancel, such as internet, phone or insurance, and shift customers to your version.
title: Why Creators Burn Out (and How to Fix It)

text: Power as a source of influence comes when someone follows a directive you gave and gets a good result. That makes them more likely to follow your later directives, as with a hiccup-cure short he tried.
title: Why Creators Burn Out (and How to Fix It)

text: Status, the fourth influence source, is relative control over scarce reinforcers, like a bartender controlling alcohol. With likeness, credibility, power and status all present, a person becomes highly influential.
title: Why Creators Burn Out (and How to Fix It)

text: He argues a creator's aim should be real influence over a large group's behavior. The strongest route is giving directives people follow and benefit from, which makes them likelier to accept later requests.
title: Why Creators Burn Out (and How to Fix It)

text: His math: 20 videos of 30 minutes equal 10 hours. With 20-second shorts, matching that would take about 1,800 shorts. He thinks people have wildly over-weighted followership and views as a stand-in for influence.
title: Why Creators Burn Out (and How to Fix It)

text: A car detailing shop pays 500 dollars for 10,000 YouTube views or 400,000 TikTok views, treating them as equal. Hormozi would still prefer the 10,000 YouTube views.
title: Why Creators Burn Out (and How to Fix It)

text: He sees short form mainly as a way to drive people forward to deeper content. It can deliver value, but the odds a viewer acts on a short and gets a result are very low.
title: Why Creators Burn Out (and How to Fix It)

text: Long-form listeners need to act on only one of many directives over a month to see life improve, which builds the host's influence. He suspects host collabs and product recommendations then convert strongly.
title: Why Creators Burn Out (and How to Fix It)

text: For an endorsement to matter, beyond just distribution, the host must have shown credibility on the topic. Without it, the endorsement works merely as an ad.
title: Why Creators Burn Out (and How to Fix It)

text: He thinks short form works like awareness ads, and its objective should be getting people to take a tiny action, such as joining a community, where faster feedback loops help build the other influence factors.
title: Why Creators Burn Out (and How to Fix It)

text: He says some creators are undervalued and many overvalued: two paid shout-outs from 100,000-follower Instagram accounts drove 10,000 customers from one and zero from the other, so followers do not guarantee influence.
title: Why Creators Burn Out (and How to Fix It)

text: He says TikTok Shop's large analysis of which content signals lead to sales found saves were the top metric for purchase intent, ahead of shares and likes.
title: The Only Metric That Matters for Short-Form Content

text: A funny meme may get many shares and views and suit the platform's goals, but he doubts the person who shares it becomes more likely to buy from its creator.
title: The Only Metric That Matters for Short-Form Content

text: People only save content when they do not already know the steps, so it cannot be obvious. Useful step-by-step advice may not go viral, but saves build the sense that the creator truly knows the subject.
title: The Only Metric That Matters for Short-Form Content

text: To make save-worthy content, show you have spent time with the problem across many clients. Go beyond the first-layer answer an AI would give, and explain why the normal advice often fails to work.
title: The Only Metric That Matters for Short-Form Content

text: He suggests treating content as removing friction from people's lives: give the normal advice, then respond to it by addressing why people struggle with it.
title: The Only Metric That Matters for Short-Form Content

text: He thinks that for services like coaching, the creator who consistently gives the most valuable content, the kind people feel they must collect, is who people trust most and most likely buy from.
title: The Only Metric That Matters for Short-Form Content

text: He says you get the best insights from people in completely different niches, and he thinks dismissing people who earn less than you is stupid.
title: The Only Metric That Matters for Short-Form Content

text: He says he has learned some of his best tactics from the smallest business owners, since those making the least often have to be the scrappiest and most creative.
title: The Only Metric That Matters for Short-Form Content

text: He notes that most buyers have jobs and paydays, and he sees buying spikes after the average payday.
title: The Only Metric That Matters for Short-Form Content

text: After losing everything and then earning more within the next 12 months, he concluded that no work is wasted, because a person is the output of the work, not just the outcome it produces.
title: Why You're Not Burnt Out (You're Just Weak)

text: More work builds a bigger work ethic and raises work capacity, so he never treats effort as wasted.
title: Why You're Not Burnt Out (You're Just Weak)

text: Using fitness as an example, he says the ability to recover from training can itself be trained. Doing more volume raises how much volume a person can withstand.
title: Why You're Not Burnt Out (You're Just Weak)

text: He applies this to feeling burnt out: you either die or adapt. In fitness terms, you die, get injured, or adapt, so mainly avoid injury and you improve.
title: Why You're Not Burnt Out (You're Just Weak)

text: Viewing work this way has been his most self-fulfilling prophecy: the more he works, the better he gets and the more productive he is per unit of time, and outcomes follow eventually.
title: Why You're Not Burnt Out (You're Just Weak)

text: Citing a friend, Dr. Cashy, he says experts in any skill become experts because they learn to be rewarded by the work itself. They measure success differently rather than having something others lack.
title: Why You're Not Burnt Out (You're Just Weak)

text: Judge yourself by your actions, not your thoughts. He became much less disappointed in himself once he judged himself only on actions taken.
title: Why You're Not Burnt Out (You're Just Weak)

text: Hormozi says regulation is the top concern in the caller's industry, and he adds that healthcare sometimes faces the same issue. The statement is cut off before he finishes the thought.
title: Scaling a $22M Hemp Distributor to $50M

text: Rather than picking a content type, he says to think about what is valuable to the people you want to attract, list their problems, make content around those problems, and tie in your product.
title: How To Turn Organic Content Into Paid Ads

text: Post lots of organic pieces, then take the ones that take off and turn them into ads. The organic version needs no CTA; add roughly 5 seconds of CTA at the end when running it as an ad.
title: How To Turn Organic Content Into Paid Ads

text: For businesses that are mostly paid, adding some organic content helps lead nurture: prospects who get on a call check the account and see the business is active, which he thinks lifts conversions.
title: How To Turn Organic Content Into Paid Ads

text: He treats organic posting as free testing: you can compare pieces against each other, and the outperformers become the ones you put ad money behind.
title: How To Turn Organic Content Into Paid Ads

text: Hormozi says many niche SEO agencies run net margins of 50% or more, so he wants the caller to drop the belief that a 13% margin is normal.
title: Helping an SEO Agency Get to $14M/Year

text: He says nearshoring was the answer a year earlier, and the current answer is to become AI-driven, because he bets around 80% of an SEO agency's work can already be automated by AI today.
title: Helping an SEO Agency Get to $14M/Year

text: Hormozi advises against seeing AI as a risk to your own business; see it as a risk to competitors, and be the wolf rather than the sheep.
title: Helping an SEO Agency Get to $14M/Year

text: He says operators need to get up to speed on agents and on tools like make.com, which he describes as a newer version of what Zapier automations used to do.
title: Helping an SEO Agency Get to $14M/Year

text: Hormozi thinks ChatGPT's huge weekly user base, and its move into recommending products, makes LLM SEO a way to future-proof an SEO agency.
title: Helping an SEO Agency Get to $14M/Year

text: He thinks a per-square-foot rate means little to ultra-wealthy clients, who mostly just compute the total. The formula can stay internal while you price the job and send them a total.
title: Helping an Interior Design Company Scale

text: He says that buyers of a premium service, whether referred or comparing several providers, choose the one that looks more polished, professional and better finished, because they want the best rather than the cheapest.
title: Helping an Interior Design Company Scale

text: Hormozi says a side hustle should not be turned into the main business. He asks callers to be clear about what their main game is, so an investment does not distract from it.
title: \"If You Lost Everything, Would You Start the Same Business?\"

text: Hormozi says real estate produces more millionaires, while private equity produces more billionaires.
title: \"If You Lost Everything, Would You Start the Same Business?\"

text: He says a low-risk, high-likelihood business, once you have the skills for it, is where the upside is.
title: \"If You Lost Everything, Would You Start the Same Business?\"

text: Hormozi says he owns a bunch of apartment buildings but treats them as a safety net that provides cash flow, not as his main game.
title: \"If You Lost Everything, Would You Start the Same Business?\"

text: Hormozi says the methods for landing a first 10 customers worked in his first business and still work across many industries in his portfolio companies today.
title: Watch this to get your first 10 customers

text: If you need to hire a team while earning only 3,500 dollars a month in total, he says that signals you are underpriced.
title: Watch this to get your first 10 customers

text: To get customers, pick one of the four promotion methods. The first step is listing friends and contacts and messaging each one individually by text, DM, email, or phone call.
title: Watch this to get your first 10 customers

text: When messaging your list, he suggests offering to work free for a period, with payment starting only if they are happy with the result.
title: Watch this to get your first 10 customers

text: If your current prospects are small, go after somewhat bigger business owners. He thinks daily outreach offering free work first would likely beat unfocused activity.
title: Watch this to get your first 10 customers

text: Make content inside the communities where your customers are, ideally local ones since trust is higher when you are nearby. Post valuable items such as teardowns of work you did free, and he thinks people will approach you.
title: Watch this to get your first 10 customers

text: Reach out to anyone who engages with your posts and offer free work. On the phone, explain that paid work covers more, then upsell from there.
title: Watch this to get your first 10 customers

text: He says a grand opening is the one exception where hard marketing works for a restaurant, but it should only be run once the model, experience and food are proven.
title: Helping a Restaurant Business Get to $100M

text: He says this matters more for restaurants because debt collection is harder and gross margins are smaller. He concludes that aggressive growth there comes mostly from the food and the experience.
title: Helping a Restaurant Business Get to $100M

text: Regrets are an unavoidable part of being human and come from opportunity cost. He once believed a regret meant a poor decision, but no decision removes them.
title: How to Make Hard Decisions

text: Since regrets will happen either way, a simpler way to decide is to ask which regret you could live with rather than which option you want. Some regrets are much harder to bear than others.
title: How to Make Hard Decisions

text: Facing a hard conversation, like telling a small business owner you are leaving, is one regret. Wasting a decade in a job you hate is another. In life you choose your regrets.
title: How to Make Hard Decisions

text: He likes the choose-your-regrets frame because it engages fear. Asking what you hate least lets you use a run-away-from drive instead of only a move-toward drive.
title: How to Make Hard Decisions

text: Hormozi says he does not try to trade away sleep; he sleeps as much as he can, which usually works out to about six hours, and he feels fine on that.
title: How to Work Harder Than 99% of People

text: Hormozi says he goes to bed around 10:00 and wakes at 4:00, and he believes he could keep that up indefinitely. In the weeks before a launch he averaged about five hours for roughly six weeks.
title: How to Work Harder Than 99% of People

text: Hormozi says he mostly drinks on date nights with his wife, prefers tequila and mezcal after years of whiskey and bourbon, and typically has one or two drinks, up to four or five.
title: How to Work Harder Than 99% of People

text: Ask leads which piece or type of content brought them in, in the application and on the sales call. If you make four or five content buckets, their answers show which bucket attracts quality rather than quantity.
title: How to Fix a Broken Sales Funnel

text: Content with a smaller audience can draw better buyers. At his workshop, where the average attendee runs a business doing 4 million a year, everyone liked his business breakdown videos, though they get fewer views than general mindset videos.
title: How to Fix a Broken Sales Funnel

text: Adding friction should be judged by whether the percentage of qualified people goes up. If the share of qualified bookings fell after adding filters, the friction did not help.
title: How to Fix a Broken Sales Funnel

text: Hormozi says most people in the room suffer from insufficient volume: they do far too little. Having reached out to 15 prospects with no result is not enough; he says to add two zeros to the effort.
title: Most Problems Can Be Solved With More Advertising

text: Hormozi says he learned marketing by going to agencies, and recommends hiring an exceptional agency with a proven track record and studying everything it does.
title: Helping a Law Firm Solve a Marketing Constraint

text: When a business has strong revenue retention and the physical capacity to serve more people, Hormozi says growth becomes purely an advertising question.
title: How to Scale an In-Person Service Business

text: Hormozi says that in a market of 100,000 people, Meta ad efficiency would likely start dropping somewhere around 7,500 to 10,000 dollars a month in spend.
title: How to Scale an In-Person Service Business

text: He notes that with Google search ads you can tell when you have maxed out, because you have already won all the keywords available.
title: How to Scale an In-Person Service Business

text: Even if return on ad spend falls from 16 to 1 to around 2 or 3 to 1 at higher spend, he says it hardly matters when you collect payment up front.
title: How to Scale an In-Person Service Business

text: In a service-based business, growth is capped by the culture you keep, and that culture is spread by the people you attract. If you are paying no one over 100,000 a year, the results rest entirely on you.
title: Helping an Online Coaching Business Get to $50M/Year

text: Talent quality jumps noticeably with pay: he describes people at 250,000, 500,000 and a million dollars a year each seeming like a distinctly higher level, and eventually finding people better than himself.
title: Helping an Online Coaching Business Get to $50M/Year

text: His hiring litmus test is feeling a desperate need in your core to have the person when you talk to them. If someone is only the least bad of the candidates, do not hire them and keep looking.
title: Helping an Online Coaching Business Get to $50M/Year

text: His company will hold a role open for weeks or months until the right person turns up, and it is always actively recruiting.
title: Helping an Online Coaching Business Get to $50M/Year

text: He started the gym largely out of ignorance and luck, and says he probably would not advise his younger self to take that lease risk today.
title: Starting a Gym at 23

text: Two weeks before the gym opened, he happened to attend a marketing workshop that introduced Facebook ads. He believes without it, his Groupon-only plan would have left him struggling to get customers.
title: Starting a Gym at 23

text: His mentor's plan of running Groupons worked for the mentor, who had 20 years of reputation and about 120 people a month, but it brought him nobody in the most competitive part of Orange County, with many gyms running Groupons.
title: Starting a Gym at 23

text: Quitting felt risky to him because it was an emotional decision, not a math one: it meant leaving the management consulting and business school path he had aimed at his whole life.
title: Starting a Gym at 23

text: He ultimately decided by preferring to be rejected by his father while accepting himself over being approved of while rejecting himself. He says he hated his job, and suspects that if he had liked it he might not be an entrepreneur.
title: Starting a Gym at 23

text: Hormozi suggests starting a podcast and using it as the lead magnet, since it gives you an hour-long conversation with a prospective CEO client.
title: How to Build a Lead Magnet That Converts

text: To build a lead magnet, start from what the target audience wants, such as credibility, then work out how to deliver that cheaply and give it away free; if they dislike it, offer more or better.
title: How to Build a Lead Magnet That Converts

text: With a large email list, split test several lead magnet candidates and compare response rates. He says this can be done in about four email cycles, and any candidate should beat having none.
title: How to Build a Lead Magnet That Converts

text: Wins only carry meaning if they were hard. Easy wins are forgettable, while difficult ones change the person who earned them.
title: Easy Wins Are Forgettable. Hard Ones Change You

text: What counted as a win at age five stops counting once you are competent. As competence grows, stakes must grow too, so you must risk more to win bigger.
title: Easy Wins Are Forgettable. Hard Ones Change You

text: As your capacity increases, your standards increase too, and standards will always outrun capacity. So you will constantly feel a gap between where you are and where you want to be, which does not mean you actually are bad.
title: Easy Wins Are Forgettable. Hard Ones Change You

text: He thinks AI makes it possible to shortcut to an outcome without the required inputs. If you detach from the journey and stop scrutinizing outputs as carefully, something is lost.
title: Easy Wins Are Forgettable. Hard Ones Change You

text: He argues the leverage crowd ignores how humans narrate their own lives. Even if the output were identical, a project produced by a shortcut would feel different from one produced through your own process.
title: Easy Wins Are Forgettable. Hard Ones Change You

text: Whether life's purpose is what changes because you were here, or who you become, is a philosophical question. He leans toward both: in hard times he sees events as happening for him, in easy times he sees himself as happening to reality.
title: Easy Wins Are Forgettable. Hard Ones Change You

text: Holding only one view creates fragility. Focusing only on outcomes means never becoming the person who can produce them and chasing shortcuts that may not work; focusing only on inputs means never checking whether the suffering amounted to anything.
title: Easy Wins Are Forgettable. Hard Ones Change You

text: He spends his mornings on maker work: models and research for big portfolio decisions using spreadsheets and data, or on content, coming up with concepts and outlining bullet points. Each is either making a decision or making a thing.
title: How I Structure My Day to Get More Work Done

text: He says he is not a full-time content creator. A large content team makes it look that way, while his own time goes to maker work and meetings.
title: How I Structure My Day to Get More Work Done

text: His second half of the day is meetings. He says the split is fluid and follows seasons, so nobody should copy his exact schedule.
title: How I Structure My Day to Get More Work Done

text: During book-writing season, Mondays were all meetings, he kept a Thursday afternoon, and the rest of his time went to book edits. In his current season, time is roughly 50/50, with Mondays still all meetings.
title: How I Structure My Day to Get More Work Done

text: Book meetings back to front: fill the end of the day first, such as 4 to 5, then 3:30 to 4, then 3 to 3:30, so the largest uninterrupted block stays free earlier in the day. He says it took 10 years to figure out.
title: How I Structure My Day to Get More Work Done

text: His earlier rule was no meetings before 1:00. Meetings then started at 1:00 and scattered through the afternoon, ending around 3:30, and he did not want to return to maker mode after that.
title: How I Structure My Day to Get More Work Done

text: He has three assistants managing calendars for him and his wife, with a fourth coming. He ends meetings at 5:00, works out, eats, then calls it a day.
title: How I Structure My Day to Get More Work Done

text: He sleeps without an alarm as long as possible and works roughly 6 to 6. He and his wife work seven days a week, and after four or five weeks of 12-hour days he takes a day off.
title: How I Structure My Day to Get More Work Done

text: His most common time off is the second half of Sunday, ending work around 2:00. His wife has about 15 meetings a day and reserves only one or two days for making content or prepping quarterlies for the team and portfolio companies.
title: How I Structure My Day to Get More Work Done

text: Businesses should stop thinking in terms of hiring for roles and instead think in workflows. A role like editor is really four or five tasks, each of which can sit in a workflow that gets automated.
title: How to Win with AI in 2026

text: Every business can be linked at a very fine level, action to action, from inbound lead onward. There may be around 120 actions, and most people will not do this granular thinking.
title: How to Win with AI in 2026

text: Building an AI workflow works like training an editor: give step-by-step instructions, keep updating the prompt as you learn, and do this for every function of the business. He calls this the future.
title: How to Win with AI in 2026

text: He thinks agencies, long a painful business, could become very lucrative for people skilled with AI. Demand for customers is endless, and the hard part is operations, which get better once the flows are systemized.
title: How to Win with AI in 2026

text: Vague instructions fail with machines and with people alike. Replace something like be more charismatic with specific observable behaviors such as voice, speed, head position and nodding, and break tasks down as if teaching a toddler.
title: How to Win with AI in 2026

text: Start with a process map of the business: begin with the big steps like idea, script, shoot, export, edit, post, then keep breaking each step into smaller actions until it cannot be reduced further. That is what gets automated.
title: How to Win with AI in 2026

text: He calls an AI automation hire high leverage, especially for online businesses. This person can sit beside teams, watch what they do, and spot things to automate. He says do it now if cash flow allows.
title: How to Win with AI in 2026

text: He puts a rough price on a loose hacker type who duct-tapes tools together at about 150 thousand dollars a year, noting that price rises with skill level.
title: How to Win with AI in 2026

text: Brand controls should be largely automated because it is pattern detection, which machines do better than people. The human skill needed is describing the pattern in concrete, black-and-white terms rather than saying something is off-brand.
title: How to Win with AI in 2026

text: He says administrative and back-office work such as invoicing, matching billables, receivables and lead nurture can already be automated now.
title: How to Win with AI in 2026

text: He thinks generalized humanoid robots will spread most, because the world is already built for the human body, while special-purpose robots face too many unique scenarios and cost too much for now.
title: How to Win with AI in 2026

text: He says text AI is ready now, while voice is very close but not quite there. He would not recommend specific voice tools since they change often.
title: How to Win with AI in 2026

text: He predicts that within 12 to 24 months much of the UX will vanish, replaced by an agent you talk or text to, and CRMs will be affected.
title: How to Win with AI in 2026

text: Humans using technology beat humans with weaker technology. Some firms will still profit on fax machines, but those who adopt the tech will earn more. He is not an AI alarmist and expects a slow shift.
title: How to Win with AI in 2026

text: He thinks businesses with heavy people and operations needs that are largely digital, such as a marketing agency adopting AI heavily, will benefit most, because they can scale operations for higher margins and less complexity.
title: How to Win in the AI Era | Hormozi Q&A

text: He thinks AI scratches a human itch without fully satisfying it, giving watered-down substitutes like porn for relationships and social media for friendships, and expects a split between fake experiences and real ones.
title: How to Win in the AI Era | Hormozi Q&A

text: He argues that believing you must be born with business skill is an excuse to avoid trying; the needed things can be learned and done.
title: How to Win in the AI Era | Hormozi Q&A

text: He says the first requirement for building a business is being willing to have colleagues, friends and family disagree with your choice; most people cannot get past one to three of these groups and stay stuck.
title: How to Win in the AI Era | Hormozi Q&A

text: He says you must accept looking cringe, since doing something new means being bad at it first; people afraid of sucking never try and keep losing.
title: How to Win in the AI Era | Hormozi Q&A

text: He judges people by the company they keep and will not befriend those whose baggage he does not want, though he distinguishes caring for a struggling sibling from voluntarily surrounding yourself with bad influences.
title: How to Win in the AI Era | Hormozi Q&A

text: He believes environment shapes behavior more than anything else, and wants his own environment to make behavior toward his goals as frictionless as possible.
title: How to Win in the AI Era | Hormozi Q&A

text: He learned from a deal story that overpaying to become number one in a market can pay off via the story it lets you tell, giving leverage in later negotiations; he is willing to lose battles to win wars.
title: How to Win in the AI Era | Hormozi Q&A

text: His biggest risk was signing a $300,000 lease for the first gym with $50,000 saved, no business or customer experience, and $5,000 monthly rent due in 14 days; he took it only out of ignorance and would not advise it.
title: How to Win in the AI Era | Hormozi Q&A

text: He likes working out at a gym with his employees, believing that normalizing hard work in the gym sets people up for better days.
title: How to Win in the AI Era | Hormozi Q&A

text: If an ad channel is already making money, do not shut it off to try something new. Keep the flow going and add the new channel on top to make more money.
title: Helping a B2B Lead Gen Agency Improve Lead Quality

text: Whatever problem you are struggling with, someone else has already dealt with it and found a solution, so you can look for their answer.
title: How to Find Motivated Sellers in a Frozen Real Estate Market

text: Before adding a second acquisition channel, Hormozi says to first spend more on the channel already working, provided it is not yet maxed out.
title: \"How Do I Increase LTV When My Product Works Too Well\"

text: When a business has enough margin, market and leads but cannot convert them, the constraint is manpower. He tests this by asking whether five times the salespeople would grow the business five times as fast.
title: Founder Has No Job (Business Prints $500K)

text: To add salespeople, first set up an acquisition channel for recruiting them. Then build the full sales org: career path, compensation, onboarding and management, run as a sales-driven organization.
title: Founder Has No Job (Business Prints $500K)

text: The more he does this work, the more he favors clear over clever in advertising.
title: High Ticket Sales Are Easier Than Cheap Ones

text: He thinks local services that are high ticket are the easiest place to start, where it is hard to lose money, because local competitors are far less sophisticated.
title: High Ticket Sales Are Easier Than Cheap Ones

text: Marketing methods used in global competition, dropped into a local market within a set radius, will crush most local competitors, who lack that sophistication.
title: High Ticket Sales Are Easier Than Cheap Ones

text: Highly credentialed competitors often have big egos and assume that if customers cannot understand them, the customers are too dumb. This makes simple communication a strong advantage.
title: High Ticket Sales Are Easier Than Cheap Ones

text: To handle hateful comments, translate them into the meaning that the person dislikes how you live your life. He says this helped him get past many negative comments.
title: High Ticket Sales Are Easier Than Cheap Ones

text: When examining what limits a business, he keeps asking why each stated limitation matters, and dismisses those that turn out not to be real issues, then continues down the list until the true constraint appears.
title: A Simple Way to Make Better Personal Decisions

text: His current constraint for the business is needing four more C-level executives to pursue what he wants to do next.
title: A Simple Way to Make Better Personal Decisions

text: His calendar is the most flexible in the companies: almost no recurring meetings, apart from a Monday one-hour meeting combining marketing, sales and media. The rest of his time is fully open to allocate.
title: A Simple Way to Make Better Personal Decisions

text: After the launch ended, his freed-up calendar is now consumed by recruiting calls, interviews, notes and introductions to vet candidates. Once the four executives are in, the company gains capacity to push his best idea from his list.
title: A Simple Way to Make Better Personal Decisions

text: Athletic training is a commonly paid category, even at high school level. Parents pay roughly $300 to $500 monthly for pitching, jumping or hockey coaches, seeing status, confidence, skills and a possible scholarship.
title: \"How Do I Sell Training Programs to Athletes?\"

text: He is not convinced amateur athletes lack money. In his view the real question is whether the remotely delivered service is something they are willing to pay for.
title: \"How Do I Sell Training Programs to Athletes?\"

text: He thinks recreational adult players are a large, probably undertapped market. Adult leagues in the US have boomed, and people want to improve so they do not look bad in front of friends.
title: \"How Do I Sell Training Programs to Athletes?\"

text: For a sports community, he would combine a champion's mindset with breakdowns of real games or fights, pausing to explain the thinking behind each move so viewers learn to play better.
title: \"How Do I Sell Training Programs to Athletes?\"

text: Hormozi says a bad year is often just a few bad days replayed in your mind. He suggests that what separates a happy life from an unhappy one may be which days you keep thinking about.
title: Advice for Hard Days

text: During a bad season, he finds it helpful to focus only on having one good day. A good day inside a bad season is a bite-sized win, and stringing several together makes the season feel less hard.
title: Advice for Hard Days

text: He says that in some seasons of life, simply maintaining counts as winning.
title: Advice for Hard Days

text: He recounts hearing Bill Ackman describe a period when he was divorcing and had lost 4 billion dollars at his firm, with no single thing he could fix that day, which made it hard.
title: Advice for Hard Days

text: Ackman's tactic for large, complex problems that cannot be solved in a day was to simply make some progress each day. A single day feels negligible, but by 30 days you see movement and by 90 it is materially different.
title: Advice for Hard Days

text: Hormozi admits his mood is still affected by circumstances. He notes many people wish to be in a great mood without anything to be happy about, and sometimes progress itself is the win.
title: Advice for Hard Days

text: He shares that business is going very well for him, but he tore his quad this year and has a lingering neck problem. His two great fears are losing his mind and chronic pain.
title: Advice for Hard Days

text: He picks one good thing, like a great podcast, and makes it the reason the day was great, then tries to expand such moments into a great week so good moments eat up the season.
title: Advice for Hard Days

text: On May 1st he decided that the rest of the year would be good. He puts heavy mental effort into minimizing the down things and focusing on good moments, treating one as making the day.
title: Advice for Hard Days

text: Life is made of small days. If you wait for a big milestone like a billion dollars or marriage before being happy, you hold your happiness hostage, so he asks whether something small could count as great.
title: Advice for Hard Days

text: He has recalibrated his scale to how little needs to happen to make his day, week or month. He imagines calling a year great because he woke pain-free about 70 percent of days.
title: Advice for Hard Days

text: He thinks the thing most likely to stop him reaching his ultimate goals is running out of steam, so he prefers making the ride more enjoyable and puts discretionary effort into that.
title: Advice for Hard Days

text: When told something cannot be done or afforded, ask what it would take. If paying contractors 50% more enables same-day responses and customers will pay for that, do it; if not, go up market to wealthy buyers who value speed, risk and ease.
title: Charge Premium Prices in a Commoditized Market

text: To improve an offer, he looks first at speed, asking what it would take to finish everything in one third of the time.
title: Charge Premium Prices in a Commoditized Market

text: For the risk lever, insure or guarantee against the customer's biggest fear. A favorite move of his is buying an insurance policy covering that fear, telling customers damages are covered up to a limit, and building the cost into price; he says it is usually cheaper than expected.
title: Charge Premium Prices in a Commoditized Market

text: If you suffer from being a commodity, he says improving the offer along speed, risk and ease is how you solve it.
title: Charge Premium Prices in a Commoditized Market

text: You can wrap your existing offer in money-model mechanics: giveaways, win your money back, decoy, pay less now or more later, and buy X get Y free, especially to get cheaper leads.
title: Charge Premium Prices in a Commoditized Market

text: After a giveaway, contact non-winners and offer a runner-up prize such as a $2,000 kitchen discount. Win-your-money-back suits service businesses where customers must act; decoy suits transactional businesses.
title: Charge Premium Prices in a Commoditized Market

text: With buy X get Y free, give away more free than the customer pays for and raise the per-unit price to compensate. Example: a 1,200 dollar year becomes buy four get eight at 300 each. Check local advertising laws.
title: Charge Premium Prices in a Commoditized Market

text: Saying lead magnets do not work is a small-business view. Straight asks give higher immediate ROI for small money, but reaching much larger scale requires softening the ask and building conversion around it.
title: Charge Premium Prices in a Commoditized Market

text: Give people something in exchange for contact details rather than a request-quote button, and make it match their desired dream outcome in their own language.
title: Charge Premium Prices in a Commoditized Market

text: There are three lead magnet types: reveal a problem, offer a trial of the solution, or a one-step of a multi-step process, which is a splinter offer.
title: Charge Premium Prices in a Commoditized Market

text: He pushes back on the claim that an offer cannot be split: there is always some piece, like a coat of paint on a door, that can be given free or heavily discounted.
title: Charge Premium Prices in a Commoditized Market

text: With a four-component offer sold for $2,000, it can be more powerful to pull one component out and give it away free or at 90% off first.
title: Charge Premium Prices in a Commoditized Market

text: Local search can be very profitable, but only so many people search and only so much inbound intent exists. Past that point, growth requires interruption-based marketing.
title: 92% of His Leads Come From One Faucet

text: Moving from intent-based to interruption-based advertising opens up a far larger audience, because only a tiny share of people actively search for a cleaner on any given day; most get prompted by an ad.
title: 92% of His Leads Come From One Faucet

text: He lays out three bets when local search tops out: go all in on content, run interruption ads (Meta first), or build a channel partner or affiliate strategy.
title: 92% of His Leads Come From One Faucet

text: He thinks it is easier to win an easy entry customer first with a cheaper service and then cross-sell, since getting a first dollar across the line is the hard part.
title: 92% of His Leads Come From One Faucet

text: He says keyword-based search advertising can absorb around 100 grand a month in spend, making it the easiest dial to move before trying a new channel.
title: 92% of His Leads Come From One Faucet

text: He suggests taking the easy option first, more of the channel already working, before attempting net new strategies.
title: 92% of His Leads Come From One Faucet

text: Finding centers of influence and striking deals with them is slower, but yields more recurring, higher-value business. He says recurring revenue matters more than commercial versus residential.
title: 92% of His Leads Come From One Faucet

text: He does not care about industry averages, joking that American averages describe people who are overweight and divorced, so he would not use them as a target. He applies that stance to most service businesses.
title: How to Triple Profit Without Growing Revenue

text: For a service business, his sequence for scaling profit is: examine the sales motion, fix pricing and packaging of each service, generate enough cash flow, hire the needed talent, then strengthen infrastructure.
title: How to Triple Profit Without Growing Revenue

text: After setting the sequence, he would frame the year as a four-part plan that shows how the company moves from its current EBITDA to a much higher target.
title: How to Triple Profit Without Growing Revenue

text: Hormozi thinks a person with strong marketing and sales skills but no product that keeps customers lacks revenue retention, and that this gap, not promotion ability, limits the business.
title: You Need Recurring Revenue

text: He says that if he could redo his gym launch business, he would focus entirely on revenue retention and set aside everything else until it was solved.
title: You Need Recurring Revenue

text: He argues that someone with enough skills, network and money can always figure out how to grow again, so the real deficiency to fix is a service or product people do not cancel.
title: You Need Recurring Revenue

text: He warns that the belief that a business will just run without you is risky, because fast, high-activity operators do many small decisions they do not notice.
title: You Need Recurring Revenue

text: He suggests that if you are good at attracting a certain audience, ask which business best monetizes that attraction, and he gives a vertical stack of brokerage, escrow and title as an example.
title: You Need Recurring Revenue

text: He believes going mass market by teaching viral content plus a video sales letter that turns organic leads into customers, backed by ten proof cases from one vertical, is less risky than pure personal development with no business model.
title: You Need Recurring Revenue

text: Hormozi wants to avoid destroying a good business over something that has not happened yet, because launching a direct-to-consumer brand is a new brand and an entirely different business.
title: \"My Industry Is Disappearing. Do I Pivot Now?\"

text: He dislikes killing businesses that are not dead but merely flat, and prefers going through one door hard: the smallest change to the existing business.
title: \"My Industry Is Disappearing. Do I Pivot Now?\"

text: He favors leveling up with a skill set you already have over starting from scratch, since the skill gap is smaller and the existing company can become more valuable.
title: \"My Industry Is Disappearing. Do I Pivot Now?\"

text: He notes that customers who consolidate may also be your best potential acquirers, so a supply deal could include an option to buy the business later, creating an elegant exit.
title: \"My Industry Is Disappearing. Do I Pivot Now?\"

text: Hormozi says he learned that after wins he often felt nothing, and that his most enjoyed times were always spent in pursuit. So he sets very big, distant goals to stay in pursuit as long as possible.
title: you’ve already achieved goals you said would make you happy...

text: He describes pursuit as his button for enjoyment. Goals matter because they give you a destination; without one you would not take the journey, which he sees as subtly different from the cliche about journeys.
title: you’ve already achieved goals you said would make you happy...

text: He suggests reminding yourself that the present moment is the golden years, when you will look back on having health, mental capacity and resources to do what you want with friends.
title: you’ve already achieved goals you said would make you happy...

text: Looking back at university or work, he thinks the best memories are the late-night struggles with friends, not the moment of submitting the result.
title: you’ve already achieved goals you said would make you happy...

text: One of his strongest motivational frames is treating the person he wants to become as the destination. He asks what hardships would forge that man, and views tough times as the process of making him.
title: you’ve already achieved goals you said would make you happy...

text: He argues that character comes from reaching for things just above your threshold repeatedly, like lifting weights to build muscle, rather than from easy times or quick wins.
title: you’ve already achieved goals you said would make you happy...

text: His strongest gratitude frame is imagining his 85-year-old self waking up in his current body. It helps him enjoy mundane days and feel present when life feels like routine, though the effect lasts only minutes.
title: you’ve already achieved goals you said would make you happy...

text: Relaying a point from Sam Harris, he says presence means finding small moments in the day to open up and notice what is happening, rather than holding yourself to master-meditator standards.
title: you’ve already achieved goals you said would make you happy...

text: He proposes a modest mindfulness goal: try to get five moments a day of being fully where your feet are, since even a single sip of coffee counts.
title: you’ve already achieved goals you said would make you happy...

text: For a low-ticket, one-to-many community, he thinks a price between $9 and $99 is plausible, and where it lands depends on the audience's affinity with you and on churn.
title: How to Pick the Right Price for Your Paid Community

text: Test several price points, and it is typically best to move upward: launch at something like $19, watch churn, then raise to $29 and see whether churn changes disproportionately.
title: How to Pick the Right Price for Your Paid Community

text: Price has two effects to watch: conversion rate, which tends to fall when price rises, and churn, which traditionally rises. The real question is by how much, judged against earnings per click.
title: How to Pick the Right Price for Your Paid Community

text: Effective earnings per click over the customer lifespan equals conversion rate times price divided by churn. Example: 100 clicks, 5% buy at $20 with 10% churn gives $1,000 total, or $10 per click, versus $1 in the first day.
title: How to Pick the Right Price for Your Paid Community

text: Rather than asking what price to use, solve for the highest earnings per click. With conversion and churn unchanged, going from $20 to $30 raises it by 50%, and dropping to $10 lowers it.
title: How to Pick the Right Price for Your Paid Community

text: No one can hand you the right price because every industry differs, even down to button color conversion. Know your audience, start at a reasonable price, and find the answer through testing.
title: How to Pick the Right Price for Your Paid Community

text: If unsure where to start, go lower, since you can always raise later. Keep raising while numbers improve; rising price also adds a sense of urgency.
title: How to Pick the Right Price for Your Paid Community

text: When numbers eventually drop after a raise, return to the price that was the sweet spot, and tell customers who left they can come back through links at the newer price. You lose a little but maximize the business.
title: How to Pick the Right Price for Your Paid Community

text: He advises hiring only when the pain of not having someone becomes real, rather than adding staff ahead of need.
title: It's unnatural for a business to make profit

text: A 70-something billionaire mentor told him profit is unnatural: over time a business slowly eats its own profits because people keep spending money.
title: It's unnatural for a business to make profit

text: Someone in the business needs to be ruthlessly focused on holding expenses down, with the stance of making more money without spending more. He says the profitable company's owner should keep that discipline since it is not normal.
title: It's unnatural for a business to make profit

text: He has usually run businesses with very high margins, even in industries where peers report around 20 percent, while he was at 73 percent.
title: It's unnatural for a business to make profit

text: Right after a time slot is chosen, ask whether anything might get in the way of showing up. He calls this an integrity tie down and says it jolts people out of autopilot, though he offers no firm reason.
title: Helping a $3M Dental Practice Scale

text: Consider pulling appointments closer to the booking date so more people show up.
title: Helping a $3M Dental Practice Scale

text: Keep automated reminders but add manual ones sent from an office iPhone at three points: the night before (about 24 hours), the morning of, and 60 to 90 minutes prior. Blue iPhone messages are preferred.
title: Helping a $3M Dental Practice Scale

text: For brick-and-mortar businesses, have the person choose something you have paid for, such as a shirt size or a color, and set it aside for them. Having incurred a cost for them gives them a reason to show.
title: Helping a $3M Dental Practice Scale

text: Let patients pick their free item for a goody bag, then send a photo of it with their name on it, so they feel a cost was incurred just for them.
title: Helping a $3M Dental Practice Scale

text: Reminding too far out is a mistake, because an appointment made Saturday feels distant by Monday. He says to use automated reminders for far-out points like seven and three days, and put real manual effort into 24 hours, morning of, and right before.
title: Helping a $3M Dental Practice Scale

text: Hormozi says every business is demand constrained, either for customers or for talent, and most problems can be solved with advertising. The real question is who you are advertising to.
title: \"I Do $10M/Year Building Luxury Homes. How Do I Attract A Players?\"

text: Hormozi says top players and leaders are found the same way as customers, mainly through outreach, although lower-level A talent can be found by other means.
title: \"I Do $10M/Year Building Luxury Homes. How Do I Attract A Players?\"

text: Hormozi says most people fail through insufficient volume. Reaching out to about 15 people and quitting is not enough; he says to add two zeros to the effort.
title: \"I Do $10M/Year Building Luxury Homes. How Do I Attract A Players?\"

text: For any service business, his rule of thumb is to start with gross margins of 80% or higher, so delivery cost on a $2,500 sale should be about $500 or less.
title: Specialists Get Paid. Generalists Get Skipped.

text: If a $100 customer acquisition cost leads into a $2,500 sale, that acquisition cost is fine, so the problem lies elsewhere, such as costs of delivery.
title: Specialists Get Paid. Generalists Get Skipped.

text: He argues that how far along the customer is when they arrive does not matter for what you sell. Sell a longer-term solution, because there is always another problem or next step to sell them.
title: Specialists Get Paid. Generalists Get Skipped.

text: He says chiropractors he knows who earn one to five million dollars a year per location get about 80% of it from supplements.
title: Specialists Get Paid. Generalists Get Skipped.

text: He notes local-market customers often accept paying for physical products more easily than services, and they don't realize a supplement costing about seven dollars sells for 60 to 100.
title: Specialists Get Paid. Generalists Get Skipped.

text: For service businesses, his rule of thumb is a gross margin of 80% or higher.
title: Helping an Accounting Business Hire Better Talent

text: If close rates are very high, such as 80%, and you are supply constrained, that signals you can double or possibly triple your price.
title: Helping an Accounting Business Hire Better Talent

text: To test a higher price, run the exact same pitch as before and, when you state the number, simply say a price twice as high.
title: Helping an Accounting Business Hire Better Talent

text: If fewer prospects close after you raise price, it does not matter when your capacity is already the limit, since supply is the bottleneck anyway.
title: Helping an Accounting Business Hire Better Talent

text: Raising price carries little risk: the worst outcome is a prospect saying no, and you can always change the price back.
title: Helping an Accounting Business Hire Better Talent

text: To find qualified staff on a professional track, build a referral program with schools where people are on that path, creating a farm system, and also reach out directly to people already in the profession.
title: Helping an Accounting Business Hire Better Talent

text: A partnership makes sense only if the other person has something you lack: money, skills, time, network or distribution. If both partners are the same, one of them is unnecessary.
title: Helping a Young Entrepreneur Decide If He Needs a Partner

text: Two similar partners will likely clash over effort levels, since each rates their own work higher than the other's, so a partnership between equals tends to break down.
title: Helping a Young Entrepreneur Decide If He Needs a Partner

text: He cites Rockefeller: great businesses rarely come out of great friendships, but great friendships often come out of great businesses. Starting with a business then becoming friends is much easier than the reverse.
title: Helping a Young Entrepreneur Decide If He Needs a Partner

text: Which path to take depends on your goal. Decide the income target first, then choose the path most likely to reach it. Owning 5% of a small company will not get you to $50 million.
title: Helping a Young Entrepreneur Decide If He Needs a Partner

text: He thinks it is greatly undervalued for someone starting out to work at a company scaling from roughly 15 to 100 people, since you learn how to do it right while someone else carries the risk.
title: Helping a Young Entrepreneur Decide If He Needs a Partner

text: If your goal is only around $100,000 a year, you can simply go sell right now and ignore his advice; a much larger goal suggests a different path.
title: Helping a Young Entrepreneur Decide If He Needs a Partner

text: Whether a business can be sold depends on its underlying economics, not its category. A school group, an Amazon store or a dry cleaner is sellable if the fundamentals are strong, and not if they are weak.
title: How to Build a Business Someone Wants to Buy

text: A sellable business example he gives: 80% annual customer retention, very high gross margins, several channels bringing in customers, and no reliance on the owner. He says such a business is absolutely sellable.
title: How to Build a Business Someone Wants to Buy

text: For an ecommerce store, what makes it a business is the product, the customers, the reviews, the brand and the awareness, rather than the platform it runs on.
title: How to Build a Business Someone Wants to Buy

text: When someone is not doing a task such as recruiting, Hormozi checks five possible causes: they don't know it's needed, don't know how, don't know when, something blocks them, or they lack motivation.
title: You Need to Hire Better Talent

text: Hormozi challenges the words have to and can't, pushing people to restate them as choose to and won't, so they see that their involvement in everything is a choice.
title: You Need to Hire Better Talent

text: He solves problems from back to front. Fix churn first in the existing flow, because the workforce may grow enough on its own. Only if a shortfall remains should you tackle attraction.
title: \"Nobody Applies. Nobody Stays. What Now?\"

text: He argues that in a business like cleaning, you cannot get huge leverage from one exceptional hire, and pay sits in a narrow range, so hunting for top talent has limited payoff. The core work is the training and people problem.
title: \"Nobody Applies. Nobody Stays. What Now?\"

text: He says the people problem is a permanent feature of this business, so most focus should go to the supply side: take almost anyone in and get them productive in 14 days, keeping them through a clear career path.
title: \"Nobody Applies. Nobody Stays. What Now?\"

text: Break what makes great employees great into observable actions rather than vague traits. Being upbeat is unhelpful; specific behaviors like smiling, nodding while others talk, and answering requests with a set phrase can be taught and roleplayed. He says this applies to AI too.
title: \"Nobody Applies. Nobody Stays. What Now?\"

text: He believes it costs almost as much to train one person as five, so recruit and train in cohorts or classes; more people also lets trainees pair off and roleplay.
title: \"Nobody Applies. Nobody Stays. What Now?\"

text: His roleplay training sequence: open with kudos for what people did well, have the trainer model the correct behavior, then split into pairs to roleplay with real-time feedback.
title: \"Nobody Applies. Nobody Stays. What Now?\"

text: Once culture is installed, managers can have staff give kudos to each other. This lets reinforcement happen without the leader and is how he says culture spreads.
title: \"Nobody Applies. Nobody Stays. What Now?\"

text: When you hit a capacity constraint, you must either sacrifice profit by paying to build capacity, or push more demand and accept a hit to your metrics or reputation.
title: Helping a B2B SAAS Scale

text: He thinks the point where you stop loving your avatar, the customer you serve, is when the pull to move on from a business appears.
title: Helping a B2B SAAS Scale

text: He believes Gym Launch could have exited for around 400 million with very little changed. At the time he saw no way to make it bigger, so he sold it.
title: Helping a B2B SAAS Scale

text: Early on his team assumed they were better than a competitor because they burned people, then realized clients simply have to do the work themselves, and blaming providers is what frustrated him.
title: Helping a B2B SAAS Scale

text: Fear of regulation ending a business overnight is usually overblown: bills are visible in advance, must be voted on, take effect later, and often include a phase-in period, so there tends to be more time than people assume.
title: Helping a Wholesale Business Doing $22M/Year Get to $50M/Year

text: He prefers to operate one way until real information changes, because otherwise you get stuck in uncertainty about what to do, and you can stay stuck indefinitely.
title: Helping a Wholesale Business Doing $22M/Year Get to $50M/Year

text: Using Ray Dalio as an example, he notes that predicting collapse for about 14 years while being almost right would have meant missing a great stock market growth period if you had held gold throughout.
title: Helping a Wholesale Business Doing $22M/Year Get to $50M/Year

text: Capitalize on an opportunity while it exists. Once you get a heads-up that it is ending, you can shift aggressively to selling other products through your existing distribution base.
title: Helping a Wholesale Business Doing $22M/Year Get to $50M/Year

text: Guessing the future is hard, so he would rather act on the information available now and change behavior once that information changes.
title: Helping a Wholesale Business Doing $22M/Year Get to $50M/Year

text: Hormozi says a business needing skilled labor has hard problems, but that difficulty makes it hard for others to copy you. The bigger the problem you solve, the bigger the price tag attached.
title: You Think Your Business Can't Scale. You're Wrong

text: He says the common brick-and-mortar mistake is opening a second location once one works only so-so. Attention splits, so both end up weak. He says you usually must fix the first model, sometimes by closing one.
title: You Think Your Business Can't Scale. You're Wrong

text: His rule of thumb for a service business is at least 80 percent gross margin, and he prefers 90 percent.
title: You Think Your Business Can't Scale. You're Wrong

text: Hormozi says a business that gets customers only from organic search and referrals has not capped its market; it has only capped people who find it unaided. Not advertising is the real gap.
title: You Think Your Business Can't Scale. You're Wrong

text: He explains that adding ad spend eats margin, so higher gross margin matters. Filling classes with more people at the same instructor cost raises profit directly.
title: You Think Your Business Can't Scale. You're Wrong

text: For a visual offer like dance, he suggests filming a group moving together on a phone, running it as an Instagram ad, leaving out the price, and selling over the phone.
title: You Think Your Business Can't Scale. You're Wrong

text: When selling to a group at once, he says to score or qualify attendees. Knowing what share are sellable leads makes close rates far steadier, whereas mixed quality makes results swing wildly.
title: \"My Funnel Stopped Working. Do I Fix It or Replace It?\"

text: He says that with good list quality, booking a call from a webinar can typically reach about 20 percent, versus the caller's 10 percent.
title: \"My Funnel Stopped Working. Do I Fix It or Replace It?\"

text: He says you can send ad traffic directly to a webinar without a lead magnet, provided the webinar's promise is compelling.
title: \"My Funnel Stopped Working. Do I Fix It or Replace It?\"

text: He explains that modern ad platforms personalize feeds, so the goal shifts from converting everyone to covering many small audience segments. Callouts can be literal text or visuals like clothing or age of the person shown.
title: \"My Funnel Stopped Working. Do I Fix It or Replace It?\"

text: He says the downside of segment-specific ads is volume: covering a hundred segments demands roughly a hundred times the creative, though results can be the best advertising has produced.
title: \"My Funnel Stopped Working. Do I Fix It or Replace It?\"

text: He says the more personalized a funnel is to one audience from ad through webinar, the better it converts, though it costs more work.
title: \"My Funnel Stopped Working. Do I Fix It or Replace It?\"

text: He says he would not stop an existing revenue flow until another flow has been built to replace it, and ideally he prefers never stopping flows at all.
title: Her Biggest Customer Is Her Biggest Competitor

text: When ad spend and lifetime value to acquisition cost are not the problem, and the only limit is the number of ads, he sees the constraint as creative volume, which he considers very solvable.
title: Her Biggest Customer Is Her Biggest Competitor

text: He suggests a target of around 50 ad creatives per week, and says producing that many is not hard, possibly doable in about an hour and a half of filming, followed by a couple of editors.
title: Her Biggest Customer Is Her Biggest Competitor

text: Your best-performing organic pieces are the ones you would put more money behind anyway. The main addition for paid is a lower-third banner with a call to action, or a slice at the end offering a freebie or lead magnet.
title: Her Biggest Customer Is Her Biggest Competitor

text: Content output works like an accordion. Making many pieces reveals a few that dominate results, so you cut to fewer, better pieces, then raise volume again at that quality, and repeat the cycle.
title: How Small Brands Should Think About Content Strategy

text: Extremely high-volume posting suits news channels because the content is supplied to them, but news has almost no long tail since it becomes irrelevant once the day or week ends.
title: How Small Brands Should Think About Content Strategy

text: For educators, quality matters more than almost anything, but you cannot tell what quality is until you have made enough repetitions to see what works and what does not.
title: How Small Brands Should Think About Content Strategy

text: He prescribes volume first for beginners because it produces a large data set. For example, after a hundred videos you can study why ten outperformed the other ninety; before that, learning is very hard.
title: How Small Brands Should Think About Content Strategy

text: Hormozi suggests placing a walkthrough video of what is included either at the very top of a sales page or at the end, so it lands at the start or the close.
title: Fixing a Fitness Coach’s Sales Page

text: He cites peak-end bias for video: viewers remember the emotional peak and how the video finishes, so key content belongs at the beginning or the end.
title: Fixing a Fitness Coach’s Sales Page

text: Testimonial slides that are hard to read get skimmed. He would use fewer, around one to three of the most meaningful, and highlight the key text so eyes go there.
title: Fixing a Fitness Coach’s Sales Page

text: Fundamentally, sales bullets say what you get and what it solves: this so you gain a benefit, or this so you avoid a bad thing. More good or less bad.
title: Fixing a Fitness Coach’s Sales Page

text: Value comes down to making results faster, easier, or more guaranteed. He likes to emphasize one of those three in each bullet.
title: Fixing a Fitness Coach’s Sales Page

text: For each feature tile, he would show a picture of the feature with one testimonial laid over it, ideally one that addresses the biggest obstacle for that feature.
title: Fixing a Fitness Coach’s Sales Page

text: Group programs offer one-to-many access rather than one-on-one, so he says to show whatever degrees of access buyers get and lead with that if it is compelling.
title: Fixing a Fitness Coach’s Sales Page

text: He thinks emojis versus check marks or bullets probably will not have a big effect on conversion, though it could be tested at scale.
title: Fixing a Fitness Coach’s Sales Page

text: Customers from inbound, intent-based sources tend to compare prices, while interruption-based ad buyers were not shopping around. So a premium of around 30% can work on interruption-based traffic if the offer is tweaked.
title: The Real Reason Your Business Isn't Scaling (It's Not CAC)

text: You can ethically run two different prices by adding one small differentiating element to the offer, so each channel gets a slightly different offer at its own price.
title: The Real Reason Your Business Isn't Scaling (It's Not CAC)

text: If you want upfront cash but prefer memberships, sell a membership that is prepaid for a set period, such as six months, then let it roll to month to month afterwards.
title: The Real Reason Your Business Isn't Scaling (It's Not CAC)

text: For a local business, reaching one customer group rather than another is done more through the messaging than through ad targeting.
title: The Real Reason Your Business Isn't Scaling (It's Not CAC)

text: He says scattered, overwhelmed thinking comes from fear of being left behind. His stance is to trust that he will change when something becomes significant enough to affect his business, and until then keep doing what works.
title: The Only 3 Things That Actually Make You Money

text: He says a conversion step like a sales script or webinar rarely needs remaking once it is known to convert; it can be automated or run weekly. The real input is more people learning about the offer.
title: The Only 3 Things That Actually Make You Money

text: He advises most people to spend the majority of their time promoting, and to go two levels deeper on the problem so it shows up in content or ads and creates differentiation.
title: The Only 3 Things That Actually Make You Money

text: As a simple split of the working day, he suggests a third promoting, a third building the product, and a third delivering it, with a timer and sticking to each block.
title: The Only 3 Things That Actually Make You Money

text: He defines focus as doing one thing, so anything else makes you less focused. He calls the ultimate productivity hack saying no, while accepting that some non-focus is unavoidable.
title: The Only 3 Things That Actually Make You Money

text: Once something begins to work, he says keep doing it until it stops working, and do not stop out of fear it will stop. Repeat successful actions. He notes even high-level entrepreneurs need reminding of this.
title: The Only 3 Things That Actually Make You Money

text: He says conversion and fixed delivery involve little volume, so the part you must actively do is the input: content and paid. He says that with the two now merged, it is finding good content and putting money behind it.
title: The Only 3 Things That Actually Make You Money

text: He lists traffic, conversion rate and churn as the places a problem may sit, and he says most people never even start on them.
title: The Only 3 Things That Actually Make You Money

text: He says early on he consumed lots of courses because he had nothing to test. Once acting, first-party data from doing the work is more accurate and relevant than third-party data of others' opinions.
title: The Only 3 Things That Actually Make You Money

text: He says with first-party data you can tune out most outside noise, because anything that truly matters will show up in your own data. He tries to work out what he can ignore.
title: The Only 3 Things That Actually Make You Money

text: When conversion is the problem, consume one video on it, take the handful of ideas, and try them all before consuming more. Until then more content adds nothing.
title: The Only 3 Things That Actually Make You Money

text: He passes along a rule from a colleague: do not change things while a solution is already on the way. Changing a test mid-run wastes it, so let enough repetitions occur to get feedback.
title: The Only 3 Things That Actually Make You Money

text: Once you have data, he says the next issue is wanting to try too many things, which is where strategy, meaning allocation of resources, matters.
title: The Only 3 Things That Actually Make You Money

text: He says the core of entrepreneurship is choosing: with limited time, money and energy, pick the option most likely to yield the biggest outcome.
title: The Only 3 Things That Actually Make You Money

text: He says most people lack the traffic to make AB testing meaningful, and they change pages too often. He suggests leaving a change alone at least a week at their traffic level.
title: The Only 3 Things That Actually Make You Money

text: He describes cowboy testing: change something and watch whether the number goes up or down. He says he often gets away with it, even at his company with heavy traffic, where few AB tests run.
title: The Only 3 Things That Actually Make You Money

text: In price-driven markets like construction, he says there are three ways to win: speed, risk, or ease. Pick at least one, and he prefers to lead with a single one.
title: Niche So Boring Nobody Competes (80 Deals/Yr)

text: When selling to business people, he suggests framing it as a logical dollars-and-cents sale. Get agreement that paying more now to save more later beats paying less and incurring larger costs.
title: Niche So Boring Nobody Competes (80 Deals/Yr)

text: He suggests gathering statistics on how often unforeseen costs occur, then presenting the top problems with their percentages. This anchors the buyer on far larger costs than your fee and shifts the price context.
title: Niche So Boring Nobody Competes (80 Deals/Yr)

text: Where subscriptions do not fit, he says the goal is reoccurring rather than recurring business, coming from nodes of referrals. He compares it to Coca-Cola, which is reoccurring rather than recurring.
title: Niche So Boring Nobody Competes (80 Deals/Yr)

text: With his software company, small business owners struggled because they lacked leads. Targeting agency owners, who onboarded around 50 clients at a time, made agency-level churn nearly zero, and he redefined the business as agency servicing.
title: Niche So Boring Nobody Competes (80 Deals/Yr)

text: He approaches referrals by partnering with referrers so their introductions frame the conversation toward a likely close and the pricing he wants. He treats referral partners as the real customers and builds a sales process to win more of them.
title: Niche So Boring Nobody Competes (80 Deals/Yr)
