text: He describes three affiliate structures. One: partners sell a small piece of your service and keep all of it, and you upsell afterward. Two: they sell your whole offer for a percentage. Three: lead gen with kickbacks later.
title: Niche So Boring Nobody Competes (80 Deals/Yr)

text: He advises building a customer journey for referral partners such as consultants, since they are the ones who keep sending business month after month.
title: Niche So Boring Nobody Competes (80 Deals/Yr)

text: He sold an upsell at his book launch, where donors gave an extra $18,000 of stuff for roughly 1,000 more books at a discount, using only an 11-minute video and a button, with no sales call.
title: You Don’t Need a Sales Team

text: Once a brand is strong enough, you can present an offer without making promises, simply pointing to the good results from everything else bought from you. Keeping that promise lets the cycle repeat on the next offer.
title: You Don’t Need a Sales Team

text: He defines the brand loop as what you say about yourself, then what others say about you, and finally what the customer thinks after you deliver, which is the last point in the cycle.
title: You Don’t Need a Sales Team

text: Starting a paid community has essentially no setup cost beyond hosting it, so the real work is building a strong offer, which he models on promise, plan, and proof.
title: Watch This Before Starting a Skool Community

text: He says the setup that seems to convert best for most people is two communities: a free lead-magnet community containing five videos (essentially the VSL) and a weekly call, which gives value and softly introduces the paid community holding everything else.
title: Watch This Before Starting a Skool Community

text: For organic traffic, the call to action goes on stories and posts, sending people to the free community, where the weekly call does the pitching toward the paid one.
title: Watch This Before Starting a Skool Community

text: To convert even more free members to paid, add a third mechanism: a free onboarding call for everyone who joins, alongside the weekly call selling one-to-many and an automated selling system aimed at those who watched all five videos.
title: Watch This Before Starting a Skool Community

text: His way of thinking about conversion is to ask how many different ways he can drive people to buy, stacking several selling mechanisms to convert as many free people as possible into paid.
title: Watch This Before Starting a Skool Community

text: Hormozi advises focusing on a single market rather than splitting across languages, choosing either English or French, instead of running offers in both.
title: You Don't Need the US Market to Build a $20M Business

text: He says a million-dollar business can be built in France, and criticizes the common obsession with needing to go to the US just because it is bigger.
title: You Don't Need the US Market to Build a $20M Business

text: He compares populations: France at roughly 70 million versus the US at about 300 million, around one fifth. So instead of a hundred-million-dollar business, you could build a 20 million one there, and expand later if happy with that.
title: You Don't Need the US Market to Build a $20M Business

text: He advises dropping the assumption that employees have hijacked, addicted brains. You cannot untrain anything; you can only train additional or better behaviors.
title: How to Get Distracted Employees to Actually Focus

text: He defines culture as the rules governing reinforcement: a long list of small behaviors, like arriving on time, that are either rewarded or not. Unpunished, unrewarded behaviors spread or persist.
title: How to Get Distracted Employees to Actually Focus

text: The method is to catch every instance of someone doing the right thing and reward it immediately, so that you become the source of the dopamine hit.
title: How to Get Distracted Employees to Actually Focus

text: Some negative reinforcement is fine, provided you give far more positive reinforcement. The positive builds the right to correct someone, otherwise you are just a hated boss.
title: How to Get Distracted Employees to Actually Focus

text: He posted a Slack request to sort through about 500 DMs from a job post; nobody responded for 40 minutes among 18 people, and he was livid until a leader stepped in.
title: How to Get Distracted Employees to Actually Focus

text: Leader stepping up on a task below his pay grade gave Hormozi a public moment to reinforce company values and show why that person has advanced.
title: How to Get Distracted Employees to Actually Focus

text: Be more public with praise and more private with criticism, and make it crystal clear what is rewarded and what is not.
title: How to Get Distracted Employees to Actually Focus

text: Reinforcing culture never ends, because new hires bring their own rules. Unless you overpower them, theirs become the norm, so culture dilutes as a company scales and leaders must be more militant about their beliefs.
title: How to Get Distracted Employees to Actually Focus

text: Lead the page with the most concrete, valuable outcome in the offer. For this videographer, that is earning $250 for a video that takes about an hour, instead of a low hourly rate.
title: How to Charge $250 an Hour as a Videographer

text: Structure a sales page around promise, proof and plan: state the result, show the method that delivers it, then show other people who achieved it. Proof like payment account snapshots makes the promise feel real.
title: How to Charge $250 an Hour as a Videographer

text: He does not think telling buyers he is not gatekeeping secrets converts. Buyers purchase because they want the outcome, so the page must make the promise believable.
title: How to Charge $250 an Hour as a Videographer

text: Define vague terms concretely. Instead of exclusive access or resources, say exactly what the buyer gets, such as direct messaging and calls during set hours. Marketing jargon leaves people not understanding.
title: How to Charge $250 an Hour as a Videographer

text: A core secret of good copywriting is simply telling people what the thing is, in plain and specific terms.
title: How to Charge $250 an Hour as a Videographer

text: Sell around the promise by showing the math: 20 hours a week at $250 is $5,000 a week, roughly $200,000 a year. The rest of the page then convinces them it will happen for them.
title: How to Charge $250 an Hour as a Videographer

text: In B2B offers, the worth of the result is usually obvious. The hard part is making buyers believe it will work for them, so effort goes into lowering risk and perceived friction.
title: How to Charge $250 an Hour as a Videographer

text: List every question a buyer would have and show you have already solved each one, such as outreach scripts, post ideas, contracts, invoices and payment setup. This makes success feel achievable.
title: How to Charge $250 an Hour as a Videographer

text: For each bonus, repeat a cycle: what it is, what it does for the buyer, why it matters, what it is worth, what it cost you to create, and that they get it now instead of paying that time and effort.
title: How to Charge $250 an Hour as a Videographer

text: He thinks many communities neglect qualifications. Who is inside the community is part of the offer, and he considers it the most underrated component, more than leaning hard on a Grand Slam Offer.
title: The Biggest Mistake Community Businesses Make With Offers

text: Like a party with a doorman, a community where everyone gets in becomes odd. Not everyone belongs, so be firm about removing people, framing it as a mismatch in vibe rather than calling them bad.
title: The Biggest Mistake Community Businesses Make With Offers

text: A community means drawing a line in the sand. Holding that line early cuts the work needed later, and he says self-policing, retention, gross margins and affiliate referrals all go up.
title: The Biggest Mistake Community Businesses Make With Offers

text: Curating strictly takes longer at first because you must turn down money. He says if you refuse money for at least six months, you shape the culture and brand of the community, which then spreads and must be protected.
title: The Biggest Mistake Community Businesses Make With Offers

text: He compares a community to a garden: it takes time to grow, and you must keep weeding. He says people are not aggressive enough about removing members because they like seeing recurring revenue rise; he has removed people paying $3,000 a month.
title: The Biggest Mistake Community Businesses Make With Offers

text: Generally, the harder a team or club is to get into, the better it is, but starting that way is difficult. He describes an accordion swinging between quantity first, then selecting, then overcorrecting and letting more in.
title: The Biggest Mistake Community Businesses Make With Offers

text: Set objective entry standards: for B2B, things like revenue, customer count, headcount or investable assets; for consumer communities, demographic criteria such as a woman over 45 with at least two kids.
title: The Biggest Mistake Community Businesses Make With Offers

text: Look at who the most active community members are, which the platform shows, then find more people like them. This narrows messaging, and with enough traffic it becomes a snowball.
title: The Biggest Mistake Community Businesses Make With Offers

text: The goal is a network effect where the community itself attracts more of the same people. In the short term you sell services like one-on-one calls, and he says that is fine.
title: The Biggest Mistake Community Businesses Make With Offers

text: Hormozi says adding qualification to a funnel will make significantly more money. He can barely recall a time when adding qualification friction cost him money.
title: You need to sell to less people.

text: When qualification is added, cost per call or per click will probably rise, but customer acquisition cost may fall and lifetime value will certainly rise, according to him.
title: You need to sell to less people.

text: Screening out unqualified prospects lifts close rate and also helps the sales team overall, since reps are no longer worn down by hearing no all day.
title: You need to sell to less people.

text: People fear going from general to specific, but going specific attracts the right people.
title: You need to sell to less people.

text: To define the avatar, study all current customers: who they are, measurable traits, geography, and ideally whether their sales-process experience differed from lower-value customers.
title: You need to sell to less people.

text: Once the avatar is known, weave it into ad callouts, landing pages, question dropdowns, funnel friction and the VSL, opening the VSL with that avatar's pains and hook. He says this will surely raise conversion.
title: You need to sell to less people.

text: Early on, a business owner need not worry about entity structure for future investors. Being profitable draws interest, and reincorporating during a sale is common and part of the negotiation. An LLC for protection is enough.
title: The Only Two Real Tax Shelters That Actually Hold Up

text: Acquirers often prefer buying assets because liability stays with the old LLC, but founders then owe regular income tax. Founders prefer selling the whole entity so liability moves to the buyer and gains are capital gains. This depends on country and is negotiated at sale.
title: The Only Two Real Tax Shelters That Actually Hold Up

text: When selling Gym Launch, the buyer's first offer was an asset purchase. His team declined and pushed for selling the entity along with its liability, and the deal was changed.
title: The Only Two Real Tax Shelters That Actually Hold Up

text: Structure matters little now because firms such as Acquisition.com, Sequoia and A16Z each want different setups (C Corp, S Corp, LLC), so buyers will restructure the business to fit anyway.
title: The Only Two Real Tax Shelters That Actually Hold Up

text: Many businesses the team looks at have been misled by strip mall CPAs promising tax avoidance. Their lawyer is frustrated by the wrong advice they have received.
title: The Only Two Real Tax Shelters That Actually Hold Up

text: He names two big real tax shelters: real estate professionals who can apply 100% of depreciation against regular income, and charitable foundations.
title: The Only Two Real Tax Shelters That Actually Hold Up

text: He says donating up to 30% of income to a charitable foundation keeps that portion untaxed, which he estimates saves roughly nine percent on regular income.
title: The Only Two Real Tax Shelters That Actually Hold Up

text: Where you live is the biggest tax lever. He argues the gap between a 50% and 37% rate is about a third in take-home terms, so move to tax-efficient jurisdictions.
title: The Only Two Real Tax Shelters That Actually Hold Up

text: Business owners can run some living expenses through the business as pre-tax money. Beyond that, he stays strictly by the book, removing anything that could sink the company.
title: The Only Two Real Tax Shelters That Actually Hold Up

text: Over the first five or six years, he was pitched tax-saving vehicles and nearly did one; after judging the promoter shady, they passed, and the man later went to prison. This happened about three times.
title: The Only Two Real Tax Shelters That Actually Hold Up

text: He cites Charlie Munger: about 95% of tax-saving schemes, even if legal now, get ruled illegal and unwound within five years, leaving back taxes, interest and penalties. The IRS lags years behind, letting sellers pitch them.
title: The Only Two Real Tax Shelters That Actually Hold Up

text: The legitimate remainder usually falls into real estate or charitable structures, but he questions whether sifting through the many bad ones is worth the time versus making more money.
title: The Only Two Real Tax Shelters That Actually Hold Up

text: Be wary of accountants who advertise by how much they will save you. He prefers a by-the-book professional who outlines strategies and the law behind them, and often just pays the tax and earns more.
title: The Only Two Real Tax Shelters That Actually Hold Up

text: Structural churn is churn built into an industry itself. Example: a gym CRM owner reported about 3% monthly churn because roughly a third of gyms close each year, so product improvements cannot fix it.
title: Helping a $1M Cold Email Agency Get to $10M

text: Large agencies like Ogilvy, NP Digital and Vayner serve Fortune 100 clients, which he says pay on time, have sales staff and process, have margins, and keep the contracts they sign.
title: Helping a $1M Cold Email Agency Get to $10M

text: He suggests an agency is likely not in the wrong business but may be serving the wrong customer. A useful exercise is comparing long-tenured clients with newly arriving ones, since the two groups may look different.
title: Helping a $1M Cold Email Agency Get to $10M

text: If a needed trait such as sales ability is hard to test for, set a requirement that guarantees it, such as a minimum company size. A $5 million a year agency must know how to sell.
title: Helping a $1M Cold Email Agency Get to $10M

text: If a cheap, simple test lets him go a little lower market, that is fine to him; otherwise he sets a firm bar that customers must meet.
title: Helping a $1M Cold Email Agency Get to $10M

text: He thinks many people have a business model better suited to bigger customers, charge too little, and see churn. They then keep adding guarantees or onboarding steps, which do not help because volatile customers stay volatile.
title: Helping a $1M Cold Email Agency Get to $10M

text: When two paths both lead up the mountain, he says obsessing over the perfect one wastes time. Recognizing that either works lets him make big decisions faster.
title: Helping a Law Firm Get to $20M/Year

text: He evaluates a move by asking how to maximize the risk-adjusted return on it.
title: Helping a Law Firm Get to $20M/Year

text: He dislikes making his growth depend on someone else opening a business and doing it well; he prefers going where the customers (fish) already are.
title: Helping a Law Firm Get to $20M/Year

text: If someone cannot sit still, ignore notifications, and stay on a single task for a full day, he says they should not expect to build anything great.
title: The 8-Hour Rule That Separates Winners From Losers

text: He says he knows no highly successful entrepreneur who lacks the ability to enter hyper-focused stretches, sometimes whole weekends or weeks without talking to anyone, working relentlessly on coding, marketing campaigns, product design, or mass hiring.
title: The 8-Hour Rule That Separates Winners From Losers

text: Greatness is driven by what a goal requires, not by what you want or whether it suits your strengths. There is a price tag, and you must be willing to pay it or you do not get the result.
title: The 8-Hour Rule That Separates Winners From Losers

text: He spends time countering the follow-your-passion idea, believing it misleads more people than it helps. Successful people who have delegated heavily and now work in their area of genius can wrongly tell others to copy their current work.
title: The 8-Hour Rule That Separates Winners From Losers

text: The behavior pattern that produces financial success can also produce dissatisfaction with life, because building a business means constantly looking for what is wrong and how to improve or fix it.
title: The Trait That Makes You Rich Can Make You Miserable

text: Continually raising the bar helps a business grow, but it can leave a person with a lasting sense of deprivation, since by the time a goal is reached they see how it could have been done better.
title: The Trait That Makes You Rich Can Make You Miserable

text: He jokes about a team member with this trait: if an event went well, he should have pushed harder, and if it went poorly, he made mistakes. So no outcome ever feels good.
title: The Trait That Makes You Rich Can Make You Miserable

text: He thinks the answer is learning when to apply the flaw-hunting pattern and when not to, by asking under which conditions it is useful and under which it is harmful.
title: The Trait That Makes You Rich Can Make You Miserable

text: Communities keep low churn when they deliver something consumable every week, like trending items or fresh deals, because last week's version loses value and members need the new one.
title: How an Online Coach Can Scale to $1M/Month

text: A one-time system is very valuable but can only be charged once. A smaller recurring charge works by selling the inputs the machine needs to keep producing output.
title: How an Online Coach Can Scale to $1M/Month

text: For beginner audiences, teach one to three business models that work, then sell the inputs. For medium and larger owners, the recurring value should be something else, likely network, access and group-negotiated discounts.
title: How an Online Coach Can Scale to $1M/Month

text: A big gap between the one-time charge and the recurring price is fine if it stays sticky. For example, $10,000 upfront then $500 monthly can hold if ongoing value exceeds the price.
title: How an Online Coach Can Scale to $1M/Month

text: Design the community so each added member adds value rather than diluting it. He describes that as a network effect.
title: How an Online Coach Can Scale to $1M/Month

text: To find out what a niche audience wants, go to places like Reddit forums and hop on calls with people. Doing that work reveals the wants and pain points that shape the promise you make.
title: You Might Make More Money From Affiliate Links Than Clients

text: The promise of an offer changes depending on the pain point. Saving money by growing your own vegetables is one promise, while being chemical-free within a year of using a system is a different promise.
title: You Might Make More Money From Affiliate Links Than Clients

text: In some niches, such as growing food at home, he thinks affiliate commissions on needed products like jars, seeds, soil, lights or watering gear may earn more than selling services to clients.
title: You Might Make More Money From Affiliate Links Than Clients

text: Some businesses suit a free community that supports the creator through affiliate links, which can give two potential income streams alongside any paid offering.
title: You Might Make More Money From Affiliate Links Than Clients

text: When earning through affiliate reviews, stay honest and never call a product good just because its commission is high. He says this earns the relationship with the community over the long term.
title: You Might Make More Money From Affiliate Links Than Clients

text: Running two offers at once, he promises, lowers the chance of succeeding at either one, so if you insist on a new offer, commit fully to it.
title: Stop the Side Hustle and Grow the Golden Goose

text: A new opportunity looks attractive because you only see its surface and have not yet met its problems, unlike the known flaws of your current business. He calls this a shiny object pattern.
title: Stop the Side Hustle and Grow the Golden Goose

text: Decide between offers with math, not feeling: you want the maximum LTV combined with conversion rate. An offer more people want, that converts better and has higher lifetime gross profit, is fundamentally superior.
title: Stop the Side Hustle and Grow the Golden Goose

text: To move from an old business model to a new one, keep selling the new offer up front until it exceeds the old business in revenue and profit, and stop replacing churned customers on the old side.
title: Stop the Side Hustle and Grow the Golden Goose

text: Questions like how much to invest versus consume have no fixed right answer. Going all-in on delayed gratification with no consumption leaves you with a life you did not enjoy, so treat these as continuums to manage, not problems to solve.
title: \"When Should You Quit a Business?\"

text: He frames quitting as a choice between pushing and pivoting. He will not quit if no new information has appeared; if the assumptions behind the original plan still hold, it is a push situation.
title: \"When Should You Quit a Business?\"

text: He would quit only when new data changes why he is pushing, what outcome pushing will bring, or shows that the way he is pushing is wrong.
title: \"When Should You Quit a Business?\"

text: He prefers the word pivot to quit because it is softer and language matters to him. In his view nothing counts as quitting unless you stop; continuing to push or pivot keeps you active, and you may stumble onto what works, then do more of it.
title: \"When Should You Quit a Business?\"

text: Even without the final outcome, look for leading indicators that show you are on the right path, and identify them ahead of time, as you would identify the problems that come with success.
title: \"When Should You Quit a Business?\"

text: Having small indicators along the way lets you keep taking steps toward the ultimate goal and keep pushing, even before reaching a huge outcome.
title: \"When Should You Quit a Business?\"

text: He says the world belongs to those who can keep working without seeing results, and it is usually whoever does so longest, because they still get leading indicators pointing to a bigger mountain.
title: \"When Should You Quit a Business?\"

text: To do something most people cannot, extend the time horizon on what most people cannot weather. Persisting on the correct path without positive reinforcement makes opportunities easier because few people can pursue them.
title: \"When Should You Quit a Business?\"

text: When a business wants growth, he starts by asking whether the current advertising method is maxed out, and says to aim for many times more customers than currently, so the current method must be increased first.
title: Helping a Coaching Business Scale

text: Fear of offering a guarantee is understandable, but it should be treated as a math problem: if it lets you close about twice as many people and you refund one in ten, you can still earn far more.
title: Helping a $1.3M Serivce Business Scale to $10M

text: A home services owner closing 80% but making no money raised prices 20% and guaranteed on-time, on-budget delivery, promising to forfeit all his profit (that 20%) if he failed. He then closed more customers and earned much more.
title: Helping a $1.3M Serivce Business Scale to $10M

text: To design a guarantee, ask what customers worry about most, then check how often you actually miss it and why. In the story, the contractor was on time and budget eight of ten jobs.
title: Helping a $1.3M Serivce Business Scale to $10M

text: Hormozi repeats advice from his first adult boss: working out what you want is 99% of the battle, and actually getting it is the easy part once you know.
title: Helping a Pest Control Company Get to $10M/Year

text: He thinks that if you stop judging yourself while you are still trying different things, you avoid constant existential worry about making the wrong choice and getting stuck in analysis paralysis.
title: Helping a Pest Control Company Get to $10M/Year

text: Getting 5% of a company makes you a holder of a stake in it, which is very different from being a real partner.
title: Helping a Pest Control Company Get to $10M/Year

text: Hormozi says he has taken companies through a 10-stage roadmap from zero to $100M+ multiple times, across software, physical products, services and brick and mortar, with stages set by headcount and broken down across eight business functions.
title: Helping a Pest Control Company Get to $10M/Year

text: He wants three things from any advice source: competence, context and alignment. Someone competent with context but misaligned incentives is dangerous, because they know exactly what would hurt you.
title: The Biggest Influence on My Life

text: He felt many modern therapies had misaligned incentives: he spent 90 minutes giving context to someone possibly less competent than him, whose incentive was for him to return next week.
title: The Biggest Influence on My Life

text: The Solomon Paradox: people gave wise advice to others yet failed to follow it themselves. Research reportedly shows people advise better when the situation is described as another person's than they act in their own.
title: The Biggest Influence on My Life

text: His ideal advisor has all three traits: his 85-year-old self, who has achieved what he wants and embodies desired traits. Every Monday's first hour, labeled Solomon on his calendar, he holds a written chat with him.
title: The Biggest Influence on My Life

text: The format can vary: a voice memo or video would work. He chooses writing because he thinks through writing. Sessions sometimes take only 7 minutes when he reaches the answer quickly.
title: The Biggest Influence on My Life

text: After a multi-year project went wrong because a vendor failed to deliver, costing about $15 million, his future-self session answered that he is the product being built, not the project, and his effort was enough.
title: The Biggest Influence on My Life

text: He stays motivated by trying to close the delta between his effort and total effort. He expects to be forgotten but wants to know at the end he left nothing in the tank.
title: The Biggest Influence on My Life

text: Friends and therapists can be enrolled in your version of events, and you can even enroll yourself. Going deeper to a future-self view reveals that part of you knows the real truth.
title: The Biggest Influence on My Life

text: The Solomon frame removes external judgment, since you imagine facing your 85-year-old self. He also imagines waking up as that older self, which gives him a fun gratitude exercise despite finding gratitude lists hard.
title: The Biggest Influence on My Life

text: When hesitating over selling his company, he realized the worry was about the opinions of just two people. Naming them made it concrete, and his future self helped show that was a silly reason to hold back.
title: The Biggest Influence on My Life

text: He thinks what everyone else believes you should do is probably not the right thing, and the future-self frame helps separate that from what you actually want.
title: The Biggest Influence on My Life

text: He says he enjoyed even the grueling daily presentation prep over a month, because he felt he was becoming his best self and living by the values he chose.
title: Stop Waiting to Find Your Passion. Create It

text: He thinks people will not identify their true north on the first attempt, and suggests learning to work is an easier guiding star to start with.
title: Stop Waiting to Find Your Passion. Create It

text: He argues you will not simply find a passion, since anything new you begin, you will be bad at first, and people tend to like what they are good at. Being willing to be bad is a prerequisite.
title: Stop Waiting to Find Your Passion. Create It

text: He told of a friend who left a fitness business to open a cookie store, driven not by cookies but by a wish to be excellent at whatever he did; that single value carried across ventures.
title: Stop Waiting to Find Your Passion. Create It

text: For someone starting out, he advises committing to the repetitive daily actions without reward and learning what hard work feels like; long term, make that the win, and just win each day without focusing on arriving.
title: Stop Waiting to Find Your Passion. Create It

text: He says dedicating yourself to excellence and repetition makes you better, and people tend to like things once they get better at them. You need just enough motivation at the start, then outside reinforcement takes over.
title: Stop Waiting to Find Your Passion. Create It

text: He says lifting works for him like ping pong: with heavy weight on your back you cannot think of anything else, and he cites Dave Tate describing the bar as making the world go quiet.
title: Stop Waiting to Find Your Passion. Create It

text: If unit economics work and hiring and onboarding can be modeled in a spreadsheet, a firm is probably already growing about as fast as its hiring and ramp-up allow. He says there are only two ways to go faster.
title: Increasing Cash Flow in a Consulting Firm

text: The other way to grow faster is raising money through equity. He calls it a classic venture play: a big opportunity, fast growth, and a need to fund hiring.
title: Increasing Cash Flow in a Consulting Firm

text: If customers starting a journey (fitness, business, anything new) need a handful of tools, affiliate relationships on those tools can usually cover the full cost of the person who handles onboarding.
title: How to Make More Money When Onboarding New Clients

text: He gave his onboarding rep a KPI: click his affiliate links together with each new client during setup, so every single person signed up through them, rather than leaving it to chance.
title: How to Make More Money When Onboarding New Clients

text: At Gym Launch, affiliate income from this process reached roughly 5 to 6 thousand dollars a month within the first month, which paid for the onboarding rep, and every month after was profitable.
title: How to Make More Money When Onboarding New Clients

text: If you hesitate to hire an onboarding person and your onboarding involves clients setting up tools, you can make that role a profit center through affiliate commissions.
title: How to Make More Money When Onboarding New Clients

text: Not knowing what you're doing is normal. If you already knew, you would be doing nothing new and therefore stagnating; doing something new is the catalyst for growth.
title: You’re Not Supposed to Know What You’re Doing

text: He argues people suffer discontent because they want opposites: strong character and an easy life, or growth without hardship. He says hardship creates growth, and one is the price of the other.
title: You’re Not Supposed to Know What You’re Doing

text: He compares growth to wanting the Jordans without paying: the price is simply what it is. Either pay it and be happy with the result, or skip the purchase, but don't complain about the price.
title: You’re Not Supposed to Know What You’re Doing

text: Beginners shouldn't expect to look or feel like they know what they're doing just because successful people appear that way. You are a white belt while they are a high-degree black belt in that field.
title: You’re Not Supposed to Know What You’re Doing

text: He says the evidence of your own results can disprove your advice before you speak. Examples: a tiny social account teaching growth, a relationship train wreck advising on relationships, an unfit person giving fitness advice.
title: You’re Not Supposed to Know What You’re Doing

text: Ask which single big domino would make everything else take care of itself, then do it. He says effort spent on anything that avoids that domino is wasted. Example: a fitness marketer who looks shredded can sell almost anything.
title: You’re Not Supposed to Know What You’re Doing

text: An employee should work out how their job directly ties to business revenue, and if they do not know, they should ask. Once they understand the link, they should push effort toward it.
title: The Question Every Employee Should Ask Their Boss

text: He says every position in a business should make the business more money if the job is well designed; otherwise there is no reason for the role to exist.
title: The Question Every Employee Should Ask Their Boss

text: Even a front-line customer service rep can tie their work to revenue: good service brings repeat purchases, fewer refunds, and supports higher prices through word of mouth. They can then focus on those drivers.
title: The Question Every Employee Should Ask Their Boss

text: Ask your boss what it would take for you to earn a specific amount, rather than stating you need it. This asks them to solve the problem and can yield an objective metric; if the boss lacks authority, ask them to check with the person above.
title: The Question Every Employee Should Ask Their Boss

text: When asking, make clear you want to make the business more money, and request a small percentage of the increase you are able to bring.
title: The Question Every Employee Should Ask Their Boss

text: He thinks small businesses are a good place for employees who want growth, since in a massive corporation you can cap out and get lost. A name-brand employer can serve as a stamp of approval to leverage into a smaller company.
title: The Question Every Employee Should Ask Their Boss

text: Most entrepreneurs are far more receptive to someone offering to help them make more money, and changing your environment often changes your behavior.
title: The Question Every Employee Should Ask Their Boss

text: Hormozi argues that few people in his life might even attend his funeral, so he questions why he should give weight to their opinions of what he does while he is alive.
title: Why I Don't Listen to People Who Can't Even Attend My Funeral

text: He says people rarely picture themselves as the one who dies. He finds it freeing that within about six months of his death people would barely mention him, so what he does today matters little, and he sees that as hopeful rather than hopeless.
title: Why I Don't Listen to People Who Can't Even Attend My Funeral

text: Learning is not a spectator activity and comes from doing. If you are not acting on the material you consume each day, you are not learning, just procrastinating.
title: Why I Don't Listen to People Who Can't Even Attend My Funeral

text: Hormozi defines intelligence as rate of learning, meaning it is a rate rather than a fixed attribute. He says this comes from his habit of operationalizing words.
title: Why I Don't Listen to People Who Can't Even Attend My Funeral

text: Learning means the same condition producing new behavior. If you attend a workshop and then repeat the same activities in the same conditions with no new behavior, he says you learned nothing, and your rate of learning is slow.

text: The hardest part of paid ads is targeting. A local business has an edge here: drop a pin on the map, pick a radius such as 10 miles, and show the ad to everyone inside it.

text: A founder can be a minority shareholder and still keep control. He points to Zuckerberg's 100-to-1 voting rights, and says it works when investors trust the founder and accept that reaching the goal needs more capital.

title: Helping a Stem Cell Clinic Scale

text: Before a raise, he talks to about ten times as many potential investment partners as he needs, collecting what each must believe. He then narrows the list by dropping unrealistic ones and picking those whose needs are affordable.
title: Helping a Stem Cell Clinic Scale

text: Sometimes one small need-to-believe, once satisfied, lets you build toward the next. He likens it to finding customers and building what they want, without letting that derail your vision or turn it into someone else's company.
title: Helping a Stem Cell Clinic Scale

text: He says investors are essentially trying to pay down risk, or have you pay it down for them. That is why control is very manageable in a raise.
title: Helping a Stem Cell Clinic Scale

title: Helping a Stem Cell Clinic Scale

text: Selling a business means selling an annuity, an annual recurring revenue stream. The buyer wants a return on it, then applies a discount based on risk that it keeps running, growing and staying profitable.
title: How to Sell a Community Business for the Most Money

text: The marketing system is what matters most when exiting a community, because it ties to the revenue. Buyers need to understand how customers arrive, not just that they exist.
title: How to Sell a Community Business for the Most Money

text: If a buyer sees customers staying about 3 months and has no clear view of how customers are acquired, the sale price might be only around 25% of annual revenue, a small exit.
title: How to Sell a Community Business for the Most Money

text: Value rises when you can prove people stay a year and show reliable, multiple acquisition sources, such as a team of outbound VAs or a network of around 20 influencer pages, rather than dependence on a single source.
title: How to Sell a Community Business for the Most Money

text: Sale value depends on how much of the business is an asset versus a job. The more the buyer has to do, the lower the value.
title: How to Sell a Community Business for the Most Money

text: Buying an asset that kicks off cash, like a building, is attractive because people are already in place and the buyer has little to do. Any asset with sellable characteristics can be sold.
title: How to Sell a Community Business for the Most Money

text: He recommends a decision test from Keith Cunningham: weigh the upside, weigh the downside, and ask whether you can live with the downside. If you cannot, do not do it. He adds how likely the downside is.
title: Helping a Wellness Clinic Scale

text: He says the more important question about a slower path, such as reaching 100M with the existing business in 10 to 15 years, is whether the owner is okay with that timeline. He calls it a risk tolerance decision.
title: Helping a Wellness Clinic Scale

text: He notes that other companies with lots of money and talent have not made this model profitable. He questions whether to bet on that instead of a business that is already good.
title: Helping a Wellness Clinic Scale

text: In insurance-reimbursed businesses you cannot control price, so you must control efficiency. He says winning comes from the bottom up, by cutting cost of goods, rather than from the top down.
title: Helping a Wellness Clinic Scale

text: He argues a 10-point margin improvement, for example from 75, would raise bottom-line profit by roughly 67 percent. He compares that to opening six more locations, which he thinks could be done in about six months.
title: Helping a Wellness Clinic Scale

text: His litmus test before licensing: first get the core business growing without the owner, by hiring capable people for disliked tasks and running an opening team for new locations. Then licensing becomes a reasonable outlet.
title: Helping a Wellness Clinic Scale

text: For a leadership team on salary, he would set aside a fixed share of profit, around 10 to 20 percent, as a pool, and let each leader receive a slice of that pool. The pool is capped, so the owner always keeps the rest.
title: Helping a Paid Ads Agency Build a Leadership Team

text: A capped pool pushes leaders to think like owners: bringing someone in means giving up part of the pie, so they should grow the pie. He notes this is the same logic founders apply whenever they hire.
title: Helping a Paid Ads Agency Build a Leadership Team

text: If a sale may come, a profits interest or sale bonus can be added to the profit share, sized in proportion to each person's share of the pool.
title: Helping a Paid Ads Agency Build a Leadership Team

text: A sale bonus in the US is taxed as income rather than capital gains. He sees no easy alternative, since giving real equity means gifting with taxes and risk, or making them buy it, which needs a valuation agreement.
title: Helping a Paid Ads Agency Build a Leadership Team

text: A simple structure: pay profit share now, pay a bonus if the company sells, and pay neither if the person leaves.
title: Helping a Paid Ads Agency Build a Leadership Team

text: Example of proportional math: with a 10 percent company profit share, someone holding 10 percent of that pool has 1 percent of profit, so they would receive 1 percent of the sale.
title: Helping a Paid Ads Agency Build a Leadership Team

text: When writing the sale bonus, define it as a percentage of cash received, not of the total headline value of the sale. He says he got burned on this before.
title: Helping a Paid Ads Agency Build a Leadership Team

text: On YouTube, consistency is what moves you from mediocre to good and solid. To reach great, you need continued improvement while staying consistent.
title: “I Have a Small YouTube Channel, How Do I Make Money ”

text: Someone who has only been seriously posting for about 8 weeks should not count the earlier inconsistent years as experience. He says they are very early and should not think about monetizing yet.
title: “I Have a Small YouTube Channel, How Do I Make Money ”

text: When a lead magnet is hard to make valuable because of tech-specific details, offer something people instantly see as valuable, such as five one-on-one calls. Five 30-minute sessions are understood as real value even at a basic level.
title: Helping a Consulting Firm Get More Leads

text: Five calls let you involve multiple stakeholders and run an enterprise-style sale. Set the frame at the start: the offer to explain how working together might look comes at the end of the fifth call, and meanwhile you provide value.
title: Helping a Consulting Firm Get More Leads

text: Use the calls to describe what will happen, not explain how to do it. Describing resets beliefs and excites people; walking through click-by-click steps loses them.
title: Helping a Consulting Firm Get More Leads

text: For his advice to the caller: content showing ROI, with a call to action of five one-on-one calls, restricted to people who qualify. The offer should center on ROI and use a calculator close.
title: Helping a Consulting Firm Get More Leads

text: When you hand a business to an operator, the test of readiness is how they answer problem scenarios such as an upset customer or a leaking ceiling: any answer other than calling you is the right one.
title: Helping a MedSpa Company Acquire Other MedSpas

text: When offering an operator an ownership position, he suggests framing it as their facility, not yours, so that they truly own it and you are free to go hunt for new opportunities.
title: Helping a MedSpa Company Acquire Other MedSpas

text: Rare talent comes from combining several skills, while commoditizing comes from breaking the work into chunks. Someone exceptional at support likely does three or four things well, so split those apart.
title: Helping an Online Coaching Business Fix His Offer

text: To replace himself as key man, he did not seek a better version of himself. He found separate people each as good as him at one function, such as phone sales or ads, even if weaker elsewhere.
title: Helping an Online Coaching Business Fix His Offer

text: Scaling a company replaces key man risk by chopping the unicorn's horn off: several people with more readily available skills together replace one rare person.
title: Helping an Online Coaching Business Fix His Offer

text: Breaking one person's skills into component parts makes them far easier to teach and removes the mysticism from the role.
title: Helping an Online Coaching Business Fix His Offer

text: The strategies he recommends for winning on school apply equally to Reddit, Instagram, Facebook and any other place where a community exists.
title: I Ran This Test, Here's What Happened

text: He avoids telling people to provide value, because people who try often produce listicles about things they have never done. He prefers to spell out what value means.
title: I Ran This Test, Here's What Happened

text: Value means making something that saves people time: not instructions, but a report of something you did so they no longer need to do it and can just take the findings.
title: I Ran This Test, Here's What Happened

text: Instead of posting a list of things to do, say you ran a test and share what happened. He notes this also pushes you to actually do things.
title: I Ran This Test, Here's What Happened

text: He thinks a particular member gives the most value per post in the community and sits near the top of the leaderboard. He suggests studying her substance, not her hooks or headlines, because she reports on things she did.
title: I Ran This Test, Here's What Happened

text: Do epic things and talk about what you did. What counts as epic depends on you, such as contacting 100 people in two days or making 100 pieces of content in 100 days, then sharing the lessons.
title: I Ran This Test, Here's What Happened

text: Lecturing with generic how-to lists carries little weight when the author has no real results behind them. Add value by doing things, then posting the findings and results.
title: I Ran This Test, Here's What Happened

text: On a small scale, as a commenter, add context to someone else's interesting post by sharing something you did and what happened.
title: I Ran This Test, Here's What Happened

text: He promises that people who leave real comments on posts get liked more by the owners of those posts, who may think the commenter took time to respond.
title: I Ran This Test, Here's What Happened

text: Without a way to get customers on demand, cutting either of two working offers just loses money, because you only sell to whatever your content brings in.
title: Helping an Online Service Business Fix Their Offer

text: When demand is capped by delivery capacity, he would fix operations first: rework how the offer is delivered to gain three to five times the capacity, so paid ads can then bring in enough people.
title: Helping an Online Service Business Fix Their Offer

text: Once capacity is expanded and ads supply enough buyers of the high-ticket offer, you can decide from total capacity whether to cut the cheaper offer and grow the premium one.
title: Helping an Online Service Business Fix Their Offer

text: Hormozi's team split business growth into 10 stages and built a quiz: enter your business details and it shows your current stage and what to do in each function, including product, marketing, sales, customer success, recruiting, IT, HR and finance.
title: I'm Clueless on How to Scale From $1.2M to $3.5M

text: Do not solve the same problem twice. If a solution is already in motion but slow, avoid launching a second one for the same problem, because the first may not be due to work yet. Sometimes you must give it time.

text: He says the person you hire for a senior role should be obsessed with the domain and should be your intellectual equal or better in it, so you should keep in regular contact with them before they start.
title: “I Make YouTube Videos. How Do I Get More Sponsors?”

text: Business owners buying software mostly care about two things: how much money it saves them and how hard onboarding will be. He would focus messaging on fast onboarding and off old systems.
title: Helping a Software Startup Hit $8.3M With Zero Revenue

text: He thinks the best answers on a model like this come more from the first 10 customer conversations than from his advice, and that the problem looks like a spreadsheet exercise.
title: Helping a Software Startup Hit $8.3M With Zero Revenue

text: He views a small monthly entry fee as a throwaway number when nearly all revenue comes from per-user seats; he would rather charge a clear onboarding price plus a price per seat.

text: When you aggregate purchasing volume for customers, you can offer them supply savings. He would pitch by asking what they pay now and promising to beat it.

text: He has trained for over 20 years, with seasons of high and low interest. Asking which workouts he enjoys most led him to prefer very long morning sessions lasting multiple hours.
title: Why I Like to Work Out

text: He likes training with someone he enjoys and, as a bonus, eating with that person afterward. He says this makes the start of an amazing day and counts the day as a win.
title: Why I Like to Work Out

title: Why I Like to Work Out

text: Hormozi holds that if you have not gotten what you want, you are not yet worthy of it. He says admitting this lets you start improving, and it is better to know you are bad for a season than pretend otherwise.
title: You're Not Suffering From Imposter Syndrome. You're Just Lying.

text: He says the test of being worthy of something is whether you have it. Repeating affirmations of worthiness does not make it true; someone not yet a billionaire is not worthy of a billion dollars.
title: You're Not Suffering From Imposter Syndrome. You're Just Lying.

text: He frames the road to success as giving yourself permission to suck, be unhappy, go unrewarded for a long time, lose friends and differ from your peers, so you can become an exception and then exceptional.
title: You're Not Suffering From Imposter Syndrome. You're Just Lying.

text: He says people feel like frauds when they teach things they have not done, not when they learn. He avoids imposter syndrome because he has done what he says he has done.
title: You're Not Suffering From Imposter Syndrome. You're Just Lying.

text: Instead of suppressing the imposter voice, he advises listening to it and gathering the evidence that makes it quiet down.
title: You're Not Suffering From Imposter Syndrome. You're Just Lying.

text: He distinguishes doing something new from being an impostor: new challenges are fine, while pretending to be something you are not, such as guaranteeing outcomes you cannot, is the impostor act.
title: You're Not Suffering From Imposter Syndrome. You're Just Lying.

text: He says the best marketing is truth. When the truth is not compelling, do not lie; change your reality so the facts become compelling.
title: You're Not Suffering From Imposter Syndrome. You're Just Lying.

text: To gain authority, list what someone in that role would need to have, treat the gaps as your action list, and once those facts are real, simply state them.
title: You're Not Suffering From Imposter Syndrome. You're Just Lying.

text: He argues that people who claim imposter syndrome feel it because they are lying, including by fudging the truth without breaking any law, and they know it.
title: You're Not Suffering From Imposter Syndrome. You're Just Lying.

text: He says stating what you have done or are doing, including that a big bet might be wrong, avoids the imposter feeling because it is truthful.
title: You're Not Suffering From Imposter Syndrome. You're Just Lying.

text: Content should demonstrate what happens as a result of your services, which for a business like this means content centered on return on investment.
title: Stop Charging Hourly (Do This Instead)

text: Content should include calls to action that generate inquiries, prompting people to respond, for example by claiming a giveaway or assessment.
title: Stop Charging Hourly (Do This Instead)

text: A high-value lead magnet can be five free one-on-one calls, restricted to companies that meet your criteria. He notes you would likely take those calls with qualified leads anyway.
title: Stop Charging Hourly (Do This Instead)

text: Hormozi says the order-of-magnitude move for a lead source capped by one person's calendar is likely learning to run a webinar, since Meta ad targeting has become very precise.
title: The 10x Move for Healthcare Service Businesses

text: For a webinar, he suggests showing many concrete examples of painful tasks the service could handle, rather than walking through how the company operates internally, which he calls boring.
title: The 10x Move for Healthcare Service Businesses

text: He suggests the second half of a webinar cover the classic frequently asked questions and worries prospects have, such as language ability, training quality, management effort and how payment works.
title: The 10x Move for Healthcare Service Businesses

text: At the micro level the measure is LTV to CAC; at the macro level, when opening more locations, the equivalent measure is return on invested capital, such as a location earning back its opening cost within months.
title: \"What If My Whole Business Model Is Broken?\"

text: He wants gross margins of at least 80 percent, ideally 90, and says that is achievable with a one-on-six ratio but harder one on one.
title: \"What If My Whole Business Model Is Broken?\"

text: He prefers semi-private lessons over private because they build loyalty to the brand rather than the teacher, who could otherwise leave and take students privately. He has seen semi-private models work very well in music and gyms.
title: \"What If My Whole Business Model Is Broken?\"

text: When capacity constrained, he gives three solutions in order: raise prices, change the client delivery ratio (for example one on one to one on four), then bring in others to deliver. Price comes first as it is fastest and easiest.
title: \"What If My Whole Business Model Is Broken?\"

text: If demand exceeds supply, raising prices is the obvious move, yet most people just suffer instead of doing it.
title: \"What If My Whole Business Model Is Broken?\"

text: He would still allow one-on-one but mainly sell semi-private, and charge a premium snowflake price to anyone wanting special treatment.
title: \"What If My Whole Business Model Is Broken?\"

text: For an initial offer, use a fixed-length challenge with a discrete outcome, or a before-and-after survey. He guesses an upfront package of 600 to 2,000 dollars, then upsell or move people into continuity.
title: \"What If My Whole Business Model Is Broken?\"

text: He says the more stressed someone is, the lower their effective IQ, and problems that seem hard under stress often get solved in minutes after rest and some time.
title: \"What If My Whole Business Model Is Broken?\"

text: With more demand than capacity, it is fine if some people refuse higher prices, since the business makes up the difference in profit.
title: \"What If My Whole Business Model Is Broken?\"

text: Comparison is an excellent measuring tool; the harm comes from the judgment attached to it. Noting that someone is doing better than you is objective, while concluding you therefore suck is where people get into trouble.
title: The Problem with Comparison in Business & How to Use It Correctly

text: He says business is an objective game where you can see how someone is doing, so a higher earner must have done something better than you at or before that point, and dissecting that is worthwhile.
title: The Problem with Comparison in Business & How to Use It Correctly

text: At 27, after a year of just under 20 million personally, he felt great at business, then saw Kylie Jenner become a billionaire younger than him. He felt terrible, but concluded she understood something he did not.
title: The Problem with Comparison in Business & How to Use It Correctly

text: His early approach was purely transactional and quantitative: conversion rate optimization, cost per impression, spend versus return, upsells. Seeing celebrities like Jenner, The Rock, Clooney, McGregor and Huda Beauty build billion-dollar brands made him admit he did not understand brand, which launched his current path.
title: The Problem with Comparison in Business & How to Use It Correctly

text: He believes that if he had explained her success away, for example by her mother's influence, to shield his ego, he would not be where he is now. Compare, pull out what they do better, and emulate it your own way.
title: The Problem with Comparison in Business & How to Use It Correctly

text: He says people mistakenly link hard work with no progress. He argues that for those who do work they enjoy, hard work does not feel like wasted time.
title: You're Not Burned Out, You're Just Focused

text: He believes the one lasting thing for an individual is who they become through the process, so work that fails to reach its goal still changes the person doing it.
title: You're Not Burned Out, You're Just Focused

text: He spent 5 years building a chain of six gyms, sold five and shut one down. He put the payout into a new venture, and his partner took the money and disappeared into bankruptcy.
title: You're Not Burned Out, You're Just Focused

text: He told a man worried about overtraining that he could worry once he looked like he trained. He explains that recovery ability and work capacity improve as volume increases.
title: You're Not Burned Out, You're Just Focused

text: He says that when people feel burnt out, the choice is to die or adapt. In fitness terms, avoid injury and you improve, and he applies the same idea to work.
title: You're Not Burned Out, You're Just Focused

text: He says this view of work has been self-fulfilling for him: the more he works, the better he gets at working and the more productive he is per unit of time.
title: You're Not Burned Out, You're Just Focused

text: With little or no capital, Hormozi would pick a business that pays for performance and needs no upfront capital. His personal pick would be recruiting, since you can work a listing without extra costs.
title: The Best Business to Start With No Money

text: When you have only skills and no capital, performance-based work means selling something to earn a small percentage of a very large amount, such as a few percent of a multimillion-dollar building.
title: The Best Business to Start With No Money

text: In recruiting, he suggests targeting higher-level roles and calling it headhunting rather than recruiting. Aim at bigger businesses able to write large checks, since VA placements are small ticket by comparison.
title: The Best Business to Start With No Money

text: Recruiting typically charges a 20% commission on the hire's total annual pay. Placing an executive earning $750,000 a year therefore yields a $150,000 commission check.
title: The Best Business to Start With No Money

text: He has lost everything twice and always worked on performance. His easy approach was asking local business owners for a commission on customers he brought them.
title: The Best Business to Start With No Money

text: His preferred approach: ask the owner the lowest price they would accept for a hundred customers, then sell at a much higher price. Tell the owner beforehand, and pay the agreed full amount anyway.
title: The Best Business to Start With No Money

text: If the owner objects to the higher price, he would point out that a higher-paying customer can spend more, so the business earns more lifetime value from them if it serves them well.
title: The Best Business to Start With No Money

text: He targeted businesses with almost no incremental cost per added customer, like semi-private gym training where the trainer is paid the same whether three or six attend. He sold upfront six or eight week packages.
title: The Best Business to Start With No Money

text: If completely broke, he would first earn about a thousand dollars, then put it into advertising, so the business owner need not front ad spend. Owners fronting spend gives them more leverage. He has also done it from zero.
title: The Best Business to Start With No Money

text: Hormozi says the report-to-manager hierarchy is an inefficient way to move information and make decisions. He links it to Roman legions and the human limit of managing roughly three to eight people, which he says leads to poor decisions at the top.
title: 85 Employees Are Eating All the Profit

text: He advises shifting from role-based thinking to workflow-based thinking, so the company's work is no longer bound by job titles.
title: 85 Employees Are Eating All the Profit

text: Hormozi says a person's actual job is usually a few steps of different multi-step processes, not their title. Understanding a company means getting very granular about what every role actually does today.
title: 85 Employees Are Eating All the Profit

text: He believes that in a company of 85 people, probably only around 10 are really running the ship, and many others are not very productive.
title: 85 Employees Are Eating All the Profit

text: He suggests watching who leans into AI and who leans away, and leaning toward the former. He thinks a business like this may need a few engineering hires to map every workflow.
title: 85 Employees Are Eating All the Profit

text: Hormozi says a business can be mapped as one continuous workflow, from ad to funnel to sales call to onboarding to delivery, and most steps of it can now be automated so people stop doing lower-value work.
title: 85 Employees Are Eating All the Profit

text: He warns that a 5% margin is a hiccup away from losing money in a service business. He still holds that a service business should always be able to survive, because costs are mostly variable.
title: 85 Employees Are Eating All the Profit

text: Hormozi says every point of margin you give up gets recaptured through growth, but it also raises your risk level.
title: How to Increase Cash Flow in a Consulting Firm

text: He describes himself as relatively risk averse despite being an entrepreneur. He likes a framework from Keith Cunningham: consider the upside, the downside, and whether you can live with the downside.
title: How to Increase Cash Flow in a Consulting Firm

text: If you cannot live with the downside of a move, he does not take it, even when the downside is small.
title: How to Increase Cash Flow in a Consulting Firm

text: Hormozi says he would start over with muscle rather than money, because he believes he would live longer that way. He notes his current training approach shortens his life.
title: Would You Rather Start Over With Muscle or Money?

text: He says beyond a certain size, each extra pound of muscle puts more strain on the organs, which he links to big bodybuilders dying young, among other causes.
title: Would You Rather Start Over With Muscle or Money?

text: In software, the business you are really in is the product business, not marketing and sales. If people do not stick with the product, marketing and everything else stops mattering.
title: The SaaS Trap Founders Walk Into

text: He says front-end marketing and sales should mainly serve to improve the product until it reaches passive growth, where it grows by itself. Only then should you pour on the gas.
title: The SaaS Trap Founders Walk Into

text: He bought School because its passive metrics were strong: it grew on its own with no marketing staff, and users who reach a certain point never leave. He says getting the small details right took 5 years.
title: The SaaS Trap Founders Walk Into

text: To get low churn, you either go upmarket to customers who do not churn, or you help create customers who do not churn.
title: The SaaS Trap Founders Walk Into

text: Expect cohort churn: for example, heavy losses in the first 6 months, then a flat retention curve for those remaining. Study what the survivors look like, then adjust your messaging to attract them.
title: The SaaS Trap Founders Walk Into

text: When a business has several overlapping offers, he says the fix is to pick one main path, cut the extras, and fold a cut low-priced offer in as a free deliverable of the main one.
title: Helping an AI Consultant Scale From $100K to $1M

text: Every piece of content can have its own freebie widget, but all of those widgets should feed a single funnel that leads to the main offer, followed by whatever follow-up cadence you want.
title: Helping an AI Consultant Scale From $100K to $1M

text: His pricing view in this exchange is that low prices exist to draw more people in so they can be sold something else, while the core offer can be priced higher, such as a thousand instead of 97.
title: Helping an AI Consultant Scale From $100K to $1M

text: If an offer is converting at 100%, people are saying yes so easily that you can add friction, such as asking for cash up front.
title: Keep Raising Your Price Until You're Closing 1 Out of 3

text: To get cash up front from a back-end split deal, move some of the later money to the front: the customer pays a set amount first, that amount is returned to them from proceeds, and afterward the split begins.
title: Keep Raising Your Price Until You're Closing 1 Out of 3

text: When a pitch is closing at 100%, keep raising the price until you close roughly one out of every three people.
title: Keep Raising Your Price Until You're Closing 1 Out of 3

text: Prospects who arrive not understanding the offer make the sale harder, so take them through an indoctrination step beforehand, such as a video sales letter, and have the qualifying questions reverse engineer the sale.
title: Helping an Agency Fix Their Sales Process

text: Pre-framing is very powerful: on a book launch opt-in, an optional VIP ticket checkbox that changed nothing else reportedly lifted sales 16%, because checkers were likelier to buy the VIP offer on the next page.
title: Helping an Agency Fix Their Sales Process

text: With heavy traffic, add a filter that qualifies people. Bad friction, like a slow page, turns everyone off; good friction repels bad prospects and lets good ones through.
title: Helping an Agency Fix Their Sales Process

text: Example: with stricter qualification, cost per call might rise from 200 to 500 while return goes from 3x to 6x. Sales efficiency can double or triple, so a smaller team closes more deals with less operational drag.
title: Helping an Agency Fix Their Sales Process

text: Most fast cash plays use resources the owner already has, like dead contacts, past customers, lists or a social following. Owners fail to grow largely because they misallocate attention and resources.
title: Helping an Agency Fix Their Sales Process

text: Test a fast cash campaign early with a few beta users and include it in the first part of onboarding, so the client can pay you back within the first 30 days.
title: Helping an Agency Fix Their Sales Process

text: His personal goal is to operate off found money: he never wants someone to pay him money they have not already made, and he has worked this way most of his life.
title: Helping an Agency Fix Their Sales Process

text: When asking who your best friend is feels hard, he suggests asking who you have the least filter around, or who you can sit in silence with without filling it. Even with no single winner, spend your time with those people.
title: What makes a good friend?

text: He says a partner should help you become more of yourself rather than dilute you, comparing them to salt that brings out flavor, while admitting analogies have limits.
title: What makes a good friend?

text: He defines authenticity, behavior-wise, as how you act when there is no risk of punishment. If you act that way around someone, they either do not punish you or have no desire to, so you behave as if they were absent.
title: What makes a good friend?

text: Instead of buying a company full of talent, it can be more efficient to pay the few key people a large sum. He cites AI hires getting a hundred million versus buying a business for four billion, as pure capital allocation.
title: “I Build and Sell Homes. But I’m Running Out of Land to Buy”

text: The test for buy versus build is how entrenched the relationships are. If they are hard to transport, buy the whole company; if the talent can carry them, strip out the talent and rebuild.
title: “I Build and Sell Homes. But I’m Running Out of Land to Buy”

text: Older owners often accept very long earnout periods, sometimes around 15-year seller financing, because it works like an annuity for them. Collateralizing against the business can make it a win-win structure.
title: “I Build and Sell Homes. But I’m Running Out of Land to Buy”

text: The quantified version of a constraint is the allocation of resources that yields the highest return. Constraints often give order-of-magnitude improvements rather than 10 to 30 percent gains, such as opening up five times the land.
title: “I Build and Sell Homes. But I’m Running Out of Land to Buy”

text: Performance-based pricing looks like the best model on paper but does not always work best in practice, because it depends heavily on how good the prospects are.
title: Helping a $2.2M/Year Cold Email Agency Scale to $10M

text: Enterprise customers with assets and obligations to protect tend to honor contracts. Small and sometimes medium business owners are less likely to, and he says US contracts mean basically nothing.
title: Helping a $2.2M/Year Cold Email Agency Scale to $10M

text: If you run performance pricing, either control the flow of money, meaning you collect payment and remit the client's share, or have complete transparency into results.
title: Helping a $2.2M/Year Cold Email Agency Scale to $10M

text: Shopify agencies can charge performance percentages, for example in email marketing, because tracking is clear and clients are unlikely to open a second store to cut the agency out.
title: Helping a $2.2M/Year Cold Email Agency Scale to $10M

text: He is fully in favor of performance deals, even zero up front, as long as he is confident he will get paid. Payment certainty is the biggest hinge: solve it and you solve the business.
title: Helping a $2.2M/Year Cold Email Agency Scale to $10M

text: Confidence in a performance model rises if clients are large, for example over $10M in ARR and venture-backed, because then they can pay and they track results.
title: Helping a $2.2M/Year Cold Email Agency Scale to $10M

text: If someone is booked out far ahead and has no demand or conversion problem, Hormozi suggests doubling the price, so they work the same amount but earn twice as much.
title: “Am I Undercharging for My Service?”

text: Most people already have a sales process even if it is unwritten; recording and comparing many calls would show the same repeated steps and questions each time.
title: “Am I Undercharging for My Service?”

text: He says you can raise your price simply because you want to, whether or not you can justify it; customers stay free to say no.
title: “Am I Undercharging for My Service?”

text: After buying a company, he told leadership his main growth move was doubling the price, with no sales retraining: the team says the same pitch but states a different number at the end.
title: “Am I Undercharging for My Service?”

text: It took nine calls to persuade the founder, and they settled on a 50% price increase. Close rates went up afterward, which he attributes to the product having been underpriced.
title: “Am I Undercharging for My Service?”

text: Selling to a higher share of people at 50% more money multiplies results, since the extra revenue from a price increase falls to the bottom line as profit.
title: “Am I Undercharging for My Service?”

text: When prices are capped by regulation or government, you must gain margin from the cost side. Hormozi's view is that such a business may need to decline new customers for a period, since demand is not its problem.
title: Helping a Disability Services Business Scale from $1.5M to $35M

text: Hormozi frames slowing intake as go slow to go fast: revenue stays flat for a while, but it is like filling the car with fuel before driving, not actually moving slower.
title: Helping a Disability Services Business Scale from $1.5M to $35M

text: Hormozi suggests charging a one-time fee to join the waitlist, signaling seriousness and pointing out that many providers are poor. It brings cash flow and sits outside capped government funding, so it is all margin.
title: Helping a Disability Services Business Scale from $1.5M to $35M

text: His goal began as matching his father's income, then exceeding it, then exceeding anything his father had ever earned. After reaching it, he saw he had been trying to beat his father at his father's game.
title: Why I Stopped Trying to Outearn My Father

text: His father introduced people by how much they earned yearly, which made clear to him that income equaled status. He notes this attitude is common in much of Asian culture.
title: Why I Stopped Trying to Outearn My Father

text: Only after winning did he realize he never asked which game he was trying to win. He believes many people chase a game whose rules they did not set.
title: Why I Stopped Trying to Outearn My Father

text: He considers himself fortunate to have hit a very hard goal relatively early, since it exposed the question of whether the goal was truly his.
title: Why I Stopped Trying to Outearn My Father

text: He believes the things he is proudest of in himself are the positive side of things he was once ashamed of. Being an outcast as a kid gave him unusual ability to work alone.
title: Why I Stopped Trying to Outearn My Father

text: Between roughly ages 6 and 16 he spent most of his time in his bedroom with audio tapes and audio books. He says this is why he can outwork anyone in solitude.
title: Why I Stopped Trying to Outearn My Father

text: Most of the time people are really buying compressed time. Anything that makes things faster or easier tends to attract people, and removing friction from their lives is something they will always move toward.
title: What Has Value in the Age of AI

text: Even though AI removes lots of friction, there is still value in giving people your own specific way of doing something.
title: What Has Value in the Age of AI

text: He accepts that what AI can do will gradually replace what humans can do, so the useful question is what humans can do that AI cannot, a list that keeps shrinking.
title: What Has Value in the Age of AI

text: He thinks that in a world full of fake things, people will crave realness and authenticity most. A community of real people sharing real struggles will stay valuable and likely become more so; he says his company is betting on this.
title: What Has Value in the Age of AI

text: A community is itself a consumable product: people want it again every month. Beyond your way of doing things, identify the part of your offer that gets consumed repeatedly.
title: What Has Value in the Age of AI

text: To find the consumable part, ask what the inputs to your system are, once someone understands your method. Deliver those inputs regularly, since they differ each period, and keep them separate from one-time components like courses or webinars.
title: What Has Value in the Age of AI

text: The second question is how their own behavior changes those metrics. Understanding the outcomes, the variables behind them, and how one's actions move those variables signals likely competence. He says most people cannot explain this, so competence is rare.
title: How to Spot a Great Hire With 2 Questions

text: People are rewarded for instantly saying yes when asked if something makes sense, so the yes says nothing about real understanding. It is a social reflex to nod when someone asks.
title: How to Spot a Great Hire With 2 Questions

text: He translates common sense, for most people, as behaving the way I would behave in the same situation. Someone acting differently has simply learned a different lesson from different experiences, rather than lacking sense.
title: How to Spot a Great Hire With 2 Questions

text: He once found a younger mentored teammate had made a mistake costing over $10 million. After first reacting with anger, he concluded he could not blame someone for not knowing what he never taught them.
title: How to Spot a Great Hire With 2 Questions

text: What looks like missing common sense is often rare sense: expertise the boss has from being very good at something. It is unfair to expect others to behave as he would without ever teaching them.
title: How to Spot a Great Hire With 2 Questions

text: Hormozi says people believe they need ideal conditions before beginning, when in fact the act of starting is the ideal condition. He says he is fully committed to this idea.
title: The Bar For Excellence Is Embarrassingly Low

text: Earlier in life he was drawn to lengthy morning routines and supplement rituals. He calls them mental busywork around the real task, noting that hours later nothing had actually been done.
title: The Bar For Excellence Is Embarrassingly Low

text: Output per unit of time rises the moment you begin working, which makes starting the greatest single hack for all other work. Everything else is procrastination around the work you should be doing.
title: The Bar For Excellence Is Embarrassingly Low

text: Starting is what puts you in the mood to work. For big mental tasks like a major content piece, he says it takes about five minutes of being in it before he gets into a groove.
title: The Bar For Excellence Is Embarrassingly Low

text: Once you know that a recruit who works through your system and resources produces a certain output per year, growth becomes a question of how many people you can feed through that system.
title: Helping a Tax Advisory Firm Scale

text: Anything a salesperson says to a customer should be scripted, and new agents should be walked through the sales process step by step rather than left to figure it out.
title: Helping a Tax Advisory Firm Scale

text: Long term, he thinks the ideal is a brand big enough to attract already-strong agents, to whom you feed leads you know will close, rather than taking people from zero to hero.
title: Helping a Tax Advisory Firm Scale

text: He suggests reinvesting a portion of profits into steadily reinforcing the brand, so that talent wants to join for status, mentorship and career help.
title: Helping a Tax Advisory Firm Scale

text: He says the current ad platform rewards many micro niches, meaning many audience-specific creatives, rather than a few big hero ads. Doubling through ads would need varied UGC campaigns aimed at many customer avatars.
title: Helping an E-Commerce Owner Build a Brand
