text: He warns that without a clear, compelling brand, a business is only in arbitrage: buying clicks cheaply, selling for more, and reinvesting. As audiences get colder and less likely to convert, margins compress until large revenue yields almost no profit.
title: Helping an E-Commerce Owner Build a Brand

text: He describes a campaign approach instead of hunting single winning ads: layer campaigns to move people from cold to more aware. Blended ROAS can rise even while some individual ad sets show lower ROAS.
title: Helping an E-Commerce Owner Build a Brand

text: He says e-commerce is a low operational drag business compared with a service business, so it is easier operationally but harder on the marketing side.
title: Helping an E-Commerce Owner Build a Brand

text: Outbound works like a snowball: early on you plant many seeds, a few hot prospects buy, and much of the rest moves into long-term nurture so you are top of mind when they become ready.
title: How to Scale Outbound Sales

text: Most people buy in one of two windows: right away when in pain and you happen to catch them, or much later when they finally become ready and remember whoever stayed present.
title: How to Scale Outbound Sales

text: He thinks content is a strong long-term nurture strategy for outbound prospects who are not ready yet.
title: How to Scale Outbound Sales

text: Most people miss their sales targets because they try to force sales to happen too fast. Outbound results should look different at month three than at month twelve.
title: How to Scale Outbound Sales

text: In almost any market, about 97% of people are not ready to buy today but will be within roughly 24 to 36 months. Most businesses stay capped by competing impatiently for the same 3%.
title: How to Scale Outbound Sales

text: Big brands are big because they sell to everyone, just at the moment each person is ready to buy.
title: How to Scale Outbound Sales

text: Judge outbound by what it produced over six to twelve months, not by what it closed today, since non-buyers still flow into email nurture and retargeting.
title: How to Scale Outbound Sales

text: Entrepreneurs must make most decisions with incomplete data. Sometimes you bet on first principles, such as that reaching more of your buyer type will make more money, and stick with it for months without early returns.
title: How to Scale Outbound Sales

text: Hormozi thinks the biggest gap for small business owners is lacking a data layer. In his view, anything unique built with AI, if it is to be useful, starts with your own data.
title: The One Thing Small Businesses Are Missing

text: His company built one repository holding sales copy, testimonials, videos and collateral, which gets split into ads in real time and matched to dynamic landing pages, all programmatically with AI.
title: The One Thing Small Businesses Are Missing

text: At acquisition.com they run several hundred landing pages against several hundred different ads, generated programmatically with AI, though he says they are not an AI company.
title: The One Thing Small Businesses Are Missing

text: On the MoreMozi highlight channel, one teenager alone puts out about 20 clips daily: five clips of roughly 3 to 10 minutes plus around 15 shorts. Software surfaces highlights, he checks quality, and CTAs are inserted automatically.
title: The One Thing Small Businesses Are Missing

text: On agencies versus in-house for content, his approach is both: he wants three agencies plus an in-house team, so every available impression gets captured.
title: The One Thing Small Businesses Are Missing

text: He watches paid-side e-commerce closely because he thinks it is nearly always the most cutting-edge. Companies going from zero to 100 million plus in 12 to 24 months run a similar playbook: decentralized UGC with an AI back-end for screening and control.
title: The One Thing Small Businesses Are Missing

text: He thinks small group is currently the best fitness model on the market, with exceptional returns on capital and easy operations.
title: Helping a $1M Gym Owner Scale

text: He says this was his first year without FOMO, which he links to realizing how hard it is to do anything well, so he is fine when others earn more in other games.
title: Helping a $1M Gym Owner Scale

text: He feels mastering a game takes a very long time and figures he has perhaps three or four more entrepreneurial seasons, meaning only that many big swings.
title: Helping a $1M Gym Owner Scale

text: At Acquisition.com the investing side has a natural bias toward no, since reasons to pass are easy to find. Some no bias helps manage risk, but refusing everything means never earning a return, which he sees as a continuum to manage.
title: The Cost of Constant Criticism

text: Friends and family doubting each new business or partner will be right almost every time, maybe 19 out of 20. But one yes, like the person you marry, can change your whole life, so the doubters are wrong on what matters.
title: The Cost of Constant Criticism

text: Cynicism grows from getting rewarded for saying no and being right. That is only short-term correctness, because big wins need big bets, which means being wrong often and being willing to look stupid.
title: The Cost of Constant Criticism

text: On his public school bet, he planned that if it fails he would document what he learned, apply it next time, and state the facts and tell the truth.
title: The Cost of Constant Criticism

text: He finds it strange that cynicism, skepticism and being cutting or aloof are treated as signs of intelligence, since people fear being called naive above all.
title: The Cost of Constant Criticism

text: Critics are right month after month that you have not hit it big, but they measure in days while you measure in decades, so they end up wrong.
title: The Cost of Constant Criticism

text: The world belongs to optimists, because doing anything big requires believing it can happen. He repeats a line that cynics get to be right while optimists get rich.
title: The Cost of Constant Criticism

text: He says he has failed more times than he has succeeded, yet optimists win more in the big ways than people who are right along the way and wrong on the big outcome.
title: The Cost of Constant Criticism

text: His editor's line: cynics are 99% right and 100% wrong, because only the big result at the end matters, even if you have several failures first.
title: The Cost of Constant Criticism

text: His first nine businesses did not amount to much, and throughout, people told him I told you so and were right at the time, but not forever.
title: The Cost of Constant Criticism

text: He holds a belief in cosmic irrelevance: he thinks that within four generations he will be completely forgotten. He says this removes the special-snowflake attitude and lowers anxiety in the daily running of a business.
title: Become the Mentally Toughest Version of Yourself

text: He considers emotional or mental stability a prerequisite for being a good entrepreneur, given how many fires arise daily. He thinks people struggle to build it because they never define it in terms of behavior.
title: Become the Mentally Toughest Version of Yourself

text: Mental toughness is your fuse: how many bad events can happen in a row before your behavior changes. Ideally it is maxed so nothing alters your behavior.
title: Become the Mentally Toughest Version of Yourself

text: Fortitude is how steep the change in your behavior is once your fuse is passed: a small dip versus going completely off the rails.
title: Become the Mentally Toughest Version of Yourself

text: Resilience is how quickly you return to baseline behavior, measured as the time between the behavior change and getting back to your original baseline.
title: Become the Mentally Toughest Version of Yourself

text: These three measures concern behavior, not moods. You can still feel upset, but if your behavior returns to baseline you resume normal function and disrupt the system you work within as little as possible.
title: Become the Mentally Toughest Version of Yourself

text: He thinks any founder benefits from an overarching worldview to frame experiences. It need not be his own; a religious one works as well, perhaps better. Without one, you become the center of your universe and slip into a victim stance.
title: Become the Mentally Toughest Version of Yourself

text: Whether the worldview is cosmic irrelevance or a creator with a purpose for you, setbacks either become unimportant or make you better. He believes this is the worldview of more successful founders.
title: Become the Mentally Toughest Version of Yourself

text: A trait like charisma is shorthand for a bucket of smaller skills. If you cannot figure out how to gain a trait, it is because the word hides many specific skills.
title: How to Become the Person You Want to Be (Step by Step)

text: The more skilled a person is, the more general an instruction can be while they still act effectively. A skilled person can be told to start a business, while a novice needs step-by-step directions.
title: How to Become the Person You Want to Be (Step by Step)

text: To understand why someone seems charismatic, list the concrete behaviors: greeting people, using names, handshakes, eye contact, nodding while listening, and asking them questions about themselves. Each is a small skill you can practice.
title: How to Become the Person You Want to Be (Step by Step)

text: When you do not know how to do something, break it into a smaller chunk. He compares this to teaching toddlers to speak by rewarding approximate sounds until they become words.
title: How to Become the Person You Want to Be (Step by Step)

text: He thinks of himself as a toddler when learning, because it removes ego from the process. Many needed skills sit on the other side of being humble enough to start small.
title: How to Become the Person You Want to Be (Step by Step)

text: Advertising can be split into doable steps: message someone, post something interesting, open with an interesting question, explain why you asked, reward the viewer at the end, then record and post it. Broken low enough, anyone can do each piece.
title: How to Become the Person You Want to Be (Step by Step)

text: He writes his books and makes content this way, on the belief that any skill you cannot figure out simply needs breaking into smaller pieces.
title: How to Become the Person You Want to Be (Step by Step)

text: Start from the daily money you want to make, work out the units you must sell, then connect that to the activities in your calendar. Time is your only resource when starting out.
title: How to Become the Person You Want to Be (Step by Step)

text: Example economics: if 100 DMs yield one customer worth $200, doing that daily makes about $6,000 a month. If customers rebuy, raise volume monthly and eventually hire someone to do it, so the business stacks.
title: How to Become the Person You Want to Be (Step by Step)

text: As you become more skilled, you can bucket many small activities into one instruction, and only need detailed breakdowns when talking to someone junior. In self-improvement, you are the junior instructing yourself.
title: How to Become the Person You Want to Be (Step by Step)

text: To close the gap, ask: what skills and traits does the person I want to become have, can I break them into individual pieces and daily activities, and do those add up to the income I want? If so, go.
title: How to Become the Person You Want to Be (Step by Step)

text: He says the advisory group performed significantly better than he expected, in member quality and in how little interaction upkeep it needs, because expectations were set clearly and onboarding was strict; it mostly manages itself at roughly a thousand members.
title: My Plan for 2026: Media, Hiring, and Strategy

text: After the launch, the company hired six C-suite executives, and he, the executive chairwoman-to-be, and the president spent most of their time interviewing candidates.
title: My Plan for 2026: Media, Hiring, and Strategy

text: He plans to grow the media team from about 20 to about 60 people next year, aiming for repeatable formats that do not depend on him and all sit under the company brand.
title: My Plan for 2026: Media, Hiring, and Strategy

text: His stated goal is a Disney of business: a universe of characters rather than a single personality, so the brand does not rest on one person.
title: My Plan for 2026: Media, Hiring, and Strategy

text: He argues the standard YouTube playbook of talking head plus clickbait headline is talent-dense, needing strong on-camera talent. Formats like Shark Tank are different because the judges can change while the format stays repeatable, ownable IP.
title: My Plan for 2026: Media, Hiring, and Strategy

text: He plans to invest heavily in Cash Cows, a deep-dive interview with an entrepreneur, as one repeatable format, and would like around eight such formats, which he expects to occupy much of his next year.
title: My Plan for 2026: Media, Hiring, and Strategy

text: One of his first jobs was at a fur coat dealer. The fourth-generation owner invented summer storage as a way to bring buyers of expensive coats back regularly, so they would then buy more often.
title: Helping a Dental Practice Create Recurring Revenue

text: He says luxury is often thought to be for rich people, but about 90% of buyers of an expensive item like a $5,000 coat are actually people of modest means who want to look rich.
title: Helping a Dental Practice Create Recurring Revenue

text: Getting customers to return regularly for other things makes them more likely to buy more frequently, according to what the fur dealer found.
title: Helping a Dental Practice Create Recurring Revenue

text: Fitness businesses take low-skilled labor and train it into skilled labor that can earn more elsewhere, so he says you need a system that makes it harder for trainers to go do it alone.
title: She Spent $14K a Month on Ads That Did Nothing

text: He says a service business run by a charismatic owner struggles to scale: with enough razzle-dazzle you cannot pay staff enough, and with too little the product suffers. Defensible four walls are needed to stop trainers leaving.
title: She Spent $14K a Month on Ads That Did Nothing

text: He describes a common boutique franchise pattern: a strong marketer crushes ads at one location, sells many franchises quickly, sells to private equity, unit economics drop, disclosed earnings disappoint, sales die, and the cycle repeats. He calls this about 90% of franchises.
title: She Spent $14K a Month on Ads That Did Nothing

text: He says most growth comes from solving problems rather than lamenting missed opportunities, since opportunities are infinite while problems are finite. One problem is the most valuable to solve, and that is how you grow.
title: She Spent $14K a Month on Ads That Did Nothing

text: He argues that big incumbents are often easy to beat; the hard part is the idea of them. He thinks they carry overhead and move slowly, while new players are leaner, faster and more current.
title: She Spent $14K a Month on Ads That Did Nothing

text: He compares premature scaling to a dieter worrying about new clothes before losing weight: make money in the current business first. Once the four walls print cash, you get breathing room and options.
title: She Spent $14K a Month on Ads That Did Nothing

text: When his work got busier and compressed, he stopped looking forward to working out. He realized he enjoys training only when he has no deadline and can go as long or as short as he wants.
title: Why I love the Gym

text: He trains for roughly two to two and a half hours because he likes it, and admits that is not efficient. If he were optimizing purely, he says it would be around 45 to 60 minutes, in and out.
title: Why I love the Gym

text: The second thing he needs to enjoy training is other people with him. He loves having partners, says he trains harder, has more fun, and is at his happiest there.
title: Why I love the Gym

text: Training with others keeps him more focused. Alone, he gets distracted, such as finishing a set, sitting on the bench and pulling out his phone.
title: Why I love the Gym

text: Hormozi says relative gains like 24% are less useful than absolute figures, so ask what clients make before and after the work in actual money.
title: Helping a Consulting Business Get More Leads

text: A lower price earlier is fair when the product was riskier then. Once the problem is solved, the price rises, even if little time has passed, because the discount was compensation for risk.
title: My Biggest Mistake in Business

text: Buyers who regret missing an earlier cheaper price may hope the product fails, since having skipped it at one tenth of the price then feels like a smaller mistake.
title: My Biggest Mistake in Business

text: Hormozi's starting premise is that life is suffering, so misery is constant whether the business is growing, plateauing, shrinking, or he is doing nothing. He notes this is a bleak view and says to ignore it if another worldview works for you.
title: \"In Your Darkest Days, How Did You Keep Going?\"

text: At 19, Hormozi dropped happiness as his mantra because he could never feel happy, and chose to be useful instead. He says this has served him well throughout his life.
title: \"In Your Darkest Days, How Did You Keep Going?\"

text: Hormozi says this is his hardest year in the last 8 years, a local minimum in his own ranking of his last 13 years.
title: \"In Your Darkest Days, How Did You Keep Going?\"

text: After a large cash number disappeared, Hormozi asked what it changed about his life: same food, wife, job, team, building and city. He concluded the suffering was optional and voluntary, since his actual life changed zero.
title: \"In Your Darkest Days, How Did You Keep Going?\"

text: The less you change your lifestyle as your business succeeds, the more resilient you are, because business volatility then changes little about your life. He compares it to anchoring far below the waves.
title: \"In Your Darkest Days, How Did You Keep Going?\"

text: Hormozi says his content is a documentary, not a sermon: it shows what worked for him, and others should use whatever works for them.
title: \"In Your Darkest Days, How Did You Keep Going?\"

text: Hormozi says he has never tried to be the happiest guy and struggles more with nihilism, the sense of why bother. He keeps going because wanting to be useful gives him a bit of meaning.
title: \"In Your Darkest Days, How Did You Keep Going?\"

text: When choosing between customer types, one being worth more and another being worth less but more numerous, Hormozi thinks from the avatar's perspective and asks what the choice changes about his day-to-day activities.
title: Helping a Wildfire Sprinkler Company Scale to $200M

text: If pursuing an opportunity requires little change to daily activities, he is much more likely to take it. If it means starting another business, it becomes a cost-benefit on how big the opportunity is.
title: Helping a Wildfire Sprinkler Company Scale to $200M

text: If delivery will not materially change, adding a sales motion to a large flow of leads is worth doing. He believes it could multiply a business several times over, possibly ten or twenty times.
title: Helping a Wildfire Sprinkler Company Scale to $200M

text: Organic and paid content have largely merged: the organic pieces that prove themselves are the ones you would put ad money behind anyway, so organic winners can simply be turned into paid ads.
title: \"Should I Fire the Customer That's 45% of My Revenue?\"

text: To turn an existing winning piece of content into a lead generator, the change may be small: add a lower-third banner with a call to action, or splice a call to action with a freebie or lead magnet onto the end.
title: \"Should I Fire the Customer That's 45% of My Revenue?\"

text: Editors can be used to ramp up organic content output, which brings in more leads, and then all of that organic content can be repurposed as paid.
title: \"Should I Fire the Customer That's 45% of My Revenue?\"

text: The gym challenge concept took the industry by storm: lose a set number of pounds in six weeks or get your money back. He reports an 80% success rate with it.
title: Teaching a Fitness Business the Diagnostic Sale

text: Do not wait for a challenge to finish before selling the next, bigger program. Sell it partway through, once people are already losing weight, and never wait until the end.
title: Teaching a Fitness Business the Diagnostic Sale

text: He considers the diagnostic sale the best way to make money in the weight-loss space: state the gap between current and goal weight, then calculate the time and total price from a weekly rate.
title: Teaching a Fitness Business the Diagnostic Sale

text: Example of the diagnostic sale math: 200 lb to 140 lb is 60 lb at 2 lb per week, so 30 weeks of loss plus 16 of maintenance, 46 weeks at 200 dollars weekly, about 9,000 dollars.
title: Teaching a Fitness Business the Diagnostic Sale

text: After quoting the price, offer prepayment with a 20% saving. If they hesitate, offer 10% off for half down with the remainder spread over payments.
title: Teaching a Fitness Business the Diagnostic Sale

text: If they decline, use a seesaw downsell: ask how low they want payments, then ask the most they can put down up front so the remainder is spread over months.
title: Teaching a Fitness Business the Diagnostic Sale

text: For weight loss, he says the approach is all prepayment. To push further, make the guarantee contingent on prepaying, which he says would crush.
title: Teaching a Fitness Business the Diagnostic Sale

text: Buyers of high-stakes services choose a specialist over a generalist, like picking a knee or back surgeon for surgery. In his view, the clients who accept a generalist tend to be the ones unwilling to pay much.
title: You need to niche down.

text: A big goal needs a way to tell whether you succeeded. Tony's food-delivery goal is easy to count, while Hormozi's goal of helping men reach $100,000 is harder to verify, so he is building a feedback loop.
title: Reflecting on the Tony Robbins Interview...

text: Hormozi recalls that going from zero to $100,000 was not his most significant moment, yet he has never felt richer than then. He wants ways to create that emotional connection to the outcome for others, but has no answer yet.
title: Reflecting on the Tony Robbins Interview...

text: Hedonic adaptation means you get used to any pleasure: a five-star dinner monthly feels special, nightly it stops being interesting. Hormozi says he does not know how this fits with people who stay happy about their results.
title: Reflecting on the Tony Robbins Interview...

text: During the launch, Hormozi saw the whole team become highly motivated when stakes were big, such as attempting a hundred million dollar weekend launch and breaking a record. He says this cannot last forever, since burnout follows, so effort must ramp up and cool down.
title: Reflecting on the Tony Robbins Interview...

text: Hormozi says he has taken multiple companies through a ten-stage roadmap from zero to a hundred million plus, which fewer than one percent finish, tied to headcount stages and across software, physical products, services and brick and mortar.
title: Reflecting on the Tony Robbins Interview...

text: Hormozi says the next level of his game is taking big bets with his wealth, accepting more risk rather than only seeking efficient cash flow from investments.
title: The Levels of Wealth

text: He expects to make major investments in media over the following 12 to 18 months.
title: The Levels of Wealth

text: His portfolio deals are currently minority stakes, but he plans to take majority ownership of interesting companies where it fits the overall portfolio, such as buying an accounting firm outright to serve the holding company internally.
title: The Levels of Wealth

text: He says he would not direct a large volume of business, on the order of 200 to 250 million dollars a year, toward companies in which he does not own a majority.
title: The Levels of Wealth

text: He expects majority purchases to get a larger share of his money allocation than the team, and thinks they will return more than the S&P. He says reaching a billion requires bigger bets.
title: The Levels of Wealth

text: His goal is to reach 10 billion, while the mission is making real business knowledge available to everyone. He says the books, courses, YouTube, shorts and podcasts all align to that mission.
title: The Levels of Wealth

text: He wants to be unassailable on the question of why people should listen to him, and expects to gain perspective as the portfolio grows from 200 million to a billion to 10 billion dollars a year.
title: The Levels of Wealth

text: If you lack good tracking, set it up early, because it only becomes harder and messier later, and every decision made without data carries higher stakes as the business grows.
title: Helping a Local Fast Food Chain Scale

text: The method you already use to acquire talent or product is often the most efficient way to acquire customers, since you already have that skill set. Not always, but often. Doing more of what you already do is the likeliest path.
title: Stop Working Part Time on a Full Time Opportunity

text: For this kind of business, content is a bonus or extra, while outbound is the main acquisition channel, especially in the beginning.
title: Stop Working Part Time on a Full Time Opportunity

text: Something you are annoyed about is not necessarily the real constraint. Focus on the actual problem, which here is acquiring customers.
title: Stop Working Part Time on a Full Time Opportunity

text: When your customers are wealthy, you are judging price from your own pocket, not theirs. Hormozi tells the caller the solution is simply naming a higher number, and that he should push price now.
title: \"How High Can I Push Prices?\"

text: Raise prices until churn starts to rise; the point where more customers leave is the signal that you have found your top limit.
title: \"How High Can I Push Prices?\"

text: For a business with an 11% net margin, a 20% price increase would triple profits, and he thinks it could probably be sustained without much change to the business.
title: \"How High Can I Push Prices?\"

text: After scaling one facility to a number you are happy with, the next step is what he calls scale zero: getting the owner to do zero in the business while it performs the same or better. Then you have a duplicable model.
title: Don’t Open a New Location Until You Do This

text: A common expansion mistake: an owner profiting from a business they work in takes the cash and all their time to a new location. The original location slips, the new one lacks staff and word of mouth, and they work twice as much for less money.
title: Don’t Open a New Location Until You Do This

text: Before asking why you cannot do more of what you are doing now, you have to measure what you are currently doing; without metrics, that question cannot be answered.
title: We're posting and praying\": A $13M CEO With No Metrics

text: When customer work is episodic, he suggests thinking one level up: count how many agencies you onboard and treat them as a distribution layer, rather than focusing only on acquiring individual customers.
title: We're posting and praying\": A $13M CEO With No Metrics

text: Once you estimate how many customers a type of agency can send yearly, you can compute the cost of acquiring one distribution node, and outreach to agency owners can show how bundling your service earns them more.
title: We're posting and praying\": A $13M CEO With No Metrics

text: He dislikes a business where about 80% of customers must be re-sold every year just to match last year, with only 20% renewing; growth then has to come on top of that.
title: We're posting and praying\": A $13M CEO With No Metrics

text: Even if customer logos change, the distributor stays constant, so agencies become your true customers: build the customer journey around making their lives easier and let them bring customers.
title: We're posting and praying\": A $13M CEO With No Metrics

text: If each agency sends one customer monthly and you add one agency monthly, you reach 12 new customers per month after a year, then 13, then 14, so the gains stack.
title: We're posting and praying\": A $13M CEO With No Metrics

text: When scaling TikTok Shop, the biggest risk is brand dilution, especially for a brand that is not yet large. He advises being harsher up front than seems necessary when selecting creators.
title: Helping a Supplement Brand Scale from $10M to $24M

text: Give every creator a brand guideline they must read and absorb before they are activated, and hand them the best-performing hooks while forbidding negative hooks, which can drive sales but hurt the brand.
title: Helping a Supplement Brand Scale from $10M to $24M

text: Check whether the creators making content match the average customer you are targeting, including how they dress and the environments they film in.
title: Helping a Supplement Brand Scale from $10M to $24M

text: Before moving content from TikTok Shop to whitelisting, require manual review once a single creative passes a daily threshold, such as 50 or 100 per day, to confirm it is on brand.
title: Helping a Supplement Brand Scale from $10M to $24M

text: Everyone has always had access to the same tools. Improving tools create a back-and-forth arms race for attention, like predator and prey, so execution remains what separates people.
title: Brutally Honest Advice for Outbound Sales

text: He sees four primary levers for converting leads into conversations and booked appointments: speed, personalization, volume and availability.
title: Brutally Honest Advice for Outbound Sales

text: Speed has several parts: speed to contact, speed of reply during back-and-forth texting or email, and how soon you can get someone in, such as today versus next week. Faster replies raise response and show rates.
title: Brutally Honest Advice for Outbound Sales

text: At a company running over 4,000 appointments a day, the strongest correlation with campaigns generating the most shows was maximum availability.
title: Brutally Honest Advice for Outbound Sales

text: He says a business that only takes sales calls Monday to Thursday afternoons could likely multiply sales about 4x by being available seven days a week, around 12 hours a day. The question is whether staffing cost is worth it.
title: Brutally Honest Advice for Outbound Sales

text: If a business is booked, customers simply go elsewhere, so limited time slots hand that business to competitors.
title: Brutally Honest Advice for Outbound Sales

text: Personalization is where AI will matter most, and it will keep improving. Personalized sales letters made for one individual are already possible, like a video sales letter tailored to each person.
title: Brutally Honest Advice for Outbound Sales

text: Marketing runs on windows of arbitrage. He thinks AI will create a large arbitrage period around personalization, speed and volume, though people will become banner blind over time.
title: Brutally Honest Advice for Outbound Sales

text: Businesses that skip AI can still make money, as some still run on fax machines or paper. Those using AI will probably get better margins, so skipping it means playing with one hand tied behind your back.
title: Brutally Honest Advice for Outbound Sales

text: Hormozi believes everyone has a unique personal brand. People come across as boring because they conform to what they think others want, and that conformity is what breeds resentment about being boring.
title: Don't Conform, Find Your True Personal Brand

text: To find your real brand, start from zero and ask what you actually want, imagining nobody else existed: how you would dress, what work you would do, and who you would date.
title: Don't Conform, Find Your True Personal Brand

text: After leaving Gym Launch, he dressed to suit his role heading a gym community. Starting over, he pictured his 85-year-old self wanting maximum comfort, and tested shoes, shorts and hats to find what let him do most things in most rooms unchanged.
title: Don't Conform, Find Your True Personal Brand

text: If the person you would truly want to date differs from your current partner, and would never date you, he suggests leaving mediocre options and taking the untrodden path, even if others reject or tease you.
title: Don't Conform, Find Your True Personal Brand

text: Sticking with things is a muscle you train. If you keep starting diets or workouts and failing, lasting a bit longer each time still counts as progress and puts you ahead of most people.
title: Don't Conform, Find Your True Personal Brand

text: Moving from selling to homeowners toward bigger customers is a fundamental change in business strategy, and that change carries risk.
title: Helping a home service company scale

text: He says the lowest-risk, best risk-adjusted move is to build on what already works: add paid search (PPC) alongside existing SEO, and write many more articles to target more keywords and lift organic traffic.
title: Helping a home service company scale

text: Hormozi calls his supplement company one of his bigger mistakes: the attention spent on manufacturing, testing, flavors, marketing and support could have gone into doubling down on the core business.
title: Helping a $10M/Year Transportation Company Scale

text: He says a growing distribution base and skill set make other opportunities look more tempting, and he now turns down a sickening number of them.
title: Helping a $10M/Year Transportation Company Scale

text: If the goal is a hundred million dollar per year business in one niche, then everything that is not that goal is what puts it at risk.
title: Helping a $10M/Year Transportation Company Scale

text: He speculates that many owners sell around 20% margins on $20M revenue, roughly $4-5M EBITDA, because an offer of 8-10x means about $40M, which feels like enough to be done forever.
title: Helping a $10M/Year Transportation Company Scale

text: He thinks it is fine if many owners sell at that level, but some companies reach $100M, usually through a more stubborn founder, which he considers a good thing.
title: Helping a $10M/Year Transportation Company Scale

text: If ad cost per customer is close to or above lifetime revenue, the business is bad. His example: 20% churn gives about 110 dollars LTV on a 22 dollar plan, so spending 90 to earn 110 is a poor deal.
title: Your $90 CPA Is Killing You (Here's How to Fix It)

text: To fix a bad CPA-to-LTV ratio, ascend a portion of buyers to something more expensive rather than only tweaking ad angles.
title: Your $90 CPA Is Killing You (Here's How to Fix It)

text: In his example, breaking even would need roughly 4x conversion. Realistically he would aim for about 2.5x, so a second transaction at 30 days brings payback to about 50%, which he calls breathable.
title: Your $90 CPA Is Killing You (Here's How to Fix It)

text: For community businesses, the first conversion point is an onboarding call included for every person who signs up. The second is messaging every group member by DM, asking about questions and selling them something else.
title: Your $90 CPA Is Killing You (Here's How to Fix It)

text: A second, pricier community is a good ascension option, and he says the people doing best use it. He bets group ads can cost about 5 to 10 dollars, and ascending 10% would halve CPA and likely lift LTV.
title: Your $90 CPA Is Killing You (Here's How to Fix It)

text: The third conversion point is a weekly Q&A call run like a webinar without slides: lots of value plus a soft call to action toward your main offer. The fourth is a scripted VSL or webinar with slides.
title: Your $90 CPA Is Killing You (Here's How to Fix It)

text: Script the modules a new member consumes first in this order: introduction with origin story and opportunity, three big concerns (circumstances, other people, personal inadequacy), then a call to action to buy more.
title: Your $90 CPA Is Killing You (Here's How to Fix It)

text: He would send ads to a free group, use the four conversion points to move people into the paid group, and could then price the paid group higher, perhaps around 99.
title: Your $90 CPA Is Killing You (Here's How to Fix It)

text: If clients agreed to a certain scope, simply deliver that scope. Often you are delivering far more than you promised, so resetting to the original promise fixes the overload.
title: Helping a Pet Care Coach Scale to $3M/Year

text: To handle people asking for your time, learn a script that sends them to a resource or to the calendar for the next available slot.
title: Helping a Pet Care Coach Scale to $3M/Year

text: Answering people quickly when they reach out rewards that behavior and trains them to do it more. You can train your audience to behave differently instead.
title: Helping a Pet Care Coach Scale to $3M/Year

text: Personal accessibility works as a differentiator while you are an underdog, but once you are big and proven enough, you can stop offering your cell phone.
title: Helping a Pet Care Coach Scale to $3M/Year

text: Delivery decreases are the equivalent of price raises: clients pay the same and get less. Pitch it as getting something different that benefits them, not as less of what they liked.
title: Helping a Pet Care Coach Scale to $3M/Year

text: Position a delivery change on the moral high ground: you made a promise, realized you were breaking it, and must change it to stay in integrity with that promise.
title: Helping a Pet Care Coach Scale to $3M/Year

text: If your mission is to help a certain number of people and your delivery prevents it, you are out of integrity. Either shrink the mission or provide something different of equal or greater value.
title: Helping a Pet Care Coach Scale to $3M/Year

text: When you change delivery you will lose some people, which is fine because it makes room for better clients who pay more and did not arrive with the old expectations.
title: Helping a Pet Care Coach Scale to $3M/Year

text: To assess a business complaint, he asks for a precise definition, quantitative evidence supporting it, and an explanation of why it matters. These questions help examine whether the proposed problem actually constrains sales.
title: Helping a $3M Restaurant Consultant Get to $10M

text: There are only a limited number of ways to get people to find out about you: use someone else's audience through affiliates, run paid ads, make content, or do outbound. Trade shows count as paying for access to another audience.
title: How to Raise Capital Without Using Your Personal Network

text: Raising money from high net worth investors works like an enterprise sale, even though it feels different. The process underneath is the same.
title: How to Raise Capital Without Using Your Personal Network

text: If he had no money and had to start raising capital from scratch, he would begin with conferences and events, since they are high leverage and face-to-face contact makes trust build much faster. An exception would be someone with media buying background.
title: How to Raise Capital Without Using Your Personal Network

text: Recognizing skill requires having some base skill yourself. Someone who does not understand a domain cannot see what is good in it, and the more skill you have, the better you appreciate exceptional performers.
title: What Looks Like Luck Is Usually Skill

text: When people credit your success to luck, he says there was probably some luck, but they also lack the skill to recognize yours. He frames it as a matter of competence, not malice.
title: What Looks Like Luck Is Usually Skill

text: He cites the idea that you only envy people whose sacrifices you cannot see, and that craving a result without the process guarantees disappointment. If you will not live the lifestyle, release the desire.
title: What Looks Like Luck Is Usually Skill

text: He thinks traits are just price tags. Something can be good and still not worth the cost to you, and people who refuse the price often call it bad instead.
title: What Looks Like Luck Is Usually Skill

text: It stings when someone dismisses a skill you paid heavily to acquire. He suggests answering without judgment: you did not pay the price, he did, and both are different people living different lives.
title: What Looks Like Luck Is Usually Skill

text: When a business is limited by supply rather than demand, he suggests redefining what business you are really in. A cleaning company is truly a cleaner-recruiting business, and a trucking firm is a contractor-recruiting business.
title: Helping a $50M Trucking Company Double Revenue

text: Alongside cost to acquire customers there is a cost to acquire talent. Once you know what a worker earns you, you can decide how much you are willing to pay to get one, and consider payback period.
title: Helping a $50M Trucking Company Double Revenue

text: Pay part of a referral bonus upfront and the rest after the recruit proves productive, such as at six months. This makes the referrer an internal champion who helps the recruit stick around.
title: Helping a $50M Trucking Company Double Revenue

text: He ran a different portfolio business that needed independent operators for brick and mortar locations. Cold traffic funnels attracting operators worked famously, with applicants jumping through hoops, and about 10 percent sticking.
title: Helping a $50M Trucking Company Double Revenue

text: He believes other people have already encountered and resolved the problems a business owner is facing.
title: You're Stuck Because Your Pricing Model Is Killing Profit

text: For nearly all businesses, and coaching businesses in particular, the constraint is rarely supply. They usually just need to advertise more, which makes it a leads problem.
title: I Hit My First Million. What Now?

text: If you can reach $1M to $3M with organic alone, that is great because it is nearly all margin. There are also levels of organic: one channel, all channels, or all channels at high volume, and usually more room remains.
title: I Hit My First Million. What Now?

text: Organic costs less than people think and more than they think at once. The content output at his company costs about $3 million a year, which is a lot but small relative to what it earns.
title: I Hit My First Million. What Now?

text: Paid-ads people treat money as in and out, while organic people avoid spending because they are used to free customers with zero CAC. He says both are right and each needs what the other has.
title: I Hit My First Million. What Now?

text: For a coach at the $1M to $3M level, if more people found out about the offer and leads doubled, the business would double.
title: I Hit My First Million. What Now?

text: Hormozi says control freak is a label low-standards people use for high-standards people. He would answer yes, because he wants it done right the first time, and thinks that saves pain since the work gets redone anyway.
title: Why I Have High Standards

text: He says people who try to pull something from their mind into reality often feel lonely, and outsiders throw labels like micromanager to make them stop. He has built defenses against these labels.
title: Why I Have High Standards

text: He argues there are no silver bullets in great products, only hundreds of tiny improvements, such as shipping, weight, color scheme, shelf placement and how a name looks on merchandise. Someone who does not care will not examine these details.
title: Why I Have High Standards

text: He uses the gap between a book with tens or hundreds of five-star reviews and one with 100,000 to illustrate how the level of detail defines what counts as right.
title: Why I Have High Standards

text: He recalls hearing that the best art is made by the artist for themselves, while commercial work made for an audience often solves nobody's problem. He thinks making it for yourself serves many similar people.
title: Why I Have High Standards

text: He says he felt ashamed for a long time about being seen as having too-high standards, feeling like a bother, and only realized last year that refusing to stop was probably a key reason for his success.
title: Why I Have High Standards

text: He says a big project involving many people still needs one vision, otherwise it becomes a Frankenstein of copied pieces that resonates with no one. Pickiness makes more work for others but yields far better results.
title: Why I Have High Standards

text: For his book launch he rehearsed the presentation three times a day for 30 days, about 100 full run-throughs: recorded aloud, watched, edited, and repeated. Live to about half a million people, it came out nearly flawless.
title: Why I Have High Standards

text: He says the first five reps feel like big improvement, but the next 95 take work from great to masterpiece, and that is where most people fall off and fail to become world class.
title: Why I Have High Standards

text: Just as customer LTV is compared to CAC up front, he says you should compare lifetime gross profit per employee to the cost of acquiring that talent on the back end.
title: “I Run a Marketing Agency. How Do I Hire Better Talent?”

text: He shows that a hire producing 1.25 million in annual gross profit, with a four-year tenure, brings about 5 million lifetime, and at an 8x multiple adds roughly 10 million in enterprise value.
title: “I Run a Marketing Agency. How Do I Hire Better Talent?”

text: He frames the hiring question as what you are willing to spend to gain an extra 1.25 million of yearly gross profit, and says he would gladly pay 125k one time for it.
title: “I Run a Marketing Agency. How Do I Hire Better Talent?”

text: A portfolio company needed a 50-person sales team in 90 days. They hired 80, kept 50, and ran 15 headhunting firms at once alongside internal sourcing, filling it in about 12 weeks.
title: “I Run a Marketing Agency. How Do I Hire Better Talent?”

text: He says a blue chip recruiting firm typically charges about 30 percent of salary, so paying around 60k for a 200k role is worth it if the hire generates 1.25 million gross profit.
title: “I Run a Marketing Agency. How Do I Hire Better Talent?”

text: He says people often have not actually counted the cost of recruiting against the payoff, so they hesitate to spend on it even when the return is large.
title: “I Run a Marketing Agency. How Do I Hire Better Talent?”

text: Absolute acceptance of criticism disarms people. If a commenter says he only succeeded because his dad gave him everything, he simply agrees, and that response takes the fight out of the exchange.
title: The Power of Absolute Acceptance

text: He is fine with being labeled by others because he will die eventually, which he says also means the label does not matter, so he can use that reasoning in either direction.
title: The Power of Absolute Acceptance

text: His ultimate self-expression is absolute agency: doing what he truly wants without fear, as long as it does not hurt people.
title: The Power of Absolute Acceptance

text: When he asks what he is afraid of, the answer is usually not a big monster but judgment, or more precisely perceived judgment from people who are not actually thinking about him.
title: The Power of Absolute Acceptance

text: He reduces fear of judgment by discounting the value of other people's opinions while raising the perceived value of his son Solomon's opinion and approval.
title: The Power of Absolute Acceptance

text: He treats identity as a continuum rather than a binary. Each day he slides more marbles toward the version of himself he wants, until most people describe him that way.
title: The Power of Absolute Acceptance

text: The hardest part of marketing is reaching the right person. Once you have them, what remains is sales motion. He compares it to 90 yards of a football field: getting them to follow, DM, opt in and book a call.
title: Instagram Keeps Banning His Growth Strategy

text: Getting the right person to follow, DM, opt in and book a call is roughly 90 percent of the work. The other 10 percent is deciding how much friction to add.
title: Instagram Keeps Banning His Growth Strategy

text: If people who book are qualified but not buying, the fix he points to is adding more friction to that step.
title: Instagram Keeps Banning His Growth Strategy

text: Making content long-term is something you need to do, and it also feeds a cold outbound motion, so the two are not cannibalizing each other.
title: Instagram Keeps Banning His Growth Strategy

text: He is more willing to accept multiple acquisition channels for local businesses because their reachable population is limited; he illustrates this with a town of 50,000 people that needs to be reached through several methods.
title: Helping a Door-to-Door Service Business Get More Customers

text: Hormozi estimates that 95% of sales organizations expand by hiring large numbers and retaining the successful sellers, making selection their main growth method rather than developing selling ability through training.
title: Helping an Online Service Business Doing $30M/Year Get to $100M

text: He argues that effective sales training can support higher margins: companies can develop inexperienced recruits, pay less than they would for established closers, and build a larger pool of capable sellers.
title: Helping an Online Service Business Doing $30M/Year Get to $100M

text: Return on invested capital asks how much money a business produces from money invested in it. He describes customer lifetime value relative to acquisition cost as a fundamental expression of business economics.
title: Helping an Airbnb Manager Get to $2M Profit

text: For the scaling swamp discussion, he illustrates a $2 million revenue business with 25% margins: $500,000 profit becomes $400,000 available after retaining $100,000 for future needs.
title: Helping an Airbnb Manager Get to $2M Profit

text: He argues that escaping the scaling swamp requires greater risk than entering it: two strong hires could consume the illustrative business's $400,000 available profit, might fail, and an already stretched owner has limited capacity to work longer.
title: Helping an Airbnb Manager Get to $2M Profit

text: He thinks beginners need rewards beyond the final result to persist. Experts already notice smaller successes within their work, such as an editor seeing an improvement immediately after a change.
title: Why Beginners Quit Before They Win

text: Hormozi found it motivating to treat personal development as the asset he was building: finishing a demanding workday meant becoming someone capable of working for 5 years without a payoff.
title: Why Beginners Quit Before They Win

text: While unable to afford separate rents for housing and his gym, Hormozi slept at the gym. Imagining himself eventually recounting that hardship helped reinforce his persistence.
title: Why Beginners Quit Before They Win

text: Hormozi says he tends to choose the option that could produce the most compelling eventual story, even when it involves a longer journey to success. He describes this as his personal filter for major decisions.
title: Why Beginners Quit Before They Win

text: Hormozi treats content receiving only 5 views as an archive people might revisit after he succeeds. That perspective reduces his need for immediate attention and gives each post value as a record of his progress.
title: Why Beginners Quit Before They Win

text: Hormozi’s test for persisting is whether evidence has invalidated a foundational assumption about the opportunity. If none has been disproved, he treats the difficulty as part of learning how to succeed.
title: When should you quit?

text: He sees an ethical problem in charging people for instruction in a business activity while losing money doing that same activity.
title: When should you quit?

text: Money can accelerate an existing skill set, but having capital does not mean someone has the ability to deploy it effectively.
title: When should you quit?

text: Hormozi says he previously lost everything and rebuilt in gym-related businesses. He attributes much of his confidence and reduced fear of financial loss to that experience.
title: When should you quit?

text: Hormozi estimates US business owners represent 9% of the population, or 32–33 million people. He says 95% generate under $1 million in revenue; the remaining 5% exceed that threshold, an audience he estimates at 1.5 million owners.
title: Social Media Is Dead. Interest Media Is Here

text: Hormozi says 0.4% of businesses, or 1 in 250, exceed $10 million in revenue. He thinks approximately 1 in 3,000 reaches $100 million annually, noting that the estimate varies by data source.
title: Social Media Is Dead. Interest Media Is Here

text: Hormozi thinks Twitter is particularly useful for improving writing because it demands brevity and provides rapid feedback on wording. He credits Twitter and the Hemingway app with helping his writing most.
title: How I Think About Growing on Social Media

text: Hormozi says he posts ideas as they occur, including during meetings, without ghostwriters or a posting schedule. Sometimes he skips 2 consecutive days; on other days he posts 11 times.
title: How I Think About Growing on Social Media

text: Some community members hesitate to participate because they feel afraid; he suggests that a personal invitation can give them permission to join in.
title: Message All 130 Members Personally to Get Engagement

text: He thinks member photos help an online community feel more connected to real life, especially when the pictures relate to the audience's interests.
title: Message All 130 Members Personally to Get Engagement

text: He advises disregarding guidance from people whose results or lifestyle you do not aspire to, and avoiding spending time defending your choices to them.
title: The Harsh Truth About What Others Think of Your Life

text: When a relative criticized his lifestyle as lacking balance, Hormozi asked whether the concern involved his health, marriage or finances. He recounts that the relative responded by saying she was less articulate than him.
title: The Harsh Truth About What Others Think of Your Life

text: Hormozi estimates that receivables financing facilities commonly cost around 1% per month.
title: He Built a $5M Paint Biz. Now He's Stuck

text: Hormozi describes challenging his explanations for relationship difficulties by considering their permanent implications: accepting them would mean accepting a future without lasting relationships.
title: Take Responsibility

text: He believes that whatever difficulty someone faces, another person has previously encountered and overcome it.
title: Take Responsibility

text: Hormozi acknowledges that Acquisition.com depends on him personally and says he does not intend to sell it.
title: Helping a Music School Expand Across the Country

text: He frames reducing key-person dependence around the owner's objective: making a company saleable or enabling a complete exit. He tells owners without those objectives not to worry about that dependence.
title: Helping a Music School Expand Across the Country

text: Hormozi says Leila makes his protected maker schedule possible. At Gym Launch, another married couple learned their respective roles by working under each of them, allowing the business to replicate their division of responsibilities.
title: Helping a Music School Expand Across the Country

text: When customers specifically value an owner's expertise, losing direct access can upset them. Hormozi frames accepting temporary revenue loss during delegation as a tradeoff against remaining personally responsible for delivery indefinitely.
title: I'm the bottleneck in my $1.6M practice

text: A sales process that relies on existing familiarity will struggle with unfamiliar prospects. Hormozi says a process designed for cold prospects also works for warm prospects and improves their conversion rates.
title: I'm the bottleneck in my $1.6M practice

text: Hormozi designed his book-launch webinar for attendees unfamiliar with him. He says existing followers accepted the introductory material, while newcomers appreciated it.
title: I'm the bottleneck in my $1.6M practice

text: Hormozi estimates that emailing his book-launch offer alone might have produced one-third of the sales; he attributes the other two-thirds to the fuller selling process.
title: I'm the bottleneck in my $1.6M practice

text: Hormozi argues that a simple intervention can produce substantial growth: if one change can double a business, there is little reason to pursue five changes.
title: \"How Should I Pay My Salespeople?\"

text: Hormozi values traditional media for reaching audiences he cannot currently access. He thinks television can offer distinctive access to attention because entering it requires more than simply publishing online.
title: Why Legacy Media Still Matters for Creators

text: Hormozi favors a barbell approach to content production: pursue exceptional quality in ambitious productions while also publishing large amounts of useful content. For the volume side, he emphasizes usefulness per second and producing more such seconds.
title: Why Legacy Media Still Matters for Creators

text: He sees polished productions as primarily expanding awareness, shaping the brand and establishing authority. He considers frequent useful content closer to purchasing decisions, while acknowledging that it can also attract people discovering him for the first time.
title: Why Legacy Media Still Matters for Creators

text: To identify a target customer profile, examine customers with the highest spending and longest relationships, then look for shared demographics, measurable characteristics, and geography.
title: Helping an Agency That Serves Wholesalers Scale

text: Hormozi describes allocating 80% of hook development to reusing past successes and 20% to new experiments. He refreshes familiar hooks with different settings, clothing or props while keeping the opening largely unchanged.
title: \"How Do You Write a Great Hook?\"

text: Hormozi saves viral organic content and ads he considers successful in a folder, then reviews them when creating ads. He adapts hooks from other industries to his own advertising.
title: \"How Do You Write a Great Hook?\"

text: Hormozi says marketers lose 80% of viewers during the opening seconds and recommends putting 80% of their effort into that opening.
title: \"How Do You Write a Great Hook?\"

text: An introductory service discount can attract buyers while a separate upfront fee covers sales commissions and acquisition costs. He says a paid introductory offer also prepares buyers to spend, reducing surprise compared with a free offer.
title: The Offer Structure a Stranger Pitched Me in a Parking Lot

text: Test equivalent discount presentations: for a $1,000 monthly service, a 20% introductory reduction can appear as 20% off, $200 saved, or an $800 opening month.
title: The Offer Structure a Stranger Pitched Me in a Parking Lot

text: He prefers discounts of at least 50% because he wants them to change purchasing behavior. In his view, reductions of 10% or 20% often sacrifice margin on customers who would have purchased anyway.
title: The Offer Structure a Stranger Pitched Me in a Parking Lot

text: For a service containing five components, he suggests discounting one component by 80% and upselling the remaining four at full price, instead of reducing the entire package by 20%.
title: The Offer Structure a Stranger Pitched Me in a Parking Lot

text: He argues that a larger initial fee can reduce churn by increasing customer investment. He especially favors startup fees when success requires customers to submit information, attend appointments, make decisions, or change behavior.
title: The Offer Structure a Stranger Pitched Me in a Parking Lot

text: To establish an upfront fee, choose its name, amount, and justification, then decide whether to collect, reduce, or waive it. Explain the fee and the associated work to every customer.
title: The Offer Structure a Stranger Pitched Me in a Parking Lot

text: He says waiving an established onboarding fee can create perceived savings even when the seller routinely waives it. He cautions that this approach must comply with applicable advertising requirements.
title: The Offer Structure a Stranger Pitched Me in a Parking Lot

text: He accepts choosing not to discount. His objection is lowering a quoted price after resistance: moving from $1,000 to $900 undermines credibility and invites an $800 counteroffer. He distinguishes that from a predetermined $500 promotion on a $1,000 offer.
title: The Offer Structure a Stranger Pitched Me in a Parking Lot

text: Hormozi defines skill compounding as combining abilities to produce a disproportionately greater result than those abilities produce separately.
title: Why Is It So Hard to Compound Skills?

text: He thinks people struggle to foresee the benefits of combining skills because acquiring another skill changes their understanding in ways they cannot anticipate beforehand.
title: Why Is It So Hard to Compound Skills?

text: He illustrates marketing uncertainty with 1,000 variables: understanding 15 influential ones might get marketers 60% toward controlling outcomes. Chance remains, but he thinks accumulated knowledge limits downside and gradually raises median results in organic content and paid advertising.
title: Why Is It So Hard to Compound Skills?

text: Hormozi argues that businesses seeking more leads often overestimate their visibility and mistakenly assume their market is saturated. Becoming widely recognized takes substantially more effort than owners expect.
title: Why You Aren’t Getting as Many Leads as You Want

text: Hormozi recalls 19 of 20 people approaching him being unaware of an earlier book launch. For a later launch, roughly 1 in 4 knew and 3 in 4 did not, despite approximately $4–5 million spent.
title: Why You Aren’t Getting as Many Leads as You Want

text: Over a month before launch, Hormozi's book accidentally became available for 24 hours; 72 people bought it within about 60 minutes. He feared widespread exposure, but observed no fallout and realized buyers would need to promote it themselves.
title: Why You Aren’t Getting as Many Leads as You Want

text: Hormozi thinks traits such as patience can be demonstrated through behavior even when feelings conflict. Repeatedly acting patiently provides evidence of patience despite wanting faster results.
title: Judge Yourself by Your Actions, Not Your Thoughts

text: Hormozi describes accumulating personal evidence as his guiding approach to self-development. He says demonstrated accomplishments can influence how others treat someone regardless of that person's feelings about their competence.
title: Judge Yourself by Your Actions, Not Your Thoughts

text: Hormozi says he only began discussing gym operations after owning six gyms. He also doubted his fitness expertise despite maintaining visible abs for ten years and holding multiple state records; repeated requests from others prompted him to share.
title: Judge Yourself by Your Actions, Not Your Thoughts

text: Hormozi favors growth bets that preserve proven elements while changing few variables. Developing additional products introduces uncertainty about whether customers want them.
title: One Channel Away From Zero

text: For intermediaries connecting sellers with buyers, poor introductions can make buyers unwilling to accept future introductions.
title: Helping a $15K-Per-Deal Connector Build His Back End

text: Information was already freely accessible before AI. Hormozi argues that when information is abundant, choosing and organizing what people need provides value.
title: What Has Value in the Age of AI?

text: Hormozi thinks a community's ongoing value is typically lower than its initial, one-time value because it depends on what members can continue consuming. He thinks pricing that ongoing value appropriately can improve retention.
title: What Has Value in the Age of AI?

text: Hormozi thinks demand for authentic human connection will increase. He points to friendships and spouses as relationships AI has not displaced, and argues that social media has left people lonelier.
title: What Has Value in the Age of AI?

text: Hormozi rejects the idea that everyone ought to pursue wealth; he believes people should choose their own goals.
title: How I Think About Goals

text: He thinks immediate financial problems need attention before ambitious planning; he says he has never met someone focused on a 10-year life vision while unable to cover rent.
title: How I Think About Goals

text: For people who have not reached their desired situation, he argues that their job is not what blocks progress: evenings and weekends provide time to pursue their goals.
title: How I Think About Goals

text: Hormozi says business gives him frequent satisfaction through activities such as writing, editing, and discussing ideas. He seeks these rewards and avoids activities he dislikes, even when others perceive his preferred work as unpleasant.
title: Why I Love Business

text: For people unsure what to pursue, he favors testing possibilities and improving direction over demanding a perfect choice. Without practical experience, they lack the perspective needed to judge which pursuit fits them.
title: Why I Love Business

text: Hormozi says dissatisfaction with his job and Baltimore prompted him to move to California and pursue fitness. His initial direction came from leaving circumstances he disliked and choosing an existing interest, rather than already knowing he would enjoy business.
title: Why I Love Business

text: When someone cannot choose among uncertain paths, he uses investing as an analogy: every investment carries risk, while holding money exposes its purchasing power to inflation. He argues that waiting for a flawless option is faulty decision-making.
title: Why I Love Business

text: He thinks inflation motivates investors to put money to work: a greater cost of holding unused capital creates more urgency to deploy it. Without that pressure, he thinks capital would move more slowly.
title: Why I Love Business

text: He recommends declining unwanted invitations or requests honestly instead of inventing excuses. He views the other person's reaction as their responsibility and honesty as a way to remain consistent with his values.
title: Try Telling the Truth More

text: He believes eliminating insincere social remarks makes genuine praise more credible. He says his team trusts his compliments because he avoids giving praise he does not mean.
title: Try Telling the Truth More

text: When an explanation is unclear, he recommends admitting confusion rather than automatically signaling agreement. Accepting a moment of embarrassment allows someone to gain understanding that lasts beyond the conversation.
title: Try Telling the Truth More

text: Faster business growth requires committing some current profit to expansion. For an owner personally making the sales, time spent building the team temporarily reduces time available to earn.
title: The $10M Solo Business That Beats Building a Team

text: Hormozi believes a difficult route should prompt changing the approach while retaining the original goal.
title: The $10M Solo Business That Beats Building a Team

text: The Theory of Constraints directs attention toward the stage that limits a business's overall output.
title: Helping a Software Consulting Firm Scale From $4M to $50M

text: When sales appointments are already at capacity, improving advertisements or landing pages cannot increase throughput through that bottleneck. Sales capacity must expand before additional demand can pass through.
title: Helping a Software Consulting Firm Scale From $4M to $50M

text: Hormozi presents a pricing rule of thumb: close rates above 80% suggest tripling prices. If doubling prices leaves conversion unchanged, he says another doubling or tripling may still be warranted.
title: Helping a Vet Owner Build a Business That Runs Itself

text: Using Jennifer Lawrence’s Hunger Games exposure as a rough proxy, Hormozi estimates A-list recognition requires $50 million in advertising or five billion impressions; at $500,000 annually, accumulating that spending would take 100 years.
title: How Much Does It Cost to Become Famous?

text: He suggests scaling his hypothetical fame estimate to the audience a business wants to reach: recognition within a local or narrowly defined market requires a smaller exposure target than national or global recognition.
title: How Much Does It Cost to Become Famous?

text: Venture funding allows companies to accelerate spending using capital they have not earned; bootstrapped companies must earn the money they spend.
title: How to Stop Feeling Behind in Your Business

text: Hormozi believes bootstrapped businesses have the strongest fundamentals over the long term.
title: How to Stop Feeling Behind in Your Business

text: How quickly a business hires is a question of risk tolerance.
title: How to Stop Feeling Behind in Your Business

text: When choosing a partner for a course or community business, Hormozi prefers someone who brings audience traffic; he believes he can then identify something valuable that person can contribute.
title: Experts Without Influence Are Just Authorities

text: For someone with a large audience, Hormozi says giving community members access to that person can sometimes provide sufficient value.
title: Experts Without Influence Are Just Authorities

text: Taking profits out of a business provides greater security but sacrifices potential upside compared with reinvesting them.
title: Helping a Dentist Get to $50M/Year

text: Hormozi says his gym business systems helped operators earn more from services, leaving supplements as an optional sale they postponed when distracted.
title: You're Thinking About Your Business Wrong.

text: For a training-led consumables business, the supplied product should underpin practitioners' primary earning activity. He explains that a more lucrative service can motivate practitioners to specialize, making its required supplies central to their business.
title: You're Thinking About Your Business Wrong.

text: Hormozi defines discipline by how often someone repeats an unpleasant behavior without a payoff. He treats discipline as a matter of degree rather than a trait someone either possesses or lacks.
title: How to Progress Faster Than 99% of People

text: He tests definitions by looking for counterexamples. Defining discipline merely as taking action fails his test because enjoyable actions need not require discipline.
title: How to Progress Faster Than 99% of People

text: He argues that trainers who enjoy their early workouts cannot use those workouts alone as evidence of discipline; his definition concerns repeatedly doing things someone dislikes without receiving a reward.
title: How to Progress Faster Than 99% of People

text: He thinks someone could hypothetically demonstrate discipline through repeated unpleasant behavior that never produces a reward, even if he considers that behavior pointless.
title: How to Progress Faster Than 99% of People

text: Hormozi says he interprets criticism of his lifestyle as another person's preference for a different way of living. He encourages people to choose the life they prefer.
title: How to Progress Faster Than 99% of People

text: Hormozi thinks the offer plays a particularly large role in attracting customers in local markets.
title: How to Get More Leads in a Local Service Business

text: A lead magnet can provide a trial or one component of a larger process. He mentions another category but does not identify it in this excerpt.
title: How to Get More Leads in a Local Service Business

text: Hormozi uses the thought that he and his critics will be gone and forgotten within three generations to reduce the influence of their judgments and pursue goals for his own satisfaction.
title: How to Build a Life You Actually Want

text: He thinks repeatedly making independent choices and accepting responsibility strengthens personal agency. For him, risking repeated failure feels more fulfilling than remaining in a merely tolerable life.
title: How to Build a Life You Actually Want

text: When minor frustrations arise, he mentally expands the scale until Earth itself disappears from view. He uses this perspective to make everyday concerns feel less significant.
title: How to Build a Life You Actually Want

text: When processing unsuitable prospects makes a funnel inefficient, he recommends adding qualification friction.
title: $15 Leads vs Medicare Part B: How to Fix the Funnel

text: He thinks developing lessons live with community members can offer more value than recordings because participants can ask questions during the teaching.
title: \"Do I need courses to start a community business?\"

text: He questions whether course libraries improve many communities: material can overwhelm members, while his observations suggest most platform activity involves member posts, comments, and interaction.
title: \"Do I need courses to start a community business?\"

text: Community operators can encourage participation by explicitly inviting members to contribute, posing questions, and requesting posts. Some members hesitate because they fear appearing foolish and feel they need permission.
title: \"Do I need courses to start a community business?\"

text: Hormozi recounts that a company he considered investing in negotiated payment terms from net 0 to net 90 and grew from $2 million annually to $5 million monthly within 18 months. He explicitly says this does not guarantee results.
title: Helping an E-Com Company Doing $1M/Year Solve Their Supply Constraint

text: He distinguishes formal ownership or control from practical leverage: lacking legal control does not necessarily eliminate influence over a business relationship.
title: He Sold $125M in Real Estate After I Fired Him

text: He considers a small income stream attractive when it requires no work, but dislikes receiving little compensation for work that still requires his involvement.
title: He Sold $125M in Real Estate After I Fired Him

text: Criticism identifies a gap between an agreed expectation and observed behavior; an insult adds a degrading judgment about the person.
title: Criticism vs Insult: Know the Difference

text: Hormozi says his team encourages frequent feedback and works to reduce its emotional weight, presenting it as a way to help people improve faster.
title: Criticism vs Insult: Know the Difference

text: He argues that the emotion behind pursuing a goal matters less than performing the necessary work; a personal explanation is useful insofar as it makes that action more likely.
title: You Don't Have to Feel Good Enough to Win

text: Hormozi recalls feeling undeserving early in his career. Achieving some wins through action helped him realize that feeling inadequate did not prevent him from doing the work and obtaining results.
title: You Don't Have to Feel Good Enough to Win

text: He describes three traits of exceptionally successful people: an exaggerated sense of superiority and ambition, intense feelings of inadequacy, and impulse control that supports sustained focus.
title: You Don't Have to Feel Good Enough to Win

text: He believes that whatever challenge someone faces, another person has previously encountered and resolved it.
title: Helping a $1.5M Nail Salon Owner Stop Doing Too Much

text: Hormozi estimates that attracting the right prospect accounts for 90% of the marketing and sales challenge; the remaining 10% concerns how much friction the sales process needs.
title: Helping a Content Agency Outgrow Cold DMs

text: When qualified prospects enter the sales process but do not purchase, he recommends increasing friction.
title: Helping a Content Agency Outgrow Cold DMs

text: Before transferring a top salesperson away from an established acquisition channel, train a replacement until their results match the original person's performance.
title: Helping a Content Agency Outgrow Cold DMs

text: He prefers testing a new acquisition channel with a proven salesperson. Combining an inexperienced salesperson with an untested process makes it difficult to identify which part is failing.
title: Helping a Content Agency Outgrow Cold DMs

text: He argues that brand growth requires some investment of resources. For someone who remains short of money despite being constantly occupied, he sees the choice of activities as the problem.
title: You Can't Be Busy and Broke

text: Creating personalized content for an audience owner and tagging them can demonstrate usefulness before a request. He says shareable contributions save the recipient time, although developing the relationship can require months.
title: You Can't Be Busy and Broke

text: Hormozi recommends assessing effort on a project in hundreds of hours. He says that investing this much work improves the result and reveals how much more a person can accomplish.
title: How to Raise Your Minimum Standard for Work

text: He says concentrating on one pursuit without distractions frees attention for repeated effort, which begins to develop mastery.
title: How to Raise Your Minimum Standard for Work

text: To refine a presentation, Hormozi drafts it, rehearses mentally, delivers it aloud, reviews a recording, and revises. He repeats the rehearsal, review, and revision cycle until the presentation feels polished.
title: How to Raise Your Minimum Standard for Work

text: Hormozi thinks AI makes polished production widely available, increasing the appeal of authenticity in short videos. He believes his own shorts look overly produced and plans to change their style.
title: How AI Will Change Social Media in 2026

text: He thinks live broadcasts and audience interaction offer unusually strong returns on content effort because AI will have more difficulty replicating them.
title: How AI Will Change Social Media in 2026

text: For longer content, he thinks greater production effort and structure remain appropriate. He favors either a format audiences strongly enjoy or a very raw podcast approach, suggesting creators avoid the middle.
title: How AI Will Change Social Media in 2026

text: An owner's boredom with an existing offering does not mean customers are bored with it.
title: Adding More Content Increased His Churn

text: He thinks subscription retention often benefits from simpler delivery and helping customers use the material. He would prioritize customers consuming 100% of an offering over expanding the amount available.
title: Adding More Content Increased His Churn

text: Choosing a goal solely to outperform someone he dislikes lets that person redirect his life, even if he ultimately wins the competition.
title: Why Most People Hijack Their Own Direction

text: Hormozi thinks resentment helps explain why people adopt socially valued goals: succeeding promises both others' respect and a feeling that their resentment is justified.
title: Why Most People Hijack Their Own Direction
