text: Around age 28, Hormozi recognized how much effort he had devoted to proving himself to his father. After his father disapproved of his departure, they had little contact for 5 years; he then received an apologetic call.
title: Why Most People Hijack Their Own Direction

text: For businesses targeting local prospects, Hormozi says in-person events produce higher conversion rates but also higher lead costs than the webinar route.
title: I'm About to Run Out of People to Sell To

text: Hormozi says national webinar funnels require more advertising, creative, technical, and selling skills than local event funnels. He argues that a local physical presence can build trust before a business has an established brand.
title: I'm About to Run Out of People to Sell To

text: For the seminar funnel discussed, Hormozi gives rough expectations: 25% of confirmed attendees arrive, half of attendees schedule a consultation, and half of those close. His attendance example is 100 confirmations producing 25 attendees.
title: I'm About to Run Out of People to Sell To

text: When someone seeks validation that their circumstances prevent success, Hormozi describes agreeing with their prediction of failure to provoke resistance and expose whether they actually accept that outcome.
title: Why Most People Don’t Win

text: Hormozi thinks actions create identity, so he rejects the personal-development premise that someone must first become a different person before taking the actions that produce desired results.
title: Why Most People Don’t Win

text: Hormozi finds it helpful to treat shortcuts as unavailable to him, borrowing a reminder from David Goggins to redirect his attention toward completing the necessary work.
title: Why I Work Triple Shifts

text: When Hormozi already understands the task but feels resistance, he finds it helpful to remind himself that he will meet its demands and that the work still needs completing.
title: Why I Work Triple Shifts

text: Entrepreneurs may use side ventures to protect against failure, but Hormozi argues that dividing attention can increase risk by weakening the business most likely to succeed.
title: Helping an Entrepreneur With Three Businesses Pick the One

text: When choosing a business, he recommends identifying the work someone would rely on if earning money became urgent, then concentrating on that proven ability.
title: Helping an Entrepreneur With Three Businesses Pick the One

text: Hormozi operated agencies serving dentists and chiropractors alongside a gym. He recalls Leila suggesting they repeatedly pursue the business they already understood well instead of continuing activities where they lacked competence.
title: Helping an Entrepreneur With Three Businesses Pick the One

text: Better sales training and repeatable processes let businesses produce consistent results with less experienced hires. Hormozi describes that ability to develop employees as valuable company know-how.
title: Why Your Sales Team Tanks After Every Big Month

text: In high-volume sales teams, employee departures can roughly match new hiring, preventing the team from growing. Hormozi describes this as a recurring talent acquisition process constraint.
title: Why Your Sales Team Tanks After Every Big Month

text: Hormozi says a separate team fully manages his venture portfolio, including investment approvals. He spends most of his own time generating demand because he sees brand building as his strongest lever for attracting talent and deals.
title: Helping a Private Equity Firm Doing $12M/Year Get to $90M

text: Hormozi approaches his role by identifying one activity that could fulfill the organization’s other objectives, concentrating on that activity, and hiring people to handle the remaining work.
title: Helping a Private Equity Firm Doing $12M/Year Get to $90M

text: Small businesses can compete through flexibility and direct owner attention, while established businesses can emphasize proven systems and extensive customer results. Hormozi argues that each competitive position offers advantages.
title: Your Downside Is Made Up.

text: For someone whose attempts could fail without worsening their current position, Hormozi argues that limited downside should make action easier and faster, rather than becoming a reason to attempt less.
title: Your Downside Is Made Up.

text: He thinks people with no objective loss at stake can still hesitate because they imagine how others would judge a future failure, even when those people are not thinking about them.
title: Your Downside Is Made Up.

text: When anticipated disapproval blocks action, identify the individual and exact interaction you fear. He thinks this usually involves one or two people; making the fear specific helps question whether their imagined judgment should govern your choices.
title: Your Downside Is Made Up.

text: Building a premium professional services firm requires finding other highly capable practitioners, which is difficult; he says successfully building that team can produce a valuable company.
title: \"I Have No Idea What I Am Doing\"

text: He argues that outside funding is needed less often than people assume, distinguishing services that earn money from current work from businesses requiring substantial product development and user growth before monetization.
title: \"I Have No Idea What I Am Doing\"

text: When additional sales are feasible, he prefers scaling an offering with strong revenue retention and gross margins over pursuing larger, high-touch transactions that would constrain delivery sooner.
title: \"I Have No Idea What I Am Doing\"

text: Lead nurturing has four dimensions: contact frequency, response speed, personalization, and convenient appointment availability. Frequency means outreach attempts per applicant, rather than the number of incoming leads.
title: \"Only 20% of My Leads Show Up. How Do I Fix It?\"

text: Personalizing lead follow-up includes matching the recipient's preferred communication format. Text, audio, and video provide different ways to reach people who may ignore a particular medium.
title: \"Only 20% of My Leads Show Up. How Do I Fix It?\"

text: For comparable offers across countries, he suggests the ratio of median incomes as a rough pricing guide. He thinks adjusting a US price of 3K by that ratio would produce an approximately equivalent Spanish price.
title: \"Only 20% of My Leads Show Up. How Do I Fix It?\"

text: He identifies branding as a way for a business to gain greater pricing power.
title: \"Only 20% of My Leads Show Up. How Do I Fix It?\"

text: He recommends trying memes in lead follow-up and says they tend to generate strong response rates.
title: \"Only 20% of My Leads Show Up. How Do I Fix It?\"

text: Hormozi thinks strong communities connect members with each other. When members depend entirely on the host, removing that connection leaves them disconnected; relationships among members can keep the group connected without the host.
title: How to Build a Community With Insanely High Engagement

text: Hormozi thinks communities become more useful and engaging when people with similar daily experiences help resolve one another's specific, recurring problems.
title: How to Build a Community With Insanely High Engagement

text: Hormozi says years of personal hardship become a roughly 30-second anecdote when he recounts his early business experience, obscuring how long that difficulty actually lasted.
title: Uncertainty Is the Point

text: He argues that calling another person's success easy can deflect the discomfort of one's own shortcomings or inaction onto circumstances, surrendering personal agency.
title: Uncertainty Is the Point

text: He says real-life improvement can take years or decades, unlike a 90-second movie training sequence, and can lack both recognition and certainty.
title: Uncertainty Is the Point

text: He recommends making initial rewards arrive quickly, then gradually increasing the wait and difficulty. He says a history of reinforcement can support working on a coding project for 6 months before receiving a reward.
title: Why Being the Youngest Won't Save You

text: Hormozi describes business funding as choosing which obligations to accept. Bootstrapping avoids financial borrowing but creates gaps in talent, infrastructure and technology. Founders should choose the obligations they can most readily resolve.
title: How do you hire A-players with limited cash?

text: Equity can attract stronger talent when cash compensation is limited, but candidates must believe in the founder's ability and prospects. He illustrates this as preferring 10% ownership alongside that founder over 100% ownership of their own venture.
title: How do you hire A-players with limited cash?

text: A money model can improve available cash by lowering customer acquisition costs, collecting payments sooner and increasing customer spending. Hormozi says this can release cash constraints on expanding advertising, staffing or infrastructure.
title: How do you hire A-players with limited cash?

text: Hormozi defines goodwill as accumulated experiences of positive reinforcement from someone, which make a person more likely to act with or for that individual.
title: How to Build a Brand

text: Hormozi thinks creators mistakenly treat asking for payment as spending goodwill: that assumption presumes the purchased product disappoints. Drawing on an account of Steve Jobs, he explains that a great paid product can instead build goodwill.
title: How to Build a Brand

text: Hormozi argues that rapid growth often feels miserable, and getting through unfamiliar challenges gives people evidence that they can handle more than their previous experience suggested.
title: You're Not Winning (You're Just Getting Used to Pain)

text: Hormozi thinks people could give themselves more credit for enduring past hardship; he treats having made it through those experiences as evidence of their ability to withstand difficulty.
title: You're Not Winning (You're Just Getting Used to Pain)

text: He defines respect as voluntarily changing your actions in response to someone's words when that person cannot compel you.
title: What Respect Actually Means

text: His POWERS model identifies six ways to earn respect: bear costs for others, repeatedly improve results, fulfill commitments, maintain boundaries, limit punishment while sharing credit generously, and remain composed under pressure.
title: What Respect Actually Means

text: Enforcement alone produces compliance that disappears when coercive power disappears. Competence and contribution without boundary enforcement can produce admiration while leaving someone routinely taken advantage of.
title: What Respect Actually Means

text: He identifies three prerequisites for justified enforcement: the person knows the expectation, can meet it, and chooses otherwise. Punishing someone for an expectation never communicated makes the leader appear tyrannical.
title: What Respect Actually Means

text: When enforcing a standard, address the person's specific action rather than insulting their character. His illustrative chef corrects a mistake while affirming that the employee still belongs on the team.
title: What Respect Actually Means

text: Consequences for violations should occur every time, follow promptly, and increase with repetition. He argues that inconsistent enforcement encourages gambling on escaping consequences; persistent violations can warrant dismissal to uphold the group's standard, even for a perceived high performer.
title: What Respect Actually Means

text: Increasing customer lifetime value allows a business to spend more on acquisition.
title: \"What Do You Do When Ads Stop Being Profitable?\"

text: Businesses stalled at $1,000 in daily advertising spend may have exhausted their creative rather than their market. Hormozi says breaking through requires better creative and increased production volume.
title: \"What Do You Do When Ads Stop Being Profitable?\"

text: After initially producing many ads, he follows a 70/20/10 allocation, assigning 70% of subsequent creative to hooks with the strongest historical performance. This excerpt does not explain the other allocations.
title: \"What Do You Do When Ads Stop Being Profitable?\"

text: He argues that comparable businesses typically face similar acquisition costs, while some achieve 10 times the customer lifetime value; he identifies that difference as their competitive advantage.
title: \"What Do You Do When Ads Stop Being Profitable?\"

text: When buying businesses, he typically improves operations working backward toward acquisition, then increases creative output to gather sufficient data, identifies the best-performing 10%, and repeatedly produces more like those winners.
title: \"What Do You Do When Ads Stop Being Profitable?\"

text: Hormozi thinks business growth speed depends partly on recognizing capable people. Experience identifying successful hires across departments and seniority levels makes rebuilding faster, while unfamiliar hiring levels slow progress.
title: Helping an E-Com Brand Scale

text: He challenges the assumption that action requires feeling motivated: people can act while lacking enthusiasm, just as courage involves proceeding while afraid.
title: How to Stay Motivated When You Don't Feel Like Taking Action

text: He proposes defining motivation as the probability of performing an intended behavior. He thinks this probability closely tracks perceived deprivation concerning the outcome someone wants.
title: How to Stay Motivated When You Don't Feel Like Taking Action

text: He thinks meeting successful people can make greater achievement seem attainable, widening the perceived distance between present circumstances and potential outcomes and increasing motivation. Comparing upward can also worsen how someone feels about themselves.
title: How to Stay Motivated When You Don't Feel Like Taking Action

text: Hormozi says an acceptable profit margin during expansion depends on the owner's individual risk tolerance; he does not endorse a universal percentage threshold.
title: You're growing too fast because cash flow can't keep up

text: For a bootstrapped business, he says net income cannot fall below zero without running out of money. The cushion above zero depends on confidence in forecasts and how much the owner wants to withdraw.
title: You're growing too fast because cash flow can't keep up

text: He thinks rapid expansion creates a greater reputational risk than financial risk: deteriorating service can reduce incoming leads, leaving employees underused and the business unprofitable.
title: You're growing too fast because cash flow can't keep up

text: When fear prevents taking a risk, he recommends writing a detailed sequence of what failure would actually involve. Specifying the feared events can make them seem more manageable.
title: You Get Paid in Proportion to Your Risk

text: He believes people in developed countries often overestimate the danger of pursuing ambitious goals, because basic survival alternatives make the actual downside much smaller than they imagine.
title: You Get Paid in Proportion to Your Risk

text: He observes that entrepreneurs can retain their earlier tolerance for financial risk even after business growth substantially increases the opportunities available to them.
title: You Get Paid in Proportion to Your Risk

text: He endorses a 10% probability of a 100-fold payoff despite nine failures in ten, but cautions that life differs from repeated gambling: an illustrative commitment of 10 years might leave only three attempts.
title: You Get Paid in Proportion to Your Risk

text: He argues that an unsuccessful attempt can still produce experience, skills, relationships, and perspective. Treating those gains as part of the outcome can encourage people to attempt more opportunities.
title: You Get Paid in Proportion to Your Risk

text: Businesses can improve customer economics through higher prices, lower costs, complementary services, upgrades in quality, additional units, or lower-quality alternatives.
title: The Ketchup-Packet Customer Problem

text: He gives 35% as a first-purchase closing benchmark for appropriate pricing. For existing customers, an add-on priced below the main purchase should reach 70%–80% acceptance when presented as the customary next purchase.
title: The Ketchup-Packet Customer Problem

text: Hormozi thinks a distinctive underlying idea is the strongest opportunity in long-form content, with exceptional substance outweighing the headline and production quality.
title: What’s Working Right Now for Long-Form Content

text: He thinks distinctive insights emerge two or three layers beneath initial observations. Sustained time considering a subject produces deeper questions that can reveal a person's expertise.
title: What’s Working Right Now for Long-Form Content

text: When creators feel genuinely interested in a topic, he recommends identifying and recreating the surrounding conditions, such as adequate sleep, rather than expecting inspiration to arrive at a scheduled posting time.
title: What’s Working Right Now for Long-Form Content

text: He argues that generating insights requires spare mental capacity and time to think; constant busyness prevents that creative space.
title: What’s Working Right Now for Long-Form Content

text: Hormozi says he follows the maker versus manager approach and keeps four or five days each week free of meetings so he can think.
title: What’s Working Right Now for Long-Form Content

text: For his Tony Robbins interview, Hormozi chose questions he personally wanted answered over an algorithm-oriented list of 10 popular topics. He reports receiving more messages about it than any other content, excluding his launches.
title: What’s Working Right Now for Long-Form Content

text: Hormozi thinks AI capability is advancing faster than human adoption. He views current competition as people using tools against other people using tools, with smarter, harder-working people gaining more from improved technology.
title: \"Is AI About to Break My Business Model?\"

text: Hormozi says choosing between aggressive reinvestment and withdrawing money has no universally correct answer; the decision depends on the entrepreneur’s personal tolerance for risk.
title: \"Is AI About to Break My Business Model?\"

text: Hormozi says he saved heavily early to establish personal security before taking larger business risks. At monthly earnings of 20,000, he spent 500; at monthly earnings of one million, household spending was approximately 10,000–15,000.
title: \"Is AI About to Break My Business Model?\"

text: Hormozi believes entrepreneurs’ household spending often creates greater risk than their business decisions. Personal living expenses are fixed survival costs, and he thinks high spending outside the business can make owners overly cautious about investing inside it.
title: \"Is AI About to Break My Business Model?\"

text: Hormozi observes that successful community operators commonly maintain two groups: a free community that attracts prospects and a paid community they can join next. He recommends this approach as a simple option for many operators.
title: \"Should I Switch My Free Community To Paid?\"

text: For community operators seeking higher conversion, he recommends adding a scheduling link and including a call when people join the free community. He treats insufficient capacity for those calls as a separate problem to solve.
title: \"Should I Switch My Free Community To Paid?\"

text: Hormozi argues that confidence comes from accumulating evidence through work that supports a person's self-image, rather than repeating affirmations.
title: I Don't Gain Confidence by Affirmations, Here's What Works Instead

text: Hormozi previously judged himself by outcomes. He now considers his work successful when he believes he has done everything he could, allowing him to evaluate his performance independently of how an event turns out.
title: I Don't Gain Confidence by Affirmations, Here's What Works Instead

text: For gyms, he suggests an annual renewal charge equivalent to 1–2 monthly payments, roughly $99–$199. His $200 illustration represents approximately 16% additional revenue.
title: You need to raise your prices.

text: He recommends offering to remove a 4% processing surcharge when customers provide another payment method. He says backup payment details can cut churn by 30%, which he values above a 3% revenue increase.
title: You need to raise your prices.

text: He recommends collecting ACH details as an additional payment option: he says ACH saves 2% in processing fees while the backup payment method also reduces churn.
title: You need to raise your prices.

text: He suggests cushioning a price increase with a temporary credit: if the additional charges total $200 across 6 months, provide $200 in gym credit. He says customers accept an expiring discount more readily than a higher price.
title: You need to raise your prices.

text: Choosing between life paths requires a clear objective. Hormozi contrasts increasing income with increasing the number of people reached: each gives a different target against which to evaluate a decision.
title: Should I Quit Med School to Go All-In on My Business?

text: Hormozi thinks many people spend years undecided because they fear committing to one future and losing the alternative; identifying what they want is harder than pursuing it.
title: Should I Quit Med School to Go All-In on My Business?

text: When choosing between competing futures, imagine looking back at age 85 and consider which missed path would cause greater regret.
title: Should I Quit Med School to Go All-In on My Business?

text: Salespeople should guide prospects through questions, identify their problems and connect those problems to the offer during the pitch, helping prospects reach their own buying decision.
title: Helping an Agency Owner Build a Sales Team

text: When a sales role requires demonstrating specialist expertise, Hormozi argues that suitable hires will be unavailable or prohibitively expensive.
title: Helping an Agency Owner Build a Sales Team

text: Given a script that already works, Hormozi considers delivering the appropriate words at the appropriate moment fully trainable through reinforcement. He argues that most businesses provide insufficient sales training.
title: Helping an Agency Owner Build a Sales Team

text: Hormozi thinks creators who struggle to attract an audience beyond their demonstrated success may need more exceptional real accomplishments, rather than additional marketing techniques.
title: The One Thing You Need to Win in Content

text: He observes that greater achievement expands the audience that sees someone as an authority. He mentions the top 10% and top 1% of success, then describes an eventual position where even other influencers regard that person as an authority.
title: The One Thing You Need to Win in Content

text: Hormozi thinks private equity firms typically respond to limited operating bandwidth by raising more capital and pursuing fewer, larger acquisitions rather than continually increasing their deal count.
title: Helping a 25M/Year Private Equity Firm Scale

text: Hormozi says his company continually searches for exceptional employees and pays at the 90th percentile across roles because he believes superior talent produces substantially greater investment returns.
title: Helping a 25M/Year Private Equity Firm Scale

text: In an illustrative hiring comparison, Hormozi argues that an exceptional sales director asking $400,000 annually instead of a $200,000 market salary could generate an additional $4 million annually.
title: Helping a 25M/Year Private Equity Firm Scale

text: Hormozi favors a recruiting team nearly as large as the sales team. He says recruiting was an early primary source of value at Acquisition.com and helped staff executive and leadership positions across portfolio companies.
title: Helping a 25M/Year Private Equity Firm Scale

text: When entering a market with an established dominant competitor, Hormozi recommends reproducing an approach that already succeeds before attempting innovations.
title: $718 Spent, 0 Leads: What This Solar Business Did Wrong

text: Hormozi argues that every competitor has some advantage, even when businesses sell identical products; the owner needs to identify that advantage.
title: $718 Spent, 0 Leads: What This Solar Business Did Wrong

text: A small business owner can compete with a large company through direct personal attention: the customer’s actual alternative is often an assigned representative rather than the entire organization.
title: $718 Spent, 0 Leads: What This Solar Business Did Wrong

text: Once entrepreneurs learn what different roles and seniority levels look like across departments, starting subsequent businesses becomes a matter of putting familiar components together.
title: Why Your Next Business Always Grows Faster

text: Hormozi argues that whatever business difficulty an entrepreneur faces, another person has already encountered it and found a solution.
title: Why Your Next Business Always Grows Faster

text: Hormozi frames declining opportunities as affirming the highest priority, rather than exercising a separate capacity for rejection.
title: Every Week 20 New Opportunities Try to Distract Me

text: Hormozi contrasts responding to suffering by harming others with trying to protect others from suffering. He credits Donald Miller for the comparison and adds that people can direct their pain constructively or be controlled by it.
title: Every Week 20 New Opportunities Try to Distract Me

text: Hormozi says an exceptional employee can deliver 10 times the output for compensation 30% above market. He considers that premium an unusually attractive investment and sees no benefit in deliberately paying below market.
title: The Best Bet in Business

text: He argues that a company's growth depends on expanding its collective knowledge. Hiring someone whose subject expertise the founder already fully possesses adds no knowledge; remaining the company's smartest person leaves its potential limited by the founder's own understanding.
title: The Best Bet in Business

text: In his lead-handling software business, Hormozi found that agency relationships persisted even as their individual small-business clients changed, making agencies a more stable customer base.
title: Helping a Building Management Agency Scale

text: Hormozi thinks many people earn less than they want because they overestimate their ability.
title: You're Not Making as Much Money as You Want Because You're Not as Good as You Think

text: He thinks the greatest financial outcomes combine drive, intelligence, accumulated skills and luck. He suggests learning from the 10,000 wealthiest people rather than concentrating only on the top five, whose outcomes also benefited from luck.
title: You're Not Making as Much Money as You Want Because You're Not as Good as You Think

text: He recommends noticing past good fortune to develop a belief that you are lucky. He thinks this encourages larger attempts because you expect to manage the downside, and repeated large attempts can eventually succeed.
title: You're Not Making as Much Money as You Want Because You're Not as Good as You Think

text: He suggests spending time around people achieving substantially more than you: opportunities that benefit them may also benefit you.
title: You're Not Making as Much Money as You Want Because You're Not as Good as You Think

text: Hormozi says taking a largely passive role while selling three companies in 2021 left him bored. Looking back, he considered building those businesses among his happiest experiences.
title: Passive Income Is Overrated

text: For Hormozi, freedom became having the choice to pursue engaging work. He says returning to business building made him happy because he could choose that activity.
title: Passive Income Is Overrated

text: When outreach drives acquisition, he views a basic organic presence as lead nurturing: it demonstrates activity and value. Relying on organic content for most demand requires a different strategy and substantially greater investment.
title: Why Most Cold Outreach Fails

text: For outbound prospecting, he suggests three relevant posts weekly as a basic credibility presence. He says prospects often inspect the sender’s profile before replying and may watch two or three pieces of content to assess legitimacy.
title: Why Most Cold Outreach Fails

text: Hormozi believes that whatever business challenge an owner faces, another person has already encountered it and found a solution.
title: Everyone is jealous of what you've got. No one is jealous of how you got it.

text: An appealing initial offer can help customers begin receiving the support they need: lead with something they already want.
title: Helping a High School Tutoring Business Scale

text: A program with a clear endpoint can open the sale of longer support. During the initial program, customers have time to learn what matters and experience progress before considering a longer commitment.
title: Helping a High School Tutoring Business Scale

text: Ongoing services are rarely sold by asking prospects to commit immediately to continuity; a limited introductory experience can precede the longer commitment.
title: Helping a High School Tutoring Business Scale

text: Hormozi advocates making the core product so exceptional that other business concerns become secondary, illustrating this with a sandwich shop whose food gives customers an extraordinary experience.
title: Be Too Good to Fail

text: In business and possibly life, Hormozi considers which single accomplishment could make other shortcomings insignificant. He urges concentrating effort on that achievement and viewing earlier mediocrity as part of the journey toward it.
title: Be Too Good to Fail

text: He says business problems often require several connected changes; working backward from the core problem can reveal what needs to change first.
title: Helping an Electrical Contractor Scale

text: He endorses the principle that continuing to want an outcome while remaining unwilling to adopt the lifestyle and effort it requires creates persistent dissatisfaction.
title: Why You Can't Get Over Your Ex (Real Reason)

text: He thinks moving past a breakup involves discovering replacement sources of enjoyment, including activities or another relationship. For an unwanted desire, he suggests reasoning through why a different pursuit would be preferable.
title: Why You Can't Get Over Your Ex (Real Reason)

text: Hormozi reports repeating his book launch presentation unchanged on the second day and generating about $25 million in sales, with many returning viewers. He attributes the decision to his belief that asking again works.
title: Advice For Anyone Who Feels Stuck

text: When an activity already produces revenue, he recommends asking how to multiply its inputs by 100. Effort and systems both help; one example is distributing a single content item across 10 destinations.
title: Advice For Anyone Who Feels Stuck

text: He argues that earlier funnel improvements offer greater throughput leverage: increasing ad click-through from 1% to 2% doubles the business, whereas doubling page conversion seems unlikely to him; a strong page improvement might yield 10–20%.
title: Advice For Anyone Who Feels Stuck

text: He considers pricing and advertising creative volume major growth levers. In the businesses he sees, insufficient traffic or churn usually deserves more attention than page conversion, while acknowledging that a poorly converting page can itself be the problem.
title: Advice For Anyone Who Feels Stuck

text: Hormozi thinks motivation reflects a perceived shortage: hunger follows missing food, and sleepiness follows insufficient sleep. He sees wanting to fill a gap as central to drive, while allowing that its source can change.
title: How to Stay Motivated All Day (this works)

text: He thinks life can have several sources of meaning. Asking what someone's life or work means to them can make an abstract question about their motivation easier to answer concretely.
title: How to Stay Motivated All Day (this works)

text: Around 31, Hormozi had enough money to stop working. About a year away convinced him he wanted activity, so he made demanding work an end in itself, an approach he says he followed for roughly five years.
title: How to Stay Motivated All Day (this works)

text: Hormozi thinks desires often reverse once satisfied, reflecting a wish for novelty. He considers deliberately balancing work and time away more demanding than either extreme, with the preferred amount of work differing between people.
title: How to Stay Motivated All Day (this works)

text: He finds that a few recurring weekly or monthly activities preserve variety in his life, helping him continue pursuing longer goals that matter more to him.
title: How to Stay Motivated All Day (this works)

text: Hormozi argues that friends' criticism of constructive changes, such as stopping drinking or building a business, can reflect their own unrealized ambitions. He encourages interpreting that resistance as evidence of progress.
title: The Lonely Chapter Every Successful Person Goes Through

text: He describes a lonely transition in pursuing success: existing friendships no longer feel compatible, while results have not yet earned entry into a new peer group. He presents this experience as common to everyone who achieves meaningful ambitions.
title: The Lonely Chapter Every Successful Person Goes Through

text: When selecting vendors, he recommends interviewing 10 providers and telling each that competing proposals are being considered. Hearing multiple pitches helps buyers understand the service and recognize stronger providers.
title: Helping an Owner Stop Getting Burned by Vendors

text: He argues that spending an additional 2 weeks selecting a vendor can avoid 6 months with a poor provider and the expense of repeating the work, which he describes as doubling the cost.
title: Helping an Owner Stop Getting Burned by Vendors

text: He treats a vendor's communication before hiring as evidence of the future working relationship. Clear expectations, responsive communication, and realistic schedules encourage confidence; extravagant promises paired with slow responses make him more skeptical.
title: Helping an Owner Stop Getting Burned by Vendors

text: He would favor a modest offer supported by 2,000 five-star reviews over an extraordinary offer without evidence. For vendors, inability to provide 5 references or a lack of visible online evidence or content raises concerns.
title: Helping an Owner Stop Getting Burned by Vendors

text: Copying the lifestyle someone enjoys after becoming successful confuses the results of success with the work required to achieve it.
title: I Live the Same Day 7 Days a Week

text: Hormozi says his enjoyable present lifestyle followed a long period of work he disliked, without encouragement and with people actively opposing his chosen path.
title: I Live the Same Day 7 Days a Week

text: For a membership, consider which work the provider can complete for customers and which risks it can absorb. Hormozi presents combining both as an especially valuable service.
title: Your Business Needs Consumable Media

text: Hormozi distinguishes three accountability sources: peers facing the same stage, alumni who have already progressed, and experts experienced in helping similar customers overcome problems.
title: Your Business Needs Consumable Media

text: In fitness coaching, experts can assess progress through multiple measures and provide corrective feedback when customers stall. Hormozi argues that a single week without progress need not become a sustained plateau.
title: Your Business Needs Consumable Media

text: A product should handle difficult work behind the scenes so customers experience an easy path to the result. Hormozi identifies solving implementation difficulties for customers, then doing so at scale, as two levels of opportunity.
title: Your Business Needs Consumable Media

text: Community operators should spend four minutes brainstorming valuable resources members can repeatedly use. Hormozi believes each community has a suitable version and probably several possibilities.
title: Your Business Needs Consumable Media

text: Hormozi thinks unusually low agency prices can make mid-market buyers doubt the provider's credibility, potentially losing customers who would accept higher fees.
title: What Agencies Get Wrong About Pricing

text: He cautions against judging customers' willingness to pay by the seller's own budget or ability to perform the service themselves.
title: What Agencies Get Wrong About Pricing

text: His pricing guideline targets a 35% close rate. He suggests a 40–50% close rate may support a 25–50% price increase, while 50–60% may support charging 1.5–1.75 times the current price.
title: What Agencies Get Wrong About Pricing

text: Under his pricing guideline, a 60–70% close rate suggests room to at least double prices; a 70–80% close rate suggests room to double or triple them.
title: What Agencies Get Wrong About Pricing

text: He recommends agency fees that rise with client ad spending while charging lower percentages in higher spending bands. Each lower rate applies only within its band, without reducing fees on earlier spending.
title: What Agencies Get Wrong About Pricing

text: He uses a parable about three workers cutting stone to illustrate how people can experience identical work differently depending on the meaning they give it.
title: Helping a Boat Rental Company Scale

text: He thinks businesses become broadly similar when viewed two or three organizational levels up: leaders face sales, marketing, technology, staffing, HR, and legal problems regardless of the product.
title: Helping a Boat Rental Company Scale

text: He discourages expecting a business to supply personal happiness. His preferred approach is to treat it as a setting for developing skills, pursuing excellence, and expressing personal values.
title: Helping a Boat Rental Company Scale

text: He rejects industry averages as standards to aspire to because he believes many average operators perform poorly and make little money.
title: Helping a Boat Rental Company Scale

text: Hormozi says celebrities often have relatively weak influence; he favors smaller creators, livestreamers, and creators whose audiences consume longer content when considering potential endorsers.
title: The Path From $1M to $100M for Service Businesses

text: Hormozi develops filming topics from coaching discussions: a team member records useful explanations and later prompts him to revisit them on camera.
title: How to Make Content People Can Understand

text: When developing written explanations, he starts with assumptions he considers reliable, connects patterns from practical experience, and tries to find counterexamples that would invalidate the resulting principles.
title: How to Make Content People Can Understand

text: He rejects dividing buyers into emotional and logical categories. He instead thinks consuming more information increases purchase likelihood and treats purchase readiness as a continuum.
title: How to Make Content People Can Understand

text: His provisional definition of influence is the probability that a person follows a request. He keeps that definition until he discovers a counterexample that defeats it.
title: How to Make Content People Can Understand

text: He thinks explanations become easier to understand when they describe observable behavior instead of relying on feelings or implied meanings.
title: How to Make Content People Can Understand

text: Rapid feedback can support learning while also reinforcing mistaken associations. He warns that people may credit an incidental behavior for a successful outcome and turn it into a ritual.
title: How to Make Content People Can Understand

text: His sales-tone model has three fixed requirements: audible volume, clear pronunciation, and an understandable pace. Its two adjustable elements are pitch and pauses; he says raised pitch invites responses, while pauses draw attention.
title: How to Make Content People Can Understand

text: He checks his writing against a third- or fifth-grade reading standard or lower. When more advanced vocabulary is necessary, he explains it simply because he believes unfamiliar words interrupt learning.
title: How to Make Content People Can Understand

text: Hormozi thinks people too readily interpret poor coaching as malicious when it may reflect limited teaching ability. Teachers improve through practice, meaning some students experience their inexperienced teaching.
title: Everyone's a Coach Now. Does It Bother Me?

text: For people who want to teach others, Hormozi recommends establishing demonstrated results first. He believes his existing business accomplishments helped his brand grow faster than those of other business commentators.
title: Everyone's a Coach Now. Does It Bother Me?

text: Hormozi limits his business guidance to outcomes he has achieved: he says he cannot guide someone to $1 billion yet, but feels confident about $100 million because he has reached it three times.
title: Everyone's a Coach Now. Does It Bother Me?

text: Hormozi treats losing peace of mind as a signal that he may be violating his values; he considers attention gained through claims he believes are wrong unworthy of that cost.
title: How I Responded to a VC Who Bashed My Clip

text: Hormozi recounts privately challenging a venture capitalist who shared a clip criticizing him. According to Hormozi, the critic conceded that Hormozi was correct and admitted overstepping in pursuit of a viral post.
title: How I Responded to a VC Who Bashed My Clip

text: Hormozi says he has benefited from challenging his assumption that feeling unhappy means something is wrong, working on his interpretation rather than automatically trying to change the situation.
title: Accept Suffering Without Letting It Run Your Life

text: He describes fading affect bias as painful feelings weakening while positive memories persist. He sees hope in remembering life more favorably, but warns that this becomes problematic when it makes the present seem disappointing.
title: Accept Suffering Without Letting It Run Your Life

text: Entrepreneurs earn greater rewards by concentrating their available time and money on fewer opportunities with higher returns.
title: The Only Way to Win in Business

text: Hormozi defines strategy as deciding how to prioritize resources. He argues that when constant work fails to grow a business, the entrepreneur is usually choosing the wrong priorities.
title: The Only Way to Win in Business

text: Reduce a long action list to 1–3 priorities, preferably 1. Focusing on 1 objective can involve 20 supporting actions, including seeking assistance from friends and hiring help, all directed toward making that objective happen.
title: The Only Way to Win in Business

text: Hormozi believes a chosen customer segment can support a $10 million or $100 million business; he says he has encountered no niche that rules out $100 million in annual revenue.
title: You NEED to niche down

text: A specialist can deliver greater value to a particular customer group than a broadly established business educator. Hormozi says an expert in insurance billing for registered dietitians can outperform him in that specialty.
title: You NEED to niche down

text: Hormozi says he lost the proceeds from selling five gyms after investing with a partner who took the money. Over the following 12 months, his profit was approximately five times his profit across the preceding five years.
title: You're Not a Victim of Your Circumstances. Keep Going.

text: He argues that losing the financial results of past work does not erase its value: the skills and experience remain, preparing someone to tackle larger challenges and achieve greater results.
title: You're Not a Victim of Your Circumstances. Keep Going.

text: Hormozi considers business emergencies rare. Even interrupted payment processing during active sales can be assessed as a tolerable sales loss rather than automatically demanding his immediate attention.
title: Most Businesses Do Lots of Small Things That Don't Matter

text: Team updates and reported metrics should inform a change in action. Hormozi says filtering communication this way removes most messages he would otherwise handle.
title: Most Businesses Do Lots of Small Things That Don't Matter

text: Hormozi thinks focus is demonstrated by both how many opportunities someone rejects and how attractive those opportunities are; declining things they actually want to pursue shows commitment to the chosen direction.
title: Most Businesses Do Lots of Small Things That Don't Matter

text: When achieving one strategic objective would resolve other problems or render them irrelevant, Hormozi argues that those secondary issues do not warrant his attention.
title: Most Businesses Do Lots of Small Things That Don't Matter

text: Four years earlier, Hormozi chose building the largest business brand as his central objective, expecting more investment opportunities, more willing deal partners, and business-content expertise that would help him grow companies.
title: Most Businesses Do Lots of Small Things That Don't Matter

text: Hormozi challenges the idea that an offer simply expires: he attributes it to poor products and says sellers should focus on delivering the outcome customers originally purchased.
title: Why Offers Eventually Stop Working

text: He sees opportunities to improve existing businesses with AI; building a business entirely around AI may also work for someone with strong product capabilities and an excellent engineering team.
title: Why Offers Eventually Stop Working

text: He predicts AI will displace more AI businesses than conventional businesses. For a proposed AI sales product, he questions whether OpenAI could reproduce its function within 6 months.
title: Why Offers Eventually Stop Working

text: For building teams, companies or revenue lines, he describes hiring 1 person to hire 10: prioritize someone with an existing network and relevant experience. Compared with training less experienced hires, this costs more but moves faster.
title: \"How Do I Grow on Social Media Working Only 1 Hour a Day?\"

text: He uses expensive headhunters for occasional specialist or leadership hires because they maintain candidate networks. He keeps recruiting internal for frequently needed roles, such as salespeople, editors and customer success staff, because those roles underpin business operations.
title: \"How Do I Grow on Social Media Working Only 1 Hour a Day?\"

text: Hormozi wants an adviser who understands the full situation, can competently interpret it, and has interests aligned with his. Missing any one of these three qualities limits the usefulness of the advice.
title: How to Give Yourself Good Advice

text: Hormozi schedules Monday’s first hour for written exchanges with Solomon, his imagined 85-year-old self. He alternates perspectives until a specific issue feels resolved; a session may take 7 or 45 minutes rather than the whole hour.
title: How to Give Yourself Good Advice

text: Hormozi reports losing about $15 million after paying a vendor several hundred thousand dollars to prevent that loss. He concluded that incompetence, rather than malicious intent, explained the vendor’s failure.
title: How to Give Yourself Good Advice

text: After a project involving two years of work failed, Hormozi found relief by treating his own development as the lasting asset and accepting his imagined older self’s approval of his effort.
title: How to Give Yourself Good Advice

text: For high achievers, Hormozi recommends measuring themselves against their desired future self. That standard can sustain motivation because outperforming others does not establish whether they have used their own full capacity.
title: How to Give Yourself Good Advice

text: Hormozi says he spent 200 hours across 28 days preparing his leads book presentation. Daily, he reviewed slides, recorded a rehearsal, watched it, and revised the slides. His calm came from believing he had exhausted his preparation options.
title: How to Give Yourself Good Advice

text: Hormozi considers his vendor choice reasonable given the information, experience, and recommendations available then. He acknowledges further checking was possible but sees a tradeoff between additional verification and excessive oversight.
title: How to Give Yourself Good Advice

text: Hormozi says he falls below his imagined older self’s standards daily, including in how thoughtfully he treats his wife. His written conversations usually address one particular concern.
title: How to Give Yourself Good Advice

text: Hormozi says research he has read places monks with over 40,000 meditation hours three to four standard deviations above typical subjective wellbeing. He presents this as a reason for considering intensive practice.
title: my thoughts on meditation...

text: He considers the ability to feel good without favorable circumstances the most valuable skill a person can develop.
title: my thoughts on meditation...

text: Hormozi believes happiness requiring substantial effort fits his worldview. Despite attaining his desired physique, marriage, business, and surroundings, he thinks a meditator with few possessions could experience greater happiness.
title: my thoughts on meditation...

text: Around age 19 or 20, Hormozi considered abandoning his existing direction for monastic meditation. He instead adopted usefulness as his life objective and stopped making happiness his focus.
title: my thoughts on meditation...

text: Hormozi personally believes people owe one another useful contributions. His wish to contribute has outweighed his wish for happiness, but he is open to pursuing both together.
title: my thoughts on meditation...

text: Hormozi evaluates ideas using three checks: clarify their meaning, examine the supporting evidence, and establish why they matter. He uses this process to filter noise, grounding his understanding in what he can observe.
title: How I Taught Myself to Think Clearly

text: Hormozi says three activities make a day good for him: exercising alongside friends, sharing meals with friends, and producing some writing.
title: How I Taught Myself to Think Clearly

text: Hormozi interprets choosing between power and peace as choosing between usefulness and personal contentment, and he favors usefulness.
title: Why I'd Pick Power Over Peace

text: He would prefer to finish life having helped many people, even if doing so involved personal costs. He thinks that contribution might also become his own route to peace.
title: Why I'd Pick Power Over Peace

text: Hormozi says he enjoys his life and work, possibly because he does something he performs well. His willingness to bear personal costs does not mean he currently experiences his life as unhappy.
title: Why I'd Pick Power Over Peace

text: He does not consider his path a personal sacrifice because he believes others have given up substantially more for him than he has given up himself.
title: Why I'd Pick Power Over Peace

text: He sees wealth and power as means rather than ultimate aims: they provide capacity to help others, including funding hospitals or protecting lives, whereas he sees personal peace as benefiting himself.
title: Why I'd Pick Power Over Peace

text: Changing surroundings need not require relocating to another city. He suggests that moving two miles away or changing living arrangements can create a different environment within the same city.
title: How to Kill Bad Habits

text: For someone trying to stop an unwanted habit, he argues that changing surroundings can remove its triggers. Returning to the previous setting can bring back the behavior associated with it.
title: How to Kill Bad Habits

text: To encourage sunscreen use, he placed supplies in three frequently used locations: his lunch table, work table, and bedside. He also chose an applicator that avoided getting oil on his hands, addressing both forgetting and discomfort.
title: How to Kill Bad Habits

text: When establishing a habit, identify and reduce what makes performing it unpleasant. Arrange environmental reminders where the behavior is practical; he explains that a phone alarm can arrive when acting on it is inconvenient.
title: How to Kill Bad Habits

text: Hormozi thinks competence and good intentions both relate to whether a company's actions fit its brand.
title: Lessons from Losing Millions | Dave Ramsey

text: Hormozi structures a video sales letter around an introduction, the offer's distinctive approach, and objections. The opening establishes the promised result, the customer's pain, evidence, and a plan.
title: How to script a VSL

text: To address an objection, identify the prospect's current belief, explain its flaw, present a better understanding, and support that alternative with evidence. Repeat this sequence for each major objection.
title: How to script a VSL

text: For entrepreneurs, he considers reinvesting in their existing business the best return opportunity. His barbell strategy puts surplus cash into passive investments after exhausting opportunities to reinvest in the business.
title: Helping a Coaching Business Scale

text: He defines a passive investment as requiring no owner time: it should be possible to leave it unattended for one or two years. Entrepreneurs must accept lower returns than they expect from their operating business.
title: Helping a Coaching Business Scale

text: When paid advertising reaches a spending ceiling, he identifies three ways forward: strengthen the offer, improve conversion, or produce better ads.
title: Helping a Coaching Business Scale

text: He believes practicing organic content improves advertising creative because organic distribution must be earned, whereas ads purchase distribution.
title: Helping a Coaching Business Scale

text: Some of his best-converting Acquisition.com ads reuse high-performing organic videos with a five-second call to action appended.
title: Helping a Coaching Business Scale

text: Hormozi thinks criticism can hurt when it contains something a person believes is true but avoids confronting. He suggests considering whether the critic is correct.
title: They Can't See You Because You're Already Successful

text: Hormozi argues that imitators reproduce the wrong features when they do not understand what produced the results. That missing understanding also leaves them unable to repair what stops working.
title: They Can't See You Because You're Already Successful

text: Hormozi endorses advice he received to pursue goals rather than retaliate against critics: retaliation keeps attention on them, while growing successful makes their influence less significant.
title: They Can't See You Because You're Already Successful

text: He estimates that e-commerce growth often becomes harder near $1 million monthly revenue, depending on market size. He qualifies this estimate by noting his direct experience covers only one e-commerce business.
title: Helping an E-Com Brand Scale Past $3M

text: For consumer brands adding wholesale distribution, he recommends pitching retailers on bringing shoppers into their stores, where those shoppers can also purchase other merchandise.
title: Helping an E-Com Brand Scale Past $3M

text: He reports that doubling average order value in a business discussed previously increased its advertising capacity fivefold.
title: Helping an E-Com Brand Scale Past $3M

text: A growth strategy needs a specific activity that produces customers; choosing a customer segment without knowing what action to take next leaves the business waiting.
title: Helping a Hospitality Consulting Business Scale

text: Customer acquisition can appear inconsistent simply because the business performs too little of the activity producing customers.
title: Helping a Hospitality Consulting Business Scale

text: Once a business identifies the activity producing customers, Hormozi suggests it may need to perform that activity at 10 or 100 times its current volume.

text: If a business already runs without a personal brand and the owner plans to sell it eventually, Hormozi would not add a personal brand on top of it.
title: Helping an In-Person Service Business Fix Their Offer

text: One behavior Hormozi would change, though he doubts it would alter the outcome, is documenting the early journey more. It need not be public: photos, voice notes or emailing yourself all work.
title: The One Thing I Regret Not Doing Early

text: When he lost his six successful gyms and was left with about a thousand dollars, he screenshotted his bank account. It was a cathartic moment that made him vow never again, and he still has and shows the screenshot.
title: The One Thing I Regret Not Doing Early

text: He says you document the early days because you believe you will become the hero who overcomes. He compares this to Kanye keeping early videos, believing he would make it and use them later.
title: The One Thing I Regret Not Doing Early

text: Hormozi describes commitment to an opportunity as excluding alternatives, including apparently superior options that appear later. He thinks unfamiliar alternatives rarely prove better because their drawbacks are still hidden.
title: My Biggest Ongoing Challenge

text: When considering switching after 2 years in a career, compare your prospective fourth year there with your second year in the new field. Hormozi argues that comparing a future alternative with your current position ignores continued improvement.
title: My Biggest Ongoing Challenge

text: Hormozi suggests that improving from the top 10% to the top 5% in a skill could triple income despite a 5-percentage-point difference. He uses this illustration to explain why continued improvement can yield disproportionate rewards.
title: My Biggest Ongoing Challenge

text: Over a long career of sustained heavy action, he has seen work swing like an accordion between doing more and doing better, and he considers this normal and expected, depending on where you are in the swing.
title: Should You Do More or Better?

text: Going from one YouTube video a week to five will likely bring more views. Then one of the five or ten usually outperforms the rest, which prompts you to cut volume and make fewer, better videos.
title: Should You Do More or Better?

text: After cutting to about three higher-quality videos every two weeks, average quality rises and total views rise. Once you are good at that, you scale back to ten like it, and again one stands out.
title: Should You Do More or Better?

text: Hormozi criticizes college entrepreneurship classes for emphasizing invention. He thinks students could often earn more by starting an existing type of business instead of creating a novel product.
title: You should start a boring business

text: Hormozi says he now seeks products customers tend to keep rather than cancel.
title: You should start a boring business

text: Inflation compounding at roughly 4% a year for 40 years shrinks what money is really worth, and people often ignore this when they plan to save.
title: Start Buying Skills

text: Example: a minimum-wage worker could pay 500 dollars for a two-day phlebotomy certification and move from 7 to 25 dollars an hour. Borrowing to do it now beats saving for eight weeks, putting her seven weeks ahead.
title: Start Buying Skills

text: Putting 500 dollars into the S&P 500 earns only a couple of dollars a year, so people who save instead of investing in skills are making assumptions without working through the math.
title: Start Buying Skills

text: When he ran ads, worked the leads and sold them himself with no employees, he made about 100 thousand dollars a month at 14-hour days. That became his baseline, which has risen as his skills improved.
title: Start Buying Skills

text: Many people in the worker's position try to earn a few dollars on saved money, when the better question is how to create another 50 thousand dollars a year of income.
title: Start Buying Skills

text: If the worker keeps living cheaply at her parents' home, tripled pay leaves about 30 thousand dollars a year, and he says that budget can buy any skill education worth under ten million dollars.
title: Start Buying Skills

text: People judge someone's age only for a couple of seconds before that person speaks. Once he opens his mouth, they care about how good he is, so age is a very thin, surface-level judgment.
title: Young Entrepreneurs: Stop Using Age as an Excuse

text: Younger people generally know less than older ones, but exceptions exist, such as Mark Zuckerberg becoming a billionaire at 21. A young person should therefore demonstrate expertise rather than worry about age.
title: Young Entrepreneurs: Stop Using Age as an Excuse

text: When he began making a lot of money around ages 26 to 27, people made a big deal of how young he was. By 36, he says, nobody cares anymore.
title: Young Entrepreneurs: Stop Using Age as an Excuse

text: Hormozi evaluates business focus by considering how serving different customers changes the work required to operate the company.
title: Helping an $830K Sports Program Get to $5M

text: To grow revenue, a business must either sell to more customers, meaning higher sales velocity, or make each customer worth more, meaning higher lifetime value.
title: \"I can't get past 3M/year. What should I do?\"

text: Each new revenue stopping point, such as 500k or a million a month, will bring a fresh moment of not knowing how to hire the next person. You fail for a while, then figure it out, so you must keep trying.
title: \"I can't get past 3M/year. What should I do?\"

text: When someone struggles to find a leader, Hormozi suggests the cause is probably searching for too much in a person or paying too little, or both.
title: \"I can't get past 3M/year. What should I do?\"

text: Acceptance means taking outcomes and circumstances as they are, including the hand you were dealt such as height, race or gender. Fighting those facts is fighting the universe, and he says the universe wins every time.
title: Acceptance vs Good Enough: The Biggest Embodiment of Failure

text: He views treating acceptance as being comfortable with who you are, unable to be better and obliged to be satisfied, as the biggest embodiment of failure he can imagine.
title: Acceptance vs Good Enough: The Biggest Embodiment of Failure

text: Saying you are good enough for your current state, given the work you have put in, differs from saying you are good. You can accept that your work produced your present outcome without treating it as the final outcome you need.
title: Acceptance vs Good Enough: The Biggest Embodiment of Failure

text: The only acceptance he practices is admitting the version of himself he wants to be is far from who he is now. He breaks that gap down one step at a time, doing things that can build that person even if he feels he does not yet deserve it.
title: Acceptance vs Good Enough: The Biggest Embodiment of Failure

text: Becoming that future version also means going through the circumstances that would create that person, which he says applies if you hold very big dreams and goals.
title: Acceptance vs Good Enough: The Biggest Embodiment of Failure

text: People tend to cheer only at the start of a race and at the finish. Neither is when support is needed, so the skill to build is getting through the long, boring, exhausting middle.
title: Everyone Who Doubts You Is Right Until They Aren't

text: Hormozi noticed people were happy for him at the beginning because he had temporarily lowered his status and was worse off than them. Their happiness seemed tied to where they stood on the ladder relative to him.
title: Everyone Who Doubts You Is Right Until They Aren't

text: Once he passed certain people, they stopped being happy for him and started saying negative things, while those still ahead kept encouraging him. He wonders whether those still ahead will flip if he passes them.
title: Everyone Who Doubts You Is Right Until They Aren't

text: After starting, you quickly pass people who have done nothing, but then face a long stretch where you have not caught those far ahead. It is lonely because you have left your original group without reaching a new one with proof behind it.
title: Everyone Who Doubts You Is Right Until They Aren't

text: He has plenty of support now but needed it most in the middle, during the many years when nobody knew who he was.
title: Everyone Who Doubts You Is Right Until They Aren't

text: The hard part is not knowing how it finishes, the fear of giving up everything for nothing. Looking back with success, the trade seems obvious, but in the moment you are placing a bet and only learn the result years later.
title: Everyone Who Doubts You Is Right Until They Aren't

text: For finding a price, start with whatever number you can say on the phone without cracking a smile. Talk to five prospects, make the offer, and keep raising it until the market says no.
title: Helping a $260K Recruiting Business Get to $1M

text: He says price is the strongest lever on profit.
title: Helping a $260K Recruiting Business Get to $1M

text: He says you can certainly raise your outbound volume from 100 DMs to 500 or 1,000, and many large companies use LinkedIn outbound as their main way to get customers.
title: Helping a $260K Recruiting Business Get to $1M

text: To get a group deal done, one person must be talking and one person must be in control; otherwise it becomes a mess, and that is the problem to solve for.
title: Helping a Business Owner Structure a Roll-Up

text: If each owner's share of sale proceeds matches their contribution to the whole, the split feels fair and everyone is motivated to push for the sale, since a bigger overall multiple benefits all of them.
title: Helping a Business Owner Structure a Roll-Up

text: Hormozi says owners selling alone may be unsellable or fetch roughly 5x, so a roll-up organizer can offer them a better multiple than they could get solo.
title: Helping a Business Owner Structure a Roll-Up

text: Subscription retention should come from customers wanting to continue receiving the product, rather than overlooking recurring charges.
title: How to Fix 75% Churn in a Subscription Business

text: Hormozi recounts bidding for a business with this model against competing buyers, including a private equity firm. The eventual price exceeded what he was prepared to pay.
title: Helping a Wellness Dentistry Practice Scale

text: Shutting a business down is harder than transferring it to someone else, so he prefers selling or handing it off, even at a lower price, to get out faster with less overhead and risk.
title: \"Which of My Three Businesses Do I Shut Down?\"

text: He says a coach does not need to operate a business of the type they teach. Clients can be told that focus on delivering them the highest returns is worth more than occasionally doing hands-on work.
title: \"Which of My Three Businesses Do I Shut Down?\"

text: When launching Gym Launch, he went from six gyms to zero in 90 days, selling all six for the price of one. Others told him it was foolish after years of building them.
title: \"Which of My Three Businesses Do I Shut Down?\"

text: He says polishing the gyms for 18 months might have fetched about 2 to 3 million. Instead, within six months Gym Launch was making a million a month, so the opportunity cost of waiting was large.
title: \"Which of My Three Businesses Do I Shut Down?\"

text: Brick and mortar locations can run seamlessly when you have around 20 of them, because that supports layers of management. One location lacks the margin to pay a capable manager without giving away nearly all the profit.
title: \"Which of My Three Businesses Do I Shut Down?\"

text: He suggests that a manager overseeing five locations makes the economics work, versus one manager per single location. Exceptions exist for models that print money, but he says this one is not that.
title: \"Which of My Three Businesses Do I Shut Down?\"

text: Before choosing an operational system to fix, he asks what actually breaks when volume doubles. The first thing to break is the operating constraint, so identify that rather than guessing at systems.
title: He Can Double His Business Tomorrow and Won't

text: He spent about five years pursuing peace, happiness or satisfaction and found it unfruitful, so he stopped chasing a feeling and chased things he could do instead.
title: I Stopped Chasing Happiness. Then I Found It

text: After he shifted his behavior and learning toward what he could do and away from what he could feel, satisfaction showed up as a result, changing his worldview toward things he can see and do with his hands.
title: I Stopped Chasing Happiness. Then I Found It

text: He describes the world in words people can grasp through sight, hearing and touch, which he thinks allows clear communication and a high share of the message reaching the other person.
title: I Stopped Chasing Happiness. Then I Found It

text: If he opposed anything, it would be vague language: phrases that sound good, rhyme or alliterate, yet listeners cannot say what they mean, so they cannot act on them.
title: I Stopped Chasing Happiness. Then I Found It

text: Growing an audience is a traffic problem, the first of the four levers: how to get more eyeballs on the offer.
title: The Simplest Way to Advertise Your Business

text: On Twitter, engage with people's feeds within a niche by commenting back and forth, then message those you have engaged with.
title: The Simplest Way to Advertise Your Business

text: There are three ways to get traffic: reach out to people, make content, or run ads. Pick one. If you are poor, start with outreach; less poor, make content; least poor, run ads.
title: The Simplest Way to Advertise Your Business

text: Hormozi says that if he had treated his whole audience like the warm buyers who respond to a special email, he would have under-converted by roughly two-thirds compared to what he should have achieved.
title: Stop Using a Warm Sales Process on Cold Leads

text: He does not consider a half conversion rate necessarily bad for cold leads when judged against warm introductions, so the comparison group matters.
title: Stop Using a Warm Sales Process on Cold Leads

text: When a premium-priced offer has low repeat buying because customers only want a few units at a time, he would split the offer into a quality piece and a quantity piece, and thinks both are needed.
title: Stop Using a Warm Sales Process on Cold Leads

text: He describes two ways to persuade, emotional and logical. On the emotional side, the upfront phase captures a representative group of avatars covering most incoming customers, using their own language.
title: Stop Using a Warm Sales Process on Cold Leads

text: He notes that reviews or testimonial stories around 18 months old lose relevance, which is why fresh ones matter.
title: Stop Using a Warm Sales Process on Cold Leads

text: For roles repeated across an organization, such as sales or video editors, he thinks of a career ladder as title plus pay. He suggests a three-rung ladder could be stretched into nine or eighteen rungs.
title: You're Stuck at $50M Because You Can't Deliver Fast Enough

text: A short ladder means people who are promoted quickly reach the top with nowhere left to advance, and lack of career advancement is often the reason they give when leaving.
title: You're Stuck at $50M Because You Can't Deliver Fast Enough

text: Each role can have junior, normal and senior levels, with a step from junior to a better-paid junior, then dropping the junior title with a perk such as no Saturday nights, then a small pay bump.
title: You're Stuck at $50M Because You Can't Deliver Fast Enough

text: The biggest turnover risk is in the first roughly 30 to 45 days, so he suggests making the first win easy so a new hire quickly feels they like the job.
title: You're Stuck at $50M Because You Can't Deliver Fast Enough

text: After the first win, keep extending the reinforcement cycle for each role so the next goal is always slightly further away while there is always something to look forward to.
title: You're Stuck at $50M Because You Can't Deliver Fast Enough

text: Hormozi is reconsidering his tendency to see entrepreneurs who stop growing as having quit prematurely: producing more also places demands on the person producing it.
title: How to Know When You've Actually Won

text: Seeing his former gym manager equally happy after roughly 10 years apart led Hormozi to regard that employee as already successful, while Hormozi still felt he was pursuing the same satisfaction.
title: How to Know When You've Actually Won

text: Hormozi repeats a line from Sam at a mastermind: every product you launch is bad at first. A first attempt at anything is rarely good, so releasing it is how you get feedback to improve.
title: Every Product You Launch Sucks

text: The goal of putting something out is to learn from it, not to win right away. Publish, then use the response to improve the next version.
title: Every Product You Launch Sucks

text: His team publishes 450 pieces of content per week without knowing which will hit. They put out the best they can, review metrics, do more of what worked and less of what did not, and repeat continuously.
title: Every Product You Launch Sucks

text: He sees perfectionism as a way of hiding from fear of rejection. His advice is to expect the content will not perform, learn from it, and produce a large amount so you learn faster.
title: Every Product You Launch Sucks

text: To justify a $1 price over a $10 price, conversion would need to be ten times higher. He says that will not happen; going to $10 might cost roughly 20% of conversion, not 90%.
title: Stop Letting Influencers Price Your Product Too Cheap

text: Creators should stop selling from their own wallet and stop fearing their audience. If the reason for building an audience was to earn income, an offer needs a real price attached.
title: Stop Letting Influencers Price Your Product Too Cheap

text: The people who get upset about paying for an offer are never the buyers, so pricing low to please them loses nothing real. He adds that a victim-minded person who buys at $1 is not someone you want in your community anyway.
title: Stop Letting Influencers Price Your Product Too Cheap

text: He thinks many community owners are missing how much pricing room exists. Unless the audience is kids, many could charge 99, 199 or 299 a month.
title: Stop Letting Influencers Price Your Product Too Cheap

text: He recalls the average community price being somewhere in the 20s, though he cannot remember when he last checked.
title: Stop Letting Influencers Price Your Product Too Cheap

text: Compare prices with simple math: take 100 clicks, multiply the conversion rate by the price. A $1 price would need 10 to 14 times the conversion of a $14 price to win.
title: Stop Letting Influencers Price Your Product Too Cheap

text: He says that if you make content you will make more money, and that content pairs well with running ads, so it is a good place to start for lead generation.
title: Helping a Concierge Dentist Get Out of the Chair

text: He says that for someone who is more of a relationship person, affiliate and referral relationships are one option for leads, though he notes this can be tougher when selling very large full-mouth cases.
title: Helping a Concierge Dentist Get Out of the Chair

text: Build content into the flow of customers already coming through, rather than creating it separately. If a business sees many people daily, even a fraction agreeing to be filmed gives far more posts than none.
title: Helping a Concierge Dentist Get Out of the Chair

text: To structure content, study accounts in your field doing it best and copy the story arc of how they show the reveal and the person walking in.
title: Helping a Concierge Dentist Get Out of the Chair

text: When deciding whether to keep a business line you already bought, treat the purchase as sunk cost. The only question is whether you would set it up that way if starting today.
title: Helping a $5M Plumber Double His Service Revenue

text: If you may want to be acquired later, a cleaner single-focus business helps, because buyers tend to want to carve out only the piece they want when two different operations sit together.
title: Helping a $5M Plumber Double His Service Revenue

text: Cutting a distracting business line that splits your attention can make the remaining one grow much faster, though it is painful in the short term.
title: Helping a $5M Plumber Double His Service Revenue

text: Changing the entire business model is, in his opinion, like an Armageddon button. Before doing it, look for less drastic options, such as finding other places to get customers who have full coverage.
title: Helping a Home Services Company Scale to $100M

text: Selling a one-time fix to someone in pain is much easier than selling a recurring solution to someone who is not in pain.
title: Helping a Home Services Company Scale to $100M

text: He has seen many home services companies, typically venture-backed, try standalone membership models, and he has not yet seen one do it profitably and well. What does work is fixing something, such as HVAC, and then enrolling people in a membership.
title: Helping a Home Services Company Scale to $100M

text: A cheap first test of a membership: keep answering emergency inquiries, and once the work is done offer a follow-up to prevent recurrence. If people will not buy that, he says not to switch the model.
title: Helping a Home Services Company Scale to $100M

text: He follows nearly any comedian who posts comedy regularly, regardless of size, but skips pages that only have one comedy video among lots of other content.
title: The Type of Content I Watch

text: The only comedy he dislikes is lazy, crude material that is crude just for the sake of it.
title: The Type of Content I Watch

text: He thinks candid comedy on podcasts beats rehearsed comedy by a wide margin, since a rehearsed bit must land every time with a cold crowd, while a warmed-up conversation can draw on earlier moments.
title: The Type of Content I Watch

text: X is his most active platform by far, and he manages his account entirely himself.
title: The Type of Content I Watch

text: For philosophy he prefers ancient authors who are dead, such as Epictetus and Seneca among the Stoics, plus darker writers like Dostoevsky.
title: The Type of Content I Watch

text: Phone-sold products typically start around $3,000. Products sold through an automated funnel straight to a checkout page usually land under $2,000. A phone-sold offer priced near $2,000 sits on the cusp between those two ranges.
title: Helping a $250K Sales Training Business Get to $1M by Fixing their Price

text: Rather than just selling a course, ask what must be added to make the offer worth a much higher price, such as $6,000 or $8,000, since the buyers already want help.
title: Helping a $250K Sales Training Business Get to $1M by Fixing their Price
