text: To help buyers actually succeed, add perceived likelihood of achievement and lower their risk by including the pieces they will struggle with most. He notes only about 27% of course buyers even make a login.
title: Helping a $250K Sales Training Business Get to $1M by Fixing their Price

text: Any routine must earn its place by increasing output per unit of time. If a multi-hour morning ritual eats the freshest hours of the day, you need a very strong argument that it improves output.
title: Copying Rich People's Habits Won't Make You Rich

text: His preferred morning routine: wake up, caffeinate, shut off distractions, and start work. The ideal is to compress the time between waking and beginning work, since you are freshest right after sleep.
title: Copying Rich People's Habits Won't Make You Rich

text: Hobbies and wellness practices are fine to keep. The question to ask is whether they fit alongside the work needed to get what you want.
title: Copying Rich People's Habits Won't Make You Rich

text: Many successful people he knows now work modest hours, but they probably worked very long hours to get there. Copying them means modeling the rise, not the plateau, though the plateau is what is more visible.
title: Copying Rich People's Habits Won't Make You Rich

text: Whether to go all in or build in stages has no single right answer because it depends on risk tolerance, which is entirely personal. Understand the risk you take on.
title: Copying Rich People's Habits Won't Make You Rich

text: He personally prefers securing his own oxygen mask first. Having a nest egg let him take bigger bets, because losing would change his life very little.
title: Copying Rich People's Habits Won't Make You Rich

text: To judge a big decision, ask what would tactically change: what you eat, wear, where you live, what you drive, who you are married to. If little changes, the decision matters less, which supports a higher risk-adjusted move.
title: Copying Rich People's Habits Won't Make You Rich

text: If you have a family, a mortgage, or costly school plans, a failed bet also puts their futures at risk. Know what you are putting at stake and how much life changes if you lose.
title: Copying Rich People's Habits Won't Make You Rich

text: Citing Keith Cunningham, he suggests asking what your upside and downside are, and whether you can live with the downside. If you cannot, do not take the bet.
title: Copying Rich People's Habits Won't Make You Rich

text: Given a long enough time horizon, every strength a business has turns into a liability. Being the best marketer or the best product person in the world helps growth now but creates dependence on that one person.
title: The Biggest Risk to Your Business

text: He is unsure how long it takes before a standout founder is replaced or their work is broken into replaceable parts. He does not know whether finding someone like them would be very hard.
title: The Biggest Risk to Your Business

text: Unless an owner needs to sell the company within a short time horizon, he would not be very worried about key-man risk.
title: The Biggest Risk to Your Business

text: To choose between a monthly price and an upfront annual price, talk to about 20 people and compare close rate and churn rather than guessing an answer.
title: \"Should I Charge Monthly or Annually?\"

text: In his example, 100 calls at $6,000 with a 20% close yields $120,000, while 100 calls at $500 a month with a 50% close yields 50 sales, about $25,000 in the first month.
title: \"Should I Charge Monthly or Annually?\"

text: If monthly customers stay longer than five months in his example, the $500 monthly offer earns more than the $6,000 upfront one, just with the money arriving later.
title: \"Should I Charge Monthly or Annually?\"

text: The cost to acquire a customer on the monthly offer would be two and a half times lower in his example, which should be weighed against the value of having cash upfront.
title: \"Should I Charge Monthly or Annually?\"

text: Compare the two prices by conversion rate multiplied by LTV for each, then add a third consideration: cash conversion cycle, meaning how fast you recoup acquisition spend to acquire more customers.
title: \"Should I Charge Monthly or Annually?\"

text: Entrepreneurs tend to chase missed opportunities instead of solving problems, yet the problems already in front of them are the opportunities.
title: Stop Chasing Opportunities, Solve Problems Instead

text: The biggest money left on the table is usually not selling customers something extra, but making the thing you already sell much better.
title: Stop Chasing Opportunities, Solve Problems Instead

text: He believes almost everyone can double lifetime value at the same price by cutting churn in half, simply by making the existing product less painful to use.
title: Stop Chasing Opportunities, Solve Problems Instead

text: If people already respond to your offer, you have figured out what they want. The harder part is discovering everything that pains them or blocks them from getting it, so focus on the pain.
title: Stop Chasing Opportunities, Solve Problems Instead

text: Advanced business owners push the bottom of the value equation (time delay, effort, sacrifice) toward zero, while newer owners make bigger promises and show more proof, which only works the top side.
title: Stop Chasing Opportunities, Solve Problems Instead

text: Consistently eliminating the downside makes a business more defensible, more valuable and more recurring, and he says it should also help a community group rank higher in the platform algorithm.
title: Stop Chasing Opportunities, Solve Problems Instead

text: There is always more to sell, otherwise you would be Amazon, but the real dollars come from making the one thing you already sell far better.
title: Stop Chasing Opportunities, Solve Problems Instead

text: Hormozi thinks first-time founders improve their chances by choosing an industry they already know through jobs, family, or friends. That familiarity reduces how much they must learn, even when the business opportunity is imperfect.
title: Start a Business Based on Your Existing Industry Knowledge

text: He argues that an initial venture rarely becomes a founder’s final business. Starting where success seems more likely can provide early reinforcement, resources, and skills that inform the next business decision.
title: Start a Business Based on Your Existing Industry Knowledge

text: Everyone has unique depth of knowledge in some areas simply from being alive and taking in information, so a person who thinks they have nothing to offer still has something to start from.
title: \"What Should I Sell?\"

text: Y Combinator, a Silicon Valley seed investor, weighs past industry experience heavily. Young founders are fine, but they want experience because knowing nothing about an industry means paying down a large amount of ignorance debt.
title: \"What Should I Sell?\"

text: You absorb knowledge of an industry just by being near it, for example a mechanic's child learns a lot about cars over 18 years. So he suggests looking at past jobs you have held, and your parents' jobs, as sources of knowledge.
title: \"What Should I Sell?\"

text: He covers the question of what to sell more fully in his upcoming leads book, which he says is roughly six months away.
title: \"What Should I Sell?\"

text: Hormozi argues you must conquer a city before a country and a country before the world, and that armies which overextend collapse, so fortify your base first.
title: You're Trapped In Your Own Business Because It's Too Local

text: His rule of thumb for service businesses is to aim for a gross margin of at least 80 percent.
title: Why Small Business Owners Always Undercharge

text: At an 80 percent gross margin, a service costing $100 to deliver has to be priced at $500.
title: Why Small Business Owners Always Undercharge

text: Lower margin targets need a much lower price: at 90 percent margin on a $100 cost, the price would be $1,000, whereas 70 percent margin lands well below $500, near the mid-$300s.
title: Why Small Business Owners Always Undercharge

text: As a business grows, the founder's identity has to move from being the best closer to being someone who can make anyone a good closer. Hormozi frames this as a necessary shift for scaling a sales team.
title: He Makes $4M Tax-Free but Can't Scale

text: Many top performers do not know why they win, so their behaviors need to be listed and codified. He compares this to Michael Jordan being a far better player than coach.
title: He Makes $4M Tax-Free but Can't Scale

text: The business you want to build cannot depend on out-earning everyone in it. He says nobody cares about the founder's personal income compared with having built an infrastructure of many reps producing large revenue.
title: He Makes $4M Tax-Free but Can't Scale

text: Saving a small amount on a negotiated lease is not worth a delay when a business already earns large sums, since the difference can be earned back in a couple of days. He says some past negotiations of his were dumb in retrospect.
title: He Makes $4M Tax-Free but Can't Scale

text: Daily sales training should take priority over sales appointments and be scheduled during the quietest selling window of the day.
title: How to Run a Sales Team

text: Managers should open daily training sessions with leadership praise and peer acknowledgments to reinforce target cultural behaviors.
title: How to Run a Sales Team

text: Department leaders bear total accountability whenever their team members fail to execute required organizational behaviors.
title: How to Run a Sales Team

text: Sales training should rotate across script stages across the week, practicing introduction, discovery, pitch, closing, and specific weekly problem areas.
title: How to Run a Sales Team

text: Sales roleplays should start with the manager demonstrating the dialogue correctly with one rep before the rest break into peer pairs.
title: How to Run a Sales Team

text: Weekly individual reviews must sequentially address personal life challenges, short-term quota hurdles using recorded struggle calls, and long-term career aspirations.
title: How to Run a Sales Team

text: High-turnover positions should be divided into junior and senior tiers to create multiple reachable promotion milestones.
title: How to Run a Sales Team

text: New hires should receive a title upgrade and compensation raise within their first thirty days upon fulfilling baseline requirements.
title: How to Run a Sales Team

text: Employee promotions and raises should depend strictly on cumulative output milestones rather than tenure to encourage faster pacing.
title: How to Run a Sales Team

text: Speed or volume targets must be counterbalanced by quality or retention metrics to prevent employees from burning leads or clients.
title: How to Run a Sales Team

text: Representatives can master scripts independently by reading aloud from two copies while blacking out words sequentially until fully memorized.
title: How to Run a Sales Team

text: Sales onboarding must verify three progressive competencies: verbatim script recall, prospect problem labeling, and closing objection handling.
title: How to Run a Sales Team

text: New closers should start with a half-capacity schedule and earn full lead allocations only after hitting target metrics five consecutive days.
title: How to Run a Sales Team

text: Allowing unpracticed sales representatives to handle inbound leads is far more costly than deducting thirty minutes daily for team training.
title: How to Run a Sales Team

text: Rehearsing a presentation dozens of times is necessary for the speaker to coordinate physical props, slide transitions, and conversational delivery.
title: How to Run a Sales Team

text: He describes the way good VCs think: they only profit from multi-billion-dollar companies, so they ask how many assumptions must come true. Each unproven assumption discounts the valuation of the large eventual business.
title: Raising $100M Almost Got Me Kicked Out of My Own Company

text: He states that the fewer assumptions still needing to be proven, the higher the valuation, because the likelihood of success is higher.
title: Raising $100M Almost Got Me Kicked Out of My Own Company

text: A big valuation step-up between rounds is justified by showing the riskiest assumption has been proven, so the company is now limited by capital rather than by unproven assumptions.
title: Raising $100M Almost Got Me Kicked Out of My Own Company

text: When justifying a higher round, he says to identify what concretely changed since the last round, such as new technology, sales velocity, audience or a finding, because that change is the story being sold.
title: Raising $100M Almost Got Me Kicked Out of My Own Company

text: He says a raise is fundamentally a pitch: investors do not want deep technical detail and their eyes glaze over; they want to believe they will make a lot of money, so it is a sale on the founder and the story.
title: Raising $100M Almost Got Me Kicked Out of My Own Company

text: Developers are an attractive audience because most earn money and have big job opportunities, which gives them both spending power and earning power.
title: “I help web developers get jobs. How do I monetize?”

text: Helping developers get better jobs is a strong thing to sell. He says he has seen many coding boot camps do this poorly, and it could be priced around $9.99 per month in a community.
title: “I help web developers get jobs. How do I monetize?”

text: Developers are a big audience but contain sub-niches. Work out the audience's end goal, such as learning a skill that lets them earn about three times as much, and build the offer around that.
title: “I help web developers get jobs. How do I monetize?”

text: Survey your group to learn what members mostly want: love of coding, upleveling skills, earning more, or getting a job. Then build the follow-on community around that main answer.
title: “I help web developers get jobs. How do I monetize?”

text: A YouTuber his team helped monetize, an engineer-focused creator, made 130k in 5 days because the audience had a lot of money.
title: “I help web developers get jobs. How do I monetize?”

text: Engineers are analytical and ask many questions, so use a logical sale: stick to facts, such as the share of people with a skill who earn a given income, and show the return on investment.
title: “I help web developers get jobs. How do I monetize?”

text: If the argument is black and white, engineers who buy logically are also less likely to refund, he says.
title: “I help web developers get jobs. How do I monetize?”

text: People are most motivated by whatever they are deprived of. Sleep, food and sex drive us most when we have gone without them, and this logic works cleanly for physical needs.
title: Find More Ways to Win

text: For intangible things like money, being deprived does not automatically create motivation, since many poor people are not very driven while some very rich people are intensely hungry. He concludes the feeling of deprivation depends on our reference point.
title: Find More Ways to Win

text: Perceived deprivation is relative to the people around you. Someone worth a hundred million among billionaire friends feels a nine hundred million gap, so may be more driven than someone earning five thousand a month who wants ten thousand.
title: Find More Ways to Win

text: He asks himself what he is deprived of, since that is what motivates him to go get it. To predict other people's behavior, he asks what they are deprived of, which he says predicts better than other approaches.
title: Find More Ways to Win

text: Treat CAC as everything spent each month on advertising and sales to get customers, including nurture aimed at past customers. Blend it all together rather than separating nurture out.
title: Helping a $5.2M Service Business Scale to $20M

text: If revenue is lumpy, widen the window and measure CAC over trailing six or twelve months. Example: one million dollars of sales and marketing spend and 50 new customers gives a CAC of 20,000 dollars.
title: Helping a $5.2M Service Business Scale to $20M

text: The longer the period you blend over, the more accurate CAC tends to be, because a single day's figure swings between terrible and amazing.
title: Helping a $5.2M Service Business Scale to $20M

text: He deliberately overestimates CAC and underestimates LTV. If the metrics still look good under those pessimistic numbers, you are safe on both sides.
title: Helping a $5.2M Service Business Scale to $20M

text: He uses fully loaded CAC, counting commissions, software, media spend and nurture.
title: Helping a $5.2M Service Business Scale to $20M

text: For a floor LTV, divide total revenue over all years in business by total customers acquired. It understates value because recent customers are young, but as the ugliest baseline it can only improve.
title: Helping a $5.2M Service Business Scale to $20M

text: Hormozi says he saved aggressively to prepare for bigger future opportunities: earning 20,000 monthly, he spent 500 on living expenses; earning a million monthly, their living expenses were about 10,000–15,000.
title: \"Should I Grow My Business or Stockpile Cash for AI?\"

text: When prospects turn down an offer, asking why they said no is valuable, because the price you charge is often not the most expensive part of buying from you; hidden costs matter too.
title: Why Nobody Wants Your Free Service

text: An agency won Hormozi over by doing the work first: it sent him shorts made from his existing content every week, and he only had to say yes. After a month of good output, it asked to be paid and he agreed.
title: Why Nobody Wants Your Free Service

text: Ask non-buyers why not. If the reason is proof, work on proof. If they expect to do lots of work themselves, they may be misunderstanding. Solving the next few friction points yields a very valuable service.
title: Why Nobody Wants Your Free Service

text: Five leads is a tiny sample. If you converted one of five, that is 20 percent, which would be a strong rate, so the real problem may be needing more leads.
title: Why Nobody Wants Your Free Service

text: Early sales conversations are usually sloppy, since you have not yet learned to frame benefits. He would keep the strategy and take another 25 to 50 appointments before judging it.
title: Why Nobody Wants Your Free Service

text: For a small business owner, the first objective is letting people know you exist. When starting out, spend the first hours of every day, until noon, on advertising and finding leads, then handle other tasks.
title: Why Nobody Wants Your Free Service

text: To prioritize any initiative, use three steps in order: what, how, who. First define what it does, then how you will do it, then who will own it.
title: Consuming Content Is Killing Your Focus

text: Any initiative must either get more customers or make them worth more, since that is the only way to grow a business. If you cannot name which goal it serves, or it does neither clearly, do not do it.
title: Consuming Content Is Killing Your Focus

text: Once you know the goal, choose how: do more, do better, or do something new. Small companies typically do more first, larger ones do better first, and new is tried only when more and better are exhausted.
title: Consuming Content Is Killing Your Focus

text: A useful test for focus: ask why you cannot do ten times more of what already works, and what would actually break if you did.
title: Consuming Content Is Killing Your Focus

text: Unless a product is viral, such as zero-cost software where adding a user costs nothing, all growth is held back by irrelevance: not enough people in the world know your business exists.
title: The Biggest Factor Limiting the Growth of Your Business

text: Whether a business is limited by supply (talent) or demand (customers), he says the underlying limit is being irrelevant in the larger universe. If everyone knew about the business, it would be bigger and could attract the talent it needs.
title: The Biggest Factor Limiting the Growth of Your Business

text: His default response to a growth limit is to reach out to more people, make more content for the people he wants to serve, and advertise more.
title: The Biggest Factor Limiting the Growth of Your Business

text: To break a sense that a goal will take a long time, he asks what you would do if something you deeply cared about depended on hitting it by month end. The urgency reveals what is actually possible.
title: The Biggest Factor Limiting the Growth of Your Business

text: Hormozi says he spends less and less time on outcome-based goals and nearly all of his time on input-based goals, which he finds makes goal setting much easier.
title: How I set Goals

text: Big money outcomes can trigger a feeling of not deserving them, but an input like a thousand emails means little emotionally. Turning the outcome into an input he can judge as doable removes that emotional weight.
title: How I set Goals

text: His example: doing the math, a thousand emails an hour for his company equals about 100 million dollars a year. He then simply asks whether he can handle a thousand emails an hour, and he thinks he can.
title: How I set Goals

text: Bad things and unmet expectations are bound to happen in business and life, so he keeps several mental frames ready for dealing with the stress they cause.
title: How I Deal with Stress and Missed Expectations

text: The frame of the veteran, which he got from Dr. Cashy: imagine the bad event repeating a thousand times, ask how you would feel by the thousandth, and if you would have habituated by then, choose to feel that way now.
title: How I Deal with Stress and Missed Expectations

text: He first used the veteran frame when his maid shrank a flannel shirt he liked. He imagined shrinking being how clothes always behaved, saw he would not be upset, chose not to be, and the annoyance ended.
title: How I Deal with Stress and Missed Expectations

text: When his cat Bill died at 18 months, he asked why he was sad and found an unmet expectation of a longer life. Imagining cats live six months turned his sadness into appreciation.
title: How I Deal with Stress and Missed Expectations

text: Upset often comes from demanding something of the universe, such as a longer life. Changing the expectation changes the feeling without changing the facts, so the shift is only one of perspective.
title: How I Deal with Stress and Missed Expectations

text: On lifespan, he says living to 75 versus 85 leaves lifespan what it is, and the only thing lost by being upset over it is the present.
title: How I Deal with Stress and Missed Expectations

text: Zooming all the way out, until you cannot even see the Earth, reminds him that an upsetting event such as losing $15 million does not matter. Then he zooms back in.
title: How I Deal with Stress and Missed Expectations

text: He plays with time and space to reframe an issue: name the expectation, see how it went unmet, and ask how it could shift or be completely different, like traffic always taking 20 minutes.
title: How I Deal with Stress and Missed Expectations

text: He thinks that using these frames regularly has let him make better decisions and react less emotionally to bad news, and that compounding the small space they create over time improves decisions.
title: How I Deal with Stress and Missed Expectations

text: When a business relies mainly on organic reach, a common trap is selling more and more products to the same limited audience. Hormozi says it makes sense until it stops working; better to find the one highest-leverage, highest-retention offer and grow the audience.
title: “I’m Stuck at $7.5M and Can’t Break $15M”

text: Hormozi prefers businesses shaped as straight lines: front door, second door, third door, done. The main question then becomes how to bring more people through the front door, which he says simplifies life.
title: “I’m Stuck at $7.5M and Can’t Break $15M”

text: Hormozi says a small business has such limited resources that doing several things well is hard, since it competes with firms that each do only one of those things as their main business. Picking one thing is sensible.
title: “I’m Stuck at $7.5M and Can’t Break $15M”

text: Customers from the first sale become the lead base for the second sale, so far fewer people are needed on ascension. He says the best one or two front-end sellers can form the back-end team.
title: “I’m Stuck at $7.5M and Can’t Break $15M”

text: Hormozi says that with high ticket sizes, two or three people handling ascension can support a business reaching a hundred million dollars a year, and that this is not hard.
title: “I’m Stuck at $7.5M and Can’t Break $15M”

text: Some people feel that succeeding would validate how they were parented, so they stay unsuccessful to avoid crediting their parents and to hurt them back. Staying stuck this way means letting those parents keep controlling you.
title: What Offends You Controls You

text: The day you decide to control yourself is the day you separate your results from your valid reasons for not winning. You may be right about those reasons, but that does not have to determine your outcomes.
title: What Offends You Controls You

text: He says he has taken companies through a 10-stage roadmap from zero to 100 million plus that under 1% of companies complete. Each stage is broken down across eight business functions, covering symptoms of the constraint and the steps taken to graduate.
title: What Offends You Controls You

text: If you have a business outside the community, it can work as long-term lead nurture, either free or low-ticket, with the goal of getting people to move up to higher service levels.
title: The 2 Ways to Use a Community Inside an Existing Business

text: Adding a small price to a nurture community creates a quality barrier that helps keep out spam bots, though making it free also works. He considers the low price not a bad idea.
title: The 2 Ways to Use a Community Inside an Existing Business

text: A community can be part of delivery for a service business, such as an ad agency. It gives customers a place to ask questions and talk to each other, adding value at very little cost or time.
title: The 2 Ways to Use a Community Inside an Existing Business

text: Do not turn your agency or service business into a community just to compete, since that forces you to serve it. Monetize through your own offer and keep the community as a feature of the services.
title: The 2 Ways to Use a Community Inside an Existing Business

text: Three folders are needed to use AI well: business context (what you have done and what your business is), an SOP repository (what you do and how), and data sources (exported past work the prompts pattern match against).
title: Get RICH in the A I  Revolution 2026

text: Data sources include your tweets, emails, setter and sales recordings, email sequences, transcripts of videos you like, product FAQs, reviews, support transcripts, best ad copy, liked social posts and your website copy.
title: Get RICH in the A I  Revolution 2026

text: Collect every email you have ever sent to your list into one master document, or export emails you like from other senders, to serve as another data source. Recorded setter or SDR calls are also an asset.
title: Get RICH in the A I  Revolution 2026

text: His newsletter used to take 60 to 90 minutes per email. With his AI setup, 16 emails take about four hours, one half day per month, which he calls 4x leverage. The newsletter drives about 20% of ACQ advisory revenue.
title: Get RICH in the A I  Revolution 2026

text: Suggested order: first get your context window right, which is a win even if you do nothing else. Second, gather data sources, which needs only capturing. Third, build the prompt repository referencing both.
title: Get RICH in the A I  Revolution 2026

text: Platforms limit how much context you can provide, so put material in Word format, which he says shrinks size dramatically compared with other formats.
title: Get RICH in the A I  Revolution 2026

text: He uses all the LLMs but uses ACQAI most for business strategy, especially offers, pricing, sales flow and sales process, because it draws on small-business-relevant context rather than general web sources.
title: Get RICH in the A I  Revolution 2026

text: If you have sales call transcripts but no VSSL, feed about 10 successful calls to an AI prompt that extracts persuasion patterns, emotional beats, objection handling and promises, and converts them into a VSSL script, then record it.
title: Get RICH in the A I  Revolution 2026

text: If you already win clients in person, one route is to keep selling that way and simply deliver the service remotely. He did this with gyms during COVID, selling one-on-one and delivering remote classes.
title: \"I Have an In-Person Service Business. How Do I Switch to Online Only?\"

text: He calls selling in person while delivering remotely a hybrid model. He finds it interesting because in-person selling has different conversion rates and lead costs than online, since people inherently trust a real person in their city.
title: \"I Have an In-Person Service Business. How Do I Switch to Online Only?\"

text: Version 1.0 of going remote is selling as you do now but offering remote services. Version 2.0 is both acquiring customers remotely and delivering remotely.
title: \"I Have an In-Person Service Business. How Do I Switch to Online Only?\"

text: For someone just starting online, the top two priorities are advertising, meaning letting people know about your offering. Without that, nobody buys regardless of anything else. He points to the leads book for the steps.
title: \"I Have an In-Person Service Business. How Do I Switch to Online Only?\"

text: Hormozi found it helpful to see each piece of content as practice for a future, better self, not the main game. He compares it to preseason, which lowers the stakes of posting.
title: How I Think About Making Content

text: He looked at impression counts and pictured them as a room of people. A hundred impressions is like a hundred-person room he would be thrilled to speak to, which made early work feel worthwhile.
title: How I Think About Making Content

text: He views growth in both absolute and relative terms. Going from 10 to 15 followers is only five more, but it is also a 50% increase, which felt exciting.
title: How I Think About Making Content

text: He projects numbers out in a spreadsheet, and the team usually hits the projection. He excludes rare viral events, which act as padding. Currently they compound at 13% a month on one platform.
title: How I Think About Making Content

text: Hormozi says people who succeed are not necessarily higher in willpower; they find other ways to reward themselves. He relays a friend's view that more skills means more ways to reward yourself, extending your time horizon.
title: How I Think About Making Content

text: You can create micro games inside a longer game to keep going, like counting down segments during cardio.
title: How I Think About Making Content

text: An Olympic lifting coach has lifters map every set and rep range at every weight, so each workout they can beat some old record. Hormozi uses this to show small frequent wins sustain long-game play.
title: How I Think About Making Content

text: Service businesses often adopt more technology over time to increase their service ratios.
title: Helping a $24M Law Firm Get to $100M

text: When a big hiring constraint appears, he and his partner pull themselves out of the business for a roughly six-week sprint of doing nothing but interviews. For C-suite hires he is personally involved, though not for directors or managers.
title: You're Stuck Because You Built the Bottom Layer, Not the Top

text: Headhunting is an outreach game, and response rates are noticeably higher when the CEO sends the message. A low-pressure approach is to ask whether they know anyone like them for a great role, stating the pay.
title: You're Stuck Because You Built the Bottom Layer, Not the Top

text: For roles outside your expertise, ask people you already pay, such as attorneys, to assess candidates. Good blue-chip headhunting firms also run technical evaluations, so you judge only culture and company fit.
title: You're Stuck Because You Built the Bottom Layer, Not the Top

text: Frame a recruiter fee as a risk-reward investment: paying 40 to earn 400 is worth it if the hire does their job. Spreading hires month over month softens the cash hit versus doing them all at once.
title: You're Stuck Because You Built the Bottom Layer, Not the Top

text: Solving one scaling problem just reveals the next; growth always brings new problems, and whatever you struggle with, someone else has already struggled with and solved.
title: You're Stuck Because You Built the Bottom Layer, Not the Top

text: Hormozi defines resilience by the time needed to resume normal behavior after adversity. He distinguishes this recovery speed from toughness, which concerns how much someone withstands before reacting.
title: How to Bounce Back From Anything Fast

text: Hormozi says placing himself and his problems within the vastness of the universe quickly reduces their emotional weight for him, making a book-printing error seem insignificant.
title: How to Bounce Back From Anything Fast

text: For an inconvenience, he imagines his reaction after 1,000 repetitions. He argues that the same accepting perspective is available on the first occurrence because the circumstance itself is unchanged.
title: How to Bounce Back From Anything Fast

text: Hormozi does not think borrowing other people's money is less risky than using your own, because lenders can take your assets if things go wrong, even though borrowing may feel safer.
title: Your bank won't fund you because you're taking too much cash out

text: For a specialized one-time role, Hormozi favors headhunters because they already hold the network and he does not want to rebuild it.
title: Your bank won't fund you because you're taking too much cash out

text: For a repeated role at the heart of the business's economic engine, such as editors for a media company or salespeople for a sales-driven one, Hormozi wants his own defined process for recruiting, hiring, onboarding and training rather than outsourcing it.
title: Your bank won't fund you because you're taking too much cash out

text: His preferred way to source for a role is to find a recruiting firm, use LinkedIn to reach the individual recruiter one level down, and offer to work exclusively for you instead of many clients, with better pay and treatment.
title: Your bank won't fund you because you're taking too much cash out

text: After selling all his businesses, Hormozi says he made more money over the following six months than the combined sale proceeds, by concentrating on just one thing. This is why he keeps advocating for focus.
title: You Need to Focus

text: Hormozi says focus never gets easier and compares it to an addiction: it has to be beaten again every single day.
title: You Need to Focus

text: Whatever a person is struggling with, Hormozi says someone else has already struggled with the same thing and found a solution.
title: You Need to Focus

text: With a large audience, inbound leads tend to be poor if you sell high-level offers, because inbound reflects the ordinary distribution of businesses, where most people make almost nothing. He gives 36,000 companies a month as his example.
title: \"I Have 3 Million Followers But No Sales\"

text: If your only avatar is a tiny group, such as around 100 Fortune 100 CEOs, you can list them all. Content then serves mainly to make them willing to pick up the phone when you reach out.
title: \"I Have 3 Million Followers But No Sales\"

text: Brand and organic content give big leverage on outbound because people answer calls from someone they recognize. He found this to be where his biggest leverage sat, and his team shifted focus to approaching companies they like.
title: \"I Have 3 Million Followers But No Sales\"

text: Using a dating analogy, he says inbound at higher-end levels gets you sixes, while outbound lets you go after tens because you can target precisely who you pursue.
title: \"I Have 3 Million Followers But No Sales\"

text: Look at how valuable the business would be at its hypothetical maximum, with all possible customers, and confirm it is very profitable at that maximum using your current delivery. If not, fix the model before trying to expand.
title: \"I Have 3 Million Followers But No Sales\"

text: Summary: reach out directly to the specific people you want, using the brand you already have.
title: \"I Have 3 Million Followers But No Sales\"

text: Hormozi says a smart machine builder prices off the value delivered, not cost. If a machine replaces a workforce costing 2 million, selling it for 400 grand is a bargain even if building it cost around 20 grand.
title: Buying the $400K Machine That 10x's My Business

text: He recounts a friend in the machine business doing about 70 million a year, selling machines at an average of roughly 400 grand that cost them about 17 grand to make.
title: Buying the $400K Machine That 10x's My Business

text: If a proprietary machine is the core of your business, it is your main defensibility, so knowing everything about how it works matters most. Needing more machines at scale makes it a big point of leverage.
title: Buying the $400K Machine That 10x's My Business

text: He suggests calling a couple of very good machine experts and bringing them to inspect the machine, to test how proprietary it really is, since a modest machine with a small add-on might be presented as a far pricier one.
title: Buying the $400K Machine That 10x's My Business

text: A landing page that only promises how to make money is too generic. He says it should be specific about who it is for, what the vehicle is and what the opportunity is.
title: You Can't Beat Me at Business, So Play a Different Game

text: The content and pages you put out decide who you attract. If your material appeals to one type of person, that is who shows up, so it will not attract a different group such as older men.
title: You Can't Beat Me at Business, So Play a Different Game

text: Narrowing your avatar is one of the biggest strategic choices in a business, since everything flows from knowing who you serve. Lead magnets, copy messaging and content all become specific and relevant to their pains.
title: You Can't Beat Me at Business, So Play a Different Game

text: Specificity lets you add more value to a group. A dentist who serves only dentists may know less about business than Hormozi, yet be more nuanced in examples and still do well in that niche.
title: You Can't Beat Me at Business, So Play a Different Game

text: He recommends niching because you will not out-compete him at general business, since he has more evidence. Counter-position by playing a different game and winning in the trenches with niche-specific knowledge.
title: You Can't Beat Me at Business, So Play a Different Game

text: Content aimed at the precise pains of a narrow group will not perform as well in reach, but it brings in leads who actually buy.
title: You Can't Beat Me at Business, So Play a Different Game

text: If you have not gotten something like a six-pack, the real issue is usually not wanting it enough. Not having it often means accepting you are unwilling to pay the price, and he says that is fine.
title: How to Get in Shape

text: Visible abs are purely a matter of body fat percentage. He says getting there is a calorie deficit, and he has tracked his macros for 20 years.
title: How to Get in Shape

text: Getting jacked as well as having abs comes from progressive overload and protein, while getting the abs themselves comes from a calorie deficit while training broadly.
title: How to Get in Shape

text: Choosing what to optimize depends on which problem you are solving. To live as long as possible, he says just walk and eat little; he expects his own muscle mass to shorten his life.
title: How to Get in Shape

text: Sequence for any body goal: work out what you actually want, find out what it costs, then be willing to pay that price.
title: How to Get in Shape

text: He thinks far more people are rich and anonymous than are rich and flaunting it. Visible influencers are a skewed sample, and many of them are not actually that successful by net worth.
title: How to Kill Your Ego

text: He estimates that the vast majority of influencers in business, roughly 98 to 99 percent, mainly sell courses or products about building a platform rather than running real businesses.
title: How to Kill Your Ego

text: He observes that the well-known business figures who are truly successful tend to be humble, and he thinks that is because they know how hard it feels and have repeatedly felt inadequate.
title: How to Kill Your Ego

text: You can only feel inadequate by moving to a higher level. Feeling amazing usually means you have not moved up.
title: How to Kill Your Ego

text: He thinks the remedy for ego is doing harder things and fighting tougher opponents. Ego survives only by believing you are a big fish in a small pond.
title: How to Kill Your Ego

text: He thinks ego appears when you feel you have beaten a level, so you keep repeating it instead of moving up to face the harder challenge waiting.
title: How to Kill Your Ego

text: He says people praise his humility, but he does not see himself as especially humble. He is reminded daily of his inadequacy because he has moved into deals and investing, where he is a small fish.
title: How to Kill Your Ego

text: He believes you cannot admit your deficits and also claim to be the best at the same time. He links this to the Dunning-Kruger effect.
title: How to Kill Your Ego

text: He compares himself daily to Warren Buffett, tracks Buffett's net worth by age against his own, and treats Buffett and Munger as heroes for how they lived.
title: How to Kill Your Ego

text: Whatever you are struggling with, someone else has already faced and solved it.
title: How to Kill Your Ego

text: After about 16 weeks testing wider topics, he got more views but concluded that knowing how to get views does not deliver what he wants, which is more business owners entering his world.
title: I Know How to Get Views. It's Not What I Want

text: He judges content decisions by asking what raises the likelihood that the outcome he wants actually happens, rather than by views alone.
title: I Know How to Get Views. It's Not What I Want

text: His fitness-flavored video drew mostly people who watch fitness content and do not care about business, so it attracted the wrong first audience.
title: I Know How to Get Views. It's Not What I Want

text: Lead with business and add other interests like dessert or philosophy on top. Business overlaps his whole audience, while the other topics only add a second layer of affinity for some viewers.
title: I Know How to Get Views. It's Not What I Want

text: He cites roughly 9% of Americans owning a business, about 27 to 30 million, but says many are solopreneurs, so the count of real business owners shrinks a lot, perhaps to around 10 million with at least one employee.
title: I Know How to Get Views. It's Not What I Want

text: He says he will not out-compete entertainment creators on views, because entertainment is reinforcing for everyone while education takes effort to consume. Entertainment lessons should not be applied to the wrong business context.
title: I Know How to Get Views. It's Not What I Want

text: Content costs resources and should produce a return, so ask which content raises the odds of attracting the desired person. Business content brings more business owners; non-business content brings non-owners.
title: I Know How to Get Views. It's Not What I Want

text: After going deeper on business, his views dropped from a previous average he gave as 400 to about 100,000 in the comparison, but business-owner opt-ins skewed toward owning a business, doubling, and book sales doubled.
title: I Know How to Get Views. It's Not What I Want

text: Chasing views and likes is reinforcing and can pull you off target. He is happy to maximize views as long as the content is about the right subject.
title: I Know How to Get Views. It's Not What I Want

text: His process is not a dialed system: the team may bring pre-prepared topic groupings and packaging outlines, but he only makes a video if he feels like making it.
title: I Know How to Get Views. It's Not What I Want

text: Investment opportunities attract heavy scrutiny, so anyone promoting them on public platforms like YouTube, Facebook or Instagram needs to be very careful about compliance.
title: \"How Do I Make My Investment Fund Actually Look and Sound Legitimate?\"

text: He thinks that when a real opportunity is underperforming, the cause may be off messaging, and that sounding more legitimate would bring a higher share of people willing to write bigger checks.
title: \"How Do I Make My Investment Fund Actually Look and Sound Legitimate?\"

text: Moving toward a more legitimate positioning means giving up money now for more money later, so it is a delayed gratification choice. Some people prefer cash today, so it is worth asking which one you want.
title: \"How Do I Make My Investment Fund Actually Look and Sound Legitimate?\"

text: Churn in SMB services tends to follow price tiers: around 300 dollars a month is where small businesses typically stay, with another tier of churn near 1,000 to 1,200, and another around 2,500 to 3,500 monthly.
title: Helping a $580K Marketing Agency Scale

text: If a business has 100% annual revenue retention, he thinks the answer to scaling is simply to add more revenue by doing more of what is already working.
title: Helping a $580K Marketing Agency Scale

text: Reaching 2% monthly churn in a model that normally has far higher churn means solving something many people struggle with. He notes it implies roughly 50-month average customer lifetimes.
title: Helping a $580K Marketing Agency Scale

text: If a company's technology already makes the business tech-enabled, the benefit is already reflected in its valuation multiple. Turning an internal tool into a product with no revenue model adds little.
title: \"Should I Sell the Tool That Gives Me My Edge?\"

text: It is normal for a business past a certain size to build internal tools to streamline processes. He advises keeping such a tool as a competitive advantage rather than selling it.
title: \"Should I Sell the Tool That Gives Me My Edge?\"

text: A buyer paying a large sum for a company knows it is not a SaaS business. A firm would not get SaaS multiples on its existing revenue, only on the small software unit.
title: \"Should I Sell the Tool That Gives Me My Edge?\"

text: In high-skill service businesses, a key employee can leave with the whole practice. Offering a path to ownership, around 20 percent, and adding more staff over time lowers that risk.
title: \"Should I Sell the Tool That Gives Me My Edge?\"

text: Law, consulting and accounting firms typically offer a path to partner, usually around 10 to 20 percent of the upside. This need not be actual equity; it can be a profit share or a profits interest.
title: \"Should I Sell the Tool That Gives Me My Edge?\"

text: Hormozi would not open a second location if the first one is not really profitable, because he expects a second one to only become less profitable.
title: \"Should I Open a Second Location?\"

text: His internal saying is nail it then scale it. He says that for a business aiming at a hundred locations, getting to two does nothing while perfecting the first does everything.
title: \"Should I Open a Second Location?\"

text: The first location must run simply and very efficiently, printing money. If a hundred small tasks are needed to keep it okay, the model needs fixing, possibly because it is underpriced.
title: \"Should I Open a Second Location?\"

text: If a location is at capacity, he says to raise prices to earn more profit.
title: \"Should I Open a Second Location?\"

text: He says the one thing successful chains share, if he had to pick just one, is an insane grand opening SOP for local. Gym Launch worked because he could fill locations in 30 days.
title: \"Should I Open a Second Location?\"

text: Test your grand opening offer on the existing location. After raising prices, learn how to acquire customers profitably at the new higher price.
title: \"Should I Open a Second Location?\"

text: Work out LTV to CAC, then capacity. Example: 50 dollars per kid, 200 kids, roughly a third efficiency means about triple cost. Filling in 30 days costs more than spreading it over a year, so budget that into location return.
title: \"Should I Open a Second Location?\"

text: He says every corporate-owned service business he knows uses a 10 to 20 percent profit share for the location manager, who acts like an owner. About 10 percent applies with a base, up to 20 if very lucrative.
title: \"Should I Open a Second Location?\"

text: The manager should make over six figures a year for a profit share arrangement to be worth it, he says.
title: \"Should I Open a Second Location?\"

text: Vague requests like being more empathetic fail because people do not know what they mean. Define the term as a list of observable behaviors, such as recapping, nodding, acknowledging feelings, and asking about feelings.
title: How to Articulate Your Thoughts More Clearly Than 99% of People

text: Recapping alone is not empathy; it is only one component, and someone who does only that comes across as robotic. Several behaviors combined make up the perception.
title: How to Articulate Your Thoughts More Clearly Than 99% of People

text: Everything is behavior, and behavior is learnable and reproducible. Framing a fuzzy quality as a behavior makes it something you can teach as a process.
title: How to Articulate Your Thoughts More Clearly Than 99% of People

text: Soft skills feel hard because they lack hard definitions, not because they cannot be defined. They involve more behaviors tied to success, while hard skills have fewer criteria and are easier to define.
title: How to Articulate Your Thoughts More Clearly Than 99% of People

text: He defines a skill as an adaptive chain of behaviors, and says this view demystified the world for him.
title: How to Articulate Your Thoughts More Clearly Than 99% of People

text: He describes his content as a first-principles approach that uses behavior to explain business phenomena.
title: How to Articulate Your Thoughts More Clearly Than 99% of People

text: Most people repeat phrases they were rewarded for saying and have no real understanding. A few have first-party experience but cannot describe it; a behavior-minded person can question them to draw out what they actually did.
title: How to Articulate Your Thoughts More Clearly Than 99% of People

text: Rapport can be reduced to behaviors: ask the other person questions, keep going until you find an answer similar to yours, link it to yourself, then ask if they are ready to begin.
title: How to Articulate Your Thoughts More Clearly Than 99% of People

text: Empathetic tone breaks down into voice controls: louder or softer, faster or slower, and where you pause. Practical versions include lowering your voice or adding variety.
title: How to Articulate Your Thoughts More Clearly Than 99% of People

text: Sounding robotic comes from reading a script. Memorizing it yields natural pauses, and what matters is that pitch and pauses vary, not exactly where they fall.
title: How to Articulate Your Thoughts More Clearly Than 99% of People

text: Hormozi says platforms increasingly distribute content according to interests, making follower counts less meaningful.
title: Helping an Online Coaching Business Scale Past $1M

text: Hormozi sees content as a way to generate brand awareness at effectively no cost. He expects stronger funnel conversion among people who benefited from that content than among completely unfamiliar audiences reached by competing advertisers.
title: Helping an Online Coaching Business Scale Past $1M

text: When Hormozi needs to learn advertising, he combines paid courses, free resources, and an agency. He makes teaching him its methods part of the agency arrangement and is willing to pay extra for that access.
title: Helping an Online Coaching Business Scale Past $1M

text: The most important life lessons are the hardest to pass on because they sound like clichés, yet sounding familiar does not remove the need to hear them.
title: Maybe It's Not That Deep

text: If you truly knew a familiar lesson well, you would not still be stuck in the same place. Being bored of hearing it, such as sleep basics or handling emotions, while still struggling shows you have not mastered it.
title: Maybe It's Not That Deep

text: When a cash shortage can be solved by borrowing, he prefers lenders that do not take equity over selling equity to investors, since lending avoids diluting the owner.
title: 12% Interest Is Actually 2%. Here's the Math.

text: Accounts receivable financing lets a business get paid early on invoices that clients settle at net 60 or net 90, easing the pain of slow-paying commercial customers.
title: 12% Interest Is Actually 2%. Here's the Math.

text: A quoted annual interest rate overstates the real cost if you only hold the money briefly. Borrowing at 12% for about 2 months costs roughly 2%.
title: 12% Interest Is Actually 2%. Here's the Math.

text: Inventory financing is especially needed by fast-growing e-commerce companies, and many solutions already exist. He says to search for lending and financing options for inventory instead of diluting equity.
title: 12% Interest Is Actually 2%. Here's the Math.

text: Whatever problem you are struggling with, someone else has already faced and solved it, so look for existing solutions first.
title: 12% Interest Is Actually 2%. Here's the Math.

text: He says his group is about to invest in a commercial cleaning chain with 48 locations, which he describes as having strong margins.
title: 12% Interest Is Actually 2%. Here's the Math.

text: Hormozi says most people built their wealth by doing one thing very well first. Only once they have resources do they expand into other verticals, so we see an ecosystem only after the single channel worked.
title: Nearly Every Fortune Was Built Doing One Thing

text: He says business owners who add multiple businesses are usually limited in getting customers, so they sell more stuff. This creates operational complexity, and they end up under-talented rather than over-expanded.
title: Nearly Every Fortune Was Built Doing One Thing

text: He calls multiple loosely interdependent businesses mutant businesses, where each supposedly feeds another, which works only in the entrepreneur's head, not in reality.
title: Nearly Every Fortune Was Built Doing One Thing

text: He defines commitment as eliminating alternatives. The most focused entrepreneurs turn down things they badly want and could win at, because saying no is saying yes to their original mission.
title: Nearly Every Fortune Was Built Doing One Thing

text: He treats spreading across several unfinished businesses as one of five or six big recurring entrepreneur errors, and likens it to pruning a tree: redirect resources to what returns the most.
title: Nearly Every Fortune Was Built Doing One Thing

text: Cash from a working business is usually best put back into that business. Feed the winner and starve the losers; it is very rare that splitting attention gains more.
title: Nearly Every Fortune Was Built Doing One Thing

text: A new idea should be compared with year five of your current business, not year one or two of the new one, since year five nearly always wins. He likens this to time in the market and time under the bar.
title: Nearly Every Fortune Was Built Doing One Thing

text: Diverting resources to a second venture is acceptable, he says, but you should understand the trade: the main business grows slower, you may be less profitable overall, and probably more stressed.
title: Nearly Every Fortune Was Built Doing One Thing

text: He uses the woman in the red dress, from The Matrix, as a recurring image for appealing distractions that pull your eye off the ball.
title: Nearly Every Fortune Was Built Doing One Thing

text: He once ran four or five gyms plus dental and chiropractor agencies and a gym launch business, and was CEO of all. Launch took about 20% of his time yet made most money, so he focused on it.
title: Nearly Every Fortune Was Built Doing One Thing

text: Consolidating required three dreaded conversations, which he held on the same day. He felt free afterward, says anticipation is worse than reality, and thinks one hard conversation builds momentum.
title: Nearly Every Fortune Was Built Doing One Thing

text: He says no lesson in his life has been truer than the return on focus, which means choosing to go all in on one thing repeatedly.
title: Nearly Every Fortune Was Built Doing One Thing

text: After selling Gym Launch he did not want to stay known as the gym guy for life, since his look and branding were tied to gyms, so he shaved the mustache he had worn for about 4 to 5 years.
title: Why I Sold My Likeness (And Shaved the Mustache)

text: The beard was not a strategic move. He simply stopped shaving during the year the company was being sold, and it grew out.
title: Why I Sold My Likeness (And Shaved the Mustache)

text: He spent about 6 months experimenting with ways to dress, looking for one outfit that works in the most situations without changing. It ended up as shoeswithout socks, shorts without underwear, a tank top, and a flannel.
title: Why I Sold My Likeness (And Shaved the Mustache)

text: He regulates body temperature by layering the flannel: buttoned up and sleeves down around 45 degrees, removed when hot. He says the outfit covers roughly 40 to 120 degrees Fahrenheit, the range in Vegas.
title: Why I Sold My Likeness (And Shaved the Mustache)

text: His shoes work for workouts, nice restaurants, and the pool, and his waterproof black shorts have belt loops for nicer places, so he never needs to change clothes between settings.
title: Why I Sold My Likeness (And Shaved the Mustache)

text: Adding more products does not create a brand. Premium associations do. AI influencers are fine as a tactic but carry no trust, so they cannot deliver the value of an association.
title: $250M CEO Explains How to Build A Brand in 2026

text: If the product is bad, nothing afterward matters: you get a first purchase and then nothing, and good promoters avoid it because it would hurt their own brand.
title: $250M CEO Explains How to Build A Brand in 2026

text: To fix a brand problem, get two to three premium associations. Once you have them, people who wish they were as cool will want to promote you too. The goal is to capture the cool.
title: $250M CEO Explains How to Build A Brand in 2026

text: AI content gives impressions and name awareness but no positive association. He calls it a reach play, not an influence play.
title: $250M CEO Explains How to Build A Brand in 2026

text: Turning an arbitrage business into a strong brand is very difficult, because the large volumes of content it produces are usually not cool, so cool people avoid associating with it.
title: $250M CEO Explains How to Build A Brand in 2026

text: Making a hundred avatars for a hundred demographics tells the market you are for everyone, which means for no one. Brand building needs saying no: pick one audience, a few problems, and repeat them in every video.
title: $250M CEO Explains How to Build A Brand in 2026

text: The chain for a brand: an aspirational hero says you are the best, which requires being cool, which requires a truly exceptional product. If the hero will not represent it, there is no long-term brand.
title: $250M CEO Explains How to Build A Brand in 2026

text: Building a brand takes longer and costs short-term cash, but that is why brands are valuable and arbitrage businesses are not. He says the choice is a trade, and he is not saying you must do it.
title: $250M CEO Explains How to Build A Brand in 2026

text: A friend runs a weight-loss business of about $300 million a year built purely on performance marketing. Buyers will not touch it, no one online praises it, and monthly revenue swings widely with cost per click.
title: $250M CEO Explains How to Build A Brand in 2026

text: For a brand-building company the north star metric should be revenue retention, not subscription arbitrage, which merely pushes bigger bundles per order (more items, not more purchase occasions).
title: $250M CEO Explains How to Build A Brand in 2026

text: A brand must be aspirational, an ideal no one fully reaches. People discount big claims, so he does huge things like the $100 million launch to show he could help someone reach a smaller goal.
title: $250M CEO Explains How to Build A Brand in 2026

text: Long-term, the brand is built by getting the cool people who capture your essence and using them for whitelisted ads, both to recruit more affiliates and for direct-to-consumer.
title: $250M CEO Explains How to Build A Brand in 2026

text: Many big brands lose money on their storefront sales, and essentially all of their profit comes from email.
title: $250M CEO Explains How to Build A Brand in 2026

text: Offer a choice: pay an upfront onboarding fee with no commitment, or have that fee waived in exchange for a long commitment such as 12 months. Leaving early means paying what month-to-month would have cost.
title: Build Ramps, Not Walls

text: The upfront sign-up fee works as an anchor: it makes the monthly price look much lower, which helps the sale.
title: Build Ramps, Not Walls

text: Frame the commitment honestly: onboarding costs money that must be recovered one way or another. He will absorb it by spreading it over 12 months if the customer commits; otherwise the customer pays it.
title: Build Ramps, Not Walls

text: Hormozi says his company puts out over 35,000 pieces of content a year, and looking back at how much work went in, the results make sense.
title: Why I Read 15 Books in 2 Weeks to Solve One Problem

text: He says a business posting roughly 700 pieces a year is doing about one fiftieth of his output, so a large gap in results is explained by the gap in volume of work.
title: Why I Read 15 Books in 2 Weeks to Solve One Problem

text: He believes results scale relatively linearly with the amount of work done. Outliers exist, but they are predictable, so the relationship is more linear than people think.
title: Why I Read 15 Books in 2 Weeks to Solve One Problem

text: Selling only low-priced products means trying to earn profit from what is effectively a loss leader. The missing piece is a back-end offer sold to the customers already arriving, like a grocery store needing more than diapers.
title: \"I Sell Thousands of Courses. Why Am I Not Rich?\"

text: Between purchase and the call, have buyers watch a short VSL that preframes the call. For extra effect, add a 7-day delay with homework between the first and second calls, and close on the second call.
title: \"I Sell Thousands of Courses. Why Am I Not Rich?\"

text: When low-ticket economics are razor thin, a back end fixes them: if 20 to 30 percent of buyers take a roughly 4,000 dollar back-end offer, the average revenue per initial sale rises sharply.
title: \"I Sell Thousands of Courses. Why Am I Not Rich?\"

text: Hormozi says proof is still underrated despite the praise it gets. He argues you should document more and show more than you do now, saying what only you can say and showing what only you can show.
title: The Most Important Factor in Great Marketing

text: He tries to demonstrate first in his marketing. With thousands of five-star reviews beside him, he needs to say little, since people who trust highly reviewed things will tend to believe him. He cites 20,000 reviews for his book.
title: The Most Important Factor in Great Marketing

text: He says the biggest issue in marketing is that nobody believes you, and everything in marketing serves that one objective. If people would want the result yet do not buy, it is because they do not believe you.
title: The Most Important Factor in Great Marketing

text: He puts belief at the top of the pyramid, above copy, selling, tactics and money models. If you lack leads, he says the cause is that people do not believe you, because you have not shown them a reason to.
title: The Most Important Factor in Great Marketing

text: The number one marketing rule at acquisition.com and his companies is to state the facts and tell the truth. If the facts are not compelling, do not warp them; change reality, meaning do more or change what you can show.
title: The Most Important Factor in Great Marketing

text: He suggests that you may need to earn something like 20,000 five-star reviews. Once you can state that, he says you will get everything else you need.
title: The Most Important Factor in Great Marketing

text: Hormozi held off making general business content until after a $46 million exit, because he wondered who would listen. Even with Gym Launch and Prestige Labs, he wanted tangible proof that he was legitimate first.
title: The Most Important Factor in Great Marketing

text: He says many people lack proof, yet proof does not take long to get. They are just not getting it, so he tells them to go get it.
title: The Most Important Factor in Great Marketing

text: Hormozi says he lost everything twice in his twenties, around age 26 or 27, in roughly one year, during the first year of dating his wife. He considers himself a product of his failures.
title: I Lost Everything Twice... (Within 12 Months)

text: He describes his relationship with his wife as a steady, consistent coal fire built on mutual respect rather than a fireworks-style relationship. They have had only one real fight, and it was about business.
title: I Lost Everything Twice... (Within 12 Months)

text: When he and his wife disagree, the first question is what information the other person has that he lacks. He reasons that since they share values and decision-making style, a disagreement usually signals an information gap.
title: I Lost Everything Twice... (Within 12 Months)

text: He pushed to start a software company while already running a supplement company and Gym Launch. His wife said they were spread too thin; he says she was right and he was wrong.
title: I Lost Everything Twice... (Within 12 Months)

text: He believes that putting his effort into improving the existing businesses would have earned more than the distracting new project. He lost money selling Gym Launch and Prestige Labs to fund the software company, and calls it his one sin.
title: I Lost Everything Twice... (Within 12 Months)

text: Hormozi objects to the head-versus-heart framing because it mixes biology with decision-making. He says the real issue is conflicting priorities, which means the person has not decided what matters most or what risk they will accept.
title: Don't Quit Until the New Thing Matches Your Income

text: Hormozi's less conventional advice is to value stability, because it keeps business fun. He wants to avoid the enjoyable venture turning into pressured work, so he prefers keeping the paycheck for now.
title: Don't Quit Until the New Thing Matches Your Income

text: He suggests not quitting a job until the new business has matched the job's income consistently, for at least a quarter and perhaps six months in a row.
title: Don't Quit Until the New Thing Matches Your Income

text: While keeping the salary, Hormozi advises living cheaply and putting that income into the new venture to learn skills: running ads, buying software or courses, and joining other communities that help growth. He notes that salary flow will eventually end.
title: Don't Quit Until the New Thing Matches Your Income

text: Hormozi thinks working two full-time jobs is useful because it teaches you to work under constraints. He warns that people who leave a job often stop working harder and coast instead.
title: Don't Quit Until the New Thing Matches Your Income

text: The key switching point is when the new business matches the job's income while using less time. Then, after making the trade, you can double or triple that income.
title: Don't Quit Until the New Thing Matches Your Income

text: For founders seeking an eventual sale, he recommends starting with value customers will repeatedly pay for. He argues that sustained delivery of that value can eventually create a business someone wants to acquire.
title: Helping an Online Coach Doing $1M/Year Scale

text: He thinks discount associations can retain members strongly when savings equal 10 times the membership fee: a $400 annual membership would save $4,000 annually.
title: Helping an Online Coach Doing $1M/Year Scale

text: A purchasing network gains negotiating leverage as membership expands, enabling better collective discounts. He contrasts this with service businesses, where adding customers typically reduces service quality.
title: Helping an Online Coach Doing $1M/Year Scale

text: For young men he strongly urges getting in shape, because it will never be easier and they will never have more time or fewer responsibilities than now.
title: How to Find the Girl You’ll Marry

text: He believes almost all humans at ideal body weight with normal musculature are physically attractive on a binary scale, so a person should not let their body be a constraint.
title: How to Find the Girl You’ll Marry

text: He told a busy salesman that if he cannot make gym time work now, he should accept never being in shape, and either do it or stop wanting it.
title: How to Find the Girl You’ll Marry

text: He suggests that wealth matters in attraction more as a signal of ability to gain resources than as having them; a hungry, ambitious young guy may beat a trust fund kid.
title: How to Find the Girl You’ll Marry

text: His three-part recipe: get in shape, get rich or signal ambition, and do not be a jerk. He says doing all three lets you attract whichever women you want.
title: How to Find the Girl You’ll Marry

text: Not being a jerk means avoiding behaviors that reduce her wish to spend time with you. It differs from doing whatever she wants: do the things that cost you little and benefit her.
title: How to Find the Girl You’ll Marry

text: He says early in dating he stated his non-negotiables, such as working a lot and working out, and that showing who you really are at baseline works better long term than performing.
title: How to Find the Girl You’ll Marry

text: He suggests keeping about three must-haves in a partner rather than a list of a hundred, since surface preferences fade over decades and core behaviors under duress matter.
title: How to Find the Girl You’ll Marry

text: He and his wife took a divorce course right after marrying, applying inversion: learn why people divorce and handle those issues up front. Money and kids are big reasons.
title: How to Find the Girl You’ll Marry

text: He practices rounding up: when something could be taken a good or bad way, assume the good meaning as the default setting in a marriage.
title: How to Find the Girl You’ll Marry

text: He says asking a partner what they would prefer instead, then requesting a specific change, makes a relationship easier to navigate without landmines.
title: How to Find the Girl You’ll Marry

text: He values his wife's responsiveness to feedback: he almost never repeats himself. If a change costs the partner nothing, make it; if it costs something, discuss the trade-off.
title: How to Find the Girl You’ll Marry

text: He used to have gyms check in with members about their results, but found many members did not care and only wanted to work out and have fun, so reminding them they were still overweight did not help retention.
title: Helping a Kickboxing Gym Cut 25% Churn

text: An internal play means reaching out to your existing list every other month with a seasonal promotion, such as a Valentine's Day or Halloween challenge, or an accountability buddy or bring-a-friend angle.
title: Helping a Kickboxing Gym Cut 25% Churn

text: Fundamentals still drive churn: sessions must be good, the music good, and the trainers solid. He also suggests reaching out roughly every other week, tied to the current promotion or bring-a-friend push.
title: Helping a Kickboxing Gym Cut 25% Churn

text: The main thing that drives churn down is consumption, meaning how much members actually use and attend what they bought.
title: Helping a Kickboxing Gym Cut 25% Churn

text: He says a business has not stumbled on something marketing cannot work for; that has yet to happen. For very high-ticket B2B, such as serving only huge companies, outbound may be the best approach instead of ads.
title: One Degree Off From a Gold Mine

text: Co-founders with the same skill set can make it work if they quickly differentiate and specialize, each focusing on the constraint or the thing that matters most. Once roles are split, each owns their area and both must work hard.
title: One Degree Off From a Gold Mine

text: He notes that lead-selling firms make a margin on leads, so a firm able to generate its own leads could print money. He says top media buyers tend to be exceptional and well paid.
title: One Degree Off From a Gold Mine

text: Selling always stays anchored to value. If a prospect drops the frame late in the sale, he says the cause is trust lost earlier in the sale, and the objection is just an excuse to exit.
title: Get U.S. Clients From Anywhere by Doing This

text: What you can charge depends on the gap between how much they believe you can help, discounted by how likely they think that result is, and then the share of that gain they are willing to hand you.
title: Get U.S. Clients From Anywhere by Doing This

text: He thinks someone with an Indian accent could absolutely sell this way, though he expects it to be harder. Of all skills for gaining access to the US market, he would pick this value-selling ability as number one.
title: Get U.S. Clients From Anywhere by Doing This

text: Hormozi says a business owner at $2 million a year is in the top 5% of business owners, and that feeling small in a room of bigger operators is normal because there are levels.
title: Agencies Charge Wrong (Here's the Fix)

text: He says his team split business growth into 10 stages and built a quiz: enter your business details and it shows your stage and what to do in each function, including product, marketing, sales, customer success, recruiting, IT, HR and finance.
title: Agencies Charge Wrong (Here's the Fix)

text: He believes people who earn more than he does offer business lessons, even when their advantage involves luck or timing; his response is to increase his exposure to opportunities.
title: You're Making Business Harder Than It Has to Be

text: Challenges that come with being on top get almost no sympathy, because nearly everyone is still climbing and the few at the top are seen as privileged, which makes it seem acceptable to attack them.
title: Why Nobody Gives You Sympathy As a Business Owner

text: Public figures get vicious, dehumanizing comments online because strangers treat them as a bundle of ideas or a representation rather than an actual person.
title: Why Nobody Gives You Sympathy As a Business Owner

text: Before you have status, nobody gains anything from tearing you down, so early on there is little incentive for others to attack you even though you are the same person.
title: Why Nobody Gives You Sympathy As a Business Owner

text: Early in his first gym business, when he had no shower and members used the YMCA, everyone cheered for him. Within nine months he had staff and a manager, and the same people mocked him for supposedly being too good for them.
title: Why Nobody Gives You Sympathy As a Business Owner

text: Hormozi says he often hears people claim their working business is not scalable and they should switch to another one. He reads this as the business having become hard, and the person wanting something easy instead.
title: How To Know If Your Business Is Actually Unscalable or Just Hard

text: To make a hard task feel doable, estimate what it unlocks in enterprise value. Example: a 500K-a-year hire adding 2 million dollars profit at a 7x valuation adds 14 million in value, which makes finding that person feel worthwhile.
title: How To Know If Your Business Is Actually Unscalable or Just Hard

text: He attaches a payoff figure to the hard thing being done. In one portfolio company, a tech buildout might lift valuation from around 80 million to the 200s, so a costly developer team is worth building.
title: How To Know If Your Business Is Actually Unscalable or Just Hard

text: Some roles are simply necessary. Asking whether a role can be avoided is a fair question, but sometimes the right answer is to hire for it.
title: How To Know If Your Business Is Actually Unscalable or Just Hard

text: Right after a customer gets full value on one need, they are often empty on a different need, so the best upsell offers something for that new gap. Sometimes peak value and new deprivation overlap, but often they do not.
title: You Don’t Need an Upsell

text: He sees poorly timed upsells as one of the big mistakes people make. Pitching more of the same thing right after the customer is already satisfied feels awkward.
title: You Don’t Need an Upsell

text: Solving a customer's first problem, such as getting more leads, can create a new problem, such as needing to work those leads. That new problem is the opening to sell the related service, like lead nurture.
title: You Don’t Need an Upsell

text: If someone has already sold a high-ticket offer for a while, adding a low-ticket offer is an easy move, because the positioning already exists.
title: “I have a small audience and sell high-ticket. How do I monetize?”

text: Hormozi prefers entering a market from the top down rather than from the bottom up, starting with a premium offer and working toward cheaper ones.
title: “I have a small audience and sell high-ticket. How do I monetize?”

text: With a premium offer at the top acting as an anchor, you can give a large share of that value in a low-ticket product at a tenth or a hundredth of the price, which makes it feel like a no-brainer.
title: “I have a small audience and sell high-ticket. How do I monetize?”

text: To pitch the low-ticket product, he suggests telling people that many wanted access to you but you can only serve a limited roster of private clients, so you are offering them many of the same resources at a low price.
title: “I have a small audience and sell high-ticket. How do I monetize?”

text: Newcomers to Skool fit one of three situations: no experience or money made, an existing business, or an audience with weak monetization. Which advice applies depends on which situation you are in.
title: 1 of 3 Paths to starting your first business

text: A beginner with no expertise should build a community around a pain they overcame, a passion, or a past profession, so others can learn the skill, overcome the pain, or pursue the passion.
title: 1 of 3 Paths to starting your first business
