text: For a beginner, he recommends launching truly free first to build engagement and learn how communities work, then moving to a free trial and paid. Early members get grandfathered in, and telling them a charge is coming gives a reason to join now.
title: 1 of 3 Paths to starting your first business

text: He says roughly 48% of free trials convert on Skool, though he hedges on the exact figure. Buying-page conversion is about the same system-wide, so the real free trial advantage is more people reaching the page.
title: 1 of 3 Paths to starting your first business

text: If you already have a different business, the simplest use is adding a link to your free community on the thank-you page or email after opt-in, to nurture leads or deliver the lead magnet.
title: 1 of 3 Paths to starting your first business

text: A community can also be a feature in the customer journey, added into onboarding after someone buys, or placed before purchase as part of nurturing.
title: 1 of 3 Paths to starting your first business

text: Someone with an audience already knows their pain, passion or professional skill, so the path resembles the beginner one: drive people to a community on that topic and monetize. He recommends a free trial.
title: 1 of 3 Paths to starting your first business

text: Skool's large dataset lets them judge features by GMV, gross marketplace volume. When free trials launched, engagement rose across communities and more revenue flowed through the platform, which he takes as evidence people earn more with them.
title: 1 of 3 Paths to starting your first business

text: If you have a good product, he says you should let people try it and lower the barrier; Skool uses a free trial itself.
title: 1 of 3 Paths to starting your first business

text: When hiring anyone, look for the candidate with the smallest skill deficiency for the role.
title: Helping a Business Solve Delegation Issues

text: In his worldview, a trait is not a separate thing; it is simply a collection of skills, so traits can be treated as skills that are learnable.
title: Helping a Business Solve Delegation Issues

text: Skills that take little time to teach should be trained rather than hired for. Sales can take about 2 days to teach while kindness takes about 2 months, so hire the kind person and train sales.
title: Helping a Business Solve Delegation Issues

text: Small jobs can lead to big ones. Hormozi says a small job is not less profitable when it keeps the relationship and keeps you top of mind for the client's next purchase.
title: Why Most Pricing Ladders Don't Actually Work

text: When pricing already scales with the size of what the client buys, Hormozi thinks pricing by category (for example a yacht, a jet, a house) makes more sense than generic tiers.
title: Why Most Pricing Ladders Don't Actually Work

text: Include the maintenance plan inside the core offer as an annual retainer, and call it something like strategy rather than maintenance. Use each visit to ask what else the client is acquiring and sell more.
title: Why Most Pricing Ladders Don't Actually Work

text: Stating up front who you serve, such as only ultra-high-net-worth clients and family offices with estates above a minimum value, lets buyers guess you cost well above a certain level, so the call has no shock.
title: Why Most Pricing Ladders Don't Actually Work

text: With bespoke work you price each job individually, so Hormozi does not care much about a ladder. He says to sell whatever you can get away with and add continuity so business stacks year over year.
title: Why Most Pricing Ladders Don't Actually Work

text: Hormozi likes a simple round rate because the math is easy to do in your head.
title: Why Most Pricing Ladders Don't Actually Work

text: Hormozi does not think paid training is the real problem in hiring sales reps. He suggests that if many hires are needed, a four-week training period seems long and could be cut to one or two weeks.
title: He Pays Recruits $750 a Week and They Quit After Training

text: For sales hiring, have applicants prepare using your script, then run a group interview where each person does a live one-minute role play and gets immediate feedback. Preparation, or lack of it, becomes obvious.
title: He Pays Recruits $750 a Week and They Quit After Training

text: One group call can screen 10 or 20 applicants. Hold one-on-one job offer conversations only with those who performed well, rather than talking to every applicant individually.
title: He Pays Recruits $750 a Week and They Quit After Training

text: He argues that talking to applicants one at a time wears you out, and that you should lower your guard and bring people in, hiring one-to-many.
title: He Pays Recruits $750 a Week and They Quit After Training

text: He says he used this hiring approach with a therapy clinic that struggled to hire therapists for its capped, insurance-based delivery, and the business grew sixfold in three weeks.
title: He Pays Recruits $750 a Week and They Quit After Training

text: He frames the 30-day profit goal around a paying customer rather than a lead, so acquisition cost is measured per customer acquired, not per lead generated.
title: How to Bootstrap Any Business

text: If acquisition cost is recovered quickly, a business can fund its own customer acquisition at essentially unlimited speed. He treats this as an ideal he strives for and has seen happen in many businesses.
title: How to Bootstrap Any Business

text: He refuses to accept that fast payback cannot be done. Instead he imagines a world where it works and asks what that would look like.
title: How to Bootstrap Any Business

text: A lead taking a couple of months to convert is acceptable to him because nurturing a lead is cheap. The real money loss comes when servicing costs stack on top of acquisition costs.
title: How to Bootstrap Any Business

text: His goal is that within 30 days of a transaction, the customer's cash covers both the cost of acquiring and of delivering to them, so that cash can be used to acquire the next customer.
title: How to Bootstrap Any Business

text: A business built purely on buying media and earning a multiple back is a cash business, not one with long-term enterprise value; he calls it a smash and grab opportunity, and growth there means spending more.
title: Helping an Online Education Business Scale

text: Growing an ad arbitrage business depends on raising customer LTV, because the amount earned per customer and the cost of attention set a natural cap, and margins tend to compress over time.
title: Helping an Online Education Business Scale

text: One improvement he suggests is split testing the first 30 seconds of a video sales letter with three to five different hooks.
title: Helping an Online Education Business Scale

text: Creative volume rule of thumb: about 50 pieces of creative for every 10,000 dollars of daily ad spend.
title: Helping an Online Education Business Scale

text: When a business already profits and has a client acquisition system, growth comes from many small improvements, such as moving from eight-to-one to twelve-to-one return, then doubling ad spend and repeating.
title: Helping an Online Education Business Scale

text: The usual prioritization rules still apply when using AI: find the thing you are not doing that currently constrains the business. He treats the question of where to start as strategy, not an AI question.
title: Are You Trying or Are You Moving Mountains? | Hormozi Hotline

text: When one thing limits the business, he says to attack it with overwhelming force rather than ten percent effort, likening it to using an atomic bomb rather than a light approach.
title: Are You Trying or Are You Moving Mountains? | Hormozi Hotline

text: He asked himself why he could not do more, traced it to missing operational capacity, and found he needed six C-suite executives. He and two colleagues spent roughly 8 weeks of free time and filled all six roles.
title: Are You Trying or Are You Moving Mountains? | Hormozi Hotline

text: He says almost none of the six executives he hired knew who he was, so he argues that brand recognition is not what makes hiring work.
title: Are You Trying or Are You Moving Mountains? | Hormozi Hotline

text: Competitors who have bigger businesses are not made of different flesh and blood; they simply did different things, so you can go do those things too.
title: Are You Trying or Are You Moving Mountains? | Hormozi Hotline

text: He would set aside at least 4 hours a week as one block, maybe 8, with zero distractions, and use each block to automate or amplify one specific task with AI. The first is hardest, then it gets easier.
title: Are You Trying or Are You Moving Mountains? | Hormozi Hotline

text: He says he learned building web pages by locking himself in a room and copying a page he liked. He expected it to take hours longer, but it took about three.
title: Are You Trying or Are You Moving Mountains? | Hormozi Hotline

text: To get better AI prompts, ask the AI which prompt you should give it for your goal, such as ideating business growth initiatives, then fill in the gaps of the prompt it writes and run it.
title: Are You Trying or Are You Moving Mountains? | Hormozi Hotline

text: He says interest-driven content distribution makes changing audiences easier than five years earlier: a strong post on a different subject can reach people interested in that subject.
title: Helping a Life Coach Make Better Content

text: He argues that publicly teaching paid training material need not undermine demand: many viewers will never apply it, while those who apply it successfully will want additional help.
title: Helping a Life Coach Make Better Content

text: He thinks messaging that reinforces a victim identity attracts people who identify that way; changing the message can attract a different audience.
title: Helping a Life Coach Make Better Content

text: Hormozi does not believe in a platform posting limit. He says this holds on every platform and cites Fox News posting a long video hourly on YouTube and a Bollywood account posting about 100 times a day on Instagram.
title: I'm an online Physical Therapist, How do I get more leads?

text: When a creator worries about fatiguing the audience with more posts, Hormozi thinks the real strain is on the editor, and that the content may simply not be good enough.
title: I'm an online Physical Therapist, How do I get more leads?

text: He suggests keeping the call to action to about 3 seconds or less, because a long one hurts view-through rate, which in turn reduces the reach the content gets.
title: I'm an online Physical Therapist, How do I get more leads?

text: A comment-to-get-an-assessment call to action is a very heavy ask. He suggests considering a cheat sheet followed by a triage question as a lighter alternative.
title: I'm an online Physical Therapist, How do I get more leads?

text: Ads sending people straight to a workshop are the heaviest ask and carry a hurdle. His scaling roadmap ads bring lower immediate return on ad spend, but he says they perform over a 60 to 90 day window.
title: I'm an online Physical Therapist, How do I get more leads?

text: Yesterday and childhood events do not decide the present moment; they only matter if you choose to make them matter.
title: Champions See Their Past as Their Origin Story

text: Whatever a person is struggling with, someone else has already faced the same struggle and found a way through it.
title: Champions See Their Past as Their Origin Story

text: He says the first step toward greater success is grasping the language successful people use, since they define common words differently from everyone else.
title: The Secret Language of the Highly Successful

text: Activities you enjoy so much that you lose track of time are usually challenging, since easy things become boring. He links this to why uncertainty about the outcome matters.
title: The Secret Language of the Highly Successful

text: He says people called addicted to work find it easy to be, because the things they do are worth doing.
title: The Secret Language of the Highly Successful

text: If people do not have the life you want, do not heed their words. He calls justifying your actions to those with a life you do not want the biggest waste of time, and frames it as a message to his younger self.
title: The Secret Language of the Highly Successful

text: First readiness test for opening more locations: the existing location must run without the owner for six months. Owner may still own it, but makes no decisions and gets no escalations, only a check, with a manager on a profit share.
title: Helping a Brick and Mortar Business Scale

text: Second readiness test: during those six months without the owner, the original location must at least hold or grow its profitability. Once both tests pass, the timeline for the next opening depends on cash needed to fund it.
title: Helping a Brick and Mortar Business Scale

text: A manager should follow a playbook and handle problems themselves. He tells a story of a godfather who asks whether a call is an emergency, and if not, why call.
title: Helping a Brick and Mortar Business Scale

text: Third test: have a strong grand opening strategy. He notes big chains dial in opening spend and targets precisely, and recommends aiming for at least 50% facility capacity before opening.
title: Helping a Brick and Mortar Business Scale

text: Before signing a lease and building out, run your best ad in several candidate areas of a city. Lead costs can differ around fivefold within one city, so cutting CAC by 80% is possible, making market selection vital for brick and mortar.
title: Helping a Brick and Mortar Business Scale

text: Give a location manager an incentive of roughly 10 to 20 percent of that facility's profit.
title: Helping a Brick and Mortar Business Scale

text: Franchising is a different business, and he often unwinds franchises he encounters because most people franchise for ego or to be a franchisor. He advises doing the math on what it takes.
title: Helping a Brick and Mortar Business Scale

text: On a franchise he acquired with 14 corporate locations and 18 franchisees, the target exit needed about 400 franchise locations versus about 67 corporate ones. He bought out franchisees over 12 months, reaching 32 corporate locations.
title: Helping a Brick and Mortar Business Scale

text: If serving smaller customers costs the same effort but requires charging less, he is not a fan. He would rather chase the bigger, higher-margin customers.
title: Helping a $400K Event Business Get to $1M

text: Changing the business model to capture a small-customer segment because your current market feels limited makes sense only when you already hold a huge share of the market, such as at 30 to 100 million a year, and can serve them with a lean process at matching margins.
title: Helping a $400K Event Business Get to $1M

text: At smaller revenue levels, the priority is getting more customers who are the right fit, not adding new segments.
title: Helping a $400K Event Business Get to $1M

text: If paid ads are working and lifetime value to acquisition cost is strong, the answer is simply to spend more on ads.
title: Helping a $400K Event Business Get to $1M

text: He frames the goal as solving the underlying problem, here deal flow, with the highest reward and lowest risk route. Thought leadership is one possible path, not necessarily the required one.
title: Helping a Real Estate Developer Doing $2.1M/Year Get to $30M

text: He suggests picking the lead path that overlaps most with your existing skills, since that gives the best odds of it working. Face-to-face people might use conferences; media lovers might make content.
title: Helping a Real Estate Developer Doing $2.1M/Year Get to $30M

text: He says paid ads can generate deal leads directly, such as an ad aimed at motel owners looking to sell, if ads are your background.
title: Helping a Real Estate Developer Doing $2.1M/Year Get to $30M

text: He ran ads aimed at payment processors doing 30 to 300 million a year and got 13 qualified companies on the phone for about $6,000 in spend, which he calls absurdly good deal flow.
title: Helping a Real Estate Developer Doing $2.1M/Year Get to $30M

text: He calls analysis paralysis the fallacy of the perfect pick: there is no perfect path, every route up the mountain has tradeoffs.
title: Helping a Real Estate Developer Doing $2.1M/Year Get to $30M

text: He names two traps: spending a year at the base choosing, when any path could have taken you far, and hopping between paths because another looks less steep, then finding it slower.
title: Helping a Real Estate Developer Doing $2.1M/Year Get to $30M

text: For thought leadership, he says to give yourself 18 months before judging whether it is a good idea, and to commit to that.
title: Helping a Real Estate Developer Doing $2.1M/Year Get to $30M

text: When he started YouTube he told his vendor he would do it for 10 years and stop only if it had not worked by then; the vendor said he had never heard that.
title: Helping a Real Estate Developer Doing $2.1M/Year Get to $30M

text: He advises doing thought leadership by sticking to what you know and only discussing topics you have a track record in, rather than imitating someone else, since you can beat others at being yourself.
title: Helping a Real Estate Developer Doing $2.1M/Year Get to $30M

text: He says social media has shifted to interest-based feeds, so to attract a certain type of lead you must make that type of content.
title: Helping a Real Estate Developer Doing $2.1M/Year Get to $30M

text: He says not to fear low view counts like 100 to 500, because if the right people watch, such as him as a metal fabrication buyer, that audience is valuable.
title: Helping a Real Estate Developer Doing $2.1M/Year Get to $30M

text: When he did direct sales, he set the frame early so prospects would know how to treat him, for example answering how are you with an enthusiastic, positive reply, which made it harder for them to be rude back.
title: How I Learned to Market and Sell

text: He says prospects are often not bad people; they may simply have forgotten, because people are busy and have low attention. He was rejected so many times that he genuinely does not take it personally.
title: How I Learned to Market and Sell

text: When calling internet leads who opted in, he used small language habits at the start to frame the call: state who he is, where they signed up, that he is a real local person, and lighten the mood.
title: How I Learned to Market and Sell

text: He believes you overcome objections by asking what the prospect was intending. A useful belief for salespeople is that an unclosed sale means you did not understand the prospect well enough.
title: How I Learned to Market and Sell

text: The number one thing he teaches his sales team is to be genuinely curious. The first question is what brought them in, then what they struggled with and what else they tried, walking through it together instead of combat.
title: How I Learned to Market and Sell

text: Hormozi says the hardest range to sell a business in is roughly 10 to 30 million, because it is too small for buyers with serious money and too large for buyers without it.
title: $25M Is the Worst Price to Sell For

text: Hormozi says that before expanding, you should compare revenue per square foot across business units, keep the most profitable service, and drop the rest, as one franchisor did by keeping only semi-private training.
title: $25M Is the Worst Price to Sell For

text: Hormozi advises looking at your most profitable times, pricing and packages, then stripping the business down so the fewest possible people can run it and someone else can operate it. He calls this the most likely path to a big exit, though not easy.
title: $25M Is the Worst Price to Sell For

text: Hormozi notes that many people he knows in fitness run five or ten locations, yet almost none of them ever sold the whole business.
title: $25M Is the Worst Price to Sell For

text: Niche matters less to him than psychographics: identify what characterizes customers who are highly successful and get the most value, and look for the fewest common denominators among the most valuable ones.
title: How to Identify Your Ideal Customer

text: As an example of common denominators among top customers, they might earn over a million dollars a year, have at least three employees, have at least 20 customers, and be organically driven. Those traits define the true avatar.
title: How to Identify Your Ideal Customer

text: People often worry that half their customers do not fit the avatar. He says the non-fitting half is the group that tends to cause reputational problems and burn out the team.
title: How to Identify Your Ideal Customer

text: With a blended customer base you usually must price for the lowest common denominator, since poor-result customers will be dissatisfied. Selling only to the avatar, who gets around ten times the value, lets you charge more and offset lower volume.
title: How to Identify Your Ideal Customer

text: Clients tend not to re-sign once their program ends, so the ascension sale should happen about halfway through, while they are still in it.
title: You need to upsell.

text: Rollover upsell: at the midpoint, credit everything the client already paid toward a longer program, offering an either-or choice such as six or twelve months, with both paid in full and a decision made that day.
title: You need to upsell.

text: Crediting the initial payment makes the first period feel effectively free, since the money already paid is applied to the next commitment.
title: You need to upsell.

text: If a business already has bonuses and a conditional guarantee, he assumes the renewal problem is the sales process rather than the offer.
title: You need to upsell.

text: Either coach the trainers to sell and pay them a percentage of the contract, or, if they hate selling, bring in a dedicated salesperson.
title: You need to upsell.

text: In the short term, the owner taking the renewal calls may be the best use of their time, framed as checking on the client's experience.
title: You need to upsell.

text: Position the upsell as keeping the party going: ask whether reaching the goal weight means being done forever, which leads the client to see this is a lifestyle change, then offer to apply what they paid toward staying on.
title: You need to upsell.

text: If the client declines the two upsell options, downsell them to continuity on the back end.
title: You need to upsell.

text: He advises testing two or three different webinar intros, specifically the first 5 minutes, and judging them by LTV, which he says will make money.
title: \"I Do $30M a Year. Why Does It Feel Unprofitable?\"

text: For upselling customers to a higher-priced back end, he says to aim for an ascension rate of at least 25 percent, and to shoot for 50 percent.
title: \"I Do $30M a Year. Why Does It Feel Unprofitable?\"

text: He says ascension should be built into onboarding: the onboarding call ends with the customer booking a goal-setting call, which leads to a setter and then a closer.
title: \"I Do $30M a Year. Why Does It Feel Unprofitable?\"

text: He says a one-on-one onboarding call earns more money than a group call but takes more operations, so a group call is a fine place to start.
title: \"I Do $30M a Year. Why Does It Feel Unprofitable?\"

text: He suggests customers can only leave the onboarding call once they show confirmation that the next call is booked, which gives a full through line to it. Because they are already customers, they show up.
title: \"I Do $30M a Year. Why Does It Feel Unprofitable?\"

text: He says to hire one strong sales director, then engage six recruiting firms asking each for 10 salespeople, which can produce a 60-person team in about 2 weeks.
title: \"I Do $30M a Year. Why Does It Feel Unprofitable?\"

text: He says his team added 40 salespeople to one of his companies in 2 weeks by paying recruiters with big networks.
title: \"I Do $30M a Year. Why Does It Feel Unprofitable?\"

text: Over time, a service business can raise route density so less time is wasted and routes get more efficient, letting it earn more than competitors or lift gross margin even while price stays fixed.
title: How to Win in a Commoditized Service Business

text: When deciding between selling fewer visits at a higher price or more visits, he says to check gross margins, but he would rather sell someone more: start at the higher frequency, then downsell to less if needed.
title: How to Win in a Commoditized Service Business

text: He suggests playing with payment terms to stack more cash up front rather than being paid quarterly, with pay in full up front as the ideal.
title: How to Win in a Commoditized Service Business

text: If an offer already worked well before, he thinks a drop in results usually means the offer is being phrased or presented badly by the salespeople, not that the offer itself is broken.
title: \"How Do I Know If My Offer Is the Problem or My People Are?\"

text: Reviewing recordings of your sales calls for the first time is often painful, and he says the problem tends to be audible within seconds of listening.
title: \"How Do I Know If My Offer Is the Problem or My People Are?\"

text: Owners often want to overhaul the offer, pricing, and marketing because of a hunch, when they simply have not listened to their sales calls. Record and review the calls first, before changing anything.
title: \"How Do I Know If My Offer Is the Problem or My People Are?\"

text: He classes this kind of problem as a data problem: the missing information was the call recordings, so gather that visibility before making big changes.
title: \"How Do I Know If My Offer Is the Problem or My People Are?\"

text: He thinks recruiting skilled media workers is difficult without an established brand because capable people can earn more than employers typically offer.
title: Helping a Business Owner Choose Between Two Avatars

text: Creating another offering is not the only way to increase earnings; expanding the existing business is also an option, even when finding additional demand is the difficult problem.
title: Helping a Business Owner Choose Between Two Avatars

text: He translates most criticism, before or after a win, as the critic saying you live or won in a way they would not prefer. They cast their preferences on you and expect you to care.
title: Stop Caring About What Other People Think

text: People are entitled to think you should care about their views, and you are entitled not to. Hormozi says this stance has cost him some friends, and he accepts that.
title: Stop Caring About What Other People Think

text: For people who react heavily to criticism, especially if they lacked input from others for a while, there is a pull to treat every comment as valuable, even though it may be harmful or a joke.
title: Stop Caring About What Other People Think

text: Ignoring everyone's opinion is not practical. Discerning good feedback is a skill to learn, and his podcast, sales presentations, emails and products improved because they responded to feedback.
title: Stop Caring About What Other People Think

text: He thinks good feedback can be filtered by two tests: aligned incentives (does the person benefit from you doing better) and competence (real domain expertise relevant to the matter).
title: Stop Caring About What Other People Think

text: He says more filters make it harder. Aligned incentives ensure the person points the same direction as you; competence ensures they know how to do the thing.
title: Stop Caring About What Other People Think

text: A friend offered a refund if buyers wrote daily plans and results in a Google Doc for 6 weeks; he said completion of twice-daily tasks is under 1%, so the guarantee was safe.
title: Stop Caring About What Other People Think

text: He thinks people underestimate how simple success is and then expect it to be easy; it is harder than expected, but rewards may also be greater than expected.
title: Stop Caring About What Other People Think

text: Owners of one to three stores should not think more locations is how they make more money. Make each store so profitable that cash piles up with nowhere to go, and only then open more.
title: You're Not Overexpanded, You're Undertalented

text: He says a good sign that it is time to expand is that the money coming in feels excessive, and the decision to open another store comes almost as an afterthought.
title: You're Not Overexpanded, You're Undertalented

text: For the caller's case he would want retail margins around 40 percent or more before scaling to something like 20 locations.
title: You're Not Overexpanded, You're Undertalented

text: He is fine with a wholesale line so long as it demands none of the owner's attention, ideally because a manager runs it.
title: You're Not Overexpanded, You're Undertalented

text: For coffee and food businesses, marketing is almost always grassroots, though some strong tactics can bring in lots of foot traffic. Cash register scripting must be nailed, and small staff incentives can help.
title: You're Not Overexpanded, You're Undertalented

text: He suspects half or more of a typical menu rarely sells and ties up cash in inventory, so trimming it would improve the cash conversion cycle.
title: You're Not Overexpanded, You're Undertalented

text: He says the real answer is usually a hundred small fixes rather than one exciting bullet.
title: You're Not Overexpanded, You're Undertalented

text: When metrics fall, either you changed something unknowingly, such as content quality, or something external changed, like the environment or the algorithm. He also warns that continuing the same approach will keep getting worse.
title: Are You Shadowbanned or Just Making Bad Content

text: Because social platforms now favor interest graphs over follower counts, a brand new account with zero followers can post a clip reaching 10 million views, so a shadow ban is much less of a death sentence than before.
title: Are You Shadowbanned or Just Making Bad Content

text: He calls Instagram the most monetizable platform, since you can directly message every follower.
title: Are You Shadowbanned or Just Making Bad Content

text: He would rather learn the problem is weak content than a ban, because content is very fixable. He notes Instagram shows shadow ban status in settings, so check there.
title: Are You Shadowbanned or Just Making Bad Content

text: Focus on controllables: improve content, make more of it and more varied. He suggests oneof10.com to find top-performing headlines and thumbnails across YouTube, then adapt them to your niche.
title: Are You Shadowbanned or Just Making Bad Content

text: A trick that worked eventually stops, and you must learn another. His own team has had to change its approach all the time.
title: Are You Shadowbanned or Just Making Bad Content

text: If customers at the low end cannot pay enough, you cannot afford the resources needed to get them results. Below a certain spend level the offer has to be do-it-yourself, which is a different business.
title: Helping a Sales Coaching and Lead Generation Agency Scale

text: Screen out prospects with a low likelihood of success and consider adjusting price so it only fits the better avatar. He frames this as an avatar issue.
title: Helping a Sales Coaching and Lead Generation Agency Scale

text: To build activation, take people with the right demographics and quantifiable traits, identify what behaviors made them activate and stay, and what similar-looking people who failed did not do. Reverse engineer the activation process from that gap.
title: Helping a Sales Coaching and Lead Generation Agency Scale

text: At Gym Launch, the team emailed a customer's list and the customer would make a sale within the first 7 days. His advice was to simply build the process around that activation.
title: Helping a Sales Coaching and Lead Generation Agency Scale

text: Each part of an offer should deliver value exceeding the entire offer’s price, because different customers may purchase primarily for different individual parts.
title: Be Clear, Not Clever

text: When explaining an offer to newcomers, use simple, everyday language and unpack technical terms. Hormozi says explaining components as though addressing a 5-year-old improves conversion because prospects understand without mentally translating unfamiliar language.
title: Be Clear, Not Clever

text: When getting each customer is hard early on, make sure every customer is worth it. He says people mistakenly sell too cheaply, and should maximize potential money from each person rather than scalability.
title: How I'd Make $100K in 90 Days From Scratch

text: To generate cash flow early, it can make sense to do unscalable things in the short term.
title: How I'd Make $100K in 90 Days From Scratch

text: The fastest route to $100,000 differs from the fastest route to a million or ten million, which is the misconception behind the question.
title: How I'd Make $100K in 90 Days From Scratch

text: After losing his money, he asked local businesses for their packages and lowest delivery price, then offered to bring customers and keep a percentage of sales while they keep the customer afterward. He made $100,000 in the first month.
title: How I'd Make $100K in 90 Days From Scratch

text: His gym offer was a weight loss challenge. He targeted the emptiest facilities, since he believed he could fill them, usually within about 3 weeks, and ad spend stayed small because returns of 10 to 1 let him recycle spend.
title: How I'd Make $100K in 90 Days From Scratch

text: His sequence: have an offer, record ads on a phone, post them to a landing page feeding a Google Sheet, call the leads to schedule, meet them, present the advertised offer and collect payment. The business delivers while he keeps the cash.
title: How I'd Make $100K in 90 Days From Scratch

text: He describes this as the easiest business to run: one person, functionally an affiliate business.
title: How I'd Make $100K in 90 Days From Scratch

text: With only basic AI knowledge, he says you could offer to observe a business free and craft an AI plan saving at least $100,000, asking for a third or 20% of savings if demonstrated. He thinks most would agree, with nothing upfront.
title: How I'd Make $100K in 90 Days From Scratch

text: Reaching businesses has many routes: knocking on doors, texting, DMs, calls, email, posting content. The bigger problem is that people lack skills; if you have skills, making money isn't hard.
title: How I'd Make $100K in 90 Days From Scratch

text: Everything that is not the work is a distraction. He treats commitment as eliminating alternatives and keeps a plaque saying focus is subtraction.
title: How I'd Make $100K in 90 Days From Scratch

text: Few activities generate money: let people know you exist, make an offer solving a specific problem, get agreement, exchange money, and deliver. Everything else is noise.
title: How I'd Make $100K in 90 Days From Scratch

text: People get paralyzed trying to pick the perfect business. He says most entrepreneurs' first business is not their last but a stepping stone.
title: How I'd Make $100K in 90 Days From Scratch

text: All of business is getting a stranger to pay you for something you make for them. You can take cash without an LLC; cards require one. Morning routines are unnecessary.
title: How I'd Make $100K in 90 Days From Scratch

text: To find a strong ad or brand manager, he says to poach: identify people who produced results for brands you admire and offer them more money to do the same work for you.
title: Helping an Online Coach Advertise Better

text: He says people who are skilled at media usually have some public presence, so they can be found by searching LinkedIn or asking a tool such as ChatGPT who worked on a brand.
title: Helping an Online Coach Advertise Better

text: Every business has three core things: attraction, conversion and delivery. He sees functions like IT, recruiting and finance as ancillary, needed for the company to keep existing but not core to creating customer value.
title: Helping an Online Coach Advertise Better

text: He would not outsource the brand manager role and recommends bringing that person in house, because for this coach the brand is arguably the most important asset.
title: Helping an Online Coach Advertise Better

text: If you already have an engaged free community and a proven way of delivering value, he thinks making that community a free trial is the best next step, so delivery and marketing become essentially the same thing going forward.
title: Don't Open a Paid Community. Do This Instead

text: Running a second, paid community alongside a free one takes more work to manage. He notes the main risk is that the free community may fade once its best members are moved into the paid one, something he says he has seen happen.
title: Don't Open a Paid Community. Do This Instead

text: He says he is recommending against his own financial interest, since he benefits when people open more communities, but he puts his reputation ahead of that when advising.
title: Don't Open a Paid Community. Do This Instead

text: Hormozi says the point of franchising is capital. If a business is not capital intensive, franchising is a poor idea, because it is the most expensive capital available: you give away nearly all the business for a royalty.
title: How to Say No to the Wrong Opportunities

text: He argues that at the top of any business the life looks the same: heads of sales, marketing, product, customer success, IT, legal and finance, whatever the product sold. He says every business feels unique, but higher up they converge.
title: How to Say No to the Wrong Opportunities

text: He says that at scale you deal daily with roughly seven to ten personalities. Changing your life therefore means managing those people and making sure they are ones you like.
title: How to Say No to the Wrong Opportunities

text: He argues that ten years can look too long, but a business built one location at a time can become huge. He cites Panda, selling chicken for 45 years, at 3.7 billion revenue and 27% net margin.
title: How to Say No to the Wrong Opportunities

text: When he was market leader and a competitor came in undercutting on price, he copied the competitor. The business ended up unprofitable, and he says the mistake cost him $50 million.
title: This Mistake Cost Me $50 Million

text: When a competitor undercuts you, do not follow them down. Let the competitor work out the consequences themselves, and concentrate on serving your customer, which he says is how you win.
title: This Mistake Cost Me $50 Million

text: When facing cheaper knockoffs, he would lead with brand rather than legal action. In his view it is better to become big first and then win legally than to try to be small and win through legal fights.
title: “I’m Stuck Doing $10/Hour Tasks in My $3M Business”

text: He says small companies that pursue legal routes get drowned in fees. Having the coolest brand and the coolest people promoting it makes customers want to buy from you even when they can see cheaper copies.
title: “I’m Stuck Doing $10/Hour Tasks in My $3M Business”

text: He warns that cycling through many SKUs and calling it a portfolio sounds impressive to outsiders, but margins and cash flow suffer, and co-founders end up wishing they had built around one product they all believed in.
title: “I’m Stuck Doing $10/Hour Tasks in My $3M Business”

text: When pitching business growth, emphasize the result customers want. Hormozi says the delivery method may need only 30 seconds of explanation as the distinctive way to achieve it.
title: Helping a Salon Coach Untangle His Offers

text: Hormozi describes education businesses as relatively easy to acquire customers for and capable of substantial gross margins, but weak at retention because customers are meant to learn and eventually graduate.
title: Helping a Salon Coach Untangle His Offers

text: Hormozi thinks technical implementation, ongoing services, and physical product delivery can provide retention and competitive protection that information alone lacks, since information is easy to copy.
title: Helping a Salon Coach Untangle His Offers

text: Hormozi sold six gyms within 90 days for roughly the price of one and a half locations to focus on his launch business. Within six months, that business approached $1 million monthly; he says this outcome was unusual.
title: Helping a Salon Coach Untangle His Offers

text: The worst advice he has heard is to follow your passion.
title: \"What is the best advice you've ever heard or received?\"

text: The lesson that took him many repetitions to learn was focus: pick one thing and go all in on it.
title: \"What is the best advice you've ever heard or received?\"

text: If he could make one law everyone had to follow, it would require people to give away all their wealth at the end of life, with the money not going to their own kids.
title: \"What is the best advice you've ever heard or received?\"

text: Growth comes from repeatedly trading: replace 40 hours of doing sales with about 2 hours of managing someone else, then later trade 40 hours of management for someone else's 2 hours, and keep repeating.
title: Helping a Real Estate Broker Get to $50M

text: Training a new salesperson may dip your revenue temporarily, but it is an investment made so you eventually get your time back and no longer have to sell yourself.
title: Helping a Real Estate Broker Get to $50M

text: He calls the 1 to 3 million revenue range the swamp. Owners there must stake most of the profit on one key hire being good, and both options, working more or betting on a hire, are unpleasant.
title: Helping a Real Estate Broker Get to $50M

text: To free up time, check what each activity earns you and how many hours it takes, then remove the two to four daily hours spent on things that do not grow the business.
title: Helping a Real Estate Broker Get to $50M

text: Any of the repeatable channels, such as social media, LinkedIn or cold outreach, can be made to work. He says you will get one of them working, so pick the channel where you and your team have the most skill overlap.
title: Pick One Sales Channel or Stay Broke

text: If your team knows social media better, double down on social media; if you are stronger at outbound, go with outbound email. He suggests sending more emails rather than adding new tactics if outbound is your strength.
title: Pick One Sales Channel or Stay Broke

text: Founders either bet on one person who can help them or work double time themselves. He says both are fine and simply reflect different risk preferences.
title: Pick One Sales Channel or Stay Broke

text: Second businesses tend to grow faster than first ones because founders have better pattern recognition. Almost everyone in the room who was on a second business agreed. You learn what a good hire looks like after hiring several.
title: Pick One Sales Channel or Stay Broke

text: As a business scales you must learn what good looks like at every role and level, from SDR to salesperson, manager, director and VP. You fail repeatedly at each until you get it right.
title: Pick One Sales Channel or Stay Broke

text: The further along a business gets, the more it feels like assembling businesses rather than building them, according to him.
title: Pick One Sales Channel or Stay Broke

text: To get from roughly one to three, he would do far more of the channel you already run, since it is likely very profitable, then put more of those resources into learning another channel.
title: Pick One Sales Channel or Stay Broke

text: Hormozi argues that when a business is underpriced, the offer and the price have to be adjusted together rather than changing only one of them.
title: You need to change your offer.

text: Hormozi says he would not disrupt a business that is working well and growing 50% a year; in his experience the breakthrough comes from improving something people already want and like.
title: Don’t Reinvent What’s Already Working

text: He defines an excellent product as one that strips out everything unpleasant about reaching the outcome, aiming to remove all friction, instead of chasing something new. Newness and excitement are marketing's job; product is about the thing everyone already wants.
title: Don’t Reinvent What’s Already Working

text: Using round numbers: $10M profit on $100M revenue could be taken out (about $6M after tax) and invested, or reinvested in advertising. If that $10M yields $30M revenue and the company is valued on top line, it creates far more value.
title: Don’t Reinvent What’s Already Working

text: He says the real question in choosing between reinvesting and taking profit is risk tolerance, meaning how much the owner will bet on the existing business. On dollars alone he sees roughly a 10x difference favoring reinvestment.
title: Don’t Reinvent What’s Already Working

text: To speed product development, lay your product out like a do-it-yourself course of about 10 modules. Then see which modules the product already handles, so customers only do the remaining ones. This ties product development to marketing.
title: Don’t Reinvent What’s Already Working

text: With paid social ads, you must keep producing new creative regularly. In a local market, new creative is needed about every 3 weeks; nationally, roughly every 6 to 8 weeks.
title: How to Pick the Right Acquisition Channel for Your Business

text: When choosing a first acquisition channel, he picks the one where your skill gap is smallest. Outbound, PPC, and Facebook or YouTube pre-roll ads all work and reach different audiences; at scale you would likely use several.
title: How to Pick the Right Acquisition Channel for Your Business

text: He says people often consume some of your content before buying, so you cannot tie it directly to sales, yet posting will make you more money.
title: How to Pick the Right Acquisition Channel for Your Business

text: If you can outspend everyone because your lifetime value is higher than competitors, PPC is the simplest route: look up competitor keywords and ads with online tools, then model their ads.
title: How to Pick the Right Acquisition Channel for Your Business

text: When a bundle sells easily but has thin margins, and the customers are upscale, Hormozi suspects they will not notice a price bump. He thinks adding around twenty could roughly double the margins.
title: Helping a Pest Control Company Fix Their Offer

text: When giving something away, expect nothing in return, so anything that comes back is a bonus. If you give in order to get something, he says you will always end up let down.
title: Give Without Expectation

text: When giving free samples to friends, the one thing he says to ask for is honest feedback, including being told it is bad. He says honesty serves the giver better than a polite lie.
title: Give Without Expectation

text: Telling friends about your stuff is one of eight ways to spread the word. He starts there because it is the cheapest and easiest.
title: Give Without Expectation

text: With services, you can adjust in real time what you offer to do for someone until they light up and ask you to handle it, which shows real interest.
title: Give Without Expectation

text: He built his brand on the thesis that giving away more and better free content than others would eventually bring opportunities to monetize, with no master monetization plan. He says it worked out that way.
title: Give Without Expectation

text: Free giving builds a goodwill deposit with an audience. The audience starts small and grows, and he says requests from people wanting to work with him keep increasing.
title: Give Without Expectation

text: Posting publicly for free is another way to let people know. When early posts got only around 17 views, he pictured a room of 17 or 22 people and treated it like a class presentation, rather than comparing to huge creators.
title: Give Without Expectation

text: He says people giving advice from your current situation are right most of the time when they doubt you, but they are wrong on the rare occasion that matters, such as when an idea hits big. They are right more often, not more right.
title: The Winner's Mindset Is a Contradiction

text: He argues that information coming from people who are not actually playing your game is effectively noise, because you are competing in a wider game with more players than their small circle and its status contest.
title: The Winner's Mindset Is a Contradiction

text: One of one meant making only content that he alone could make. A generic Coca-Cola breakdown is something anyone can do, but sharing how he doubled a company's sales with four specific changes is something only he can say.
title: What Would You Do If You Weren't Afraid?

text: Around the launch of the book One of One, the idea grew beyond doing only what only they can do into doing things they did not yet know they could do. That became one of zero, the brand he plans to carry for the next few years.
title: What Would You Do If You Weren't Afraid?

text: When he debated quitting his job, his most difficult decision, he told himself that if entrepreneurship failed, he would still probably get a job and would have a strong entrepreneurship story for business school applications.
title: What Would You Do If You Weren't Afraid?

text: People tend to catastrophize failure into losing everything and dying alone. He suggests playing it out two natural steps: if he lost everything, someone he knows would probably lend him a couch or floor, since he has not burned his relationships.
title: What Would You Do If You Weren't Afraid?

text: His genuine plan B was driving Uber and stripping. He estimated roughly 70 to 80 thousand dollars a year from Uber and 150 to 200 thousand from stripping, and he says shame around this does not matter to him.
title: What Would You Do If You Weren't Afraid?

text: Burnout happens when the reward cycle you are used to becomes too delayed, too weak, gets habituated to, or stops occurring, so an activity that once felt good no longer does after many repetitions.
title: What Burnout Actually Is and How to Fix It

text: Punishment works like reward: people habituate to it, so to keep it effective you must vary both its type and its intensity.
title: What Burnout Actually Is and How to Fix It

text: Burnout is essentially an extinction curve on a behavior: you still do the same things but no longer get the satisfaction you used to.
title: What Burnout Actually Is and How to Fix It

text: Burnout is harder to resolve when competing priorities, such as a family relying on your income, make leaving difficult, especially once others stop praising your work and expect it as normal.
title: What Burnout Actually Is and How to Fix It

text: Reinforcement means anything that makes a behavior happen more. Pay can keep reinforcing a job even after its other rewards, like challenge, have faded because you have mastered it.
title: What Burnout Actually Is and How to Fix It

text: Identity labels, such as being a good provider, are themselves reinforcing and create rules for yourself. To change someone's behavior, give them a label they can live up to, then align their actions with it.
title: What Burnout Actually Is and How to Fix It

text: Advertisers who hit an artificial spending ceiling usually need many more creatives. The gap between stalling and scaling comes down to creative quality, which covers both the hooks aimed at the target audience and the creative itself.
title: At 21, He Makes $600K a Month. His Ads Are the Ceiling.

text: For a VSL funnel, after the headline is tested, test the first five minutes: cut them out, retell them tighter, put more proof up front, make clear the viewer is in the right place, and run several variants. He says this can cut CAC by 20 to 30 percent.
title: At 21, He Makes $600K a Month. His Ads Are the Ceiling.

text: Better creative and conversion rate optimization both lower the cost to acquire a customer. The back end works on a different side, raising how much you can afford to spend, which helps when you are in a bidding war with competitors.
title: At 21, He Makes $600K a Month. His Ads Are the Ceiling.

text: Low-ticket upsells alone are not enough for a phone-sales business; add a high-ticket upsell in the range of five to ten thousand dollars.
title: At 21, He Makes $600K a Month. His Ads Are the Ceiling.

text: Adding a phone team to sales can typically double or triple lifetime value, so the real question is when to pull that lever.
title: At 21, He Makes $600K a Month. His Ads Are the Ceiling.

text: He thinks ads mostly reach further into slightly colder people beyond your existing base, so unless you have a proven cold conversion mechanism, figuring that out is not his first bet.
title: Helping a Fitness Coach Double His Business in 6 Months

text: He prefers creating spare capacity, such as hiring a head, before turning up lead flow. Otherwise people either cannot take the extra calls or drop the ball on content.
title: Helping a Fitness Coach Double His Business in 6 Months

text: He says many big creators do not do their own scripting or research, and that he saw his own content do better after he stopped scripting and others helped.
title: Helping a Fitness Coach Double His Business in 6 Months

text: To earn around 500,000 a year as an employee, unless you are CEO, you likely need a company doing at least 10 million a year, probably 20 million or more.
title: How to Make More Money as an Employee

text: Many companies making 100 to 500 million a year, such as family-owned manufacturers, are not on the S&P 500, so there are far more large businesses than people expect.
title: How to Make More Money as an Employee

text: To raise income in a job, tie yourself as close to revenue as possible and take on as much risk as possible, effectively becoming an internal entrepreneur.
title: How to Make More Money as an Employee

text: What you earn from making someone else money is always a discount on the value you create; for example, a business owner would likely give 10% of an extra 5 million they could not otherwise get.
title: How to Make More Money as an Employee

text: Think of yourself as a vendor to the business rather than an employee, and ask whether you can clearly explain how your role makes the company money.
title: How to Make More Money as an Employee

text: Many roles are second or third order removed from revenue. Articulate your link, such as proposing to cut churn from 10% to 5% and asking for a raise if you hit it.
title: How to Make More Money as an Employee

text: Pitch that you can generate a stated amount of value and ask to be paid a small percentage of it. If the owner refuses, your upside is capped and he says to leave.
title: How to Make More Money as an Employee

text: The more of an outcome you own in money and time invested, the more upside you can unlock.
title: How to Make More Money as an Employee

text: Hormozi identifies four sources of influence: status from controlling scarce resources, power from giving guidance that produces benefits, credibility from external evidence, and likeness through shared appearance, behavior, or values.
title: The 4 Things That Build a Powerful Brand

text: A single achievement can establish multiple sources of influence. Hormozi illustrates this with selling a company: the completed sale supplies evidence of accomplishment, while its financial proceeds confer status.
title: The 4 Things That Build a Powerful Brand

text: For businesses using educational content, including trades, give viewers practical instructions that produce useful results. When people benefit from following that guidance, they become more willing to follow future instructions from the same source.
title: The 4 Things That Build a Powerful Brand

text: Hormozi argues that a branding mistake leaves an association that cannot be erased. Recovery comes from reducing negative associations and creating enough positive ones to diminish the mistake's relative influence.
title: The 4 Things That Build a Powerful Brand

text: Hormozi ranks three sources of brand influence from weakest to strongest: a business's statements about itself, endorsements from people the audience respects, and the audience's own experience using its products or services.
title: The 4 Things That Build a Powerful Brand

text: Social proof carries different weight: an influential person the buyer knows is more persuasive than an unfamiliar reviewer. Among unfamiliar reviewers, people resembling the buyer exert more influence than people unlike them.
title: The 4 Things That Build a Powerful Brand

text: Strong marketing associations can secure an initial purchase, but customers then judge the product through experience. Hormozi argues that the product must reinforce the brand because promotional strength cannot compensate for a poor experience.
title: The 4 Things That Build a Powerful Brand

text: Business owners should create content relevant to prospective customers rather than pursue views alone. Hormozi argues that niche demonstrations and problem-solving content can attract buyers despite smaller audiences because recommendation systems distribute content according to viewers' interests.
title: The 4 Things That Build a Powerful Brand

text: For an e-commerce brand aiming at $100M, he says the long-term problem to solve is building a brand, and that happens through customers coming back to buy again.
title: \"Do I Lower Prices to Grow Faster?\"

text: If he bought the apparel company, he would put all effort into lifting repeat buyers from 30% to 65%, so two of every three customers return. Better product experience also brings free referred sales that are hard to attribute.
title: \"Do I Lower Prices to Grow Faster?\"

text: Big apparel brands like Gymshark keep scaling into colder markets because a strong brand and repurchases from the existing base counter the rising difficulty of acquiring new customers.
title: \"Do I Lower Prices to Grow Faster?\"

text: Even if customers cost more to acquire, when they refer others the overall blended CAC drops, which lets the business expand much further.
title: \"Do I Lower Prices to Grow Faster?\"

text: As you keep investing in the brand and demand rises, selling into B2B channels gets easier because you have leverage: you can promise to drive foot traffic from people who want your products.
title: \"Do I Lower Prices to Grow Faster?\"

text: A stronger brand comes from the people you choose to associate with, and it need not be the founder. Five to ten influencer faces can work, though generic picks are not enough.
title: \"Do I Lower Prices to Grow Faster?\"

text: He says most online fitness sellers get only one purchase, since clients buy a set block such as 12 weeks or six months and then stop. Consistent renewals from clients signal that your time is well spent.
title: how to scale as a fitness coach

text: Scaling decisions start from how much money you want and what lifestyle you want. Check whether the number of in-person days your model demands hits a wall before or after your income goal.
title: how to scale as a fitness coach

text: If you want to keep scaling beyond your current in-person setup, he suggests trying offers that are online only, since they let you grow without in-person time.
title: how to scale as a fitness coach

text: He has never liked personal training as a business because it does not scale. If you hire a trainer for one-on-one clients, they are loyal to that trainer, not to you, and follow him if he changes gyms.
title: how to scale as a fitness coach

text: His first step for moving beyond one-on-one is going to one-on-six, for two reasons. You earn six times the money, and small groups retain customers to the business better.
title: how to scale as a fitness coach

text: In small groups, clients are accountable to each other, and getting all four people to leave is much harder than one person leaving. Even if a trainer leaves, clients stay for the other members.
title: how to scale as a fitness coach

text: Alternating coaches gives stability, and so does having more than one customer per session. This is why he has always favored semi-private training over one-on-one.
title: how to scale as a fitness coach

text: In a luxury market you win on total dollars, not on number of transactions, so if you have done the work of positioning as luxury you should capitalize with very high price options.
title: Charge $100K or Don't Call It Luxury

text: He describes luxury as a Veblen good, where raising the price for the right buyer makes them want it more. He would bet that doubling or tripling prices would raise close percentage, though he says it is not a promise.
title: Charge $100K or Don't Call It Luxury

text: A request-for-quote opt-in is about the lowest converting option available.
title: Charge $100K or Don't Call It Luxury

text: Use a questionnaire as the opt-in, framed as matching the buyer to the ideal experience. Qualified budgets go straight to the calendar; others get a PDF or similar.
title: Charge $100K or Don't Call It Luxury

text: Send the VSL before the call with a hidden request, such as texting back the head count. This commits people to watching, proves they did, and lets you pause the call for them to watch if not.
title: Charge $100K or Don't Call It Luxury

text: Build a frame using surveys and statistics: people forget food choices but remember how good a time they had. Spend should follow what contributes most to memory, which supports pricing entertainment high.
title: Charge $100K or Don't Call It Luxury

text: Anchor around very large comparable expenses at the start of the call and in the VSL so the stated price feels much better.
title: Charge $100K or Don't Call It Luxury

text: Anchor upsell: make the top price the true offer, then downsell to a version missing one niche feature at about a third of the price. Some buy the top tier, and many take the cheaper one.
title: Charge $100K or Don't Call It Luxury

text: An anchor only works if you truly commit to selling the top offer so the buyer seriously considers and starts justifying it; tossing it out casually fails.
title: Charge $100K or Don't Call It Luxury

text: He does very few podcasts. He says the many appearances on one philosophy-themed show make people assume he is always a serious philosopher, which overrepresents that side of how he actually lives.
title: My Framework for Brand Associations

text: One reason for a big-audience podcast appearance: many people who have never heard of him enter through that host's world, and viewers see a different side of him.
title: My Framework for Brand Associations

text: Influence means people's behavior changes because of you, whether they love or hate you. A brand with high influence and large reach is bigger; parents have very high influence but tiny reach.
title: My Framework for Brand Associations

text: When choosing associations, he asks whether he will lose audience, whether he will gain people not yet exposed to his content, and whether he gains more than he loses.
title: My Framework for Brand Associations

text: He will discuss business with anyone who wants to. He thinks the biggest loss of reputation would come from doing or saying things that contradict his stated values; beyond that he sees associations as mostly exposure.
title: My Framework for Brand Associations

text: Positioning matters: being introduced to a poor-quality person's audience as similar to that person is a bad move, so he generally avoids speaking on other people's stages and does not headline events.
title: My Framework for Brand Associations

text: He says the speaking circuit is incestuous and his business is much larger than nearly everyone on it, and he expects to be paired with other speakers whether he wants it or not.
title: My Framework for Brand Associations

text: He considers the strongest branding move to be continuing to act as himself and achieving what he says he will do.
title: My Framework for Brand Associations

text: In direct-response alternative education, coaching, helping people and courses are fine. The problem is lying about credibility, results, and through unrealistic claims and expectations.
title: My Framework for Brand Associations

text: To keep a reputation, he says to do the opposite of typical marketing: promise nothing and deliver a great deal. It is hard to sell that way, which is why branding matters.
title: My Framework for Brand Associations

text: Hormozi cites Keith Cunningham's test for risky moves: ask what the upside is, what the downside is, and whether you can live with that downside. If the downside is not livable, skip it. He adds likelihood as an optional fourth question.
title: Watch this if you keep chasing every shiny business model

text: He points out that taking a fee off the top line can beat running the operation yourself when your own margin is thin: a licensing fee equal to half your margin, taken from revenue, is not a bad trade.
title: Watch this if you keep chasing every shiny business model

text: Hormozi sets a gate before adding a new model: only move to licensing once the current business can open a new location roughly each quarter with a team the owner is not involved in.
title: Watch this if you keep chasing every shiny business model

text: Hormozi defines sales culture as explicit and implicit behavioral expectations, and says those expectations govern team performance.
title: Helping a B2B SaaS Scale

text: Allowing an experienced new salesperson to behave in ways leadership discourages elsewhere signals that existing standards no longer matter, potentially changing the whole team's behavior.
title: Helping a B2B SaaS Scale

text: Hormozi says his recruiting process typically starts with 500–1,000 resumes for one solid hire, narrowing through conversations to roughly three qualified finalists before selecting one.
title: Helping a B2B SaaS Scale

text: Hormozi asks recruiters to produce several candidates strong enough to make selection difficult. He considers an obvious winner a sign that they have not supplied enough strong alternatives.
title: Helping a B2B SaaS Scale

text: When people found things hard while expecting them to be easy, he told them plainly that this is what hard feels like. Their expectations then matched reality, they felt relief, and the situation felt less awful.
title: Why 99% of People Quit

text: Hormozi says that giving people permission to feel bad about a hard thing they chose helps them stop feeling as bad. It becomes their new normal.
title: Why 99% of People Quit

text: As a fraternity president, he told pledges that 8 weeks of effort gets them 3 and a half years of benefits, such as others driving and cleaning for them. He framed it as a good investment.
title: Why 99% of People Quit

text: He credits the line 'this is what hard feels like' as a source of motivation. He connects it to why most people stop and why they don't win.
title: Why 99% of People Quit

text: Cam Haines keeps a 'Must be nice' sign behind his power rack in response to people saying that about his sponsorships. Hormozi has seen him carry an 80 lb rock labeled poser up a hill with no audience.
title: Why 99% of People Quit

text: When someone online calls him an asshole, he replies that they are right. He sees little point in working to prove critics wrong, since he would not change their minds anyway.
title: The Trick to Never Being Insulted Again

text: He says he has probably acted badly many times in his life, so agreeing with an insult is honest for him. He notes that this ends the endless back-and-forth when people criticize him.
title: The Trick to Never Being Insulted Again

text: He says he has never had people pick fights with him because of his size, and he thinks the idea that big men attract challenges is a farce. He suspects he gives off little fight energy.
title: The Trick to Never Being Insulted Again

text: He argues that character traits are not binary. Everyone has been impatient and patient, nice and mean at different times, so the real question is to what degree you have a trait.
title: The Trick to Never Being Insulted Again

text: He thinks many people get upset at a name because they believe a label from one individual means something about them. For him, such a label carries no meaning.
title: The Trick to Never Being Insulted Again

text: A stranger bumped into his partner and called her skinny; she took it as a compliment. He uses this to show an insult only stings because we choose to accept it as one.
title: The Trick to Never Being Insulted Again

text: If you can make one insult okay once, he says you can do it every time, because how you perceive it is a choice.
title: The Trick to Never Being Insulted Again

text: He says he cannot know what someone intends by their words. All he can observe is the fact that they said something, so he responds only to that.
title: The Trick to Never Being Insulted Again

text: He says you must believe before anyone else that your service is not a commodity. To start, list every reason a bad provider of the service is bad, then fix each of those things.
title: Fixing Pricing in a Service Business

text: He defines good as the absence of hard. You cannot make something easy, only remove what makes it hard. Removing those frustrating elements raises the value of a product or service.
title: Fixing Pricing in a Service Business

text: If customers see two offerings as the same, they buy the cheaper one, which is a bad fight. He puts his effort into answering why his offering is different before thinking about pricing.
title: Fixing Pricing in a Service Business

text: He says you should be able to state the difference simply: the several things that make the alternatives bad, how you avoid them, and why the higher price in exchange is worth it.
title: Fixing Pricing in a Service Business

text: Hormozi relays Glover's three essences of an attractive man: being comfortable in his own skin, knowing where he is going, and having fun on the way there. He calls it a lovely frame.
title: The 3 Things That Make a Man Attractive

text: Hormozi treats the three traits as ideals to aim for, and asks whether a married man would really want to let himself become unattractive. He says direction, inner comfort and fun each contribute to attractiveness.
title: The 3 Things That Make a Man Attractive

text: Hormozi says a man with only one of the three can still find a mate. If he clearly knows he is going somewhere, people will rally behind him even without fun or comfort.
title: The 3 Things That Make a Man Attractive

text: Hormozi says a man who is simply comfortable with himself, or one who has lots of fun, can still attract people even lacking the other two traits. He would personally rank direction and comfort above fun.
title: The 3 Things That Make a Man Attractive

text: Hormozi says the question of why work hard if unhappy assumes happiness is the life goal. His own goal is to do epic things and be useful, not to be happy.
title: Why I Work Even Though It Doesn’t Make Me Happy...

text: Looking back, Hormozi finds the things that gave him the most joy were those he was willing to sacrifice for over an extended period. He says they pay memory dividends far larger than the momentary cost.
title: Why I Work Even Though It Doesn’t Make Me Happy...

text: In college Hormozi was obsessed with happiness, nearly went into positive psychology, and consumed all that material. He says it drove him mad and left him sadder and more depressed.
title: Why I Work Even Though It Doesn’t Make Me Happy...

text: Hormozi gave up on happiness and just did things. Some time later he noticed he was not miserable. For a long time he identified as not a happy person and accepted that.
title: Why I Work Even Though It Doesn’t Make Me Happy...

text: By dropping happiness as a requirement for his activities, Hormozi enjoyed them more, because good moments became pleasant surprises. Permitting himself to be unhappy for a long stretch to get what he wanted brought him great relief.
title: Why I Work Even Though It Doesn’t Make Me Happy...

text: Despite finishing school in three years and landing a good job, Hormozi found his life empty and spent a few years in a funk.
title: Why I Work Even Though It Doesn’t Make Me Happy...

text: When an owner runs two very different businesses that make similar profit, the most useful thing is to choose one, free up the time, and put everything into it.
title: He's Doing $3.4M But Wants Out of the Stress

text: Choosing is only half of it; you then have to commit and stay on the path so the split focus does not recur. He says focus matters most for someone already making millions.
title: He's Doing $3.4M But Wants Out of the Stress

text: If customers cost 200 to 250 euros each to acquire, the problem is usually not a cash shortage but a front-end price that is too low. He says to charge more up front.
title: He's Doing $3.4M But Wants Out of the Stress

text: A fitness onboarding challenge can be framed around what customers fear: injury and lack of accountability. Onboarding addresses injury, money at stake drives attendance, and measured progress shows what works.
title: He's Doing $3.4M But Wants Out of the Stress

text: The goal of a money-back challenge is not that people hit the target but that they start the process. Pitch the continuation halfway through, not at the end.
title: He's Doing $3.4M But Wants Out of the Stress

text: Hormozi considers agencies relatively easy to grow to $1 million, $3 million, or even $10 million annually. Beyond that, growth becomes much harder because recruiting people capable of more advanced work becomes increasingly difficult.
title: The Problem With the Agency Model

text: He views Fortune 100 clients as the agency model’s ideal endpoint: reliable payment, no churn, and five-year agreements worth $5 million annually. His broader principle is that agency growth requires progressively upgrading the clients served.
title: The Problem With the Agency Model

text: A lead-generation agency should select clients who can already sell. Feeling compelled to take over additional client functions signals a poor client fit; identify businesses suited to the narrow service the agency delivers at strong margins.
title: The Problem With the Agency Model

text: Every new business accumulates some form of debt, including gaps in talent, technology, finances, or reputation. He recommends choosing the kind that will be easiest to resolve.
title: The Problem With the Agency Model

text: For big strategic decisions, his team asks which problems they would prefer to have. They list the problems each option would bring, ignore the upside, and pick the problems they are best equipped to handle.
title: The Better Way to Make Big Decisions

text: He believes that spelling out the problems of each path, without thinking about upside, sometimes produces real innovation and solid decisions that reduce regret after the decision.
title: The Better Way to Make Big Decisions

text: Regrets usually come from the path not chosen, because people imagine it with only its upside and forget the negatives that would have come with it.
title: The Better Way to Make Big Decisions

text: Good decision-making and regret minimization mean considering the downsides when deciding and remembering them afterward. He calls this one of his strongest frames for feeling glad about paths he did not take.
title: The Better Way to Make Big Decisions

text: He treats a sales team's inconsistent results as a sales operations issue. His first step is to do everything that should already be in place, starting with all reps reading the same script.
title: We hit $700K then crashed to $200K. Why?

text: He says sales reps need daily training so they say things the right way, and should memorize the script so thoroughly they can deliver it word for word.
title: We hit $700K then crashed to $200K. Why?

text: If reps keep going off script to close deals despite training, he says that signals a cultural problem, which is a leadership problem, since the leader is reinforcing off-script behavior with no consequences.
title: We hit $700K then crashed to $200K. Why?

text: For a consistent world-class sales team, he says the process must always rank above the individual player, and no one is above the process.
title: We hit $700K then crashed to $200K. Why?

text: He believes roughly 95 to 98 percent of sales teams do not understand how sales training and sales culture work.
title: We hit $700K then crashed to $200K. Why?

text: For a local business, he says you must avoid burning through your reputation. Losing around half of customers each year is a warning sign, especially on a product that should be sticky.
title: Helping a Service Business Owner Build Systems

text: Cutting churn from about 50 percent per year to 20 percent or less would, by his estimate, double the business in roughly two and a half years even if nothing else changed.
title: Helping a Service Business Owner Build Systems

text: Fixing churn involves setting expectations correctly in marketing, on the sales call and in top-of-funnel offers, plus defining key activation points and the conversations needed across the early steps.
title: Helping a Service Business Owner Build Systems

text: Retention gains hit profit disproportionately, so profit would rise by significantly more than double when churn is cut, and he says it could double, triple or quadruple.
title: Helping a Service Business Owner Build Systems

text: At the teeth whitening chain he owns, doubling lifetime revenue per customer led to 2.4x revenue and 7.5x profit per location, which is why he bought the company.
title: Helping a Service Business Owner Build Systems

text: Hormozi says most businesses die because the entrepreneur quits. If the founder keeps going, the business can change its model, structure and pricing and survive, so he would rather ask why entrepreneurs quit.
title: The Real Reason Most Businesses Die

text: Businesses, products, markets and technology naturally come and go, which he treats as normal. In his view, the real failure is someone starting and then not persisting.
title: The Real Reason Most Businesses Die

text: Story: at a dinner, college-aged friends said they were starting a business. Six months later they were still setting up the LLC, which he says takes about 30 minutes online, so he asked what else they did.
title: The Real Reason Most Businesses Die

text: Newer entrepreneurs often convince themselves they did real work by sitting at a computer. He asks whether they figured out something to sell, told people about it, and asked for money.
title: The Real Reason Most Businesses Die

text: Because a service business is mainly headcount cost, it can be collapsed down to just the founder doing the work for pay. He says there is little reason for one to fail, and it dies only if the founder stops.
title: The Real Reason Most Businesses Die
