text: He says he barely knows anyone who failed at a business. He knows people who changed businesses many times, and he believes most people do not give up, they just never start.
title: The Real Reason Most Businesses Die

text: When a client changes the scope after a guaranteed bid, he says you can tell them the terms changed, so the guarantee no longer holds, though you still try to hit the goal. This no-change contingency protects you.
title: My Favorite Offer for Home Service Businesses

text: If the client keeps the terms unchanged and you still go over, you refund the price raise you added, so you keep what you would have earned anyway. He says this covers you on both sides.
title: My Favorite Offer for Home Service Businesses

text: In a commoditized business, you can win on lower risk, meaning people believe you are more likely to deliver the result due to reputation. Without a brand, covenants and guarantees can substitute, but long-term it is reputation.
title: My Favorite Offer for Home Service Businesses

text: Other ways to win when a market is commoditized are speed, such as healing or seeing the horse faster than competitors, and ease, meaning less friction so the customer can hand over the keys and not worry.
title: My Favorite Offer for Home Service Businesses

text: Hormozi currently believes a business grows by resolving one main constraint. He finds that aligning everyone around it and tackling problems sequentially gets them resolved faster than pursuing competing departmental priorities.
title: Helping a $9M Tax Firm Get to $25M

text: Leaders must decide which objective matters most so their teams can prioritize. Selling and routine business operations still continue alongside that objective.
title: Helping a $9M Tax Firm Get to $25M

text: When evaluating acquisitions, he asks whether the company fits the deal box and whether he likes the founders, since he often removes founders and installs a trusted operator; many possible reasons to pass make deals harder.
title: My Criteria for Buying Companies

text: His minimum for acquisitions is roughly $3 million in top line and at least $1 million EBITDA, because below that a company is usually still figuring things out; he wants at least basic product market fit and won't build it himself.
title: My Criteria for Buying Companies

text: His head of biz dev says to look for companies incompetent in exactly the areas his team is excellent, such as a weak sales process or poor demand generation despite high LTV and sticky backend.
title: My Criteria for Buying Companies

text: His team bought a 32-location teeth whitening chain whose product experience was fine but sales process was weak; the first rollout of a improved sales level 5x'd LTV, which he framed as creating about $50 million enterprise value once rolled out across all locations.
title: My Criteria for Buying Companies

text: The hard part of acquiring is discipline: about 3,000 companies apply monthly, but more deals don't mean more money, so he stresses picking the best deals for them rather than merely good ones and avoiding eyes bigger than stomach.
title: My Criteria for Buying Companies

text: He expects the deal box may expand over time as ex-operators join, for example someone who scaled and exited a software business for a hundred million plus could bring deals into his flow instead of building a deal machine.
title: My Criteria for Buying Companies

text: While he slept on the gym floor and showered at the YMCA, clients cheered him on. Within nine months, after hiring staff and a manager, the same people teased him about being too good for them.
title: You're on the Right Path.

text: He earned a college writing scholarship, served as vice president of the newspaper and edited the creative writing magazine, so he has written for a long time.
title: You're on the Right Path.

text: Hate can be treated as an indicator that you are on the right path, rather than something to internalize.
title: You're on the Right Path.

text: Nothing worthwhile comes without an associated amount of discomfort. When friends push back on your changes, such as with jokes about not drinking, expect it to hurt, but it comes with the path.
title: You're on the Right Path.

text: Hormozi thinks the long-term content play is finding content you enjoy making so you can keep going: either enjoy what you make or record yourself doing things you already like. The rest is tolerating pain.
title: Helping an E-Com Brand Make Better Content

text: He gives himself permission to make whatever he wants, since no content police will arrest him for skipping a day or for not optimizing for the algorithm. His content shifts as he changes.
title: Helping an E-Com Brand Make Better Content

text: People need reminders more than teaching, and audiences even more so. Seeing the same message again in a slightly new context is welcome, so creators need not feel content must be as novel to the audience as to them.
title: Helping an E-Com Brand Make Better Content

text: He cites Dave Ramsey, who has answered similar money questions for 35 years, as proof that repeating a core message across differing situations works, with each case's nuance making it fresh.
title: Helping an E-Com Brand Make Better Content

text: He thinks creators underestimate how much audiences enjoy repeated versions of the same thing, citing his own habit of watching the same gym equipment reels dozens of times, so posting today's version is fine.
title: Helping an E-Com Brand Make Better Content

text: He advises finding a format you like first, then working out the algorithm and clickability around it, starting from yourself and working backward. He notes Ramsey lasted 35 years partly because he enjoys it.
title: Helping an E-Com Brand Make Better Content

text: He calls paying roughly 20 to 30 percent more for A+ talent one of the biggest remaining arbitrages in business, because such people are worth more than three or four times a B-level hire. He says most people get this wrong out of fear of the extra cost.
title: When Should a Founder Step Out of Day-to-Day Operations?

text: To judge whether a costly hire is worth it, compare the hit to profit against the extra revenue needed to cover it. He frames a $100,000 salary as requiring $400,000 of added revenue to break even, and asks whether the freed-up time can produce that.
title: When Should a Founder Step Out of Day-to-Day Operations?

text: Setting up incentives so that people naturally behave the way you want in a community takes a long time to build, but it is what makes the behavior self-sustaining.
title: What It Takes to Build a Good Product

text: The look and feel of a community platform can be deliberately light and fun, so that negative or trollish long posts feel out of place and stand out.
title: What It Takes to Build a Good Product

text: For creators, the goal is making it as leveraged as possible to host a community. With thousands of members, a creator cannot answer every question personally, so members answering each other helps.
title: What It Takes to Build a Good Product

text: He says a Facebook post from a creator or customer reaches only around 5% of people, and a post that is not good simply disappears.
title: What It Takes to Build a Good Product

text: Add a small amount, like 99 cents, to every menu item and a plus 3% card fee at the bottom of the menu; he says these small margin increases go mostly unnoticed by customers.
title: How I’d Scale a Restaurant

text: Order each menu section from highest to lowest absolute gross profit in dollars, not price, and box the top three best-margin meals as can't-miss picks for visitors who only eat there once.
title: How I’d Scale a Restaurant

text: Because liquor carries the highest margins, run three prongs: pair each meal with a wine or spirit on the menu, have a mixologist create a weekly drink special the team tastes, and put it on a table A-frame.
title: How I’d Scale a Restaurant

text: Adding the card fee in fine print gets tacked on with nobody objecting, and he says it is worth an extra 4 or 5% to the owner.
title: How I’d Scale a Restaurant

text: Great food is the biggest driver of restaurant success; his tips are business-side only, and if the food is bad, nothing else will work.
title: How I’d Scale a Restaurant

text: Script four daily team conversations: first-time greeting, drink special, drink pairing prompt, and review request. He says great establishments deliver the same interaction every time, like Chick-fil-A.
title: How I’d Scale a Restaurant

text: Servers should pitch the drink special early so one or two get ordered per table, and offer the menu's pairing when items are ordered unless guests already have drinks or don't drink.
title: How I’d Scale a Restaurant

text: Have the manager check on tables when the bill arrives, then ask for a review and leave a QR code to Yelp; reward the server with a spiff. He says this could reach thousands of reviews in six months.
title: How I’d Scale a Restaurant

text: Run as many grand openings as possible since no one knows you exist. Wendy's gave the first 500 attendees a Frosty keychain for free Frosties, which he says creates 500 regulars who bring paying friends.
title: How I’d Scale a Restaurant

text: He prefers fixing monetization and profitability on the back end first, then driving more traffic on the front end.
title: How I’d Scale a Restaurant

text: For reopenings, invite local influencers or locals found through nearby hashtags to eat free with a red carpet feel, then reuse their videos as ads.
title: How I’d Scale a Restaurant

text: Require promo recipients to leave a five-star review and post a video, producing hundreds of ads, reviews and organic buzz; he suggests requiring several review platforms.
title: How I’d Scale a Restaurant

text: For a promotion in a busy-neighborhood location, put an A-frame just inside the door so people walk into it, and handwrite it because he says print never works.
title: How I’d Scale a Restaurant

text: Set a carryout spend bonus a bit above average order value, such as a gift above 75 or 80 dollars if average is 60, to nudge orders up and add margin.
title: How I’d Scale a Restaurant

text: He uses a Matrix scene as a metaphor: a woman in a red dress distracts Neo from his lesson, standing for attractive opportunities that pull you off your main objective. Internally his team uses the phrase for such tempting distractions.
title: You're Distracted by the Woman in the Red Dress (Business Lesson fr...

text: The more successful and capable you become, the more attractive the distracting opportunities get. Early on the temptations are modest, but as you improve, the bigger opportunities make the choice to decline much harder.
title: You're Distracted by the Woman in the Red Dress (Business Lesson fr...

text: A mentor told him right as they sold Gym Launch that if a opportunity is not worth a billion, it is not worth his time. He calls this a great razor for all decisions.
title: You're Distracted by the Woman in the Red Dress (Business Lesson fr...

text: About 3,000 companies a month reach out to Acquisition.com to do a deal, roughly 100 a day, and they have completed 13 deals in 2 years, showing how low the acceptance rate is.
title: You're Distracted by the Woman in the Red Dress (Business Lesson fr...

text: He says capital is never really scarce, only good deals are; a good deal never starves for funding, so a weak investor return is a deal problem.
title: Helping a Home Builder Scale from $30M to $50M

text: He guesses the market return for a riskier small-business real estate deal like this is closer to 13-17%, maybe 13-15%, not 9%.
title: Helping a Home Builder Scale from $30M to $50M

text: He suggests finding one funder who provides a facility that rolls over across the builder's projects, instead of raising money from many small investors.
title: Helping a Home Builder Scale from $30M to $50M

text: He says visionary, future-based language can be too vague; ask how you will know you succeeded and define it in measurable terms, which also helps the team.
title: Helping a Home Builder Scale from $30M to $50M

text: He argues that if the current business can plainly keep growing, you should do more of it rather than switch to an unfamiliar model, since the new one may bring problems you have not seen.
title: Helping a Home Builder Scale from $30M to $50M

text: He notes that owners often think that to do more they must do something different, and he advises simply doing more of what works.
title: Helping a Home Builder Scale from $30M to $50M

text: Looking back on a year, he says he forgets about 95% of it because nothing notable was recorded; what people recall is mostly a small handful of short moments.
title: The Power of Moments: Why 95% of Our Year Goes Unnoticed

text: A few bad moments, maybe five lasting about five minutes each, can get replayed in the mind until they turn a whole season into a bad one. He asks whether the same can be done with positive moments.
title: The Power of Moments: Why 95% of Our Year Goes Unnoticed

text: To grow a business, he thinks about everything that could destroy it. He credits Charlie Munger's advice to always invert, which Einstein is also said to have given.
title: The Power of Moments: Why 95% of Our Year Goes Unnoticed

text: Instead of asking how to grow, ask how you would destroy the business in the fewest moves, list those moves, then do the opposite. He says this taps a stronger mental engine and has produced some of his greatest creative moments.
title: The Power of Moments: Why 95% of Our Year Goes Unnoticed

text: If a business is supply constrained and has more demand than it can serve, raising prices probably makes sense as a way to grow profit.
title: How to Scale a $3M Tennis Business to $10M

text: To grow a space-limited business, Hormozi would examine revenue per square foot for each service category, after a deeper look under the hood at the business.
title: How to Scale a $3M Tennis Business to $10M

text: When a friend who owns a personal training gym brand began franchising, he compared each service category and picked the one with the highest revenue per square foot and the lowest CAC to LTV ratio.
title: How to Scale a $3M Tennis Business to $10M

text: Hormozi argues a high-ticket business owner is really in the acquisition business. The biggest risk is depending on something you cannot control, so he thinks the big competitor probably controls its own customer acquisition.
title: Helping a $4.6M Implant Center Fix Its No-Shows

text: Physicians and dentists are so skilled locally that beginner marketing tasks feel beneath them, yet at scale that skill matters far more, so many jump to ownership and outsource everything.
title: Helping a $4.6M Implant Center Fix Its No-Shows

text: If you outsource lead generation with no knowledge, you can only believe pitches and hope. Learning enough to be dangerous lets you judge an agency, or recruit its top ad person to work with you.
title: Helping a $4.6M Implant Center Fix Its No-Shows

text: Hormozi strongly advocates vertical stack entrepreneurship: the best entrepreneurs he knows can run ads, write copy, build landing pages, and also make strategic decisions.
title: Helping a $4.6M Implant Center Fix Its No-Shows

text: If you are missing pieces of the business, you get stuck and stay stuck until you get lucky or learn. Hitting a wall of ignorance or time forces a bet, and losing some bets is a feature of business.
title: Helping a $4.6M Implant Center Fix Its No-Shows

text: Hormozi relays a mentor's saying that making a billion means losing a hundred million, and that to make 100 million you lose about 10. He frames losses as tuition paying down ignorance.
title: Helping a $4.6M Implant Center Fix Its No-Shows

text: He suggests roughly 70% of effort go to repeating actions already proven to work, 20% to adjacent things, and 10% to moonshots unrelated to the core. He mentions Google's approach to this split, and thinks big discoveries often come from the smaller buckets.
title: How to Fix Creator Burnout

text: His analogy: content variables are bricks scattered on a floor, and you must reshuffle many times before they form a building. Once one format works, reshuffling again is unlikely to yield an even bigger building.
title: How to Fix Creator Burnout

text: Keeping a 20% bucket of one-step-adjacent experiments keeps creative energy alive, and a 10% wild bucket gives breathing room, while the core stays funded because income stopping would end everything.
title: How to Fix Creator Burnout

text: The market cares about what it cares about and will signal that. That does not mean you skip other projects; it means you may not expect a return from them, and the return may be non-monetary, such as improving your life, which he values as much or more.
title: How to Fix Creator Burnout

text: He thinks adding the 20% and 10% buckets increases total output, not weekly but over a five-year span, because you avoid wanting to quit.
title: How to Fix Creator Burnout

text: The Mr. Beast approach, caring nothing about yourself and enduring constant pain, gets the fastest and biggest results, with the caveat of how long a person can sustain it. He acknowledges it is tempting.
title: How to Fix Creator Burnout

text: People tend to use AI to do foolish things quickly. Current models lean toward agreeing with the user, so people get weak ideas confirmed and then act on them wrongly.
title: AI Just Helps People Do Dumb Things Faster

text: An AI calling an idea good does not make it good. Human judgment is still needed to make sound calls, at least for now.
title: AI Just Helps People Do Dumb Things Faster

text: A good decision can carry more leverage than AI does. He notes some older businessmen who skip AI personally still earn far more than young people using it, so AI is one form of leverage, not a replacement for all leverage.
title: AI Just Helps People Do Dumb Things Faster

text: He compares AI skill to basic tools: five years ago he would not have hired someone unable to use the internet, Excel, Slack, email or Zoom, and he now tests prompting proficiency even more, especially for AI-native roles.
title: AI Just Helps People Do Dumb Things Faster

text: What remains for him is taking responsibility and risk. No AI is currently accountable for anything, nor can it form an LLC, process payments or file taxes, so a human must carry the risk. He is paid for risk and decisions.
title: AI Just Helps People Do Dumb Things Faster

text: Even with AI assisting, the person is still the one who makes the final decision. AI offers suggestions and recommendations, but the human decides.
title: AI Just Helps People Do Dumb Things Faster

text: He describes a way to build a creator ad program outside TikTok Shop: gather micro creators in a group, commit a monthly ad budget only to their ads, and split a portion of it as a pot proportional to spend.
title: How to Use Affiliates to Grow Your Business

text: Getting affiliates or customers to promote comes down mainly to product rather than affiliate strategy. Outside TikTok Shop, he rarely sees an affiliate strategy be the reason something grows.
title: How to Use Affiliates to Grow Your Business

text: Growth comes from a good product with a wrapper of clear incentive around it. He cites Dropbox and PayPal as great products that then added referral incentives.
title: How to Use Affiliates to Grow Your Business

text: Referral programs need four things: right product, right incentive, right timing and right way (low friction). He ranks product first, incentive second, with timing and method tied for third.
title: How to Use Affiliates to Grow Your Business

text: The cost to a promoter is the social capital they spend recommending you, so the product must be very good. A bad restaurant recommendation makes the recommender look bad.
title: How to Use Affiliates to Grow Your Business

text: He notes most products are only mediocre or above average, which is not enough for people to go out of their way to promote them.
title: How to Use Affiliates to Grow Your Business

text: Making people complete many steps to become an affiliate does not work. He thinks TikTok Shop works because it has no friction, people already post, and the incentive is built in.
title: How to Use Affiliates to Grow Your Business

text: He frames referral design like the value equation: make it easy, fast and low risk, with timing added as the question of when to ask.
title: How to Use Affiliates to Grow Your Business

text: The moment of greatest satisfaction is often also the moment to upsell, and he would prefer the upsell then. Ask for a referral when the customer is very satisfied but not deprived of a next thing.
title: How to Use Affiliates to Grow Your Business

text: He cites the summary of about 400 founder interviews by David Senra as two words, focus and patience, and says he stands by it: you do one thing for an extremely long time.
title: \"I Have a Software Business and a Coaching Business. Should I Shut One Down?\"

text: Quality comes from depth rather than moving to the next feature. He compares it to coats of paint: let one layer dry, return with fresh perspective, and look at the problem again.
title: \"I Have a Software Business and a Coaching Business. Should I Shut One Down?\"

text: He says you can roughly judge a solution's quality by how many angles of attack were used on the problem. First passes rarely cover them all, and later passes, like the fifth or eighth, unlock the most.
title: \"I Have a Software Business and a Coaching Business. Should I Shut One Down?\"

text: He thinks most people miss order-of-magnitude outcomes because they split their time and never give a problem enough surface area.
title: \"I Have a Software Business and a Coaching Business. Should I Shut One Down?\"

text: He gives himself only one big project per year. At ACQ all decisions are written in memos so the thinking can be defended; next year's plan was on memo seven and its rollout on memo three.
title: \"I Have a Software Business and a Coaching Business. Should I Shut One Down?\"

text: He says the $100 million launch made $100 million in three days because the plan had been refined for two years, covering risks and contingencies, so nothing went differently than planned.
title: \"I Have a Software Business and a Coaching Business. Should I Shut One Down?\"

text: If you want a nine-figure exit, he says your competitors are doing this depth of thinking, so he would protect it at all costs.
title: \"I Have a Software Business and a Coaching Business. Should I Shut One Down?\"

text: Revenue retention is only one proxy for whether a business keeps making money. A buyer mainly wants confidence it will keep earning and growing, so a business without recurring revenue, like home building, can still sell for a lot.
title: Helping a Criminal Defense Firm Scale to $100M

text: If a business serves a market where new problems keep arising each year, such as collisions for a law firm, that steady inflow of demand can stand in for recurrence when arguing the business will continue.
title: Helping a Criminal Defense Firm Scale to $100M

text: The fastest and likely most valuable path is buying unprofitable firms, layering centralized marketing and sales on each, and adding EBITDA. This is how markets get consolidated, and it makes you a platform that others would buy.
title: Helping a Criminal Defense Firm Scale to $100M

text: Choosing between building from scratch and acquiring comes down to return on capital and effort. Some businesses can be bought for almost nothing, which makes starting from zero pointless.
title: Helping a Criminal Defense Firm Scale to $100M

text: If acquired operators are competent at delivery but weak at marketing and sales, buy them cheaply, run marketing and sales centrally, and keep the operation centralized so quality can be controlled.
title: Helping a Criminal Defense Firm Scale to $100M

text: He does not take creatine. He points out that meat already contains creatine, though he adds that getting the full daily amount from food would take a very large quantity of meat.
title: Why I Don't Take Creatine

text: He says much of fitness follows a bell-curve meme: beginners and experts land on the same simple advice, which is to pick the right parents, eat protein, and lift progressively heavier weight over time, with the elaborate set and rep schemes in between being noise.
title: Why I Don't Take Creatine

text: His own recent testosterone reading was 124, and the highest he has ever measured is 270. He has always been low, well under the commonly cited 300 to 1,000 range, yet he is very muscular.
title: Why I Don't Take Creatine

text: People differ in androgen sensitivity, so the same testosterone or anabolic input produces very different muscle responses. Genetic potential from parents is one factor and responsiveness to anabolic hormones is another, so a sensitive person needs less testosterone to build the same muscle.
title: Why I Don't Take Creatine

text: He calls the standard testosterone ranges arbitrary. His disclaimer is that he is not giving scientific advice. If a man is below 300 but has no symptoms such as erectile dysfunction, morning fatigue, depression, moodiness or unusually low muscle mass, he is probably just androgen sensitive and fine.
title: Why I Don't Take Creatine

text: When content attracts the wrong audience, he thinks the problem may be only the framing, not the whole content approach. Keep the substance and change the wrapper so it speaks from the viewpoint of someone who would buy.
title: I Baited the Hook With the Wrong Bait

text: Even when reframing content for buyers, you still must follow the laws of content and make it interesting. The frame should reflect what a person who will buy your product would experience.
title: I Baited the Hook With the Wrong Bait

text: If your marketing presents you as a practitioner of the service, you attract clients for that service. If you actually sell something else, such as training, your content should attract people who want that.
title: I Baited the Hook With the Wrong Bait

text: To duplicate a salesperson, identify what you do on calls that the hire does not do, and what the hire does that you do not, then have him adopt and drop those behaviors. Roleplay is the way to do it.
title: The Two Questions Every Sales Rep Must Ask

text: Hormozi suggests a price can be so low it drops below a point of marginal cheapness, where buyers stop believing you can deliver and see you as small-time.
title: The Two Questions Every Sales Rep Must Ask

text: If your customers are large businesses making deals worth hundreds of thousands, your fee is a rounding error to them, so payment plans should not matter and a low price hurts credibility.
title: The Two Questions Every Sales Rep Must Ask

text: Hormozi thinks brand is the single most valuable thing to build in a business, because it is persuasion, suggestion or influence delivered at scale. He also believes it is widely misunderstood and is why few people build big things.
title: Brand Is Just Persuasion at Scale

text: The word brand comes from marking cattle. Its purpose is to change how others behave toward the marked animal, since people treat a branded cow differently from an unbranded one depending on who owns it.
title: Brand Is Just Persuasion at Scale

text: Branding is essentially teaching through pairing: linking things people know with things they do not. Repeated enough, people adopt the item, such as a hat, if they like what it has been associated with.
title: Brand Is Just Persuasion at Scale

text: The same message lands differently depending on who says it. A crude tweet works for the richest man in the world because it is read in his context. Hormozi is building context for delivering his messages at scale.
title: Brand Is Just Persuasion at Scale

text: His personal brand is a 10, 15 or 20 year plan, revealed one piece at a time. The book launch is one piece, with another coming next year.
title: Brand Is Just Persuasion at Scale

text: Charging gets a higher share of consumers to follow through, but free reaches far more people, so he says free gives a bigger total impact.
title: Brand Is Just Persuasion at Scale

text: Information, media, software and sometimes tools can be given away free, but intensive hands-on work like flying to people's homes should not be. Serving huge numbers and adding a bar people can clear earns more money, in his view.
title: Brand Is Just Persuasion at Scale

text: He sets his bar deliberately high because he needs only one Facebook-scale deal. About 2,400 companies a month contact him, and in two years he did 22 deals total.
title: Brand Is Just Persuasion at Scale

text: Branding at the top of a market lets a business also capture people beneath that tier, but it cannot capture people above it. Being anchored at the top is therefore an advantage.
title: Helping a Fitness Coach Escape a Broke Niche

text: He tries to build a loop into every business: one-time advertising effort from him brings customers, customers produce testimonials and reviews, and those fuel more advertising. It becomes self-sustaining once testimonials outnumber the ad creative needed.
title: Helping a Fitness Coach Escape a Broke Niche

text: For enterprise-level sales, he says shows and conferences are valuable because all the prospects gather in one place and attendees get elevated status. He describes enterprise sales as typically combining conferences with affiliate partners.
title: Helping a consulting firm doing $15M/year scale

text: Affiliate partners in enterprise work are centers of influence: you do joint-venture style deals where each side covers an element the other does not, sharing deal flow and co-participating in deal work.
title: Helping a consulting firm doing $15M/year scale

text: Warm outreach is always the first thing to do. He jokes that for gym memberships it yields about five dollars a year, showing that adding zeros to the price of what you sell lets the same effort go much further.
title: Helping a consulting firm doing $15M/year scale

text: Cold outbound serves as the front end for the other two channels: use it as the primary action to land conferences and affiliates, then secure the deals with both so a repeatable playbook feeds the funnel.
title: Helping a consulting firm doing $15M/year scale

text: He treats affiliates as a second customer base. In his software company there were three levels: small businesses, agencies above them, and agency influencers above those, requiring three tiers of service.
title: Helping a consulting firm doing $15M/year scale

text: He initially thought he would serve small businesses, then found agencies were who needed the software to serve them, which became major leverage for scaling quickly.
title: Helping a consulting firm doing $15M/year scale

text: To improve affiliate activation, compare partners who send leads with those who do not, on demographics and behaviors, then reverse-engineer those differences into actions in a regular activation cadence.
title: Helping a consulting firm doing $15M/year scale

text: Hormozi says medical practices commonly struggle because reception staff lack lead-handling skills; they need a dedicated sales position, even if selling in healthcare feels uncomfortable.
title: Why Doctors Need a Sales Role

text: He concluded you should always hire to cover the smallest skill deficiency. Kindness is also a skill, just a harder one to teach than something like setting calls, so the right hire depends on which gap is cheaper to train.
title: The One Hiring Rule That Fixes Almost Every Bad Hire

text: If the skill gap is large, such as a healthcare CFO with big M&A experience, training a nice outsider costs too much. Better to hire the experienced person and coach the behavior gaps, choosing the highest return per hire.
title: The One Hiring Rule That Fixes Almost Every Bad Hire

text: No hire fits perfectly, so you need a bridge over the skill gap. How quickly someone learns determines how fast that gap closes, which is where raw intelligence matters.
title: The One Hiring Rule That Fixes Almost Every Bad Hire

text: He notes that top firms like Google, Goldman Sachs and Bain recruit raw talent from elite schools and train them through an 8-week boot camp. He has put growing weight on learning potential as his training improved.
title: The One Hiring Rule That Fixes Almost Every Bad Hire

text: Given equal soft skills, he would pick a smart hard-working HR person with 3 years over a 10-year veteran. It takes about 4 months to match the veteran, then the smarter one keeps growing, giving better overall return.
title: The One Hiring Rule That Fixes Almost Every Bad Hire

text: He suspects Bezos attracted people smarter than himself because he is an admirable leader. Admirable character traits plus a mission people believe in help draw top talent.
title: The One Hiring Rule That Fixes Almost Every Bad Hire

text: The talent he can attract to Acquisition.com differs from what Gym Launch could attract. The opportunity and external brand matter, since top candidates have many options and must be sold on joining.
title: The One Hiring Rule That Fixes Almost Every Bad Hire

text: The higher the role level, the more the dynamic shifts from candidates coming to you toward you courting them. Low-level roles may need less courting.
title: The One Hiring Rule That Fixes Almost Every Bad Hire

text: Three things to figure out: who you sell to, how much you charge them, and how you will reach them.
title: Helping a Software Business Break Into Enterprise Sales

text: If a product already has a clear enterprise use case, Hormozi would hunt whales rather than minnows.
title: Helping a Software Business Break Into Enterprise Sales

text: In a sales conversation, name the biggest number you can think of and watch the reaction. You can always come down but never go up; the worst feeling is a quick yes to a price that was too low.
title: Helping a Software Business Break Into Enterprise Sales

text: He thinks the pain of one-off contracts and endless contingencies comes from the price being too low to care about; at a high enough price you would accept those terms.
title: Helping a Software Business Break Into Enterprise Sales

text: Pricing decides who can afford you, and that in turn decides what selling friction is worth bearing; it is not worth it at 10 grand a month but is at a million a year.
title: Helping a Software Business Break Into Enterprise Sales

text: When the delivery or operations differ materially between customer types, it is important to focus on one avatar, because otherwise it is like running two different businesses, which he says you do not want.
title: \"Should I Chase Bigger Clients or More Clients?\"

text: Giving a community away free is fine, as long as you already have a plan for what you will sell afterwards.
title: How to Make Money as a Coach in the Finance Niche

text: He thinks Dave Ramsey became a guru without being labeled one, because in personal savings nobody disputes the claim: if you cut spending by $2,000 a month, you have $2,000 more, no math to prove.
title: How to Make Money as a Coach in the Finance Niche

text: Promising to help someone earn more carries risk because they may not do it, while savings claims are easier to make since spending less leaves the difference in hand.
title: How to Make Money as a Coach in the Finance Niche

text: He describes Ramsey's business as four revenue streams: media, an app for saving money, coaching, and courses plus events. He cites publicly stated figures of roughly 300 million top line, with media around 120 million.
title: How to Make Money as a Coach in the Finance Niche

text: Give away the information and sell implementation. He suggests remote semi-private coaching, such as one coach to six clients, which can earn about as much as one-on-one while keeping people accountable.
title: How to Make Money as a Coach in the Finance Niche

text: After a remote group, you can add an in-person experience as another paid tier.
title: How to Make Money as a Coach in the Finance Niche

text: The same information can sell for different prices depending on medium: free or PDF is cheapest, a live eight-week remote program is worth more, and an in-person classroom is worth even more.
title: How to Make Money as a Coach in the Finance Niche

text: He thinks in-person is worth more partly because attendance makes consumption and action more likely, and mainly because people get questions answered in real time, which addresses a major concern about whether they will get the result.
title: How to Make Money as a Coach in the Finance Niche

text: Consider the medium you deliver information in; you can put paywalls around the same concepts by changing the delivery mechanism.
title: How to Make Money as a Coach in the Finance Niche

text: Hormozi thinks a business that runs both catering and a restaurant will probably need to pick one of them, and he says catering looks like the more scalable option.
title: Helping a $1.2M BBQ Caterer Pick a Lane

text: A restaurant is limited by its four walls relatively quickly, whereas catering is not, and a lot of catering in one local area can still generate a lot of money.
title: Helping a $1.2M BBQ Caterer Pick a Lane

text: Seasonal volatility is part of a catering business and will not really change. The aim is to make a large profit in the busy season to cover the slow season. Volatility alone does not mean the business is broken.
title: Helping a $1.2M BBQ Caterer Pick a Lane

text: For home-services companies at roughly the scale of five sales reps, he says you need an internal sales academy: a recruiting machine that mirrors the customer-facing pipeline of lead gen, nurture, sales, onboarding, retention and ascension.
title: Helping a $20M Fence Company Scale to $50M

text: Just as a business spends money reliably on demand generation, it needs to spend reliably on supply generation for salespeople. He says the two must exist as parallel functions inside the business.
title: Helping a $20M Fence Company Scale to $50M

text: He says you should know your recruiting funnel numbers the way you know ad numbers: applicant generation, nurture, interview, onboarding, and retention stats, tracked like CTR, opt-in rate, close rate and show rate.
title: Helping a $20M Fence Company Scale to $50M

text: Hormozi says decision-making is among the highest-leverage things a person can do, and he guesses Musk's edge is finding the minimum context needed for an accurate decision, then spotting problems and correcting course quickly.
title: Lessons from Elon Musk

text: Hormozi does not think raw horsepower can be trained, but believes skills can be, and he describes skill as almost a reallocation of horsepower. He admits he is unsure how much of this ability is skill.
title: Lessons from Elon Musk

text: The one constant in Hormozi's business career is that the quality of talent he brings in has only risen, and his income has correlated directly with the quality of people he brings in and what he is willing to pay them.
title: Lessons from Elon Musk

text: Hormozi sees a limiting belief in how much people think they can pay someone. He points to the reported multibillion-dollar deal for a famous designer as proof that a price exists for the best in the world at anything.
title: Lessons from Elon Musk

text: Hormozi repeats a principle he attributes to Leila: avoid solving the same problem twice. If a fix takes three months, being one month in without results does not mean it failed; it may just need its full 90 days.
title: Why Nobody Good Applies to Your Job Post

text: When you plan to grow volume many times over, work out how much faster you must add people. Twelve times the volume with one hire every three to four months means roughly one hire per week, so build that acquisition machine early.
title: Why Nobody Good Applies to Your Job Post

text: For a role where you train people from scratch, Hormozi says to look broadly across trades groups rather than only existing specialists, since everyone congregates online somewhere such as groups, forums, associations, discords or school communities.
title: Why Nobody Good Applies to Your Job Post

text: To triage many applicants, run job ads on sites like Indeed and Facebook Marketplace into group interviews. Assume only about 30% of booked people show, so book roughly 30 per session, with one or two sessions weekly.
title: Why Nobody Good Applies to Your Job Post

text: In a group interview you can sense a person's vibe within a minute or two, then follow with a one-on-one. This lets you sort through a huge number of applications for a low-skilled role.
title: Why Nobody Good Applies to Your Job Post

text: Recruiting talent is its own machine that must be built deliberately. If acquisition of customers is already proven, the team must still multiply talent acquisition to match growth.
title: Why Nobody Good Applies to Your Job Post

text: He rarely speaks on stages because promoters use his face to sell, and attendees then buy whatever the event host sells. He has no association with that person and no time to vet them, so speaking is not an endorsement.
title: Most Entrepreneurs Are Too Arrogant to Focus

text: After about an hour talking with eight or nine entrepreneurs at Yogurtland, he saw that all of them were distracted and running several ventures at once. This led him to rebuild his talk around focus.
title: Most Entrepreneurs Are Too Arrogant to Focus

text: Any of several business options could work, but only the one you actually work on will. So you must commit to a single one.
title: Most Entrepreneurs Are Too Arrogant to Focus

text: He calls it arrogant to put 25% effort into four things while competing in a real market. Someone giving 100% to one thing will not be beaten by your fractional effort.
title: Most Entrepreneurs Are Too Arrogant to Focus

text: He likes defining commitment as the elimination of alternatives. To be committed, you must cut off other options, and he links this to the Latin root of decide, which means to kill off.
title: Most Entrepreneurs Are Too Arrogant to Focus

text: He compares focus to pruning a tree: soil nutrients, minutes in a day, and attention are all limited, so you must choose what to cut and where to allocate them.
title: Most Entrepreneurs Are Too Arrogant to Focus

text: Staying on one project for a long time lets you peel back layers and gain depth of understanding that surface-level work across many things never gives. Spread thin, you only react and put out fires, so progress stalls.
title: Most Entrepreneurs Are Too Arrogant to Focus

text: He cites Warren Buffett as saying the difference between successful and really successful people is that the really successful say no to almost everything.
title: Most Entrepreneurs Are Too Arrogant to Focus

text: Repeat the same title sequence at each level, so employees are always roughly three to six months from another promotion. This keeps career advancement visible whenever someone might be thinking of leaving.
title: Scaling a $50M Pest Control Company to $1B

text: Alternate title bumps with perks. A title alone works for some people, but pairing it with something like a better parking spot, no Saturday nights, a choice of calendar, or a better truck makes promotions feel more rewarding.
title: Scaling a $50M Pest Control Company to $1B

text: At orientation, show new hires where they are now and where they will be if they hit each milestone. Tie promotions to objective measures, such as total volume of deliveries combined with a count of five-star reviews.
title: Scaling a $50M Pest Control Company to $1B

text: Place the first milestone, such as twenty five-star reviews to reach junior plus, very early, because he says the biggest turnover happens in that initial stretch.
title: Scaling a $50M Pest Control Company to $1B

text: When people attack you, their statements are often projections that are not real. He notes that a relative telling him she did not want his life prompted the answer that she should simply not live it.
title: My Family's Intervention Went Horribly Wrong

text: A mentor taught him that when someone says you are a terrible person, you can just reply that they are right. They then have nothing to say, and you move on. He sees it as accepting their idea of you.
title: My Family's Intervention Went Horribly Wrong

text: He says he became very angry during a family intervention where relatives, believing he was misguided, gathered to talk to him. He thinks they genuinely wanted to help rather than being envious.
title: My Family's Intervention Went Horribly Wrong

text: Improv has one rule, do not punk the game, meaning refuse to make an allowed move. He says this can be destructive to those playing, yet sometimes constructive for the person doing it.
title: My Family's Intervention Went Horribly Wrong

text: He says people uncomfortable with emotions in a meaningful conversation may turn scathing, mocking or laugh to avoid discomfort. He calls this punking the game in a destructive way, both externally and internally.
title: My Family's Intervention Went Horribly Wrong

text: Refusing to play by rules someone else set, in a game you never agreed to, is the best protection against entering a situation you do not want. He says wealth affords this.
title: My Family's Intervention Went Horribly Wrong

text: Once a business earns enough profit, owners should think about return on invested capital: giving up a slice of profit, such as 200,000 out of 2.5 million, to fund a hire who could bring in an extra million.
title: Helping an Online Coaching Business Scale to $50M/Year

text: He still believes the biggest arbitrage opportunities in business today are in talent.
title: Helping an Online Coaching Business Scale to $50M/Year

text: Growing revenue without upgrading people builds talent debt. He wants to shrink the gap between current team and needed team as fast as possible to pay it down. Businesses can take on financial, technical or management debt instead.
title: Helping an Online Coaching Business Scale to $50M/Year

text: Paying people less to save money always costs something; you end up paying with whatever you care about least.
title: Helping an Online Coaching Business Scale to $50M/Year

text: For businesses below $1 million, he says apparently erratic acquisition results commonly reflect too little activity to produce consistent outcomes.
title: 200 Cold Calls, 2 Customers: That's Not Luck, That's Math

text: He describes presenting sales alternatives so that one looks clearly preferable, steering the buyer toward the intended selection.
title: 200 Cold Calls, 2 Customers: That's Not Luck, That's Math

text: When a business struggles to get customers, he treats it as a demand problem. Expanding the existing business is much preferable to launching a direct-to-consumer line, which adds risk and distraction while old objections remain.
title: \"My Industry Is Being Bought Up. Do I Start Over?\"

text: Feeling rushed comes from believing you fell behind, and that belief often arises because you are in a different season than the people you compare yourself to. In his framing, you are not behind, just early.
title: You're Not Behind. You're Just Early

text: The typical mistake is comparing someone else's output to yours without comparing the inputs behind it. His example: a podcaster asking why their show is not like Rogan's, when Rogan has about ten more years of episodes.
title: You're Not Behind. You're Just Early

text: He thinks most people making this judgment error are earlier in their careers, so they are usually simply early rather than failing.
title: You're Not Behind. You're Just Early

text: He says people should compare themselves to top figures, using himself and Elon as an example, in order to see the size of the discrepancy.
title: You're Not Behind. You're Just Early

text: Without promotion nobody knows your offer and you earn nothing, so you must let people know it exists first. Scale the promotion only once you know the product is good; early on, accept it will be weaker.
title: How to Build a Good Product

text: Free samples lower the stakes, especially for your personal reputation. If nobody will even take the free version, that is useful feedback that people probably will not pay for it.
title: How to Build a Good Product

text: Giving something away can pay off in three ways: the person becomes a paying customer, leaves a review or testimonial, or refers another customer to you.
title: How to Build a Good Product

text: If you think your offering is poor, give it free and ask for honest feedback on how to improve it. Ask unhappy people for private feedback rather than a public review, then keep iterating.
title: How to Build a Good Product

text: You will not get it right the first time. Nearly every entrepreneur, apart from rare exceptions like Bezos and Zuckerberg, has a trail of earlier attempts that each taught lessons applied to the next business.
title: How to Build a Good Product

text: He sees marketplace friction as serving to build who you become, which he views as the asset that ultimately matters, since accumulated results will not matter in the end.
title: How to Build a Good Product

text: If your product is weak, give it to more people, ask for feedback, and ask what it would take to be less bad; eventually it becomes good.
title: How to Build a Good Product

text: When asking referral sources for more business, he prefers asking which specific people they saw this week would be a good fit, rather than asking whether they have any. He calls it small wording training that still matters.
title: “Why Isn’t My Business Scaling?”

text: Hormozi says media buying is becoming a more commoditized skill, so he would hand it off first.
title: $16M a Year and Still a One-Man Show

text: He advises building a self-feeding loop where the business's normal activities produce the creative that fuels it, keeping the business centered on customers rather than the founder. He says he has done this in every business he owns.
title: $16M a Year and Still a One-Man Show

text: Hormozi suggests an unlockable digital bonus available in a customer's first 7 days, small but attractive, so customers earn it by sending a video. Each such mechanism acts as a creative cadence.
title: $16M a Year and Still a One-Man Show

text: A referral push in a community, monthly or quarterly, can be aimed less at gaining referrals than at getting people to post publicly, since the posts themselves become creative.
title: $16M a Year and Still a One-Man Show

text: He says almost no e-commerce companies reach $100M a year without a brand. Smash-and-grab operators exist but tend to come and go, vanishing overnight.
title: $16M a Year and Still a One-Man Show

text: For a much bigger move, Hormozi says to bet on one to three creators or authorities who embody the brand's values, whitelist their ads, and use their leverage to recruit micro and nano influencers beneath them.
title: $16M a Year and Still a One-Man Show

text: He notes smash-and-grab doctor brands often turn a doctor into a celebrity, using the white coat's credibility and having them read the VSLs. He contrasts that with building something lasting.
title: $16M a Year and Still a One-Man Show

text: Hormozi says direct response is now a game of massive creative. Ads once targeted broad audiences like 45-year-old women; now the aim is capturing a hundred small ponds rather than the ocean.
title: $16M a Year and Still a One-Man Show

text: He explains Meta's Andromeda update tries to make all content, ads included, feel relevant, and AI can read what ads say and perceive videos and backgrounds. He says national campaigns are gone, replaced by hundreds of micro ads.
title: $16M a Year and Still a One-Man Show

text: Hormozi says advertisers newer to Meta may see lower cost per result but burn through creative quickly: a piece runs efficiently for a shorter period, then cost jumps, so the machine needs constant micro creative.
title: $16M a Year and Still a One-Man Show

text: When a business is showing signs of the wrong customer or too many customers, Hormozi says he would not add complexity to the business.
title: \"Should I Turn My Service Into Done-With-You?\"

text: He likes a team bonus pot that pays everyone once the whole team passes a shared target, so teammates push to help the lowest performer improve instead of competing against each other.
title: How I Give Bonuses to Sales Teams

text: He wants the team's enemy to sit outside the company, such as competitors who do a poor job for customers, so staff stand side by side and try to outsell those rivals.
title: How I Give Bonuses to Sales Teams

text: His earlier content was cutthroat, with the view that salespeople should compete hard against each other. Over time, with bigger teams and more revenue, he shifted and thinks the cooperative approach builds a much better culture.
title: How I Give Bonuses to Sales Teams

text: If he had to keep one of four skills, it would be the ability to give people directions that lead to a good result. Martha Stewart's instructions worked for years, so her audience trusted her when she asked them to buy.
title: Why People Don’t Listen to You (And How to Fix It)

text: Many people stuck scaling ads past a certain daily spend are stuck because of who they target. The reverse pyramid from Eugene Schwartz runs problem aware, solution aware, product aware, then most aware, usually existing customers.
title: Why People Don’t Listen to You (And How to Fix It)

text: Most creators make ads and content only for a narrow, lower-awareness slice, such as people who already know about affiliate marketing. Going broader on the pyramid gives a much larger addressable market, and curiosity is what captures that wider group.
title: Why People Don’t Listen to You (And How to Fix It)

text: Attention captured too low in the funnel makes too few people find the message relevant. Downstream products such as info products or coaching come after the attention is captured.
title: Why People Don’t Listen to You (And How to Fix It)

text: Start with unaware people using curiosity and relatable questions, not the label of what you do or your leaderboard rank. Introduce credentials once they are curious. Tactical videos are fine but he expects them to get less reach.
title: Why People Don’t Listen to You (And How to Fix It)

text: Curiosity sits at the top for unaware people. Beneath it are problem-aware people, who do not know what you do but know they dislike their situation, and pain-based hooks work strongly on them.
title: Why People Don’t Listen to You (And How to Fix It)

text: For a problem-aware person, suggest the problem may be the opportunity they chose, not them. Use an analogy, then match their problems to your solution.
title: Why People Don’t Listen to You (And How to Fix It)

text: Hormozi notes that when different leaders would run two initiatives, they can often be done at the same time. He says he does not normally recommend running concurrent efforts, but here the leadership differs.
title: Move the Factory or Fix Sales First?

text: When deciding whether to do two big projects together, Hormozi checks whether capital is the constraint, which is why he asked about profitability and what share of yearly free cash flow the move would consume.
title: Move the Factory or Fix Sales First?

text: Hormozi separates one-off roles from repeated roles because he handles them differently, and he asks which type a founder is trying to fill before advising on delegation.
title: \"I'm Still Working at 11PM. How Do I Let Go?\"

text: For one-off roles, he prefers buying over building: he will pay a recruiter a premium to bring in someone experienced who has done the job many times, since recruiters already have the network.
title: \"I'm Still Working at 11PM. How Do I Let Go?\"

text: For repeated roles in a service business, he sees the core economic arbitrage as buying talent for less, adding your own special sauce, and charging more for the result.
title: \"I'm Still Working at 11PM. How Do I Let Go?\"

text: Because of that arbitrage, all repeated roles need an in-house university. Training effectiveness must rise and cost to train must fall, since training five people costs almost the same as training one.
title: \"I'm Still Working at 11PM. How Do I Let Go?\"

text: A common expansion pattern: owners split up to launch a second and third site, the new one underperforms and the original slips, so liabilities double while profit stays flat or falls, leaving several barely profitable stores.
title: You're the reason your margins look good.

text: His litmus test before expanding: the business must be able to grow without the owners for 6 months, with a general manager who is treated as an owner.
title: You're the reason your margins look good.

text: The general manager trade is that the owner's phone does not ring and the manager earns a share of profit; if it rings, he wants the money back.
title: You're the reason your margins look good.

text: Owners should write down the many small things they do, as observable behaviors someone else can do, then divide that list into daily tasks for the manager and the team.
title: You're the reason your margins look good.

text: Nail the model at the first location before scaling, rather than iterating the model location after location; a wrong location or market can leave you stuck for years and lowers cash flow.
title: You're the reason your margins look good.

text: If a shop runs profitably for six months without you, more options open: open more shops, buy failing ones and flip them, license, or franchise.
title: You're the reason your margins look good.

text: Because he would not know whether something else was better, the worry about missing out does not bother him. He believes he would adapt to any hypothetically better experience and drift back to his baseline anyway.
title: \"Are You Wasting Your Life by Working So Much?\"

text: He does not think finding out about more things is the path to happiness. He points to people who never leave their tribe and are happier than most of us.
title: \"Are You Wasting Your Life by Working So Much?\"

text: His own way of living is doing what he wants for as much of his day as he can, with the people he wants to do it with.
title: \"Are You Wasting Your Life by Working So Much?\"

text: When family says he works too much, he sees it as their projection: their idea of work is negative, and they would prefer he live the way they want. He answers that he lives his life his way, and that is enough.
title: \"Are You Wasting Your Life by Working So Much?\"

text: Output per unit of time rises the moment you begin working, which makes simply beginning the single greatest hack for everything else you do in work, since starting puts you in the mood to work.
title: Why Your Brain Hates Finishing Tasks

text: For big mental tasks like a major content piece, he needs about five minutes inside the work to get a lay of the land. He used to spend hours delaying those first five minutes, and has since compressed that gap heavily.
title: Why Your Brain Hates Finishing Tasks

text: Rather than finishing work at a clean stopping point, he suggests stopping partway through a sentence. The unfinished thread creates an open loop that pulls you back, which he links to the Zeigarnik effect.
title: Why Your Brain Hates Finishing Tasks

text: Hormozi recounts an acquired business where pricing research supported doubling the price. Convincing its founder required nine calls; conversion subsequently increased, which he attributes to the original price undermining credibility.
title: Helping an Online Service Business Fix Their Broken Offer

text: Doing or saying something truthful that changes someone's behavior is not manipulation. He calls it persuasion. Deception, meaning saying something untrue, is what he treats as the more problematic part.
title: Where's the Line Between Persuasion and Manipulation?

text: A first rule of marketing for his team: state the facts and tell the truth. If the truth is not compelling on its own, find a way to make the true thing more compelling.
title: Where's the Line Between Persuasion and Manipulation?

text: Rather than claim to be the greatest marketer ever, which he cannot verify, he would cite a checkable result: a launch that did $106 million in a weekend using methods from his free books. Specific proof is honest and persuasive.
title: Where's the Line Between Persuasion and Manipulation?

text: He places little weight on intent as the line between helping and manipulating, because good intentions can produce bad outcomes and bad intentions can produce good ones. He cares more about learnable skills that raise the odds of action.
title: Where's the Line Between Persuasion and Manipulation?

text: In the short term, you raise someone's motivation by changing how valuable a reinforcer seems, often by simply bringing up the true cost of inaction that they have pushed out of mind.
title: Where's the Line Between Persuasion and Manipulation?

text: Example he gives: telling someone more than 50 pounds overweight that it costs about 5 years of life, possibly meaning not meeting great-grandkids. If that matters to them, the true fact may push them to act.
title: Where's the Line Between Persuasion and Manipulation?

text: He thinks teaching, selling, persuasion and manipulation all share the same core: doing or saying something to get another person to act. He notes that this is also the purpose of communication.
title: Where's the Line Between Persuasion and Manipulation?

text: Hormozi says a million Instagram followers and 200,000 TikTok followers are not worth the same. He notes the caller has probably already seen the difference in value between the two audiences.
title: You need to post more.

text: Every deal carries risk, speed and ease. Buyers want the outcome with as little risk as possible, delivered fast and with little effort, so these are the levers of value people pay for.
title: The Best Offer for a Construction Company

text: For a home builder, he suggests an on-time, on-budget guarantee: finish on schedule and on budget or give the customer the builder's profit, expressed as roughly 20% of the deal, and pair it with a 20% price increase.
title: The Best Offer for a Construction Company

text: The guarantee is conditioned on the customer not changing their mind. Since customers usually do change things, the builder rarely has to pay out, yet the guarantee still helps close the deal.
title: The Best Offer for a Construction Company

text: Pitch the premium by comparison: custom homes often run 10 to 20% over budget, and a 15% overrun on a $2 million home is $300,000, so a $250,000 fee is already offset by the savings.
title: The Best Offer for a Construction Company

text: Add the speed argument: other builders are typically 3 to 9 months late, and a half-year delay costs the owner appreciation on the home. He also cites better appraisal versus cost when building the right features.
title: The Best Offer for a Construction Company

text: Frame the higher price as paying now rather than paying more later: cheaper builders cost more through overruns, delays and inefficiency, so customers pay in different ways anyway.
title: The Best Offer for a Construction Company

text: Tell the customer that changes are welcome but void the guarantee, using an absurd example like gold toilets that add sourcing time and cost. This keeps the builder from being held to it.
title: The Best Offer for a Construction Company

text: Even if a payout happens, he argues the excess earned on the other roughly 95% of deals more than covers it.
title: The Best Offer for a Construction Company

text: When asked how to pick one sales channel and how long to test it, Hormozi says he would reject the premise of the question and prefers the owner stick with one channel and do more of it.

text: Hormozi suggests the risk-adjusted first move is to scale a channel already producing customers, such as going from one local event a week to several, before starting channels never tried.
title: Helping a Junk Removal Company Scale

text: He says that until roughly three million dollars a year in revenue, owners must learn everything themselves, because nobody truly skilled can yet be afforded. He calls this the math behind why that stage is so painful.
title: Helping a Junk Removal Company Scale

text: His illustration: a two million dollar business at 30% margin makes about 600,000 a year; after reinvesting some, perhaps 350,000 in free cash remains, and the owner's living costs leave maybe 200,000.

text: Looking back, his good days share three things: he worked hard on something he felt was worth doing, he exercised, and he spent time with people he enjoys. Doing all three means the day was good.
title: Most People Abhor Work Because They Misunderstand It

title: Most People Abhor Work Because They Misunderstand It

text: Work he enjoys is the kind where you lose track of time, and it is usually challenging, because easy work turns boring. He links this to why uncertainty about whether something will succeed matters.

text: Typical affiliate deals that give 20% back to anyone who sends a customer fail because nobody cares about 20% of what you have. The affiliate needs a grand slam offer instead.
title: Helping a Lead-Gen Company Create a Reverse Affiliate Offer

title: Helping a Lead-Gen Company Create a Reverse Affiliate Offer

text: In a reverse affiliate deal, your cost per qualified lead equals your cost of delivery. If delivery costs about 200 dollars, that is the price of a qualified customer on your calendar, and a customer who paid 10,000 is more qualified than one who paid nothing.

title: Building a $46M Company

text: He recommends attempting sales before studying sales material: practical failures reveal specific gaps and give later instruction a concrete situation to address.

title: Building a $46M Company

text: He believes the best moment to sell is when a customer initially feels most excited about the desired outcome, before experiencing the effort required to achieve it.

text: If you already know you won't do business long-term with a partner, he would start by asking whether they feel the partnership is working, then, if they agree it isn't, propose a shared plan to exit.

title: \"My Business Partner Has a Huge Ego\"

title: \"My Business Partner Has a Huge Ego\"

title: The Difference Between Guilt and Shame

text: He mentally places nearly everything near death as a perspective tool. Since everyone dies and is forgotten, he thinks people who insult you are irrelevant to your goals and outcomes.

text: When insulted, he checks whether the critic is right about something he dislikes in himself. If so, the right response is to agree, which he says is the frightening part.
