text: He says the acquisition AI tool, as it exists today, does not do the outreach work itself. Multi-step workflows involving third-party tools fall outside what it covers.
title: \"How Can I Use AI to Get More Customers?\" | Hormozi Hotline

text: He agrees that AI can help by producing assets such as VSLs placed between calls or texts, which add trust so prospects are more willing to call or text.
title: \"How Can I Use AI to Get More Customers?\" | Hormozi Hotline

text: He believes people online, and humans generally, will keep moving toward whatever source seems most truthful. Edited content can be faked, so he sees live content as gaining ground.
title: Live Streaming Is the Future of Content

text: To his knowledge, AI cannot live stream at present, so he calls live streaming the last human domain. He would fully bet its growth continues, and thinks it is a good idea.
title: Live Streaming Is the Future of Content

text: He suggests structuring live streams so portions can be clipped out, with the full stream serving as long form content and the clips as short form.
title: Live Streaming Is the Future of Content

text: He ran a full-time career streaming himself sleeping, with viewers paying to mess with him. It reached about a million followers in a year, and he later did IRL streams doing whatever paying viewers asked.
title: Live Streaming Is the Future of Content

text: He built backpacks to stream in public back when the tech did not exist for it, and notes it has since become a huge industry.
title: Live Streaming Is the Future of Content

text: Before adding new projects, a scattered owner should remove what consumes their time. He suggests they likely have many half-built bridges, so starting more efforts is the wrong move.
title: Helping a MedSpa Business Owner Scale

text: If profit were only about 400k including the owner's pay, he would see real business issues and could not yet afford extra hires. Roughly 30% margins on seller discretionary earnings mean the business is okay.
title: Helping a MedSpa Business Owner Scale

text: He tests whether sales is the constraint by asking if an extra 300k in profit would change the owner's life. If not, sales is not the bottleneck; the owner's time is, so add manpower.
title: Helping a MedSpa Business Owner Scale

text: To decide between more headcount, more skilled headcount, or doing fewer things, he asks which activities are most profitable and how the owner's time splits, seeking the highest use of their time.
title: Helping a MedSpa Business Owner Scale

text: Hormozi says that as a founder hands off tedious work, more tasks will pile up, and the founder keeps the more important, valuable work while someone else takes the rest.
title: Helping a Dropshipping Company Build a Brand

text: Hormozi suggests VAs and project-based workers are well suited to tedious tasks that do not feel high leverage or high value to the founder.
title: Helping a Dropshipping Company Build a Brand

text: Only around 1 or 2 percent of your audience sees a given organic post, and many people who know you have not followed. Running ads reaches that much larger group beyond those who see organic posts.
title: \"How do ads work?\"

text: People who earn a modest amount from organic content can usually reach 25 or more by paying to promote their content with ads, according to what he has observed.
title: \"How do ads work?\"

text: For an ad strategy when you already have media, run your best organic content as ads to your audience, plus a small batch of direct-to-camera clips that simply state the offer.
title: \"How do ads work?\"

text: He suggests roughly 35 short pieces of content per week serving as ads, plus about five to 10 straight direct-to-camera offer videos.
title: \"How do ads work?\"

text: The three most common ManyChat automations are new follower, story call to action (replying with a keyword), and post comments (commenting a keyword). Each triggers a DM that can run if-then logic and collect information.
title: \"How do ads work?\"

text: Keyword comment or reply triggers work orders of magnitude better for lead generation than telling people to click the link in bio. A normal video gets 1,000 to 2,000 comments, while a link-in-bio video gets about 50 clicks.
title: \"How do ads work?\"

text: When customers have just paid a large upfront sum for a big project, a recurring monthly fee looks small by comparison, so there is a lot of room to raise it. He frames it as insurance on what they just bought.
title: Helping a Home Service Business 3x Profit Without Getting More Clients

text: He describes a Bezos page, paraphrasing Dawkins, that applies biological reversion to the environment to life: surroundings push you to blend in and dilute yourself. Bezos calls the pull natural and inevitable, yet worth fighting even though it is hard.
title: How to Think About Your Own Insignificance Without Losing Your Ambition

text: He likens this pull to a cosmic regression to the mean and says it is inevitable for everyone.
title: How to Think About Your Own Insignificance Without Losing Your Ambition

text: He deliberately pictures humbling things, like worms eating his body or an animal killing him and making a meal of him. Doing so lowers the sense that his goals are all-important and gives him a big exhale.
title: How to Think About Your Own Insignificance Without Losing Your Ambition

text: A free community functions as a lead magnet: it attracts people into the business’s audience and should make them more likely to purchase its product.
title: Free vs Paid Communities: You’re Doing It Wrong

text: He proposes splitting a webinar or sales video into five modules: an introduction, three stories addressing doubts about oneself, other people, and external circumstances, then an offer invitation. Stories should feature similar people achieving the audience’s desired result.
title: Free vs Paid Communities: You’re Doing It Wrong

text: Looking back, the past seems smoother than it was because we know how the story ended. Using the stock market's last 15 years as an example, he says this hindsight hides the dips and uncertainty people lived through.
title: How to Deal With the Stress of Entrepreneurship

text: He finds it a helpful framework that a current terrible-feeling situation always either resolves or you die, and in both cases there is nothing left to worry about.
title: How to Deal With the Stress of Entrepreneurship

text: He argues that what makes entrepreneurship hard is not tactics. Learning things like setting up a landing page is a knowledge deficiency that will not hurt you; unpredictable crises are what cause stress.
title: How to Deal With the Stress of Entrepreneurship

text: He gives examples of the stressful stuff: a manager leaving with half the team, a payment processor shutting down, and leads arriving while payroll cannot be made.
title: How to Deal With the Stress of Entrepreneurship

text: He reminds himself that the future is likely to be better and the past was not as good as remembered, and he sees this as a hopeful message for entrepreneurs.
title: How to Deal With the Stress of Entrepreneurship

text: You cannot pursue every opportunity. He says you effectively have to decline every opportunity so that the one you choose becomes worth pursuing.
title: The Price of Building Something Big

text: He says he sat through massive multi-year plateaus because he wanted to pursue every single thing. His conclusion is that you must trade novelty for loyalty to the business.
title: The Price of Building Something Big

text: He thinks business is like a fine wine: you understand it at a deeper level as years and seasons pass, and he believes chasing new ventures means missing that depth.
title: The Price of Building Something Big

text: To estimate a business's hypothetical maximum, multiply units sold per month by lifetime value. Example: 10 units monthly at 5K price with 5% churn gives 100K LTV each, so about 1 million monthly, or 12 million yearly.
title: \"I Run a $7M/year Agency. How Do I Sell the Company?\"

text: When revenue is projected to grow without changes, make sure both existing revenue and the incoming additional revenue drop to the bottom line, meaning margin work matters.
title: \"I Run a $7M/year Agency. How Do I Sell the Company?\"

text: His rule of thumb for service businesses he runs is an 80% gross margin.
title: \"I Run a $7M/year Agency. How Do I Sell the Company?\"

text: He says to throw out industry averages, since most people are mediocre at their business and measuring against that benchmark only anchors you to lower standards.
title: \"I Run a $7M/year Agency. How Do I Sell the Company?\"

text: Hormozi argues that reporting hierarchies compress information at successive management levels, contributing to poor decisions by leaders distant from the work.
title: Helping a Dental Marketing Agency Scale From $10M to $20M

text: Hormozi thinks much of the human work across an agency's customer journey can be automated, freeing employees to perform more valuable tasks.
title: Helping a Dental Marketing Agency Scale From $10M to $20M

text: Hormozi believes a services company should generally be able to remain viable because most of its costs vary with activity.
title: Helping a Dental Marketing Agency Scale From $10M to $20M

text: Hormozi believes paid advertising and content have fully merged already, and his paid team and media team now operate as a single team.
title: Ads Have Changed Forever

text: His company produces around 450 pieces of content per week, lets the algorithm show which ones perform best, and then runs those winners as ads.
title: Ads Have Changed Forever

text: About a year earlier his team added calls to action at the end of content used as ads. Now they skip that and just place a banner overlay inviting a click.
title: Ads Have Changed Forever

text: If the content was good, viewers will take whatever action the platform offers, so the same piece can lead to a workshop, roadmap or books as long as it is relevant to the topic.
title: Ads Have Changed Forever

text: Deeper work-related content from the middle or bottom of the funnel, especially content with many saves, suits being run as ads. A broad philosophical talk fits less well when leading to a book.
title: Ads Have Changed Forever

text: To choose ad candidates, look at the content with the most saves rather than the most follows or views, and try running those as your ads.
title: Ads Have Changed Forever

text: He says that with Andromeda you lose very little by running a bad ad. If you only make around 20 pieces a week, put all 20 up as ads.
title: Ads Have Changed Forever

text: A perfect platform would have no ads, so if you make every ad look like content, the platform favors you. Running content as ads aligns with platform objectives.
title: Ads Have Changed Forever

text: Copy gets stronger through specificity. Broad phrases like lose weight fast trigger banner blindness because people have heard such claims many times and learned to tune them out.
title: Specificity Gets Past the Spam Blocker in People's Brains

text: People have a mental spam blocker much like the one on a computer, built up after being let down by dishonest claims. He says the way past it is to be specific.
title: Specificity Gets Past the Spam Blocker in People's Brains

text: Replace a vague statement about entrepreneurs working harder with concrete sacrifices, such as missed dance recitals, missed baseball games, and payroll stress at month end when taxes are due. Specifics show what working hard looks like and draw a stronger response.
title: Specificity Gets Past the Spam Blocker in People's Brains

text: Do not copy his entrepreneur example. Pick specific details relevant to your own audience and be as specific as possible.
title: Specificity Gets Past the Spam Blocker in People's Brains

text: Hormozi illustrates specialization with time-management offers: $19 generally, about $100 for salespeople, and potentially $2,000 for outbound sellers. He argues niche-specific messaging can support a 100-fold price difference despite similar fundamentals; broader targeting does not necessarily yield 100-fold volume.
title: You Need to Niche Down

text: He recommends starting with an audience you can serve exceptionally well, then expanding as reputation grows. Incoming questions indicate possible breadth, but he advises waiting until demand makes the expansion opportunity more valuable than current revenue.
title: You Need to Niche Down

text: Hormozi describes progressing from local and remote weight-loss help to gym ownership, gym-business guidance, national service-business scaling, and broader business advice after building a diverse portfolio. Requests for help accompanied that widening scope.
title: You Need to Niche Down

text: He ranked his last 13 years and rates the current one as the fifth worst overall, but the worst of the past eight. His worst year was the first year of his business.
title: \"How Do You Keep Going When It Sucks?\"

text: He says problems are relative: his present problems are better than earlier ones, yet still problems. His reason for continuing is that he has nothing else he'd rather do, and he would switch immediately if he found something he enjoyed more.
title: \"How Do You Keep Going When It Sucks?\"

text: He says people adapt to suffering just as they adapt to pleasure. To keep punishment effective, its intensity and variety must change, and business is good at supplying new kinds of pain.
title: \"How Do You Keep Going When It Sucks?\"

text: He notes repeat setbacks hurt less: the second time an employee burns you or you get sued, it stings less. Staying in the same vein of business makes it less painful, since fewer unfamiliar things remain.
title: \"How Do You Keep Going When It Sucks?\"

text: Hormozi came from powerlifting, trained almost only legs at first, and treated upper body work as a distraction, before shifting toward the view that looking jacked is the most functional thing.
title: The Real Reason I Work Out

text: He argues that being jacked counts as functional, more so than niche mobility drills, because he is far likelier to be on camera than chased by a lion. He prefers high return on what he is most exposed to.
title: The Real Reason I Work Out

text: He says that when two fighters are equal in skill, the one with more muscle wins. When skill is unequal, the outcome depends on the size of the skill gap, and it may not take much extra skill to beat someone slightly stronger.
title: The Real Reason I Work Out

text: He believes the life you want lies beyond a few hard conversations, and that many people live a life they hate because they are too afraid to have them.
title: The Conversation That Will Change Your Life

text: When he feels anxious, insecure, angry or sad, he asks himself which conversation he is not having. Usually a short think reveals the one he has been putting off, and then he has it.
title: The Conversation That Will Change Your Life

text: He says the gap between knowing he must have a conversation and actually having it keeps getting shorter. After a breakup, firing or quitting, he feels relief and wants to have more such talks.
title: The Conversation That Will Change Your Life

text: Remembering he nearly died because he avoided a conversation gave him courage, so whatever the reaction, he preferred being alive. He says death has been a recurring theme in gaining the nerve to confront people, including his dad.
title: The Conversation That Will Change Your Life

text: He argues that if you feel you have nothing going for you, you can reframe it as having nothing to lose by acting, which makes you a much more dangerous person.
title: The Conversation That Will Change Your Life

text: When a sales team underperforms, the cause may be who was hired rather than how they were trained. He cites a Chick-fil-A people leader's idea that teams often lose in the playoffs what they actually lost in the draft.
title: Helping a $16M Clinic Get Doctors to Sell

text: He advises being selective about the beliefs candidates hold, since certain beliefs are needed to work well in a given business model. He skipped yoga and spin studios despite the identical model, because their outlook clashed with his approach.
title: Helping a $16M Clinic Get Doctors to Sell

text: He has found nothing more effective than modeling and role-playing for transferring skill. He notes sales skill transfers fairly fast to smart people, who tend to get lost in medical jargon instead.
title: Helping a $16M Clinic Get Doctors to Sell

text: To ease reluctance to sell, he suggests reading testimonials from patients who were undersold, showing that not offering solutions hurts people. He also frames it as making offers available to those who need them, not selling.
title: Helping a $16M Clinic Get Doctors to Sell

text: Some models keep the doctor in the back and use a patient care coordinator, who is effectively the salesperson. He has seen this work but is not convinced a structural change is needed here.
title: Helping a $16M Clinic Get Doctors to Sell

text: A clipboard with the script and checkmarks makes it hard for a physician to mess up the sales conversation. It walks through pain, what they cannot do, what they have tried, then asks permission to share the recommendation.
title: Helping a $16M Clinic Get Doctors to Sell

text: Hormozi says he long described himself as an impatient person, then realized he should judge himself with the same evidence-based lens he uses on other people.
title: Reflecting on Why I Was Wrong About Myself (Patience & Self Judgment)

text: He argues that claiming a trait like honesty or loyalty means little without evidence; someone who has not been tested in a situation has not yet shown they have that trait.
title: Reflecting on Why I Was Wrong About Myself (Patience & Self Judgment)

text: He believes you can act patient even when you do not feel patient, and doing so builds a growing stack of undeniable proof that you are who you want to be.
title: Reflecting on Why I Was Wrong About Myself (Patience & Self Judgment)

text: He does not believe in binary traits such as patient versus impatient; he prefers asking how patient, how honest or how loyal someone is, treating traits as continuums.
title: Reflecting on Why I Was Wrong About Myself (Patience & Self Judgment)

text: Using a penny-on-the-scale image, he says each patient act adds a bit of proof, and enough pennies eventually let you honestly say you are fairly patient, even though each act feels unwanted in the moment.
title: Reflecting on Why I Was Wrong About Myself (Patience & Self Judgment)

text: He says to drop the phrase industry average from your vocabulary, because it lowers what you accept as good enough and frames decisions as beating others rather than beating your own standard.
title: Helping a Concrete Business Owner Fix His Margins

text: For a business around one to three million with 10-20% margins, growth needs either the owner doing a second full-time job's work or a big bet on a hire who absorbs half or more of profit. He calls this the swamp.
title: Helping a Concrete Business Owner Fix His Margins

text: The best price point is not where you close the most deals but where you make the most money, which sits past peak close rate. Expect to lose more deals and earn more profit.
title: Helping a Concrete Business Owner Fix His Margins

text: He states that raising prices 10% consistently doubles a business's profit. He also says pricing and sales process changes are faster than operational efficiency, needing about a week of sales training.
title: Helping a Concrete Business Owner Fix His Margins

text: A 10% close rate signals a sales motion problem, and that is why owners hesitate to raise prices. He orders fixes as sales motion first, then pricing, and thinks a good job could reach 30-40% closing.
title: Helping a Concrete Business Owner Fix His Margins

text: Never email quotes. On the setting call, qualify and give a very wide range, such as 5,000 to 50,000, saying the exact number depends on seeing the job, like diagnosing a car not yet in the shop.
title: Helping a Concrete Business Owner Fix His Margins

text: Tell the prospect up front that the visit will end with a quote and a deposit, so the intent to close is set early. He says in-person close rates run about three times email close rates.
title: Helping a Concrete Business Owner Fix His Margins

text: He says he ran on a ruthless focus on dollars per hour: anything that could be traded away for more time spent on the activity that actually earned money, he traded away.
title: The Ruthless Focus That Got Me to My First Million

text: After a first $500 sale that took 30 minutes, he decided that any task worth less than about $250 per 30 minutes would be handed to someone else, including cooking, grocery shopping and cleaning.
title: The Ruthless Focus That Got Me to My First Million

text: For him, the useful question was what creates an input-to-output equation that ends in money; he poured everything possible into the input and eliminated the rest.
title: The Ruthless Focus That Got Me to My First Million

text: While running six gyms and planning locations seven through ten, he already worked all waking hours and had given up Saturdays, so he also gave up football and Netflix to make the expansion happen.
title: The Ruthless Focus That Got Me to My First Million

text: He finds it more useful to write down everything you are willing to sacrifice than to write to-do lists, because once everything else is sacrificed only the one important thing is left to do.
title: The Ruthless Focus That Got Me to My First Million

text: He cites Jerry Seinfeld sitting down to write for two hours daily with nothing else allowed, as an example of removing alternatives so only the key work remains.
title: The Ruthless Focus That Got Me to My First Million

text: He believes most people who are not achieving what they want are careless with their time, and their real output is probably lower than they assume.
title: The Ruthless Focus That Got Me to My First Million

text: He argues the ultimate productivity hack is no: stop doing unimportant things to create space, then fill it with what matters. Adding more to a schedule while refusing to sacrifice anything is why people fail.
title: The Ruthless Focus That Got Me to My First Million

text: As a rule of thumb, he suggests gathering about ten testimonials from people you have helped, ideally written, highlighted around key points, with images or screenshots from inside the community.
title: Your About Page Isn't Selling — Here's Why

text: If you lack social proof, he says to help people for free and ask them for testimonials in return.
title: Your About Page Isn't Selling — Here's Why

text: Each feature on a sales page should be paired with one or two testimonials showing that specific feature was valuable, ideally the thing that unlocked the customer's result.
title: Your About Page Isn't Selling — Here's Why

text: A page section needs a promise and some proof. The promise states a result in a time period through a unique method, and the proof is a stat such as a share of members hitting a result in month one.
title: Your About Page Isn't Selling — Here's Why

text: Survey your members so you have data to back the claims you make on your page.
title: Your About Page Isn't Selling — Here's Why

text: Pick either a rock bottom or a rock top story, not both. He notes wealthier people tend to have rock top moments, so it fits if you sell to them.
title: Your About Page Isn't Selling — Here's Why

text: He is not against leading with a story, but if most visitors already know who you are, he would start with the promise of what you will help them do.
title: Your About Page Isn't Selling — Here's Why

text: Be tangible about what customers get, why it matters and how it works. Poetic wording that leaves the buyer unsure what they receive does not sell.
title: Your About Page Isn't Selling — Here's Why

text: Use a spread of testimonials across ages, backgrounds and demographics to cover different avatars, especially when trying to reach a wider market.
title: Your About Page Isn't Selling — Here's Why

text: Before building a sales page, answer who you serve, what you help them do, how, and by when. The rest of the page is proof for each of those points.
title: Your About Page Isn't Selling — Here's Why

text: Hormozi suggests building a quiz-based funnel first, then recruiting many health-and-wellness influencers to send traffic into it, with a low-barrier offer at the front.
title: I make $50M/Year Selling Supplements but I Feel Lost With My Messaging

text: Hormozi would give influencers or affiliates one hundred percent of the profit on a front-end test so as many people as possible get tested, then earn through follow-up segmentation sequences and ancillary purchases.
title: I make $50M/Year Selling Supplements but I Feel Lost With My Messaging

text: Early on, his goal was learning rather than earning. He had saved 50 thousand dollars, which he knew could cover at least two years of living costs, so he kept expenses minimal and spent his remaining time at the gym trying to learn.
title: Lessons from My First Business

text: He kept living costs very low in that period: about 400 dollars a month to split a bedroom and about 100 dollars a week on food.
title: Lessons from My First Business

text: When optimizing a page, if forced to choose, Hormozi would rather have a few visual tiles plus a simple call to click and join than a page of all words and no tiles.
title: Sales Pages: How to use proof, promise plan

text: His test for any page element is whether it raises the likelihood that he would buy. He judges a page by what a normal visitor experiences, and a visitor should quickly learn what they actually get.
title: Sales Pages: How to use proof, promise plan

text: Insider jargon from your own world makes it harder to convert outsiders. Remove it and state a clear promise, as if explaining the offer to a toddler without fancy words.
title: Sales Pages: How to use proof, promise plan

text: A sales page should follow promise, plan, proof: a headline promise first, then the plan showing how the person gets there, with each element matching a key part of the plan.
title: Sales Pages: How to use proof, promise plan

text: The proof should deliver on the promise made at the start. If the promise is quitting a habit, proof is someone reporting lasting results and life improvements that match it.
title: Sales Pages: How to use proof, promise plan

text: He frames a sales page as a hero's journey the reader walks through in advance: promise, plan, then fulfillment via someone else's story. That vicarious fulfillment makes them willing to risk money to live it.
title: Sales Pages: How to use proof, promise plan

text: Include a PS statement on every sales page, saying who the offer is for and who it is not for, to attract the right people and ward off the wrong ones.
title: Sales Pages: How to use proof, promise plan

text: He suggests treating each sale the founder has to close as a failure of the sales team, not a win, so the sales lead shifts from being a great closer to being a great trainer of closers.
title: Why You’re Still the Only Closer in Your Business

text: He would consider withholding commissions on sales the founder helps close, which he thinks would quickly stop reps from asking the founder to step in.
title: Why You’re Still the Only Closer in Your Business

text: A founder-driven sales process leans on consultative selling and deep industry expertise. He says it can work but takes far more effort to run, and it is not what he prefers because it does not scale well.
title: Why You’re Still the Only Closer in Your Business

text: A young rep facing a large business owner cannot copy the founder's approach, since that approach rests on the founder's authority. A scalable process centers on the prospect, not the salesperson.
title: Why You’re Still the Only Closer in Your Business

text: In a scalable sales process, the knowledge that matters is the set of questions to ask and the correct order for asking them.
title: Why You’re Still the Only Closer in Your Business

text: Hormozi says he had taken only 11 days off since the start of this year, and he does not picture the great builders vacationing for long stretches while growing their companies.
title: How to Know When to Rest and When to Keep Pushing

text: He keeps examining which expectations he thinks others hold for him that he does not hold himself, and drops things he only does because he feels he is supposed to.
title: How to Know When to Rest and When to Keep Pushing

text: He recharges in a dark, quiet, low-stimulation room, such as an audiobook in a recliner or Netflix with pizza, and this takes about 3 hours rather than a whole season.
title: How to Know When to Rest and When to Keep Pushing

text: He has a theory that you get much more output by skipping days off and working fewer hours per day. He himself works roughly 6 to 6, seven days a week, sometimes stopping at 4 on Sunday.
title: How to Know When to Rest and When to Keep Pushing

text: He thinks work capacity expands with use: fatigue builds up more slowly and the ability to focus for long periods improves. He says he works more and has more energy now than at Gym Launch, despite being older.
title: How to Know When to Rest and When to Keep Pushing

text: He is not sure he believes in seasons of rest. His approach is to sleep when tired and keep sleeping until no longer tired, which he admits most people do not do.
title: How to Know When to Rest and When to Keep Pushing

text: When launching a new offer, keep it simple: launch with one offer, test it, and only consider adding a downsell or upsell later if you want to.
title: Helping a Course Business Scale

text: Get as many people as possible into the core membership offer, then put your effort into the retention side of it.
title: Helping a Course Business Scale

text: A network's value depends on the quality of its members. Harvard keeps its reputation by turning away 91% of applicants, not just by charging high tuition.
title: Helping a Course Business Scale

text: To build an enduring business, make it the best networking community in its field, so that over the long term membership becomes something people aspire to and can list on a resume.
title: Helping a Course Business Scale

text: Exclusivity comes down to whom you decline to take money from. You cannot be exclusive while accepting every buyer, which is why most people fail at it: it takes a much longer time horizon.
title: Helping a Course Business Scale

text: Without a long horizon, you can simply learn to market and sell and make around $10 million a year. Building a household brand instead requires patience to build over a decade.
title: Helping a Course Business Scale

text: Raising price in theory raises the bar, but by itself it does not. Price draws a certain type of person, yet you must still be able to turn people away. It takes both.
title: Helping a Course Business Scale

text: Hormozi likes controlling the whole funnel from click to close. Being vertically integrated, for example by acquiring a volume wholesaler, gives a better way to monetize what the business already buys, so the two businesses boost each other.
title: I'm so confused. Walk me through how you make money

text: If he needed to make money tomorrow without anything complex, he would call everyone he had dealt with over the past year and ask what it would take to become their exclusive buyer.
title: I'm so confused. Walk me through how you make money

text: With a strong return on capital, you can afford to spend more to get more deals. Even a lower cash-on-cash return could leave you happy if it lets you double your deal count.
title: I'm so confused. Walk me through how you make money

text: Hormozi says a company doing about 3M a year is nowhere near saturating a state-wide market. He tells the caller to drop the belief that the market is tapped.
title: I'm so confused. Walk me through how you make money

text: Guilt is the feeling of having broken your own rules, while shame is the feeling of having broken other people's rules.
title: When Guilt and Shame Are Actually Holding You Back

text: Guilt and shame are only useful after a bad behavior, and only when they push you to change that behavior for the better. Feeling bad just to feel bad, without changing anything, serves no purpose.
title: When Guilt and Shame Are Actually Holding You Back

text: Advertising means making people aware of what a business offers.
title: You Have 4 Options. Pick One.

text: To scale a low-ticket software product, he says it comes down to virality: the product must compound by itself through word of mouth, product quality, and growth factors built into the software and customer experience.
title: How To Fix a 12 Month Ad Payback Period in SaaS

text: To find what drives retention, he suggests studying customers who stayed 12 months, working backward to see their actions and demographics, and ranking each factor by how much it raises the chance of reaching month 12.
title: How To Fix a 12 Month Ad Payback Period in SaaS

text: After ranking the retention-linked actions, he says to build them into the front-end onboarding flow and reduce friction at each step. This begins as a data problem and then becomes an engineering problem.
title: How To Fix a 12 Month Ad Payback Period in SaaS

text: He says fix retention before virality: once people stop leaking out, work on encouraging them to bring friends. Growth in SaaS looks like signups where half never leave, so you keep compounding.
title: How To Fix a 12 Month Ad Payback Period in SaaS

text: He does not think fixing this is mainly a money matter. It needs a good data engineer and tracking of in-software user actions; if that tracking is missing, put it in place first.
title: How To Fix a 12 Month Ad Payback Period in SaaS

text: Part of churn from users who did not make money is a marketing issue. If you promise they will make money, they blame the software when they do not; framing it as a way to build communities lets smaller wins count as success.
title: How To Fix a 12 Month Ad Payback Period in SaaS

text: He thinks personal excellence largely comes from letting your own private judgment matter more than what everyone else will think of the work.

text: Deciding how much debt to take is a math exercise about risk: look at the business's seasonal volatility, the payments due, cash flow relative to debt covenants, and what coverage you can commit to over the period.

title: Scared of Debt? Your Business Will Stall

text: Consumer debt and business debt are different. A 100,000 dollar truck that produces 400,000 dollars yearly gross profit, paid over 5 years at 20,000 a year, is not very risky in his view.
title: Scared of Debt? Your Business Will Stall

text: How comfortable someone is with the chance of defaulting is a purely individual matter. He notes Dave Ramsey considers even 1% debt and 99% cash too risky, and says that is fine.

text: He thinks exceptional achievement can come from following the ordinary path of sustained work: someone succeeding after a decade remains exceptional, even if their progress attracts less attention than a teenage success.

text: Customers do not inherently value an app less because its developer is 14 rather than 40.

text: For young people who repeatedly feel dismissed because of their age, he suspects inadequate competence is a more likely explanation than age itself.
title: How to Get Taken Seriously When Nobody Thinks You're Ready

text: When staff grow uneasy about price increases, Hormozi prefers to confront it directly and hold the awkward conversation face to face instead of avoiding it.
title: \"Every Time I Raise Prices My Team Wants a Raise\"

text: To address staff discomfort about higher prices, he walks them through the vision he promised and asks whether having money or having none lets the company reach and help more people, and fund their training and growth.
title: \"Every Time I Raise Prices My Team Wants a Raise\"

text: He says that in the social sector, money is often demonized, and leaders should present it as neutral: it is power or unused energy that can build hospitals or bombs, depending on how it is used.
title: \"Every Time I Raise Prices My Team Wants a Raise\"

text: He asks team members to trust the commitment to the vision, stating that extra revenue will be allocated to deliver the impact that was promised.
title: \"Every Time I Raise Prices My Team Wants a Raise\"

text: Hormozi says that for a business at roughly 6 to 8 million in revenue aiming for 50 million, his team split the journey into 10 stages, each with guidance on what to do next.
title: “I Sell Custom Luxury Home Products. How Do I Get More Leads from Google Ads?”

text: Hormozi believes that whatever a business owner is struggling with, someone else has already faced and solved the same problem.
title: “I Sell Custom Luxury Home Products. How Do I Get More Leads from Google Ads?”

text: Parents pay for college because they believe it leads to a job for their kids. An offer that guarantees the job outcome can be positioned against a year of college cost, and worsening industry stats help that pitch.
title: How to Sell a $30K Offer With a 50% Close Rate

text: Sell the higher-priced follow-on before the first program ends, since afterward it becomes a separate buying decision. Pitch while the customer has had a quick win but is not finished yet.
title: How to Sell a $30K Offer With a 50% Close Rate

text: When unsure how to qualify buyers on a new sales motion, talk to everyone at first. Then see who buys and reverse engineer the qualifications, and aim front-end marketing at that profile to raise ascension buyers.
title: How to Sell a $30K Offer With a 50% Close Rate

text: Add a halfway check-in call with the parent to show progress, plus an end call showing next steps. He says a pitch can be made on both calls.
title: How to Sell a $30K Offer With a 50% Close Rate

text: Push to collect as much cash up front as possible for more skin in the game. Ask for the full price, then downsell to a large down payment with the rest spread over a year, then downsell again.
title: How to Sell a $30K Offer With a 50% Close Rate

text: Frame a second-phase sale as completing a multi-step process already started, not a new sale. Crediting the earlier payment toward it makes the buyer feel better and reduces the urge to stop midway.
title: How to Sell a $30K Offer With a 50% Close Rate

text: Whatever difficulty a person is facing, someone else has already dealt with the same thing and found a solution to it.
title: The Only Metric of Success That Actually Matters

text: He spends the rest of his day doing business and does not garden, because he does not care about gardening.
title: The Only Metric of Success That Actually Matters

text: He records once a week, going live for three or four hours, doing back-to-back YouTube videos with chat interaction, then open Q&A at the end that becomes clips. He finds it efficient and interactive.
title: Building a Content Team From Scratch

text: He says his energy stays much higher when talking to live people than when staring at a few young staff behind a camera.
title: Building a Content Team From Scratch

text: His team has a dedicated person per platform: YouTube shorts, YouTube long, a long-form strategist, a long editor, Instagram, LinkedIn and Facebook. Each sources and clips moments from his recordings for their platform.
title: Building a Content Team From Scratch

text: Early on, one or two people can cover several platforms; as the operation grows, specialization becomes important.
title: Building a Content Team From Scratch

text: Platforms are fragmented: his YouTube shorts do not do well on Instagram, and his Instagram content does not do well on TikTok. That is why he assigns people per platform.
title: Building a Content Team From Scratch

text: Split content work into pre-production (idea, packaging, research, key points, stories, visuals), production, and post-production. Pre-production offers the highest leverage and return on time.
title: Building a Content Team From Scratch

text: He recommends doing the content format that energizes you, and trying not to hate what you do for long periods. He has high tolerance for disliked work but advises against relying on it.
title: Building a Content Team From Scratch

text: He thinks most creators miss the pre-production step by posting only when inspired. Inspiration is fine to capture, but hitting high volume needs structure and planning what you will say.
title: Building a Content Team From Scratch

text: Each platform person has a weekly expectation of what to post from the recorded content. A 30-hour launch live gave them plenty of material to clip into 30-second pieces.
title: Building a Content Team From Scratch

text: First capture in whatever way is most natural so you have material; once volume exists, raise quality through pre-production.
title: Building a Content Team From Scratch

text: Trying to maximize content production on every platform yourself will burn you out; eventually you need a production or media house. The talent should be in a good state of mind, with personalization happening in post.
title: Building a Content Team From Scratch

text: Platform specialists know which moments suit their platform. A clip might work on TikTok but not YouTube, though sometimes all three pick the same moment and post it asynchronously.
title: Building a Content Team From Scratch

text: Showing that you can acquire other businesses and fold them in typically raises a company's valuation multiple by one to two turns, because it makes the business look more like a platform.
title: \"My Customers Can't Afford to Buy Twice. Now What?\"

text: Horizontal expansion (more locations or acquiring competitors) and vertical expansion (owning a distributor to lift margin percentage) both make a company more valuable. He would pick either before franchising or adding new products.
title: \"My Customers Can't Afford to Buy Twice. Now What?\"

text: Enterprise multiples work opposite to wholesale discounts in consumer goods: the larger the EBITDA, the higher the premium, so the core task is simply making more money.
title: \"My Customers Can't Afford to Buy Twice. Now What?\"

text: Going vertical first gives an immediate boost to every later add-on acquisition. The tradeoff is that doing it later makes the boost larger at the moment you make the move.
title: \"My Customers Can't Afford to Buy Twice. Now What?\"

text: He believes a movement sticks when people relate to you, you stay consistent, and the person on camera matches who you are in person. Word of mouth from those who met you carries weight with those who have not.
title: \"My Customers Can't Afford to Buy Twice. Now What?\"

text: He says any movement around his brands was not built by design; he had not really thought about building one.
title: \"My Customers Can't Afford to Buy Twice. Now What?\"

text: When rolling out a change to existing clients, he suggests presenting it broadly to everyone: describe how things were, what new information or decisions arose, what is happening now, and why it benefits them.
title: Helping an Agency Get More Clients

text: He suggests framing the change around what clients gain, such as reinvesting in things they care about that the owner could not previously deliver, rather than centering it on the owner's own concerns.
title: Helping an Agency Get More Clients

text: Whether clients feel under-delivered to is not up to the owner. He thinks the owner must sell the new direction rather than defend the current way of working that the owner does not want.
title: Helping an Agency Get More Clients

text: In education businesses, selling and running are hard because once customers learn your secrets, nothing keeps them. Consumables are needed to make the offer sticky, and he says they drive long-term LTV alongside a sales motion.
title: Helping a Tattoo Artist Get to $35M/Year

text: He says young people in the Western world are largely obsessed with independence, freedom and optionality: wanting to keep all options open, avoid being tied down, and not commit to a career or anything else.
title: Why Your Generation Is Obsessed With Freedom

text: Options work like money: they only have value when spent or used. Hoarding them your whole life and never using them is a wasted life, like an ant that saves forever and never eats.
title: Why Your Generation Is Obsessed With Freedom

text: Part of growing up is making commitments, meaning eliminating alternatives and walking through one-way doors with no return. He sees this as a strong sign of maturity.
title: Why Your Generation Is Obsessed With Freedom

text: He holds that there are no solutions, only trade-offs, and people struggle because they are unwilling to make trades. Example: marriage swaps novelty for loyalty, and eventually loyalty becomes worth more.
title: Why Your Generation Is Obsessed With Freedom

text: The worst trade is the one you never make: sitting on the sideline with a big stack of options unused, you end up with neither of the things you wanted.
title: Why Your Generation Is Obsessed With Freedom

text: Some options expire, so not committing can close doors anyway. His extreme example: a woman waiting until 60 to decide about kids has very likely lost that option.
title: Why Your Generation Is Obsessed With Freedom

text: One of the biggest changes in his own maturity is realizing, viscerally, that you cannot have it all. A house with mountain view, beach, seclusion and walkable shops cannot exist, since these things sit separately.
title: Why Your Generation Is Obsessed With Freedom

text: Hormozi says running many gyms gave him a larger base to test on, so he learned faster and now knows the gym business better than when he operated the gyms himself.
title: I Own a Marketing Agency and Teach People How to Start One. Which Should I Shut Down?

text: His R&D process: pick 10 to 20 representative markets, find the biggest problem across the whole distribution base, and spend a monthly budget of about 50,000 dollars plus his time on it. He says the budget can scale with revenue.
title: I Own a Marketing Agency and Teach People How to Start One. Which Should I Shut Down?

text: He gave test participants direct access to him in a separate group and released results monthly. Even failed tests helped, since others could cross ideas off their lists without taking the risk.
title: I Own a Marketing Agency and Teach People How to Start One. Which Should I Shut Down?

text: When a test worked, he rolled it out to the whole distribution base, and improved the gym model piece by piece that way.
title: I Own a Marketing Agency and Teach People How to Start One. Which Should I Shut Down?

text: If you already have a personal brand, he thinks it will be about you, and people will buy whatever you send that traffic to, provided they trust you.
title: I Own a Marketing Agency and Teach People How to Start One. Which Should I Shut Down?

text: When increased advertising spending brings poorer leads, he identifies three possible explanations: weak creative, insufficient fresh creative, or expansion from familiar audiences into colder traffic.
title: Helping a $1.35M Education Business Scale Past Its Lead Cap

text: Over a normal career of 40 years or more, someone might earn one or two million dollars. He would rather cram that span of work into four years and spend the other 36 doing what he wants with far greater resources.
title: How to Buy Back 36 Years of Your Life

text: He believes a certain amount of work must be done to generate income, so he prefers to do it all in a concentrated burst instead of spreading it across a lifetime.
title: How to Buy Back 36 Years of Your Life

text: On an early date, his future partner said she only wanted to help people. He asked whether she could help more people if she made more money, she agreed, and she shifted away from being a bleeding heart.
title: How to Buy Back 36 Years of Your Life

text: Personal resources are very limited, so anyone wanting to help many people must learn the game of making money.
title: How to Buy Back 36 Years of Your Life

text: He says winning that game probably means outworking many people and being criticized by people whose lives you do not want. Working hard and smart will not necessarily feel exciting.
title: How to Buy Back 36 Years of Your Life

text: He thinks a business with a large ticket size could reach roughly five to ten million dollars from a single market like Quebec alone, so there is likely more room there than the caller assumes.
title: Helping a Financial Services Business Scale

text: To expand to a new region with paid ads, little changes besides targeting and headline. Either use one generic headline aimed at the whole country, or run many campaigns with local ads for each market.
title: Helping a Financial Services Business Scale

text: He would bet local ads per market perform better, but very broad targeting can sometimes lower cost, so he recommends testing both approaches.
title: Helping a Financial Services Business Scale

text: Hormozi observes that successful businesses in this dental treatment category frequently publish collaborative results posts with people who have some public visibility, though he acknowledges limited familiarity with the category.
title: One Location Prints Cash. The Other Bleeds It.

text: Adding software to a business does not by itself make it valuable. You do not become a software company or earn a software multiple unless the software you build is exceptional.
title: How to Sell Your Education Business for 8 Figures

text: The economics that make software valuable are growth (ideally viral), high gross margins where extra customers cost little, and strong revenue retention. Those traits, not the software label, drive value.
title: How to Sell Your Education Business for 8 Figures

text: Net negative churn means that even if you lose some customers, the remaining ones upgrade or grow enough that you keep more than 100% of revenue. He gives an example of keeping 80 of 100 customers.
title: How to Sell Your Education Business for 8 Figures

text: In professional services like accounting or law, it is common to sell annual continued-education memberships priced around one to three thousand dollars a year, with monthly expert webinars, law updates and a Q&A forum. He says this could be sellable.
title: How to Sell Your Education Business for 8 Figures

text: If you build software, bring in a technical co-founder with a meaningful slug of equity, and reserve additional equity for other key engineers you need to hire.
title: How to Sell Your Education Business for 8 Figures

text: A common owner mistake is billing recurring for a one-time deliverable. Hormozi calls this labeling a payment plan a membership, and says churn looks high because customers simply finished paying for what they bought.
title: Stop Calling a Payment Plan a Membership

text: Be clear which parts of your offer are consumed monthly versus learned once. Only the consumable parts, such as calls, community access and meetups, suit recurring charges.
title: Stop Calling a Payment Plan a Membership

text: Many business owners past a certain size want to be around peers of similar size to learn from them, and it is less lonely, so community carries real value.
title: Stop Calling a Payment Plan a Membership

text: Hormozi says he looks at gross margins and revenue retention. If something costs little to deliver, people keep paying, and it earns well, he prefers it over building a bigger, costlier product.
title: Stop Calling a Payment Plan a Membership

text: Charging four times as much requires a robust team able to deliver that value; without one, customers will come to resent you.
title: Stop Calling a Payment Plan a Membership

text: Illustration: selling six or seven more of a 10K item with tiny cost can match the margin of a 100K product costing 30K, so why bother building the bigger thing.
title: Stop Calling a Payment Plan a Membership

text: If you have a supply problem or want to serve fewer customers, raising the price is fine.
title: Stop Calling a Payment Plan a Membership

text: He thinks the red pill movement exists because a disparity grew too large, leaving a big share of men feeling disenfranchised.
title: The Real Reason the Red Pill Movement Exists

text: He argues that as women out-earn men and outperform them in many areas, a mating mismatch appears: men generally date at the same level or below, women at the same level or above, so if outcomes were truly equal many women would lack partners.
title: The Real Reason the Red Pill Movement Exists

text: He notes there is no popular solution: nobody wants to say women should do worse, while telling men to step up will not get a whole population of men to improve when incentives point elsewhere.
title: The Real Reason the Red Pill Movement Exists

text: He cites a clip by Williamson that calls this the tall girl problem: a tall woman can date only very tall men, a tiny pool, so many women compete for few men who then face little pressure to settle down.
title: The Real Reason the Red Pill Movement Exists

text: He says he does not think a politically correct answer to this problem exists.
title: The Real Reason the Red Pill Movement Exists

text: Hormozi says education businesses offer many monetization options but attract narrower audiences, making broad growth harder. Entertainment businesses have an easier time attracting views.
title: Teaching a YouTuber how to build a real business

text: For large entertainment audiences, he favors an everyday consumable that many followers already buy. Audience affection can give buyers a reason to choose the creator's version.
title: Teaching a YouTuber how to build a real business

text: Hormozi considers building businesses his creative pursuit; producing content supports that pursuit.
title: Teaching a YouTuber how to build a real business

text: Hormozi thinks his lifetime allows roughly four major business-building attempts, each requiring seven to ten years, so he wants to choose those commitments carefully.
title: Teaching a YouTuber how to build a real business

text: If you already have a winning model, Hormozi sees little reason not to get even better at it and compound the competitive advantage you already have, rather than branching into other things.
title: The $10M Trucking Owner Who Wants to Sell the Product Too

text: Hormozi points out that adding a second business line piles a new cash constraint on top of existing ones, and asks why do it instead of simply doubling the current business.
title: The $10M Trucking Owner Who Wants to Sell the Product Too

text: When he ran Gym Launch and Prestige Labs, he tried selling supplements through his gym distribution base. It looked smart on paper but completely slowed the growth of his main business.
title: The $10M Trucking Owner Who Wants to Sell the Product Too

text: He calls the phrase about not wanting to leave money on the table his favorite entrepreneur statement, using a contractor who did roofs, general contracting and house flipping as an example of spread-thin focus.
title: The $10M Trucking Owner Who Wants to Sell the Product Too

text: Once the business model is nailed and returns on capital look attractive, you can afford patience and owning every location yourself becomes more appealing than partnering.
title: Helping a $1.8M Roofing Company Get to $70M

text: A franchise model can make sense when opening a location takes a lot of capital and needs heavy oversight, though he still views franchising fundamentally as impatience.
title: Helping a $1.8M Roofing Company Get to $70M

text: He sees franchising as the most expensive form of capital: the franchisor gives up a large share of each location, roughly a 25 to 30 percent partner, for something like 8 percent of top line.
title: Helping a $1.8M Roofing Company Get to $70M

text: He has seen many franchise systems of about 20 locations that earn little. Maintaining 20 franchised locations takes about the same work as 20 owned ones, but owning yields much more money, just more slowly.
title: Helping a $1.8M Roofing Company Get to $70M

text: He tends to flip franchises into company-owned locations. In the teeth whitening chain, he started with 14 corporate stores and 18 franchisees, bought all 18 out within 12 months, and now owns 32.
title: Helping a $1.8M Roofing Company Get to $70M

text: After buying out the franchisees, administrative headaches largely disappeared because he runs the stores his own way, and the business makes more money.
title: Helping a $1.8M Roofing Company Get to $70M

text: He says a business spending around $20,000 a month on ads has not saturated its market, and he thinks a niche like custom gaming products could go toward $2 million a month before nearing saturation.
title: Burn $200K on Google Ads to 5x a Boring Business

text: He argues that $20,000 a month in ad spend is very small, and that plenty of traffic exists; most people simply do not know how to access it. His own launch spent $500 a day.
title: Burn $200K on Google Ads to 5x a Boring Business

text: For a highly visual, high-ticket product, he would reach out to influencers, send them custom products, ask to be tagged, then whitelist the best-converting influencer story as an ad on Instagram and Meta.
title: Burn $200K on Google Ads to 5x a Boring Business

text: Defining what a successful businessperson is really means deciding what success means for you in the game of business, since even the best-known founders have given up points in other areas like family.
title: When do you become successful?

text: He encourages trying to win at the game of life, with business as just one component; winning too hard at business alone may leave you at life's end feeling you missed things.
title: When do you become successful?

text: Many people are dissatisfied because they want the rewards of every area of life while paying the cost of none, but trade-offs are unavoidable and highly individual.
title: When do you become successful?

text: You will stay wishy-washy about your goal until you define it for yourself; once you do, you can respect others' different choices with certainty, even if they would not work for you.
title: When do you become successful?

text: You are allowed to change your target: success at 20 will differ from success at 30 or 40, and shifting targets is pursuing something else, not having lost.
title: When do you become successful?

text: If your business is seasonal, avoid labeling the slow months the off-season. Hormozi says that once you use that label, everyone treats the period as off, and you keep losing money during it.
title: Helping an Indoor Golf Business Scale

text: Hormozi says the best way to choose what to act on from content is to notice which idea you cannot stop thinking about, keep retelling to friends, or keep clipping and sharing. That idea is the one to work on.
title: How to Actually Learn From Every Podcast You Hear

text: He says taking even half of one idea from a podcast or book and working on it for a month produces a lot of progress.
title: How to Actually Learn From Every Podcast You Hear

text: He argues people today are unusually fortunate: you can search for any problem, find top minds discussing it, listen, and implement the next day. He says this shifts both you and the world around you.
title: How to Actually Learn From Every Podcast You Hear

text: When a business has a low-cost education offer and a higher-priced service offer, the education side can act as the front end and the service as the back end, even if the owner sees them as two separate businesses.
title: Stop Worrying About Your Niche Being Too Small

text: Put ad spend behind the offer with the better LTV to CAC ratio and the much larger addressable market, then focus effort on moving those customers up into the higher-level back end, accepting that not every customer will fit it.
title: Stop Worrying About Your Niche Being Too Small

text: When two businesses have different owners and must stay separate, treat the relationship like an arms-length affiliate deal and pay a kickback. The customers then cost only the kickback amount.
title: Stop Worrying About Your Niche Being Too Small

text: Hormozi predicts that if a done-for-you business signs 50 customers, about four will produce roughly 70% of revenue, leaving the rest as small minnows, and the owner will then question why he is doing it.
title: The Real Problem With Done-For-You Businesses

text: He thinks done-for-you models are hard to scale, because you cannot control many of the things you are liable for, and he challenges the caller to name one big business built this way.
title: The Real Problem With Done-For-You Businesses

text: He says only about 5% of franchisors ever reach 100 locations, yet many people dream of being one, spend around 250,000 on legal work, open 10 to 15 locations to friends and family, then stall because they cannot attract customers.
title: The Real Problem With Done-For-You Businesses

text: He describes the ideal franchise opportunity as a franchisor with a good business model who does not know how to promote, and says such franchisors are fairly common.
title: The Real Problem With Done-For-You Businesses

text: Any e-commerce brand can put a large QR code on each purchase linking to a community, with a strong incentive to join, to get real contacts and repurchases instead of faceless marketplace buyers.
title: Put a QR Code on Every Package

text: Low-ticket businesses usually scale through brick and mortar distribution, such as getting products into large grocery chains or vitamin shops.
title: Put a QR Code on Every Package

text: For retail distribution, packaging matters a lot. He would test it heavily, such as with small polls, and would spend ad money on packaging tests so products move and get reordered.
title: Put a QR Code on Every Package

text: In direct-to-consumer low-ticket ads, offer multi-month supplies, since the average buyer takes about three months, to recover acquisition cost up front, then focus effort on repurchase.
title: Put a QR Code on Every Package

text: Low-ticket and ecommerce businesses revolve around breaking even on acquisition cost, while needing to reinvest in both inventory and re-engaging customers so gross profit expands.
title: Put a QR Code on Every Package

text: Repurchase rate is the most important metric for a physical products business. Without it, retail buyers try the product once, stop buying, and the store eventually drops you.
title: Put a QR Code on Every Package

text: Once the product is right, marketing becomes very solvable.
title: Put a QR Code on Every Package

text: How to scale depends on the goal: making money can mean just you raising prices with a few helpers, while building an asset requires systems.
title: Put a QR Code on Every Package

text: What looks like magic is a set of behaviors, maybe 17 of them. Documenting them lets others perform them and even outdo the original person, enabling service scale.
title: Put a QR Code on Every Package

text: Scaling a service business means the real business is recruiting, hiring and training, which falls under culture.
title: Put a QR Code on Every Package

text: In the traditional private equity model, company cash flow services the debt, often interest-only for about five years. If the company doubles, repaying the loan at sale leaves the enterprise value increase as the buyer's gain.
title: Put a QR Code on Every Package

text: The model that seems to work best is showing customers how to do the thing, then also selling them your product once taught. Recurring revenue comes from them continuing to buy the product, as with Gym Launch or Prestige Labs.
title: Teach the Skill, Then Sell the Supplies Forever

text: For a business teaching customers and then supplying them, what makes it very valuable is proving what percentage of education buyers become permanent sellers of the product, continuing to sell year over year.
title: Teach the Skill, Then Sell the Supplies Forever

text: When most enterprise value comes from the product side, treat the education as a way to offset acquisition cost for the product business. The goal becomes getting the most people possible to sell the product.
title: Teach the Skill, Then Sell the Supplies Forever

text: Set the education price at the highest level that still sells the most, stopping before the next tier where you would start losing buyers you would otherwise have had.
title: Teach the Skill, Then Sell the Supplies Forever

text: At Prestige Labs, gyms bought a supplement stack for each trainer, roughly $5,000 worth, and got the education free. Trainers ran a 30-day challenge, gained conviction from their own results, and that made back-end sales easier.
title: Teach the Skill, Then Sell the Supplies Forever

text: It is much easier to sell a physical product than information, because people can see and hold it, whereas info sellers are used to selling something intangible.
title: Teach the Skill, Then Sell the Supplies Forever

text: Hormozi says he rarely prefers a low-ticket business, but when it has lower churn and (he bets) higher gross margins than the core service, and a large pool of buyers, it can be the better business.
title: Helping an Agency Owner Bet on a $500/Month Offer

text: He says 1% monthly churn on a sticky, low-priced product aimed at a prosumer avatar that has many potential buyers is a very strong number, and that it adds high enterprise value.
title: Helping an Agency Owner Bet on a $500/Month Offer

text: With any affiliate there are two elements: a launch and an integration. The integration is worth more, while the launch gets their audience to buy faster.
title: Helping a Nonprofit Scale

text: For a new affiliate with an existing customer pool, ask for a launch where they refer around 10 people, offering to do the work free in exchange for permission to use their story as a case study.
title: Helping a Nonprofit Scale

text: After the initial launch, get the partner to include your value proposition in their own pitch and plug yourself into their onboarding process, so you capture all their new customers instead of only those they choose to refer.
title: Helping a Nonprofit Scale

text: When a strong offer closes only about 10 percent, the sales process is likely the problem, and fixing it could plausibly triple the business without any other change.
title: Helping a Nonprofit Scale

text: Hormozi attributes his content's originality to recording experiences from his daily life, including conversations in business meetings, instead of choosing subjects based on current trends.
title: How to Make Content Nobody Can Copy

text: He argues that creators need their own source of material: relying on another creator's ideas keeps them behind that creator and makes continued participation dependent on someone else.
title: How to Make Content Nobody Can Copy

text: Copying his content word for word does not make someone him, because copycats did not originate the ideas. They cannot apply them well or diagnose why something fails, since they never reasoned from first principles.
title: You Need More Proof...

text: The second reason copycats lack his influence is that they have no proof, meaning no results like a sold company, a large tech platform, or a big advisory and private equity business.
title: You Need More Proof...

text: You can make money in almost any market, but climbing to higher-end markets requires progressively more compelling proof. Impressing poor people takes little; impressing rich people takes much more.
title: You Need More Proof...

text: Rich people tend to influence many poorer people, so the aim is to be an influencer's influencer, like a favorite rapper's favorite rapper, which requires being genuinely good and demonstrating it.
title: You Need More Proof...

text: Assume the market begins as a skeptic, because many people were burned early by things like MLMs. Only after you prove enough things do they accept you as a real source of information.
title: You Need More Proof...

text: People listen to authority figures because it is the lowest-effort way to consume information: they skip judging whether it is true and act on it directly. He calls this persuasive because it happens without thinking.
title: You Need More Proof...

text: A teacher earning $50,000 a year could repeat Buffett's investing advice, even more skillfully, yet nobody would believe them. So to be seen as the best marketer, go market and prove it.
title: You Need More Proof...

text: A lead magnet can be a short list of six actions someone does right before going on stage, which is then used to invite people into a paid mentorship community offering weekly calls and video feedback.
title: The Lead Magnet That Will Sell Your Mentorship Program

text: The company's mission is to make business accessible to everyone, so the plan was to put everything out for free with no paywalls, including courses on the site and books priced at 99 cents.
title: Who Is Alex Hormozi?

text: He shares learnings from portfolio companies so the content stays relevant, fresh and cutting edge, reflecting what is working today.
title: Who Is Alex Hormozi?

text: Giving lots of value also attracts companies to work with them. The goal is to deliver more value to a company before any conversation, effectively paying for themselves in advance.
title: Who Is Alex Hormozi?

text: He did not know whether the approach would work at the start, but it has gone pretty well. His belief is that constantly giving and focusing on audience value will eventually return to you.
title: Who Is Alex Hormozi?

text: Top closers speak and move differently, with changes in tonality and body language. He wants those behaviors documented in fine detail so others can copy them and string together more closes in a row.
title: Door-to-Door Sales Secrets That Print Cash

text: Door-to-door reps should treat the work as a numbers game. Set a goal for doors knocked per hour, adjusted for how far apart doors are, so a bad door is expected and does not discourage them.
title: Door-to-Door Sales Secrets That Print Cash

text: If one location or trainer already performs better than another, that proves the weaker one can reach the same result, since it is already happening in the business.
title: Door-to-Door Sales Secrets That Print Cash

text: He believes that selling with the correct messaging attracts the right prospect.
title: Door-to-Door Sales Secrets That Print Cash

text: Meta usually produces more leads than PPC because it interrupts people instead of catching existing intent, but those leads are colder. Hormozi notes there is a huge audience on Meta, so far more money can be spent.
title: The Real Reason Your Meta Ads Aren't Converting

text: For a high-ticket dental sale like implants, he would expect to spend roughly five to ten thousand dollars in ad spend per sale, calling that about industry average.
title: The Real Reason Your Meta Ads Aren't Converting

text: Screen leads on the setting call with BANT: budget, authority, need, timing. Unqualified people should be filtered by phone before they ever show up in person.
title: The Real Reason Your Meta Ads Aren't Converting

text: For the need question, ask for a one to ten rating. Whatever they say, ask why it is not a ten, or why it is not a one, so they sell themselves on its importance.
title: The Real Reason Your Meta Ads Aren't Converting

text: For timing, ask when they would want it solved if a magic wand existed. Prospects wanting it today or within days are worth pursuing; those pushing it far into the future are tire kickers unlikely to close.
title: The Real Reason Your Meta Ads Aren't Converting

text: He would require a deposit if show-up rates were a problem. When show rates are fine and the weakness is the setting call, the fix is better qualification instead.
title: The Real Reason Your Meta Ads Aren't Converting

text: Cost per lead for this kind of offer of roughly 50 to 150 dollars is probably about right. Five leads for ten thousand is too expensive, and an enormous lead count would signal something wrong.
title: The Real Reason Your Meta Ads Aren't Converting

text: Meta finds people resembling the avatar shown in the ad, so make ads look premium and feature someone matching the ideal customer.
title: The Real Reason Your Meta Ads Aren't Converting

text: He believes PPC tends to work better for high-ticket dental because its leads are hotter, though quality may be lower initially. Someone hands-on at a PPC dental agency can be paid hourly to explain keyword choices.
title: The Real Reason Your Meta Ads Aren't Converting

text: No matter what a business struggles with, someone else has already struggled with and solved the same problem.
title: The Real Reason Your Meta Ads Aren't Converting

text: He suggests separating a vision from a plan: the wider the territory you must defend at once, the harder it becomes, so the plan should cover less ground than the vision.
title: Helping a Nail Salon Build a Franchise Model

text: A business model is only proven if it works without the owner's social media bringing in customers. He would want the model to reach a margin of around 30 or higher independent of that.
title: Helping a Nail Salon Build a Franchise Model

text: A sign that a service model is truly nailed is turning away new customers because all staff are fully booked and no chairs remain, leaving the question of whether to expand.
title: Helping a Nail Salon Build a Franchise Model

text: He states that nail salons only work when roughly half of revenue or so goes to technician pay, given the caller's example of cutting labor from 70 percent to 50 percent.
title: Helping a Nail Salon Build a Franchise Model

text: Franchising is essentially a capital play: it lets you use other people's money to open a hundred or a thousand locations over about ten years.
title: Helping a Nail Salon Build a Franchise Model

text: He believes the next five years will change business massively, comparable to the internet arriving again, with humanoid robots trainable once and then performing consistently.
title: Helping a Nail Salon Build a Franchise Model

text: He says a nail salon chain he considered buying used a gamified system to lift technicians to six-figure incomes, which produced loyal staff, retained customers, and 43 percent net margins across five locations.
title: Helping a Nail Salon Build a Franchise Model

text: If the ultimate version of a business is not what you want to own, Hormozi says to make an exit plan and build the business you would want, likening it to not marrying someone who wants different things.
title: Helping a $1.5M Business That Runs on 30 Minutes a Day Scale

text: If a business depends on one person doing the selling, Hormozi says it is not really a business yet. Once someone else does the sales, you have something, though then you could simply sell it to that person.
title: Helping a $1.5M Business That Runs on 30 Minutes a Day Scale

text: To exit to a team member, Hormozi describes offering the buyer the profit for two years and then ownership, or giving half the profit in exchange for never being called again.
title: Helping a $1.5M Business That Runs on 30 Minutes a Day Scale

text: Hormozi role-plays crisis scenarios with prospective successors, such as an injury or breakdown. The right answer to each is anything other than calling him. When they pass, the handover starts.
title: Helping a $1.5M Business That Runs on 30 Minutes a Day Scale

text: He credits strategy for his success, defining strategy as prioritization: not doing more things, but getting more return from the things you do.
title: You Don't Understand Strategy

text: He believes most people spend much of their time on activities that do not matter, since working faster or with frenetic energy does not multiply results.
title: You Don't Understand Strategy

text: His content output is far larger than most people's because of a team and infrastructure that repurpose and reproduce content. He describes content ten times better, with ten times the views on twenty times the content, as roughly 200 times the output.
title: You Don't Understand Strategy

text: He and his wife have worked nearly every day for about 13 years, and he worked the first 100 days of last year without a day off. He says he does not recommend this for everyone.
title: You Don't Understand Strategy

text: He counts a day as a work day only if it runs past about two in the afternoon, meaning more than 10 hours of work.
title: You Don't Understand Strategy

text: He thinks a maniacal sense of urgency is good, and the better question is how to finish in a tenth of the time rather than half the time.
title: You Don't Understand Strategy

text: Asking how to make 10 times more money is better than asking for double. Doubling just means doing more of the same, the best risk-adjusted move, while 10x or 100x forces you to find different levers.
title: You Don't Understand Strategy

text: He aims to be the best student and best success story of anything he buys. A downside is that providers then claim ownership of his results, with many people saying they were behind his launch.
title: Why We Refused to Join the $100K Club

text: He works from replicate before you iterate: follow the instructions exactly, reproduce the original person's results, and only then apply a few tweaks based on his general knowledge and start diverging into his own solutions.
title: Why We Refused to Join the $100K Club

text: He almost always buys access to expertise because it is faster. He warns against assuming a purchase will solve everything, since nothing does, but it can reduce the time needed to get there.
title: Why We Refused to Join the $100K Club

text: Because investing in his education has paid off so much, he spends money wherever he can to learn more and arranges his life so he learns more by default.
title: Why We Refused to Join the $100K Club

text: He and his partner decided both must be exposed to the same information: they never joined masterminds or attended events separately, and when one read a book, that person gave the other the cliff notes.
title: Why We Refused to Join the $100K Club

text: A very premium network accepted both of them but allowed only one to join, and even asked him to lie to get in. He refused, keeping his integrity and treating the two of them as a package deal.
title: Why We Refused to Join the $100K Club

text: Hormozi says he is always willing to pay an affiliate the full customer acquisition cost, since he would rather pay a known partner than pay an ad platform.
title: Helping a $5M Coaching Business Build an Affiliate Program

text: His preferred affiliate setup is to peel off a narrow part of the core product as a lead magnet. Affiliates keep 100% of what they charge for it, either separately or bundled, and it becomes lead gen for the main offer.
