title: Helping a $5M Coaching Business Build an Affiliate Program

text: He thinks the standard flat percentage affiliate commission, such as 20%, is a poor approach.
title: Helping a $5M Coaching Business Build an Affiliate Program

text: He says paying in man-hours, such as about $50 of labor for a referred customer who shows up, beats paying an ad platform far more per show, and he thinks businesses resist it wrongly.
title: Helping a $5M Coaching Business Build an Affiliate Program

text: He says that across many businesses studied, the biggest ones often get less revenue from affiliates than people assume, and they drive more of it themselves. He warns smaller businesses about this.
title: Helping a $5M Coaching Business Build an Affiliate Program

text: Returns are best at the very top of achievement, but reaching the highest levels means giving up amounts of the things you hoped success would bring, in proportion to the level reached.
title: The Price of Being Exceptional

text: He argues hardship persists because, just as with punishment, what keeps the suck sucking is rising intensity and variety, and life supplies both without playing fair.
title: The Price of Being Exceptional

text: He thinks the hard stays because the currency you pay changes: first convincing friends and family, then overcoming yourself to act, then learning through failure, then closing large skill gaps quickly.
title: The Price of Being Exceptional

text: Habituation to failure is narrow, so each new type of failure hurts afresh. His event desk problem recurred three times in different forms, and each still stung.
title: The Price of Being Exceptional

text: He calls this year financially the best of his life, yet it also brought health and legal problems, which he sees as a change in the currency he pays.
title: The Price of Being Exceptional

text: He has habituated to paying in long hours and reduced social life, no longer regarding them as sacrifices, which he says is the state you want to reach.
title: The Price of Being Exceptional

text: He challenged his eight-person team to finish a 12-week project in 7 days, hoping for under 50 total working hours. They worked roughly 12 to 14 hour days, and everyone said they loved it.
title: The Price of Being Exceptional

text: Once you learn how to work, he says, the work itself is self-reinforcing and enjoyable; the hard part is everything else you must sacrifice to get back to working.
title: The Price of Being Exceptional

text: He compares business to the Bulgarian weightlifting system, which breaks nearly everyone except the one person who can sustain it. He says achievement science is straightforward: pursue high-leverage opportunities.
title: The Price of Being Exceptional

text: Working smart instead of hard only wins against dumb competitors; when rivals are smart and also work hard, you must work hard too.
title: The Price of Being Exceptional

text: Hormozi argues that entrepreneurs should concentrate on mastering one business because dividing their effort across ventures makes competing against a fully focused operator harder.
title: How to Get Rich by Doing Less, Not More

text: Hormozi says a person can effectively lead only one business as CEO; owning multiple companies differs when each has a separate CEO responsible for its financial results.
title: How to Get Rich by Doing Less, Not More

text: He thinks referrals are harder to scale when a business serves business customers on both sides, compared with consumer software where a measurable viral coefficient can guide improvements.
title: Helping a Marketing Agency Scale

text: Doing exceptional things means accepting isolation and the pain of rejection. Some rejection is not customers declining but people rejecting your behavior, your choices and who you are becoming.
title: Why the Path to Exceptional Is So Lonely

text: He thinks rejection of your changing behavior is often harder than sales rejection, because it shows up as edgy jokes with a bit too much truth, snide remarks, or quiet exclusion from invitations.
title: Why the Path to Exceptional Is So Lonely

text: He describes a no-man's-land: you give up those social moments for many hours alone, not wanting your current life and not wanting to be with the old group either. He sees this as the start of transformation.
title: Why the Path to Exceptional Is So Lonely

text: He calls the lonely chapter the most powerful idea he and his partner have come up with. He thinks it resonates because of the doubt you endure when nobody understands, you are discouraged, and success is not promised.
title: Why the Path to Exceptional Is So Lonely

text: The lonely experience happens on every mountain, first and second alike. After a success others consider enough, pursuing the next summit starts the whole cycle again.
title: Why the Path to Exceptional Is So Lonely

text: He thinks for many people the first big lonely chapter comes after their first success, since that success happens inside the frame they already live in. Driven people may need to reach the top to realize it is not what they want.
title: Why the Path to Exceptional Is So Lonely

text: He built one of the UK's biggest events companies, with status, wealth, freedom and being the boss. Everyone said he should be satisfied, but it felt wrong, and finding something new meant letting go of what others said he should want.
title: Why the Path to Exceptional Is So Lonely

text: Others see only as far up the mountain as their local maximum. Once you reach a new one, you perceive the next peak and they cannot. He thinks many people need to climb the first peak to see this.
title: Why the Path to Exceptional Is So Lonely

text: Telling yourself you are far better than a competitor gives you nothing except complacency and a greater chance of looking foolish if they beat you.
title: Never Underestimate Your Competition

text: Leaders at the top have the most resources and the best perspective, so what usually topples them is hubris. Egos make people lose, since admitting someone might be better hurts.
title: Never Underestimate Your Competition

text: He points to a tweet of his: people underestimate how much smarter you can come across with just 20 minutes of preparation.
title: Never Underestimate Your Competition

text: Not preparing only makes you look more naturally gifted, and you then win by less than if you had prepared. Practicing hard makes you better, so skipping it is purely ego. He prefers a reputation for work ethic.
title: Never Underestimate Your Competition

text: He falls into the trap of assuming his company will outperform others too, so he reminds himself to assume he is always the underdog and that rivals hold a trick he does not know about.
title: Never Underestimate Your Competition

text: He warns that health clinics offering blood work and supplement tests are also businesses, and he knows from the fitness industry that there are games behind them, so he keeps his own approach as simple as possible.
title: What Is My Fitness Routine?

text: He eats about 2 lb of meat daily to reach roughly 200 g of protein, and adds dessert beyond that to hit his calorie goal.
title: What Is My Fitness Routine?

text: He adjusts weight by changing dessert: less to lose weight, the same to maintain, and to gain he adds extra calories such as pasta or rice to meat meals.
title: What Is My Fitness Routine?

text: His training has been progressive overload with resistance work using weights, machines and plate-loaded machines for almost two decades.
title: What Is My Fitness Routine?

text: He has tried kettlebell-only, barefoot, swim sprint, high intensity interval and strongman training, and competed in powerlifting for 5 years, and now trains more like a bodybuilder. He does not currently do preventative screenings like MRIs, though he may later.
title: What Is My Fitness Routine?

text: To sell a business built on a digital product, you need a real brand plus a distinctly better product. Buyers must want it because of who you are and what it is, since copycats will appear once it succeeds.
title: Hormozi Tells $1M Founder His Exit Plan Won't Work

text: Growth comes from making each customer worth more or selling to more customers, and most businesses probably need to do both.
title: Hormozi Tells $1M Founder His Exit Plan Won't Work

text: Ask what you can sell your customers that they will not want to leave. Adding a back end and then using the extra cash to fund ads is the lowest operational change route to growth, though it will not produce a sellable company.
title: Hormozi Tells $1M Founder His Exit Plan Won't Work

text: Two ways to raise customer value: add a higher-touch back-end service, or keep the product digital and add a recurring element. He says simply adding a more expensive offer is significantly easier.
title: Hormozi Tells $1M Founder His Exit Plan Won't Work

text: Relying on organic and SEO for leads works mainly because the local market has strong demand relative to supply, not because it is a sound practice. Learning to acquire customers through paid channels could let a business beat competitors who never do.
title: You're distracted by shiny objects instead of scaling what works

text: In businesses where clients bond with individual providers, the aim is to make customers loyal to the brand rather than the provider. He admits this is harder when clients prefer a specific person who knows their preferences.
title: You're distracted by shiny objects instead of scaling what works

text: Keeping and attracting better talent often requires paying people more, even when margins feel thin. Fix the sales motion first, then the membership model to maximize revenue per day per technician, then fund a better career path.
title: You're distracted by shiny objects instead of scaling what works

text: A better career path draws higher quality talent, so the owner can step away and the business still makes money. That is what turns it into a replicable model.
title: You're distracted by shiny objects instead of scaling what works

text: The entrepreneur's job is to break the whole business into granular steps, each with clear directions. An editor asked simply to make a video may know only some steps, so every stage of the pipeline should be spelled out.
title: How to Win with AI in 2026

text: Breaking a business into granular steps matters because AI agents are now doing each of those steps. As an example, he says ACQ's media output roughly tripled in the last month.
title: How to Win with AI in 2026

text: His example content pipeline runs: rank what is performing well, cross-list against brand and expertise to build a reservoir of ideas, then outline, intro, hook and road map with stories woven in, then packaging.
title: How to Win with AI in 2026

text: Hormozi stopped consulting for equity because he considers the ownership offered insufficient for the expected work. He prefers investing cash, negotiating promotional or brand support separately, and avoiding vague obligations or recurring weekly time commitments.
title: How to Make Offers for Equity

text: Hormozi sees a clearly bounded advisory arrangement, such as meeting quarterly alongside other advisers, as an exception to his dislike of consulting for equity, although it remains outside his preferred approach.
title: How to Make Offers for Equity

text: He has generally seen higher-priced offers churn more, but he attributes this not to price itself but to customers poorly matching value and to weak qualification of who is allowed to buy.
title: \"Does Pricing Affect Churn?\"

text: Lowering price while keeping everything else the same would almost certainly lower churn, but that alone doesn't tell you whether you earn more. Cutting price 50% to gain a 20% churn drop would be a bad trade.
title: \"Does Pricing Affect Churn?\"

text: The real target is lifetime value rather than churn alone. Churn is a big multiplier on LTV, but it is only one input to optimize.
title: \"Does Pricing Affect Churn?\"

text: Every input, including price, churn and page conversion, ultimately rolls up into earnings per click. Since everyone is driving traffic into a money-making box, each input should be made as valuable as possible.
title: \"Does Pricing Affect Churn?\"

text: From experimenting with many prices across service levels, he finds the price curve much less extreme than people assume. Being deliberate about pricing is smart, but obsessing over it is not warranted.
title: \"Does Pricing Affect Churn?\"

text: A price increase does not mean everyone who would have bought at the old price buys at the new one. Raising 50% might cut conversion 40%, so the net effect could be roughly 10% more or less, and higher prices bring other issues like expectations and card declines.
title: \"Does Pricing Affect Churn?\"

text: The bigger driver is how good the product is. If it is good and priced appropriately for the qualification of your prospects, you will make a lot of money.
title: \"Does Pricing Affect Churn?\"

text: For a business making 500,000 a month, nudging price from 1250 to 1350 would probably yield only around 2% more revenue, not the full 7-10%, and it is unlikely to deliver the order-of-magnitude growth needed.
title: \"Does Pricing Affect Churn?\"

text: He says that when you judge your success by whether you did everything in your control to prepare, a lucky win feels tarnished by guilt, and success starts to feel under your own control.
title: The Minimum Standard That Changed My Career

text: He says the downside of defining success by your own full effort is realizing you can do very few things, which makes life feel short.
title: The Minimum Standard That Changed My Career

text: He told a public CEO friend with a few hundred thousand followers, who posted one piece of content a day, that his team puts out 300 a week. The CEO thanked him for resetting his minimum standard.
title: The Minimum Standard That Changed My Career

text: His presentation process: write it, run it in his head, deliver it out loud, watch the recording, edit, and repeat until it is polished. He says repetition like this unlocks mastery.
title: The Minimum Standard That Changed My Career

text: He listened back to every podcast he recorded for roughly the first two and a half years. At the time he thought they were great, though he now finds his early episodes awful.
title: The Minimum Standard That Changed My Career

text: Hormozi says running ads is not that complicated. He once feared it, then paid an expert $750 an hour to sit beside him for six hours, and he learned the whole thing.
title: Business Isn't Complicated.

text: His method for learning from an expert: pay by the hour, forbid the expert from touching the computer, make them watch him work, and have them explain the reasoning behind bids and targeting as he goes.
title: Business Isn't Complicated.

text: He reasoned that he would try harder than any agency would, so he chose to learn ads himself instead of paying agencies large sums.
title: Business Isn't Complicated.

text: To choose a growth path, ask which of the options has the highest likelihood of success for you: content, affiliates with big networks, direct outreach, or ads.
title: Business Isn't Complicated.

text: Content is slow, so he suggests starting it anyway so the business shows some internet presence, but not relying on it for near-term growth.
title: Business Isn't Complicated.

text: Ad targeting can be simple: buy a list of the target profession, which is readily available online, build a lookalike audience from it, and run an ad offering something free and amazing.
title: Business Isn't Complicated.

text: On the thank-you page after opt-in, invite people to a free call and tell them to leave their credit card at home. He says this makes it a two-call sale and lowers pressure.
title: Business Isn't Complicated.

text: If a sales process is too consultative, it depends on specialized, hard-to-find salespeople. A tighter script that people simply follow, looping off-track questions back to the main line, lets ordinary reps succeed.
title: How to Recruit Elite Sales Directors for Your Agency

text: He says his own sales team averages around 23 years old. They do not know the client's business better than the client, but they know how to sell what his company offers.
title: How to Recruit Elite Sales Directors for Your Agency

text: In his view, a sales director's job is mostly maintaining culture and running daily training rather than selling on calls, so they need less product knowledge than frontline reps, since teaching sales is teaching sales.
title: How to Recruit Elite Sales Directors for Your Agency

text: He would begin splitting a sales team around 10 people per manager; two groups of seven or eight feels better to him personally.
title: How to Recruit Elite Sales Directors for Your Agency

text: When choosing between a big outcome far away and a small one right now, the small immediate one wins every time, so give people an immediate reinforcer for acting.
title: How to Scale a Webinar/Events Funnel

text: Once a card is on file from a trial, a one-click upsell to the annual plan becomes possible, which he says is rolling out in his school community.
title: How to Scale a Webinar/Events Funnel

text: He suggests building the whole event around upgrading people to annual rather than getting them to buy at all.
title: How to Scale a Webinar/Events Funnel

text: When designing performance pay, he recommends first deciding earnings for ordinary and exceptional performance, with poor performers dismissed, then calculating the incentive percentage needed to produce those earnings.
title: Helping a $5.5M Auto Hail Repair Company Scale to $15M

text: He says achievements and material success are meaningless if they change nothing about your daily life. If they change your day to day, then pursuing them had a purpose.
title: What Money Taught Me That I Couldn't See Before

text: He defines goals almost entirely by asking what the goal would change about his life. If it would change nothing, he likely will not make it a goal.
title: What Money Taught Me That I Couldn't See Before

text: Citing Arthur Brooks, he says fluid-intelligence fields like mathematics peak in the teens and twenties, while pattern-recognition roles such as historians peak later. He thinks explaining, teaching and breaking things down improve with age.
title: What Money Taught Me That I Couldn't See Before

text: He expects his 85-year-old self to still care about being valuable, though how he is valuable may change, and to have more proof and a longer track record than now.
title: What Money Taught Me That I Couldn't See Before

text: He holds strong beliefs loosely and will change them given new information. He says people build a caricature of someone from short online snippets, which he accepts as the nature of short-form content.
title: What Money Taught Me That I Couldn't See Before

text: He optimized for freedom and optionality for a long time, but says you sometimes choose to give up optionality through commitments and dependencies like family. He thinks the point of options is to select the one you want.
title: What Money Taught Me That I Couldn't See Before

text: He thinks young people in the western world are obsessed with independence, freedom and optionality, refusing to commit to a career or anything else. He suggests this may be the most valuable point of the podcast for them.
title: What Money Taught Me That I Couldn't See Before

text: To fix churn, call about 20 customers from the recent cohort who stayed and 20 who left. Ask stayers why they bought, what worried them, and what moment showed them it would be great.
title: He Took Over His Dad's Business and Churn Exploded

text: The most important interview question for retention is what moment made the customer realize the product was going to be great. The why-buy and fear questions mainly help marketing.
title: He Took Over His Dad's Business and Churn Exploded

text: To dig deeper, study monthly subscribers who kept renewing. Annual customers reveal little about retention because they did not churn simply because they could not.
title: He Took Over His Dad's Business and Churn Exploded

text: Once you learn which action retained customers took, all onboarding should be directed toward getting new customers to take that activation action.
title: He Took Over His Dad's Business and Churn Exploded

text: In School, people who join multiple communities and get at least three members into one community reach about 11x lifetime value, so onboarding pushes getting those first three members.
title: He Took Over His Dad's Business and Churn Exploded

text: Finding the activation point is granular work: look at what retained customers did, map the activation point to it, and expect two or three candidates you must then sort out.
title: He Took Over His Dad's Business and Churn Exploded

text: Acquisition.com buys a minority interest in businesses and then deploys his growth model in them; the photography company is one where the firm holds a 20% interest.
title: The Types of Businesses I Like to Buy

text: He prefers service businesses over software, even though software gets hot valuations, because he likes high cash flow. He says services let him change price, product and client experience without much development work.
title: The Types of Businesses I Like to Buy

text: He says service businesses are simple, and margins come easily in them if you know how to deliver value.
title: The Types of Businesses I Like to Buy

text: His current targets are niche e-learning businesses, brick and mortar chains with several successful locations, and tech-enabled services that may have a minor software part. He mentions a fourth but forgets it.
title: The Types of Businesses I Like to Buy

text: With the children's photography business, the firm owns all of it, unlike the other deals. It went from one location to about 13 in roughly a year, and he thinks it may be worth more than all his other businesses combined.
title: The Types of Businesses I Like to Buy

text: When the photography founder came to him he had one location and about 100 B2B customers in a coaching-style business, which Hormozi disliked. After learning studios earned a lot and cost far less to open than they made, he proposed fronting the costs and building them all.
title: The Types of Businesses I Like to Buy

text: He sees the next five to ten years as polar, either in-real-life or AI, with no in-between. He sorts bets into things he is confident will not change and things he is sure will change.
title: ACQ's Business Strategy

text: He keeps investing in Skool because he thinks people will always want to connect in community, even when it is digital. He also owns lots of real estate because he thinks people will always need a place to live.
title: ACQ's Business Strategy

text: On the AI side, he looks for components that will not be disrupted within six to twelve months. He points to proprietary data that cannot be duplicated another way, since a superior data set to train on creates alpha and arbitrage opportunities.
title: ACQ's Business Strategy

text: His money is roughly 80 percent in bets he is confident will not change and 20 percent in small, venture-style bets he thinks have disproportionate upside.
title: ACQ's Business Strategy

text: Hormozi has always been a maximizer rather than an optimizer: once he finds an input-output equation, he wants to push as much input into it as humanly possible instead of fine-tuning it.
title: Maximizing vs. Optimizing

text: He sees competitors who depend on optimizations, such as a required eight hours of sleep, a morning routine, supplements or coffee, as weak and easy to exploit, and he likes competing against them.
title: Maximizing vs. Optimizing

text: He says optimizations turn into superstition, and he holds the extreme view that you should be able to make money with just an internet connection, a laptop and a fold-out chair, with everything else being extra.
title: Maximizing vs. Optimizing

text: He bought a sleep-tracking ring and chased sleep personal records; stressing about missing them made him sleep worse than before tracking. After he dropped the ring, he slept fine the next night.
title: Maximizing vs. Optimizing

text: He still believes in tracking progress in general, but warns against becoming so romantic about optimization routines that you cannot break them. Sometimes you must be violent about it and sacrifice sleep or health during a season.
title: Maximizing vs. Optimizing

text: For about two years he did gym turnarounds, flying around the country and doing a new gym each month, eating gas station food and gaining weight. He says it was temporary, he is in shape now, and it was worth it.
title: Maximizing vs. Optimizing

text: He credits absolute dedication to maximization, until it becomes part of your identity and character, as one of the outsized returns in his life. He says to list what you are unwilling to give up for your dreams, since the person who beats you will give up those things.
title: Maximizing vs. Optimizing

text: For the present moment, his answer to getting ahead fastest is AI, with no caveats. He describes it as applying AI to any function of a business, such as marketing, sales, delivery, finance, recruiting or IT.
title: How to Get Ahead Faster Right Now Using AI

text: AI skills are in high demand from businesses, and AI also gives leverage, since one person can run agents and serve many people. Building AI skills therefore shifts the demand curve in your favor.
title: How to Get Ahead Faster Right Now Using AI

text: He defines technology as something that lowers the value of humans in general while raising the value of an individual human. Base labor is becoming less valuable, while a person who uses AI becomes more valuable.
title: How to Get Ahead Faster Right Now Using AI

text: He thinks the need for lots of years of experience and for degrees and accreditation has been largely dispelled, even at top institutions and more so at lower ones, aside from classic fields like law and accounting.
title: How to Get Ahead Faster Right Now Using AI

text: To fast-track to money, learn everything you can about AI and keep learning. Pick one specific business problem that needs lots of headcount or training to perform, and get AI to do it. Do that and you can earn as much as you want.
title: How to Get Ahead Faster Right Now Using AI

text: Having a billion-dollar AI idea is worth zero dollars by itself. To make it tactical, apply AI to one specific business function.
title: How to Get Ahead Faster Right Now Using AI

text: Businesses have eight functions: marketing, sales, product, customer success or support, IT, recruiting, HR and finance, with legal optional. Small businesses may lack some. Every business needs these to continue, so pick one and apply AI there.
title: How to Get Ahead Faster Right Now Using AI

text: Trying to make everything AI at once is like boiling the ocean. He advises picking a single function instead.
title: How to Get Ahead Faster Right Now Using AI

text: Narrowing your avatar and pricing for that niche can let you charge roughly five times more. Going wide gives more sales volume; going narrow gives premium pricing because the deliverable is specific to that avatar.
title: Niche Down and 5x Your Price

text: If you sell broadly to 100 people and only 10 are the ideal customer, your reputation suffers and you cannot price for the value delivered, since you must price so the mismatched customers are not too upset.
title: Niche Down and 5x Your Price

text: Better to offer free material to everyone and work together once someone fits your ideal customer. He says this brings a stronger brand, more goodwill, higher ascension rates, and selling from your back foot, his preferred way to sell.
title: Niche Down and 5x Your Price

text: Before worrying that a niche is limiting, check its size. He notes there are more YouTube channels above 10k subscribers than gym owners, so that audience alone can support a very lucrative business.
title: Niche Down and 5x Your Price

text: Tracking and publishing graduates' real outcomes, such as median income, lets a business frame its price against the results it delivers. He says this allows much higher pricing, including honest disclosures about people who do not get jobs.
title: They Pass My Exam and Triple Their Income (Then Ghost Me)

text: Think one level up about who the customer is: when institutions buy, they are the customer rather than the individual students. He suggests mapping the whole network of them and aiming for full-time partnerships.
title: They Pass My Exam and Triple Their Income (Then Ghost Me)

text: When negotiating with partners, ask what it would take to make the deal exclusive or lock it in for 5 years. He presents this as the magic question for building an entrenched position.
title: They Pass My Exam and Triple Their Income (Then Ghost Me)

text: To reach institutional buyers, trade shows and conferences are an easy way in because the buyers are there. A higher-end option is hiring a salesperson who already sold into that sector and brings their contacts.
title: They Pass My Exam and Triple Their Income (Then Ghost Me)

text: For larger clients on a fixed fee, set up tiers where each range of size has its own price, and layer them as a waterfall, which he calls a very powerful selling approach.
title: Helping a Data Firm Price Bigger Clients

text: Customers tend to assume they will reach the top tier, thanks to survivorship bias and optimism, yet the blended rate ends up nearer the middle. Make the tiers non-retroactive so each band is charged at its own rate.
title: Helping a Data Firm Price Bigger Clients

text: Tie tiers to a core value metric: something that rises as the customer gets more value from you, such as revenue for e-commerce or number of providers for healthcare practices.
title: Helping a Data Firm Price Bigger Clients

text: Structure it as a fixed fee up to a threshold, then a smaller fee above it. Once they accept the first amount, the rest feels like a shoe-in, since buyers mostly fixate on the first number.
title: Helping a Data Firm Price Bigger Clients

text: Add a very high, small top tier that you expect nobody to reach; it works as a reverse anchor on price. He says he has done this with every software company he has had and it works well.
title: Helping a Data Firm Price Bigger Clients

text: He disagrees that a business cannot scale; any business can, often through a slight permutation of what it does now, such as running more events.
title: Helping a Data Firm Price Bigger Clients

text: When the founder is the bottleneck in a heavy service business, hire a team, list the intangibles you personally provide, and train others to duplicate them; the work becomes recruiting, hiring and training.
title: Helping a Data Firm Price Bigger Clients

text: For high-skilled delivery people, he would usually give a percentage of the profit from events they run so they do not feel underpaid.
title: Helping a Data Firm Price Bigger Clients

text: Rather than changing everything, confront what is hard and learn the skill. Growth past a million a month may mean the constraint becomes advertising, i.e. what share of the market you capture.
title: Helping a Data Firm Price Bigger Clients

text: Stop complaining about results from work you did not do. If you only followed your diet half the month, or only planned content rather than publishing it, missing results should not surprise you.
title: The #1 Trait That Almost Guarantees Success

text: The work does not care about your intentions or planning. He asks what you actually did, as opposed to what you prepared to do.
title: The #1 Trait That Almost Guarantees Success

text: He cites Charlie Munger's speech that inverts success by asking how to guarantee failure. He recalls about seven items, one of which is inconsistency, so being inconsistent is a sure route to failing.
title: The #1 Trait That Almost Guarantees Success

text: Hormozi says that if you rank around number two out of roughly 3,000 reps, you are in the top fraction of one percent, and that is a strong reason to stay with that skill rather than chase other ideas.
title: \"If you went broke today, how would you start over?\"

text: He notes that alternative businesses will always sound sexy and interesting when described, so how appealing they sound should not be trusted as a reason to switch away from something you are proven at.
title: \"If you went broke today, how would you start over?\"

text: He believes e-commerce operators are the best at branding because low ticket prices force them to earn retention and hold up click-through rates at scale.
title: I Spent 7 Years Building a Brand With a Sh*tty Product

text: The shift he describes: rather than making sales to get customers in the short-term sense, you make sales in order to acquire customers who keep buying.
title: I Spent 7 Years Building a Brand With a Sh*tty Product

text: He says Meta's Andromeda ad update demands a large volume of creative, so he recommends building an army of people producing content for you.
title: I Spent 7 Years Building a Brand With a Sh*tty Product

text: To scale ads on a current channel you need more creative. Options: build it yourself until you hit a wall, partner with a huge influencer, or build a horizontal army of many creators.
title: I Spent 7 Years Building a Brand With a Sh*tty Product

text: His order of operations: first fix email on the back end, second confirm repeat purchases by checking what share buy second and third items, third use known lifetime gross profit per customer to set incentives for bringing in people and content.
title: I Spent 7 Years Building a Brand With a Sh*tty Product

text: When he taught gym owners, he hoped they would all end up earning more than his own gyms did, so that nobody compared their results to his.
title: The Real Reason I Can't Scale Two Businesses at Once

text: When selling a tool, the easiest offer is implementation help, such as six or twelve calls to apply the steps. It can also cover the cost of acquiring the customer, making the offer self-liquidating.
title: The Real Reason I Can't Scale Two Businesses at Once

text: His two favorite upsells that always work are more of what the customer just bought, and more help with what they just bought. He says they work about 30 percent of the time, or all the time.
title: The Real Reason I Can't Scale Two Businesses at Once

text: Onboarding for a software tool priced at three or four hundred dollars monthly can probably be sold for around $5,000, since buyers of tools want help.
title: The Real Reason I Can't Scale Two Businesses at Once

text: He describes the perfect long video as around 20 shorts combined around a single theme. Think of a long as a string of sound bites rather than one topic talk.
title: The Real Reason I Can't Scale Two Businesses at Once

text: For his brutally honest advice videos, he reads his best tweets from the previous 30 to 45 days in a row, then explains each. Nearly all of these reach a million views because the quotes are pre-tested.
title: The Real Reason I Can't Scale Two Businesses at Once

text: He suggests that businesses can achieve a 50% conversion rate on inbound leads.
title: \"Why do my employees keep quitting?\"

text: Break a role into stages such as junior, standard and senior, each with a pay bump after a set period or output. Editors can move up after 100 videos and 6 months, then again after another 6 months.
title: How to Set Up Career Paths

text: Repeating the junior, standard, senior ladder across several tracks multiplies the steps. Six tracks with pay bumps give 12 career progressions, which he says keeps people invested much longer.
title: How to Set Up Career Paths

text: He says this ladder approach works well in med spas and nail salons, where levels of aesthetician each have junior, standard and senior versions, giving many progression steps.
title: How to Set Up Career Paths

text: Tie each promotion to a mini certification created in house. It unlocks more expensive, complex procedures, which raises hourly billables, and workers feel they are always learning and progressing.
title: How to Set Up Career Paths

text: He says feeling lost when you attempt something new is normal, because if you already knew what to do, it would not count as growth.
title: It's Okay to Not Know What You're Doing

text: He strongly dislikes mental medication, believing it is over-prescribed and that people self-diagnose online. He thinks people treat ordinary human states like hunger, sadness or frustration as defects, driven by a social norm against them.
title: It's Okay to Not Know What You're Doing

text: He holds that nothing is wrong with you, and questions what you gain by accepting a something-is-wrong label. He tries to remove the word should from his vocabulary, asking according to whom.
title: It's Okay to Not Know What You're Doing

text: He rejects any if-then structure for happiness, such as the idea that changing your outside conditions or taking a pill will make you feel better.
title: It's Okay to Not Know What You're Doing

text: He has seen people close to him damage their lives by hopping between antidepressants and piling up pill combinations. He says America turns to the pill bottle first, unlike the UK.
title: It's Okay to Not Know What You're Doing

text: He argues that anxiety or heavy drinking often points to a specific stressor. In his view, you should confront that underlying cause rather than search for a medication or treat the symptom as the problem.
title: It's Okay to Not Know What You're Doing

text: He believes many people waste their lives hunting for an answer that does not exist, because they do not accept reality and think something is wrong with them.
title: It's Okay to Not Know What You're Doing

text: He believes friends who belittle someone's attempts to change will become increasingly rejecting as that person pursues their desired identity, eventually leaving little shared ground.
title: How to Know When It's Time to Cut a Friend

text: In his opinion, a friendship whose conversations revolve exclusively around shared history is a signal that it may be time to end the relationship.
title: How to Know When It's Time to Cut a Friend

text: Truly seeing what someone went through to become who they are helps you understand their behavior. Without that understanding, we tend to assume people are simply evil, though most are not and act as they do because of past reinforcement or punishment.
title: How I Diffused a Decade-Long Family Fight

text: When he returned home from college freshman year, a familiar fight with a relative was triggered. He felt nothing, told her he understood and was sorry she had a hard life, and she broke down crying because she felt understood.
title: How I Diffused a Decade-Long Family Fight

text: Douglas Murray told him that Christopher Hitchens once said that in life we must choose our regrets. Hormozi noted it down right away at Murray's apartment and reflected on it for about a year.
title: How I Diffused a Decade-Long Family Fight

text: Writing ideas down when they arrive matters because a tipsy mind will not remember them; the note he made was the trigger for a year of thinking.
title: How I Diffused a Decade-Long Family Fight

text: Because opportunity cost is built into existence, choosing one option rules out another, so even a correct choice leaves an open loop of what if. Regrets are therefore inevitable, not just a result of bad decisions.
title: How I Diffused a Decade-Long Family Fight

text: To get more outlier videos rather than an occasional one, study the game of YouTube more, including the hooks, since the aim is consistently producing videos that break out.
title: How to Get Better at YouTube

text: He suspects weak videos may not have been edited for retention, and suggests using open loops and a clear road map inside the video.
title: How to Get Better at YouTube

text: His rule of thumb for opening a video is the five Ps: promise, pain, proof, picture, plan. Open with the big promise, the pain avoided, evidence you can deliver, then a visual road map of the video.
title: How to Get Better at YouTube

text: Plan and picture are nearly the same thing; the picture is just the visual version of the plan, though a plan can exist without a picture.
title: How to Get Better at YouTube

text: Proof matters especially in B2B and education. The credibility you show should relate to the video topic: for a sales video, citing having over 200 salespeople and scaling sales across several businesses beats citing portfolio profits.
title: How to Get Better at YouTube

text: Almost everything in education comes down to the messenger. He notes Elon Musk could post something trivial and still get around 10 million views because of who he is, not the content.
title: How to Get Better at YouTube

text: A common misconception in education is that the message exists apart from the messenger; he says they are consumed together in the same context, which is why proof matters.
title: How to Get Better at YouTube

text: He had Guinness judges at his event so a third party, whose business rests on the credibility of its claims, could confirm the sales were legitimate.
title: How to Get Better at YouTube

text: Initial offers can be structured so bonuses or discounts unlock only when the customer takes a required action, and guarantees can depend on three actions being completed.
title: “We Have More Demand Than We Can Handle. How Do I Get to $10M?”

text: The initial offer shapes the application, the sales motion and the first activation point in the business. Collect fast cash and tie it to the customer completing specific required steps.
title: “We Have More Demand Than We Can Handle. How Do I Get to $10M?”

text: When asked whether conditions on an offer can really be enforced, he says to state the facts, tell the truth and be upfront about the conditions.
title: “We Have More Demand Than We Can Handle. How Do I Get to $10M?”

text: Achieving your goals is a general skill that can open doors to new relationships, and sometimes you must give up part of what you currently have in order to get what you want.
title: How to Become Your Future Self Faster

text: Whatever you are struggling with in your business, he says someone else has already faced and solved the same problem.
title: How to Become Your Future Self Faster

text: If your business is driven by sales, Hormozi says the CEO should know how sales works firsthand. Otherwise whoever runs sales holds leverage over you and can make demands, like threatening to leave unless paid double.
title: Helping a Real Estate Company Scale

text: Hormozi says a strong closer can also come from a mission-driven persona: someone who wants to help and to win at whatever they do, rather than a psychopath type. He cites Jacob, who rose from call floor to setting to closing.
title: Helping a Real Estate Company Scale

text: Home service businesses are among the worst offenders at cost-plus pricing, which he links to the low industry averages in trades like roofing, plumbing and HVAC. Customers do not care what the job costs the provider.
title: Why Cost-Plus Pricing Is Killing Your Roofing Business

text: Cost-plus pricing gives a disincentive to cut costs: raising costs raises absolute profit dollars on each job, even though net profit percentage falls, so there is little reason to lower prices.
title: Why Cost-Plus Pricing Is Killing Your Roofing Business

text: In home services, customers mostly fear going over budget, the work failing long term, and the job dragging on too slowly. He says to pick one or more of these and guarantee against it.
title: Why Cost-Plus Pricing Is Killing Your Roofing Business

text: When a business guarantees against the customer's downside, the offer stands apart from competitors, and the customer is willing to pay a premium for that insurance.
title: Why Cost-Plus Pricing Is Killing Your Roofing Business

text: A business charging the highest prices must accept that some customers will decline. Hormozi says the tradeoff is earning three, four, or five times as much when it does sell.
title: Helping a $3M Balloon Arch Business Fix Their Offer

text: A recent customer departure over price can distort an owner's judgment about raising prices. Hormozi warns against letting that single event determine the pricing decision.
title: Helping a $3M Balloon Arch Business Fix Their Offer

text: Hormozi considers pricing by adding a markup to costs almost always the weakest approach. He defines value-based pricing as charging according to customers' willingness to pay.
title: Helping a $3M Balloon Arch Business Fix Their Offer

text: For businesses at $1–3 million in revenue, Hormozi recommends narrowing customer focus and standardizing delivery around the segment with the strongest lifetime-value-to-acquisition-cost ratio.
title: Helping a $3M Balloon Arch Business Fix Their Offer

text: Commercial buyers may push suppliers into price comparisons that treat their work as interchangeable. Hormozi recommends broadening the discussion to overall business returns, including coordination effort and the buyer's time.
title: Helping a $3M Balloon Arch Business Fix Their Offer

text: Hormozi describes the mockery aimed at people doing something different as group think, the worst kind of shared thinking where everyone holds the least useful beliefs of the others. He says it only lowers the bar for everyone.
title: Why You Should Ignore the People Closest to You

text: When someone says what you are doing is lame, he suggests agreeing with them and carrying on. Their game differs from yours, and they want you to follow their rules so they can beat you at the status game of their small circle.
title: Why You Should Ignore the People Closest to You

text: Hormozi says that if you are playing a wider game with more players, the information coming in from those close to you comes disproportionately from people you are not competing against. He therefore calls it noise and irrelevant.
title: Why You Should Ignore the People Closest to You

text: When choosing how to fix a lead problem, he thinks first about the smallest operational change: build on something already known to work. Example: invite likely customers onto an existing podcast as guests via outbound, for high response and show rates.
title: Why Your Leads Are Feast or Famine (And How to Fix It)

text: For a conference booth, he tries to get the spot right where attendees enter and turn right. He says about 70% of people turn right, and organizers usually price booths by size alone, so that spot yields more return.
title: Why Your Leads Are Feast or Famine (And How to Fix It)

text: He suggests running a giveaway at a conference booth, revealed on the second or third day, so people must hand over contact details to enter. This collects leads throughout the event.
title: Why Your Leads Are Feast or Famine (And How to Fix It)

text: He likes framing a giveaway prize with a value sandwich: it is described as better than one lower-value item and less than a higher-value one, giving a sense of up and down value.
title: Why Your Leads Are Feast or Famine (And How to Fix It)

text: When a conference asks for a speaking fee, he says you can propose alternatives: send one email to the attendee list, or offer slides in exchange for emails, then ask a few extra questions to sort out the most engaged audience members.
title: Why Your Leads Are Feast or Famine (And How to Fix It)

text: Staying driven and in control is a skill built over time. Early on he had general motivation but no skill, and he got better at pursuing his goal with practice.
title: The Biggest Predictor of Future Success

text: Early on, he says, you can wander and try lots of activity to see what gives feedback, then move in the direction that responds.
title: The Biggest Predictor of Future Success

text: He was a high achiever early: many AP credits, finishing college in 3 years with honors, vice president of the powerlifting team, and fraternity president.
title: The Biggest Predictor of Future Success

text: Not having succeeded earlier in life has no bearing on whether you can succeed now. The work required is the same, and whenever you begin, what came before that moment does not matter.
title: The Biggest Predictor of Future Success

text: Even with zero momentum, if you do the work it still works. He grants that momentum makes things easier.
title: The Biggest Predictor of Future Success

text: Generalizing from discipline in one area, like school or exercise, to another, like a job, is plausible though not guaranteed.
title: The Biggest Predictor of Future Success

text: Stack wins starting from the lowest common denominator. For someone struggling badly, getting out of bed counts as a win. Then add weight to your goals gradually, like adding weight to a bar.
title: The Biggest Predictor of Future Success

text: Your bar keeps moving because your standards for excellence keep improving, as a toddler's approximate mom is celebrated but a ten-year-old's is not. Use your own standards, not someone else's.
title: The Biggest Predictor of Future Success

text: Hormozi's rule of thumb for everyone: build your process for cold audiences and it works everywhere, whereas a process built only for warm audiences works only on warm ones.
title: Stop Using a Warm Sales Process on Cold Leads

text: Using a warm sales process on cold leads is a mismatch he names as a problem, since inbound leads already in a buying cycle behave differently from outbound ones.
title: Stop Using a Warm Sales Process on Cold Leads

text: When everyone on a small team is doing everything and the owner is stuck chasing people to do their jobs, he thinks it is likely a roles and responsibilities problem that needs workflow organized.
title: My Team Is Spread Too Thin and I Can't Scale

text: He names small agency owners as one of his favorite sources of good marketing leaders, since they enjoy marketing, practice it in spare time, and can run a tiny team.
title: My Team Is Spread Too Thin and I Can't Scale

text: Agency owners with mid-six-figure agencies often take home little, around 100,000 a year with high stress, so leaving to work for a brand can appeal to them.
title: My Team Is Spread Too Thin and I Can't Scale

text: He prefers a marketer who never had an organic brand, since they learned to make money cold and can then apply that skill to a brand. He calls this a good avatar for a scrappier starter marketer.
title: My Team Is Spread Too Thin and I Can't Scale

text: Business owners can remain constrained by low prices, unsuitable employee compensation, or serving unsuitable or excessive customer types because they fear losing customers, employees, or revenue when they change.
title: Four Traps Keep Businesses Small. He's in One.

text: Hormozi says his persistence developed incrementally: continuing through business difficulties felt preferable to returning to work he disliked.
title: Four Traps Keep Businesses Small. He's in One.

text: He thinks feelings of being an impostor arise from insufficient work. He describes responding to his own sensitivity to those feelings by doing enough work to feel his credibility is defensible.
title: Four Traps Keep Businesses Small. He's in One.

text: Hormozi describes sharing methods that produced his own results without promising equivalent outcomes for others. He prefers explaining his experience over prescribing what another person ought to do.
title: Four Traps Keep Businesses Small. He's in One.

text: Because platforms now work on interest-based distribution, a strong piece of content gets shown to people interested in its topic. So to attract a certain audience, make content about that topic.
title: Helping a $3M/Year Business Owner Make Better Content

text: If you want life coaching customers, he says to make your content about life coaching: its philosophies, its frameworks, and how to get life coaching clients, including the frameworks taught inside your training.
title: Helping a $3M/Year Business Owner Make Better Content

text: He says worrying about giving away secrets in content does not matter: most people never act on it, and those who do and get results will want more from you.
title: Helping a $3M/Year Business Owner Make Better Content

text: Changing what you say in your videos changes who you attract. He thinks a provictim narrative draws victims, so the fix is to change the message, not the whole approach.
title: Helping a $3M/Year Business Owner Make Better Content

text: He advises talking in content about the thing you sell, rather than avoiding it because of the audience it currently attracts.
title: Helping a $3M/Year Business Owner Make Better Content

text: He decides which podcasts to accept largely by interview quality, and he thinks in-person recordings outperform Zoom ones. In his view even the best Zoom episode is roughly as good as the worst in-person one.
title: How I Choose Which Podcasts to Go On

text: He says he tires out faster and gets less interested during long Zoom conversations, which he attributes to staring at a screen. He enjoys longer in-person conversations more.
title: How I Choose Which Podcasts to Go On

text: There is power in knowing you are doing everything possible to win. If you can say you controlled the controllable, you can accept uncontrollable events, like a launch hit by bad luck, with a clear conscience.
title: Volume Negates Luck. Violence Is the Answer

text: He thinks nothing is more satisfying for a man than knowing he gave everything he had to an endeavor he considered meaningful, leaving nothing in the tank.
title: Volume Negates Luck. Violence Is the Answer

text: He and his wife often repeat that a man must have a quest: something to move toward, whether being the best father, musician, businessman, or anything else.
title: Volume Negates Luck. Violence Is the Answer

text: He thinks people become lost and hopeless when they are aimless and never apply their capacity for violence to a meaningful pursuit.
title: Volume Negates Luck. Violence Is the Answer

text: The destruction he means is figurative: it targets the ideas, doubts and imagined risks in your way, not people. He uses strong language deliberately.
title: Volume Negates Luck. Violence Is the Answer

text: He considers having someone in your corner who believes in a better version of you one of the rarest gifts in life.
title: Volume Negates Luck. Violence Is the Answer

text: He suggests everyone wants a partner who rewards the good fight, and he thinks dying while trying is about as good a life as anyone can ask for.
title: Volume Negates Luck. Violence Is the Answer

text: If sales reps are already booked out, improving the landing page or ad click-through rate accomplishes nothing, because the choke point is sales. Fix sales capacity first, then push more volume into the front end through marketing.
title: Helping a $4M Consulting Firm Grow Its Exit Multiple

text: Not knowing how to do something is ignorance rather than a focus problem, and that is acceptable because everyone lacks knowledge they should have.
title: Helping a $4M Consulting Firm Grow Its Exit Multiple

text: Letting more people know about your business is unlikely to make you less money, so posting more content is a sensible move.
title: Helping a $4M Consulting Firm Grow Its Exit Multiple

text: His stated approach to his own content: use it only if it is useful, treat it as a documentary showing what is happening rather than a sermon, and expect it to change if he changes his mind.
title: Why Most People Never Win (Even With Good Advice)

text: He calls the ability to tell which things to use and which to discard the greatest skill, describing it as the core story of noise versus signal.
title: Why Most People Never Win (Even With Good Advice)

text: He has focused heavily on behavior because advice that cannot be turned into what to do is not useful. He thinks value is most crystallized as do this instead of that.
title: Why Most People Never Win (Even With Good Advice)

text: The best version of your life is not copying someone. It is applying principles that generalize across domains, with the discernment to fit nuance to your situation. He credits this skill for his outsized returns.
title: Why Most People Never Win (Even With Good Advice)

text: He says he has never bought from anyone in the alternative education space without getting an exceptional return. Even from bad experiences he noted what he would never do to a customer.
title: Why Most People Never Win (Even With Good Advice)

text: His gym price-raise approach suits service businesses with trainers, classes or semi-privates, not facility-usage gyms. A gym owner who went from 29 to 200 dollars a month lost 90% of members by ignoring that context.
title: Why Most People Never Win (Even With Good Advice)

text: He says winners keep winning because they find a silver lining even in terrible experiences, and that giving advice with all conditions attached would take ten minutes of disclaimers.
title: Why Most People Never Win (Even With Good Advice)

text: He wants to be like dwarven steel, which absorbs only what makes it stronger. Many people lose because they try to prove something did not work instead of asking how to make it work.
title: Why Most People Never Win (Even With Good Advice)

text: He says persuasion fundamentals learned in the disreputable education market are powerful; if you can sell there against heavy buyer resistance, selling something like insurance becomes easy.
title: Why Most People Never Win (Even With Good Advice)

text: Passion is not found but created: you begin doing something you are bad at, improve, come to enjoy it, and only later do people call it a found passion.
title: Why You Don't Find Your Passion, You Create It

text: When he opened his gym, his interest in it faded because it turned into work. He had earlier been choosing among fitness, test prep and frozen yogurt as his supposed passions.
title: Why You Don't Find Your Passion, You Create It

text: A later mentor, a successful businessman, told him never to build work around your passion because it will become work. Hormozi thinks about this more than he shares it.
title: Why You Don't Find Your Passion, You Create It

text: Chasing passion assumes your daily work is whatever currently interests you, which may not make money. New activities mean you will be bad at them and likely dislike them at first, so behavior has to change.
title: Why You Don't Find Your Passion, You Create It

text: He prefers assuming everything will be unpleasant and that you will eventually get good. Competence brings status, and enjoying that status outweighs the pain of the work, creating a loop that keeps you going.
title: Why You Don't Find Your Passion, You Create It

text: Set the baseline expectation that things are hard and aim to become someone who does them anyway, rather than waiting for perfect conditions. Whatever condition you start in was the perfect one.
title: Why You Don't Find Your Passion, You Create It

text: Hormozi says that about 20 minutes of preparation for a meeting can make a person seem dramatically smarter, in his words around 50 IQ points.
title: How to Appear 50 IQ Points Smarter in Meetings with Just 20 Minutes...

text: Before one of his three lifetime consulting days, he spent roughly four hours researching the client, reviewing every landing page and offer, and produced seven pages of ideas. He walked through them line by line, and the client was shocked by the preparation.
title: How to Appear 50 IQ Points Smarter in Meetings with Just 20 Minutes...

text: He aims for people to get more from him than they give him, and he treats a few hours of prep as trivial next to the value it creates.
title: How to Appear 50 IQ Points Smarter in Meetings with Just 20 Minutes...

text: He uses a cheap twist kitchen timer on his desk, about seven dollars, and calls it probably his biggest focus hack so far. He sets it when he begins working.
title: How to Appear 50 IQ Points Smarter in Meetings with Just 20 Minutes...

text: Setting the timer to a guessed duration, such as 35 minutes, trains him to get better at predicting how long a task will take.
title: How to Appear 50 IQ Points Smarter in Meetings with Just 20 Minutes...

text: In a roll-up, get an option on 100% of the business plus drag-along rights to sell above a set price, with everyone agreeing upfront. Otherwise the greediest holdout can hurt everyone at closing, which he says he knows from experience.
title: Make an Offer So Good They Feel Stupid Saying No

text: If you want to keep your own IP when selling businesses to an acquirer, treat it as a negotiation: for example, grant the buyer a free license limited by time period or by territory.
title: Make an Offer So Good They Feel Stupid Saying No

text: If you want to build something big, he suggests reserving roughly two-thirds of the equity pie for future talent rather than spending it all now, since the best people are likely to arrive later.
title: Never Give Real Equity (Do This Instead)

text: Revenue retention measures the percentage of revenue generated from a customer cohort in one year that is retained into the following year.

text: Without revenue retention, an entrepreneur is trapped in the sales business instead of building a compounding resale business.

text: Logo retention measures the percentage of customer accounts retained over time, whereas revenue retention measures the dollar value retained from that same customer cohort.

text: Logo retention inherently decays over time and can never exceed 100% due to involuntary structural churn such as relocation, business closures, or employee turnover.
title: What Makes The Perfect Business (5 Things)

text: Involuntary churn occurs from natural operational events like business dissolution or death, while voluntary churn happens when dissatisfied clients deliberately leave because of poor service quality.

text: Net revenue retention can exceed 100% if existing customers expand their spending enough to outweigh the revenue lost from departing clients.

text: To achieve net revenue retention above 100%, provide clear pathways for lower-tier customers to upgrade their spending and qualify prospects to verify genuine need before closing sales.

text: Across subscription businesses, the highest cancellation rate occurs in the first thirty days, with initial churn exceeding 20% across all categories.
title: What Makes The Perfect Business (5 Things)

text: Recurring subscription churn experiences steep secondary drop-offs around month three at roughly 10%, before declining to nearly 2% monthly after month six across all categories.
title: What Makes The Perfect Business (5 Things)

text: To maximize lifetime value in recurring models, direct operational effort toward guiding customers through the first thirty days and third month to reach the six-month mark.
title: What Makes The Perfect Business (5 Things)

text: Standalone educational programs, roofing services, and vehicle sales lack retention stickiness because customers complete the transaction and do not require immediate repeat purchases.
title: What Makes The Perfect Business (5 Things)

text: Combining educational communities with recurring consumable content converts one-time instruction into sticky ongoing subscriptions that members pay month after month.
title: What Makes The Perfect Business (5 Things)

text: A company with high retention requires acquiring far fewer customers to achieve identical top-line revenue compared to a high-churn business that must constantly replace lost accounts.
title: What Makes The Perfect Business (5 Things)

text: Attempting to rapidly increase customer acquisition in a single year often inflates marginal acquisition cost two to three times higher than acquiring customers steadily over multiple years.
title: What Makes The Perfect Business (5 Things)

text: Retaining existing customer cohorts unlocks compounding revenue, creating predictable future cash flows and higher overall profitability without frantic vehicle switching.
title: What Makes The Perfect Business (5 Things)

title: What Makes The Perfect Business (5 Things)

text: Hormozi reflected on the nature of mental toughness following the unexpected death of his mother.
title: If You Have a Hard Life, Watch This

text: Hormozi defines mental toughness as the likelihood that an adverse event causes an individual to act against their own long-term objectives.
title: If You Have a Hard Life, Watch This

text: Mental toughness operates on a measurable continuum rather than a binary state, where higher toughness reflects a minimal behavioral reaction to negative circumstances.
title: If You Have a Hard Life, Watch This

text: Overall mental toughness consists of four distinct behavioral dimensions—tolerance, fortitude, resilience, and adaptability—which provide an accurate assessment only when evaluated in combination.
title: If You Have a Hard Life, Watch This

text: Tolerance measures the volume or duration of hardship someone can endure before their conduct deviates from their normal baseline.
title: If You Have a Hard Life, Watch This

text: Fortitude represents the degree of behavioral disruption or how severely someone deteriorates once their tolerance threshold has been crossed.
title: If You Have a Hard Life, Watch This

text: Resilience is the duration needed for someone to restabilize their behavior back to baseline following an emotional disruption.
title: If You Have a Hard Life, Watch This

text: Hormozi suggests that prolonged suffering after a tragedy does not demonstrate greater love, and people possess agency over how long they choose to mourn.
title: If You Have a Hard Life, Watch This

text: Adaptability reflects whether a person stabilizes at a higher, equal, or lower behavioral baseline compared to before an adverse event occurred.
title: If You Have a Hard Life, Watch This

text: Trauma is defined as any lasting behavioral alteration resulting from an aversive experience, which can produce either constructive or destructive long-term patterns.
title: If You Have a Hard Life, Watch This

text: Since adversities are inevitable, individuals can intentionally use painful events as positive catalysts to develop greater behavioral capability.
title: If You Have a Hard Life, Watch This

text: Deconstructing mental toughness into explicit behavioral elements allows people to cultivate it as a trainable skill instead of treating it as an unchangeable identity.
title: If You Have a Hard Life, Watch This

text: To develop tolerance, prioritize being more frustrated by relinquishing personal self-control than by the external provocation itself, keeping baseline behavior intact.
title: If You Have a Hard Life, Watch This

text: To increase fortitude, notice behavioral deviations immediately and review past negative consequences to stop a downward cascade before compounding poor choices occur.
title: If You Have a Hard Life, Watch This

text: To improve resilience, uncouple emotional feelings from physical conduct, focusing entirely on resuming baseline habits promptly regardless of inner mood.
title: If You Have a Hard Life, Watch This

text: To build adaptability, ask how hardship can be utilized constructively, adopting the deliberate actions an admired fictional protagonist would take toward a triumphant ending.
title: If You Have a Hard Life, Watch This

text: Emotions like guilt and shame offer utility only while driving positive behavioral adjustment; lingering in them afterward yields no functional benefit.
title: If You Have a Hard Life, Watch This

text: Emotional maturity is defined as the trained capability to experience negative feelings without translating them into harmful conduct toward oneself or others.
