title: 5 Ways To Increase Lead Quality (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Targeting by zip code, income level, or profession is the first lever for raising lead quality; wealthier zip codes also attract more competitor spend and raise costs.
title: 5 Ways To Increase Lead Quality (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Requiring more steps before a prospect reaches a sales call filters for higher intent, because people who take more action are in more pain and more motivated to buy.
title: 5 Ways To Increase Lead Quality (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: A straight-to-call offer produces more qualified prospects than a giveaway opt-in, though a giveaway generates far more volume and can still be profitable with the right monetization system behind it.
title: 5 Ways To Increase Lead Quality (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Adding an application before granting access to a sales call raises lead quality; paragraph-style answers require more effort and yield higher quality than checkbox questions.
title: 5 Ways To Increase Lead Quality (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Application questions should get prospects to state their goal, admit they have a problem, reveal their biggest unknowns, and confirm willingness to invest in a solution.
title: 5 Ways To Increase Lead Quality (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Including a minimum spend threshold in an application (e.g., asking if they are willing to invest at least half the actual price) sets expectations and filters out price-sensitive leads before the call.
title: 5 Ways To Increase Lead Quality (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Providing genuine tactical value inside the ad itself is the fifth lever; a prospect who has already benefited from free content arrives with stronger trust and views the seller as an authority.
title: 5 Ways To Increase Lead Quality (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Hormozi's personal default is to start with the broadest possible targeting and maximum volume, then build offers, upsells, and indoctrination sequences on the back end rather than restricting the front end.
title: 5 Ways To Increase Lead Quality (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Operators should know their revenue-per-dollar-spent at day 15, day 30, and day 60 for every lead source; without those numbers, marketing decisions are much harder to make.
title: 5 Ways To Increase Lead Quality (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: The right time to add lead-quality friction is when volume is so high that prospect quality is unacceptably low, or when the team lacks the operational capacity to handle the existing flow.
title: 5 Ways To Increase Lead Quality (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Hormozi prefers placing responsibility for profitability on the monetization model and sales sequence rather than on front-end marketing restrictions; he believes this approach tends to produce more revenue.
title: 5 Ways To Increase Lead Quality (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: He applied the wide-net-then-optimize model across several businesses: a gym, a supplement company, Gym Launch, and an online fitness model that moved seven-figure gym owners online at roughly one-fifth the cost per lead.
title: 5 Ways To Increase Lead Quality (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: To change behavior, change the environment first. Removing someone from the context where a habit lives is more effective than willpower alone.
title: 'What now?' [Ep 009]

text: Vietnam-era data suggests that changing environment produced roughly a 90% success rate in dropping heroin use, while U.S. recovery centers see roughly 90% relapse when people return home.
title: 'What now?' [Ep 009]

text: Patience is not a feeling; he defines it as knowing what to do in the meantime while waiting. Operationalizing the word makes it actionable.
title: 'What now?' [Ep 009]

text: He defines love as how much someone is willing to sacrifice to maintain a relationship, making an otherwise abstract word measurable.
title: 'What now?' [Ep 009]

text: He used every advertising method described in his book to market the book itself, treating the launch as a live demonstration of its own concepts.
title: 'What now?' [Ep 009]

text: The book launch drove roughly 137,000 sign-ups from paid ads, 104,000 from affiliates, across 27,000 affiliate promoters.
title: 'What now?' [Ep 009]

text: He added a referral incentive: refer 10 people and receive two bonus chapters not included in the public release.
title: 'What now?' [Ep 009]

text: For future books he intends to continue the meta-theme of using the book's own concepts to market and promote the book.
title: 'What now?' [Ep 009]

text: One of One means doing only what you can do; One of Zero means doing what no one else would do, or what you are not even sure you can do yet.
title: 'What now?' [Ep 009]

text: He thinks the best content rule is to say only what you could say and show only what you could show, making output impossible to replicate.
title: 'What now?' [Ep 009]

text: Mathematically, one divided by zero is undefined; he uses that as a metaphor for work that goes beyond conventional definition or expectation.
title: 'What now?' [Ep 009]

text: He believes the four markers of a great podcast interview are: host rapport, host familiarity with the guest's work, quality of follow-on questions, and comfort letting silence exist.
title: 'What now?' [Ep 009]

text: When a host simply reads the next prepared question instead of diving deeper, the conversation becomes a series of short clips rather than a real exchange.
title: 'What now?' [Ep 009]

text: He thinks the best hosts let a pause sit after an answer, which often draws out the real insight or crystallization of thinking from the guest.
title: 'What now?' [Ep 009]

text: His biggest personal unlock over the past year has been redefining winning as working as hard as he can on a thing, rather than an external outcome.
title: 'What now?' [Ep 009]

text: He thinks fear and punishment are the strongest short-term motivators but cannot sustain marathon-length effort; a redefined sense of winning is needed for the long run.
title: 'What now?' [Ep 009]

text: Because he does not believe in legacy or being remembered thousands of years from now, he had to make the act of working as hard as possible the reward itself.
title: 'What now?' [Ep 009]

text: He measures perfect work by imagining a future version of himself with full context, skills, and resources, and asking what that person would consider maximum effort on this project.
title: 'What now?' [Ep 009]

text: Holding that standard of maximum effort means he can pursue very few projects at once; many things simply will not get done, which he sees as a necessary trade-off.
title: 'What now?' [Ep 009]

text: The biggest mistake content creators make is letting the algorithm take over: they post one off-brand topic that gets likes and gradually become a channel about something they do not actually care about.
title: 'What now?' [Ep 009]

text: He thinks comedians and philosophers are the two great truth-tellers of society, and considers comedy one of the most philanthropic careers because its purpose is to bring joy.
title: 'What now?' [Ep 009]

text: His two major projects for the next two years are a third book and the One of Zero brand; he expects the third book to help a lot of people make money.
title: 'What now?' [Ep 009]

text: Post-launch, his plan is more of what was working before, done better — summarized as more, better — alongside the two new projects.
title: 'What now?' [Ep 009]

text: Becoming a billionaire requires owning something worth a billion dollars, not earning a billion in income — wealth is built through equity appreciation, not salary accumulation.
title: How Billionaires Make Their Billions

text: When a business grows its annual profit by one million dollars and trades at a 10x multiple, the owner's net worth rises by ten million — far more than the after-tax cash they actually receive.
title: How Billionaires Make Their Billions

text: The after-tax cash received from a profit increase is much smaller than the corresponding increase in equity value, so obsessing over passive side income instead of growing your core business is a poor trade.
title: How Billionaires Make Their Billions

text: To reach billionaire status an owner needs roughly 70–100 million in EBITDA, since companies of that size typically trade at around 15 times earnings, putting equity value at or above one billion.
title: How Billionaires Make Their Billions

text: Generating that level of EBITDA requires producing approximately 1.3–1.5 million dollars per week in profit, which at a 30% margin implies roughly 300 million dollars in annual top-line revenue.
title: How Billionaires Make Their Billions

text: The size of your goal shapes how you think and plan: someone targeting 100,000 dollars breaks the world into tiny units, while someone targeting 10 million is forced to think in large-scale systems and high-ticket offers.
title: How Billionaires Make Their Billions

text: If you cannot identify what to sell for 10,000 dollars, figure out what creates 100,000 dollars of value for a customer — you can then price at roughly one-tenth of that value.
title: How Billionaires Make Their Billions

text: Insufficient earnings usually trace back to insufficient value delivered, not to execution or hustle problems.
title: How Billionaires Make Their Billions

text: Finance professionals build wealth by accepting large pools of capital, generating returns above what they pay investors, and pocketing the spread — a model that scales independently of personal labor hours.
title: How Billionaires Make Their Billions

text: A buyer pays a high multiple for a growing business because compounding annual growth over several years produces total earnings that often exceed the purchase price, while the asset itself also appreciates substantially.
title: How Billionaires Make Their Billions

text: Using leverage — putting down a fraction of the purchase price and financing the rest — dramatically amplifies the effective return on a business acquisition when the asset grows as projected.
title: How Billionaires Make Their Billions

text: Hormozi would not pursue any opportunity capped at 100 million dollars annually; he only targets opportunities that are not limited by personal time, serve a very large market, carry very high gross margins, and play out over a very long time horizon.
title: How Billionaires Make Their Billions

text: To think like a billionaire, an entrepreneur should set goals large enough that they are forced to consider leverage, scalable markets, and long time horizons — the goal size itself changes the strategy.
title: How Billionaires Make Their Billions

text: There are exactly seven categories of things that can be sold: products, services, access, attention, risk, money, and endorsements/brands — each available in physical and digital form, yielding 14 total sellable types.
title: 'I'm Broke, What Should I Sell?'

text: A digital product is something like a PDF; a physical product is something like a water bottle. The format changes the delivery, not the underlying category.
title: 'I'm Broke, What Should I Sell?'

text: Services in the digital realm include producing ads or buying media for clients — activities that occur and are delivered in digital space.
title: 'I'm Broke, What Should I Sell?'

text: Access as a category means leasing entry to something — a physical building or a digital content library like a streaming service.
title: 'I'm Broke, What Should I Sell?'

text: Attention is a sellable commodity: physical attention is a billboard, digital attention is social-platform advertising — both involve selling eyeballs to an audience.
title: 'I'm Broke, What Should I Sell?'

text: Risk can be sold as a paid guarantee or warranty on a physical product, or as cyber-threat insurance in the digital realm — AppleCare is an example of a paid guarantee.
title: 'I'm Broke, What Should I Sell?'

text: The entire banking industry is built on buying and selling money; the price charged for that money is the interest rate.
title: 'I'm Broke, What Should I Sell?'

text: An endorsement or brand is sellable: letting someone use your logo for a revenue share in the physical world, or a verified badge on a platform in the digital world, both transfer status for a fee.
title: 'I'm Broke, What Should I Sell?'

text: Offerings can combine multiple categories simultaneously — a live concert sells access plus physical products like drinks and shirts, and the recorded version adds a digital product layer.
title: 'I'm Broke, What Should I Sell?'

text: Choosing what to sell comes down to two things: the resources you have available, and the skills, knowledge, or experience you already possess.
title: 'I'm Broke, What Should I Sell?'

text: Even first-time entrepreneurs carry more expertise than they realize: knowledge absorbed from parents, people who raised them, and early odd jobs is a legitimate starting inventory of skills.
title: 'I'm Broke, What Should I Sell?'

text: When starting with very limited capital, physical products and software are usually out of reach; selling time through services is typically the most accessible starting point.
title: 'I'm Broke, What Should I Sell?'

text: The ideal first or next thing to sell is the offer where you deliver the most value to someone while it costs you the least — that intersection is the sweet spot.
title: 'I'm Broke, What Should I Sell?'

text: The Delivery Cube has six frames that let a business owner adjust how valuable, scalable, or profitable any offer is without changing the core product.
title: 'I'm Broke, What Should I Sell?'

text: Delivery Cube frame 1 is group size: one-to-one, small group, or one-to-many — each format carries a different perceived value and a different revenue ceiling.
title: 'I'm Broke, What Should I Sell?'

text: Delivery Cube frame 2 is fulfillment mode: DIY (do it yourself) scales unlimitedly but commands lower prices; DWY (done with you) sits in the middle; DFY (done for you) is typically the most expensive and easiest to sell but the hardest to deliver.
title: 'I'm Broke, What Should I Sell?'

text: Delivery Cube frame 3 is support medium: chat, email, phone, or live video — email support is far more scalable while live video support is far more valuable.
title: 'I'm Broke, What Should I Sell?'

text: Delivery Cube frame 4 is consumption format: visual, audio, live, recorded, or text — live and in-person is perceived as most valuable and least scalable; recorded digital content is most scalable and least valuable.
title: 'I'm Broke, What Should I Sell?'

text: Delivery Cube frame 5 is speed and convenience: variables include hours of availability, days per week, and guaranteed response time — businesses can choose to absorb inefficiency so customers never wait, or maximize staff utilization by having customers wait.
title: 'I'm Broke, What Should I Sell?'

text: Delivery Cube frame 6 is the 10x/one-tenth test: ask what would need to change to justify charging ten times more, then ask what scalable low-cost additions would let you charge one-tenth the price while maintaining perceived value.
title: 'I'm Broke, What Should I Sell?'

text: Forcing yourself to justify a price ten times higher than your current one shifts your thinking toward the quantity of value required — for example, moving from a ten-thousand-dollar to a hundred-thousand-dollar offer.
title: 'I'm Broke, What Should I Sell?'

text: The one-tenth price direction of the test reveals what additions would be perceived as valuable but cost so little to deliver that you could maintain margins at a fraction of the current price.
title: 'I'm Broke, What Should I Sell?'

text: Together, the seven categories and the Delivery Cube give an entrepreneur a starting point for deciding what to sell first and a mechanism for making that offer more scalable, more profitable, or more valuable over time.
title: 'I'm Broke, What Should I Sell?'

text: A network becomes more valuable as each additional member joins; the first movers who establish large customer bases attract even more users simply because of size.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: A product ecosystem — where proprietary software and hardware only work together — locks customers in through one champion product and forces adoption of the entire lineup.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Most traditional service businesses degrade as more customers arrive; network-effect businesses do the opposite — each additional customer adds value for all existing ones.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: A buyer group — for example, dentists pooling purchases — gains greater leverage over vendors as membership grows, functioning as a demand-side monopoly.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Exclusive control over an essential resource — like a dominant share of mining and distribution for a commodity — lets the owner set prices by managing supply and demand.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Proprietary data accumulated over years cannot be replicated legally and cannot be caught up to quickly, making it a near-permanent barrier to entry.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Hormozi thinks the best AI model will win, not the first; users will immediately switch to a better one, so being early matters less than being superior.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Google has decades of search data, location data, email data, purchase data, and phone-search data that will let it personalize AI better than newer entrants, even if it appears behind in the AI race.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: A business owner does not need all 13 competitive strategies — finding one and weaving it deeply into the company's structure from the start is enough to build a very large business.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: A government-granted exclusive right to operate in a market — such as a utility franchise or transit route — can make it literally illegal for competitors to enter.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Simply knowing how to navigate government regulations and obtain a license or grant is itself a competitive advantage, even at small scale — a liquor license being a straightforward example.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: There is no advantage to being the second-cheapest competitor in a market; a low-cost leadership strategy is only valuable when a business is definitively the cheapest.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Each of these 13 competitive advantages compounds over time — unlike most businesses, which get harder and more costly as they scale.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Any single one of these 13 competitive moats, executed correctly all the way, is sufficient to build a multi-billion-dollar company.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Vertical integration — owning the entire chain from raw inputs to the end customer — lets a business capture margin at every step and deliver a better product at a lower price than competitors who rely on third parties.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Owning every step of the supply chain reduces business risk because dependency on third-party vendors is a hidden threat: if a key vendor fails, it can threaten the whole business.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Brand power allows a business to attach its logo to a commodity, achieve higher conversion rates, lower customer acquisition costs, and charge premium prices — all simultaneously.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Anyone can build a brand by consistently keeping promises, deliberately building associations with what their customers value, and clearly disassociating from what their customers do not value — over time.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Brand is Hormozi's personal favorite moat because it can be built with skill alone, without large capital or regulatory complexity — making it accessible to small and early-stage businesses.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Predatory pricing — temporarily pricing at a loss to outlast competitors — is most effective in software, where incumbents can copy a new feature, bundle it at no extra charge, and starve out the challenger.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Price discrimination — selling the same product at different prices based on a buyer's spending power — maximizes total profit; airlines use collected spending data to show different prices to different buyers.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Pricing is one of the fastest and easiest levers to change compared to building economies of scale or navigating government regulation; it can be implemented quickly at any business size.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: To price ethically at different levels, make small but real differences to each offer version so that, if two customers compare what they paid, the owner can point to a genuine distinction.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Exclusive contracts on the supply side — locking up a critical input so no one else can source it — force any would-be competitor to either buy from the incumbent or not enter at all.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Long-term government contracts, such as defense procurement, create multi-year exclusivity; a competitor who missed those years of revenue and relationship-building is extremely unlikely to win the next round.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: When a company already owns broad distribution, it can instantly make any acquired product worth many times its acquisition price by immediately pushing it through that network.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Physical distribution networks are especially durable moats because physically reaching human beings cannot be easily or quickly replicated, unlike digital distribution.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: A smaller business can win distribution agreements from established players by offering incentives the incumbents no longer bother with — lower wholesale cost, retail kits, free staff training — to get a first foothold.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: High capital requirements for market entry are a competitive advantage in themselves; choosing a business category that requires significant capital automatically shrinks the competitor pool.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Pharmaceutical development requires years of losses, extensive regulation, and many failed attempts before a single approved drug can generate decades of profits — that barrier is the moat.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Patents, copyrights, and trademarks give a business owner legal protection that makes it worth investing heavily in creating valuable assets, because competitors cannot legally copy them.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Trade secrets are difficult to maintain as a moat because employees who learn them can leave and apply that knowledge elsewhere, making enforcement very hard in practice.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Copying someone's ad, offer, or content is generally not actionable as intellectual property infringement; IP protection is specifically about preventing someone from pretending they own or created something they did not.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: A licensing strategy — paying established brands a royalty to use their name and flavor — lets a small business immediately benefit from decades of brand equity and consumer familiarity without building it from scratch.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Acquisitions and mergers effectively eliminate competition by assimilation rather than outcompeting; buying competitors consolidates market share under one entity.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Private equity uses outside capital to roll up fragmented markets — acquiring supply chains, competitors, or distribution — then captures economies of scale, brand strength, and pricing power all at once.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Small businesses stay small through competition; large businesses think about consolidation — combining fragmented players into one entity creates a company worth far more than the sum of its parts.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Innovative business models disrupt markets by giving away what incumbents charge for, then monetizing through a separate revenue stream — making the incumbent's core product unprofitable to defend.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: The cost to acquire a paying customer in a freemium model equals the cost to deliver the free product divided by the conversion rate from free to paid; the free delivery cost replaces traditional marketing spend.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Free gets roughly ten times the interest of any paid offer; dropping a service from even a low price to zero generates disproportionate demand that funds a higher-margin attached sale.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: Owning a distribution channel — not just holding contracts with one — means a business also profits from every other seller who needs access to that channel, not just from its own products.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: All 13 competitive strategies are variations of one underlying concept: monopoly — structuring a business so that only one seller can operate, whether by controlling supply, demand, technology, capital, media, or regulation.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: A business does not need to become a billion-dollar company to benefit from monopoly thinking; owning a small but tightly controlled niche creates life-changing wealth at any scale.
title: 13 Ways to DESTROY Your Competition (Legally)

text: If a market is not declining and is flat or growing, the right question is which market you can provide the most value to given your existing skill set.
title: The Key To Finding a Profitable Market

text: Personal experience in a market trumps all other selection criteria because familiarity with the customer's pain leads to better products and a higher likelihood of winning.
title: The Key To Finding a Profitable Market

text: Criterion one for market selection: the market must have a desperate, urgent need — not a nice-to-have — for the product or service being offered.
title: The Key To Finding a Profitable Market

text: Health, wealth, and relationships are timeless human needs and therefore reliably painful markets in any economic environment.
title: The Key To Finding a Profitable Market

text: Criterion two for market selection: the market must be growing, not shrinking, because even a skilled operator cannot overcome a structurally declining industry.
title: The Key To Finding a Profitable Market

text: Criterion three for market selection: prospects must be easy to find — through associations, groups, or shared channels — so that marketing can reach them directly.
title: The Key To Finding a Profitable Market

text: Criterion four for market selection: the target customers must have enough money to actually purchase the offer; pain and growth mean nothing without purchasing power.
title: The Key To Finding a Profitable Market

text: All four criteria — pain, growth, findability, and purchasing power — must be present simultaneously; having only three is insufficient and will cause the business to fail.
title: The Key To Finding a Profitable Market

text: The same core value proposition applied to a market with stronger purchasing power will likely generate more revenue than one applied to a market that is painful but cash-poor.
title: The Key To Finding a Profitable Market

text: When evaluating investment opportunities, Hormozi checks whether the founder has personal experience in the market and whether the problem being solved meets all four market-selection criteria.
title: The Key To Finding a Profitable Market

text: Even if a bias against you is real, the only productive question is what you will do about it—not whether the bias exists.
title: Business Owners: You're (Probably) Not Good Enough

text: The victim mentality Hormozi observes hurts people far more often than it has ever helped them, across both employees and business owners.
title: Business Owners: You're (Probably) Not Good Enough

text: Biases will always exist because bias is how humans learn: people form expectations from repeated experience and those expectations persist as long as the underlying patterns do.
title: Business Owners: You're (Probably) Not Good Enough

text: Wishing for a world without bias is wishing that humans stop learning, which will never happen.
title: Business Owners: You're (Probably) Not Good Enough

text: Proving empirically that a bias exists is good for society but bad for the individual, because it changes nothing about the individual's situation.
title: Business Owners: You're (Probably) Not Good Enough

text: No single person has ever improved their circumstances by proving they were a victim of something.
title: Business Owners: You're (Probably) Not Good Enough

text: When facing bias, the only viable path is to be better than the bias—to overcompensate so thoroughly that the bias cannot hold.
title: Business Owners: You're (Probably) Not Good Enough

text: Volume negates luck: if you are at a disadvantage, find the best performer and do twice as much as they do, because matching them only keeps you behind.
title: Business Owners: You're (Probably) Not Good Enough

text: Believing a bias applies to you makes it true and gives it more power rather than less.
title: Business Owners: You're (Probably) Not Good Enough

text: A person who defies an expected stereotype is more memorable and interesting than one who matches it—they earn a separate mental category in others' minds.
title: Business Owners: You're (Probably) Not Good Enough

text: Personal excellence is the ultimate rebellion—a principle Hormozi attributes to Andy Frisella and endorses fully.
title: Business Owners: You're (Probably) Not Good Enough

text: Accepting bias as the reason for not advancing gives a comfortable excuse that protects the ego but prevents growth.
title: Business Owners: You're (Probably) Not Good Enough

text: The more biases you face and overcome, the more compelling your story becomes—a story no one without those disadvantages can ever tell.
title: Business Owners: You're (Probably) Not Good Enough

text: A restaurant with a location disadvantage can still win if its product is exceptional enough—the bar is simply higher, not insurmountable.
title: Business Owners: You're (Probably) Not Good Enough

text: The only thing anyone can control is whether they are willing to do the extra work the bias demands of them.
title: Business Owners: You're (Probably) Not Good Enough

text: Six levers increase customer lifetime value in a coaching or service business: raise prices, lower cost of goods, increase purchase frequency, cross-sells, upsells, and downsells.

text: Raising prices on the exact same offer is the simplest way to make more money per customer, and is something many business owners simply never do.

text: In a recurring-revenue business, increasing purchase frequency means reducing churn. Keeping a client one extra month on a three-month average tenure is a 25% increase in LTV.

text: A cross-sell is selling a different, complementary product or service to the same customer—distinct from the core offer but addressing a related need.

text: If 20% of customers take a cross-sell priced at the same level as the core offer, average monthly revenue per customer rises by 20%.

text: An upsell is selling more of the same thing the customer already bought—more access, more sessions, higher service tier—not a different product.

text: Only about one in 250 businesses, roughly 0.4%, passes $10M a year in sales, and about 9% cross $1M, while 90% never reach $1M.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: He now sees character traits as skills: patience or people skills are bundles of trainable micro skills. Soft skills are simply harder to measure than hard skills.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: He argues the best entrepreneur has many skills and beliefs that don't limit them; deeply held beliefs are invisible, so unknown unknowns cap potential most.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: He moved from gyms to done-for-you turnarounds to licensing with the same skills; each was a higher leverage vehicle. He says many entrepreneurs stall before $1M or $10M due to the wrong vehicle.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: He cites Buffett: it matters less how hard you row than what boat you are in, since a smarter, harder-working friend in steel faced headwinds.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: He lists four types of leverage, borrowed from Naval and renamed: collaboration (people), capital (other people's money), code (software), and content (media).
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: You don't need all four leverage types; maxing out one, for example fundraising or software, can be enough, since a thousand times return on any is still a thousand times.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: People who seem to move faster don't move faster; they get more from every input. Every vehicle switch restarts you at zero, so leverage per step must be disproportionate.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: He cites Panda Express: sticking with one vehicle for 45 years built capital and collaboration at scale, with owners taking home large margins; he thinks staying long makes it hard to fail.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Instead of seeking more leverage types, you may need more of the one you use; each type is a bucket of micro skills such as recruiting, negotiating or understanding platforms.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: He thinks content creators should have real experience before educating; if lacking, document what you are doing instead. He says he cannot yet teach nine-figure months.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: He thinks switching to a new business means an apples-to-apples comparison is impossible; compare your year ten of one against year three of another, and the starting field has the longest lever.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: He notes Y Combinator screens for industry and personal experience, and suggests someone with years in one industry take a half pivot within it rather than switch fully.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: He frames not knowing how to earn more as ignorance debt, a yearly cost equal to the gap between current income and the income you don't yet know how to make.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Strategy is allocating limited time and money to options with the most leverage; he cites Munger's advice to do whatever it takes to earn your first hundred thousand.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: He compares index investing at roughly 9-10% a year to skills: a thousand-dollar sales course lifting income from $40K to $220K beats it, and pairing capital with know-how is acquisition.com's edge.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: He passes on his father's view that education can't be taken by governments, divorce or lawsuits, and that skills compound as you stack the next one.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: If someone is better than you, do twice what the top person does; equal hours leave them ahead. He cites Kobe's extra summer sessions.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Join groups ahead of you and give first, repeatedly, until they ask what they can do for you; asking up front is doing it wrong.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Transfer skills by having the teacher document, demonstrate, and then watching you duplicate; the learner must execute.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: He favors jobs as a way to get paid to learn, and says to change conditions if your workplace teaches nothing; he took a big pay cut himself for learning.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Tell your employer which skills you want to learn; when growth slows, ask for a training budget. He says paying 25% more for an A player yields about five times output.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Step one of leaving a job: live below your needs, since less personal risk allows more business risk and offense.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Start a side hustle only as a path to your main business; run it until it matches your income, then sustain it six months before quitting.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: He likes service businesses as starting points, since they cost only time and teach other skills; he says running gyms made Gym Launch possible.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Separate your identity and self-worth from the business; he says this lets you treat it as an asset and make hard decisions.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Business, health and marriage are infinite games; approaching them with a finite frame loses. The goal is to keep playing and find games you won't quit.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Many people quit an industry when they just disliked a function; he suggests staying in the industry and switching roles, since all businesses share marketing, sales, product and finance.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Baseline skills rise over time; he says once he learned marketing and sales together, his minimum became about a million dollars a year.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: He says his first step out of the sub-million category was learning to sell, since without sales nothing else matters.
title: How to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: A private chain means you open more locations yourself, keeping all ownership, taking all risk, fronting all capital, hiring all labor and controlling the brand end to end.
title: The Only 4 Ways To Scale A Service Business (PICK ONE)

text: A franchise has three components: name, business systems and fee. Using all three while calling it a license makes it an illegal franchise, risking fines and shutdown. Licenses typically include only two of the three.
title: The Only 4 Ways To Scale A Service Business (PICK ONE)

text: A private chain suits cases where a new location costs little to build. His rough test: opening cost under about six months of first-year profit from that location.
title: The Only 4 Ways To Scale A Service Business (PICK ONE)

text: The more specialized the skills needed to deliver the service, the harder it is to scale privately because inconsistent service becomes a problem. Productize the service and lower the skill needed from labor to make it scalable.
title: The Only 4 Ways To Scale A Service Business (PICK ONE)

text: He moved a portfolio company from licensing to owning locations because licensees earned so much and openings cost so little. In about 14 months it went from roughly half a million to 12 million dollars a year.
title: The Only 4 Ways To Scale A Service Business (PICK ONE)

text: Starting a franchise costs roughly 750,000 dollars for setup, legal and filings, and usually takes one to two years to show profit, since the roughly 50,000 dollar upfront fee mostly covers acquiring the franchisee.
title: The Only 4 Ways To Scale A Service Business (PICK ONE)

text: Franchising fits when opening a location takes a lot of capital, so you shift that risk to other owners and take a slice of top line. You generally need 100 plus locations for it to make sense.
title: The Only 4 Ways To Scale A Service Business (PICK ONE)

text: He says 90 to 95 percent of franchises never exceed 100 locations, so becoming a franchise is the start of the next journey, not the end goal.
title: The Only 4 Ways To Scale A Service Business (PICK ONE)

text: Licensing costs almost nothing to start, has high margins and generates cash from day one, but is hard to defend and gets low exit multiples unless licensee retention is very sticky, around six times or more.
title: The Only 4 Ways To Scale A Service Business (PICK ONE)

text: Licensing can suit newer owners with little money who want cash flow sooner; he used it for Gym Launch, his first business.
title: The Only 4 Ways To Scale A Service Business (PICK ONE)

text: Software has the highest exit value but needs heavy cost, time and low early cash flow. Yearly retention must be above roughly 80 percent or buyers see a normal service with some tech.
title: The Only 4 Ways To Scale A Service Business (PICK ONE)

text: He chooses a vehicle by weighing the IP, needed cash flow, upfront investment, time, owner risk appetite and how sure the return is. Cheap, sure-win openings mean owning privately; costly ones may mean franchising; easily copied offers favor licensing for speed.
title: The Only 4 Ways To Scale A Service Business (PICK ONE)

text: Keeping options open feels like delayed gratification, but he says options are valueless until exercised. At some point you must decide and cut off one future, which invites criticism.
title: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.

text: He notes that priority was used only in the singular in English until around 1950, since only one thing can come first, yet people claim ten important priorities.
title: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.

text: Whatever decision you make, people will push the opposite extreme back at you. He says this is because they are too afraid to make their own decisions and fear consequences and conflict.
title: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.

text: Decide comes from a Latin root meaning to cut off, so each decision asks which future you are cutting off today.
title: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.

text: He thinks maturity is directly related to how many commitments you have made and how many people rely on you, since commitments cash in optionality.
title: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.

text: With twelve focused hours a day, giving each of ten priorities about an hour and ten minutes cannot cover everything, so trade-offs are unavoidable. He advises ranking them for yourself.
title: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.

text: His one tactical tip: pick activities that check multiple priorities at once. He lifts with coworkers who are friends, covering recreation, career growth and physical health, so he can block more time for it.
title: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.

text: At the end of life you will wish for benefits of other priorities, but you want them while already enjoying your chosen trade. You pick your regrets, or they get chosen for you.
title: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.

text: He says people always want what they cannot have: singles want marriage, married want singlehood, childless want kids, parents want a night off, employees want businesses, employers envy employees clocking out.
title: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.

text: He recounts a founder on a podcast saying to seek the most dominant game. Facebook beat MySpace by optimizing monthly active users rather than total users, a superior game.
title: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.

text: He argues that the person with the most context on your life is you, so uninformed outside opinions matter little, while distinguishing legal laws from spoken and unspoken rules whose consequences are often milder than feared.
title: It took me 37 years to realize what I'll tell you in 18 minutes.

text: Hormozi says a fifty-thousand-dollar burger looks different once you compare it to income: for someone earning about 100 million a year over 2,000 hours, it costs less of their earnings than his twelve-dollar lunch did at seven dollars an hour.
title: How The World’s RICHEST Man Made His Money

text: Rather than mocking people who buy ten-thousand-dollar purses or fifty-thousand-dollar jackets, he urges empathizing with the buyer: when the price gap is tiny relative to their wealth, they simply want the best one.
title: How The World’s RICHEST Man Made His Money

text: Any market has four positions: bargain (cheapest, poor quality), best value (like Target), premium (like Lexus or BMW), and luxury, where price has no cap and the known cost is part of the product's value.
title: How The World’s RICHEST Man Made His Money

text: In luxury goods, raising prices increases the number sold instead of lowering it, because buyers tie their status to the purchase. He says this creates enormous profit.
title: How The World’s RICHEST Man Made His Money

text: Rich people have the same problems as everyone else but want them solved differently. With them, speed and convenience matter most, and the question is how much of their time and pain you ask for, not the money.
title: How The World’s RICHEST Man Made His Money

text: A friend serving Fortune 100 clients manages 1.2 billion a year in ad budget, fronts the spend through a multi-billion credit line, and charges six percent, earning 18 million on a 300 million month, purely for convenience.
title: How The World’s RICHEST Man Made His Money

text: To appeal to the rich, deliver the same service in half the time and accept requests through any channel, such as phone, text, email or WhatsApp, so it feels effortless.
title: How The World’s RICHEST Man Made His Money

text: Solving rich people's problems lets you charge rich-people prices, and he says they have unlimited upside and are better customers.
title: How The World’s RICHEST Man Made His Money

text: Charging more increases customers' emotional investment, since very cheap items get no attention, and he says this raises the likelihood they get results.
title: How The World’s RICHEST Man Made His Money

text: In a wine study, people ranked identical wines by price, rating the expensive one best and the cheapest worst. A pricier item is perceived as more valuable even when the core product is the same.
title: How The World’s RICHEST Man Made His Money

text: Higher emotional investment and perceived value lead customers to get better results, such as those in personal training versus a ten-dollar-a-month gym membership.
title: How The World’s RICHEST Man Made His Money

text: Higher prices attract less demanding customers: bigger contracts mean fewer payment plans and easier clients. Taking fifty dollars from someone with a hundred in the bank is half their net worth, so being willing to pay does not mean you should accept it.
title: How The World’s RICHEST Man Made His Money

text: Higher prices leave more margin to deliver: a five-dollar cost sold at eight leaves three dollars, but sold at fifty leaves forty-five to reinvest in product, value and higher-level talent.
title: How The World’s RICHEST Man Made His Money

text: Higher-paying, less demanding, happier customers create a snowball of testimonials and momentum. The reverse is a vicious cycle of chargebacks and refunds from demanding customers with unrealistic expectations.
title: How The World’s RICHEST Man Made His Money

text: He argues there is no advantage in being the second cheapest in a marketplace, but there is an advantage in being the most expensive.
title: How The World’s RICHEST Man Made His Money

text: A first diagnostic question in any business: is it limited by supply or by demand? If doubling leads can be handled, demand is the limit; if not, build capacity first, since fixing one problem can worsen another.
title: Building a $2,500,000 Business for a Stranger in 36 Minutes

text: Raising prices can lift close rates for ordinary businesses because customers grow more convinced you can deliver, raising perceived likelihood of achievement in the value equation.
title: Building a $2,500,000 Business for a Stranger in 36 Minutes

text: Higher prices raise emotional investment, perceived value and results while lowering customer demandingness, and fund better delivery. Underpricing can lose sales by making a business look like a shaky operation; for owners under roughly three to five million revenue, charging more is a big lever.
title: Building a $2,500,000 Business for a Stranger in 36 Minutes

text: Close rates above 80% signal room to raise prices. A price rise pays as long as the close rate stays above the break-even level.
title: Building a $2,500,000 Business for a Stranger in 36 Minutes

text: He leans toward the Dave Ramsey side on debt: debt adds risk, and risk over a long horizon tends to come due. Businesses face seasons and volatility, and lasting firms often run debt free.
title: Building a $2,500,000 Business for a Stranger in 36 Minutes

text: Each extra step before a conversion typically loses about half or more of visitors, so send ad traffic to a dedicated page with a clear offer above the fold, not the home page.
title: Building a $2,500,000 Business for a Stranger in 36 Minutes

text: If each dollar spent on ads returns several dollars, spend as much as possible. If unsure of the return, you have an attribution data problem to fix first.
title: Building a $2,500,000 Business for a Stranger in 36 Minutes

text: Check ad creative at real phone size, since desktop design tools hide unreadable text. Lead with location and the offer in the headline, and run many colour and image variations.
title: Building a $2,500,000 Business for a Stranger in 36 Minutes

text: Test new ad content cheaply by posting it organically. Take the best organic posts, add a short call to action at the end, and use them as ads since the algorithm already tested them.
title: Building a $2,500,000 Business for a Stranger in 36 Minutes

text: For reactivating past customers, test frames like owing them a checkup or money, or admitting a mistake, and split test week by week. Highlight no cost in bold, since people scan.
title: Building a $2,500,000 Business for a Stranger in 36 Minutes

text: Collect customer bills before and after service to show savings; he thinks savings stats are the strongest pitch and pair well with a higher price. Send exceptional customer stories too.
title: Building a $2,500,000 Business for a Stranger in 36 Minutes

text: Pick one or two seasonal pain points and run messages before, during and after each, twice a year, to get year-round sign-ups, as with gym New Year and summer cycles.
title: Building a $2,500,000 Business for a Stranger in 36 Minutes

text: Bid on your own brand and name search terms even if it costs money, so competitors cannot take those clicks; you can beat rivals on profitability for your own name.
title: Building a $2,500,000 Business for a Stranger in 36 Minutes

text: Treat reactivation as monthly mini campaigns of two or three emails each, with angles like allergies, savings and environment, and case study follow-ups.
title: Building a $2,500,000 Business for a Stranger in 36 Minutes

text: Referrals are promised by everyone and delivered by few, so a true affiliate program needs a compelling offer for partners. Pick one approach, outbound events or partners, rather than both.
title: Building a $2,500,000 Business for a Stranger in 36 Minutes

text: Affiliate offer: partners sell a low-ticket lead magnet and keep all revenue; you deliver it cheaply, then upsell your core offer. Acquisition cost equals delivery cost divided by upsell take rate.
title: Building a $2,500,000 Business for a Stranger in 36 Minutes

text: Referral-swap partnerships are less scalable long term, because you rarely have enough referral volume to feed twenty partners.
title: Building a $2,500,000 Business for a Stranger in 36 Minutes

text: Fix the landing page and ads before raising spend, since better conversion might double or triple lead flow and you could hit capacity limits first.
title: Building a $2,500,000 Business for a Stranger in 36 Minutes

text: He suspects the ads work mainly because competitors in the industry are weak at advertising, not because the ads are good.
title: Building a $2,500,000 Business for a Stranger in 36 Minutes

text: The fastest way to become the person you want to be is to surround yourself with people who leave you no choice but to become them.
title: We Made a BIG Decision...

text: Because the relationship was deep, deal terms were easy: Shiron emailed his proposal, they replied all with counsel and asked to paper it. He says if final terms break down, something was wrong earlier.
title: We Made a BIG Decision...

text: Some skill and experience levels cannot be hired; replicating a partner's depth would take effort that detracts from the whole, so bringing in a partner was worth the brand risk.
title: We Made a BIG Decision...

text: He asks people bringing in a partner whether they like having dinner with them, and questions why anyone would give half a business to someone they do not enjoy.
title: We Made a BIG Decision...

text: Resources are like bullets, and at some point a business needs another barrel: someone who can build something from nothing at his level. Hiring someone with your skill set is a different thing.
title: We Made a BIG Decision...

text: Everything comes down to return on time. He advocates aggressive focus, and says businesses never really overexpand, they undertalent, meaning they lack enough barrels to pursue their ideas.
title: We Made a BIG Decision...

text: He capped around 2-3 million a year solo with six businesses; adding Leila as a barrel, who focused him on one opportunity, took the company to nine figures plus.
title: We Made a BIG Decision...

text: He believes a business's potential equals the aggregate skill set of its people. If one person does every job, one brain is the maximum; each added brain raises the peak and unlocks opportunities none could pursue alone.
title: We Made a BIG Decision...

text: The more people who can say I got it and deliver, the more powerful the organization; he would support and clear friction for people with that competence and care.
title: We Made a BIG Decision...

text: A good new leader makes things feel lighter and returns attention to you; if someone makes things feel heavier, they are not helping. He is willing to sacrifice some today to avoid being hurt tomorrow.
title: We Made a BIG Decision...

text: A new leader meeting every employee gives a three-dimensional view of the company, better than one person's document.
title: We Made a BIG Decision...

text: Growth speed derives from decision speed. Without data, patterns from past experience help, compressing decisions that would take weeks into 30 minutes.
title: We Made a BIG Decision...

text: A players start providing value immediately, within the first work week. Someone who says they need a quarter to get their bearings is probably not the right person, in his experience.
title: We Made a BIG Decision...

text: Leaders new to a team should ship tangible artifacts early, because if the team sees no wins, they will not assimilate you.
title: We Made a BIG Decision...

text: His two pieces of advice for new people: do not tell others what to do or that they are wrong, and offer help to everyone.
title: We Made a BIG Decision...

text: When introducing a new leader, do not promise things will be better; say it will be different, and explain what changes and stays for impacted people.
title: We Made a BIG Decision...

text: He frames acquisition.com 1.0 as helping themselves directly, 2.0 as also helping others indirectly through documenting, and 3.0 as helping themselves and others directly.
title: We Made a BIG Decision...

text: Many owners voice dreams far beyond their capacity; when you bring in more barrels and talent, your realm of believability expands and new possibilities appear.
title: We Made a BIG Decision...

text: With enjoyable people, timelines expand and there is no rush; miserable founders want the misery to end, which creates pressure and pushing energy.
title: We Made a BIG Decision...

text: When he started Gym Launch, a lawyer told him the podcast applied to law; you can swap gym and membership for contract and services.
title: We Made a BIG Decision...

text: Hormozi names five Ps that must align before a sale: promotion, prospect, price, product and process. He looks at them across the whole sales pipeline.
title: My SIMPLE voice tweak that EXPLODED OUR REVENUE...

text: If a team follows a proven script but does not close, they may be saying the right things in the wrong way. Delivery has two parts: tone and cadence or emphasis.
title: My SIMPLE voice tweak that EXPLODED OUR REVENUE...

text: The same words carry different meanings depending on emphasis, as with a comedian's script that only works for the person whose pauses and intonation fit it. Reading a script is not enough.
title: My SIMPLE voice tweak that EXPLODED OUR REVENUE...

text: One fix is becoming a master salesman by controlling tone: slow down and lower your voice to signal importance. This skill builds through repetition and noticing what worked on good sales.
title: My SIMPLE voice tweak that EXPLODED OUR REVENUE...

text: Review recordings of your calls from hot streaks, when you felt able to close anyone. He calls them game tape. Beginners without such footage can study other people's hot calls.
title: My SIMPLE voice tweak that EXPLODED OUR REVENUE...

text: He says the gap between average and master salesmen is like a 250 versus 300 batter. Great salesmen never go cold because they know how to recreate success.
title: My SIMPLE voice tweak that EXPLODED OUR REVENUE...

text: His sales team closed the highest percentage on days when clients finished the program and many success stories were shared. The team then sold with strong conviction.
title: My SIMPLE voice tweak that EXPLODED OUR REVENUE...

text: The faster fix is believing in what you sell. Since a product is never perfect, he focuses on having perfect intentions, which you can control.
title: My SIMPLE voice tweak that EXPLODED OUR REVENUE...

text: Believe the prospect is better served with you than anyone else. This is especially true where the client must do the work, as in coaching, weight loss or business training.
title: My SIMPLE voice tweak that EXPLODED OUR REVENUE...

text: You cannot guarantee results because you cannot control the variables, but you can say you are the best shot the person has at success. He says this helped him in weight loss sales.
title: My SIMPLE voice tweak that EXPLODED OUR REVENUE...

text: People feel conviction and choose to believe you based on how you say things, not only what you say. A sale is fundamentally a transfer of belief, and you cannot transfer belief you lack.
title: My SIMPLE voice tweak that EXPLODED OUR REVENUE...

text: Email costs nothing per customer once the lead exists, so gross profit from email sales drops straight to the bottom line. He compares email to a 401k that compounds, versus ads as a paycheck.

text: Hearing out your team's ideas matters: if you reject every one, they stop bringing ideas. Choose which hills to die on and let them try ideas that will not damage the brand.

text: Trust team members partly because they are closer to the data; a CEO only sees snippets, more so as the company grows.

text: The number of offers made to a prospect correlates directly with money made, but each offer spends goodwill, so deposit enough value to earn the ask. Email is free one-to-many content he fully controls.

text: Asking again for the sale is fine, since people get busy and forget. It works as long as enough goodwill has been deposited to earn the right to ask.

text: Selling the same offer through different mediums, like webinar, phone, live workshop or email, reduces offer fatigue and gives more chances, because people judge goodwill by the medium.

text: The same information is priced differently by delivery medium: book, digital course, virtual live, and in-person live each carry different price points, as with in-person versus online college.

text: Quarterly cleanup: once a quarter, run the list through a conversion event, such as a challenge or lead magnet, with a deadline and a big promise you can deliver.

text: Test on about 10% of the list or less before going to the whole list. Testing subject lines, calls to action and landing pages can sometimes double or triple campaign throughput.

text: Hormozi avoids holiday trips home because familiar people and settings can pull him toward an identity he deliberately left behind.
title: Why I Don't Go Home for the Holidays

text: When someone addresses a person disrespectfully, he recommends identifying the unacceptable treatment and controlling the response rather than trying to control the speaker. The resulting discomfort is part of establishing different expectations.
title: Why I Don't Go Home for the Holidays

text: When someone applies an outdated negative label, he recommends responding from the identity a person wants to embody. He argues that describing oneself as still improving can concede the very label being challenged.

text: Hormozi evaluates customer lifetime value as cumulative gross profit rather than revenue. This accounts for delivery costs but differs from net profit, which also subtracts other business expenses.

text: A higher price can itself make a product more appealing or place it in a different perceived category, prompting buyers to investigate what makes it different.

text: Getting existing customers to purchase more often increases their lifetime gross profit. Even one additional purchase from each customer increases customer value across the business.
title: 6 Hacks To Make More Money [Increase LTV] Without More Customers

text: An upsell offers a larger quantity or a better version within the same product category. A cross-sell addresses a related need with an additional product.

text: Cross-sells can generate most of a business's profit. A loss-leader model can work when the initial purchase leads to a higher-margin follow-on purchase and the business understands its numbers.

text: When prospects cannot afford the primary service, a business can earn referral commissions by directing them to suitable partners with good products who specialize in serving those customers.

text: The ratio of lifetime gross profit to cost of acquiring a customer is the core economic unit of a business; all profit flows from it. A 20 to 1 ratio makes a business that can be scaled endlessly.
title: Million Dollar Equations

text: Rough way to get average customer lifespan: take customers at the start of a period, see how many remain at the end, compute churn, and divide 1 by it. Losing 10 of 100 means 10% churn and a 10-month lifespan.
title: Million Dollar Equations

text: Lifetime gross profit per customer equals monthly gross profit per customer times lifespan. Example: $6,000 monthly gross profit across 10 customers is $600 each, times 10 months gives $6,000.
title: Million Dollar Equations

text: Owners often judge ad spend against lifetime revenue instead of lifetime gross profit. Spending $50 to win $100 revenue that yields only $10 gross profit loses money, so use gross profit.
title: Million Dollar Equations

text: CAC should include labor and software as well as ad spend. Total monthly cost divided by customers acquired that month gives CAC.
title: Million Dollar Equations

text: Aim for lifetime gross profit at least three times CAC; below that you are too constrained to scale. A very weak ratio can end interest in a business, and an exceptional one may offset weaker metrics.
title: Million Dollar Equations

text: For expansion, compute the full cost to open a location, including marketing, buildout and hiring, then assess payback, one-year return and capacity profit. He wants at least 3:1, ideally 5:1.
title: Million Dollar Equations

text: For active, non-passive investments he wants roughly a 300% annual return at minimum, because his time and opportunity cost must be justified, unlike passive dividend investing.
title: Million Dollar Equations

text: Payback speed depends on how big the buildout is and how good the team is at launching new locations. He prefers opening near capacity by spending more on the launch.
title: Million Dollar Equations

text: Faster payback on customer acquisition indicates a more cash-flow-positive business, which matters most to small owners. Levers: upfront first and last month, fees, upsells, third-party financing.
title: Million Dollar Equations

text: Sales velocity times lifetime gross profit shows where revenue will level out if nothing changes. A business above that level will shrink; one below will grow.
title: Million Dollar Equations

text: Sales velocity divided by churn gives the customer count at the hypothetical max, for example 100 monthly sales at 10% churn gives 1,000 customers, which informs headcount planning. Use trailing 90-day, 6-month and 12-month averages.
title: Million Dollar Equations

text: Market size is very important but hard to assess, since many big companies began with a niche and expanded. Focus on the knowable risks that could break the equation.
title: Million Dollar Equations

text: Plan clip moments proactively: when a good question arrives, answer it with clear next steps so the clip has a payoff, and open the stream with hooks from proven content.
title: I Live Streamed For 30 Days. Here's What I Learned.

text: Slow mode and heavy moderation (four moderators) kept spam out, and asking chat to focus on a theme gave the stream structure. Cameos from Layla outperformed solo streams, and chat interaction is the best engagement.
title: I Live Streamed For 30 Days. Here's What I Learned.

text: His biggest point is that production quality does not matter for livestreams; an iPhone worked as well as his fancy camera. He says iPhone 17 and later need no external mic.
title: I Live Streamed For 30 Days. Here's What I Learned.

text: Edit livestreams like regular videos: trim fast, start with hooks, keep value per second high. Post-live views can double or triple the live viewership.
title: I Live Streamed For 30 Days. Here's What I Learned.

text: When choosing between two hard options, ask what he wants to happen and what problem he is solving, then check that the planned action actually gets that result.
title: I Live Streamed For 30 Days. Here's What I Learned.

text: Wanting to act because of emotion has no correlation with whether the action produces the result you want. Pausing to add those two filters saved him time and made him money.
title: I Live Streamed For 30 Days. Here's What I Learned.

text: He and Layla only move forward when both agree; they make sure both have the same information, and when they disagree, each asks what information the other has that they lack.
title: I Live Streamed For 30 Days. Here's What I Learned.

text: Before a hard discussion, frame it as being about the issue, not each other: critique is about the idea, not the person, and you are a team.
title: I Live Streamed For 30 Days. Here's What I Learned.

text: Working on the business means growing it: get more customers and make them worth more. Ask if you could handle 50% more customers; yes means demand constraint, no means supply constraint.
title: I Live Streamed For 30 Days. Here's What I Learned.

text: For a local business, ads on Meta and Google PPC typically work fastest; content builds recognition; outbound suits very high ticket sales with few, valuable targets.
title: I Live Streamed For 30 Days. Here's What I Learned.

text: He says advanced owners are not right more often; they act faster when wrong. Keeping bad teammates too long sacrifices the rest of the team.
title: I Live Streamed For 30 Days. Here's What I Learned.

text: To overcome hesitating to fire, imagine the business were breaking even or losing money. If you would feel fine letting them go then, the hesitation is just a story.

text: He thinks contract legal help is enough until roughly 30 million in revenue, when bills justify a general counsel who coordinates niche vendors. He has never had in-house legal.
title: I Live Streamed For 30 Days. Here's What I Learned.

text: There is no magic moment to build your own product. If you have the skills for product, delivery and sales and enough cash, you take on risk and are disproportionately rewarded.
title: I Live Streamed For 30 Days. Here's What I Learned.

text: For an unpaid invoice, he usually moves on to the next client rather than sue, since time is better spent earning. He would qualify customers better and take half up front.
title: I Live Streamed For 30 Days. Here's What I Learned.

text: He thinks one bad review is catastrophized; the fix is collecting many more five-star reviews rather than fretting over it.
title: I Live Streamed For 30 Days. Here's What I Learned.

text: On School, he says high-but-not-perfect ratings such as 4.9 convert better than a perfect 5.0, because a flawless score looks fake.
title: I Live Streamed For 30 Days. Here's What I Learned.

text: If you love an industry, he suggests working at a successful, fast-growing company to trade earning for learning, since business skills are easier to learn than falling in love with a field.
title: I Live Streamed For 30 Days. Here's What I Learned.

text: A former partner emptied the account holding prepaid customer money, so Hormozi used his savings to serve customers and wind down over about six to eight weeks, following a mentor's advice to do right by everyone.
title: I Live Streamed For 30 Days. Here's What I Learned.

text: In a failing business, be honest, do right by everyone you can, stop the bleeding fast, and deliver services with your own time if needed rather than take on more debt. Bankruptcy of the LLC is the worst case.
title: I Live Streamed For 30 Days. Here's What I Learned.

text: He thinks most businesses at high level have the same functions and parts that suck, so someone who no longer needs money is romanticizing another business.
title: I Live Streamed For 30 Days. Here's What I Learned.

text: In a hard conversation, say everything you would tell a friend, including your fears about the relationship, up front rather than hiding it.
title: I Live Streamed For 30 Days. Here's What I Learned.

text: Stay in a job for an outcome only if it is big enough to boost your authority and earnings for life, such as taking a company public, and worth the time.
title: I Live Streamed For 30 Days. Here's What I Learned.

text: Stay in a job while your rate of learning is high and it raises your opportunity size; move full-time to the side business when learning drops off.
title: I Live Streamed For 30 Days. Here's What I Learned.

text: Every entrepreneur must learn to promote, convert and deliver; accounting, legal and tech can be outsourced. Learn a key salesperson's motion before removing them.
title: I Live Streamed For 30 Days. Here's What I Learned.

text: To learn a new field, work at a small founder-driven company of about 10 to 40 people and talk to every coworker. He apprenticed about three months at a gym before opening his own.
title: I Live Streamed For 30 Days. Here's What I Learned.

text: He suspects entertainment audiences pay far less per follower than educational ones; make your audience valuable by selling to it or helping advertisers earn more.
title: I Live Streamed For 30 Days. Here's What I Learned.
