text: Hormozi thinks handing people a lot of money they did not earn is bad for them, noting that everyone he knows who was given money had their life ruined, so he would not leave it to descendants.
title: We're giving away all our money.

text: He believes the desire for permanence through legacy is a human condition that is not real; even whole ancient civilizations like the Sumerians are remembered only as having existed, and descendants' genes and traits thin out over generations.
title: We're giving away all our money.

text: He has shifted from crediting hard work and sacrifice for success to thinking people are naturally predisposed to business, much as athletes are physically; work hones the skill, but some people get disproportionate returns on effort.
title: We're giving away all our money.

text: Since the estate will be donated at death anyway, he reasoned it makes more sense to start giving now, and he sees skills, experiences and lessons as more valuable to give than money.
title: We're giving away all our money.

text: He and his wife have donated about a million dollars over the last few years to charities they believe in.
title: We're giving away all our money.

text: Acquisition.com is their portfolio holding company, fully owning seven companies plus stakes in others, doing about 85 million a year; the channel, books and free courses exist to transfer lessons while alive.
title: We're giving away all our money.

text: His first businesses came from scarcity, insecurity and deficiency, which made building them a grinding, rage-filled experience; he notes that people far richer than him do not seem to act that way.
title: We're giving away all our money.

text: He thinks that if you only satisfy personal needs, drive fades once you cross your number, so you either make money the ultimate scorecard or change what drives you.
title: We're giving away all our money.

text: He likens entrepreneurship to a casino where everyone gets a seat, you cannot cash out or keep your chips when you leave, and they go back to the table, which reinforces that it is only a game.
title: We're giving away all our money.

text: Money only solves money problems, and once those run out it has little utility; more of it changes nothing beyond that.
title: We're giving away all our money.

text: He sees money as raw power, like a weapon without the skill to wield it; the more you have, the more skill you need, and he thinks it is too much for one person to be handed.
title: We're giving away all our money.

text: Giving money to individuals robs them of the chance to earn and achieve for themselves, which is why he directs it to causes.
title: We're giving away all our money.

text: In college he felt dread while a Powerball drawing ran, because winning would make everything he wanted to do meaningless and deny him credit for earning it; he ties this to ego and insecurity.
title: We're giving away all our money.

text: He estimates their estate at 60 to 80 million, and says waiting 40 to 50 years at ten percent would make it over a billion dollars even with no new earnings.
title: We're giving away all our money.

text: Acquisition.com does not sell time or do one-on-one consulting; it takes positions in companies, nominally three to ten million but skewing to five to ten million plus, and the smallest portfolio business then made eight million a year.
title: We're giving away all our money.

text: Hormozi says he sold two businesses, a $12 million business, two exotic cars and a $4 million Austin house last year to get a reset from feeling weighed down by possessions.
title: I sold everything

text: He describes his life in three-to-five-year seasons: college and consulting, running gyms, licensing gyms and building three bigger companies, and now investing in service or e-learning businesses making 1 to 10 million in profit.
title: I sold everything

text: After living in various areas, he concluded that about 90 percent of daily life depends on what is within walking distance, so he wanted nature, restaurants, a strong gym and a grocery store close by.
title: I sold everything

text: He argues that opinions about a city rest on a few people and places visited, so they are near irrelevant; experience depends on the submarket you land in.
title: I sold everything

text: He and his wife visited 33 cities in 18 months, staying two to three weeks each, and found higher-end areas so similar in chains that he sometimes forgot which city he was in.
title: I sold everything

text: Because he sees no marginal difference in living between areas, he prefers to pay less tax, so zero-tax became a preference rather than a driver.
title: I sold everything

text: He prefers living in ultra-wealthy areas because upper-middle-class neighbors had different priorities from his, making meaningful conversations and relationships hard.
title: I sold everything

text: He prefers a large airport with direct flights, since connections in smaller markets are a massive pain for him and for visitors.
title: I sold everything

text: After a period of leasing luxury places at roughly $50 to $100 thousand a month, he missed familiarity and social circles, since a month in one place is too short to build real relationships.
title: I sold everything

text: He thinks the more money and self-knowledge someone has, the more particular they become, because certain things drain attention; he wants his own gym, studio and kitchen items.
title: I sold everything

text: He believes the ideal setup for the very wealthy is two to three, maybe four, primary homes stocked with your things, giving flexibility plus familiarity; having no home base felt like free-floating.
title: I sold everything

text: Hedonic adaptation means new things stop conferring value once you get used to them, as with a new car losing its thrill within a month or two.
title: I sold everything

text: He found buying for status not worth it: his Bentley, over 300 thousand dollars, improved service but he felt it made him view people worse, and he says it was not worth the money.
title: I sold everything

text: He justifies private jets by relative cost: taking home over a million dollars a month means a flight costing 10,000 is like 50 dollars to an average family, at 200 times income.
title: I sold everything

text: The biggest benefit of flying private, he says, is turning travel from a negative experience into a positive one, removing wasted days, exhaustion and recovery time and making him likelier to travel.
title: I sold everything

text: He bought an eight-figure mountaintop home because he prefers a headquarters holding his things, and he gets stimulation from work so he needs no outside stimulation and is more productive with familiar surroundings.
title: I sold everything

text: His unifying rule for material goods is function over form: spend even large sums when it improves function, and skip costly items when cheap ones serve better, like cheap cotton tees over expensive tank tops.
title: I sold everything

text: He gave away 90 percent of his clothes and felt better, since a full closet made him feel guilty; now buying one item means discarding the lowest-utility one so quality rises while size stays constant.
title: I sold everything

text: His plan is two to three homes in different climates, such as beach, mountain, lake or desert, for novelty and weather without the nomad feeling.
title: I sold everything

text: He advises a middle path between owning nothing and everything, and says a unifying theory works as a decision algorithm that pre-makes decisions and saves mental bandwidth for new ones.

text: Reframing is the one to three sentences said after a prospect says anything other than yes, meant to raise the odds that whatever comes next leads them to buy.
title: After Closing 4000+ Sales, I Discovered a New Method to Close Deals Faster

text: When a prospect asks a trap question where they judge your answer, answer with a question about the question, such as asking which certifications they are looking for.
title: After Closing 4000+ Sales, I Discovered a New Method to Close Deals Faster

text: The person asking the questions controls the conversation; once you start answering, you are on defense.
title: After Closing 4000+ Sales, I Discovered a New Method to Close Deals Faster

text: The 3A framework: acknowledge by restating what they said, associate the question with what top customers ask, then ask your next question.
title: After Closing 4000+ Sales, I Discovered a New Method to Close Deals Faster

text: Restating the prospect's words shows you are listening and buys thinking time before you respond.
title: After Closing 4000+ Sales, I Discovered a New Method to Close Deals Faster

text: Like a lawyer, only ask questions you already know the answers to, and only answer when sure you have the right answer.
title: After Closing 4000+ Sales, I Discovered a New Method to Close Deals Faster

text: To a think-about-it objection, ask what their main concern is, what variables they are weighing, or what would make it a no.
title: After Closing 4000+ Sales, I Discovered a New Method to Close Deals Faster

text: Prospects believe almost nothing you say about them, so ask questions that lead them to conclude they are a good fit themselves.
title: After Closing 4000+ Sales, I Discovered a New Method to Close Deals Faster

text: Do you have any questions is the worst question in sales because it invites objections and hands over control; train it out of your team.
title: After Closing 4000+ Sales, I Discovered a New Method to Close Deals Faster

text: If pressed for answers, compare it to asking a receptionist about your surgery, or a mechanic who must look under the hood first; anyone answering before assessing is suspect.
title: After Closing 4000+ Sales, I Discovered a New Method to Close Deals Faster

text: For a timing objection, acknowledge it, call it smart that they are thinking about implementation, note best customers think similarly, then ask what would make it a good time.
title: After Closing 4000+ Sales, I Discovered a New Method to Close Deals Faster

text: For a spouse objection, agree it is sensible, then ask which parts they think the spouse would dislike, returning the talk to specific concerns you can address.
title: After Closing 4000+ Sales, I Discovered a New Method to Close Deals Faster

text: Beginners treat statements like disliking a feature as deal enders; keep asking why, since best closers make the most asks.
title: After Closing 4000+ Sales, I Discovered a New Method to Close Deals Faster

text: A wealth manager pitching him reframed his already-have-an-advisor brush-off by saying most of their clients did too, which made him feel like a typical buyer.
title: After Closing 4000+ Sales, I Discovered a New Method to Close Deals Faster

text: Bad selling includes selling an unqualified prospect; if you state facts and tell the truth and they are qualified, you are ethically obliged to keep asking.
title: After Closing 4000+ Sales, I Discovered a New Method to Close Deals Faster

text: Use straw men or foils to deliver tough truths without insulting the prospect, since permission-based lines like coach hat can fail for a young seller with an older buyer.
title: After Closing 4000+ Sales, I Discovered a New Method to Close Deals Faster

text: Three associations: describe someone else who asked the same thing today, cite a successful past customer, or cite an authority such as the CEO, so you are just the messenger.
title: After Closing 4000+ Sales, I Discovered a New Method to Close Deals Faster

text: Validating phrases like that is smart or reasonable make people like being sold to, similar to calming an angry customer rather than disagreeing.
title: After Closing 4000+ Sales, I Discovered a New Method to Close Deals Faster

text: Rule five: keep childlike curiosity; saying huh, smiling, and seeking to understand changes tone and buys a few seconds.
title: After Closing 4000+ Sales, I Discovered a New Method to Close Deals Faster

text: Keep the human first: if you believe the product helps a qualified prospect, imagine advising your past self with empathy and ask their concerns.
title: After Closing 4000+ Sales, I Discovered a New Method to Close Deals Faster

text: You close by making the prospect right, not by being right; feeling combative or winning logically loses the sale.
title: After Closing 4000+ Sales, I Discovered a New Method to Close Deals Faster

text: Labels given through associations, like family man, can be recalled near the close to pair their earlier obstacles with reasons to buy.
title: After Closing 4000+ Sales, I Discovered a New Method to Close Deals Faster

text: Deeper in a sale, asking what are you afraid of gets to the core issue fast, but only works with established rapport.

text: Newcomers often try to fix problems that do not exist yet, like fulfillment overload before a first sale. Hormozi says close deals first, and deal with being overwhelmed once it actually happens.
title: 3 Steps To Starting (Or Fixing) Any Business

text: Give so much in the offer that the buyer would feel foolish refusing. Later, once sales bring in money, you can peel back the parts that consume the most time and add the least value.
title: 3 Steps To Starting (Or Fixing) Any Business

text: One of his standing rules is to create flow, then monetize flow, then add friction, in that order. Early on, that can even mean selling one-on-one time or doing unreasonable things to get yeses.
title: 3 Steps To Starting (Or Fixing) Any Business

text: Before you have made a single sale, stop thinking about scale. He says the details of the delivery matter little, since customers mostly remember feeling understood and finding the solution unique, easy and believable.
title: 3 Steps To Starting (Or Fixing) Any Business

text: He believes money is made in your mind first. If you cannot picture yourself earning from something, it will not happen, and he says poor expectations keep people poor while rich people expect rich outcomes.
title: 3 Steps To Starting (Or Fixing) Any Business

text: When starting out, being overwhelmed is normal and expected. Sell the most extreme offer you can think of, get one yes, then another, and optimize for profit only after you have money and a business.
title: 3 Steps To Starting (Or Fixing) Any Business

text: Early on you cannot tell which promised items buyers value and which are costly to deliver. So stack as much value as you can, then over time trim toward an offer that is both profitable and attractive.
title: 3 Steps To Starting (Or Fixing) Any Business

text: At 23 he paid three thousand dollars he did not have for a weekend conference run by a business coach. There he heard that the sales secret is an offer so good people would feel stupid saying no.
title: 3 Steps To Starting (Or Fixing) Any Business

text: He realized he could earn even without strong sales skill: if someone said no, he could keep adding to the offer until they said yes. He kept his price and added more instead of cutting it.
title: 3 Steps To Starting (Or Fixing) Any Business

text: In the beginning he was willing to scale the unscalable, doing whatever was needed to get people saying yes and start the flow.
title: 3 Steps To Starting (Or Fixing) Any Business

text: Hormozi defines work as output, where output equals volume times leverage. Work rate is that output divided by time, so working faster means more output per minute.
title: How to get SO rich you question the meaning of making money

text: He says working longer hours or trying harder are poor definitions of work, since many people already work all their waking hours and cutting sleep is bad for knowledge workers.
title: How to get SO rich you question the meaning of making money

text: Doing more is capped by time and physical ability, while leverage has no cap. He says to beat competitors you should out-leverage them rather than outwork them.
title: How to get SO rich you question the meaning of making money

text: Using callers, he shows leverage stacking: skill, automated dialer, best list, right season, better offer, recorded pitch, then a team, each producing more output for the same hours.
title: How to get SO rich you question the meaning of making money

text: Passive versus active is not binary; income is on a spectrum of how active it is. Everyone has the same time, and what matters is what you get back per unit of it.
title: How to get SO rich you question the meaning of making money

text: Hearing about a friend's lucrative venture triggers uninformed optimism: you only see the highlights. After switching you learn the hidden steps, hit informed pessimism, and many then restart something new.
title: How to get SO rich you question the meaning of making money

text: In a game you restart in seconds after dying, but in entrepreneurship you restart years later. People who keep quitting at the valley of despair fight the same boss repeatedly.
title: How to get SO rich you question the meaning of making money

text: Hormozi had nine businesses and was broke. He says the faster you push through the valley of despair, the sooner you make money, and every business has its own problems.
title: How to get SO rich you question the meaning of making money

text: The money left on the table is the focus you fail to give the one thing that matters. He points to the top self-made women on Forbes, whose wealth came from single industries like roofing supply.
title: How to get SO rich you question the meaning of making money

text: Learning means changed behavior under the same conditions. If you return home from a workshop and behave the same, he says you learned nothing.
title: How to get SO rich you question the meaning of making money

text: He says to do one thing for a long time, get help, observe others, make each mistake only once, and choose a vehicle that compounds with time.
title: How to get SO rich you question the meaning of making money

text: Which one you pick matters less than picking one. He argues the ability to say no, and who you become from the decision, drives the outcome rather than the vehicle.
title: How to get SO rich you question the meaning of making money

text: Magic wand test: imagine all side projects vanish except the one with most opportunity. He says the riches lie behind a few hard conversations most people avoid for life.
title: How to get SO rich you question the meaning of making money

text: Saying no must be relearned at every level: the opportunities get bigger as you grow. He launched a supplement company while Gym Launch made 26 million a year and later called it a strategic mistake.
title: How to get SO rich you question the meaning of making money

text: Layla told him patience is about the behaviors you do, not how you feel. He says to gain traits like focus or courage, act like the person who has them despite discomfort.
title: How to get SO rich you question the meaning of making money

text: Better is better than new, because doing existing things better yields more from the same input. Improvements apply to call scripts, content, websites, follow-up sequences and offers.
title: How to get SO rich you question the meaning of making money

text: Quitting something uncomfortable once got you rewarded, so you learned to jump ship. He says this lesson must be unlearned, since it stops you from staying with a possible billion dollar opportunity.
title: How to get SO rich you question the meaning of making money

text: List everything you already know you should be doing in your business but are not. He says most people know what to do and avoid it for something more stimulating.
title: How to get SO rich you question the meaning of making money

text: He says calling leads within five minutes would triple results for many, though setting up CRM, round robin and call prioritization is boring. Better gets more for what you put in.
title: How to get SO rich you question the meaning of making money

text: Ask what you would tell yourself to do if you were coaching yourself with all your information and no agenda, then follow that advice. He says it often differs from what he was doing.
title: How to get SO rich you question the meaning of making money

text: In his distracted period he ran six gyms, a launch business, and dental and chiropractor agencies and stayed poor. After selling and closing others, Gym Launch reached 1.5M a month in 12 months, then 4.5M.
title: How to get SO rich you question the meaning of making money

text: Doing one thing longer and more than anyone makes it unreasonable to be bad. He credits 4,000 sales calls for his sales skill, and says become best by out-volume-ing others.
title: How to get SO rich you question the meaning of making money

text: Most people fail by moving fast on a weak foundation, such as a poor product marketed hard. Customers then tell others it is bad.
title: How to get SO rich you question the meaning of making money

text: If ad costs rise faster than CPMs, he says it signals negative word of mouth. He argues spending a year, even at break-even, getting the product right makes the long game easy.
title: How to get SO rich you question the meaning of making money

text: Boring better looks like weekly split tests of landing pages and emails, new ads before you need them, daily sales role plays and customer success role plays, and extra interviews per role.
title: How to get SO rich you question the meaning of making money

text: He promises that doing only what you already know you should do will make you more money in 12 months than you can imagine. Separating actions from outcomes builds identity through repetition.
title: How to get SO rich you question the meaning of making money

text: He says a 9.5 out of 10 book takes about 20 times the work of a 7 but sells about a thousand times more, a 50x gain per unit of input.
title: How to get SO rich you question the meaning of making money

text: The reason an education or coaching business gets big quickly is the same reason it is unlikely to make you a billionaire. Speed to the first million and ceiling at the top trade off.
title: I Discovered The Easiest Million Dollar Business to Start in 2024

text: Among information businesses started from scratch without a brand, only a handful reach $100M a year, and he says he knows them all; all have deep brands and about 30 plus years. Roughly a dozen or so reach $30M.
title: I Discovered The Easiest Million Dollar Business to Start in 2024

text: Many information businesses sit at roughly $1-3M a year because they need little operational infrastructure; a team of 10 can get there. He says many entrepreneurs cap out there because they lack leadership and management skills.
title: I Discovered The Easiest Million Dollar Business to Start in 2024

text: Education businesses are hard to turn into assets because knowledge is not sticky: once taught, customers know it and leave, so recurring revenue is low. He compares it to four-year degrees.
title: I Discovered The Easiest Million Dollar Business to Start in 2024

text: Selling an education business faces three key man risks: the founder brings customers, creates the product, and holds team loyalty. A buyer cannot easily replace all three.
title: I Discovered The Easiest Million Dollar Business to Start in 2024

text: Traditional business owners who teach beginners jump ahead on income at first, but in the long run the traditional business curve goes higher, especially if you can exit because you no longer rely on it.
title: I Discovered The Easiest Million Dollar Business to Start in 2024

text: He says most people quit just when they hit a boss they do not know how to beat. Chains and service businesses stall because they cannot bring in the next layer of leadership.
title: I Discovered The Easiest Million Dollar Business to Start in 2024

text: The satisfaction of helping others fades: after hundreds of weight-loss testimonials in gyms he became numb, and he expects owners helping other owners to feel the same.
title: I Discovered The Easiest Million Dollar Business to Start in 2024

text: Do not straddle two business models. Commitment means eliminating alternatives, and focus is measured by how many things you say no to.
title: I Discovered The Easiest Million Dollar Business to Start in 2024

text: A traditional business gives up faster income and lifestyle compared to education, but you usually reinvest more cash into new locations and hires. Which is better depends on your goal.
title: I Discovered The Easiest Million Dollar Business to Start in 2024

text: Education business growth needs no capital expense, while traditional growth needs reinvestment, especially for new locations. Because it is slower and costlier fewer succeed, and the result is an asset someone else could own.
title: I Discovered The Easiest Million Dollar Business to Start in 2024

text: He bought out all 30 plus franchise locations of a chain acquisitions.com purchased, making them corporate. He reasoned franchising earns about 8% for half the opening work, and franchisees resist the process and hurt reputation.
title: I Discovered The Easiest Million Dollar Business to Start in 2024

text: He cites Panda Express as more valuable because its owner owns every location, the land and the net income: about 2600 locations, nearly $4B sales, 27% net margin. He did not begin coaching other restaurant owners at five locations.
title: I Discovered The Easiest Million Dollar Business to Start in 2024

text: Starting out he wanted money and did not care about exits; goals change with time. Successful software founders who switched from information businesses stopped one thing and did the other.
title: I Discovered The Easiest Million Dollar Business to Start in 2024

text: He rejects keeping a test kitchen business while moving to education. Test new plays on about 10 customers spanning market and skill bands, rather than only top performers, giving representative data.
title: I Discovered The Easiest Million Dollar Business to Start in 2024

text: At gym launch he sampled two gyms from each 20% performance band, ten total across markets. If a play works for the bottom it works for everyone, but top gyms give bad data.
title: I Discovered The Easiest Million Dollar Business to Start in 2024

text: A side business consumes mental bandwidth far beyond its income share because the brain handles urgent issues. So when switching, sell or cut the old business rather than keeping an appendage.
title: I Discovered The Easiest Million Dollar Business to Start in 2024

text: He has yet to see anyone succeed big while straddling both, yet most people do so.
title: I Discovered The Easiest Million Dollar Business to Start in 2024

text: Hormozi says the food and exercise quirks common among entrepreneurs, like special glasses, toe shoes and biohacking, are make-believe that mainly helps sell things to people. He says this from a fitness background.
title: My Unconventional Diet Explained in 15min

text: He has eaten ice cream every day, plus cookies and alcohol, for almost 20 years and says he has stayed in shape throughout. Several mastermind peers later told him they got in shape from his presentation.
title: My Unconventional Diet Explained in 15min

text: To change your body, locate your current spot on a fat-versus-muscle grid and your target spot. The direction between them tells you whether to raise or lower calories and training volume.
title: My Unconventional Diet Explained in 15min

text: He argues keto, low-fat, portion control and intermittent fasting all work by cutting calories, not through carbs or fat themselves. In his view calories are what matters.
title: My Unconventional Diet Explained in 15min

text: He explains that keto fails for some people because they add so much extra fat and protein, such as butter or ribeyes, that the total calories end up higher than what they cut.
title: My Unconventional Diet Explained in 15min

text: He says 99 percent of people only need three numbers: daily calories, daily grams of protein, and training volume. In this video he covers just calories and protein.
title: My Unconventional Diet Explained in 15min

text: Set calories as body weight times a goal number: around 15 for maintenance on the high side, about 10 for faster fat loss, 11 for moderate loss. If loss is too slow, lower the number.
title: My Unconventional Diet Explained in 15min

text: He says formulas for calories burned are hard and imprecise, since controlling intake is easy but measuring expenditure is not. So adjust your intake based on results.
title: My Unconventional Diet Explained in 15min

text: Eat about one gram of protein per pound of body weight per day. He says a diet should be something you can do forever, not just for eight weeks.
title: My Unconventional Diet Explained in 15min

text: A hundred grams of protein roughly equals one pound of lean meat, so a 200-pound person needs about two pounds daily. Any mix of lean meats works, such as chicken breast, shrimp, tilapia or lean steak cuts.
title: My Unconventional Diet Explained in 15min

text: Estimate protein calories by multiplying protein grams by five, not four, to cover the small amount of fat in lean meat. Subtract that from total calories; the remainder can go to any food.
title: My Unconventional Diet Explained in 15min

text: Worked example: 200 pounds, moderate loss at 11 times body weight gives 2,200 calories. 200 grams of protein takes about 1,000, leaving about 1,200 for whatever you want.
title: My Unconventional Diet Explained in 15min

text: Get protein in first, then fill remaining calories with anything. Meal count does not matter, whether one, three or five. Big-volume eaters may choose potatoes and rice; he prefers smaller amounts of tastier food.
title: My Unconventional Diet Explained in 15min

text: He says eating ice cream or cookies daily makes them stop being special, and restricting foods pushes people toward obsession and splurging. With nothing forbidden, you cannot fall off the plan.
title: My Unconventional Diet Explained in 15min

text: To gain or lose weight, keep the same protein base, which protects muscle, and change only the extra calories. He says everyone loses weight in a calorie deficit, at different speeds.
title: My Unconventional Diet Explained in 15min

text: When meeting someone, he says their name as he shakes hands and keeps using it at the start of sentences, aiming for about ten repetitions in a conversation so it sticks in his memory.

title: How I make friends with BILLIONAIRES [5 Steps]

title: How I make friends with BILLIONAIRES [5 Steps]

text: He treats bad simply as against your preferences. His model tracks baseline behavior, the trigger, how low you drop, how long you stay down, recovery, and whether you end up better or worse than before.
title: Build a Mind So Strong It Scares People

text: Hormozi says mental toughness is four separate components: tolerance, fortitude, resilience and adaptability. He says the definitions matter more than the labels he gave them.
title: Build a Mind So Strong It Scares People

text: Resilience is how long it takes to return to a new baseline after acting out. He says it is the most workable component and the one he would most urge people lacking what they want to develop.
title: Build a Mind So Strong It Scares People

text: Someone can have low fortitude yet high resilience: a big behavioral swing that recovers quickly still counts as high resilience.
title: Build a Mind So Strong It Scares People

text: He uses trauma to mean a permanent behavior change after an aversive event. By that definition, getting better from a bad experience is also trauma, and changing for the worse is low adaptability.
title: Build a Mind So Strong It Scares People

text: When someone says they were traumatized, he would ask how their behavior permanently changed. If it did not, they showed resilience, fortitude and adaptability.
title: Build a Mind So Strong It Scares People

text: Telling people to toughen up does not help. Naming the components gives clear instructions, which makes mental toughness a skill that can be developed rather than a trait you are born with.
title: Build a Mind So Strong It Scares People

text: For a short fuse, practice not giving an event power over your behavior. He does not say do not be upset; be more upset about letting it change your behavior than about the event.
title: Build a Mind So Strong It Scares People

text: First notice you diverted from normal behavior. Then ask what you would say if you were not in a bad mood, and do that. Practicing helps you catch yourself sooner.
title: Build a Mind So Strong It Scares People

text: To improve adaptability, ask how the bad event can serve you. He says his biggest growth followed his biggest upsets, and suggests acting as a movie protagonist would to move toward a happy ending.
title: Build a Mind So Strong It Scares People

text: Guilt means you broke your own rules; shame means you broke others' rules. Both are useful only if they change behavior for the better, and feeling bad for its own sake serves no one.
title: Build a Mind So Strong It Scares People

text: He is not telling people to numb themselves, only that you need not act out your feelings. Separating feelings from behavior signals maturity, which depends on skill rather than age.
title: Build a Mind So Strong It Scares People

text: He wrote this after his mother's death to understand his feelings and behavior changes. He asked how he could become better from it, and reasoned she would not want him permanently worse off.
title: Build a Mind So Strong It Scares People

text: Sleep and food affect toughness: people are less tolerant when unslept or unfed, so all stats rise when biology is better. Bad events still arrive unexpectedly, so you must respond with what you have.
title: Build a Mind So Strong It Scares People

text: Citing Frankl, he says there is a gap between stimulus and reaction where we choose. He notes eulogies give accomplishments one or two sentences, and mostly discuss service and character.
title: Build a Mind So Strong It Scares People

text: He writes to understand: putting thoughts on paper exposes gaps in your thinking and forces you to learn, because you cannot hide from the words.
title: Build a Mind So Strong It Scares People

text: He says the best business strategy fails if you have low tolerance, fortitude, resilience or adaptability. Many people chase tactics but cannot execute consistently because they let the world dictate their actions.
title: Build a Mind So Strong It Scares People

text: Getting through a day without others knowing you were in a bad mood counts as a win. The skill compounds, and people start labeling you unshakable, which you then live up to, forming a virtuous cycle.
title: Build a Mind So Strong It Scares People

text: Hormozi says writing down his mistakes and successes after losing everything the second time was a major factor in his faster progress; he has not lost everything since and built a net worth of over $100 million.
title: Your Failures Can Make You Rich (if you write them down)

text: He kept a yearly email thread to himself of short lessons and failures, revisiting early opinions later to see what actually happened, which sharpened his decisions when he recognized a familiar situation.
title: Your Failures Can Make You Rich (if you write them down)

text: He compares entrepreneurship to a video game: known levels go fast, new levels are slow with many failures, and the experience carries into later companies.
title: Your Failures Can Make You Rich (if you write them down)

text: Documenting acts as a time machine: records from a winning period let you compare how you saw things then versus now, rather than trusting memory that current mood distorts.
title: Your Failures Can Make You Rich (if you write them down)

text: He says the only thing worse than a mistake is learning the wrong lesson from it, since you will repeat it. He calls asking what someone learned from a failure one of his favorite questions.
title: Your Failures Can Make You Rich (if you write them down)

text: People blame failure on outside circumstances but credit success to themselves. Hormozi, citing Dr Burgman as he recalls it, says succeeding without knowing why is worse than failing and knowing why correctly.
title: Your Failures Can Make You Rich (if you write them down)

text: Outcomes often need two or three things at once, so people who credit a single factor draw wrong lessons. Better operators see business more clearly and predict more accurately what it takes to repeat a result.
title: Your Failures Can Make You Rich (if you write them down)

text: The four scarcest skills, each applied at maximal scale, are raising and multiplying money, capturing and multiplying attention, returning time to others, and influencing mass behavior. He says any one of them can build a billion-dollar fortune, and they are not ranked.
title: The 4 RAREST skills on earth that make BILLIONAIRES...

text: These skills are not have-or-have-not. What matters is how far along you are and how masterful you are at each one.
title: The 4 RAREST skills on earth that make BILLIONAIRES...

text: The money skill has two parts: getting money from other people, and allocating it so it multiplies faster than alternatives. With that skill at scale, he says you can build endless fortunes.
title: The 4 RAREST skills on earth that make BILLIONAIRES...

text: Attention must be captured and then multiplied organically at no added cost to you, as with Rogan and Zuckerberg. That absence of incremental cost is what he calls the key to unlimited leverage.
title: The 4 RAREST skills on earth that make BILLIONAIRES...

text: If you are not earning what you want, he says it is usually because your time is not going to the scarcest, highest-value skills. Such skills often cannot be taught but can be learned, a line he credits to Naval Ravikant.
title: The 4 RAREST skills on earth that make BILLIONAIRES...

text: To build a fortune from time, find something many people spend time on and automate it, usually with software, at no incremental cost to you. Saving everyone ten minutes daily would make you a billionaire.
title: The 4 RAREST skills on earth that make BILLIONAIRES...

text: Because a time-saving product costs almost nothing to deliver, you can sell to everyone, since everyone pays something for time back. He cites Google, which consolidated searching in one place.
title: The 4 RAREST skills on earth that make BILLIONAIRES...

text: Changing people's beliefs and thoughts changes their decision-making and thus their downstream behavior, as when someone adopts a new faith. Doing this at scale can change the world and make large money.
title: The 4 RAREST skills on earth that make BILLIONAIRES...

text: He argues top persuaders often end up aggregating power, since at some point people run out of needs for money and start seeking power.
title: The 4 RAREST skills on earth that make BILLIONAIRES...

text: The four skills match four kinds of leverage: labor (others act for you), capital, technology (returning time), and media (multiplying attention).
title: The 4 RAREST skills on earth that make BILLIONAIRES...

text: A technologist friend told him all technology automates luxury, and luxury is a function of convenience, effort and sacrifice. Technology scales by returning those to people at no incremental cost.
title: The 4 RAREST skills on earth that make BILLIONAIRES...

text: All four skills compound rather than add. Compounding means growth on top of growth, like repeated 10 percent gains, and it works through people telling people, money making money, time saved attracting users, and attention returning.
title: The 4 RAREST skills on earth that make BILLIONAIRES...
