text: Route the best leads to the best closers and weakest to weakest. He tells of a timeshare rep whose income and company output rose after leads stopped being round-robined.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Give kudos for highest show rate weekly, not just close rate, since a 20% show boost may be easier than a 20% close gain. He says this can beat sales training.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Layer manual reminders on automation at 24 hours, morning-of, and one hour before, with personalized prep in the 24-hour one. He prefers iMessage with voice or video.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: He prefers same-day or next-day availability only, since shows are higher, and says to hire more reps if that limits capacity.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Drill a correct phrasing several times in quick succession and stay on one skill for a week or two. Set expectation beforehand that you will interrupt often.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: He says the best closer is often not the best sales manager, likening it to coaches. Managers should drop ego and say the team may outsell them.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: He favors competing against a common outside rival over internal rankings, suggesting internal edging out may lose closers suited to team settings.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Record every call and review it with sales and customer success together, including onboarding calls. He says this aligned expectations and reduced cancellations after closing.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Record heavily when you feel hot and analyze those calls for tone, pauses and transitions. He says great closers systematize what makes them hot.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: He believes conviction beats tone drilling, and reading testimonials to the team builds it. Credit the rep who closed that customer.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: He describes sales as transferring conviction over trust, filling only the gaps needed. He calls it unethical if a buyer who knew everything would refuse.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: The sale begins at first engagement, so setter questions and communication between click and call shape close rates independent of the call.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Edify the business and closer during qualification with specific results of similar customers, rather than vaguely handing off.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Confirm BANT before asking for money: budget, authority, need, timing. Do it in the call or application, and again on the closing call.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: He likes outbound voicemail or email saying you are calling about the recipient's competitor, which he thinks lifts response rates.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: When calling an opt-in, pause after your name, remind them what they opted into with several cues, and offer two time options.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Spend five minutes prepping and keep notes in the CRM so prospects never repeat themselves. He says repeating their answers back helps the sale.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Open calls with a short proof, promise, plan agenda of about 15 seconds. He says the agenda gains rapport and control of frame.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Script adherence is the first thing to drill: if all follow the script and fail, the script is the problem, and changing it is only possible then.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Emphasis, tone and pacing change meaning. Write scripts with formatting cues such as underline, caps, italics for them.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: His Closer framework starts with clarify why they came, then label the gap between present and desired.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Reviewing past pain deepens deprivation and motivation. He says the pain is the pitch, including cost of inaction and what they already tried.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: What prospects tried before is an advantage, since it failed to solve the problem. Show what each lacked.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Chunk any pitch up to three pillars, since people remember threes. State the pillar then give a metaphor, within about two minutes.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Talk about the prospect, not the product. He says spending about 90% of learning on prospect pains lets you sell almost anything.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Explain pillars through metaphors comparing something unfamiliar to something known, such as a stool, toothbrush habits, or a local guide.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: For ghosted leads send a meme. He says the Kevin Hart where-you-at meme had the highest response rate, re-engaging about five to ten of 200.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Train closers back to front: payment collection first, then asking for payment, since they cannot close without them. Expect a no.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: When the prospect says yes, stop selling and ask for payment info, since extra details can turn yes into maybe.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Being surprised by an objection means underpreparation. Know your reply instantly, using acknowledge, associate, then ask, so it sounds natural.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: For stalls ask: main concern, what are you afraid of, what variables decide, and what makes this a yes. Then acknowledge, associate, and ask to proceed.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: All-purpose close: restate their objection as the reason they have not succeeded before, asking if it is why they are on the phone.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: The 1-to-10 close asks their score, then what would make it a 10. If six, ask why not a one so they state the positives.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Never give blind answers to detail questions. Ask a question about their question first, and if pressed appeal to business authority with the mechanic or secretary analogy.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: He says a detail obstacle is really a preference obstacle. Reply that changing variables changes outcomes and their own approach has not worked.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Ask why they care about a detail, then chunk up to the reason behind it and close on that instead of debating specifics.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: He says AAA separated his top salespeople from mediocre ones: acknowledge, associate with something positive or a third party, then ask. Acknowledging buys time and builds rapport.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Approach prospects with childlike curiosity: aim to understand, not win. If they don't buy immediately, respond with curiosity instead of a hard close, since proving them wrong makes no money.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: The person asking questions controls the sale. Sales is an education process: figure out what information the prospect needs to decide, and use questions to guide them to the conclusion.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Never disagree with prospects, though this differs from agreeing with everything. Questions cannot be disagreed with, while statements are bombs. Before answering, check which answer they want.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: For a detail question, ask what the right answer would be. If you have it, confirm. If not, ask why, chunk up to the reason, and ask whether they'd care how you get there.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Handle predictable objections like budget, authority, need and timing early, during fact-finding, before asking for money. Before money there are no stakes; afterward, the same questions feel like extraction.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: When unsure what to say, repeat the prospect's question back to buy time and keep rapport instead of falling into silence.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Before a harsh truth, get permission. If you lack authority, use a foil such as someone similar to them, a senior engineer or the founder. Asking to be a coach fits consumer weight loss.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Learn to stack closes, weaving several in a row after the first one. Understand the theory behind each close rather than memorizing scripts.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Objection themes: time is prioritization, decision-maker is support not permission, details are preferences, money is value and resourcefulness, and stalls are decision avoidance.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Keep only two or three closes per obstacle type that you like and can say in your own language.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: When lost, zoom out with best case worst case: both options are risk-free, one guaranteed not to change anything, the other with a chance. Guarantees make the decision a simple yes or no.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: After the sale, reinforce the decision by handshaking the customer to customer success, passing full conversation knowledge and booking the next meeting, which he thinks reduces drop-offs, backouts and early refunds.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Cheap competitor close: ask which they'd choose if yours cost the same, and let them list why you're better. Price comparison usually signals they're close to buying.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: In person, ask for their ID before payment and trade it for the card they choose. On Zoom, ask them to hold the ID by the camera to match the profile.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: For decision-maker objections, bring the partner in early. Otherwise ask what would happen if they said no, then what the partner's main concern would be, isolating concerns through a hypothetical foil.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Next use past agreements: if they already dislike their situation, why would the partner oppose solving it? Last resort is support versus permission, asking who they'd blame.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Decision-maker has four reasons: they have authority (smokescreen), they fear telling you their real objection, they lack authority but past agreements exist, or they should claim authority over their own life.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: If a spouse or partner is required, involve them earlier in the process. For give me some time, ask what they'll do instead and ask permission before sharing a hard question.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Time objections are priority issues: raise the value of yours or lower theirs. Put math on it and cover the cost of inaction, but stop selling if the prospect is truly better off not buying.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: I'm busy is a priorities objection; give me time to decide is decision avoidance. Ask why after answers to chunk up to the underlying reason.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Without a guarantee, sell around it: offer more guarantee the more control you have. Frame it as for serious people, and ask if it's fair to guarantee work you don't control.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: When a prospect wants to try your free material first, agree and say do it: either they succeed and hit another problem you can solve, or they fail and you help now.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: For government or Fortune 100 sales with 6 to 12 month cycles and committees, much of this doesn't apply. He says more people connected on both sides raises closing odds.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Whoever cares most about the prospect wins the sale. Caring keeps rapport, and telling unfit prospects not to buy raises closing percentage.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Volume negates luck: sales is a numbers game, and the best salespeople do the most volume. Force-feed yourself early reps to pass the terrible period quickly.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Find your team's best closer and do double their effort. Skill grows slowly while income lags, and the best returns come late in mastery, so people who quit early miss them.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Sales resumes don't matter in transactional selling with one or two call closes. He prefers group interviews of one to two minutes each, since stars speak up and encourage nervous others.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Hire for the lowest skill deficiency: consider training cost and ramp-up time. Attitude bundles many skills, though rare expertise may flip this, more so in higher roles.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: In his experience compensation attracts salespeople but rarely changes behavior, except paying on cash collected raises collections. Fast feedback like Slack kudos tied to processed sales works better.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Sales and marketing sit on one continuum. He puts them under one roof, which he says removes conflict between them.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Sales is personalized marketing: marketing covers some information a buyer needs and salespeople fill the rest for each prospect. A sales team improves return on acquisition.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Trust and belief are continuums, not binary. Bigger purchases need more of both, like a bigger plane needing a longer runway.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: If you need many calls to close, pre-market more so prospects arrive further along the continuum. Aim for the prospect to speak roughly two-thirds of the time.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Let prospects keep talking without jabbing back; people like talking about themselves and build rapport. A CEO told him not to be cute; sales is like backyard football.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Great salespeople never skip fundamentals: prepare, warm handoffs, use notes, set the agenda with proof promise plan. Consistency sustains high close rates.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: No for now isn't no forever. Reach out every three to six months as a pulse check, since obstacles may be legitimate and timing changes.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: New salespeople should take low-scored yellow and red leads for training, closing hard prospects makes easier ones easier. Never sell to someone who cannot benefit.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Objections do not always mean no. Wow that's expensive may just be a reaction, so unless they say they don't want to buy, don't waste bullets overcoming it.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Never change price to close a deal. Test prices ahead of time. When asked to do it for less, answer that you could do it for more to re-anchor; change terms or features instead.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: People want to buy and need an excuse. Be kind, not nice: ask hard questions before asking for money and through foils.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: Prioritizing the close over the person creates commission breath and loses them. Coming from human first keeps you on their side of the table with aligned incentives.
title: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]

text: You must coach yourself in your own business because you make most of its decisions; outside coaching helps, but you are the main coach of your own company.
title: If you're struggling with cash flow, Watch This

text: When a business owner is stuck, Hormozi first listens for cash flow opportunities lying around and for major threats, and only after those are checked does he look at strengths and weaknesses.
title: If you're struggling with cash flow, Watch This

text: If a business is bleeding cash, fixing culture will not save it tomorrow. Actions must be ranked by importance, and urgent cash needs come before important-but-slow fixes.
title: If you're struggling with cash flow, Watch This

text: With payroll due within 30 days, a retention system will not solve the problem since it takes about 12 weeks to pay off. Do it after big opportunities are captured and threats handled.
title: If you're struggling with cash flow, Watch This

text: Losing around 30% of customers per month is not merely a weakness; it is a threat to the business itself.
title: If you're struggling with cash flow, Watch This

text: Picking which opportunities to pursue is usually the core job of a good coach, and experience matters because a veteran has more proven plays to draw from than a novice who only says run more ads or sell better.
title: If you're struggling with cash flow, Watch This

text: When you need money fast, the only options are selling to your existing customers, since starting campaigns and bringing in new people takes too much time. He names three such plays.
title: If you're struggling with cash flow, Watch This

text: Easiest cash play: offer a limited number of spots, for example three people at $3,000 for a one-year transformation, with a reason why. Limit it, since cash pops buy time for better judgment.
title: If you're struggling with cash flow, Watch This

text: Marketing a challenge to your existing base at $100 to $200 typically gets a take rate of roughly 20 to 25% of all customers.
title: If you're struggling with cash flow, Watch This

text: To make more, give the challenge away free and upsell participants into food, supplements or other services; he cites about an 85% take rate into the challenge and 80 to 90% closing on the upsell.
title: If you're struggling with cash flow, Watch This

text: Adding one-on-one nutrition and accountability creates recurring revenue and, in his view, lowers churn because members get regular contact.
title: If you're struggling with cash flow, Watch This

text: Give all members a free 14 to 28 day taste of one-on-one accountability, then offer to continue at half the new-customer price. He believes more than half would stay, and uses half for the math.
title: If you're struggling with cash flow, Watch This

text: Match the play to how fast you need money: text blast with paid in full for tomorrow, internal play if you can wait two weeks, hybrid free trial into paid if you can wait a month.
title: If you're struggling with cash flow, Watch This

text: Once cash flow is secured by the big opportunities, you can afford to pay for solving root problems like retention and wait the 12 weeks for results.
title: If you're struggling with cash flow, Watch This

text: He argues most growth advice is wrong because if it were right everyone would follow it and grow; most real growth is counterintuitive, and most people spend effort on things that do not move the business.
title: It's Actually Pretty Easy to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Small side improvements act like offshoots on a tree, pulling resources away from the trunk. Cut them off so resources go into the one thing that lifts revenue most. What counts is growth per task, not tasks finished.
title: It's Actually Pretty Easy to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: He defines commitment as eliminating alternatives, and calls it the recipe for growth: put all resources on the single growth path that returns the most.
title: It's Actually Pretty Easy to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: People do easy problems all day because they know how to solve them and get quick dopamine. The most important problem is messier, with more variables, systems, analysis and iteration, so it gets left undone.
title: It's Actually Pretty Easy to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: When running a prioritization meeting, he declares that nothing before today is anyone's fault and that questions about causes are to understand the problem, not to blame. This makes the team feel on the same side.
title: It's Actually Pretty Easy to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Give people explicit, specific permission to let smaller fires burn, naming who can say the boss approved it. Most staff want to do a good job and fear being blamed for neglected issues.
title: It's Actually Pretty Easy to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: On a paid ads team, if the pixel is wrong nothing else matters because conversion optimization cannot work on bad traffic data. Ignore other ugly problems until that root issue is fixed.
title: It's Actually Pretty Easy to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: After fixing the top item, reassess rather than forcing a ranking of a whole list. Fixing one thing often makes items two through five irrelevant, or reveals a different next priority, so earlier work on them would have been wasted.
title: It's Actually Pretty Easy to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: He cites Frank Slootman, who limits each company to a single objective instead of three or five.
title: It's Actually Pretty Easy to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: He bases this on the theory of constraints: one thing in the business limits growth, and it should be the focus.
title: It's Actually Pretty Easy to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Strategy is prioritizing limited resources against unlimited opportunities. The best strategists see moves others miss, for example a 10x move beyond a 2x number-one item.
title: It's Actually Pretty Easy to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Speed is about how much distance each unit of effort covers, not how fast you do things. Seek the big wheel that makes many small-wheel spins irrelevant, and accept that the A+ problem may take days.
title: It's Actually Pretty Easy to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: To signal a priority, meet daily or twice daily rather than weekly. He says more frequent meetings show how much more important the work is and install faster feedback loops.
title: It's Actually Pretty Easy to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Once the priority and deadline are set, explicitly tell the team everything else they are working on matters less, and let some fires burn.
title: It's Actually Pretty Easy to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Increase communication between meetings too, such as checking in an hour later, and make progress visible with a dashboard or thermometer. He also suggests a shared reward on completion, like dinner or a day off.
title: It's Actually Pretty Easy to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Saying you are committed is easy; showing it is hard. His process for a team is to prioritize, create urgency with meeting times and deadlines, and eliminate everything else on their plates.
title: It's Actually Pretty Easy to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Piling an urgent priority on top of normal work does not work. If you prioritize, add urgency and eliminate other work, the problem gets solved faster than expected; then reassess and repeat.
title: It's Actually Pretty Easy to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: When assigning tasks, ask for estimates in minutes and hours, not days, set a check-in meeting a few hours later, and have each person repeat back what they will do to confirm they understood.
title: It's Actually Pretty Easy to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Many businesses build a graveyard of half-built bridges, spending resources without finishing anything that gets money across. He says this is where most businesses lose their money.
title: It's Actually Pretty Easy to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: A portfolio company had a low show-up rate at its sales event. Reaching the industry benchmark would lift revenue 35%, and at roughly 10% margin more than triple profit, so everyone focused on it and the business grew over 35%.
title: It's Actually Pretty Easy to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: A stream of small easy wins never moves the business forward; the day fills up and the number one problem stays untouched, so breakthroughs and growth never come.
title: It's Actually Pretty Easy to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Top problems are hard because they are full of unknowns: you do not know where to start or how it ends. Start by pulling the thread to understand the problem, and the next step becomes clearer.
title: It's Actually Pretty Easy to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: He has been loosening his grip on information and increasing transparency, sharing financials, conversion rates and margins, because more people knowing everything means more people can help solve problems. He calls the fear of sharing irrational.
title: It's Actually Pretty Easy to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Regularly ask team members to show everything they are working on. Old requests may linger and cause anxiety; retire stale ones and give clear direction on what matters now, plus quick praise.
title: It's Actually Pretty Easy to Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Sticking to a few core products lets you get steadily better at them, and better gives leverage: the same input yields more output, whereas many items force more input for each one.
title: 7 Secrets Behind Chick-fil-A’s $50B Empire

text: Small margins of improvement can bring outsized returns, like Olympic runners separated by a tenth of a second whose lives differ hugely. He says winning comes from being better rather than being new.
title: 7 Secrets Behind Chick-fil-A’s $50B Empire

text: Boston Market took on heavy debt, grew very fast, then imploded, while Chick-fil-A ignored criticism for not taking debt or growing faster and focused on long-term compounding.
title: 7 Secrets Behind Chick-fil-A’s $50B Empire

text: He argues that building to last 70 years means winning by default, since competitors are unlikely to survive that long. Asked to be richest, he says answer with for how long.
title: 7 Secrets Behind Chick-fil-A’s $50B Empire

text: Chasing only money makes people get diluted by shiny easy wins that distract from core items; he says lasting growth beyond the founder comes through a mission rather than a mercenary cause.
title: 7 Secrets Behind Chick-fil-A’s $50B Empire

text: Restricting operators to one store lets them pour heart and soul into it. He sees wisdom in this, plus a path from entry-level worker to owner with uncapped earning.
title: 7 Secrets Behind Chick-fil-A’s $50B Empire

text: Say no to obvious money-makers that conflict with your values. Staying closed Sundays gets harder as the forgone revenue grows, and he says holding to values pays off long-term though it costs short-term.
title: 7 Secrets Behind Chick-fil-A’s $50B Empire

text: Values must be true to you and the business, few in number, and actually lived rather than wall slogans. People learn far more from what you do than what you say, so a late CEO undermines a punctuality value.
title: 7 Secrets Behind Chick-fil-A’s $50B Empire

text: Chick-fil-A studied hospitality, hired Ritz Carlton people, and built a service culture where staff say my pleasure, which spread only after the founder changed how he spoke.
title: 7 Secrets Behind Chick-fil-A’s $50B Empire

text: Build a compounding vehicle inside the business: Chick-fil-A uses store cash to buy land and fund next locations, gaining high returns and tax benefits. He prefers reinvesting where he has control and skill over external funds.
title: 7 Secrets Behind Chick-fil-A’s $50B Empire

text: Owners tire of their offers long before customers do; buyers might visit once a month. Constant changes feel inconsistent to them, and they value getting the same thing they liked before.
title: 7 Secrets Behind Chick-fil-A’s $50B Empire

text: Repeating the same product the same way makes improvement easier, since improving one or two things is far easier than improving a hundred.
title: 7 Secrets Behind Chick-fil-A’s $50B Empire

text: Chick-fil-A has about a quarter of the menu items McDonald's has and makes twice the money; fewer items mean fewer order mistakes, faster drive-through, and less spoiled food, following 80/20.
title: 7 Secrets Behind Chick-fil-A’s $50B Empire

text: Even the sandwich is simplified: he says a Big Mac has six ingredients and a Whopper seven excluding bun, while Chick-fil-A's has just butter, pickles and chicken, aiding speed and consistency.
title: 7 Secrets Behind Chick-fil-A’s $50B Empire

text: Chick-fil-A found each added menu item just split sales away from its main product. Launching a new offer that shifts customers from the old one leaves you with two things for the same revenue.
title: 7 Secrets Behind Chick-fil-A’s $50B Empire

text: A growth executive there said he was hired to do what the other twenty percent aren't doing, and the company even rehearses drive-through in an indoor arena for efficiency and accuracy.
title: 7 Secrets Behind Chick-fil-A’s $50B Empire

text: He asks what business he could stay in for a hundred years, believing solving one problem that long makes you very good at it.
title: 7 Secrets Behind Chick-fil-A’s $50B Empire

text: Hormozi says closing 14% of total webinar leads is very high, not low, and a solo founder that small should not worry about wanting out of the business forever.
title: Answering Your Sales Question Live

text: When traffic, conversion and delivery are all scalable and unit economics are positive, the main job is turning up ad spend and making more creatives with different angles for different avatars.
title: Answering Your Sales Question Live

text: He suggests testing selling the annual plan on the webinar first, then downselling non-buyers to monthly with an extra bonus after cart close.
title: Answering Your Sales Question Live

text: To get low-skilled staff to follow a process, adherence is low with a plain request, so build a roadblock into the flow, such as not completing exit unless the review ask is done.
title: Answering Your Sales Question Live

text: Make the critical metric the first number in the daily huddle, review recordings and roleplay; frequent repetition signals priority, and a short two-sentence script helps.
title: Answering Your Sales Question Live

text: He says the constraint metric should be the headline of daily reports until solved; at a portfolio company, daily focus reportedly cut churn by more than half.
title: Answering Your Sales Question Live

text: Quotes should be delivered by phone with the sale asked at delivery; only if they decline, book a follow-up meeting to decide.
title: Answering Your Sales Question Live

text: One person does not effectively run two businesses; split focus makes getting ahead very difficult.
title: Answering Your Sales Question Live

text: When revenue drops but costs rise, cutting weaker performers can lift culture, since stars are happy to see non-contributors leave.
title: Answering Your Sales Question Live

text: He thinks outbound to property managers would work well, since they are usually dissatisfied with current vendors, and advises fully focusing on that channel.
title: Answering Your Sales Question Live

text: If one business has strong margins and an acquisition channel, put effort into scaling it rather than rescuing a weaker one, since the same effort yields a bigger delta.
title: Answering Your Sales Question Live

text: Labor and software are not truly fixed costs; add up only truly fixed ones like leases and truck payments before deciding how much baseline must be covered.
title: Answering Your Sales Question Live

text: Beat price objections by reframing before price: in a commoditized space, show value beyond price such as speed, rework and risk, and shift from local savings to global value.
title: Answering Your Sales Question Live

text: A missing pre-call video may hurt framing; local savings from a cheaper vendor can cost more globally through delays, rework and opportunity cost.
title: Answering Your Sales Question Live

text: With a toxic star salesperson, first isolate the actions she takes that others don't, then set a 30-60 day improvement plan; in his experience, removing such stars lets the team's average rise.
title: Answering Your Sales Question Live

text: A dramatic outlier salesperson usually signals missing process and training; if everyone follows the killer process, everyone earns more.
title: Answering Your Sales Question Live

text: In entrenched markets, sell the outcome rather than the technology, and consider doing it free or at cost to take on risk.
title: Answering Your Sales Question Live

text: With no case studies, work free to get a track record; free clients teach you, become customers, give referrals and reviews.
title: Answering Your Sales Question Live

text: Dislike of pushiness is dislike of bad salesmanship; aim to sell better rather than harder, since unqualified or unframed prospects cause the problem.
title: Answering Your Sales Question Live

text: After a price objection, agree and ask a follow-up question rather than disprove; add to their logic. Most sales close from proper intro, discovery and framing, not harder closing.
title: Answering Your Sales Question Live

text: He says a business that requires you is not really a business in spirit: most people start for freedom, but end up with liabilities, dependencies and a job they cannot quit.
title: How to Build a Business That Runs Without You

text: Illustration: an owner clearing $500,000 a year in cash is far poorer than one whose team runs a $2 million profit business valued at six times profit, worth $12 million.
title: How to Build a Business That Runs Without You

text: Run a time study: set a timer every 15 minutes and note one word about what you did, then break the list into tasks that become a project, a process or a person.
title: How to Build a Business That Runs Without You

text: Sort each task red, yellow or green: green can be handed to someone now, yellow needs a one-time project or process you can build, red means you lack the skill or person. Solve green first.
title: How to Build a Business That Runs Without You

text: Write decision rules as if-this-then-that for common scenarios. The more people in a function, the more standardized the questions become.
title: How to Build a Business That Runs Without You

text: Set dollar limits on what each person can decide alone, possibly with a total cap, and review financials monthly. He learned from spending on surprise dinners that mistakes happen and feedback corrects them.
title: How to Build a Business That Runs Without You

text: Ask each person how their role makes the company money; for support roles, reverse the costs of doing it badly into measurable standards.
title: How to Build a Business That Runs Without You

text: Graduation test: can someone do the job at about 80 percent and still give you the full result? He believes one person can be beaten by another giving it full time.
title: How to Build a Business That Runs Without You

text: You cannot outwork everyone in your business. Trade doing for managing: swapping about 200 hours a month of work for 20 hours managing is a tenfold improvement, repeated by hiring managers.
title: How to Build a Business That Runs Without You

text: His litmus test: does the business burn down without you? Better still is leaving a month and returning to a business in better position, which buyers want.
title: How to Build a Business That Runs Without You

text: Handoff has three steps: they watch you do it, you watch them do it, then you support their independence while staying available. He accepts 60 to 80 percent quality if improvement is clear.
title: How to Build a Business That Runs Without You

text: Systemize marketing without your face: weekly screenshots of nice comments become ads, testimonial incentives like credits or trials, and lifecycle ads built from recorded calls.
title: How to Build a Business That Runs Without You

text: Stress test: hire people better than you for red items, learn from them, then take 90 days off and fix what breaks until nothing does.
title: How to Build a Business That Runs Without You

text: He argues businesses are not big or valuable or self-running because the owner is not as good as they think; the best people only work for someone they respect.
title: How to Build a Business That Runs Without You

text: To attract top talent you need track record and ability to sell the future; track record can generalize to traits, but mostly you need proof.
title: How to Build a Business That Runs Without You

text: He says he had to build Gym Launch to prove he could build something 100 times bigger, and talent quality at acquisition.com is orders of magnitude higher.
title: How to Build a Business That Runs Without You

text: He argues enterprise value is the most tax-efficient way to build wealth, and you can borrow or raise capital against it; it matters once your needs are covered.
title: How to Build a Business That Runs Without You

text: For growing a software app, pick one of the Core Four or an others path; early on retention matters more, then it is a CAC to LTV math problem.
title: How to Build a Business That Runs Without You

text: The value equation has a dream outcome offset by time delay, effort and sacrifice, and likelihood; you find out value by asking people to pay.
title: How to Build a Business That Runs Without You

text: People are more sensitive to monthly fees than one-time fees, so pull cash forward by selling extra things customers need anyway at a transition point.
title: How to Build a Business That Runs Without You

text: Adding qualification friction to a funnel almost never lost him money; cost per lead may rise but CAC may fall and LTV rises.
title: How to Build a Business That Runs Without You

text: Find your avatar by studying top spending, longest staying customers: demographics, quantifiables, geography, then weave it into ads, landing pages, forms and VSLs.
title: How to Build a Business That Runs Without You

text: Some businesses need retention measured one level up: track referral partners or repeat clients rather than individual projects, as his agency software did.
title: How to Build a Business That Runs Without You

text: He says tracking data lets you predict performance and reduce the guesswork in volatile results across partners.
title: How to Build a Business That Runs Without You

text: A patent means little unless you can fund defending it; until the business succeeds it is worth nothing, and copycats arrive with success.
title: How to Build a Business That Runs Without You

text: If Meta ads did not work for you, it means your ads and conversion process failed, not the channel.
title: How to Build a Business That Runs Without You

text: He advises using AI for leverage rather than fearing it, noting adoption follows a curve and laggards still earn.
title: How to Build a Business That Runs Without You

text: Hormozi says that if you are not earning what you want, your product is not good enough. Anyone with customers has already been discovered, so lack of exposure is not the cause when they do not refer others.
title: How MILLIONAIRES become BILLIONAIRES...

text: Citing Dan Kennedy, he says small entrepreneurs chase customers to make bigger sales, while bigger entrepreneurs make sales to gain customers. The first is short-sighted about money; the second builds a lasting relationship and compounds value over time.
title: How MILLIONAIRES become BILLIONAIRES...

text: A billionaire friend told him that if something will not grow on its own over time, it is not worth doing. Hormozi says ultra wealthy people invest in one-time efforts that compound.
title: How MILLIONAIRES become BILLIONAIRES...

text: If you must constantly show up, promote and sell to keep a business going, the product itself is not good enough, since people are not referring business on their own.
title: How MILLIONAIRES become BILLIONAIRES...

text: First product question: if you made your existing offer ten times more pricey, even a hundred thousand or a million dollars, what would the experience and delivery need to be to justify it? This pushes you to think about value creation.
title: How MILLIONAIRES become BILLIONAIRES...

text: Second product question: if the product cost one-tenth as much but had to be better than now, which one-time assets could you build that deliver value at scale and still be profitable?
title: How MILLIONAIRES become BILLIONAIRES...

text: Third question, his favorite: if you could sell to only one more customer and all growth had to come from that customer telling others unprompted, what would the experience need to be?
title: How MILLIONAIRES become BILLIONAIRES...

text: The three questions target different things: the expensive-price question targets product value, the one-tenth-cost question targets profit to the owner, and the one-customer question targets the surrounding customer experience that creates raving fans.
title: How MILLIONAIRES become BILLIONAIRES...

text: He observes that very wealthy people he knows talk almost only about product, while small operators talk only about promotion. In his view promotion should exist to get the product right, then be juiced and left to run.
title: How MILLIONAIRES become BILLIONAIRES...

text: He lists six ways of getting customers: paid media, earned media (organic following), contact list, manual outbound, affiliates, and word of mouth.
title: How MILLIONAIRES become BILLIONAIRES...

text: Of the six, word of mouth is the only one that compounds; the others scale roughly linearly, such as doubling outbound or ad spend to roughly double customers.
title: How MILLIONAIRES become BILLIONAIRES...

text: When the product is good enough that people tell friends, he says you get unending scale and the profit, with less worry about churn, negative reviews or customers leaving.
title: How MILLIONAIRES become BILLIONAIRES...

text: He notes that early in his career he talked more about promotion, and now talks far more about people and product. He says the ultra wealthy do things that grow with time, making time an asset.
title: How MILLIONAIRES become BILLIONAIRES...

text: He advises no half measures: either sell or do not sell, and avoid sitting in between.
title: How to sell a product - The most PURSUASIVE tactic you can use...

text: At a fitness mastermind with a three-hour slot, he gave mostly value, rushed through his slides and made the pitch with no pre-frame. The $2,000 offer bombed, and the Q&A turned combative.
title: How to sell a product - The most PURSUASIVE tactic you can use...

text: He says intense emotional moments put the brain in a hyperlearning state, so he deliberately asks what lesson he wants to ingrain in the moment. He credits conversations with Dr. Cashy for this idea.
title: How to sell a product - The most PURSUASIVE tactic you can use...

text: One of his gym-business execs half-pitched by telling the audience they did not need scarcity, guarantees or bonuses. Hormozi says those are the very things that persuade people, and audiences still need them to decide.
title: How to sell a product - The most PURSUASIVE tactic you can use...

text: He says he has usually been better served by holding back his ask. If you keep giving and build enough goodwill, you may never need to ask.
title: How to sell a product - The most PURSUASIVE tactic you can use...

text: He proposes that long stretches of giving followed by receiving can beat the standard jab jab jab, right hook pattern, because people feel they must reciprocate what they receive.
title: How to sell a product - The most PURSUASIVE tactic you can use...

text: He thinks the biggest difference between big and small business owners is that big ones understand and apply goodwill. Many of the best things in his life came from it.
title: How to sell a product - The most PURSUASIVE tactic you can use...

text: Making an ask draws down relational capital built with your audience. So when you ask, make it clear and strong rather than small repeated asks, and otherwise keep investing and overdelivering.
title: How to sell a product - The most PURSUASIVE tactic you can use...

text: Ideally you never need to pitch because of the goodwill you have built, but if you must pitch, do it as though you mean it.
title: How to sell a product - The most PURSUASIVE tactic you can use...

text: Thinking about mortality has been the biggest driver of his major decisions. He uses it routinely because it gives clarity and context, showing most decisions do not matter, and it helps him drop other people's playbooks.
title: Why I chose to disappoint my dad

text: He argues that on a long enough time horizon legacy is fragile: his great-great-grandfather ruled in Iran with 400 children, yet he cannot recall the name, and revolution can take lands and accounts.
title: Why I chose to disappoint my dad

text: He finds that dropping pressure from society, family, friends and perceived expectations is freeing, and he chooses to live that way, seeing the long-horizon view as both disheartening and liberating.
title: Why I chose to disappoint my dad

text: At 23 he chose to disappoint his father over losing himself, quit consulting, sold everything, moved to California for fitness, apprenticed a few months, and slept on the floor of his first facility for nine months.
title: Why I chose to disappoint my dad

text: He judged that taking about $200,000 over two years, equal to the degree's economic value, to start something himself would teach more and might yield a business earning comparable money to a job offer.
title: Why I chose to disappoint my dad

text: His deciding factor was not knowing what would make him happy but knowing his current life did not; preferring not to be alive in that life opened up his decision-making.
title: Why I chose to disappoint my dad

text: Sometimes you must try a path on to see if it fits, and give yourself permission to change. Advice from elders is right in its own context but may not translate to a new era.
title: Why I chose to disappoint my dad

text: He prefers joy over happiness, seeing joy as internal and happiness as circumstantial. He notes it is harder to name what brings joy than what you hate, so fix the hated things first.
title: Why I chose to disappoint my dad

text: He suggests inversion: imagine what you would do to build the worst possible life, then reverse those things. He considers this an easier route to a good life.
title: Why I chose to disappoint my dad

text: He says the simplest way to turn free members into paid ones is by price point: low ticket gets an onboarding call, high ticket gets a webinar or VSL inside onboarding so people self-select.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He bets more offers will shift toward roughly $1,000 a month, since boosting acquisition lowers CAC and improves the LTV to CAC ratio; he says brand, content and value in advance keep growing in importance.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He says if restarting Gym Launch he would price around $10K a year and focus on keeping 80-90% renewing, with a value-to-price gap so large nobody leaves.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He says once you can sell, you become obsessed with retention; he favors businesses with word-of-mouth growth and high annual retention, since keeping customers compounds growth year over year.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He moved from pricing as high as possible to making customers smile at the value, believing they then stay longer and tell friends.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: In Gym Launch's early days ads returned 100 to 1, which he attributes to customers making money with the product rather than exceptional ads.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He says pricing is the strongest profit lever, beyond more customers or longer retention; optimize conversion rate times LTV, with four levers: traffic, conversion, price, churn.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: To compare prices, compute LTV at each price (price divided by churn), then check whether the higher price loses less conversion than the LTV gain; compare earnings per click.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He cites a study finding that the more often a company reviews price, the more profitable it is: annual beats never, quarterly beats annual.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: In a high-ticket upsell test at 50k, 35k, 25k and 15k, revenue was identical; he would prefer more customers at a lower price if margins hold, for word of mouth.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He suggests high ticket is less price sensitive because buyers who believe in the outcome find both prices worthwhile; the difference is affordability for some buyers.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: For community churn he says under 20% monthly is average and roughly 5-10% is good.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: To find LTV, look at churned members' LTVs and average them, then reverse engineer churn from that LTV and price.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: Price divided by churn equals LTV; traffic times conversion is the other input. Price and churn affect conversion both ways.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He distinguishes value posts (six tips nobody cares about) from valuable posts where you took risk, spent money or did work so others skip it.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He says client experience can matter more than results: with great results and poor experience people leave when someone else delivers; great experience with mediocre results keeps them.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He says prompts asking members to share about themselves, like favorite book or a photo of workspace, beat long polished posts for comments.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He suggests answering comments with questions instead of statements, which keeps conversations going and reveals members' problems.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He recommends rotating pinned posts, ideally featuring members' posts, so the community sees they could be pinned too.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He defines culture as the rules governing what gets rewarded and punished in an organization.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He says categories signal what to post and act as innate rules; gamifying category names can increase posting.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He rewards good behavior by praising publicly, pinning, DMing his most engaged members, and bringing them closer; he warns against not correcting bad posts.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He says separate one-time value like education from ongoing value like calls, community, ads; price the ongoing part as monthly and the one-time part as the upfront (big head, long tail).
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He says the model reaching $20M fastest may not reach $100M fastest, because churn eats fast-start models while low-churn businesses compound.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He advises against spreading payments over a year; charge clearly for what is delivered, since claimed price versus what you collect after churn differ.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He suggests a lower upfront price with a small monthly could raise LTV and conversion, potentially multiplying earnings per click.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He says a community where members connect to each other outlasts one where everyone connects only to the owner, who becomes a bottleneck.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He says sell the outcome to convert, then use community and member-to-member rewards to keep them; the owner cannot reward everyone often enough alone.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: A new community needs only a few intro posts and one recurring call, such as an agenda-free coffee hour. Let engagement occur first, then build modules to serve what members show they want.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: Bring people in on what they want, then give them what they need. He says this reversal produced roughly 98% retention across his communities.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: Most people do not want to start a business; they want to feel good and have fun. Making things more fun and interesting, not just more logical, widens the market.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: Business growth comes from four levers: traffic, conversion, price and churn. Scale as far as possible until something breaks, fix it, then scale again.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: Every task should ladder up to one of the four levers. Pick work by the biggest constraint and compare alternatives, such as more ads, before choosing a task like reactivating a group.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: Most times you can do more of what works or do it better, so he rarely does new things. Small entrepreneurs stall by dropping what works and chasing other ideas.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: His business mantra is more and better: do more of what works, do it better, and fix whatever blocks either, then return to more and better.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He says overwhelm is the main cause of churn, and that people keep adding to communities thinking it improves them. A weekly group onboarding is a simple fix for low ticket.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: To improve something, define the actual problem, test explanations on extreme cases and gather feedback across many versions before launch. Cut what people do not value and reword what they misunderstand.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: Making every detail perfect requires limiting the number of details. He describes his school games offer as one short course, one call per week and one monthly Mastermind session.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: To add value in a community, spend most time listening, validate problems with power users, prioritize the top problem, fix it through research and experiments, then announce the fix.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: Compare business models on earnings per click by isolating conversion, price and churn; traffic sits outside the box. Separate promotion from delivery, and put extra content energy into promotion.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: Listen to customers, but the right ones. He widened content beyond business, grew the wrong audience, and reoriented content back to business-only.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: Makers need whole blocks of time while managers can work in small slots, so interrupting makers is costly. He keeps meetings to Mondays and mornings free of them.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: When hiring a mediocre person, it is worth it if the time you save goes into higher-value work and compensates for the quality gap.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: Laundry, cleaning and food add up to about 96 hours a month by his calculation. Paying roughly 1,500 dollars monthly makes sense if your time earns more than that hourly cost.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: For a videographer, he says liking the person matters more than skill, since skills can be learned. He would prioritize someone he likes and who likes him.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: Great talent needs a vision big enough for their dreams. Hiring mirrors the customer funnel, and brand counts twice: for customers and for talent.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: With the right people little communication is needed; the wrong person cannot be fixed by communication. Google's ads-suck story is his example of good talent.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: Batch calls on the meeting day and record them, so one hour delivers value, makes content, and brings in customers.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: Niching down lets you productize delivery, so results are more consistent than generic consulting. His sales training for gyms ran under an hour, a script, not psychology.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: Hormozi describes making gym nutrition delivery highly explicit and controlling execution variables so different locations could produce consistently good customer outcomes.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He thinks moving toward more established customers usually improves economics: they can pay more and require less support because they arrive with more skills.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: When choosing between offers, he weighs the lifetime-value-to-acquisition-cost ratio alongside total addressable market. Attractive economics and a large market leave room to increase sales volume.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He recommends choosing customers according to where the business can deliver the greatest value.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: As a business learns which customers it serves best, specializing requires deliberately declining revenue from customers outside that focus.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: Lifetime offers create an ongoing delivery obligation funded by a single payment, making a later change of direction difficult.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: Hormozi recalls meeting a business operator facing chargebacks who refused all refunds. He contrasts that policy with his own practice of refunding customers who request it.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He argues that returning a dissatisfied customer's money can prevent a prolonged personal conflict, especially when the payment matters much more to the customer than to the business.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He is unsure that threatening to prevent former members from returning improves community retention. In communities where that threat carries weight, he thinks the community's quality may explain the effect.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: Customers should be able to cancel easily. A business can invite them to a conversation after cancellation and attempt to win them back.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: An onboarding call can naturally surface an upgrade opportunity by exploring a customer's goals, obstacles, current situation, and previous unsuccessful attempts.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He sees an in-person component as an advantage for an online business because a paid event can also generate advertising material for both its local and online offers.
title: 3 Hours of Money Making Advice You Needed To Know Yesterday

text: He uses 10x as his test for which opportunities deserve his attention: at about 100 now, a project must have a billion or more of potential to be worth his time.
title: 'I'm Facing A Billion Dollar Decision' [Ep 012]

text: Reputation damage is irreversible because you get only one, and money cannot fix a bad one. He says do not take reputational risk with only downside, unlike a stance that trades one audience for another.
title: 'I'm Facing A Billion Dollar Decision' [Ep 012]

text: Time is the base asset everyone has, and people who trade it for more stuff get more stuff. Every moment spent carries the opportunity cost of a higher-return use.
title: 'I'm Facing A Billion Dollar Decision' [Ep 012]

text: He recounts a Tony Robbins story: rich people make bets that win either way, like a billionaire hoarding nickels expecting to melt them for about 40 percent profit if removed. He says seek high-return, low-risk bets.
title: 'I'm Facing A Billion Dollar Decision' [Ep 012]

text: He gave a long value talk at a personal trainer conference, then rushed the pitch in 15 minutes. It flopped with about two sales. His lesson: either sell or give value, do not mix them.
title: 'I'm Facing A Billion Dollar Decision' [Ep 012]

text: To commit fully to a decision, eliminate the possibility of going back on it.
title: 'I'm Facing A Billion Dollar Decision' [Ep 012]

text: Being half in, half out is effectively not in at all, and gives people an excuse to feel like they are progressing. He says make a bet and accept being wrong, since no bet guarantees being wrong.
title: 'I'm Facing A Billion Dollar Decision' [Ep 012]

text: Hearing your own name is a favorite word for people. He notes that forgetting someone's name costs you leverage, while remembering it gives you more in the conversation.
title: 'I'm Facing A Billion Dollar Decision' [Ep 012]

text: He wants people to want to do what he asks, not feel they are doing a favor. Tone, laughs and jokes get them in a good mood first, since people do nice things in nice moods.
title: 'I'm Facing A Billion Dollar Decision' [Ep 012]

text: Measure success by whether you completed actions that make failure unreasonable, and then you succeed by default. Write a list of things to do and change behavior back in the same environment.
title: 'I'm Facing A Billion Dollar Decision' [Ep 012]

text: He has enough singles, doubles and triples in his career that he decided to take a bigger swing, where he will either win or learn.
title: 'I'm Facing A Billion Dollar Decision' [Ep 012]

text: At a crossroads between two paths on a first attempt, he encourages taking the lower-risk path with the higher chance of success, since many entrepreneurs who bet big lose years of their lives.
title: 'I'm Facing A Billion Dollar Decision' [Ep 012]

text: If you take the big swing, go fully in: burn the boats, eliminate alternatives, no half measures. Control everything within your control so you lose only to things outside it.
title: 'I'm Facing A Billion Dollar Decision' [Ep 012]

text: If others in your industry succeed doing what you do, the vehicle is viable and success is possible for you too. Lack of income after a short time usually reflects limited skill, not a bad business.
title: 1 SKILL That Is HARD To Learn, BUT Will Pay Off FOREVER

text: Experts see finer distinctions than beginners, like people who live with snow daily. Hormozi says he sees many more ways to monetize than just free and non-free offers because of his volume of experience.
title: 1 SKILL That Is HARD To Learn, BUT Will Pay Off FOREVER

text: He says real conviction comes only two ways: lying, or having actually done the thing. Having done it lets you rebut criticism with certainty.
title: 1 SKILL That Is HARD To Learn, BUT Will Pay Off FOREVER

text: He ran 33 gym turnarounds over two years, selling supplements to rooms of strangers. He closed nobody the first six months, then had scattered wins that became a repeatable system.
title: 1 SKILL That Is HARD To Learn, BUT Will Pay Off FOREVER

text: Learning from other people's mistakes and successes is the fast track; making every mistake yourself is wasteful. Wise people learn from others' experience as well as their own.
title: 1 SKILL That Is HARD To Learn, BUT Will Pay Off FOREVER

text: He says every successful entrepreneur has a rocky cut-scene: two to six unseen years repeating the same thing until mastery, then applying that skill to a new vehicle and appearing to blow up overnight.
title: 1 SKILL That Is HARD To Learn, BUT Will Pay Off FOREVER

text: An entrepreneur he spoke with built a sales system by making hundreds of daily dials to neglected opt-in leads, step by step getting first call, second call, then offer, over years.
title: 1 SKILL That Is HARD To Learn, BUT Will Pay Off FOREVER

text: Hormozi did 4,000 in-person sales consultations. He says nuance comes only from repetition, time under the bar, with no shortcut.
title: 1 SKILL That Is HARD To Learn, BUT Will Pay Off FOREVER

text: Skill is the foundation of a pyramid: a shallow base limits the peak, a deep base supports a skyscraper. No one can take your experience from you.
title: 1 SKILL That Is HARD To Learn, BUT Will Pay Off FOREVER

text: When you see someone doing better, observe and replicate exactly before changing anything. Only once you match or beat them have you earned the right to iterate on their system.
title: 1 SKILL That Is HARD To Learn, BUT Will Pay Off FOREVER

text: To learn from successful owners, offer value you can actually provide, such as front desk or cleaning work. He did front desk at 33 gyms and learned layout and sales.
title: 1 SKILL That Is HARD To Learn, BUT Will Pay Off FOREVER

text: Billy Gene did cold calling for two or three years before starting marketing, which Hormozi describes as his sword-sharpening rocky cut-scene period.
title: 1 SKILL That Is HARD To Learn, BUT Will Pay Off FOREVER

text: He says passions and interests tend to be very narrow. He describes addiction as a narrowing of what brings joy, while fulfillment is a broadening of it.
title: If you’re ambitious but inconsistent, please watch this

text: He left a consulting job with $50,000 saved to pursue fitness, went from free programs to a gym, then turnarounds, licensing to 6,000 locations and a supplement company, selling to private equity at $46.2 million.
title: If you’re ambitious but inconsistent, please watch this

text: Truly doing only your passion would mean only a very narrow activity, yet getting paid for it requires lots of unrelated work. So it is fine to earn from one thing and be passionate about another.
title: If you’re ambitious but inconsistent, please watch this

text: Passion is a bad judgment filter. Running a business means facing the hardest, worst problems tied to the thing you love, so most of it will be unpleasant.
title: If you’re ambitious but inconsistent, please watch this

text: The only way he can conceive of living purely on passion is not scaling: make only what you want, when you want, and be so good that you keep raising prices.

text: A friend built a successful high-end cookie business without loving cookies; he was passionate about being a certain kind of person. Hormozi took this as a reframe: let your values show in how you do business.

text: He suggests the lesson the young man needed was consistency after things get boring, because that is where people fall off, more than where it gets hard.

text: He made roughly 5,000 ads this year including the book launch, and started making ads 14 years ago, recording weekly to fund rent, payroll and equipment, without being passionate about it.
title: If you’re ambitious but inconsistent, please watch this

text: People do what they are reinforced for, which is not the same as what they are rewarded for. A negative event can be reinforcing if it protects loved ones, while a reward can lose power over time.

text: He thinks the unlock is being compassionate about the difficulty of the pursuit and who you become through it, and accepting that refunds and chargebacks are part of your duty to those you provide for.

text: Citing Phil Knight, he says you are not out of business until someone physically stops you working. Failure besides death is made up, since we draw the goal lines ourselves.

text: Frustration tolerance is how many times you can be rejected and try again. It is learnable, and repeated unpleasant tasks push you to find better ways, which is called getting better.

text: When you start you will be cringey and awkward with no track record, and people may judge you. Quitting over that means caring more about their disappointment than your own.
title: If you’re ambitious but inconsistent, please watch this

text: Instead of vague others, name the one to three people whose opinion you actually care about. He asks whether any one person's opinion should be the voice you hear for the rest of your life.
title: If you’re ambitious but inconsistent, please watch this

text: Of course you are not good when you just started; you suck for a long time and improve until you suck so little you are good. Frustration tolerance is continuing without reward.

text: He pictures the man he wants to become and asks whether that man would be proud of quitting; the shame of falling short brings him back. He says he must suffer even more than so far.

text: He compares follow-your-passion to Hollywood romance, tidy in ninety minutes but ignoring later reality. He says nostalgia is memory minus pain, so early hard years look better than they felt.
title: If you’re ambitious but inconsistent, please watch this

text: Pursuing a different life puts you in the minority, against wiring to follow the pack. Every path can succeed, all will suck longer than expected, and winners keep going.

text: Being someone competitors know will not stop makes you dangerous. Trying that many times at one thing makes you very good. He advises picking a path and committing, because the pain is what stands between you and who you want to be.
