text: Traffic-rich audiences without monetization and money-making businesses without traffic are two separate worlds; combining them produces very large earnings. He cites Logan Paul with Prime and Mr Beast with chocolate as examples.
title: Building a brand, but it’s on easy mode instead

text: If you already run paid ads, starting organic content makes them more profitable: people look at ads, then your organic, then take the next step, show up to booked calls, and close at a higher rate.
title: Building a brand, but it’s on easy mode instead

text: Early on, ignore views and think of organic content as lead nurture; as it grows it becomes acquisition.
title: Building a brand, but it’s on easy mode instead

text: For each new platform he starts with an agency because he prefers to buy lessons and shrink timelines. His first one cost about five grand a month and mostly kept him accountable to three videos weekly.
title: Building a brand, but it’s on easy mode instead

text: He thinks calls to action inside content hurt reach and feel awkward; put them in descriptions and bio link instead and people will naturally take the next step.
title: Building a brand, but it’s on easy mode instead

text: Make all content give only and let ads carry the ask. This avoids balancing a give-to-ask ratio and protects the brand, since a feed shows several free pieces followed by one ad.
title: Building a brand, but it’s on easy mode instead

text: Wider-topic content can bring in the right people at the top of funnel even with a third of the views. His rough guess: about three or four niche long videos for each broader one.
title: Building a brand, but it’s on easy mode instead

text: Bigger creators post less often because of power laws: ten times the effort on one video can yield a hundred times the views. Make lots of content early to learn what quality looks like.
title: Building a brand, but it’s on easy mode instead

text: After watching the first three minutes of his top 35 videos, he found three shared elements: promise, proof, path. Promise and proof answer why stay; path sets expectations and he believes affects watch time.
title: Building a brand, but it’s on easy mode instead

text: For educational content, he thinks proof of why to listen matters more than matching the thumbnail words exactly, unlike entertainment. He holds this as a current view that may change.
title: Building a brand, but it’s on easy mode instead

text: A brand is an association between two things. Its strength has three parts: influence on behavior, direction (toward or away), and reach.
title: Building a brand, but it’s on easy mode instead

text: He rejects the idea that all publicity is good publicity: it raises reach but not necessarily influence or direction. Since brands are built on associations, be careful who you appear next to; he avoids stages.
title: Building a brand, but it’s on easy mode instead

text: Avoid platform hacks because they stop working when platforms close the loop. Align with the constant platform goal: content people click, watch through, and follow with more of your content.
title: Building a brand, but it’s on easy mode instead

text: Treat a long video like several shorts strung together, and structure it the same way. Long content only takes three formats: lists, steps, and stories, which can be mixed.
title: Building a brand, but it’s on easy mode instead

text: His team publishes about 350 pieces a week. He advises starting at a volume you can commit to and ramping up, reusing each idea across formats.
title: Building a brand, but it’s on easy mode instead

text: He captures ideas by tweeting them in real time, and the team turns tweets into videos, posts, and reels. Keep a repository for ideas.
title: Building a brand, but it’s on easy mode instead

text: Topic sources: real-time notes, last week's calendar, far-past lessons that shifted beliefs, and manufactured challenges. These keep content endless.
title: Building a brand, but it’s on easy mode instead

text: To build a framework, gather lots of data, list what each example contains, find what they all share, cut the rest, and name it, ideally with alliterative letters or an acronym.
title: Building a brand, but it’s on easy mode instead

text: Gym Launch retention: he interviewed about 20 gyms with under 3% monthly churn; each did 20-plus things but only five in common, which became the five horsemen of retention.
title: Building a brand, but it’s on easy mode instead

text: He does not think you can be canceled unless all channels to communicate are removed; you become uncancelable if you keep making content and do not accept it.
title: Building a brand, but it’s on easy mode instead

text: Controversy helps reach but not necessarily influence or direction; he avoids it to not attach to many controversies.
title: Building a brand, but it’s on easy mode instead

text: He started with agencies, then hired Caleb, who managed them and built an in-house team. Pay both for a period until your team beats theirs, then the agency goes away.
title: Building a brand, but it’s on easy mode instead

text: To find a good agency, talk to ten and you will quickly see who is competent; ask for referrals. He notes the best agencies do not need ads.
title: Building a brand, but it’s on easy mode instead

text: Hormozi recalls that the word decision comes from a Latin root meaning to cut off. Not deciding meant killing the future with his dreams, so he chose which future to end.
title: 17 Life-Changing Conversations I Wish I Had Earlier

text: Instead of mastering manipulation and scripts, find what people really want, like a chicken sandwich chain that simply makes great sandwiches. He starts products by asking how to get the most people to say yes, then works backward.
title: 17 Life-Changing Conversations I Wish I Had Earlier

text: Going slow to go fast: compounding comes from doing the same thing for a long time. What feels slow in the short run looks fast over the long run, while erratic activity keeps restarting from zero.
title: 17 Life-Changing Conversations I Wish I Had Earlier

text: Any change carries a guaranteed cost that must be paid, while success from the change is not guaranteed.
title: 17 Life-Changing Conversations I Wish I Had Earlier

text: His 300 flyers proved nothing; a mentor tests with 5,000 and then 5,000 a day. He resolved that volume or duration should never be why advice fails, since young entrepreneurs often quit too soon or do too little.
title: 17 Life-Changing Conversations I Wish I Had Earlier

text: Seeing a disorganized founder at a mastermind stuck at $300-400K a month broke his and Layla's limiting belief. Using others' success as inspiration rather than criticism, they reached $1M a month within six months.
title: 17 Life-Changing Conversations I Wish I Had Earlier

text: A multimillion-dollar founder told him fat pitches are rare, so when things get easy you should go hard. He says you may get only two or three in a lifetime and should sacrifice short term for long term.
title: 17 Life-Changing Conversations I Wish I Had Earlier

text: When something works, the real win is doing ten times more of it rather than starting a new venture. He delayed a supplement business 18 months, tripled ad spend, and went from 400K to 780K, to 1M, then 2M within months.
title: 17 Life-Changing Conversations I Wish I Had Earlier

text: After product market fit, innovation should go toward increasing volume rather than reinventing the product.
title: 17 Life-Changing Conversations I Wish I Had Earlier

text: Set aside a fixed percentage of marketing spend, such as 10 to 20 percent, for new ideas and expect to lose it. A founder said four in five ideas fail but one becomes the next leading edge.
title: 17 Life-Changing Conversations I Wish I Had Earlier

text: A learning budget extends your return horizon and gives permission to be creative and fail. He committed to one and it became a pivot point for scaling.
title: 17 Life-Changing Conversations I Wish I Had Earlier

text: A pastor's marriage advice: if you don't agree, don't move forward. He and Layla slow down, avoid false urgency, and first ask what information each is using, since they share values and reach the same conclusions.
title: 17 Life-Changing Conversations I Wish I Had Earlier

text: Larger peers at a half-billion-dollar mastermind were not smarter or harder working; they had a bigger total addressable market. Start in a niche, but eventually widen the aperture, as Facebook did.
title: 17 Life-Changing Conversations I Wish I Had Earlier

text: A billionaire told him growth is about everybody else. Stuck at $30-40M for three years, he hired experts and gave them big slices of the pie, since ten people with 20 years each provide 200 years of experience.
title: 17 Life-Changing Conversations I Wish I Had Earlier

text: If everyone learns everything from you, the organization is limited to one brain and one lifetime. Getting talent who make decisions for you breaks that limit.
title: 17 Life-Changing Conversations I Wish I Had Earlier

text: Fame has costs like lost privacy, but he believes the pros outweigh them: great teammates with shared values, more alignment and inbound business. He now considers his earlier dismissal of inbound a mistake.
title: 17 Life-Changing Conversations I Wish I Had Earlier

text: An influencer told him to post on every platform and denied any flowchart, saying to simply do far more volume. He posted ten times more content and grew ten times faster.
title: 17 Life-Changing Conversations I Wish I Had Earlier

text: With plenty of money, deal flow is easy; what is missing is rules. Allocate capital in proportion to how much of your brain knows each area, such as 85 percent real estate and 15 percent stocks for one expert.
title: 17 Life-Changing Conversations I Wish I Had Earlier

text: He invests only in businesses because he knows them. Declining anything outside that saves time, lawyer calls and diligence, and he moves faster.
title: 17 Life-Changing Conversations I Wish I Had Earlier

text: An exceptional product grows quadratically through word of mouth, while marketing and sales grow linearly. Perfect one product before making new ones; his book sells more each month with no ad spend.
title: 17 Life-Changing Conversations I Wish I Had Earlier

text: Brand can be quantified as the premium you can charge over the commodity version. Extra pricing power drops to the bottom line, and the brand compounds through audience and awareness.
title: 17 Life-Changing Conversations I Wish I Had Earlier

text: Hormozi's Rule of 100: doing 100 of an acquisition action every day, such as outreaches or dollars of ad spend, makes you better at it and gives enough volume to see an outcome.
title: Easiest Way To Get Your First 5 Clients [if you have no budget]

text: He says the most common mistake in getting clients is insufficient volume of outreach or advertising.
title: Easiest Way To Get Your First 5 Clients [if you have no budget]

text: A true master needs less volume for the same result, but mastery only comes from volume. Volume creates skill, and getting better makes you like doing it more, so the cycle reinforces itself.
title: Easiest Way To Get Your First 5 Clients [if you have no budget]

text: If you are not currently acquiring customers, he says you are not doing the Rule of 100. The numbers can be scaled up or down, but this baseline applies per person working on it.
title: Easiest Way To Get Your First 5 Clients [if you have no budget]

text: Most people do outbound once a week or every two weeks when motivated, or spend a single 100 dollars on ads. He says you must do it daily.
title: Easiest Way To Get Your First 5 Clients [if you have no budget]

text: Expect to be poor at first and hope to break even on ad spend; over time skill improves and returns rise. He says people want high skill with low volume, but skill requires the volume first.
title: Easiest Way To Get Your First 5 Clients [if you have no budget]

text: When someone says they want more clients, his first question is whether they do 100 outreaches or spend 100 dollars daily. If not, do one of them first; which one hardly matters.
title: Easiest Way To Get Your First 5 Clients [if you have no budget]

text: If you are alone in the business, outreach is the cheapest method since it only costs your time. Later you can teach others the skill and have them repeat it.
title: Easiest Way To Get Your First 5 Clients [if you have no budget]

text: Hires will likely perform at half or a third of your level, but with returns like 10 to 1 or 30 to 1 on outreach, ten people at fifty percent effectiveness still beat you alone.
title: Easiest Way To Get Your First 5 Clients [if you have no budget]

text: He says moving from you selling to others selling requires a short step back, but you can then grow from one to three to five sellers because you stop being the bottleneck.
title: Easiest Way To Get Your First 5 Clients [if you have no budget]

text: If you struggle to get clients, spend 100 dollars or do 100 reach outs every day for 90 days. He guarantees you will have customers by the end.
title: Easiest Way To Get Your First 5 Clients [if you have no budget]

text: With no money and few skills, he would build a boring service business tied to the body, such as nail, lawn or dental work, since human contact is valued and AI disruption is less likely.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: Coco Fit tried to automate personal training with machines and failed, because people hire trainers for a human to talk to and hold them accountable, not for information.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: After losing everything, he made 100 grand in a month by finding a local business, fronting marketing money, negotiating a low bulk rate for services, and selling at a higher price to keep the spread.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: The three core skills are building, selling and leading. Leadership is getting people to do what you want at scale; selling includes marketing and conversion; building is the product.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: He prefers solving a business from back to front: first find a product people like and keep paying for, since marketing is close to commoditized and mediocre products leak customers.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: For creative or communication work he optimizes for flow across a week rather than fixed rules; brute-force work like cold calls can be pushed through regardless of how he feels.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: When you have nothing to lose, high-risk decisions have a disproportionate upside. He compares quitting a job you want to leave to refusing a free lottery ticket.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: Offers are a mental exercise that feels like fast progress, while leads require activity. He thinks more people make money by letting people know about their stuff than by polishing offers.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: Being number one versus number two captures 80 to 90 percent of the economics, so working ten times harder for a slightly better solution can be worthwhile.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: If he looked at one metric for a business, it would be the ratio of cost to acquire a customer against lifetime value; fix retention before spending on acquisition.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: For a subscription app he suggests churn under 3 percent monthly, ideally retaining at least 80 percent annually, and staying quiet until metrics are right.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: Anyone can market to a big monthly number by spending enough, but income then lasts only as long as spend does; he does not want that kind of business.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: He writes books at a basic level and includes steps like turning on the computer, so about 70 percent of readers get leads instead of 10 percent; experts still benefit.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: Teaching is training: choose what to reward, punish or extinguish. Someone has only been taught if behavior changes in the real context that triggers it.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: He rewards almost exclusively: punishment works faster but only while the punisher is present and needs escalating intensity, while reward lasts longer and can be faded out.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: He decides what to work on using constraints: find the weakest link, fix it, then move to the next; if growth does not follow, the wrong constraint was picked.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: To grow a business you sell to more clients, make them worth more, or reduce risk; ask why you do not have ten times the customers.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: A brand exists to change behavior in the widest share of a target audience by pairing something unknown, like your logo, with positive things people already know.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: He models brand on two axes: direction (toward or away) and strength. A brand is a bouquet of associations, and one rotten flower can damage the whole.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: He sees brand as the ultimate cheat code: with one, people show up, skip price objections and refer friends. It takes long because it is teaching through associations.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: To prioritize problems, he ties each to sales velocity, customer lifetime value, or risk; if it does not, or another has bigger effect, he deprioritizes it.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: Four market positions: luxury, where high price itself adds value; premium, slightly better with utility; commoditized mid-tier; and low-cost leaders. Higher-ticket services are premium, not luxury.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: Price too far above value creates a negative experience; he is extreme about price-to-value discrepancy, as with Chipotle, so customers tell friends and acquisition cost falls toward zero.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: Charging more weeds out bad customers, but premium pricing is earned by reinvesting in the product and serving a clearly defined avatar based on top customer data.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: His portfolio company stalled at 30 locations because finance was the constraint; he told the CEO to build a finance function, growing to 38 locations self-funded.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: Judge skill in a hire by the quality and quantity of data they collect about their department; his marketers who cited many funnel metrics but few product metrics revealed weaker product skill.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: When hiring for a function you lack, interview 10 to 20 people for information first, so you learn what the role should look like.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: Coaching models are hard to scale since customers come for your expertise. Two paths: a partner track like law firms, or narrowing and productizing so anyone can deliver.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: Gym Launch only served micro gyms with at least 30 members, one employee and a certain model, so unskilled staff could follow playbooks.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: Agencies fall into being everything to everyone; focus on the problem and audience solves about 90 percent of strategic issues. Talent quality is proportional to service-business growth.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: To justify price, spell out the many small steps behind one outcome like leads, since owners do not know the work involved.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: Agencies with large clients are harder to replace and clients stick; small business owners are erratic and can cancel from a bad month.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: For price-sensitive small businesses, price by what they will keep paying in their worst month, not the value in their best; he saw an automated SEO service at 300 dollars monthly work.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: Study your top 10 to 20 percent of clients on hard data and experience, then serve only that type; selling one and delivering well beats signing five who leave.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: Most people stay poor because they cannot say no; taking bad-fit customers creates an operational rat race. A nine-figure company is possible in almost any niche.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: To stand out in fitness, be authentic and lean into your own odd interests; superfans overlap on a few of them and only one version of you exists.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: To get owner-like behavior in a sales org, he suggests a contracted profit share, not equity, since equity deals get litigious and slow.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: A limit test for senior talent: you should be learning from them on the call; if you have to teach them, they are not the right person.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: He prefers repeated materials like webinars or VSLs to share information, so closers open by asking if the prospect is ready to buy and use the call to close.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: Hard closing tactics exist because of no brand; without one, understand the avatar deeply, since knowing their pains matters more than product education.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: There are no silver bullets for show rates: a lead nurture checklist of 17 items each adding 2 to 5 percent moved show rates from 30 to 40 percent up to 85 percent.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: With brand, show rate on calls at acquisition.com is nearly 100 percent even with a nine-day wait; ask why people do not trust you.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: Vista Equity analyzes what its top 20 percent of customers share, chases only those and says no to others; he says this can multiply the business fivefold at same sales velocity.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: Reward sales reps for adhering to the script, not closing. Then change the script if it does not close; paying five dollars for adherence worked, and approval mattered more.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: Sales has false positives: a rep who goes rogue and closes gets reinforced for the wrong behavior, which later stops working.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: Sell the outcome, not the emerging tech; that you use AI is irrelevant. He says most AI businesses he sees are weak wrappers or ignore normal business laws.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: To enter AI for main street, pick an industry you know from experience and one specific problem common across firms; narrowness makes you an expert an inch wide and mile deep.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: Choose which problem to solve by value created times ease of implementation, meaning customers times gross profit per customer.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: In a service business, the people delivering are the product; give them pay and upside so they feel like owners, ideally real owners.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: For a tech company, he says the key hire is a technical co-founder, because you cannot judge developers you lack context to assess; one great developer beats 100 mediocre ones.
title: 81 Minutes of Money Making Advice You Needed to Know Yesterday

text: He proposes measuring happiness by how strongly you want to stay alive, on a scale from actively wanting to die to actively wanting to live, because unhappiness is easier to recognize than happiness.
title: What really matters at the end of life (life & death discussion)

text: To raise that score, install contingencies in your life that make you want to reach tomorrow, such as interesting work or people you want to see. He says meaningful long-term projects help a lot.
title: What really matters at the end of life (life & death discussion)

text: He believes people compete on quantifiable things, so they play status games rather than happiness games. Quantifying happiness would be great, but it would need a definition first.
title: What really matters at the end of life (life & death discussion)

text: Hopelessness is a perceived lack of options. When you do not know what to do, build capacity: sleep, exercise, save money, make content. Dig the well before you are thirsty.
title: What really matters at the end of life (life & death discussion)

text: He thinks philosophy cannot be pursued in isolation, because wisdom requires living in the world. The best philosophy comes from practitioners of reality.
title: What really matters at the end of life (life & death discussion)

text: His view of death: nobody knows, and we were not alive for nearly all of the universe's history and things were fine, so he presumes non-existence after death is similar. He calls it his best guess.
title: What really matters at the end of life (life & death discussion)

text: Moods behave like weather and change within minutes or hours, rarely more than a day. Do not take drastic action while feeling bad, and remember hard times pass.
title: What really matters at the end of life (life & death discussion)

text: When stressed, he thinks of alligators, ancient animals that eat rarely and mostly bask, as a reminder that things are not a big deal.
title: What really matters at the end of life (life & death discussion)

text: To start a business, offer a service people do not know how to do, do not want to do, or lack time for, in exchange for money. He says ignore advice against trading time for money.
title: What really matters at the end of life (life & death discussion)

text: Keep doing the service until you run out of time; at that point you are probably underpriced and should raise prices, then use the extra money to hire help.
title: What really matters at the end of life (life & death discussion)

text: Early entrepreneurship is a rite of passage requiring uncertain pain for uncertain time. Marrying the process reduces the pain, and interest leads to skill. Use any fuel you have, and expect it to take longer.
title: What really matters at the end of life (life & death discussion)

text: The feeling of being stuck often comes from rushing and comparing yourself with others. Growth map: let people know, get them to pay, deliver, then raise prices as you improve.
title: What really matters at the end of life (life & death discussion)

text: His story frame for hard times: he will tell this story in his 70s and 80s, and the harder the conflict, the better the story.
title: What really matters at the end of life (life & death discussion)

text: He sees brain differences like physical differences: different, not worse. Judge them by what they actually affect in your life, and he avoids I-am labels, preferring to say he expresses tendencies.
title: What really matters at the end of life (life & death discussion)

text: To reduce self-sabotage, change your environment: add friction to what you should avoid and make the right choice easiest. He says he relies on setup rather than willpower.
title: What really matters at the end of life (life & death discussion)

text: Delayed gratification can be overlearned; aim to maximize gratification over a whole lifetime by balancing consuming now and investing for later, otherwise what you delay never happens.
title: What really matters at the end of life (life & death discussion)

text: He never wore his saved-for orange glasses, and skipped croissants in Paris for fear of carbs; he calls both examples of delaying gratification too long.
title: What really matters at the end of life (life & death discussion)

text: His biggest surprise in business was that his traits can change; he used to lead more by fear and punishment, and as he changed, his sense of identity became more fluid.
title: What really matters at the end of life (life & death discussion)

text: To disrupt a market you need a product ten times better, which he attributes to Elon Musk as a rule of thumb.
title: What really matters at the end of life (life & death discussion)

text: He finds the beginning of a business most fun and loses interest once it makes lots of money, so he puts creative energy into marketing, which keeps changing.
title: What really matters at the end of life (life & death discussion)

text: Stress adapts: things that once stressed you now seem trivial, so your future self will view your current stress as no big deal.
title: What really matters at the end of life (life & death discussion)

text: Getting married, getting in shape and building a business are easy; staying at them is hard. He thinks marriage is mostly about commitment and loving the essence of the person.
title: What really matters at the end of life (life & death discussion)

text: His time approach is to ask what will move him furthest forward, do that, and skip the rest.
title: What really matters at the end of life (life & death discussion)

text: He says getting rich depends more on courage and character, like risk-taking, persistence and frustration tolerance, than on intellect. Spend the first four to six hours of the day moving the ball forward.
title: What really matters at the end of life (life & death discussion)

text: He sees no moral problem in making money; the issue is deception. If it feels off, you are probably misrepresenting something, so make your story true and tell it.
title: What really matters at the end of life (life & death discussion)

text: Creators need a long period of high volume while unknown to get good; only afterwards can you cut volume and raise quality. Each new viewer sees you for the first time.
title: What really matters at the end of life (life & death discussion)

text: He lists his struggles: physical ailments, wanting to be a better husband and father, legal nuisances, hard staff conversations, and working to be more upbeat.
title: What really matters at the end of life (life & death discussion)

text: Getting rich is an outcome and getting better is an input. Entrepreneurs who fixate on the outcome scatter their focus, while improving the thing that creates wealth makes wealth follow.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: If the only way you grow is selling more units to more customers, you must market and sell forever and restart from zero each month. He says most businesses live this way.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: Pouring more customers into a business with many holes in the bucket is a mistake. He says he chased revenue and profit early in his career, sacrificing long-term growth for short-term growth.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: Build something people keep buying or immediately tell friends about. Recurring billing is not required. His books sell nearly a million dollars a month without ads because readers post and recommend them.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: The offer gets people in the door, but delivery is what keeps them paying and sending referrals. He calls the offer important early on but secondary long term.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: A friend baked and numbered 365 cookie batches over a year, gave them to tasters, and gathered their contacts as leads. He then opened a successful premium cookie shop.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: When every business owner says they need more leads and none grow, he treats that as a sign they are looking at the wrong thing. Find out why customers do not rebuy or refer.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: After early testing, the aim is to refine product, service, onboarding, hiring and training so quality stays the same or improves when you scale.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: Improving sales or lead generation shows immediate jumps, which is addictive, but product gains arrive with a delay and bring the big money on the back end. Improving product exercises delayed gratification.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: Traffic is effectively unlimited across many media. The real problem is that you cannot afford leads because your product is weak, so build back to front.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: If you earn the same per customer as competitors, you are in a race to the bottom on CAC, hunting short-lived hacks. The biggest companies skip such hacks because they have won the LTV game.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: He rephrases Dan Kennedy: the one who can make customers most valuable wins. Spending capacity depends on gross profit and purchase frequency, and frequency depends on product quality.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: He states that ad costs per eyeball keep rising, and scaling reaches colder, less aware audiences, which lowers efficiency and requires more education. He calls these unchanging facts.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: Building a community around a business is one way to raise LTV for almost any business, giving one place to deliver value and announcements.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: Referrals counter rising ad costs. Each customer bringing extra customers cuts CAC, and better product also lifts LTV through more purchases, longer stays and premium pricing.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: Brand is a reinforcing loop: you promise, deliver, and customers tell others you delivered, lowering CAC. Marketers who change offers every six months likely cannot deliver on promises.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: Quantitative test: if your cost to acquire customers rises faster than average CPMs in your market, word of mouth is working against you. He says detractors outnumber promoters.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: Making brand the end goal lets you charge more for the same thing, since buyers perceive higher likelihood of achievement and lower risk and accept slower results.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: He says brand-driven advertising is more profitable than pure direct response, though slower, with returns of perhaps 30 to 100x rather than 2 to 3x, citing Apple.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: About a year into Gym Launch, some gym owners who missed his webinar asked to buy the automated lead nurture launch sight unseen. This showed him how important keeping promises is.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: Keep price, value and cost as far apart as possible: high value, premium price, and large margin over cost, achieved by doing the many small details competitors skip.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: Success comes from many small details rather than silver bullets, and competitors are lazy. Even asking customers what pace they want may improve the experience.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: Customers can be near-detractors while owners think all is well; some pay yet tell others not to buy, because switching is a hassle.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: You often do not know why you win. Gym owners credited features when convenience was the real reason. Owners blame outside forces for losses but credit themselves for wins.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: Ignore because statements from your team. Ask how do you know; if there is no tracked data, gut feel is not evidence. He says many successful people also do not know why they succeeded.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: Excuses about a weak product license you to skip work you know you should do. That neglected work is the opportunity because competitors skip it too.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: Sometimes hold revenue and advertising at a level until referrals exceed 30%. The first phase of a business is to learn, not to earn.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: If you lose no customers, the business keeps growing even at a modest pace, such as adding 10 a month. He calls entrepreneurship a battle of wills over intellect, needing delayed gratification.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: For most businesses the compounding vehicle is product quality. Sales-and-marketing-driven growth slows, while a compounding product lets you scale profitably with referrals and repeat purchases.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: Companies that grow only by pushing marketing and sales get lower valuation multiples, while buyers pay much more for those that compound. He says this also makes an entrepreneur's life calmer.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: Improving product is the highest-leverage move because everyone gets it: work once, sell many times. Marketing is linear, needing more effort for each new customer.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: Track product quality through price commanded, repeat purchases, average orders per lifetime, and churn. These outputs reflect quality, while activation metrics are the inputs.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: Find activation points by comparing customers who stay against those who cancel across many variables, then steer onboarding toward that experience and remeasure.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: His first book still sells thousands of copies monthly years later, and many buyers bought the second book. He urges doing unscalable things early to build a compounding model.
title: You Get Rich By Not Focusing On Getting Rich

text: Hormozi says people almost never truly leave home without any way to pay, so a wallet excuse usually signals something else went wrong earlier in the sale.
title: How to CLOSE THE SALE when the prospect says, 'I left my wallet at home..'

text: At the end of the sale, ask whether they have their ID on them. Asking for ID is easier than asking for a payment method, and it is usually stored next to their payment cards.
title: How to CLOSE THE SALE when the prospect says, 'I left my wallet at home..'

text: Take the ID, note details and chat about where they are from, then give it back. Handing it back builds trust because it shows you took nothing they must fear losing.
title: How to CLOSE THE SALE when the prospect says, 'I left my wallet at home..'

text: Holding their ID, offer to trade it for the card they want to use, and gesture with it toward their wallet, phone case or purse so they know to take payment out.
title: How to CLOSE THE SALE when the prospect says, 'I left my wallet at home..'

text: If they still resist, back up and ask what would make this not a fit, or return to why they came in, reminding them of the original goal of the sale.
title: How to CLOSE THE SALE when the prospect says, 'I left my wallet at home..'

text: Everyone has a phone, so first option is to have them open their banking app, go to statements, and read the account number at top right, then record it in place of a card.
title: How to CLOSE THE SALE when the prospect says, 'I left my wallet at home..'

text: Businesses should set up the ability to take bank transactions with their payment processor, since it opens another route to making a sale.
title: How to CLOSE THE SALE when the prospect says, 'I left my wallet at home..'

text: Second option is Apple Wallet. He does not use it first because nearly everyone with a bank has the banking app and statements available, making the bank route close to certain.
title: How to CLOSE THE SALE when the prospect says, 'I left my wallet at home..'

text: If they lack other options, ask them to put down a card they do not want to use, framing it as standard policy, then delay the charge so they can swap cards at home.
title: How to CLOSE THE SALE when the prospect says, 'I left my wallet at home..'

text: Hormozi says the trade-for-card step handles about 80 percent of scenarios. Final fallback is using one of their other cards, delaying the date, and texting to swap it later.
title: How to CLOSE THE SALE when the prospect says, 'I left my wallet at home..'

text: If the objection is not enough money, ask what day they get paid and schedule the charge for that day, such as Friday when it is Wednesday.
title: How to CLOSE THE SALE when the prospect says, 'I left my wallet at home..'

text: Ask if they truly still want to do it, since hesitation can mean they are unsure about money or unsure about the program. If they confirm, put a card down to lock the spot.
title: How to CLOSE THE SALE when the prospect says, 'I left my wallet at home..'

text: He says he learned these small tweaks through a huge number of sales, adding steps one at a time that raised his odds of closing.
title: How to CLOSE THE SALE when the prospect says, 'I left my wallet at home..'

text: He says dissatisfaction comes from wanting to keep everything gained from past trades while also retrading what was given up for something else, without accepting the downsides of the new choice.
title: give me 14 minutes and you'll learn how to be absurdly happy with your life

text: People regret the lives they have because of paths not taken, without counting the trades they made then. He suggests playing out the other path, which also has costs and may be worse than imagined.
title: give me 14 minutes and you'll learn how to be absurdly happy with your life

text: He argues that spouse dissatisfaction rises because expectations are higher, not because people are worse: one partner is expected to be business partner, sparring partner, housekeeper, parent, hobby buddy and lover, like cramming ten humans into one.
title: give me 14 minutes and you'll learn how to be absurdly happy with your life

text: He describes stages: first you blame others for not having what you want; then you learn to get things but crave the other path's benefits without its costs, imagining both lives and feeling short.
title: give me 14 minutes and you'll learn how to be absurdly happy with your life

text: He says demanding everything, an impossible standard, and changing the target once reached amounts to choosing dissatisfaction.
title: give me 14 minutes and you'll learn how to be absurdly happy with your life

text: He gives little weight to deathbed regrets, seeing them as a human tendency to want another life's benefits while keeping one's own, which does not inform decisions well.
title: give me 14 minutes and you'll learn how to be absurdly happy with your life

text: From looking at what lasting marriages share, he narrowed it to high commitment with low expectations, and thinks this applies to any big life choice. Commitment means eliminating alternatives.
title: give me 14 minutes and you'll learn how to be absurdly happy with your life

text: With low expectations, reality tends to exceed them, so you stay above expectations. He notes he is sharing a thought, not claiming to have life figured out.
title: give me 14 minutes and you'll learn how to be absurdly happy with your life

text: He warns that refusing to choose between contradictory options while waiting for more information leaves you stuck and without the benefits of either.
title: give me 14 minutes and you'll learn how to be absurdly happy with your life

text: Some doors are reversible but big ones, like marriage or a business, are hard to undo. He says the ability to make decisions and make good ones is a prized trait.
title: give me 14 minutes and you'll learn how to be absurdly happy with your life

text: He lists three skills: learning to decide, deciding well so outcomes work, and staying satisfied without changing what you wanted from the decision. He calls being happy with decisions underrated.
title: give me 14 minutes and you'll learn how to be absurdly happy with your life

text: He finds it helpful to acknowledge the trades he made, accept them, and remind himself that alternative paths carry costs and probably weaker upsides than imagined.
title: give me 14 minutes and you'll learn how to be absurdly happy with your life

text: He believes he would be about as happy or unhappy across three different lifetimes, and that thinking this lowered his anxiety.
title: give me 14 minutes and you'll learn how to be absurdly happy with your life

text: He points out that wives of rich men and of poor men are not always happy, concluding humans stay dissatisfied regardless of circumstance.
title: give me 14 minutes and you'll learn how to be absurdly happy with your life

text: When dissatisfaction creeps in, he tells himself that he is the problem, then asks which arbitrary expectation he set that the world failed to meet; removing it is as good as having it.
title: give me 14 minutes and you'll learn how to be absurdly happy with your life

text: When an attack contains some truth, he gives three options: ignore it, agree with it, or agree and one-up the attacker. He names ignoring as his personal favorite because it costs the least time and effort.
title: The Alex Hormozi Guide to Haters [REVEALED]

text: He points out that people who attack him spend their own audience's attention on him, and some of those viewers become customers, so he is happy for the haters to continue.
title: The Alex Hormozi Guide to Haters [REVEALED]

text: Agreeing with an insult removes the conflict, since a fight needs an opposing side. If you take the attacker's side of the table, there is nothing left to push against and they have to leave.
title: The Alex Hormozi Guide to Haters [REVEALED]

text: The third level is agreeing and adding to the insult, mocking yourself better than they can. You know yourself better than they do, so you have more material.
title: The Alex Hormozi Guide to Haters [REVEALED]

text: Attacks fade like an extinction curve: yelling at a rock stops when the rock gives no feedback. Without a reaction, haters lose interest and disappear, so he aims to be the rock.
title: The Alex Hormozi Guide to Haters [REVEALED]

text: He views hate as coming only from below, so being hated tells him the hater is beneath him and follows him.
title: The Alex Hormozi Guide to Haters [REVEALED]

text: Against smaller people making silly insults, any of the three levels works. Against smaller people accusing you of lying, he ignores them, even though it is painful to watch.
title: The Alex Hormozi Guide to Haters [REVEALED]

text: He says you beat hate by drowning it out with a louder message, not by answering it. Time spent on attackers is time not spent giving value to your audience.
title: The Alex Hormozi Guide to Haters [REVEALED]

text: Responding to a smaller attacker can be a Pyrrhic victory. Even if you win, you lose credibility, and letting them provoke you shows they control your actions.
title: The Alex Hormozi Guide to Haters [REVEALED]

text: When someone bigger than you makes a false or mocking attack, lean hardest into the third level. A joke response makes the attacker look petty and can even send attention your way.
title: The Alex Hormozi Guide to Haters [REVEALED]

text: He states a rule: never attack back. Reputation is won by deflection or by amplifying above the attack, never by direct conflict.
title: The Alex Hormozi Guide to Haters [REVEALED]

text: He argues brand is built on association, so repeatedly saying you are not something links you with it, like the pink elephant. Denying a claim can feed the narrative you want to kill.
title: The Alex Hormozi Guide to Haters [REVEALED]

text: He advises putting anxious energy into a louder message about your mission instead of replying. People follow you for the value you give, so ignoring a rumor should not halt growth.
title: The Alex Hormozi Guide to Haters [REVEALED]

text: By the law of large numbers, 500 hateful comments is 0.1% of the audience he cites, so the other 99.9% are positive. He says to focus on them.
title: The Alex Hormozi Guide to Haters [REVEALED]

text: His summary: if the claim is true, lean into it. If false and the attacker is smaller, ignore it. If false and bigger, make them seem petty. Beyond that, only getting louder wins.
title: The Alex Hormozi Guide to Haters [REVEALED]

text: You only lose by getting quieter or by changing your message, and both stop delivering value. He says people who came for the value tend to defend you.
title: The Alex Hormozi Guide to Haters [REVEALED]

text: He says humor counters hate better than anything, and self-mockery is the best humor. Nobody keeps kicking someone who admits their flaws, so the conflict fades.
title: The Alex Hormozi Guide to Haters [REVEALED]

text: He says about 99% of his attention goes to amplifying his message, and levels two and three together are the tiniest slice of his responses, with ignoring dominant.
title: The Alex Hormozi Guide to Haters [REVEALED]

text: With a million followers and 500 haters a day, the haters are a tiny share but feel huge. Social media amplifies hate we are not built to handle.
title: The Alex Hormozi Guide to Haters [REVEALED]

text: He says you get canceled only if you accept it or if platforms make it impossible to spread your message. Otherwise continuing to put out value dilutes negativity over time.
title: The Alex Hormozi Guide to Haters [REVEALED]

text: He calls hate a prerequisite for success, citing Winston Churchill on enemies. He says only invisible people get no hate, and if you stand for something, some will oppose you.
title: The Alex Hormozi Guide to Haters [REVEALED]

text: His recap: ignoring is by far the biggest part. If others can push a button and get a reaction, they will; if you keep doing your thing regardless, you become very hard to beat.
title: The Alex Hormozi Guide to Haters [REVEALED]

text: Building a company so it could be sold someday was among the most valuable things he did as an entrepreneur, whether or not he ever plans to sell. It gave him optionality and more freedom, the real goal of the business.
title: I OWN 6 multimillion dollar companies...this is how I do it...

text: He made the mistake of being CEO of one company and then starting a second while planning to be CEO of both. It cost him dearly in time and stress, because being CEO is a full-time role.
title: I OWN 6 multimillion dollar companies...this is how I do it...

text: CEO and owner are different roles. Buffett owns companies like See's Candies and Geico without running them. The question is whether your business can hold and grow without your involvement, as with equity in a stock.
title: I OWN 6 multimillion dollar companies...this is how I do it...

text: He treats all portfolio companies the same way, whether he owns 100% of three of them or holds minority stakes in five others. He meets quarterly with leadership teams, plus extra meetings as needed.
title: I OWN 6 multimillion dollar companies...this is how I do it...

text: Nose in, hands out, a phrase from a mentor: in strategic meetings he leaves with no homework or to-dos, acting as an adviser who offers experience and bounces ideas rather than leading. Otherwise he could never get anything done.
title: I OWN 6 multimillion dollar companies...this is how I do it...

text: To become a true owner, you must build the business with that intention from the start. His earlier businesses depended on him partly from his own interpersonal needs and partly because he did not know better.
title: I OWN 6 multimillion dollar companies...this is how I do it...

text: A personality-based brand makes owner independence harder than a faceless brand. See's Candies and Geico are not about Buffett; Geico has a gecko mascot.
title: I OWN 6 multimillion dollar companies...this is how I do it...

text: Ownership test: if you claim to be passive but have no CEO, he would challenge that. The company must grow and innovate without you, which means bringing someone up to operate as CEO.
title: I OWN 6 multimillion dollar companies...this is how I do it...

text: His litmus test: put someone new in charge and give them six months. The company should grow in both top line and profit without him, barring things like planned capital investment.
title: I OWN 6 multimillion dollar companies...this is how I do it...

text: To remove yourself, leave the company-wide Slack or Asana so nobody can reach you there. His portfolio uses one separate Slack containing only executives from each company, whose teams reach those executives directly.
title: I OWN 6 multimillion dollar companies...this is how I do it...

text: Ownership, not CEO, is the goal. He thinks acting as an owner leads to better long-term decisions and less stress over short-term details, and better serves the business and its customers.
title: I OWN 6 multimillion dollar companies...this is how I do it...

text: He defines a millionaire as someone whose net worth, excluding their primary residence, exceeds a million dollars; net worth is assets minus liabilities, and liquid net worth counts only assets tradable in and out.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: There are two routes to a million: earn it or own it. Owning, such as a business sold at a multiple of profit, gets there faster because taxes and living costs do not erode it each year.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: He says diversification is for people who do not know what they are doing; early on, the scarce resources are time and attention, so put them into one thing.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: The wealthiest people have multiple income streams, but they got there by going all in on one until it overflowed, and diversified only afterward to maintain wealth.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: Any opportunity could work or fail depending on which one you work on, so move quickly through the phase of not knowing what you are doing.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: Entrepreneurs pass through uninformed optimism, informed pessimism, and a valley of despair where most quit and jump to a new opportunity, repeating the cycle without progress.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: Building fast and flimsy caps growth. If a business is built wrong, the fastest way to a much larger size can be to restart and build it properly.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: Do not just push marketing and sales harder; keep improving the product until customers tell their friends, otherwise a bad product raises advertising costs as reputation suffers.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: The market is the strongest variable in how much you earn, then the offer, then your ability to persuade.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: When picking a market, look for four things together: people in pain, ability to buy, ease of targeting, and a growing market. Missing any one is a problem.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: The simplest formula to reach two million plus is one avatar, one product, one channel.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: Under a million dollars, adding more products or channels adds complexity; instead sell more of the same product to the same person through the same channel, and if it cannot scale profitably it is a business or pricing problem.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: Value has four variables: dream outcome, perceived likelihood of achievement, time delay, and effort plus sacrifice. Raise the first two, lower the last two.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: The ideal offer is a huge dream you are guaranteed to get instantly with no effort; costs like time, effort and sacrifice reduce value.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: Hidden costs, meaning things the buyer must start doing, are often the most expensive part of an offer. Removing them can make the same service far more valuable.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: He says offers are one of the largest levers in any business because changing the offer changes marketing, sales scripts, sales process, and delivery.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: There are eight ways to advertise: four you do (warm outreach, content, paid ads, cold outreach) and four others do (referrals, employees, agencies, affiliates). If nothing sells, you are not doing enough of the core four.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: For your first million, pick just one advertising method and stick to the core four before involving other parties.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: Founders should be involved in marketing and sales early because it is cheaper, the skills are needed long term, and it lets you teach and test others later.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: Build a sales process by trying steps, noting what got a response, and repeating; then write a script so others can sell, since successors lack founder conviction.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: He regrets taking nothing out of his gyms while reinvesting all profit, then losing everything when he sold; he says pay is personal and depends on risk tolerance.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: He likes growing a bank balance as a goal because it forces cash out of the business and lowers spending, and a full account leads to less stressed decisions.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: A back-of-napkin split for capital-heavy portfolio businesses is 33% to the owner, 30% to growth, with the rest to reserves for the business and the owner.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: Alternative to a split: a watermark. Calculate the monthly cost of planned growth, keep that above a level in the account, and distribute the rest.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: Set goals on activities rather than outcomes, because inputs are controllable and drive outputs.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: The rule of 100: 100 primary actions over 100 days usually produces the first result you want; count in hundreds, such as 100 outreaches or $100 of ads per day.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: Portfolio goals use the scientific method: the problem, an if-then hypothesis, how to measure doing it and result, then whether it was done and worked.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: Relaying a mentor's saying, he says you should only need to get rich once and afterwards never make bets that risk the farm.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: Fortunes are created by taking huge risks with small amounts of money and preserved by taking small risks with large amounts.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: Market in four directions: to prospects, customers, candidates and employees, so delivery capacity grows with sales.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: Removing the founder-as-genius by building people and systems adds enterprise value without changing revenue or profit; he uses a 7x multiple example.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: Reputation is like a bouquet of associated experiences, and one negative one can distort perception of the rest. A brand is an association between something known and unknown.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: Customer surplus, or goodwill, is value received beyond what was paid; in his experience it compounds multiplicatively when repeated.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: He says goodwill compounds faster than revenue, and a hundred million dollar brand can be built faster than that much revenue.
title: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]

text: At a quarterly meeting, the private equity partner who owns two portfolio companies cared about only two topics: building technology into the business and value-adding acquisitions, aimed at a large sale price. The rest he treated as routine blocking and tackling.
title: Top 10 Fast Business Lessons From My Last 10 Years

text: Your wealth depends on the weight of your slice, not owning the whole pie. Building big requires more people, so tie leaders in with profit sharing and bonus pools.
title: Top 10 Fast Business Lessons From My Last 10 Years

text: After his companies introduced profit sharing and bonus pools for leaders, returns grew well beyond what was given up, so the smaller retained share became worth more than full ownership without that growth.
title: Top 10 Fast Business Lessons From My Last 10 Years

text: Looking at the richest people, most do not own all or even the majority of their companies. He takes from this that making more people wealthy makes you wealthier, including people vested in your success.
title: Top 10 Fast Business Lessons From My Last 10 Years

text: Big things take time. He was once obsessed with fast wins, and learned from the Panda Express owner that customers must love the product and that success took decades, with much growth arriving late.
title: Top 10 Fast Business Lessons From My Last 10 Years

text: Ask what you could do for a very long period, and stay unmoved by shiny objects. Test decisions by whether they matter in 10 years and limit everything else.
title: Top 10 Fast Business Lessons From My Last 10 Years

text: Brand is your reputation, what people say behind your back. It is built by making promises and delivering beyond them, which quietly lifts advertising returns as more people hear of you from friends.
title: Top 10 Fast Business Lessons From My Last 10 Years

text: Many people over-promise and under-deliver, so acquisition cost rises faster than ad costs. He says negative word of mouth is stronger than positive, and people wrongly blame platforms.
title: Top 10 Fast Business Lessons From My Last 10 Years

text: Brand gives pricing power, which flows straight to profit, as with coffee, or a plain versus logo t-shirt. Margins form a moat when costs rise, while commodity sellers without brand go under.
title: Top 10 Fast Business Lessons From My Last 10 Years

text: Simple scales, fancy fails. His largest portfolio companies have the simplest models, since scale adds complexity itself. Keep offers, customer journey, audience, messaging and pricing as simple as possible.
title: Top 10 Fast Business Lessons From My Last 10 Years

text: The most successful portfolio founders are the least emotionally reactive. Projected upsides and threats usually land less extreme than imagined, so estimates should be conservative in both directions; big returns often come from the unexpected.
title: Top 10 Fast Business Lessons From My Last 10 Years

text: He has often thought he would lose companies he owned, yet in about ten years has lost none. He says fear-driven thinking that things are dying is the mind fooling you.
title: Top 10 Fast Business Lessons From My Last 10 Years

text: Learned from a Blackstone founder: building anything big needs top-level talent, which is drawn only to big opportunities. Think how large it can be so others' dreams fit, and leave room for future talent.
title: Top 10 Fast Business Lessons From My Last 10 Years

text: Compounding needs time, which people hate adding. Portfolio leaders chase small steady gains; 10 percent growth per quarter gives about 40x over a decade, so a $1M business could reach $40M.
title: Top 10 Fast Business Lessons From My Last 10 Years

text: His goals for portfolio and own companies have grown more conservative. Most entrepreneurs he talks with set unrealistic goals, so he favors achievable targets, such as 10 percent per quarter, leaving room to overachieve.
title: Top 10 Fast Business Lessons From My Last 10 Years

text: Only take a company-sized risk when not taking it risks the company more, and you have strong evidence. He says founders often destroy healthy businesses by betting on non-core exciting opportunities.
title: Top 10 Fast Business Lessons From My Last 10 Years

text: Once you have product market fit in an enduring demand market, growth mostly comes from boring work: getting better at fulfilling the promise. About 80 percent of his portfolio is non-tech.
title: Top 10 Fast Business Lessons From My Last 10 Years

text: Improve what you already sell: shorten time to value, improve customer health, segment customers by need and match products. This builds brand, pricing power, word of mouth and moat.
title: Top 10 Fast Business Lessons From My Last 10 Years

text: A portfolio company wanted a new high-ticket upsell line. He proposed a survey; 85 percent of customers wanted more of what they already bought and 15 percent wanted the new product.
title: Top 10 Fast Business Lessons From My Last 10 Years

text: Lead with data rather than ego, and sell what customers want, even when boring. Ignoring customers can off-road and destroy a business.
title: Top 10 Fast Business Lessons From My Last 10 Years

text: His success recipe: make and keep promises, build brand, use it for pricing power, spend extra profit on better people and acquisition channels, share pie, then give it time.

text: In a service business, he says getting churn below roughly 1 to 2 percent is very unlikely, and doing so usually means growth is purely from organic referrals. To get massive you must grow from organic, outbound and paid.
title: Your Inflow Is Your Bottleneck (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: To reach a 200 to 500 member facility you need to sign roughly 20 new clients weekly. Otherwise you will not get there.
title: Your Inflow Is Your Bottleneck (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Services are easy in and easy out, unlike software, which is stickier because switching is painful. If you sell services and want to be big, accept a back-end churn and use fast scaling of inflow as your advantage.
title: Your Inflow Is Your Bottleneck (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Even people who sign straight onto recurring billing usually must be resold on a longer term. There is a try-it phase and a commit phase, and they stick only after the second sale.
title: Your Inflow Is Your Bottleneck (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Example: capped at 10 new trials weekly with 10 percent monthly churn, reaching 300 members would require converting 75 percent weekly, which few do.
title: Your Inflow Is Your Bottleneck (ALEX HORMOZI)

title: Your Inflow Is Your Bottleneck (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Running ads for a couple weeks then turning them off does not scale. Inflow must continue every week while you fulfill concurrently, which requires scheduling the team accordingly.

text: Growth is a volume game. Champions have short memories and are unaffected by losses. If you meet 200 people, about 100 will say no, and you must be emotionally fine with that.

text: He says priorities are just ranked. Conflicts mean one is secondary, so decide what matters most and put the required work on the calendar.

text: After reading 14 self-help books around age 21 or 22 with no life change, he vowed to do everything in the next book before reading another, then quit his job and drove across the country.
