text: What you do next matters more than what you did before; a long history of inaction does not limit the impact of your next choice.
title: 15 Brutal Truths I Know at 36 That I Wish I Knew at 20

text: He prefers believing you will eventually learn anything with enough volume, and says people badly underestimate the repetitions needed to get good; his own early videos did not sound natural.
title: 15 Brutal Truths I Know at 36 That I Wish I Knew at 20

text: Extrapolate any past success, such as school or fitness, to your next challenge; work ethic is a generalizable skill, and repeated application builds a snowball of confidence.
title: 15 Brutal Truths I Know at 36 That I Wish I Knew at 20

text: If you are under 30 with no responsibilities and want your situation improved, he recommends working as many hours as possible, since you will never have fewer obligations and early effort compounds for decades.
title: 15 Brutal Truths I Know at 36 That I Wish I Knew at 20

text: Starting later with family has trade-offs, but experience lets you spend effort more strategically, like veteran athletes. Having nothing to lose gives unlimited lottery tickets, since fear comes from having something to lose.
title: 15 Brutal Truths I Know at 36 That I Wish I Knew at 20

text: Entrepreneurship is a strong vehicle for personal development because the market gives honest feedback where friends and family protect your feelings; he says the person limiting the business is you.
title: 15 Brutal Truths I Know at 36 That I Wish I Knew at 20

text: The hard part is continuing when excitement fades; your potential depends on how much uncertainty you can tolerate and for how long, and inability to work without reward hurts more than lack of talent.
title: 15 Brutal Truths I Know at 36 That I Wish I Knew at 20

text: If you are stuck in bills, get out of the hole fast, even with multiple jobs, since above water options open up and long-term thinking becomes possible.
title: 15 Brutal Truths I Know at 36 That I Wish I Knew at 20

text: He defines sadness as coming from a perceived lack of options; the question to ask is which trade you are unwilling to make, since changing what you tolerate creates options.
title: 15 Brutal Truths I Know at 36 That I Wish I Knew at 20

text: Fear lives in the vague, not the specific; play out feared decisions step by step in concrete detail and the costs often turn out bearable.
title: 15 Brutal Truths I Know at 36 That I Wish I Knew at 20

text: Trying to be good at everything makes you good at nothing; decisions mean cutting off paths, so compounding requires saying no to other opportunities and sticking with one thing for months.
title: 15 Brutal Truths I Know at 36 That I Wish I Knew at 20

text: He says entrepreneurs are rewarded for believing in themselves more than others do; the few who earn far more stuck with an uncommon path long after quitting made sense and made trades others refused.
title: 15 Brutal Truths I Know at 36 That I Wish I Knew at 20

text: The pi equation is inflow divided by outflow. Because it divides rates, it outputs a hypothetical max, which he uses in three variations to see where a business is heading.
title: How to Scale Your Business Fast

text: If he signs up five customers a month and loses 10% monthly, the business tops out near 50 clients (5 divided by 0.1). It cannot exceed that unless sign-ups rise or churn falls.
title: How to Scale Your Business Fast

text: With 30 clients, two new sign-ups a month and 10% churn, the hypothetical max is 20. The business will shrink from 30 toward 20 unless he fixes something.
title: How to Scale Your Business Fast

text: Lifetime value is monthly revenue per client divided by monthly churn. At $1,000 a month and 20% churn, a customer is worth $5,000, giving a number to market against.
title: How to Scale Your Business Fast

text: Knowing customer value gives rough math for acquisition spend. He says spend under about a third of value, aiming for roughly a 3 to 1 return, so under $2,000 on a $5,000 customer.
title: How to Scale Your Business Fast

text: Applied to revenue: $10,000 of new business monthly with 10% revenue churn caps out at $100,000 a month. Comparing current revenue to that cap shows whether the business is shrinking or growing.
title: How to Scale Your Business Fast

text: Without negative churn, growth slows over time because churn takes a bigger share each month as the customer base rises, so the business approaches its max in a flattening curve.
title: How to Scale Your Business Fast

text: Because business results fluctuate, he says companies usually end up capping around 80-90% of the theoretical max rather than hitting it exactly.
title: How to Scale Your Business Fast

text: The golden ratio compares the share of customers who refer a new customer monthly to the share who leave. If referrals are 10% and churn is 5%, the business grows without limit, called net negative churn.
title: How to Scale Your Business Fast

text: He notes that in practice growth is not truly endless, since mistakes eventually lower the referral rate or raise churn, but holding the golden ratio for a period brings very fast growth.
title: How to Scale Your Business Fast

text: Combining lifetime value with inflow gives the revenue ceiling: 20 new clients a month at $5,000 lifetime value levels out at $100,000 a month.
title: How to Scale Your Business Fast

text: Inside the business, 20 clients at $1,000 looks like only $20,000 a month, so you cannot tell if you are winning. He says to keep going, avoid shiny object syndrome, since recurring revenue takes time to build.
title: How to Scale Your Business Fast

text: Only three levers move the ceiling: price, churn, and inflow. Raise lifetime value through higher price or lower churn, or raise inflow.
title: How to Scale Your Business Fast

text: When advising struggling owners, his first questions are inflow, churn, average price per user, and current revenue. From these he can tell growth direction, speed, and where they will level out.
title: How to Scale Your Business Fast

text: Hormozi stresses profit over revenue: he was earning a couple million a year in revenue across his ventures yet took home almost nothing, because he chased revenue for status.
title: My 7 year journey to making my first million.

text: He believes in the theory of constraint: a system grows until it hits its bottleneck. Most people are constrained without noticing, and limiting beliefs are one form of constraint.
title: My 7 year journey to making my first million.

text: He was running nine or ten businesses at once, spread too thin, working all hours and drinking heavily to sleep, before the crash pushed him to focus on Gym Launch.
title: My 7 year journey to making my first million.

text: His done-for-you offer: he flew to gyms, paid all ad, hotel and food costs, and filled the gym in 30 days free; he kept the upfront cash and the owner kept contract value. Average result was about 200 sales in 21 days.
title: My 7 year journey to making my first million.

text: When closing a business, he says the best advice he got was to write the checks and do right by everyone, which left him without emotional scars.
title: My 7 year journey to making my first million.

text: After four years and six gyms he was left with about 23 thousand dollars, and concluded the entrepreneurial journey improves you: skills, experience and character are the assets.
title: My 7 year journey to making my first million.

text: He learned a payment processor can hold your money. He wired a 22 thousand dollar commission on funds never received, leaving 1 thousand, and launched six gyms funded by a 100 thousand dollar limit credit card.
title: My 7 year journey to making my first million.

text: After processor cancellation, he got a high-risk processor with a reserve and 50 thousand monthly limit, then added more processors of similar size to handle volume.
title: My 7 year journey to making my first million.

text: About 35 percent of sales in the done-for-you model were refunded, with margins near 20 percent; nearby gym owners undercut by telling clients to refund and sign up with them.
title: My 7 year journey to making my first million.

text: He learned to control everything end to end: since others fulfilled contracts he sold, he had no customer relationship and refunds spiraled.
title: My 7 year journey to making my first million.

text: He wrote a sales page in two or three days out of need, and online sales hit about 1,000 dollars a day with no fulfillment middleman.
title: My 7 year journey to making my first million.

text: He quoted 6 thousand then 8 thousand dollars to teach his sales guys the method, and all said yes, reaching about 60 thousand in a day; then he sold the same to the 32 launched gyms, doing 300 thousand in a month.
title: My 7 year journey to making my first million.

text: The average gym using the consulting program collected about 30 thousand dollars cash in 30 days, and word of mouth drove Gym Launch's growth more than marketing.
title: My 7 year journey to making my first million.

text: He priced Gym Launch at 16 thousand because it made customers roughly double their money in 30 days, while franchises charge around 500 thousand for similar systems.
title: My 7 year journey to making my first million.

text: He knew every piece of the process from doing it himself: markets, sales training, offer positioning, sales-room layout, and next-day nutrition consults to cover ad spend.
title: My 7 year journey to making my first million.

text: He says the foundation you build dictates the peak height, and income is predicted by the value you provide to the marketplace.
title: My 7 year journey to making my first million.

text: A product delivering great results earns forgiveness from customers, letting him build infrastructure while scaling.
title: My 7 year journey to making my first million.

text: He moved from service to media licensing, with no cost of reproduction and higher gross margins: about 3 million profit in four or five months, then 17 million the next year.
title: My 7 year journey to making my first million.

text: With the same skills, changing beliefs and traits let him move into better opportunity vehicles: gyms, then done-for-you sales, then licensing and media with the highest gross margins.
title: My 7 year journey to making my first million.

text: AI will not disrupt all creators equally. Creators sit on a continuum from low to high risk, based on what the consumer is being asked to risk when they act on the content.
title: The New Way of Making Content In The Age of AI

text: He defines entertainment as content whose goal is simply to be consumed. Its value is delivered fully in the viewing, like a laugh at a comedy clip, with nothing after.
title: The New Way of Making Content In The Age of AI

text: He expects AI to disrupt low-risk B2C educator content first, since viewers would likely follow tips from an AI avatar if the advice seems sensible.
title: The New Way of Making Content In The Age of AI

text: As stakes rise, as with savings and investing, audiences want more third-party proof from the creator, such as a legal career, Wall Street background or business success.
title: The New Way of Making Content In The Age of AI

text: Creators with zero proof may exist in higher-risk niches, but they are not the biggest, because following their advice is riskier than following someone with visible proof.
title: The New Way of Making Content In The Age of AI

text: He thinks AI could copy credibility through large follower counts, but until AIs run huge companies with no human involved, their ability to earn trust for business advice stays low.
title: The New Way of Making Content In The Age of AI

text: With identical advice, the person with real-world experience wins a much larger following, because audiences take proof as a signal that lowers their own risk in acting on it.
title: The New Way of Making Content In The Age of AI

text: To build a brand when AI can duplicate anything, focus on proof and demonstration. The further toward higher-risk content, the safer, at least short to medium term. Real-time demonstration is hard to fake.
title: The New Way of Making Content In The Age of AI

text: One content method: transcribe your virtual meetings, ask AI to surface interesting moments, and talk about those real examples instead of inventing stories.
title: The New Way of Making Content In The Age of AI

text: Better still, engineer proof into your existing business motion so serving customers generates marketing, creating a loop where customers produce content that brings more customers. He wants this in every business.
title: The New Way of Making Content In The Age of AI

text: For B2B, bring customers in and walk through their results, like a campaign for an agency. With few customers, do free work for people and document it publicly.
title: The New Way of Making Content In The Age of AI

text: AI will disrupt from the lowest-risk creators upward, so protect yourself by doing what is harder for AI: demonstrate expertise and product quality, ideally with customers, on camera.
title: The New Way of Making Content In The Age of AI

text: He says he usually is not making content but capturing it, by documenting work he already does, such as Q&A with business owners, which keeps volume high without extra time.
title: The New Way of Making Content In The Age of AI

text: Proof comes in two forms: third-party proof like exits, revenue and headcount, and demonstration, where people see you use your expertise live. Products can be physically demonstrated.
title: The New Way of Making Content In The Age of AI

text: If your work seems undocumentable, create the opportunity: run a sweepstakes, email your list, or visit your five or ten customers at home.
title: The New Way of Making Content In The Age of AI

text: There are only two ways to grow a business: get more customers, or make each customer worth more.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: If you can acquire customers at a net cash-positive profit, acquisition stops being a bottleneck and a cash-poor business can compete against far richer rivals who lack the skill.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: Example: borrow $100 to acquire two customers at $50 each, each spends $300, fulfillment costs $100 total, leaving $400 cash plus two customers. Repeat and double each round until operations break.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: A strong offer lets you sell without price comparison, forcing a values-based decision. It lifts click-through, opt-in and close rates together, a multiplicative effect that means more leads, sales and higher prices.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: For agencies using his software, he switched from a monthly retainer to a large one-time fee plus pay-only-when-appointment-shows. Returns rose from half-to-one up to about 11-to-1 in the first 30 days.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: He checks seven offer elements: promotion (free, discount or premium), core offer, bonuses, scarcity, urgency, guarantees, and the magic naming formula for reskinning tired offers.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: With a new business he starts with something free, creating flow first, then monetizing, then adding friction. Free offers typically convert five to ten times better than other types.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: A discount can be displayed four ways: percentage off, absolute amount off, relative equivalent (like a month's mortgage), or new price versus old price. Switching keeps a tired promotion fresh.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: Premium offers usually need a much higher price than you think, and competitors rarely sell at those levels. He layers premium upsells after a free entry offer, getting 30-to-150-to-1 returns.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: Value rises with dream outcome and perceived likelihood of achievement, and falls with time delay and effort and sacrifice. Mature companies gain mostly by cutting time, effort and sacrifice.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: Perceived likelihood rises with social proof, testimonials and videos, raising value without changing the product. Shrinking time by delivering an early win and cutting the time to result also raises value.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: Bonuses added after the core ask make the core look worth more. Stack them when the prospect hesitates, instead of discounting, and rewrap bonuses to keep a supply of limited bonuses.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: Scarcity is about units, urgency about time. Ethical scarcity can use limited bonuses. Urgency can be cohort-based (new group starts Monday) or name-based, with monthly renamed promotions ending.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: Stack guarantees: an unconditional trial period, plus a conditional guarantee on a different timeline tied to activation steps the customer must complete. This raises close rates and makes the offer more compelling.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: Reskin the same offer with new names and reasons why, like seasons, anniversaries or birthdays, so marketing stays fresh without changing operations. Name parts include a magnetic reason, avatar, and container.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: He suggests picking a monthly ad budget you are willing to burn, starting near $100 a day, and always spending it, so learning is forced without ego attached.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: Limited free: someone comes in for a free but inferior offer, then you upsell them to the primary offer. You may not even mention the inferior one.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: Free with deposit: customers pay for a program up front and get it refunded or credited if they hit the outcome. He says it made more money than any other offer, since money creates accountability.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: Giveaways: first prize is your core, biggest package; second prize is a meaningful discount for everyone else. Everyone gets an offer, which generates leads.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: Free with prepay: buy three get three free or similar with services, pulling in cash up front. He says prepaid customers churn at one-fifth of month-to-month.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: Bid on your own brand terms. Returns on branded search are around 20 to 40 to one, setup takes about 10 minutes, and it goes to a simple opt-in page.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: Do a quarterly four-day push to your list with a real scarcity offer, promoting hard for four days; most businesses never do this.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: For outbound he advises starting with 100 reach-outs a day across multiple channels, giving it six months. His outbound took about a quarter to break even and now returns roughly 20 to 1.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: For partners, aim for full integration into their onboarding rather than one-off talks, by solving their biggest problem. Prestige Labs sells supplements inside every partner gym's onboarding.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: Being an affiliate can pay 40 to 50 percent of top-line revenue with no fulfillment, and partners tend to send business back once you sell theirs first.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: About 30 percent of his customers come from referrals. His golden ratio: the share of customers who refer should exceed the share who leave, which gives growth on its own.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: Build the referral ask into onboarding at a fixed point and ask right after the first magical moment, when goodwill peaks. Unlockable bonuses can reward referrals without paying cash.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: Eyeballs will never be cheaper than today, so the lever for outspending everyone is earning more per customer. Higher lifetime gross profit lets you use any channel.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: In his genie example, doubling clients or doubling purchases per customer each doubles profit, but doubling price yields about six times the profit at a 20 percent margin. Price is the top lever.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: Estimate lifetime gross profit by multiplying total revenue by gross margin and dividing by total customers ever signed. For recurring, divide by churned customers instead.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: The owner who can make a customer more valuable than competitors do wins, since he can spend more on acquisition, reach deeper into channels and the market, and outbid rivals for the same audience.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: Six lifetime gross profit levers: raise price, cut fulfillment cost, increase purchases, upsell (quality or quantity), downsell, and cross-sell.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: Gym owners he works with raise recurring price by about $38 on average from around $129, which he says triples profit at a typical 12.5 percent net margin.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: Cost-cutting options: outsource admin work to cheap overseas staff, use tools and software, apply technology, and buy wholesale. This raises margin and lets you spend more aggressively.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: Upsells come in two types: more of the same (units or time) or a better version (quality, speed, access and convenience). Surveying customers reveals options.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: Against a free competitor, speed beats free. He also suggests pricing the upsell at about five times the core price, since roughly one in five customers buys, and margins can be higher.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: Downsells fit people who say no then yes, and people about to leave. His downsells often have near-100 percent margins, and he buys lunch for the salesperson who sells the cheapest product that day.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: For cross-sells, map what customers do just before and after buying and provide those needs. Refer out for commission, or build it yourself if partners earn more on your customers than you do.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: A cross-sell business can be built on a loss leader: sell the core at cost or below, then earn on higher-margin adjacent items, like a burger sold cheap while fries and Coke earn six times the profit.
title: KEYNOTE: Small To BIG. The Big 4 Customer Acquisition Models.

text: Hormozi says being busy but broke comes from spreading effort across too many things, not from too little work. His first company stalled below $3 million a year until he applied effort deliberately.
title: You're Setting Goals Wrong

text: He defines strategy as prioritizing limited resources against unlimited options: choosing what you will do and what you will not do.
title: You're Setting Goals Wrong

text: He thinks entrepreneurs were rewarded for quitting a job and starting a business, so they wrongly keep starting new ventures instead of concentrating on the better vehicle they already have.
title: You're Setting Goals Wrong

text: Priority originally meant a single thing that comes first, so having a list of several priorities means having none. Concentrate your network and promotion on one thing.
title: You're Setting Goals Wrong

text: Early on, everything is manual brute force to get the first people in; word of mouth and reputation only snowball if effort stays on one offering.
title: You're Setting Goals Wrong

text: The biggest productivity hack is doing nothing except the task you set out to do. He sees most productivity systems as guilt-free procrastination.
title: You're Setting Goals Wrong

text: Focus, commitment and deciding all mean cutting off alternatives. What remains is your priority, so the key decision is what remains.
title: You're Setting Goals Wrong

text: To choose a priority, ask which item you would complete with full certainty in a year to get furthest. If the others depend on it, that one is your priority and the rest can be ignored.
title: You're Setting Goals Wrong

text: In his experience, teams finish things faster one after another than in parallel, because when all resources aim at one point, everyone feels responsible for holding the company back.
title: You're Setting Goals Wrong

text: He estimates every change in a business costs about 20% of revenue upfront before any uncertain upside. A test should offer at least 20% plus upside for him to take it.
title: You're Setting Goals Wrong

text: Most tests are not worth running because they will not change the business. Optimizing small hacks will not get you to a 10x when they are not the constraint.
title: You're Setting Goals Wrong

text: Businesses stuck at $1 million, $3 million or $10 million for years are typically changing too many things and working on the wrong thing, so they lack bandwidth for the one that matters.
title: You're Setting Goals Wrong

text: Accept that things which are not the constraint are good enough. Nothing will be perfect, so make details perfect but limit how many details you handle.
title: You're Setting Goals Wrong

text: Highest leverage sits at the ends: a product so good people talk about it endlessly, or marketing so good everyone hears about you, not the middle.
title: You're Setting Goals Wrong

text: If metrics for an area you love are at or above industry benchmark, leave it alone and free bandwidth for the real constraint, likely something you dislike and outsource.
title: You're Setting Goals Wrong

text: Small business owners have the most ideas but the lowest capacity to pursue them, so the best hope of competing is doing one thing well.
title: You're Setting Goals Wrong

text: Ask yourself: if all I did was this, would nothing else matter? If so, stop letting other things matter. Good ideas fail from lack of execution, and all fail if you execute all of them.
title: You're Setting Goals Wrong

text: His shorts editor working on two platforms made both suffer; on one platform alone, views exceeded the combined total of both.
title: You're Setting Goals Wrong

text: His team ran monthly events with zero new things four times in a row and got the best scores each time. He says changes lowered scores, and customers lack context on what changed.
title: You're Setting Goals Wrong

text: You get tired of your business long before customers know anything about it, since they have no context.
title: You're Setting Goals Wrong

text: Keep a big list of ideas so you know what to do meanwhile. He has 200 plus items, and in 18 months he pulled only three from it.
title: You're Setting Goals Wrong

text: Dropping the undone to-do list brings relief, since much anxiety comes from it. Do well what you already do; he promises more money and a realization that execution, not ideas, is the problem.
title: You're Setting Goals Wrong

text: Using Buffett's twenty-punch idea, imagine one optimization punch per year. Constraint forces you to see which single item would change everything, making side quests pointless.
title: You're Setting Goals Wrong

text: With low skills, your time trades for little, so the first goal is to free up time to learn a valuable skill while supporting your family, even if the family suffers short term.

title: watch this if you're tired of being broke

text: Entry-level at-home phone sales jobs often need no experience and pay 40,000 a year or more; take one and keep your other job in between. Driving Uber is an option if you have a car.
title: watch this if you're tired of being broke

text: Sadness comes from lack of options; when you feel hopeless, treat it as ignorance meaning you do not yet know enough, which is fixable.
title: watch this if you're tired of being broke

text: The game is trading up repeatedly: cut costs, work more and apply to better jobs while learning to sell, then sell pricier things and eventually your own.
title: watch this if you're tired of being broke

text: Anyone not helping you reach your goals in this season does not deserve your time; both your minutes and dollars must be earned by people who help you.
title: watch this if you're tired of being broke

text: He owned a roughly 5 to 6 thousand dollar car in cash and paid 400 a month sharing a room in a house with six others, using savings for courses and seminars.
title: watch this if you're tired of being broke

text: Balance can be viewed over a lifetime and across a family unit; for now one partner may focus on the kid while the other focuses on career.
title: watch this if you're tired of being broke

text: If people around you have smaller dreams for you than you do, ignore their advice entirely.
title: watch this if you're tired of being broke

text: Pick one skill and spend four hours daily studying only that, using a cheap physical timer that stops whenever you look away. He says about 20 hours gets you the basics.
title: watch this if you're tired of being broke

text: Without experience, prove hustle by messaging several people at each company, such as recruiters and talent heads, with personalized notes rather than copy-paste, plus a tailored cover letter based on the job description.
title: watch this if you're tired of being broke

text: For low-level roles, resume matters less than hustle. Employers want someone who goes above and beyond, so show it through actions.
title: watch this if you're tired of being broke

text: After applying, visit in person politely to say you are excited and will outwork other candidates. Once hired, do twice what the top performer does, like Kobe with three daily practices.
title: watch this if you're tired of being broke

text: To pass the top person you must match their effort and then work extra when they clock out.
title: watch this if you're tired of being broke

text: Volume negates luck. He told this to his teenage son. Do more reps daily, like ten personalized messages and cover letters, each day, timer-based.
title: watch this if you're tired of being broke

text: Outwork everyone for a year, two years, and more. He frames it as a 36-month season with everything you want on the other side.
title: watch this if you're tired of being broke

text: You can rely on volume rather than luck; you only need one yes, so a great deal of opportunity sits on the other side of willingness to be rejected.
title: watch this if you're tired of being broke

text: Rejection costs nothing: you either learn or win. Like asking many people to prom, each no leaves you where you were with more experience, and one yes can change your life.
title: watch this if you're tired of being broke

text: A hard beginning means a bigger monster to slay, which makes a more epic story to later share with others in the same situation.
title: watch this if you're tired of being broke

text: To reduce fear of a risk, write down in exact step-by-step detail what you fear will happen if you fail. He says it is often not so bad once spelled out, since fear lives in vagueness.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: Commit to the effort you will put in, separate from the outcome. Give full effort to what you control, then accept the rest.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: He breaks mental toughness into four parts: how much bad it takes to change your behavior, how much it changes, how fast you rebound, and whether you rebound above baseline.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: Power follows where you point blame. Blaming others hands them control; saying you lacked resilience gives you something to act on.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: Record-breaking outcomes require work nobody has done before. His launch involved 400 pages of email copy, six VSLs and 1,700 slides, and no one gives credit for it.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: When work goes unseen, he asks himself what kind of man he wants to be, and he tells himself the story he will someday be able to tell.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: He believes employees whose spouse or partner is not supportive of their work will not reach their potential, so he pays attention to team members' home environments.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: High agency means reasoning for yourself rather than picking identities and beliefs off the shelf. Ask what do I want and does this help me get it.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: Have hard conversations and written contracts upfront, even with friends. He had eight lawsuits this year, all with friends or friendly parties, from deals done years earlier without clear agreements.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: Cover in agreements what happens if either partner wants out, dies, or disagrees on money use or selling. Better to settle while stakes are low.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: Chiron's five friend levels by what you can discuss: past, other people, ideas, doing things together, and making, losing and spending money together.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: Learn the laws and contracts that apply to your business. Knowing the rules reduces stress and gives strategic advantage in legal conflicts.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: He hit his financial goals this year and feels he has enough. He now plans personal life first and lets business fill the gaps.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: At very large scale he thinks you are paid for quality of judgment rather than quantity of work, so he reorients life to improve decisions.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: Before reacting, ask what do I want to happen and what raises the odds of that. Gut reactions like punishing usually work against the goal.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: Doing nothing is often the best response in conflicts; he calls it the heavyweight champion. It is physically efficient but emotionally painful.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: Once a business works, changing variables is likely to make it worse. The highest risk-adjusted move is doing more of what works; he allows himself one new thing per year.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: Ask why you can't do more of what works, and remove distractions to solve that hard problem. Long fixes like culture can feel worse midway; give them time.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: Third marshmallow fallacy: delaying gratification forever means working for nothing. Savers must learn when to reap, weighing investing against consuming.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: Clear beats clever. Percentages at each funnel stage are small, so simplicity matters; he advises one big benefit with ten reasons rather than ten offers.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: The offer still matters most. His three-book shipping-only offer converts better than anything in his career, even at a loss.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: He expects hyperpersonalization with AI-generated creative volume in 2026, and wants a machine where customers create ads that bring more customers.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: Side quests suit visionary founders of larger businesses only if they do not drain resources from the main business. Books serve this role for him.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: Delegation is the price of scaling. Hard workers try to outwork problems; his razor is that if it requires him, it does not work, so he scales himself to zero.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: At equilibrium he now favors increasing supply before demand, since demand growth risks reputation. Hiring four leaders in the prior 90 days enabled the launch.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: Talent has the best ROI in business: spending heavily on recruiting a high-profit hire is worth it when they produce hundreds of thousands in gross profit yearly.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: Mixed teams pull A players down. He cut a 14-person sales team to six who closed more deals than all 14.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: He says he identifies A players within the first 14 days, and his tolerance for non-A players has dropped. Character and work ethic show early.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: Money attracts talent but culture keeps it. Real-time reinforcement beats infrequent financial rewards, and winners want to win more than earn.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: Leaders driving revenue lines should be incentivized on bottom line; if they need him to drive revenue they don't deserve it. If nobody could succeed alone, you lack good people.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: He says he is 0 for 12 on executive assistants but believes his latest is his first world-class one, though he cautions it is early and to take this with a grain of salt.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: The top quality he needs in an executive assistant is speed: a reply within 60 seconds whenever he messages, since in that moment the assistant is his constraint.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: Founders should make the decisions about their own time, since they are the best allocator of it. The blocking and tackling of scheduling can be outsourced.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: He admits he under-screened for general intelligence in assistants. With a very intelligent one he trusts her judgment more and can hand off tasks for a first draft that gets about 80% done.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: When a department or revenue line is weak, look at the leader. He holds that the leader is always the problem: either leader alone or leader plus team, never the team alone.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: In a world where services and content are easily commoditized and copied, brand becomes the moat. Brand is built from who and what you associate with.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: For a local business, brand is mostly word of mouth and online reviews. Most other businesses add all the content they publish publicly.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: To build a brand, choose curated associations that reinforce the position you want in prospects' minds, and think about what they like that you want them to link to you.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: Demonstrate a skill few in your market can do better than anyone, and do it repeatedly, past your own boredom, because the market takes a long time to notice.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: He says the PR blast planned after his record launch fell flat because the PR firm got little of his attention, and he sees it as a miss that could have been fixed with queued-up PR.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: He argues the greatest risk to a business is the founder no longer wanting to do it; most businesses die because the founder runs out of will, not money.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: He says shrinking or volatile businesses carry the most pain, growing ones are painful but pay off, and plateaus can be endured for years because the pain is not quite enough to quit.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: What helped him most is having something outside yourself that the business drives toward, such as societal impact, a problem to solve, or who he wants to become. It must be real, since money alone runs out.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: He feels he must be willing to let Acquisition.com do some things he simply wants to do, even if not best for the business, because his own interest keeps him going.
title: 26 Harsh Lessons I Learned in 2025

text: Skills are developed first to a proficient level, then deepened through consistent repetition. Deepening requires character traits such as focus, determination and drive, plus resisting the pull of new opportunities and side projects.
title: Leveling Up Why We Get Stuck (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: He says the higher you climb, the more tempting new opportunities become, so the discipline needed to say no has to be upgraded at each new level of income.
title: Leveling Up Why We Get Stuck (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: He waited almost two years after launching Gym Launch before starting the supplement company, because his partner insisted he stay focused. He credits that with explosive growth, though he now thinks he might skip the supplement company entirely.
title: Leveling Up Why We Get Stuck (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: The first step is filling skill holes and stacking skills until you reach proficiency, not expertise. Most skills need only a couple of hours of study, but people avoid it because being bad at something is uncomfortable.
title: Leveling Up Why We Get Stuck (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: You learn more from your first 20 sales than from your first 20 hours studying sales, and stepping into a real fight teaches more than practice does, because it is real.
title: Leveling Up Why We Get Stuck (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Citing the book Grit by Angela Duckworth, he says the most successful people stick with a path. Early-stage entrepreneurs jump between opportunities and never give any one a chance to work.
title: Leveling Up Why We Get Stuck (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: When a friend ran contracting, roofing and house flipping at once, Hormozi told him to pick one, since each could become a billion-dollar business but not all three together.
title: Leveling Up Why We Get Stuck (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Deepening a skill requires sticking with it, patience, focus, saying no and repeating things over and over, and breaking through to the next proficiency level can take years.
title: Leveling Up Why We Get Stuck (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Using a fitness analogy, he says there is a wide gap between the effort that maintains muscle and the effort that forces adaptation. Most people train above minimum but below the threshold for growth, and skills work the same way.
title: Leveling Up Why We Get Stuck (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: If your income has stayed flat for years, your skill set has stayed flat too. He says that usually happens because you lack the character traits needed to deepen those skills.
title: Leveling Up Why We Get Stuck (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: People get stuck because what needs improving changes as they level up: first skills, then character traits. People wrongly assume growth follows the same linear path each time.
title: Leveling Up Why We Get Stuck (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Sometimes the skill itself is not doing other things and staying the course. Getting to the next level can mean doing less and removing constraints.
title: Leveling Up Why We Get Stuck (ALEX HORMOZI)
