text: He suggests that spending part of an ad budget on a giveaway or challenge, for example 50 thousand out of a million a month, may beat spending five percent more on ads.
title: REVEALING Black Friday Secrets To Use In Your Business (feat. Shopify's President)

text: He treats marketing and sales as one continuum; acquisition is education, meaning changing behavior under the same conditions.
title: REVEALING Black Friday Secrets To Use In Your Business (feat. Shopify's President)

text: He suggests an accountant could post short 60-second videos on each tax change, and small firms can beat big ones because they avoid compliance committees.
title: REVEALING Black Friday Secrets To Use In Your Business (feat. Shopify's President)

text: He likes moves that double or triple dip, such as a single Advent calendar producing PR, sales, fan rewards and data.
title: REVEALING Black Friday Secrets To Use In Your Business (feat. Shopify's President)

text: Hormozi says many aspiring founders hunt for one perfect business that fits passion and could become huge. He calls that a fallacy, because the first business mainly teaches skills and shows what step to take next.
title: If You Want to Start a Business in 2024, Watch This Interview

text: When people cannot decide what to sell, he suggests solving your own problem. He says almost every really good business he has had came from scratching his own itch.
title: If You Want to Start a Business in 2024, Watch This Interview

text: Advertising is the process of making something known. If nobody knows about your offer, nobody can buy it, so telling people about what you do matters from the start.
title: If You Want to Start a Business in 2024, Watch This Interview

text: He names two groups to surround yourself with: mentors who are ahead of you, and a community of peers. Both increase your luck surface area, meaning your exposure to opportunities. Online communities work if you cannot move.
title: If You Want to Start a Business in 2024, Watch This Interview

text: He thinks the difficulty of entrepreneurship is what makes the goal worthwhile. If everyone could do it, it would not be valued, and difficulty is another barrier competitors must cross.
title: If You Want to Start a Business in 2024, Watch This Interview

text: With entrepreneurship this accessible, he describes it as endless lottery tickets: if one fails you try another. He sees strong risk-adjusted return, since the upside remains and many people want you to win.
title: If You Want to Start a Business in 2024, Watch This Interview

text: His framing for growth offers: make them so good that people feel stupid saying no. He says he modeled a Shopify-style competition at Skool, with a fun, competitive structure where participants all win.
title: If You Want to Start a Business in 2024, Watch This Interview

text: If you lack an audience and are more of a product person, find a brand champion who already has distribution. He compares it to finding your Michael Jordan, and says being generous in the deal can pay off.
title: If You Want to Start a Business in 2024, Watch This Interview

text: For a local business like a chiropractor, he suggests partnering with businesses that share your customers, such as gyms or smoothie shops. Offer something like a free adjustment coupon to raise their value at no cost to you.
title: If You Want to Start a Business in 2024, Watch This Interview

text: He says he has built almost as much revenue through partnerships and affiliate relationships as through direct sales he generates himself, and that being a good partner means leaving enough on the table for them.
title: If You Want to Start a Business in 2024, Watch This Interview

text: Three partnership tips from Hormozi. First, send the partner customers before asking for a deal. Second, be willing to pay a referral partner at least your cost to acquire a customer. Third, never count the other side's money.
title: If You Want to Start a Business in 2024, Watch This Interview

text: He believes referral customers from a partner will likely be worth more in lifetime value than customers bought from ad platforms. He says that gives a better LTV to CAC ratio.
title: If You Want to Start a Business in 2024, Watch This Interview

text: He admits he lost deals early on by getting greedy over how much the partner would earn. He advises making the deal work for your side alone and being happy if they make a killing.
title: If You Want to Start a Business in 2024, Watch This Interview

text: He observes that the wealthiest people he knows do not treat business as zero-sum, and that everyone can win, unlike in many games.
title: If You Want to Start a Business in 2024, Watch This Interview

text: He estimates from the entrepreneurs he has looked at that you keep about one tenth of the wealth you generate for others. His conclusion is to focus on making other people a lot of money.
title: If You Want to Start a Business in 2024, Watch This Interview

text: His main tactical takeaway is to create individual contributor tracks. A star media buyer may not want to manage others and may want to become world-class, so ask each person which track they are on.
title: If You Want to Start a Business in 2024, Watch This Interview

text: He runs open-book financials across his companies each quarter: where money was made and where spending failed. He says it keeps everyone on the same page and nothing hidden.
title: If You Want to Start a Business in 2024, Watch This Interview

text: Employees who state their flaws openly cannot be faulted for them; people speak to their face instead of behind their back. Saying you are not well-rounded invites others strong in that area to join you.
title: If You Want to Start a Business in 2024, Watch This Interview

text: He says leadership frameworks like mission and values matter for companies between $10 and $30 million a year aiming for $100 million. This is when leaders must start passing decisions to others.
title: If You Want to Start a Business in 2024, Watch This Interview

text: He believes everyone has a unique thumbprint of interests, like Joe Rogan's odd mix. People become rounded stones by pulling back their pointy bits, which makes them look uniform when they are not.
title: If You Want to Start a Business in 2024, Watch This Interview

text: He says writing down a goal alone means little, because winners and losers share the same goals. Since the goal cannot be what separates them, the behaviors underneath it must be.
title: How to get what you want...

text: He defines advertising as making your product known. More private one-to-one outreach or more public posting means more people find out, but people usually already know this and still fail to do it.
title: How to get what you want...

text: He views identity as a voting system where each action casts a vote for the type of person you become. A single repeated question is easier than remembering a fifty-point checklist.
title: How to get what you want...

text: He dislikes affirmations because saying them does not make them true. He argues you need evidence you are that type of person, and evidence starts with doing the activity.
title: How to get what you want...

text: Rather than fixing habits directly, he suggests fixing the being, and the habits follow. The question can use any ideal self, such as a person with a six pack or the best husband in the world.
title: How to get what you want...

text: He notes identity comes from roots suggesting repeated beingness, so what you repeatedly do becomes who you are. Changing your actions therefore changes your identity, in a reinforcing loop.
title: How to get what you want...

text: He argues the question handles situations you could not predict, because you cannot foresee most variables. He compares it to what would Jesus do, which ties decisions to a real identity.
title: How to get what you want...

text: He personally asks what King Solomon, or Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger, would do, depending on the situation. An external person who embodies desired traits works as well as a future version of yourself.
title: How to get what you want...

text: He observes that as you level up you simply change who you compare yourself to, so you can always find a way to feel bad, even as the best in the world.
title: How to get what you want...

text: His advice to his friend: committing to the activities is the goal. Making a lot of money in one month achieves nothing because the goal is the activities. Write down what a billionaire would do rather than goals.
title: How to get what you want...

text: Hormozi says most tax tricks promoted online are tiny and make little difference, and that adopting the ultra-wealthy mindset about taxes matters more than any single hack.
title: How the rich avoid paying taxes...MY strategy - Part 1

text: He says the biggest first difference in taxes comes from where you live: a zero-income-tax state versus a high-tax one like California, so moving to a lower-tax state is the obvious first step.
title: How the rich avoid paying taxes...MY strategy - Part 1

text: He reports spending roughly 750,000 dollars on tax advisors and strategies, and paying about 18 million dollars in US taxes over three years.
title: How the rich avoid paying taxes...MY strategy - Part 1

text: He says US residents face global taxation, and the only ways around federal tax are living in Puerto Rico six months a year while exporting services (about 4 percent federal rate), or expatriating.
title: How the rich avoid paying taxes...MY strategy - Part 1

text: He states that most of your net worth over time comes from asset growth rather than contributions, and mostly from starting early.
title: How the rich avoid paying taxes...MY strategy - Part 1

text: He advocates living on as little as possible for as long as possible to start compounding early; he says 500 a month at age 20 beats 5,000 a month at 45.
title: How the rich avoid paying taxes...MY strategy - Part 1

text: Buying something worth 100 dollars for 30 dollars gives an instant gain with no tax owed, and it can keep compounding untaxed. He says the wealthy structure purchases this way.
title: How the rich avoid paying taxes...MY strategy - Part 1

text: Tax rate only matters if you sell and realize capital gains. He points to Warren Buffett holding companies like See's Candy, Coca-Cola and Geico for decades because holding is tax-efficient.
title: How the rich avoid paying taxes...MY strategy - Part 1

text: He says the ultra-wealthy think in long horizons and generational wealth, buying things likely to last 30 years rather than flipping or chasing something trendy.
title: How the rich avoid paying taxes...MY strategy - Part 1

text: He explains that loans are not treated as income yet can be spent. If assets grow faster than the loans taken against them, you can live off loans while the assets compound untaxed.
title: How the rich avoid paying taxes...MY strategy - Part 1

text: He regards conservation easements and captive insurance as small hacks. He passed on a captive insurance idea that would have saved about 250,000 a year, and the IRS later reversed its stance and charged back interest and fees.
title: How the rich avoid paying taxes...MY strategy - Part 1

text: He warns the tax code can change rules and apply them retroactively, so he simply plays within the rules and avoids selling, so as not to be taxed.
title: How the rich avoid paying taxes...MY strategy - Part 1

text: He chose not to move to Puerto Rico because extra net worth would not change his life, and he refuses to trade freedom for a better tax rate, calling money a means not the goal.
title: How the rich avoid paying taxes...MY strategy - Part 1

text: He thinks Puerto Rico may make sense when you are smaller and building net worth, but he says Texas versus California costs him no lifestyle change while saving taxes.
title: How the rich avoid paying taxes...MY strategy - Part 1

text: He summarizes the big rocks: buy low for less than value, then either never sell or borrow against the appreciating assets to live off them.
title: How the rich avoid paying taxes...MY strategy - Part 1

text: Hormozi says he spent over 20 million dollars on influencer payouts for Prestige Labs and over 22.8 million for the software company Alan, and had over 23,000 affiliates promote his book.
title: How to 10x Your Business Overnight with Influencers

text: If you reach a million people for free, you profit as long as the product sells for more than it costs, so the question becomes which product earns the most, not whether it earns.
title: How to 10x Your Business Overnight with Influencers

text: Nike bet its whole basketball budget on Michael Jordan instead of spreading it across several players, hoping for 2 million in sales and getting 122 million the first year.
title: How to 10x Your Business Overnight with Influencers

text: Two models exist: you have a branded product and find an influencer to promote it, or you find the influencer and build a product branded around them and deliver it.
title: How to 10x Your Business Overnight with Influencers

text: To find influencers, define who buys your product, find the influencers they follow, then choose super influencers that fit. Contact in layers, starting with people you know personally, then your network's contacts.
title: How to 10x Your Business Overnight with Influencers

text: Message on multiple platforms and try their website, support or email, since inboxes there are less crowded than Instagram DMs. Superstars often cost far less than people assume, sometimes a couple hundred thousand a year.
title: How to 10x Your Business Overnight with Influencers

text: Of 1,200 people interested in an editor role, only about 60 submitted a test edit, one in twenty, so taking action leaves the odds in your favor.
title: How to 10x Your Business Overnight with Influencers

text: Verify yourself: pay for the blue check, which he says raises response rates five to ten times, and write a bio stating what you do and want, with a clear friendly photo.
title: How to 10x Your Business Overnight with Influencers

text: Magic message: longtime fan, first-time messenger, you partner with influencers, estimate their monthly recurring income, show screenshots of others, they get most profit, you do most work, ask for a 15-minute call. Personalize it.
title: How to 10x Your Business Overnight with Influencers

text: Offering to fly out shows seriousness and incurring cost makes them take you more seriously; frame it casually as being in their area anyway.
title: How to 10x Your Business Overnight with Influencers

text: Gifts and paid-time offers must be relevant and valuable to that influencer; the thought and effort visible in a gift matter, and gifts should carry their logo, not yours.
title: How to 10x Your Business Overnight with Influencers

text: Send 100 messages a day across platforms, which takes about four hours, and keep repeating until replies come.
title: How to 10x Your Business Overnight with Influencers

text: Sharing a target influencer's stories is an easy way to give them value and makes them like you more from the start.
title: How to 10x Your Business Overnight with Influencers

text: Before the call, prepare mockups of their version of the product and projections based on their followers, posting frequency, reach and a click conversion assumption.
title: How to 10x Your Business Overnight with Influencers

text: Prove you will work hard by doing the work first: giving value before the partnership is the best sign of value after. You gain more than the influencer, so prep time is worth it.
title: How to 10x Your Business Overnight with Influencers

text: Structure the pitch as promise, proof, demo if you have a product, and plan covering next steps and who does what, then make the offer.
title: How to 10x Your Business Overnight with Influencers

text: Make an offer so good they feel foolish saying no. For mid-sized influencers, growth help may matter more than money, so offer extra resources, since their growth lifts you too.
title: How to 10x Your Business Overnight with Influencers

text: Every position has an advantage and disadvantage. As the new player, sell personal attention, care, flexibility and owner mentality.
title: How to 10x Your Business Overnight with Influencers

text: As the established player, sell track record, best practices, infrastructure, specialists and brand association.
title: How to 10x Your Business Overnight with Influencers

text: Reuse polished decks made for other influencers as samples, and show alternative structures, to look legitimate and prompt them to ask for a version like it.
title: How to 10x Your Business Overnight with Influencers

text: Tony Robbins' company and Matthew McConaughey launched The Art of Living, with over two million registrations and nearly half a million attending live.
title: How to 10x Your Business Overnight with Influencers

text: If you have no product, build a paid community for an influencer, since fans want more access; the top fans pay and others keep free content.
title: How to 10x Your Business Overnight with Influencers

text: Hormozi says he owns a portfolio of companies generating over $250 million in combined revenue per year, and that about 15 years ago he was sleeping on the floor of his gym while building his first business.
title: I can’t hide this anymore.

text: Many people choose socially acceptable options, like staying in college, when the deeper reason is protecting themselves from facing the reality of not being successful yet.
title: How To Level Up In Business - Understanding Tradeoffs

text: When picking between paths, first decide logically which one gets you closer to the goal, then look for the emotional driver preventing you from choosing it.
title: How To Level Up In Business - Understanding Tradeoffs

text: Starting his gym, his mindset was not to outwork everyone but to outsacrifice anyone, putting everything he had into his success.
title: How To Level Up In Business - Understanding Tradeoffs

text: He gave up his 20s for his business. He does not claim it is the right path, only that any decision should be made for the right reasons.
title: How To Level Up In Business - Understanding Tradeoffs

text: The stories we tell ourselves about why we made choices shape our identity, so the story behind a decision matters as much as, or more than, the decision.
title: How To Level Up In Business - Understanding Tradeoffs

text: Naming exactly what you fear gives clarity and removes some of its power over you, letting you face it.
title: How To Level Up In Business - Understanding Tradeoffs

text: He prefers a maybe over a never: do not let fear of failure push you down a path that never realizes your potential.
title: How To Level Up In Business - Understanding Tradeoffs

text: Three or four years into his entrepreneurial journey he wrote down extra things to give up, including Sunday football, all TV and going out. He says others need not copy this.
title: How To Level Up In Business - Understanding Tradeoffs

text: He does not believe anything great was ever achieved by a balanced person; unreasonable goals take extreme effort and unreasonable sacrifice.
title: How To Level Up In Business - Understanding Tradeoffs

text: Between two coders, one dropping out and coding 16 hours daily for three and a half years versus one coding a couple hours a day while socializing, the first would reasonably be far ahead.
title: How To Level Up In Business - Understanding Tradeoffs

text: Imbalance can be limited to a season of life rather than forever, though sometimes the season truly requires being lopsided.
title: How To Level Up In Business - Understanding Tradeoffs

text: Decide by asking which option gets you where you want to go, what sacrifice it requires, and whether you will make it, so life does not make decisions for you.
title: How To Level Up In Business - Understanding Tradeoffs

text: Hormozi calls the balance between making good content and making lots of content qualium, meaning quality volume. He personally leans toward volume, but thinks the value sits in the middle.
title: My Actual Social Media Strategy For 2027 - The Algorithm

text: He treats content creation as digital manufacturing: raw recorded video goes in, and posts that earn views, likes, shares and leads come out. He applies the five-step Algorithm from the book to it and made it mandatory for his direct reports.
title: My Actual Social Media Strategy For 2027 - The Algorithm

text: When testing a requirement, he asks what it means, how anyone knows it matters, and so what. If there is no evidence it changes results, the requirement gets removed.
title: My Actual Social Media Strategy For 2027 - The Algorithm

text: A rule of thumb he borrows from Elon: delete so much that you sometimes have to add things back. Most steps are reversible, so fear of deletion is usually unwarranted.
title: My Actual Social Media Strategy For 2027 - The Algorithm

text: Because editors have other work, he would rather ship one and a half or two videos at 95% quality than one at 100%, arguing the last bit of polish is not worth about 40% of the cost.
title: My Actual Social Media Strategy For 2027 - The Algorithm

text: He ends meetings with who, what, when. When someone gives a deadline, he asks how much actual time on task it needs and what they are doing that matters more in the meantime.
title: My Actual Social Media Strategy For 2027 - The Algorithm

text: To speed up a team, shorten communication cycles, such as end of day instead of end of week. He claims this makes a team roughly seven times faster, and he asks why something cannot be done earlier.
title: My Actual Social Media Strategy For 2027 - The Algorithm

text: He presses vendors for progress updates as often as hourly to force accountability and pull deadlines forward.
title: My Actual Social Media Strategy For 2027 - The Algorithm

text: Automation comes last, because eliminating a task is more efficient than automating it. People now start with AI automation of things that should not be done at all.
title: My Actual Social Media Strategy For 2027 - The Algorithm

text: Test AI use by asking whether views, leads or revenue are rising. If token costs climb month over month while money does not, you may be spending on things that do not matter.
title: My Actual Social Media Strategy For 2027 - The Algorithm

text: He says we are in show-me times, not tell-me times. Content should demonstrate expertise across varied conditions and with avatars representing the customers you serve, solving their specific problems.
title: My Actual Social Media Strategy For 2027 - The Algorithm

text: Entertainment and memes make you a media business selling attention to advertisers. If you sell your own products or services, educational content is the door to influence and authority.
title: My Actual Social Media Strategy For 2027 - The Algorithm

text: For people to follow your instructions they must be easy to understand, in plain words, and they must believe the payoff justifies the risk. Lower comprehension cost, raise conviction.
title: My Actual Social Media Strategy For 2027 - The Algorithm

text: Proof is the whole point in a trust economy. You cannot credibly teach growing stores, selling or content without having done it yourself.
title: My Actual Social Media Strategy For 2027 - The Algorithm

text: To build a personal brand, do real work for years first, then start the brand. Documenting along the way is fine if you state facts and tell the truth. He views imposter syndrome as shame from misrepresenting the truth.
title: My Actual Social Media Strategy For 2027 - The Algorithm

text: Hormozi calls the money ladder the order in which people get paid. He says one belief shift, changing how he viewed the flow of money, helped make him wealthier: look at who gets paid when to see who holds control.
title: Wealth Principle #1: Get Paid First

text: An employee sits at the bottom of the ladder because they front their labor and time first, then get paid two or four weeks later. He says nothing is wrong with this, but you should understand the hierarchy.
title: Wealth Principle #1: Get Paid First

text: Contractors and gig workers can move up the ladder. At the low end they work then get paid, as employees do; better ones take half upfront and half on delivery; the top ones get paid first or as they work.
title: Wealth Principle #1: Get Paid First

text: Getting paid first, as a doctor does before surgery, is a higher level of wealth and control. He says the more a customer pays upfront, and especially in full, the higher you sit on the ladder.
title: Wealth Principle #1: Get Paid First

text: Banks rank above workers because they are preferred creditors in the capital stack. If things go badly they get paid first and everyone else is left with the scraps. He says to watch who fronts, who splits, and who is paid first when things fail.
title: Wealth Principle #1: Get Paid First

text: Insurance sits above banks because insurers are paid for years, even decades, before they may have to fulfill anything, and they may never have to. He calls this money for doing nothing.
title: Wealth Principle #1: Get Paid First

text: He describes insurance as the opposite of a depreciating asset: insurers collect cash upfront and let it appreciate over time before paying claims. He ties this to insurers being among the oldest companies in the world.
title: Wealth Principle #1: Get Paid First

text: Moving up the ladder is driven by demand and how good you are. Doctors and great consultants get paid before delivering. Above them, banks get paid first from a defined pot, and insurers get guaranteed money with unguaranteed work.
title: Wealth Principle #1: Get Paid First

text: Watching where money flows and who gets paid when made him a lot wealthier, and he says it changed the way his companies wrote agreements.
title: Wealth Principle #1: Get Paid First

text: Hormozi says he had $1,036 at age 27 after losing everything on a new venture, and two years later had over $17 million in the bank, which he credits to stumbling into one of four ways fortunes are made.
title: The 4 Ways Fortunes Are Made (and how I stumbled into one)

text: Money is just a medium for transferring wealth between people and has little value itself; it matters because it lets you acquire assets. Wealth means assets that earn without you trading time.
title: The 4 Ways Fortunes Are Made (and how I stumbled into one)

text: Lawyers, doctors and accountants cannot become super wealthy while selling their own time. They must shift from practitioner to owning a whole practice with many doctors working for them, creating an asset that earns while they sleep.
title: The 4 Ways Fortunes Are Made (and how I stumbled into one)

text: Fortunes have been made in four ways: labor, capital, code and media. Labor came first because it was the only option, as with kings and their servants, the pyramids and Rockefeller's oil business.
title: The 4 Ways Fortunes Are Made (and how I stumbled into one)

text: Labor is the hardest leverage to employ, according to him, and anyone with 50 to 500 plus employees knows it. Labor and capital are both permission-based, meaning you need other people's approval to use them.
title: The 4 Ways Fortunes Are Made (and how I stumbled into one)

text: Capital means using other people's money. If you finance an asset that doubles in five years, repay the principal plus interest and keep the rest, your return on your own money is effectively infinite. He names Buffett and Munger as examples.
title: The 4 Ways Fortunes Are Made (and how I stumbled into one)

text: Code is permissionless leverage: adding one more user to software costs nothing extra, and this is why the big tech companies built new fortunes.
title: The 4 Ways Fortunes Are Made (and how I stumbled into one)

text: Media is the fourth leverage he stumbled into when he moved from a service business selling others' time to media. Zuckerberg, Google and Bloomberg sell attention, and once you hold an audience, selling it costs nothing incremental.
title: The 4 Ways Fortunes Are Made (and how I stumbled into one)

text: Media margins are close to 100 percent because there is no added cost, and exceptional margins are what build fortunes. His margins soared when he moved from flying out as a done-for-you sales team to licensing media.
title: The 4 Ways Fortunes Are Made (and how I stumbled into one)

text: Combining multiple leverage types boosts returns further. Much of today's super wealth uses other people's capital and labor to write code that is then sold as media once the audience is captured.
title: The 4 Ways Fortunes Are Made (and how I stumbled into one)

text: You can build blogs, YouTube videos and podcasts for almost no money and distribute them at zero incremental cost. He points to Joe Rogan selling his podcast for 100 million dollars as an example of owning media.
title: The 4 Ways Fortunes Are Made (and how I stumbled into one)

text: Over time the ways to build fortunes have multiplied and the permission required has shrunk. If you are best at capturing attention or coding, you can build a fortune without anyone's approval, which he says makes now the best time to be alive.
title: The 4 Ways Fortunes Are Made (and how I stumbled into one)

text: To make your business more valuable, tap into one of the four types of leverage. He says he guarantees more money and a shot at a super fortune, and that he now looks for the fourth type deliberately.
title: The 4 Ways Fortunes Are Made (and how I stumbled into one)

text: A drop in price never produces a matching rise in sales, so cutting price to fix demand or retention tends to disappoint.
title: This Lesson Cost me $5,000,000...

text: Employees who worried the offer was too expensive pushed to lower the weekly price from 800 to 600 while adding coaching services. Clients who had paid more complained, profit fell by 400 dollars a month, and churn stayed unchanged.
title: This Lesson Cost me $5,000,000...

text: He says the price-cut episode, driven by staff opinion, cost him around a million dollars, and he believes others need not repeat that lesson.
title: This Lesson Cost me $5,000,000...

text: He says US household net worth is extremely concentrated: scaled to 100 dollars, the bottom 50 hold about 2.50 and the top 1% hold more than the bottom 90% combined.
title: Why you aren't making as much money as you want

text: Telling people to sell to the rich is not a slogan but reality; people often take years to learn it, often because everyone they know is poor, so they compete over the small money at the bottom.
title: Why you aren't making as much money as you want

text: Pareto applied to business: about 20% of customers produce 80% of profit, roughly 4% produce 64%, and the top 1% produce about 51%. A high-paying customer costs little more to serve.
title: Why you aren't making as much money as you want

text: He favors building top-down, as Tesla did from the Roadster: anchoring high gives a stronger brand narrative and lets operations handle low volume before scaling to cheaper products.
title: Why you aren't making as much money as you want

text: Rule of thumb: each new tier should cost 5 to 10 times the previous price, expect about 20% to take it, and it should add roughly another full doubling of revenue or the extra operations may not be worth it.
title: Why you aren't making as much money as you want

text: Because a top tier often rides on existing overhead, its revenue can drop mostly to profit. His example goes from 10 to 90 profit per month by adding two customers at 50.
title: Why you aren't making as much money as you want

text: He prefers starting with the unscalable high-end: 100 grand is a smaller share of a rich person's wealth, and serving one 100K customer is easier than serving a thousand 100 customers, based on his gym-membership experience.
title: Why you aren't making as much money as you want

text: Serving low-budget masses requires heavy capital and automation, which is why big consumer companies relied on outside funding. Since most US businesses are service-based, he says go the opposite direction and serve the best customer at the highest price.
title: Why you aren't making as much money as you want

text: Sellers misprice next tiers: going from 1,000 to 1,500 does not work. The buyer for the next tier sits at 5K to 10K from a 1K offer.
title: Why you aren't making as much money as you want

text: Stop selling from your own wallet or listening to friends and family without money. Be too cheap and buyers may doubt you; a health company's 50% price raise increased close rates.
title: Why you aren't making as much money as you want

text: Make the upsell 5 to 10 times the price and design something you would happily deliver at that price. If it feels like too much work, either do less or charge more; he prefers charging more.
title: Why you aren't making as much money as you want

text: Expect only one in five to one in ten to say yes to a high tier. The goal is most money, not most yeses, and a crazy anchor helps sell everything else.
title: Why you aren't making as much money as you want

text: Think in absolute profit: one person paying 10,000 for something costing 2,000 equals 400 people paying 50 for something costing 25.
title: Why you aren't making as much money as you want

text: His first high-ticket breakthrough: after selling 500 dollar packages, he quoted a gym owner 6,000 expecting a no, got yes, then sold others at 8K and 10K, collecting about 60 grand in a day.
title: Why you aren't making as much money as you want

text: Rules of thumb: consumer impulse purchases are about 500 to 600 dollars, higher-ticket services 3,000 to 10,000. For small businesses, cheap is about 400 to 800 a month and mid-tier 2,000 to 3,000 a month.
title: Why you aren't making as much money as you want

text: Poor buyers react to the price alone while rich buyers judge return versus cost. Before saying the price, tell them it is expensive; this anchors each buyer to their own scale.
title: Why you aren't making as much money as you want

text: Close-rate check: 60 to 80% suggests 2 to 3x room on price, 50 to 60 suggests 1.5 to 2x, 40 to 50 suggests 1.25 to 1.5x, 30 to 40 is about right. Below 30, improve selling.
title: Why you aren't making as much money as you want

text: Qualify and score leads: people with more money are more likely to buy the expensive thing, so speaking only to the right audience raises close rates.
title: Why you aren't making as much money as you want

text: Avoid commodity offers where buyers compare and pick the cheaper. Rich buyers want fast, easy and guaranteed, so do more of the work for them and charge for it.
title: Why you aren't making as much money as you want

text: When demand exceeds supply, raise price. Higher price gives higher gross margin, better talent, better service, reputation and demand, which drives price further.
title: Why you aren't making as much money as you want

text: Hormozi took every sale himself early on out of fear others would waste opportunities. Seeing a first sale made by someone else showed him the business could work without him.
title: The day when everything changed for me...

text: A new hire he had not yet trained closed a walk-in customer paid in full without knowing the pitch. This taught him it is better to find great salespeople and point them in a direction than to train them.
title: The day when everything changed for me...

text: Elite institutions like Harvard and top service firms succeed largely by selecting from a huge pool of talent rather than by the quality of their training.
title: The day when everything changed for me...

text: He has moved toward nature over nurture for roles, especially sales. Rapport and energy are traits he sees as natural, and a rep can win on rapport alone.
title: The day when everything changed for me...

text: Equal training hours give more return on someone with a high starting level: ten hours moving a person from six to nine beats moving a two to four and a half.
title: The day when everything changed for me...

text: Hiring reps from similar companies shortens ramp-up because only the product changes, and it lets you judge their skill faster.
title: The day when everything changed for me...

text: He notes that top sales trainers such as Belfort and Bradley were exceptional sellers from the start, and he had closed thousands of deals before any sales training.
title: The day when everything changed for me...

text: Training should remind good salespeople how good they are, not make them good. Finding a good rep costs far less than training a mediocre one.
title: The day when everything changed for me...

text: A founder weak at sales can invest heavily in self-training with their own time, which a business could not reasonably spend on an employee.
title: The day when everything changed for me...

text: 24 Hour Fitness takes almost anyone, then filters through demanding requirements; about 10% make it past 90 days. Training focuses on their process, not sales fundamentals.
title: The day when everything changed for me...

text: His rule: a rep who has run a full sales cycle without closing a deal is not a killer. Every killer he has had closed deals in the first cycle.
title: The day when everything changed for me...

text: Removing people who drag the team down lifts the team, because cutting the bottom moves the top up, and it sets a higher bar for new hires.
title: The day when everything changed for me...

text: Hire when you feel a strong tingle of needing this person, not when you think they could probably do the job.
title: The day when everything changed for me...

text: The longer he does business, the shorter his tolerance for a non-exceptional rep becomes, because he recognizes exceptional people immediately.
title: The day when everything changed for me...

text: Most people who grow multi-location businesses and then try licensing or franchising fail because the locations are not profitable enough; the unit economics are poor. He says a franchisor needs strong per-unit profit before scaling.
title: 7 figure CONFIDENTIAL meeting LEAKED - business growth STRATEGY exposed...

text: He says most franchise systems never get past 30 locations, and he attributes this to weak unit economics. The founder may enjoy telling friends about being a franchisor, but the units stay unprofitable.
title: 7 figure CONFIDENTIAL meeting LEAKED - business growth STRATEGY exposed...

text: Before anyone would buy into a license or franchise, the corporate-owned locations should be exceptional, with margins of 30 percent or more, according to him.
title: 7 figure CONFIDENTIAL meeting LEAKED - business growth STRATEGY exposed...

text: In small markets, costs are lower and competition is lighter, so margins should be higher, not lower. The trade-off is that leads dry up after the start, so word of mouth and retention matter more.
title: 7 figure CONFIDENTIAL meeting LEAKED - business growth STRATEGY exposed...

text: If the goal is money rather than status, he suggests merging locations onto one fixed overhead and making one unit wildly profitable and running without the owner. That creates an asset that can be sold, licensed or franchised.
title: 7 figure CONFIDENTIAL meeting LEAKED - business growth STRATEGY exposed...

text: He tells a story of his Las Vegas neighbor who owns Panda Express: about 3.8 billion in sales last year at 26 percent margin, and the secret he named was repeating the same thing for 45 years.
title: 7 figure CONFIDENTIAL meeting LEAKED - business growth STRATEGY exposed...

text: He advises making the business profitable out of pride in building the best product, not as a means to something else, because turning the next goal into the target distorts the effort.
title: 7 figure CONFIDENTIAL meeting LEAKED - business growth STRATEGY exposed...

text: Doubling the number of customers per month doubles revenue, profit and cost together in his example, taking profit from 2,000 to 4,000 a month when everything scales proportionately.
title: A Magic Business Genie Grants You 3 Wishes...

text: Doubling how long customers stay eventually reaches the same top line as doubling new customers, but raises lifetime value. Since acquiring and onboarding usually cost more than keeping a customer, he says this route leaves more bottom line.
title: A Magic Business Genie Grants You 3 Wishes...

text: Doubling lifetime gross profit per customer lets the cost of acquisition be larger than it could otherwise be.
title: A Magic Business Genie Grants You 3 Wishes...

text: In his example, doubling price with the same 100 customers and 8,000 in cost takes profit from 2,000 to 12,000 a month. He calls this a sixfold profit gain from one change.
title: A Magic Business Genie Grants You 3 Wishes...

text: He says raising prices often does not lower demand proportionally. If doubling price loses a third of buyers, profit per customer is six times higher and total business profit still triples.
title: A Magic Business Genie Grants You 3 Wishes...

text: Higher prices can make people perceive more value, and a higher price tag can fit better with a strong brand. He says that in one case, raising price 50% with no product change led to more buyers.
title: A Magic Business Genie Grants You 3 Wishes...

text: Pricing is the strongest of the three profit levers and the one people forget to test, though they split test pages, scripts and offers. He says fear of breaking things holds people back.
title: A Magic Business Genie Grants You 3 Wishes...

text: First step to raise price: survey existing customers with the Van Westendorp pricing survey. Ask about their background and reason for buying, then the four price questions (too expensive, too cheap, a stretch, a bargain), plus which offer components they would keep or drop.
title: A Magic Business Genie Grants You 3 Wishes...

text: Announce a price change internally to the team first, then to existing customers with the past, present and future reasoning, and then to new prospects. Expect fewer sales by volume after the change because the pipeline was cleared beforehand.
title: A Magic Business Genie Grants You 3 Wishes...

text: He says the root of passion is a Latin word for suffering, and the word was first used for the crucifixion of Christ, so passion means something worth suffering for, not doing what you love.
title: It took me 36 years to realize what I’ll tell you in 26 minutes…

text: He argues passion exists only in the vague, not the specific: in a successful business most of each day will not be the thing you love, and that specific thing will likely change.
title: It took me 36 years to realize what I’ll tell you in 26 minutes…

text: He says doing the same loved thing constantly would make you stop loving it; rarity is what makes it enjoyable. He calls follow your passion advice easy and politically correct but untrue.
title: It took me 36 years to realize what I’ll tell you in 26 minutes…

text: He says lacking passion is often an excuse hiding inability to handle difficulty, and repeatedly doing things you dislike to reach something meaningful.
title: It took me 36 years to realize what I’ll tell you in 26 minutes…

text: He says new entrepreneurs see their suffering as a sign something is wrong and change course, but change also causes suffering, and they sacrifice the goal by never walking the path.
title: It took me 36 years to realize what I’ll tell you in 26 minutes…

text: The goal is to reframe experience so bad things count as good, changing perceptions rather than conditions, like accepting that both rain and sunshine bring benefits.
title: It took me 36 years to realize what I’ll tell you in 26 minutes…

text: He argues you suffer the same amount whether you pick a hated path, a moderate goal or a swing for the fences, so aiming big makes sense; delaying to find your passion is foolish.
title: It took me 36 years to realize what I’ll tell you in 26 minutes…

text: Find something people value and do it even though it is hard; there is no greener grass, as both sides of the fence are hard.
title: It took me 36 years to realize what I’ll tell you in 26 minutes…

text: He advises being passionate about why and how you work rather than what, because why and how are internal and persist while the what is external and only a treat.
title: It took me 36 years to realize what I’ll tell you in 26 minutes…

text: He says self-serving motives cannot be the goal since you satisfy your own needs quickly; the why must be bigger than you, or you only overcome obstacles smaller than you.
title: It took me 36 years to realize what I’ll tell you in 26 minutes…

text: He cites research where people tolerated shocks until a pain threshold, and when told loved ones would be spared each shock they took, their threshold tripled.
title: It took me 36 years to realize what I’ll tell you in 26 minutes…

text: His own passion, the thing he will suffer for, is helping men provide; he spends much effort on books and content because he thinks that matters most on his deathbed.
title: It took me 36 years to realize what I’ll tell you in 26 minutes…

text: He says you can become passionate about your work by being passionate about what it gets you; in some ways it is about the destination so you can tolerate the journey.
title: It took me 36 years to realize what I’ll tell you in 26 minutes…

text: He believes a man must have a quest, and that you need something you cannot fully achieve to keep striving, because people habituate to the good but still suffer through the bad.
title: It took me 36 years to realize what I’ll tell you in 26 minutes…

text: He started a gym believing lifting and eating with friends all the time would make him happy, and instead the first year was the most miserable of his last 15.
title: It took me 36 years to realize what I’ll tell you in 26 minutes…

text: He says the gap between who you are and who you must become is the pain of growth; if suffering while pursuing something meaningful, nothing is wrong with you and you are on the right path.
title: It took me 36 years to realize what I’ll tell you in 26 minutes…

text: He took out $42 million in distributions before a $46 million exit at 31, then felt miserable on a year off with no quest, and chose to return to this work.
title: It took me 36 years to realize what I’ll tell you in 26 minutes…

text: He predicts that after your next major life change, well-being improves briefly then returns to baseline; so the suffering is a fixed cost, but you can change what or who you do it for.
title: It took me 36 years to realize what I’ll tell you in 26 minutes…

text: At 22 he slept on his gym floor under a parking garage for about six months on four to five hours a night, opening at 4:15 am.
title: It took me 36 years to realize what I’ll tell you in 26 minutes…

text: He quit a white-collar path to run a gym and lost social status among peers, with no promise it would work.
title: It took me 36 years to realize what I’ll tell you in 26 minutes…

text: He got through hard times by committing to not stopping, reasoning that if he never stopped he could not be called a failure; he suggests thinking through the specific worst case.
title: It took me 36 years to realize what I’ll tell you in 26 minutes…

text: He says money gives options but does not dramatically change subjective well-being, which is internal.
title: It took me 36 years to realize what I’ll tell you in 26 minutes…

text: He says the suffering never stops, so accept it as the toll on all paths; then at least you get to choose where you go.
title: It took me 36 years to realize what I’ll tell you in 26 minutes…

text: Reciprocity: kindness and generosity make people more likely to return the favor and to like you. The gift should be proportional to the person you are trying to win over.
title: HOW TO GET WHAT YOU WANT (6 Proven Methods)

text: He and his partner donated a million dollars to Arnold Schwarzenegger's charity to get his attention, and afterward sat down with Arnold multiple times.
title: HOW TO GET WHAT YOU WANT (6 Proven Methods)

text: Stores offering cold water at the door works because visitors feel indebted, so they stay longer, listen more and buy more. He thinks it is probably among the highest-return items in the business.
title: HOW TO GET WHAT YOU WANT (6 Proven Methods)

text: Waiter example: a mint with the bill raised tips by 3 percent, two minutes of attention raised them by 14 percent, and leaving a mint then returning with a second one raised tips by 23 percent.
title: HOW TO GET WHAT YOU WANT (6 Proven Methods)

text: A local entrepreneur he found annoying began sending expensive gifts monthly for nine months to apologize. Even though Hormozi saw what was happening, it still worked and he agreed to meet him again.
title: HOW TO GET WHAT YOU WANT (6 Proven Methods)

text: Consistency: get someone to publicly commit to an identity or action, then later remind them of it when making the ask so they act consistently with it.
title: HOW TO GET WHAT YOU WANT (6 Proven Methods)

text: In a study, few homeowners accepted a huge drive slowly yard sign, but many agreed to a bigger sign after first putting a small note-card sign in a window. Small yes first can lead to the big yes.
title: HOW TO GET WHAT YOU WANT (6 Proven Methods)

text: Social proof: people look to others for cues on how to behave or what to believe. Examples include high review counts on Amazon and laugh tracks making people laugh more.
title: HOW TO GET WHAT YOU WANT (6 Proven Methods)

text: He framed every five-star review and before-and-after photo so his gym lobby was covered floor to ceiling, and used that proof when prospects doubted results.
title: HOW TO GET WHAT YOU WANT (6 Proven Methods)

text: Liking: people are more persuaded by those they like and want to be like. In a study, people liked flatterers even when told they were paid to compliment, and flattery had no cap if genuine.
title: HOW TO GET WHAT YOU WANT (6 Proven Methods)

text: ACA framework for likability in conversation: acknowledge what they said, compliment them on it, then ask the next question to move the conversation forward.
title: HOW TO GET WHAT YOU WANT (6 Proven Methods)

text: He bounced on a mini trampoline during consults and did a cartwheel before handshakes at his gym. He says people bought partly because they liked the feeling he gave them.
title: HOW TO GET WHAT YOU WANT (6 Proven Methods)

text: Authority works because people apply fewer filters and accept more as true, independent of the message itself. This is why mentors speed decision-making.
title: HOW TO GET WHAT YOU WANT (6 Proven Methods)

text: Build authority by showing credentials, awards and track record, plus third-party accreditation. He printed certifications for himself and his trainers, including some he certified internally.
title: HOW TO GET WHAT YOU WANT (6 Proven Methods)

text: Urgency is a function of time, such as a promotion ending tomorrow. Scarcity is a function of units, such as only a hundred left. People value what is scarce.
title: HOW TO GET WHAT YOU WANT (6 Proven Methods)

text: Implement scarcity with limited time, limited supply and one-time offers, and use loss language, since people feel loss aversion more strongly than desire to gain.
title: HOW TO GET WHAT YOU WANT (6 Proven Methods)

text: Luxury brands centrally control supply, withhold how many items stores will get, and during covid some stores kept lines outside to signal demand and exclusivity.
title: HOW TO GET WHAT YOU WANT (6 Proven Methods)

text: Scarcity must be real. If you can serve only a set number of customers or have limited product, state those limits explicitly and you will sell more.
title: HOW TO GET WHAT YOU WANT (6 Proven Methods)

text: Hormozi argues that what separates billionaires from people in massive debt is mainly the quality of their decisions, and that a single decision can redirect a life.
title: I Sold My Company at 31: My Detailed Breakdown of the Decision

text: After the banker valued his company at $150 million, he shifted from building to selling; growth stalled, and he says he does not know whether burnout, the pandemic or his mindset caused it.
title: I Sold My Company at 31: My Detailed Breakdown of the Decision

text: Once selling dominated his thinking, he judged decisions by what an acquirer would think rather than customer goodwill. He cut prices to lower churn, lost about $5 million of profit, and thinks this hurt the business.
title: I Sold My Company at 31: My Detailed Breakdown of the Decision

text: He went from $17M profit on $26M revenue to $13.4M profit on $37M, with about 135 employees at peak, after hiring extra staff to look legit for buyers.
title: I Sold My Company at 31: My Detailed Breakdown of the Decision

text: Ahead of the sale, he stopped attending product meetings and client-facing calls and events, built an outbound call team handling 50% of sales, and promoted gym owners as the consulting brand's face.
title: I Sold My Company at 31: My Detailed Breakdown of the Decision

text: He tested reasons to sell and found weak ones: proving legitimacy, proving a model can be sold, boosting net worth, or spiting doubters. His friend countered each.
title: I Sold My Company at 31: My Detailed Breakdown of the Decision

text: Sometimes you must give up something good and known for something unknown that could be great; he says people regret what they did not try more than what they tried and failed.
title: I Sold My Company at 31: My Detailed Breakdown of the Decision

text: He views diversification as a hedge against ignorance; if you know your space well, he says you can go all in on it and let it grow disproportionately.
title: I Sold My Company at 31: My Detailed Breakdown of the Decision

text: He believes you can own many things but only run one actively; split attention is among the most dangerous things in entrepreneurship, and his revenue flatlined when he started other companies.
title: I Sold My Company at 31: My Detailed Breakdown of the Decision

text: Bankers may inflate valuation promises because they want you to sign on with them.
title: I Sold My Company at 31: My Detailed Breakdown of the Decision

text: He says selling is a story, not reality: you will still lie awake thinking about the team and company, so you may not get the mental freedom you imagine.
title: I Sold My Company at 31: My Detailed Breakdown of the Decision

text: A friend suggested he replicate the conditions he imagined after selling while keeping the company. He doubted it works, comparing it to children who keep occupying your thoughts even when grown.
title: I Sold My Company at 31: My Detailed Breakdown of the Decision

text: Selling means losing the resources and leverage of an owned company, like getting recruiting, sites and books done by asking; he saw this as a possible advantage since it would force faster decisions.
title: I Sold My Company at 31: My Detailed Breakdown of the Decision

text: Hormozi noticed that the argument for keeping the company was driven by fear of losing what he had, rather than by analysis.
title: I Sold My Company at 31: My Detailed Breakdown of the Decision

text: Buffett gives contradicting advice: never sell wholly owned companies, and get into the best boat. Hormozi finds both fair, and it mirrors his selling-versus-keeping dilemma.
title: I Sold My Company at 31: My Detailed Breakdown of the Decision

text: His first decision framework: accept there is no wrong answer, since he would stay wealthy and likely be happy either way, so none of it matters much materially.
title: I Sold My Company at 31: My Detailed Breakdown of the Decision

text: Using the horse parable, he says you cannot know whether something is good or bad until you die, and then it will not matter.
title: I Sold My Company at 31: My Detailed Breakdown of the Decision

text: He calls quitting his job, selling his gyms, and selling majority stakes in these companies his three hardest decisions, ranked in that order, each trading status for something bigger but unknown.
title: I Sold My Company at 31: My Detailed Breakdown of the Decision

text: He thinks the hardest decisions in life are giving up the sure thing for the uncertain bigger one, and that quantum leaps need big risks.
title: I Sold My Company at 31: My Detailed Breakdown of the Decision

text: He asks what he is most afraid of; selling scared him most (fear of being a one-hit wonder), which pointed toward selling.
title: I Sold My Company at 31: My Detailed Breakdown of the Decision

text: His 85-year-old self test: imagine what your 85-year-old self thinks. He calls it his most effective decision framework, and it told him to do what excites him.
title: I Sold My Company at 31: My Detailed Breakdown of the Decision

text: His ultimate reason was that the next venture could be 10x or 100x bigger and anything distracting from it would be a net loss; he did not want to regret gripping too hard.
title: I Sold My Company at 31: My Detailed Breakdown of the Decision

text: He felt the loss of the business but not the gain of money; relief lasted about three days. He now feels sure the decision was right.
title: I Sold My Company at 31: My Detailed Breakdown of the Decision

text: He says unmade decisions weigh heavily and consume mental capacity, so making the decision unlocked his future and creative energy.
title: I Sold My Company at 31: My Detailed Breakdown of the Decision

text: People skip things they know they should do because a short-term reinforcement beats the long-term one. The long-term fix is to act, then label the pattern as an identity, such as being organized, and stay consistent with it.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Ask Me Anything)

text: Warm traffic only yields what warm traffic yields. Cold traffic run through a warm sales motion does not convert, so the motion must become a cold one that warms people up first.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Ask Me Anything)

text: A paid workshop priced around 49 to 99 dollars, with real value delivered, makes buying easier than a high-ticket offer and lets people see proof before the pitch.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Ask Me Anything)

text: Small friction such as a low-price purchase can cut unqualified attendees from around 90 percent to about 40 percent, and buyers tend to buy more afterward.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Ask Me Anything)

text: He cares more about the qualified conversion rate than the overall event conversion rate; if qualified people close well, the problem is traffic, and qualified counts predict revenue better than lead counts.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Ask Me Anything)

text: Insufficient ad volume feels like volatility. With high-ticket offers and high CAC, daily spend must be much higher, which then requires far more creative.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Ask Me Anything)

text: To make many video ads quickly, walk with a phone and teleprompter app showing hooks of past winners; reuse winning hooks while tweaking the body and background.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Ask Me Anything)

text: Optimize the ad pixel on an event with enough volume, like applications, rather than closes, and place the pixel only on the qualified-applicant thank-you page.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Ask Me Anything)

text: If you are underpricing in a small market, going after a bigger market can multiply revenue; he suggests taking current pricing and adding a zero for US customers.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Ask Me Anything)

text: Make content about doing your clients' work, teaching everything you do, so prospects see the effort and want to hire you instead of doing it themselves.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Ask Me Anything)

text: When churn is high and data is thin, drop scalability for the short term: run manual onboarding calls and watch customers use the product to find friction.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Ask Me Anything)

text: Match the billing cycle to the value cycle; if customers only need value quarterly, offer quarterly or annual billing.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Ask Me Anything)

text: Keeping a monthly option gives a faster feedback loop for fixing the product; once churn is solved on monthly, push everyone to annual. Cutting churn by two thirds would triple the business.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Ask Me Anything)

text: If an employee brings substantial gross profit, paying 10 to 20 percent of it as a referral bonus is reasonable, and paying staff beats paying an outside recruiter.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Ask Me Anything)

text: For one-off roles use recruiters; for repeatable roles build a system, with a cost of acquiring talent and lifetime gross profit per employee, using ads, VSL and group calls.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Ask Me Anything)

text: Service businesses need demand-generation funnels and supply-generation funnels, a bow tie, and most miss the supply side.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Ask Me Anything)

text: Emergency-driven customers can be flipped into ongoing ones by offering to credit today's visit toward a recurring plan; sell thrive rather than survive.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Ask Me Anything)

text: Intent-based inbound leads price shop, while interruption-based leads from ads do not compare shops, so a premium is possible with one extra differentiating element.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Ask Me Anything)

text: Until the model works, treat the business as an experiment: marketing spend exists to get reps on the offer and sales motion, then scale.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Ask Me Anything)

text: Messaging aimed at the correct top avatar cuts out lower slices, while speaking broadly attracts unqualified people; qualify who you sell to.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Ask Me Anything)

text: Track churn separately for ideal customers; he says under 3 percent monthly would be excellent.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Ask Me Anything)

text: Constant pivoting follows a cycle: uninformed optimism, informed pessimism, valley of despair, new shiny object. Get out by pushing through the valley to informed optimism.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Ask Me Anything)

text: Year one of a new venture equals year four or five of the old one, so switching sacrifices compounding; depth comes from staying with one opportunity.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Ask Me Anything)

text: He suggests starting AI implementation with a customer and problem rather than learning to code first, so tools are learned in context.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Ask Me Anything)

text: For enterprise clients, go where they are: trade shows, conferences and centers of influence such as law firms and architects; long-term build a brand.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Ask Me Anything)

text: Consistency over long periods, doing the same thing without immediate reward, is what almost nobody is willing to do and where people win.

text: Hormozi says value is a loosely used word entrepreneurs rarely define, and he built the Value Equation with four components to define and measure it.
title: How I got 700 people to pay me $40,000 each...no bs..

text: Dream outcome is the first component. He observed that for men, money-making things cost more than weight-loss things, because making money raises status more.
title: How I got 700 people to pay me $40,000 each...no bs..

text: Dream outcome sets the product category; within a category, the other three variables decide what is cheap or expensive. A five dollar ebook and liposuction share the same outcome, weight loss.
title: How I got 700 people to pay me $40,000 each...no bs..

text: Describing the dream outcome more vividly makes it seem more appealing, so prospects deem it more valuable and will pay more.
title: How I got 700 people to pay me $40,000 each...no bs..

text: Perceived likelihood of achievement raises value: a surgeon with ten thousand procedures commands more than a novice even if he spends less time. Time taken to fulfill should not be part of your value equation.
title: How I got 700 people to pay me $40,000 each...no bs..

text: Hormozi calls escalating promises the most beginner move, where he started. He raised perceived likelihood by adding more testimonials, since many testimonials make prospects believe the provider is good and lower perceived risk.
title: How I got 700 people to pay me $40,000 each...no bs..

text: Time delay is between paying and getting the result. Doing what the best competitor does in half the time makes you more valuable, because people pay for speed.
title: How I got 700 people to pay me $40,000 each...no bs..

text: Against a free competitor, compete on speed. A friend's expedited DMV services charge fifty dollars versus free government service and do very well.
title: How I got 700 people to pay me $40,000 each...no bs..

text: Hormozi says he raises value by strengthening the dream outcome and how it is expressed, so prospects believe it matches what they truly want.
title: How I got 700 people to pay me $40,000 each...no bs..

text: Precision Nutrition's cofounder said their breakthrough was realizing certifications sell community with like-minded people, not continuing education; certification was a socially acceptable excuse. Defining that outcome correctly helped the business.
title: How I got 700 people to pay me $40,000 each...no bs..

text: The equation is a fraction: if time delay and effort are near zero, even a small promised benefit becomes infinitely valuable.
title: How I got 700 people to pay me $40,000 each...no bs..

text: He once focused only on the top of the equation. He notes Amazon, Netflix and Uber grew by cutting the downside, and he thinks that is where the biggest competitive moat is.
title: How I got 700 people to pay me $40,000 each...no bs..

text: Scoring personal training one of four and liposuction four of four explains why one takes an hour of arm wrestling to sell a thousand dollar package while the other sells forty thousand in under fifteen minutes by phone.
title: How I got 700 people to pay me $40,000 each...no bs..

text: Hormozi says his group aims to build a portfolio of companies reaching a billion dollars yearly revenue, and was then at about eighty-five million.
title: How I got 700 people to pay me $40,000 each...no bs..

text: He estimates 25 to 30% of independent gyms have permanently closed, and thinks this could climb to 40 or even 50% over the next six months.
title: My Address To The Gym Industry At The Onset of COVID

text: An investing saying holds that when a strong operator meets a weak market, or a weak operator meets a strong market, the market wins. He uses it to contrast growing, static and shrinking markets.
title: My Address To The Gym Industry At The Onset of COVID

text: He thinks consumers have been permanently retrained to meet fitness needs differently: if all clients tried a new solution, some amount above zero would stick, so he believes the gym market keeps shrinking.
title: My Address To The Gym Industry At The Onset of COVID

text: Gym Launch is loyal to gym owners, not to gyms. Gyms were only the vehicle, for the past three to four years, for owners to package their skills.
title: My Address To The Gym Industry At The Onset of COVID

text: He reports in-person lead cost averaging about $30 across markets, even for a free offer, and says extra friction can double people's resistance to going to the gym.
title: My Address To The Gym Industry At The Onset of COVID

text: Online lets the owner live anywhere, skip early and late gym hours and no-show appointments. He says the model is less constrained by geography and time and is more profitable.
title: My Address To The Gym Industry At The Onset of COVID

text: He argues one-on-one online coaching gives many people better results than group workouts, so fulfillment is better for the client and more profitable, and the model avoids rent as a fixed cost.
title: My Address To The Gym Industry At The Onset of COVID

text: Cold outbound messaging works but takes two to four hours a day and does not scale. He thinks an okay vehicle builds only an okay business, and that this explains why gurus lack large businesses.
title: My Address To The Gym Industry At The Onset of COVID

text: Webinar-to-application models sell $2,000 to $3,000 offers, but he says the webinar fatigues and applications can cost around $100. Even experienced operators often get only one to two dollars back per ad dollar upfront.
title: My Address To The Gym Industry At The Onset of COVID

text: He calls the five-day group challenge model effort-heavy, stop-and-go and hard to scale, noting no massive online weight loss companies run on it. He would not recommend these models to people without a following.
title: My Address To The Gym Industry At The Onset of COVID

text: A free trial front end needs little skill to sell, unlike a $3,000 high-ticket fitness sale, which he says is hard to outsource. Unlimited leads give consistent operations and cash flow.
title: My Address To The Gym Industry At The Onset of COVID

text: Selling a supplement first, then a follow-up sale, is easy enough to scale and break even or close to it on the first transaction. He says by day 30 customers convert at gym prices, with higher profit.
title: My Address To The Gym Industry At The Onset of COVID

text: The model has three roles: trial seller, the person converting the same-day offer and nutrition sale, and the owner. One person can cover all three at scale, and each sale is simple.
title: My Address To The Gym Industry At The Onset of COVID

text: He says the in-person business mentality, skills and sales choreography are the same as online; only fulfillment via an app differs. He says the same $5,000 of marketing yields more online clients.
title: My Address To The Gym Industry At The Onset of COVID

text: Sunk cost fallacy: past investment is irrelevant to the current decision. For an existing gym lease, he suggests walking away, which he thinks is easier during this period, or funding the lease from online profit.
title: My Address To The Gym Industry At The Onset of COVID

text: He thinks there is a golden window with high demand for online services and little supply, and does not know how long it lasts, so those on the fence should act now.
title: My Address To The Gym Industry At The Onset of COVID

text: He says many top seven-figure gym owners have gone 100% online, some selling their gyms, because they saw the math. He adds experienced fitness professionals have an advantage over influencers.
title: My Address To The Gym Industry At The Onset of COVID

text: He did not take a vacation for five years while running his gym, and returned early from Christmas trips three years running because of stress.
title: My Address To The Gym Industry At The Onset of COVID

text: He lists his bets: free weight loss offers always draw signups, low-skill people can sell free trials, supplements sell in a one-step upsell, and customers stay on continuity at $39 to $59 a week.
title: My Address To The Gym Industry At The Onset of COVID

text: He says the app automates 80% of fulfillment, removing worries like trainers, broken equipment, cleaning and music, and that Gym Launch will support owners whether they go online or stay in person.
title: My Address To The Gym Industry At The Onset of COVID

text: Hormozi does not think offering to buy a millionaire lunch or work free is realistic, since you have little to offer. He says start by being honest about your current value, then increase it.
title: A BILLIONAIRE told me how to make BILLION DOLLARS...here's my plan...

text: Rule of thumb he gives: the people you can get access to are roughly at your level multiplied by five. Someone earning 100 thousand a year might reach people making about a million. Otherwise you pay for access.
title: A BILLIONAIRE told me how to make BILLION DOLLARS...here's my plan...

text: Hormozi says the breakthrough from mid-30 millions toward 100 million was focusing on people. An entrepreneur's influence dilutes across management levels, so you cannot remain the source of everything.
title: A BILLIONAIRE told me how to make BILLION DOLLARS...here's my plan...

text: The billionaire told him a self-sustaining growing business needs three superstars: one owning acquisition, one owning delivery, one owning operations and shared services. With those three, he said, the business can grow on its own.
title: A BILLIONAIRE told me how to make BILLION DOLLARS...here's my plan...

text: Hormozi says he observes that the richest people are willing to give up part of the pie so it grows. He regrets early partnering with people sharing his skills instead of complementary ones.
title: A BILLIONAIRE told me how to make BILLION DOLLARS...here's my plan...

text: Early in a career you need not give equity for a needed skill like accounting; you can pay a vendor. He notes early equity is the most expensive kind, so level up skills instead.
title: A BILLIONAIRE told me how to make BILLION DOLLARS...here's my plan...

text: The billionaire said he never misjudged someone as non-superstar who later became one. Hormozi's takeaway: if you do not immediately see a leadership hire as a superstar, they are probably not the fit.
title: A BILLIONAIRE told me how to make BILLION DOLLARS...here's my plan...

text: Hormozi says going from 30 to 100 million requires giving up control over high-level decisions, since superstars want authority and responsibility, and the credit for outcomes.
title: A BILLIONAIRE told me how to make BILLION DOLLARS...here's my plan...

text: The billionaire gave profit shares only to CEOs of his companies, and believed creating profit is unnatural and the CEO's responsibility, since businesses left alone tend to break even.
title: A BILLIONAIRE told me how to make BILLION DOLLARS...here's my plan...

text: He shared five percent of profits with company CEOs and let them buy in over time; one CEO went from five or ten percent to owning thirty-something percent.
title: A BILLIONAIRE told me how to make BILLION DOLLARS...here's my plan...

text: Hormozi says advanced people are advanced because they consistently do the basics. He believes success is simple but not easy, and finding good people is the number one business problem.
title: A BILLIONAIRE told me how to make BILLION DOLLARS...here's my plan...

text: Hormozi concludes that a corporation's size is proportional to its number of superstars. As companies grow, the billionaire said, you need fewer drivers and more tenders who make incremental improvements.
title: A BILLIONAIRE told me how to make BILLION DOLLARS...here's my plan...

text: Growth often comes in steps, with plateaus in between, because of bottlenecks. Hormozi says you usually remove a bottleneck by hiring someone experienced in that area.
title: A BILLIONAIRE told me how to make BILLION DOLLARS...here's my plan...

text: The billionaire invests in multifamily real estate, focusing on return of capital over return on capital, and said he never bought below an eight cap rate.
title: A BILLIONAIRE told me how to make BILLION DOLLARS...here's my plan...

text: Hormozi says as you grow, decisions become about downside mitigation: doubling net worth changes little in your life, but halving it does.
title: A BILLIONAIRE told me how to make BILLION DOLLARS...here's my plan...

text: The billionaire said his firm stalled at 100 million for four or five years, then split into about 100 pieces with profit sharing and phantom equity for superstars. It reached 500 million five years later and a billion five after.
title: A BILLIONAIRE told me how to make BILLION DOLLARS...here's my plan...

text: His wife notes that wealth among employees often does not track pay; some mid-tier earners have more savings and less debt than higher earners, so cutting downside matters more than raising upside.
title: LEAKED: Street millionaire employee training...how he REALLY got rich..

text: Making not spending fun works as a game: try to beat last month's spending total every month and see what else can be trimmed. He says couples must do it together.
title: LEAKED: Street millionaire employee training...how he REALLY got rich..

text: When sleeping on his gym floor, he was already earning profit that grew from $5,000 to $35,000 monthly; he felt anxiety spending non-negligible income and pushed money into his bank account.
title: LEAKED: Street millionaire employee training...how he REALLY got rich..

text: Saving $500 a month from age 35 to 75 means contributing $240,000 and retiring with about $3 million in the S&P, which is why you cannot outwork money and must let it work for you.
title: LEAKED: Street millionaire employee training...how he REALLY got rich..

text: Debt compounds against you like the eighth wonder of the world in reverse; credit card rates around 10 to 16% would delight an investor, but the bank collects them.
title: LEAKED: Street millionaire employee training...how he REALLY got rich..

text: Step one: save a starter emergency fund of $1,000 to $5,000 before paying debt, because unexpected bills are predictable in that they will happen, and interruptions would otherwise derail debt payoff.
title: LEAKED: Street millionaire employee training...how he REALLY got rich..

text: Step two: pay off all debt except the mortgage, smallest balance first, even if a larger one has a higher rate, because you need emotional wins and momentum.
title: LEAKED: Street millionaire employee training...how he REALLY got rich..

text: Debt is risk; over a long enough horizon, risk can multiply your returns by zero. He and his wife bought their home and cars in cash and hold no debt.
title: LEAKED: Street millionaire employee training...how he REALLY got rich..

text: Step three: after clearing debt, expand the emergency fund to three to six months of living expenses, sized to your need for security; it is not invested. Living on less makes this easier.
title: LEAKED: Street millionaire employee training...how he REALLY got rich..

text: He says buying the Bentley was his biggest financial regret and he got no enjoyment from it; he preferred the cracked-windshield Prius, chose confidence of a strong bank account over impressing others.
title: LEAKED: Street millionaire employee training...how he REALLY got rich..

text: Turning in a lease early and buying a $5,000 car in cash turns the monthly payment into a permanent flow toward net worth.
title: LEAKED: Street millionaire employee training...how he REALLY got rich..

text: Step four: if you keep your mortgage, refinance to a 15-year fixed so more payments go to principal. He notes no capital gains tax on a primary home sale after living there over two years.
title: LEAKED: Street millionaire employee training...how he REALLY got rich..
