text: Step five: invest 15% of pre-tax income in the S&P 500, which he says rose about 9 to 10% yearly over 80 years. He disclaims that this is not professional investment advice.
title: LEAKED: Street millionaire employee training...how he REALLY got rich..

text: Before Gym Launch he had under $300,000 in an index and treated it as nonexistent, never touching it, and earned money another way when needed. He says this builds character.
title: LEAKED: Street millionaire employee training...how he REALLY got rich..

text: He suggests buying index funds through the free Robinhood app rather than an adviser, whose fees he says would hurt returns.
title: LEAKED: Street millionaire employee training...how he REALLY got rich..

text: He suggests going further: pay the 15-year mortgage off early with excess cash, after checking there is no prepayment penalty, and then everything beyond food goes into building wealth.
title: LEAKED: Street millionaire employee training...how he REALLY got rich..

text: He says he and his wife earned more from their investments this year than from their companies.
title: LEAKED: Street millionaire employee training...how he REALLY got rich..

text: His wife says vices cover short-term pain, and possessions add attention demands and complexity that increase anxiety; saving buys back attention.
title: LEAKED: Street millionaire employee training...how he REALLY got rich..

text: He defines the top 1% as $1 to $5 million in assets and says nobody will come to save you; the math works for everyone.
title: LEAKED: Street millionaire employee training...how he REALLY got rich..

text: There are three ways to get leads: assemble a list manually, buy from brokers, or scrape with software. He usually starts with scraping because it tends to be the cheapest.
title: I Helped 6 Business Owners Make More Money

text: To choose a scraping tool, he runs his avatar search in the top four or five tools, works a sample of 100 or 500 leads from each, and doubles down on the one with the highest response rate.
title: I Helped 6 Business Owners Make More Money

text: To create a free offer people reply to, give away something people normally pay for, even on a micro level. Generic free stuff everyone gives is weak; you must be significantly better.
title: I Helped 6 Business Owners Make More Money

text: The top way to change behavior is to change environment. He suggests even moving thirty minutes away, which shifts the people you frequent, and accepting you will lose many friends.
title: I Helped 6 Business Owners Make More Money

text: When shared interests shrink to just reminiscing about the past, those friends are not helping build your future. As he advanced, he cut such people sooner, reasoning he would cut them eventually.
title: I Helped 6 Business Owners Make More Money

text: When opening his sixth gym, working sales twelve hours daily, he gave up football, fantasy, and Netflix to make time. Cutting things creates a vacuum, and new people and positive behaviors fill it.
title: I Helped 6 Business Owners Make More Money

text: He recommends connecting with people online for community, since online groups pursuing the same goal are far bigger than local ones. Decide which behaviors to give up, since you only have 24 hours.
title: I Helped 6 Business Owners Make More Money

text: With family, reset the rules of engagement and enforce them by lowering contact cadence and proximity. He treats family and strangers the same and expects no debts either way; he notes this is an extreme view.
title: I Helped 6 Business Owners Make More Money

text: Give free value until people ask for more, then notice the common thread in requests, poll the audience about a paid product, and build it once they say yes. Free content does not mean everything is free.
title: I Helped 6 Business Owners Make More Money

text: Illustration: asking 100 people to buy might yield one sale; offering to solve a problem free might get 20 yeses, and half of those may buy a follow-up, giving ten sales. Trust before the ask can 10x conversion.
title: I Helped 6 Business Owners Make More Money

text: Block the first hours of each day to make the free asset exceptional, and document the making so people see the effort. Good work gets shared, multiplying interest.
title: I Helped 6 Business Owners Make More Money

text: Exceptional work prevents doing multiple things well. Ignore other opportunities, focus on what earns most now, and improve it via the value equation: faster, less effort, higher perceived likelihood of success.
title: I Helped 6 Business Owners Make More Money

text: Pick one avatar and master it first, like mastering a puddle before a pond. Choose work where you lose track of time, since exceptional results need that volume of effort.
title: I Helped 6 Business Owners Make More Money

text: He prefers a semi-private gym model at about 300 to 400 dollars monthly, two to three sessions weekly, targeting avatars with more money. Micro gyms typically cap around 120 to 150 members because human-connection systems get complex.
title: I Helped 6 Business Owners Make More Money

text: For a gym launch he would run a three-month pre-launch and spend disproportionately on pre-sales, opening at full capacity so the location is profitable in month one.
title: I Helped 6 Business Owners Make More Money

text: Challenge names are just wrapping paper. Rotate them locally so ads do not fatigue, but funnel everyone into the same sales process so operations stay unchanged.
title: I Helped 6 Business Owners Make More Money

text: Good partnerships have a yes person and a no person. He suggests asking the cautious partner for a checklist that must be met before the next location, then repeating it each time.
title: I Helped 6 Business Owners Make More Money

text: He and his wife solved a different problem than most couples chase: not Hollywood romance, which he says fades, but shared work and direction. Respect came first, romance after about two and a half years.
title: I Helped 6 Business Owners Make More Money

text: He frames a partner search around three things: goals (where), values (how), and lifestyle (interests). Where he wants to go is non-negotiable, so a partner must share it.
title: I Helped 6 Business Owners Make More Money

text: He suggests learning skills in order of making money: a base sellable skill, then promotion, then conversion (sales), then leadership and operations.
title: I Helped 6 Business Owners Make More Money

text: He tweeted that the gap from a thousand to a million is skills, a million to 100 million is character, and 100 million to a billion is time (which he says we will see). Scale speed tracks talent recruitment.
title: I Helped 6 Business Owners Make More Money

text: There is a two-sided funnel: attracting customers and attracting talent. Knowing only how to attract customers means things keep breaking and you cannot scale.
title: I Helped 6 Business Owners Make More Money

text: In enterprise sales, involve as many stakeholders as fast as possible and pitch so they look good with no job risk. Never leave a meeting without booking the next one.
title: I Helped 6 Business Owners Make More Money

text: Reframe long enterprise sales cycles as hours of work rather than calendar time: forty-eight one-hour meetings can stretch two years or fit in three months, and cover the budget approvers.
title: I Helped 6 Business Owners Make More Money

text: Enterprise lead gen through gated content still works, as with white papers. He gets a name from anyone who downloads and uses scripted questions about objective and stakeholders to pull the thread.
title: I Helped 6 Business Owners Make More Money

text: Hormozi proposes normalizing a six-day, twelve-hour-per-day work week for men aged 16 to 28, arguing young people have little utility but lots of energy, so should trade energy for experience and become useful.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: The first rule of entrepreneurship, he says, is to use what you have. Lacking capital or connections is no excuse; resourcefulness matters more than resources, and skill comes from repeated failure and small improvements.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: If you have under $100,000 saved and want more, he advises cutting spending hard, then using savings to make bets on education, opportunities, inventory or software.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: A big savings stockpile lets you think long term, because you do not have to worry about paying for tomorrow. Without it you stay in survival mode.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: Very broke people should stop eating out, buy only discount groceries, buy clothes only at Goodwill, and attend only free friend events.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: He says people who do not support your goals are not really your friends, and some people called friends are actually enemies to the goal.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: To earn more when broke: apply to higher-paying jobs, take side work, learn skills that pay a higher hourly rate, then find the hardest worker in the room and double their input.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: After making these changes, wait 36 months: be patient with outputs and impatient with inputs. Direction changes instantly, but the fruit takes time.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: Skill development equals repetitions times improvement between repetitions; volume helps most when paired with feedback on what you did.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: Review your top ten videos of the last month, work out what made them good, and apply one of those things in every new video, building a checklist. Also do less of the bottom 10 percent.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: His early sales skill came from no training, watching others, and a huge volume: 15 to 20 in-person consults a day plus phone calls, starting Facebook ads in 2013.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: On appointment-setting calls he used a positive, high-energy tone with pauses, which made people more likely to show up and made objections easier to handle.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: He is not naturally high energy, so he bounced on a small trampoline of about a hundred dollars between sales appointments to lift his mood.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: His biggest improvements came from reviewing data, not advice: compare the top 50 of 2,000 ads with the bottom 50, do more of the winners' traits, and repeat for calls, content and meetings.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: If you are under roughly 28, humbling yourself to people ahead of you and asking them to mentor you can earn free advice worth thousands of dollars.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: He says he spent ego, money, time and social capital to learn faster, and credits his father with the belief that you are the asset you invest in.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: Skills stack disproportionately: knowing two, such as sales and finance, or code and marketing, can make far more than knowing one.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: Citing Munger, he says avoiding stupidity is easier than pursuing intelligence, and he defines intelligence as rate of learning.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: Your reference group, the five people you compare yourself to, strongly shapes what you achieve. He says you sometimes have to like your goals more than your friends.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: Everyone pursuing something goes through a lonely chapter: you no longer fit with old friends but lack the achievements to fit a new group.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: Leasing a Ferrari early in your career impresses only poor people, and rich people would say to reinvest instead. He adds that context matters, and outsourcing things you dislike, like cooking, is sensible.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: He bought a roughly 1.7 million dollar Austin house in cash from one month of pay, noting that whatever you spend is taken from the future and you must balance consumption and investment.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: He bought a Bentley, returned it six months later and lost about 20 thousand dollars, concluding he did not care about it.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: Distraction, meaning research and delay, keeps you from doing what you already know you should; start with your basic guess instead of searching for the perfect program.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: Getting better is a meta skill: learning to improve at one thing makes you better at improving at everything, so see being bad at something new as an opportunity.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: The perfect moment arrives when you decide you are fed up with waiting and act; it only looks perfect in hindsight.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: He argues that having demons or self-sabotage really means a skill deficit in behaving under certain conditions, and the fix is repetition.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: Bad salespeople have a few good days, good ones get hot streaks, and great ones never go cold; being on fire is just behaving differently, which is learnable.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: He defines trauma as a permanent behavior change from an aversive stimulus, and says whether it is good or bad depends on whether the new behavior serves your goals.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: To test a story about your past, define it in behavior terms, ask what evidence exists and how often it happened, then ask what utility it has.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: He was terrified by the thought of winning a lottery in college because he would never achieve anything that felt his own.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: Everyone has had their version of ten out of ten pain, and the chapter you are in is a requirement for becoming who you want to be.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: Build a figure-it-out muscle: before quitting, try for 20 hours. Often it is not hard, you just have not tried yet.
title: How To Actually Get Rich In Your 20s

text: To pick your next hire, list your activities and find the lowest-cost one that eats the largest share of your time. Value each activity by what it earns you, not just market rate.
title: This first hire nearly bankrupt me...but was worth it..

text: Early on, do not outsource work crucial to the business, such as sales. Hand off admin and billing first, since they are less likely to hurt the business. Hiring is played as defense.
title: This first hire nearly bankrupt me...but was worth it..

text: He says entrepreneurship is essentially buying back time and building skill to do higher-revenue work, ending with you making decisions, then supplying a shared vision people use to decide on your behalf.
title: This first hire nearly bankrupt me...but was worth it..

text: Most people solve problems that do not exist in their business. Picking the problem you are truly solving is among the most important entrepreneurial skills.
title: This first hire nearly bankrupt me...but was worth it..

text: Early first hires are usually either general admin help or a first follower who believes in your vision. Spouses often fill this role and give far more effort than a normal employee.
title: This first hire nearly bankrupt me...but was worth it..

text: The other common first hire is someone to help with fulfillment. This requires productizing your service by narrowing customer type and outcome so others can replicate results, freeing you to run the business.
title: This first hire nearly bankrupt me...but was worth it..

text: While productizing, you will work overtime, roughly one and a half to double, since you run the business while building the infrastructure others will work within.
title: This first hire nearly bankrupt me...but was worth it..

text: For founder-owned bootstrapped businesses, which he says are 99% of businesses, the first two hires are typically admin help and customer fulfillment help. VC-backed startups may hire differently.
title: This first hire nearly bankrupt me...but was worth it..

text: Outsource in order: first the tasks taking the most time for the least value, so you climb toward work that earns the most money in the least time.
title: This first hire nearly bankrupt me...but was worth it..

text: His first lens for an opportunity is how many people could potentially buy the offering, which shows how long the game can run. He tests the assumptions that would keep demand true, like weight loss demand persisting.
title: What I look for to invest in companies [no bs]

text: His second lens is potential profit per unit, a function of the value customers get and the cost to deliver it. Very valuable but very costly offers leave little profit, so he is less interested in them.
title: What I look for to invest in companies [no bs]

text: His third lens is competitive dynamics. Phone service has huge demand and near-zero marginal cost, but beating giants like Verizon and AT&T makes it fail this third box.
title: What I look for to invest in companies [no bs]

text: A business is more interesting when few competitors exist and the space is new. He judges these by asking whether many new entrants are arriving or established players could price him out.
title: What I look for to invest in companies [no bs]

text: To raise your own opportunity, ask whether you can make the offer apply to more people, and whether you can raise the outcome's value or cut fulfillment cost to increase gross profit per unit.
title: What I look for to invest in companies [no bs]

text: For any service business he likes gross margins of 80% or higher. Selling at $1,000 a month should cost under $200 to deliver.
title: What I look for to invest in companies [no bs]

text: Gross profit is not owner profit; it must cover marketing, admin, payroll, HR, finance and legal. Starting at 80% and targeting 50% margins leaves 30% for those functions.
title: What I look for to invest in companies [no bs]

text: Small businesses often think charging more is bad, but he says you need gross profit to scale and help more people. The biggest companies sell high-value things with tiny incremental cost.
title: What I look for to invest in companies [no bs]

text: Information and education businesses have near-100% gross margins like software without development costs, but tend to suffer higher churn because value declines once the skill is learned.
title: What I look for to invest in companies [no bs]

text: To improve retention in education businesses, separate one-time consumables (the skill) from ongoing consumables such as community and accountability, and note that skills often create new problems needing new solutions.
title: What I look for to invest in companies [no bs]

text: He views problems as blank checks with a dollar amount attached; business owners choose whether to cash them by solving them.
title: What I look for to invest in companies [no bs]

text: He thinks TAM is a weak indicator of company size because founders expand vision over time, and a company dies or sells when its founder runs out of vision.
title: What I look for to invest in companies [no bs]

text: He advises against switching avatars early; one avatar can likely reach around 100 million a year. Over a long horizon, adjacent markets and acquisitions can expand TAM, so he weighs TAM mainly over 3 to 5 years.
title: What I look for to invest in companies [no bs]

text: He says money invested early compounds at roughly three to four times the rate it does later, so extra dollars saved young can outgrow later earning gains. His example: one dollar at 25 might become $90 by 70, a third of that at 35, a ninth at 45.
title: My honest advice to someone who wants to get rich.

text: His compounding argument is not that everyone should put all their money into the S&P 500. It is that dollars invested in any form early in a career get disproportionate returns.
title: My honest advice to someone who wants to get rich.

text: Skills learned young also compound disproportionately, because getting good takes a certain number of repetitions. He cites Bill Gates, who coded early and so built software first and kept a lasting advantage.
title: My honest advice to someone who wants to get rich.

text: The same accomplishment earns more reputation when achieved young. He says a person with $700,000 saved by 19 impresses far more than a 65-year-old with the same, so a smaller win can be leveraged more when young.
title: My honest advice to someone who wants to get rich.

text: He says you are considered young only until about 30. After that, the reputational boost fades. Youth multiplies every win, whether press, network, mentors or access to capital.
title: My honest advice to someone who wants to get rich.

text: He wrote a $500,000 check to an 18-year-old who had built a $30 million a year e-commerce business. The founder's age and that achievement convinced him the person was sharp.
title: My honest advice to someone who wants to get rich.

text: Early success can be laddered into bigger later success as stepping stones. His path: getting fit, then personal and online training clients, a gym, multiple gyms, Gym Launch, and its sale funded acquisition.com and the family office.
title: My honest advice to someone who wants to get rich.

text: Young people have more energy, and getting repetitions takes energy. Now nearly 40, he notes he has less energy than some 18-year-olds, which he sees as a clear advantage to use.
title: My honest advice to someone who wants to get rich.

text: Younger people usually have fewer obligations such as kids, spouses or location ties. That lets them live cheaply, reinvest excess cash aggressively in skills or investments, and move to where learning happens faster.
title: My honest advice to someone who wants to get rich.

text: Go where the reps are: DC for politics, New York for finance, LA for media. Skills and network are what you fish for early, before strings tie you down.
title: My honest advice to someone who wants to get rich.

text: Quoting James Clear, he says winners and losers share the same goals. The difference is the actions taken, the risk tolerated, and the pain endured for long periods with an uncertain payoff.
title: My honest advice to someone who wants to get rich.

text: Waiting for certainty means never moving, since the world never provides it. He says you eventually realize failing will not kill you, you will just learn and improve.
title: My honest advice to someone who wants to get rich.

text: You never finish or fully win, because by the time you reach a goal you have planted a bigger one. Goals get within shooting distance as you progress, as with his bench press of 315.
title: My honest advice to someone who wants to get rich.

text: When someone misses a request, first ask whether they knew you wanted it done. Unfollowed verbal asks may be taken as casual chat, so write requests down to give both sides proof.
title: How to Get Anyone to Do Anything You Want

text: Define what you ask in terms of behavior or outcomes, including format. Spending a couple of extra minutes on clarity can save the other person hours; he calls clarity high-leverage work.
title: How to Get Anyone to Do Anything You Want

text: Labels like harassing or creepy mean different things to different people. Until you break them into concrete behaviors, people cannot know what to change; they often do not know what good looks like because nobody taught them.
title: How to Get Anyone to Do Anything You Want

text: He holds that everything is trainable; some things take longer because the broad concept, like being kind, sits on hundreds of behaviors, while aptitude has far fewer.
title: How to Get Anyone to Do Anything You Want

text: When someone cannot do a task, find which sub-step they lack. Then the person is not an idiot; they may know most steps and only need one shown.
title: How to Get Anyone to Do Anything You Want

text: The more skilled and expert the person, the vaguer your instructions can be; the less skilled, the more specific they must be, chunked down further.
title: How to Get Anyone to Do Anything You Want

text: To transfer skill: write the steps down, do them in front of the person, then have them do the steps in front of you. He covers this in his leads book around pages 207-208.
title: How to Get Anyone to Do Anything You Want

text: For deadlines, ask when they can deliver, how long the actual work takes, and what else they have on. This shows their workload and lets you reprioritize if something else matters more.
title: How to Get Anyone to Do Anything You Want

text: He wants end of day as the default deadline. He argues an organization defaulting to end of day moves far faster than one defaulting to end of week or month.
title: How to Get Anyone to Do Anything You Want

text: Leadership means spreading culture and holding the line against regression to the mean. He asked a leader to think of the role as driver: pushing things forward and asking what can be removed from their plate.
title: How to Get Anyone to Do Anything You Want

text: Circumstances are asked last because people blame them first to protect their ego. Probing how hard the obstacle was to solve reveals their agency and problem-solving ability.
title: How to Get Anyone to Do Anything You Want

text: Asking someone directly whether they were unmotivated will never get a yes. The first four questions give many chances for the issue not to be an attack on the person.
title: How to Get Anyone to Do Anything You Want

text: Everything is trainable but not everything is worth training; some skills you expect people to arrive with, which is why jobs have prerequisites.
title: How to Get Anyone to Do Anything You Want

text: He defines motivation, persuasion and sales as temporarily changing the relative value of an outcome so behavior changes. His mother lost weight only when a doctor tied it to seeing her grandchildren.
title: How to Get Anyone to Do Anything You Want

text: Reframing a struggle, like boredom in sales, as a skill deficiency on the way to what the person wants can be highly motivating. If motivation is truly absent, they may not belong on your team.
title: How to Get Anyone to Do Anything You Want

text: Turn statements like no one can sell like me into how questions such as how to find someone who can; the statement is unsolvable, the question is solvable.
title: How to Get Anyone to Do Anything You Want

text: Be wary of beliefs you treat as facts; they are rules that exist in your mind. He challenges limits like we cannot charge more or pay more because industry standards say so.
title: How to Get Anyone to Do Anything You Want

text: Most business owners copy peers and end up in commoditized services; if everyone does something, that is a reason not to. He cites Henry Ford paying above competitors to get top talent.
title: How to Get Anyone to Do Anything You Want

text: Frame underperformance conversations by comparing output to what you believe they are capable of, separating performance from the person, then ask whether the gap is know, how, what, when, blocked, or motivation.
title: How to Get Anyone to Do Anything You Want

text: Framing feedback as a shared problem, with both on the same side of the table, avoids defensiveness that comes from telling someone they are subpar.
title: How to Get Anyone to Do Anything You Want

text: Customers form first impressions in the 24-48 hours after purchase. Getting that window right raises upsell uptake and retention, and adding onboarding to a recurring service can add two to three months to lifetime value.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: Reinforcing the decision after purchase means restating the customer's goal, why they want it and their problem. Tying next steps to their stated personal goal sharply raised follow-through, he says doubled or tripled.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: Onboarding should give a quick win, such as getting login working and a tour, and connect people to support live during the call so they finish set up and understanding the basics.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: Delivering an excellent, on-time experience before asking for money raises perceived likelihood of achievement, so the next offer feels credible. Providing value today makes people expect value later.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: Two upsells work in almost any business: more of what they just bought, or more help with it.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: If you believe in your product, he says you have an ethical duty to present the offer. Buying happens in a short burst after a problem appears, then almost stops, so sell related items then.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: Purchases shift identity, such as runner or investor, and related products go with that identity. Offering them immediately is congruent with the promise; selling only one item suggests you did not believe in it.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: End onboarding with three things: send notes so they need not take any, links to tutorials matching their interests, and a live-introduced point of contact.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: BAMFAM means book a meeting from a meeting: pick the next time on calendars before hanging up. Sales, onboarding and account reps should each pass the baton so the customer always knows who is next.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: Too techy, not enough support and slow results map to value equation drivers: effort, perceived likelihood and time delay. Fix by setting better expectations up front or adding to the back end.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: Rescripting sales to set more realistic expectations did not change close rates. He says lowering expectations can raise perceived likelihood because people believe you.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: To lift perceived support, make existing support easier to reach, such as in-software chat bubble plus an assigned account rep for the account and general support for daily questions.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: Chat support data showing which pages trigger requests reveals where users get stuck and guides product roadmap; he cites one point producing 82% of complaints.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: Run emails, ads and scripts through a reading-level grader and lower the grade level. He claims this improves conversion, experience, expectations and refunds.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: Do not make salespeople handle last week's unhappy customers. It destroys their conviction, which shapes how they speak and is among the strongest predictors of close rate.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: Customer success conversations should be scripted like sales ones, since about 90% of customers present the same few issues. Unscripted calls beginning with what can I help with are a poor approach.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: Create a dedicated escalations team acting as triage, so sales morale and close rate hold up, and give it commission so lost customers carry real cost.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: A lost customer costs more than the refund: unhappy people discourage others, so you may lose several would-be customers, and they will not buy your next thing.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: CAC should rise only roughly with CPM increases per year; if it doubles or triples quickly, he suggests bad word of mouth may be a cause. LTV can be raised to offset.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: They paid a 10-15% commission for saving customers, reasoning that paying $200 to keep a $2,000 sale beats getting nothing.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: Script and practice responses to common escalation problems. With commission, the CS team began texting, emailing and calling three to five times.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: Lead outreach tapers over time, but customer outreach in an issue should escalate: one attempt across channels the first day, two the next, three after.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: Results across the company: 61% fewer cancellations, 25% of escalation calls chose a higher service level, and 2.4x overall ascensions.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: Expect worse initial stats when introducing change, but treat them as opportunity, since problems and solutions are known and only need execution.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: Not tracking lets you ignore problems; many unhappy customers never request refunds. Tracking satisfaction, NPS and similar metrics can itself act as an intervention.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: No company is too big for good customer service; he cites Chick-fil-A and Amazon as examples.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: Talk to unhappy customers, as that is where the insight lies. If one in four buys something four times pricier, the escalation recovers the losses from the other three.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: Follow-up frequency should match avatar: low-ticket buyers tolerate frequent contact, while wealthier buyers often want it to just work and be left alone.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: Retention matters as much as acquisition: two firms both reach 300 customers, but the one keeping customers needs far less selling. As an investor, he watches how many last year's customers still pay.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: Test costly interventions on a small slice first, define in advance what results make it worthwhile, then roll out. Hiring a CS rep for ~$70-100K who saves far more yields strong return.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: Reach out to customers as fast as with leads. At another company, proactively downgrading customers using only some services led to them never cancelling, and that group had the second-highest LTV.
title: Watch this to keep more customers

text: After reaching a nine-figure net worth and pulling out of his businesses, he felt depressed because he had nothing to need and kept hunting for another goalpost, hoping a second championship would make the first more valuable.
title: The Truth About Retiring At Age 31

text: He argues humans wither without adequate challenge and are shaped by opposition; having removed his challenges, he felt stagnant, and he now wants meaningful work with real stakes.
title: The Truth About Retiring At Age 31

text: He believes the goal cannot be to stop working, because anyone wanting to keep growing must work; he sums up his mantra as hard work, and paraphrases a proverb that work shapes you more than you shape it.
title: The Truth About Retiring At Age 31

text: He says his best entrepreneurial memories were the struggling, high-stakes periods where he had to perform anyway, because of what it revealed about himself, not outside circumstances.
title: The Truth About Retiring At Age 31

text: Values are not real until tested: you cannot claim loyalty or honesty without an easy chance to cheat or steal unpunished and choosing not to. Likewise growth needs a challenge matching your current ability.
title: The Truth About Retiring At Age 31

text: Saying hard work will make other things follow is still outcome-seeking. He found that dropping the outcome and making the work itself the goal was liberating and made him more present.
title: The Truth About Retiring At Age 31

text: He applies the mantra in small moments: reporting gym reps honestly, improving a book paragraph even when tired, and giving his wife emotional energy. He now seeks chances to work hard.
title: The Truth About Retiring At Age 31

text: Making work the goal lets the process become meditative and bring flow, one of the best human feelings. He accepts he will sometimes fall short but commits to trying in the present moment.
title: The Truth About Retiring At Age 31

text: Your capacity to work hard and well is improvable: working hard and well increases how much work you become capable of.
title: The Truth About Retiring At Age 31

text: He describes seasons of motivation: first outcomes to impress others, then outcomes to impress himself, and now hard work itself as the goal.
title: The Truth About Retiring At Age 31

text: Having reached what most call the mountaintop, he says there is nothing there; achievements feel no more meaningful, and moving the goalpost does not make the earlier one more meaningful.
title: The Truth About Retiring At Age 31

text: He says he feels the same at a nine-figure net worth as at 10 million, 1 million or 100,000 dollars, and would rather look back on a life of working to his true capacity.
title: The Truth About Retiring At Age 31

text: Most people work just enough to avoid negative status consequences, so they cannot claim to know how to work hard. If only consequences motivate you, you do not truly hold the value.
title: The Truth About Retiring At Age 31

text: Each day offers a test: he can ship work others call good while knowing it could be better, then try to raise the bar the next day.
title: The Truth About Retiring At Age 31

text: Hormozi says a poor or sketchy environment should not make you feel unable to sell. In his view the problem is usually the pitch, not the circumstances, and you can sell wherever you are.
title: Sell Anywhere (SELL TO ANY CUSTOMER in 2018)

text: Hormozi is opening a gym in a run-down, sketchy-looking residential area, and he says people still come up to see it despite the rough appearance.
title: Sell Anywhere (SELL TO ANY CUSTOMER in 2018)

text: Quoting a yearly contract total as monthly revenue is misleading: 100 people at 2,500 a month sold as 30,000 contracts is about 250,000 collected, not 3 million a month. Ask how much cash was collected and how reliable the contracts are.
title: How gurus lie about how much MONEY they make...I'm calling it out..

text: Contract-based figures can be legitimate when contracts are secured against assets or the company has net negative churn, where clients spend more over time, as with Salesforce or HubSpot. Most people citing them are not in that situation.
title: How gurus lie about how much MONEY they make...I'm calling it out..

text: Lifetime revenue is hugely inflated as a yardstick: a McDonald's employee collects about a million dollars of income over a career. It flatters ego and impresses people who do not know the terms.
title: How gurus lie about how much MONEY they make...I'm calling it out..

text: When someone cites a 50 or 100 million business, ask whether they mean yearly revenue, profit, or total since starting. Many newer entrepreneurs also mix up revenue with cash; he uses revenue to mean cash collected.
title: How gurus lie about how much MONEY they make...I'm calling it out..

text: Valuation depends on who assigns it. He says small businesses under 5 million a year typically sell at two to three times EBITDA, mid-market at six to eight, and above 100 million sometimes 12 to 15. Top-line multiples are very rare.
title: How gurus lie about how much MONEY they make...I'm calling it out..

text: Huge EBITDA multiples like 100x or 500x usually mean the business made almost no profit, and people quote them because they sound impressive.
title: How gurus lie about how much MONEY they make...I'm calling it out..

text: Businesses sell every day at one to three times EBITDA; outliers get the press. When entrepreneurs boast, he asks about bottom line per year.
title: How gurus lie about how much MONEY they make...I'm calling it out..

text: Net free cash flow, what owners can extract after reinvesting to keep the competitive edge, matters because Munger and Buffett dislike businesses needing lots of extra capital. He asks owners what they take home.
title: How gurus lie about how much MONEY they make...I'm calling it out..

text: Most businesses fail and, he says, nearly all never actually sell, so entrepreneurs should de-risk by extracting cash flow from the business.
title: How gurus lie about how much MONEY they make...I'm calling it out..

text: Ten years at a million total revenue means about 100,000 a year; at 50 percent margin that is a 50,000 owner income, near US median. He would hesitate to treat such a person as an authority.
title: How gurus lie about how much MONEY they make...I'm calling it out..

text: Net worth has two parts: after-tax wealth extracted and reinvested, and the value of the businesses owned. A business needing the owner's face gets a lower multiple than one that does not.
title: How gurus lie about how much MONEY they make...I'm calling it out..

text: His ratings: contract value is a no, lifetime revenue is a no, valuation is acceptable only if the multiple and its basis are defended, and yearly revenue is only a partial answer.
title: How gurus lie about how much MONEY they make...I'm calling it out..

text: Revenue must be read alongside profit: a software company with 20 million revenue and 500,000 profit sold for 168 million because buyers saw the reinvestment. Low profit on small revenue is far less valuable.
title: How gurus lie about how much MONEY they make...I'm calling it out..

text: Net free cash flow gets a yes from him; multiplying it gets close to what a buyer might pay, barring monopoly-style situations.
title: How gurus lie about how much MONEY they make...I'm calling it out..

text: Net worth also gets a yes, as it is what is left after everything. He has had 21 businesses, and only two firms from the Fortune 500 of 50 years ago remain.
title: How gurus lie about how much MONEY they make...I'm calling it out..

text: He believes profitable owners should purposely take some profit out every month rather than bet everything on themselves, even if this is unpopular in Silicon Valley.
title: How gurus lie about how much MONEY they make...I'm calling it out..

text: Entrepreneurship is hard because it forces your identity and worldview to change as you grow. The jump from little control to complete control is what usually stifles growth, since there is only one of you.
title: How to buyback your time as a business owner

text: The buyback principle means continually buying back your time as the company grows. Owners typically start with lower-skilled support tasks, then higher-level admin like billing, collections and contracts, then selling.
title: How to buyback your time as a business owner

text: Every level of entrepreneurship is uncomfortable because the thing you are holding onto is the thing you must give up next, partly because owners identify with being that thing.
title: How to buyback your time as a business owner

text: If you have work worth a hundred dollars an hour, you should not be doing work the market pays fifteen an hour for, such as training classes, even if you feel no one does it like you.
title: How to buyback your time as a business owner

text: Hormozi used to insist on watching the money himself until he found someone better at tracking it than him. He gave up control of it while still looking at it.
title: How to buyback your time as a business owner

text: Up to about a million dollars a year you can sell yourself with helpers around you. Past a million it usually becomes difficult, and you must scale sales and give up that control.
title: How to buyback your time as a business owner

text: After sales control comes managing a sales team: recruiting, hiring, training and compensating. Around three to ten million he places this stage. Going from ten toward thirty million, the control given up is leadership, leading leaders who lead others.
title: How to buyback your time as a business owner

text: If your business model only works with sales at your personal level, the model is broken. Others should close half as many as you and it should still work, though over time you want them to sell better than you.
title: How to buyback your time as a business owner

text: When you relinquish control you still keep full accountability and responsibility for results.
title: How to buyback your time as a business owner

text: His rule of thumb is to know where the bodies are buried: if you cannot name the flaws in a department, you are too far away. This signals a need for more transparency, not that you gave up too much control.
title: How to buyback your time as a business owner

text: If you only hear good news from a department and nothing negative, you are too far away. He calls this his managerial leadership rule of thumb.
title: How to buyback your time as a business owner

text: You cannot build something great without trusting other people. Trust issues can be overcome by taking back power and responsibility for your outcomes rather than blaming others.
title: How to buyback your time as a business owner

text: The order of control he lists relinquishing is doing, admin, operations, sales, then a sales team, then leadership, and it continues beyond.
title: How to buyback your time as a business owner

text: Sales is a transference of conviction: one person believes, another does not, and trust completes the transfer. A rep with no belief in the product has no conviction to transfer.
title: $100M Salesman Reveals #1 Persuasion Hack

text: When a rep who started hot begins closing less, he says it is usually not a skill gap, so training will not fix it. They likely heard something negative from a prospect they sold.
title: $100M Salesman Reveals #1 Persuasion Hack

text: Hold a weekly meeting where customer success shares client wins with the sales team. Each side sees the other's work, sales learns what to avoid saying, and gains ammunition to feel more convinced.
title: $100M Salesman Reveals #1 Persuasion Hack

text: Build a pipeline for collecting testimonials and reviews, and ideally have clients join the sales team to tell their story.
title: $100M Salesman Reveals #1 Persuasion Hack

text: At his gyms, Saturdays with program graduation weigh-outs had near 100% closing on walk-ins. Sales consults then took about half as long, because the team's strong conviction overcame prospect doubts.
title: $100M Salesman Reveals #1 Persuasion Hack

text: Training and logical frameworks compensate for weak conviction. Prospects mostly buy on recommendations from people they believe, so a sales team that truly believes acts like a referral.
title: $100M Salesman Reveals #1 Persuasion Hack

text: Read customer testimonials to the sales team every morning. It sets the day's cadence and reminds them why they do the work.
title: $100M Salesman Reveals #1 Persuasion Hack

text: Sales directors, including founders of small businesses, must keep breathing conviction into reps. Prospects transfer doubt to them, so their conviction drains and must be refilled regularly.
title: $100M Salesman Reveals #1 Persuasion Hack

text: One of his key sayings in sales: people need to be reminded more than taught.
title: $100M Salesman Reveals #1 Persuasion Hack

text: What predicts closing ability is not whether you believe in the product but how deeply you believe. This is why founders often make the best promoters.
title: $100M Salesman Reveals #1 Persuasion Hack

text: Reps who genuinely believe the product will help the prospect fight for the sale far longer than reps focused on their commission check.
title: $100M Salesman Reveals #1 Persuasion Hack

text: He argues that actively selling your own sales team with proof yields outsized returns in effectiveness, beyond drilling scripts, though drills are still necessary.
title: $100M Salesman Reveals #1 Persuasion Hack

text: Prospects must believe in your conviction more than their own doubts. Skills only communicate clearly and build trust so conviction can cross that bridge, but conviction must exist first.
title: $100M Salesman Reveals #1 Persuasion Hack

text: He calls missing conviction the number one thing absent from sales trainings, and one of the easiest to implement.
title: $100M Salesman Reveals #1 Persuasion Hack

text: Hormozi points out that the weekend is a very recent invention, under 100 years old, first passed by a union in England in 1929, because people disliked what they did for a living.
title: Why selfcare makes you poor & fragile [trigger warning]

text: If you want relief, he says to stop hating your daily work and stop spending time with people who drag you down, rather than schedule self-care to escape a life you dislike.
title: Why selfcare makes you poor & fragile [trigger warning]

text: He says there are no rules for how you live. Before accepting someone's advice on what you should be doing, ask whether those are rules you actually want applied to your life.
title: Why selfcare makes you poor & fragile [trigger warning]

text: He says that if you like what you do, you can work a full year straight, and people who criticize this are projecting their own dislike of their lives because they cannot imagine liking daily work.
title: Why selfcare makes you poor & fragile [trigger warning]

text: He grants that sleep and rest are necessary, but distinguishes that from feeling you need a full escape such as a spa day. If that is how you relax, fine, but insisting others must relax a certain way makes no sense.
title: Why selfcare makes you poor & fragile [trigger warning]

text: He argues that since everyone dies and is forgotten within about ten generations, you should do what you want. He sees growth as identifying limits that only exist in your mind.
title: Why selfcare makes you poor & fragile [trigger warning]

text: He calls the self-care movement soft and says that people have dealt with much harder things than a boss's deadline. Recall your hardest life experiences to see you will survive, and self-care is fine only if you do not project it on others.
title: Why selfcare makes you poor & fragile [trigger warning]

text: Hormozi's early rapid success, millions in profit within months and nearly twenty million in his second year, became a poisonous benchmark. He judged any business below that as failing.
title: Don't Start a Business Until You Watch This...

text: He notices that investors and bigger-business owners look at things over long time horizons, while entrepreneurs get caught in weekly and monthly goals and neglect long-term investments that are important but not urgent.
title: Don't Start a Business Until You Watch This...

text: He tries to favor actions he can repeat consistently that, over a long enough horizon, will inevitably reach his goal, rather than fast results. This changes how he views tasks, projects and initiatives.
title: Don't Start a Business Until You Watch This...

text: He uses a five-year horizon because he can believe in it, though a mentor urged a hundred-year one. Extending the horizon turns time from a threat into an asset, with compounding working for him.
title: Don't Start a Business Until You Watch This...

text: He changed his view on inbound marketing over the previous year. Building an asset that steadily produces more inbound interest each month appeals to him, so he wants a third reliable channel alongside outbound and paid ads.
title: Don't Start a Business Until You Watch This...

text: Comparing yourself to someone who started at the same time matters less when you compare against twenty years out. He now asks whether their company will still exist and aims to build something enduring.
title: Don't Start a Business Until You Watch This...

text: Choose projects that may not pay off this quarter or year but would inevitably pay off disproportionately in five years. He believes consistency is most people's constraint, and consistent people can exploit this.
title: Don't Start a Business Until You Watch This...

text: He told his Gym Launch general manager not to measure ROI on an inbound initiative until the next year. He found it freeing and thinks it improves execution because the team does not declare failure after a week.
title: Don't Start a Business Until You Watch This...

text: Instead of tracking weekly or monthly sales growth, ask which non-revenue metric, if tripled, would make it unreasonable for the company not to triple too. For him it is the number of qualified applications.
title: Don't Start a Business Until You Watch This...

text: He had leading indicators for churn, like customer activation, but never one for growth. He now uses sales accepted leads: leads who showed up, are qualified, and are the type he can serve.
title: Don't Start a Business Until You Watch This...

text: A goal of raising inbound applications by five percent monthly is more consistent and controllable than a sales growth goal, since many other variables affect sales in the short term.
title: Don't Start a Business Until You Watch This...

text: Day-to-day activity around the leading metric is like the stock market, up and down. Viewed over years, the true value shows, so he treats qualified inquiries as his primary predictive metric.
title: Don't Start a Business Until You Watch This...

text: He now values smaller reliable inflows, like an initiative he expects to add about twenty clients monthly, even if it will not double lead generation. He wants to start the snowball.
title: Don't Start a Business Until You Watch This...

text: Thinking like a shareholder, board member or adviser rather than CEO greatly lowered his stress. Monthly ups and downs no longer affect him, and his ego is less impacted by business fluctuations.
title: Don't Start a Business Until You Watch This...

text: His profit was cut roughly in half in 2020, about 13.4 million the prior year versus around 6 million. He sees it as a temporary pandemic disruption and expects to recover and grow within three years.
title: Don't Start a Business Until You Watch This...

text: Hitching yourself to something inevitable like the passage of time aligns you with forces that grow you without your permission.
title: Don't Start a Business Until You Watch This...

text: He believes the ultimate version of niche B2B agencies and info businesses is rolling up the customers they serve, since they already do the integration work and stop short of monetizing it.
title: 7 Millionaires Asked Me How to Get Rich(er)

text: Do-it-yourself fits an avatar whose current income is low, since learning marketing pays off more for someone earning $35,000 than for someone earning a million who can hire it out.
title: 7 Millionaires Asked Me How to Get Rich(er)

text: Reoccurring revenue differs from recurring: customers buying repeatedly without a membership is still reliable. Tracking that, for example half of customers buying again each year, makes a business valuable.
title: 7 Millionaires Asked Me How to Get Rich(er)

text: When people complain of heavy competition, he sees it as a sign of many buyers in the market, provided you are number one.
title: 7 Millionaires Asked Me How to Get Rich(er)

text: Whatever business he is in, an ultimate version already exists, so he studies it and aims to do it better. Its owners are often corporate people who no longer know how the business works.
title: 7 Millionaires Asked Me How to Get Rich(er)

text: He distrusts what customers say when leaving, such as already got the value; he thinks it is often just a wish to leave.
title: 7 Millionaires Asked Me How to Get Rich(er)

text: Frequent communication works if it is pushed to the client and asks nothing of them; updates on work done make clients feel you work for them constantly.
title: 7 Millionaires Asked Me How to Get Rich(er)

text: Clients judge quality by their experience of communication and expectations, and cannot see internal work, so poor communication suggests sloppy work.
title: 7 Millionaires Asked Me How to Get Rich(er)

text: For a SaaS company, the business is the product: retention and word of mouth matter most. Marketing and sales up front serve to improve the product until growth is passive, then push hard.
title: 7 Millionaires Asked Me How to Get Rich(er)

text: Find the cohort whose retention curve flattens, study who they are, then adjust messaging and marketing to attract more of them. That loop is what he would focus on.
title: 7 Millionaires Asked Me How to Get Rich(er)

text: To reverse-engineer top customers he looks at four lenses: psychographics, demographics, geographics and activities.
title: 7 Millionaires Asked Me How to Get Rich(er)

text: Vista Equity story: a pricing head told him their secret is knowing acquired companies' customers better; they cut marketing to other customers and push the best ones. He says people stay poor by refusing to say no.
title: 7 Millionaires Asked Me How to Get Rich(er)

text: As a framework, look at the biggest version of the business, how it got there, its model, how many steps away you are; skill gaps become the opportunity.
title: 7 Millionaires Asked Me How to Get Rich(er)

text: Every element of a sales script should be a question, never a paragraph or statement, because reps who get statements will read them aloud. Questions let reps pause and ask the next one without needing special intelligence, so it scales.
title: How I Built A 20+ Sales Team [The Process]

text: Start the call by clarifying why the person is there: what made them get on, their goal, why it matters, and what the ideal outcome looks like 12 months out. Then restate the problem back and confirm it.
title: How I Built A 20+ Sales Team [The Process]

text: Overview the prospect's past pain by asking what they tried before and why it failed, repeating until they run out, then recap the pain. They are on the call because earlier attempts did not work.
title: How I Built A 20+ Sales Team [The Process]

text: Reps need to know only three short stories, about 30 seconds each, that illustrate the elements the customer is usually missing (for weight loss: fitness, nutrition, accountability). Each story explains why that element matters.
title: How I Built A 20+ Sales Team [The Process]

text: Normal buyers have concerns, so objection responses must be drilled with flash cards. He says all objections fall into three types: price, stall, and decision maker.
title: How I Built A 20+ Sales Team [The Process]

text: A price objection is a gap in perceived value. A decision-maker objection is handled by leaning on what the partner already implicitly knows and agreed to, such as that the problem exists and a solution is wanted.
title: How I Built A 20+ Sales Team [The Process]

text: Closing means teaching someone to decide, since people fear mistakes. Walk them through yes/no questions on liking you, the product, likely results and access to the money, then ask for the card and address their main concern.
title: How I Built A 20+ Sales Team [The Process]

text: Reinforce the decision right after purchase because people back out. Examples: a 30-second personalized video from the founder, a handwritten card, or a t-shirt.
title: How I Built A 20+ Sales Team [The Process]

text: Record every sales call. It is a compliance matter, and reps follow the script more when they know they are recorded. Managers should review them. He strongly recommends Gong for teams selling over Zoom.
title: How I Built A 20+ Sales Team [The Process]

text: Communication cadence: quick daily huddles sharing testimonials so reps remember why they sell despite daily rejection, weekly one-on-ones, and monthly meetings.
title: How I Built A 20+ Sales Team [The Process]

text: In one-on-ones, have each rep tag their best, worst and average call. Check where they clarified the problem, explored pain, asked for the sale and overcame objections. Without pain and the ask, no sales happen.
title: How I Built A 20+ Sales Team [The Process]

text: Regularly cut the bottom 10% of the sales team, even when things are going okay. He claims this yields about a 30% productivity jump each time and calls it the top driver of sales teams.
title: How I Built A 20+ Sales Team [The Process]

text: Keep a published leaderboard updated daily, and notify the team when anyone makes a sale, using a bell in person or a thread of bell images remotely, to show momentum and activity.
title: How I Built A 20+ Sales Team [The Process]

text: Run sales competitions of about six weeks with trips as prizes, using teams of three so reps share practices and root for each other. Budget about 25% of one month's commission check per person.
title: How I Built A 20+ Sales Team [The Process]

text: Hormozi thinks most so-called productivity hacks are really procrastination hacks, suited to people who like making lists more than doing work. He prefers to spend his time working and keeps few routines.
title: Unconventional Productivity Habits That Made Me Successful

text: He plans the night before, because he struggles to fall asleep until he has thought through the next day. He limits himself to one to three things, with no fixed rule on the count, and starts them upon waking.
title: Unconventional Productivity Habits That Made Me Successful

text: He reduces repeated daily decisions, especially ones whose outcome is basically mood, such as food. He eats the same meals for breakfast, lunch and dinner, enjoys them, and feels no stress about it.
title: Unconventional Productivity Habits That Made Me Successful

text: He believes clearing out belongings and trinkets frees up attention, similar to how cleaning a garage feels good. He thinks the recovered bandwidth shows up as better quality decisions.
title: Unconventional Productivity Habits That Made Me Successful

text: He argues a bedtime matters more than a wake-up time. Set an alarm for going to bed and wake when you wake, rather than dragging yourself up exhausted. He says he decides better when well rested.
title: Unconventional Productivity Habits That Made Me Successful

text: Elaborate routines create superstition about how you work, making you reliant on them just to function. He believes short-term boosts often become crutches, and prefers being resilient enough to wake, have coffee and work.
title: Unconventional Productivity Habits That Made Me Successful

text: He thinks many people use productivity hacks and routines as a crutch to feel productive instead of getting work done. In his experience, the habits that stuck were the simple ones.
title: Unconventional Productivity Habits That Made Me Successful

text: Successful people keep wildly different sleep hours, such as a billionaire friend who works nights. Hormozi says to find the sleep schedule that gets your best work done and reserve time to think.
title: Unconventional Productivity Habits That Made Me Successful

text: He says that as entrepreneurs move up, results depend more on the decisions they make than on the actions they take.
title: Unconventional Productivity Habits That Made Me Successful

text: Hormozi names overkill, wanting to change everything when something feels uncomfortable, as one of his biggest weaknesses, second only to lack of focus.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Part 1)

text: If nobody in your industry has reached the size you want, there is probably a reason. Then either you are a true innovator, or the model is very hard to scale, and you may need to blow up your vehicle.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Part 1)

text: Owners stuck at a local peak must be willing to step back, lose status mostly in their own eyes, and ask how to best deploy their raw skills, assets and money.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Part 1)

text: His litmus test: if you have been stagnant and no version of your business has reached your goals, consider dramatically changing it.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Part 1)

text: If the business is doing well and trending up, do not use a cannon or chainsaw. Use sandpaper and a chisel for fine details rather than rebuilding from scratch.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Part 1)

text: Constant reinvention leaves team and customers in whiplash, because others only grasp the few words you communicated and lack the context behind your conclusions.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Part 1)

text: Alex Becker shut down a large information business and started High Ross, which became more valuable. Sam Evans shut down consulting.com, earning about 3 million a year, and School then took off.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Part 1)

text: Summary rule: if you are winning, change very little; if you are losing, consider changing a lot. Losing depends on your goals.
title: Alex Hormozi Answers Your Questions (Part 1)

text: He and his wife declined two offers of $50,000 for a single day of consulting, because the attention required would take more from their business than the money would give.
title: Why I Turned down two people who offered me $50K (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: He believes an entrepreneur can make any single business as big as they want, so splitting attention across several businesses to see which takes off is fundamentally flawed and ensures none work.
title: Why I Turned down two people who offered me $50K (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: He says many entrepreneurs fail because they cannot focus: they keep switching products, industries and customer avatars and launching new things rather than sticking with one.
title: Why I Turned down two people who offered me $50K (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: He says a $30 million a year business and a $100 million one are virtually the same: the larger one does more of the same, such as 15 sales a day instead of 5, for the same customer avatar and problem.
title: Why I Turned down two people who offered me $50K (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Side deals like JVs, 50/50 partnerships or extra services always come with strings attached, and the strings attach to your attention, which he calls your most valuable asset, more than time.
title: Why I Turned down two people who offered me $50K (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: A mentor who was COO of a $10 billion company taught him that sometimes you must go slow to go fast, getting good at one thing and doing more of it.
title: Why I Turned down two people who offered me $50K (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: He says the people who make the most money do the fewest things, meaning a small number of things done extremely well, not less work.
title: Why I Turned down two people who offered me $50K (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: For a gym owner, he advises saying no to meal prep, online training and small corporate deals, and instead delivering great results and getting customers to send more people, repeated continually.
title: Why I Turned down two people who offered me $50K (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: He says entrepreneurs often self-sabotage by piling more onto their plate. If you have several locations or businesses, focus on the one that makes money and repeat it until you are sick of it, then do more.
title: Why I Turned down two people who offered me $50K (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Hormozi says he found his strongest sales tactic by accident, not from a book. After adopting it he sold everyone, and newcomers he taught closed 80 to 90 percent of walk-ins in a physical-product retail setting.
title: My Best Sales Tactic (to Make a TON of Money)

text: Telling a customer they can buy an item cheaper elsewhere, or that they do not need it, made people buy everything else he recommended. He later called these items ghost products, formerly sacrificial lambs.
title: My Best Sales Tactic (to Make a TON of Money)

text: If the buyer does not yet know they need something, a concession via a ghost product can build trust faster. You may stock the item without selling it, but he found he always gave those away.
title: My Best Sales Tactic (to Make a TON of Money)

text: Send customers elsewhere for your lowest-margin products, giving those away to earn trust, and keep the high-margin products for yourself to sell.
title: My Best Sales Tactic (to Make a TON of Money)

text: Before asking for the sale, paint a picture of their life with the benefits and explain exactly how to take the product. Ask what they do every morning and attach usage to it, like placing it next to the toothbrush.
title: My Best Sales Tactic (to Make a TON of Money)

text: After walking through each product, close by asking to use the card on file, so they make no new purchase decision. He calls this a one-click upsell combining a prescriptive close with ghost products for trust.
title: My Best Sales Tactic (to Make a TON of Money)

text: Getting people to form or break habits is very hard, so tie product usage to habits they already have. This makes you a better salesperson and coach.
title: My Best Sales Tactic (to Make a TON of Money)

text: On a budget objection, offer to rank items by importance and remove the lowest one. Do not imply the removed item is unimportant; instead show what they would need to do to replace it.
title: My Best Sales Tactic (to Make a TON of Money)

text: If they decline an item, reintroduce the problem it solves. Also ask what old-identity spending they will cut, like going out or drinking, to show the money is already there.
title: My Best Sales Tactic (to Make a TON of Money)

text: Insert yourself into the sales process of a business with many low-ticket transactions, such as car washes, massage, nails or hair. The repetitions teach selling better than any course and made higher-ticket sales feel easy.
title: My Best Sales Tactic (to Make a TON of Money)

text: For a service business, name things you could do but are not core, and offer to connect the buyer to a cheaper outside provider. Owners can coach salespeople to seem to lean to the buyer's side.
title: My Best Sales Tactic (to Make a TON of Money)

text: He believes the education system is broken: people pay huge sums for schooling that adds little value, and government-backed debt is hard to escape.
title: This is my plan to become a BILLIONAIRE.

text: He thinks the guru boom of the last 10 to 15 years exists because demand for high-value skills is unchanged and still unsatisfied by formal schooling.
title: This is my plan to become a BILLIONAIRE.

text: He predicts education will fragment into niche skills, such as gym running, plumbing or online training, that people can exchange for money in the marketplace.
title: This is my plan to become a BILLIONAIRE.

text: He and his wife donate about a million dollars a year and plan to leave most of their wealth to charity. He says sharing skills scales further than money does.
title: This is my plan to become a BILLIONAIRE.

text: His goal is to help people reach 1, 3 or 5 million a year, and later, if they reach roughly 5 to 20 million, offer to invest to help them reach 50 or 100 million.
title: This is my plan to become a BILLIONAIRE.

text: The first of ten planned courses is $100 Million Offers, with a 99-cent book and free downloads of checklists and SOPs, plus videos on YouTube, all without opt-in.
title: This is my plan to become a BILLIONAIRE.

text: He says money only solves money problems; having solved his, he gives away skills and beliefs to find meaning.
title: This is my plan to become a BILLIONAIRE.

text: He releases a course only when it is better than what people already have, using repeated refinement and simplification so knowledge transfers quickly and is not boring.
title: This is my plan to become a BILLIONAIRE.

text: If you struggle to sell or get leads, the offer is usually the problem. Structuring it better makes far more people buy.
title: This is my plan to become a BILLIONAIRE.

text: His course order follows building a business: offers, lead generation, money models, sales scripting, scaling sales teams, then pricing and lifetime gross profit per customer.
title: This is my plan to become a BILLIONAIRE.

text: His companies grew without outside capital through client-financed acquisition: customer cash funds growth, acquisition cost is lower than what is collected, and he says more than that comes back within 30 days.
title: This is my plan to become a BILLIONAIRE.

text: Earning more per customer lets you spend more on acquisition, so the backend informs the front end.
title: This is my plan to become a BILLIONAIRE.

text: He says the product ultimately determines a company's success, and fortune builders make a sale to gain a customer rather than gaining customers to make sales.
title: This is my plan to become a BILLIONAIRE.

text: Customers feel they got a good deal from the gap between what they pay and what they receive, so a good deal depends on value, not price.
title: This is my plan to become a BILLIONAIRE.

text: An executive coach helped him design a life around reading, writing and teaching frameworks, which about a year and a half earlier started the idea for Acquisition.com.
title: This is my plan to become a BILLIONAIRE.

text: Hormozi lists four ways to pay for anything: past money (savings), income money (monthly earnings), debt money (future earnings), and new money, which he prefers.
title: How to Buy Anything You Want Without Going Broke

text: He told a business owner who wanted a much pricier, nicer office that he could take it if he could pay it off within a year, and the owner said he could.
title: How to Buy Anything You Want Without Going Broke

text: Hormozi bought a roughly 36,000 sq ft building he did not strictly need, and promised his partner it would earn more than it cost. He asks whether he can find something to pay for a purchase.
title: How to Buy Anything You Want Without Going Broke

text: Sawdust money is income generated from existing resources you underuse, aimed at funding one specific project, rather than drawing on savings, income or debt.
title: How to Buy Anything You Want Without Going Broke

text: The richest people he knows fund a wanted item by earning extra, such as working one more day per week for a year, instead of touching savings, income or debt.
title: How to Buy Anything You Want Without Going Broke

text: He takes on debt only if he will repay it within a year, with no prepayment penalty and a clear plan for earning the money in a defined period.
title: How to Buy Anything You Want Without Going Broke

text: Paul McCartney reportedly wanted a swimming pool without using savings, income or debt, so he wrote a song and paid for the pool with its earnings.
title: How to Buy Anything You Want Without Going Broke

text: Use the thing you want as motivation to find new resources, being resourceful with assets you already control rather than draining what you have.
title: How to Buy Anything You Want Without Going Broke

text: A single-mom gym member could not afford membership, so she drove Uber one day a week to pay for it. She stayed a long-standing member and lost 100 pounds.
title: How to Buy Anything You Want Without Going Broke

text: Everyone has a lifestyle-based minimum demand for money. Real wealth comes from raising what you earn while keeping that minimum low.
title: How to Buy Anything You Want Without Going Broke

text: He started advisory services partly to keep his promise that the building would generate income covering its cost, so he could enjoy his home gym.
title: How to Buy Anything You Want Without Going Broke

text: For those further along, he suggests not raising lifestyle with income but raising new money against each purchase. Those who are broke should only focus on new money.
title: How to Buy Anything You Want Without Going Broke

text: The extra work can be temporary, such as overtime for a year, six months or a month, just long enough to afford the item.
title: How to Buy Anything You Want Without Going Broke

text: Some wealthy people do not enjoy their money because they are afraid to spend it. He says the happiest people use money as a tool.
title: How to Buy Anything You Want Without Going Broke

text: For consumption purchases that are not good investments, use underused resources like your time, such as taking a new client project or one-on-one services for a defined period.
title: How to Buy Anything You Want Without Going Broke

text: He gets more excited about earning money earmarked for a specific thing than about his regular earnings, and enjoys the work more knowing where it goes.
title: How to Buy Anything You Want Without Going Broke

text: If a nicer business machine cannot be justified, earn the price difference yourself. He says he has never regretted doing this, since it avoids using money he would want elsewhere.
title: How to Buy Anything You Want Without Going Broke

text: A study he recalls (he is unsure if Fidelity or Schwab) found the best-performing stock accounts belonged to people who died or forgot their passwords, meaning no activity at all.
title: How I Lost $217,000 on A Day Trade & How I Trade Now

text: He reads that result as showing flaws in human judgment and the power of compounding. Doing the least across accounts resembles holding a market index, and those people ended up with the most money.
title: How I Lost $217,000 on A Day Trade & How I Trade Now

text: About 97 percent of his net worth sits in very stable assets. Only three to five percent is investable money he plays with to scratch an entrepreneurial itch.
title: How I Lost $217,000 on A Day Trade & How I Trade Now

text: He argues people should not try to beat the market by trading, noting that large quant firms with hundreds of analysts compete against them.
title: How I Lost $217,000 on A Day Trade & How I Trade Now

text: He guesses roughly 75 percent of people who try to beat the market lose money, for example by buying dips that fall another 50 percent.
title: How I Lost $217,000 on A Day Trade & How I Trade Now

text: Frequent trading turns gains into regular income taxed around 43 to 45 percent, instead of capital gains. Doubling 100 dollars to 200 leaves about 155 after tax versus about 180 when held.
title: How I Lost $217,000 on A Day Trade & How I Trade Now

text: To end with 180 dollars after regular income tax, trading would need to turn 100 into about 245, roughly 45 percent more gain than a holder needs to match it.
title: How I Lost $217,000 on A Day Trade & How I Trade Now

text: He sold a holding at a good time within a year, but the price returned to where he sold. Doing nothing would have left him with more money because of the regular income tax.
title: How I Lost $217,000 on A Day Trade & How I Trade Now

text: If you need the itch to trade, he suggests putting aside about three percent for pure speculation, treating it as a way to manage your own foolishness.
title: How I Lost $217,000 on A Day Trade & How I Trade Now
