text: Early on he once changed his business model dramatically because someone was soliciting his clients, and it only hurt his own business; most customers never knew it was happening.
title: How I CRUSH copycats, thieves and competition.

text: He reassures himself that copycats need him and not the reverse: their customers and model come from his, so they stay a subset of him and cannot outgrow him.
title: How I CRUSH copycats, thieves and competition.

text: He argues that people who copy are followers who operate from scarcity, hoard, and focus on you instead of their customers, signaling to the market that you are the focus.
title: How I CRUSH copycats, thieves and competition.

text: When a rival gets loud, get louder about your own solutions, purpose and mission, and never name or acknowledge them, since acknowledgment elevates them to your level.
title: How I CRUSH copycats, thieves and competition.

text: Use a competitor's noise as fuel to market and sell harder; his company saying is to beat them in the field and watch the scoreboard.
title: How I CRUSH copycats, thieves and competition.

text: Whoever gives customers the most wins. If a competitor worries you, put that nervous or angry energy into increasing the value you deliver to customers.
title: How I CRUSH copycats, thieves and competition.

text: Having something worth having means people will try to take it; he treats attempts to take yours as a sign of success and desirability.
title: How I CRUSH copycats, thieves and competition.

text: He suggests guiding responses to others by which values you want your life to show, and avoiding actions your 80- or 90-year-old self would be ashamed of.
title: How I CRUSH copycats, thieves and competition.

text: He reports being 22 for 22 against people who tried to take what is his, yet winning brings no victory lap; rivals simply fade away.
title: How I CRUSH copycats, thieves and competition.

text: Real hot battles are rare; most of it happens in your mind, and most rivals lack skills to compete and eventually leave, after which you forget them.
title: How I CRUSH copycats, thieves and competition.

text: He credits four habits with the most outsized returns: waking at 4 a.m., keeping consistent sleep and wake times including weekends, giving to his network without expectation, and taking absolute ownership. He also describes a fourth-style habit of jumping into unfamiliar skills.
title: The 4 Tiny Habits That Made Me The Most Money

text: Sleeping in and going to bed late on weekends while waking early on weekdays does not suit the body. He advises the same bedtime and wake time every day, weekends included.
title: The 4 Tiny Habits That Made Me The Most Money

text: He believes entrepreneurs tend to be more emotionally reactive and scattered by nature, so controlling space and attention matters, and waking at 4 a.m. lets him finish self-work and still have several dedicated hours for big projects.
title: The 4 Tiny Habits That Made Me The Most Money

text: His 4 a.m. to 9 a.m. block is protected time for big projects, because during the day his attention still gets pulled by calls and personnel issues once others are up.
title: The 4 Tiny Habits That Made Me The Most Money

text: Time spent working in the business is like an expense, while time spent on the business is an investment that moves the whole business forward and accelerates growth.
title: The 4 Tiny Habits That Made Me The Most Money

text: Waking at 4 a.m. is made possible by going to bed at the same time on weekdays and weekends; waking at 9 twice a week then much earlier the other days will not make you productive.
title: The 4 Tiny Habits That Made Me The Most Money

text: Highly successful entrepreneurs live a certain way, which involves sacrifice. He chooses it, for example scheduling dinners with friends around 5:45 so he is home by 7:30, and says others must accept their own trade-offs.
title: The 4 Tiny Habits That Made Me The Most Money

text: Genuinely giving to people in your network without expecting anything is a habit his wife observed in him. He links leadership to serving rather than being the big boss.
title: The 4 Tiny Habits That Made Me The Most Money

text: Some of his highest-return giving was going the extra mile on an intro request: connecting the person with several people, screening them first, and sharing his own experience.
title: The 4 Tiny Habits That Made Me The Most Money

text: Helping people with nothing expected back builds stronger relationships, and he has many favors to call on. He says that if you help people, you get more back and your reputation follows.
title: The 4 Tiny Habits That Made Me The Most Money

text: The habit tied to skill acquisition is diving into a skill you are bad at while expecting zero return on your first 20 hours.
title: The 4 Tiny Habits That Made Me The Most Money

text: Most people avoid starting new skills because they fear being bad at them. He says the first 20 hours yield about 70 percent of gains, with heavy diminishing returns after.
title: The 4 Tiny Habits That Made Me The Most Money

text: He claims that spending 20 hours watching videos on running Facebook ads would put you ahead of 99 percent of people who try marketing, since most people do little. Ego makes people stop learning.
title: The 4 Tiny Habits That Made Me The Most Money

text: Take absolute ownership of every situation. Blaming circumstances, past, upbringing, spouse or employees gives your power away to whoever you point at, so you should drive the victim mindset out of yourself.
title: The 4 Tiny Habits That Made Me The Most Money

text: Giving first came most naturally to him, which he thinks stems from insecurity and wanting to be liked. In new groups he asks what people struggle with and works to overdeliver, which later brought monetary value.
title: The 4 Tiny Habits That Made Me The Most Money

text: He argues everyone is self-made, but only millionaires and billionaires own that; the type of person who says it has habits and outlooks that achieve what they want.
title: The 4 Tiny Habits That Made Me The Most Money

text: He strongly recommends the first two habits, regular bedtime and wake time, as easy to do: he says they bring more energy, focus and leadership, and he gets more done because he is not exhausted.
title: The 4 Tiny Habits That Made Me The Most Money

text: His PhD friend says clients pay him to tell them things they already know, like going to bed on time. Tired people on stimulants often improve just by sleeping.
title: The 4 Tiny Habits That Made Me The Most Money

text: Eating consistently every day, regardless of what, starts making people healthier. He notes that being consistent is itself something many people cannot do.
title: The 4 Tiny Habits That Made Me The Most Money

text: Show rate is the share of booked appointments that attend. With 100 appointments and 70 attending, the show rate is 70 percent.
title: I Doubled A Business in 60 Days to Show It's Not Luck (Part 1)

text: Offer rate is the share of attendees who actually receive an offer, since not everyone is qualified. He treats it as an indicator of lead flow quality.
title: I Doubled A Business in 60 Days to Show It's Not Luck (Part 1)

text: Track close rate both off shows and off offers, plus team and individual stats. A rep can inflate close rate by offering only to sure buyers, and comparing offer rates exposes it.
title: I Doubled A Business in 60 Days to Show It's Not Luck (Part 1)

text: Good data lets you tell whether a problem is low quality leads or weak salespeople, so you can fix the right thing.
title: I Doubled A Business in 60 Days to Show It's Not Luck (Part 1)

text: Read close rate together with cash collected upfront: low close with high cash percentage suggests a hard line, while high close with low cash suggests reps taking tiny deposits just to get a yes.
title: I Doubled A Business in 60 Days to Show It's Not Luck (Part 1)

text: The biggest driver of show rate is total time slots available. Targeting and the offer also affect it, independent of nurture or salespeople.
title: I Doubled A Business in 60 Days to Show It's Not Luck (Part 1)

text: Instead of optimizing ads for cheapest leads or appointments, optimize toward cost per sale so ad delivery shifts toward the people who actually buy.
title: I Doubled A Business in 60 Days to Show It's Not Luck (Part 1)

text: Splitting setters between cold calling for appointments and nurturing existing appointments hurts, because they are two very different activities.
title: I Doubled A Business in 60 Days to Show It's Not Luck (Part 1)

text: Phone tips: dial twice because first calls often get screened, contact leads fast rather than after hours, and remind people on the day of their appointment.
title: I Doubled A Business in 60 Days to Show It's Not Luck (Part 1)

text: For a two-call close on a mid-priced consumer service, he thought about 40 percent close rate was right; ideal close rate varies hugely by price and sale type.
title: I Doubled A Business in 60 Days to Show It's Not Luck (Part 1)

text: Discovery should dig into why they want the result and what changes in their life, not just surface questions, since those intentions supply the ammunition for the close.
title: I Doubled A Business in 60 Days to Show It's Not Luck (Part 1)

text: Obstacles arise before price is discussed and objections after. Address obstacles up front or they blow up at the close; shallow discovery produces more of both.
title: I Doubled A Business in 60 Days to Show It's Not Luck (Part 1)

text: Making your best closer the sales manager is a common mistake because the skills differ; high team churn signaled it here.
title: I Doubled A Business in 60 Days to Show It's Not Luck (Part 1)

text: Raising setter minimums from two to three sets per day is a 50 percent increase; if the bar is set low, people shrink to it.
title: I Doubled A Business in 60 Days to Show It's Not Luck (Part 1)

text: When the same problem recurs for quarters under the same person, it may be a who issue rather than a what issue. He fixed the sales director role first, since other fixes would have fallen flat.
title: I Doubled A Business in 60 Days to Show It's Not Luck (Part 1)

text: To judge a candidate, ask what data they plan to collect and how they would fix issues; vague answers signal shallow thinking. A good sales director pairs developing people with tracked metrics.
title: I Doubled A Business in 60 Days to Show It's Not Luck (Part 1)

text: Cutting the lowest closers when there is spare capacity raises overall close rate. Reps with more calls sell more calmly, and low performers demotivate high performers.
title: I Doubled A Business in 60 Days to Show It's Not Luck (Part 1)

text: He promoted one good setter to lead nurture specialist as a bridge between setters and closers, with a checklist to maximize attendance, and raised setter expectations from two to four per day.
title: I Doubled A Business in 60 Days to Show It's Not Luck (Part 1)

text: Reminder tactics: a three-way intro between setter, closer and prospect by phone, and a personalized voice memo or video text from the closer the morning of the call.
title: I Doubled A Business in 60 Days to Show It's Not Luck (Part 1)

text: Surface objections early, like killing zombies while far away. Before the appointment, ask if anyone else must be part of the decision and reschedule to include them.
title: I Doubled A Business in 60 Days to Show It's Not Luck (Part 1)

text: Looping means handling an objection then asking again, repeatedly. He says sales made are directly proportional to how many times you ask, and the concern should be resolved each time.
title: I Doubled A Business in 60 Days to Show It's Not Luck (Part 1)

text: Results after 60 days: show rate 49 to 70 percent, close rate 27 to 41 percent, cash collected upfront 47 to 82 percent, monthly sales 56 to 93.
title: I Doubled A Business in 60 Days to Show It's Not Luck (Part 1)

text: He tells of an HR director who spent about ninety days studying pay, then raised underpaid staff without explanation. He reckons it wasted roughly $100,000 of payroll effort and cost him around $600,000 in profit.
title: Recruiting and Hiring Tips - How to Hire The Best Employees

text: He says making employees happy is not the job of an owner, manager or HR director. People are responsible for their own happiness; the job is to hire people with a positive inclination who fit the culture.
title: Recruiting and Hiring Tips - How to Hire The Best Employees

text: He says the customer of a manager or HR director is the company, not employees. The company has three stakeholders to balance: shareholders, customers who pay, and employees who run it.
title: Recruiting and Hiring Tips - How to Hire The Best Employees

text: He says growth and surviving unseen future storms require profit, which funds new product lines, legal defense and other needs. Spending on things with no value puts the company in a weaker position.
title: Recruiting and Hiring Tips - How to Hire The Best Employees

text: He once put operations first on mentors' advice and the company started making less money. He reversed it: marketing, sales and product come first, and operations supports and enables them.
title: Recruiting and Hiring Tips - How to Hire The Best Employees

text: A superstar salesperson who replaces two or three normal salespeople can justify above-market pay. Judge value by what that person returns to your specific company, not just by what the market pays.
title: Recruiting and Hiring Tips - How to Hire The Best Employees

text: He says to think like an owner about pay requests: ask what the company loses if the person leaves. A customer service person can earn more only if you can show the money they save.
title: Recruiting and Hiring Tips - How to Hire The Best Employees

text: He says people are paid by the value they provide, not equally; not everyone gets a trophy. He considers this the real world, and assessment should rest on contribution to the bottom line.
title: Recruiting and Hiring Tips - How to Hire The Best Employees

text: He says HR protects the company first by making the initial answer to a hiring request likely no. Ask to see hour-by-hour utilization before agreeing that a team is truly overworked.
title: Recruiting and Hiring Tips - How to Hire The Best Employees

text: He claims many people who say they are overworked are undisciplined and cannot focus, not truly overloaded. A law firm partner once told him he did not yet know what work is.
title: Recruiting and Hiring Tips - How to Hire The Best Employees

text: He says good HR is largely good recruitment, since company value rests on people, the who. Recruiting sits with HR, development with departments, and retention with department heads and compensation packages.
title: Recruiting and Hiring Tips - How to Hire The Best Employees

text: He says the only reasons to change compensation are that you cannot attract talent or cannot retain it. Without one of those problems, there is no reason to change pay.
title: Recruiting and Hiring Tips - How to Hire The Best Employees

text: He says Gym Launch has very low attrition despite firing often, because of a high-performance culture where low performers do not last. He repeats a remark that it is a dangerous place to work.
title: Recruiting and Hiring Tips - How to Hire The Best Employees

text: He says a strong winning-team culture makes newcomers either assimilate or get rejected. That lets you remove poor fits quickly while also helping retain the people who fit.
title: Recruiting and Hiring Tips - How to Hire The Best Employees

text: He thinks a star employee is often worth paying more to keep, since they may produce the output of three to five employees. He thinks pay based on value provided is the ultimate fairness.
title: Recruiting and Hiring Tips - How to Hire The Best Employees

text: He says if you are not attracting or retaining people poorly, your pay is fine and needs no change. Non-core roles that cannot show direct value will likely be paid less, and he says that is okay.
title: Recruiting and Hiring Tips - How to Hire The Best Employees

text: He warns that managers who focus on keeping staff happy with perks may waste money and not learn what creates value. Owners may sideline them. Aligning with the company helps you move up.
title: Recruiting and Hiring Tips - How to Hire The Best Employees

text: He has cut planning down to roughly the next 12 weeks, plus one or two year-end targets, because detailed long-range projections rest on too many unknown variables and went stale within a year.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: Pick the single biggest-domino priority and put all resources behind it; he says other items then tend to get faster. Failing to choose means the leader is not doing the job.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: A good strategist looks at all options given current resources and picks the one that resolves the most problems at once; he calls that leverage.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: Two things matter most: a supply and demand curve in your favor, then leverage to capitalize on it. He designed the acquisition.com logo to represent these.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: Supply-constrained businesses (cleaning, accounting, legal, high-end consulting) find customers easily but struggle to find staff; their real business becomes recruiting, training, managing and incentivizing people.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: In supply-constrained firms, work out what a hire yields in yearly gross profit and be willing to pay a large share, such as 20%, including to staff who refer great people.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: He thinks owners underpay for the talent that constrains them. A $1,000 referral bonus on a role worth $400,000 gross profit a year is dumb next to $25,000 or $50,000.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: He holds that good people are among the highest-leverage assets and are still undervalued; big companies fight talent wars because a top hire is worth more than their pay.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: He observes that entrepreneurs obsessed with work tend to do better, and that people who work most tend to make most; he says do whatever you want.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: He works about seven days a week, roughly 12-hour days with a few 16-18 hour days, around 90 hours weekly; he says he prefers this to a five-day week.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: He bought acq.com from Yahoo for $480,000 and stood up acq Ventures, a family office arm focused on SaaS and tech-enabled services, taking active, larger positions.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: He built a $100 million scaling roadmap across eight departments with ten stages each, letting owners see weakest areas to fix first.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: Slow growth is usually a lack of good people and of focus. The CEO must pick one objective that makes others less important and delete everything not aligned with it.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: When fixing a department, eliminate as much as possible first (meetings, processes), since it can be added back; he says most of it turns out to be waste.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: When told something is impossible, ask what it would take: which resources and trade-offs. He says this assumes success and works backwards, and applies to deals and sales.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: A company he evaluated gave away a rarely taken downsell worth about 5% of revenue for free, and lead flow tripled the next week.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: The largest portfolio company ran three to ten split tests continuously on key funnel points and won lifts of 20%, 50% and 28%, mostly by one person and a couple of developers.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: He suggests comparing three or four third-party tools with the same use case by their conversion rate on customer-facing user experience, noting it is a heavier lift.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: He observed that portfolio stars had spouses who actively supported long hours, while a spouse who pulls them away can hurt performance; he suggests talking to a candidate's spouse.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: SCALE loop: start, compound (do more), augment (do better), leverage (make consistent/automate), expand to the next channel or product, then repeat.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: Optimization sequence: question requirements, delete, optimize priorities by result per cost, pull up timelines, then automate.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: On taking over the media team, he cancelled recurring meetings and one-on-ones and replaced them with a daily huddle, to protect deep work.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: Move end-of-week deadlines to end-of-day; he says this can speed a team sevenfold and uses spare capacity now, as future priorities are unpredictable.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: If at full capacity but not making money, you are likely underpriced; raise price until people stop buying, accepting more no's for more profit.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: Five and 20 rule: after five customers accept, if net money is equal or higher, raise price 20% and repeat until net revenue drops.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: If overpaying an employee, first bring in a backup who can do the job at the new rate, then renegotiate, giving a delay of a couple months before new pay applies.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: If serving too many avatars (common below $3 million), find your top 20% of customers, craft a message and offer just for them, and price for the value they get.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: Overextension, like opening second and third locations early, is typically a who problem; either hire strong people at your own income's expense or prune and reconcentrate.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: CEO and owner are different. Test by leaving for a month, then require six months of holding or growing without your direct involvement.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: Running multiple businesses because you cannot pick prevents any from growing to size; he says the opportunity lies in the problems needing solving, so pick one.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: Track a metric only if a rise or fall would change your behavior; a business with no data (lead cost, close rate) cannot know its problem.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: Problems are finite while missed opportunities are infinite; he now asks whether something is a problem or a missed opportunity, and solves problems first.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: Keep a big money ideas list and write new ideas down instead of acting; later he often finds he no longer cares about them.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: He concludes that his sense of rush comes from whom he compares himself to, so it is arbitrary; change the comparison or ask whether it serves you.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: New Balance's CMO flipped spend from 70% bottom to 70% top of funnel; returns fell for 18 months, then rose strongly from month 19.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: He aims for at least three or four value-giving touches per ask, matching a 3:1 content-to-ad ratio studied on TV and radio.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: For B2B branding: help the audience reach goals, help people like them, and achieve or showcase aspirational outcomes; extreme results lower perceived purchase risk.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: He says to work with people who move toward you rather than spending time convincing people of your rules of the game.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: Hormozi believes a team that admires none of your traits is hard to influence without punishment. He prefers a team that respects some of your skills or behaviors, while still allowing healthy disagreement.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: His favorite businesses are built from someone else's waste or unused capacity, like Airbnb and Uber. Businesses also hold their own excess capacity, which he calls sawdust.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: Hormozi prefers initiatives that check several boxes at once. The workshops in unused office space at acquisition.com generate deal flow, cash flow, content and talent flow using costs already paid.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: He lists everything the company does regularly, such as calls and conferences, then looks for recombinations that add value at no extra cost. One example is turning SOPs and checklists into lead magnets.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: Hormozi bets that in-person and AI sit at opposite ends and doubling down on both is wise. He thinks IRL demand persists because in-person customers are more loyal, refer more and buy more often.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: He argues that hard-to-scale but valuable things, such as in-person experiences, are worth scaling. Each bit of scaling provides resources to keep scaling.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: On School, the more optimized a page is, the more likely changes lower results. Of 16 major split tests on the games page, only two won.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: He repeats a Paul Graham idea: almost any business problem in marketing, sales or product can be addressed by talking to customers more, no matter how big you are.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: Hormozi says overwhelm is the top reason people cancel. He advises improving by removing things rather than adding, and making outcomes faster and easier along the value equation.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: Giving customers every feature they request creates Frankenstein products. Keeping simplicity, speed and ease as primary goals takes hard product discipline.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: Draw your business as a loop where each step causes the next. Multiple self-reinforcing flywheels compound growth; find the friction points that stop the wheel spinning and smooth them.

text: Decide role by role whether it needs to be in person. Remote forces structured communication; in-person gave him better training, culture, visible deep work and faster feedback, but harder talent attraction.

text: To move people to an in-person office, he suggests signing bonuses for some roles and a 30-day hotel stay first. About 30% of his portfolio is in person.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: His sleep basics: pitch black room, very cold room (temperature-control mattress pad if partners differ), and foam earplugs, which lowered his resting heart rate by four beats per minute.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: A kneeling chair allowed him many sitting positions and removed his neck and shoulder pain. He also cut workouts to two weekend sessions during a heavy work season.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: He defines culture as the rules governing reinforcement: what is good, neutral or bad. He prefers three values, since people won't remember more, each with many behaviors beneath.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: Hormozi rejects a no man left behind approach: if someone can't keep up, they can't stay. He says great things require sacrifice, which only feels costly to someone not aligned with the goal.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: An insult attaches a negative label to a person; a criticism states the gap between desired and actual factually. Framing feedback as criticism removes emotional charge and lets you coach.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: Give criticism plus concrete steps, and tell people what to do instead of what not to do. Skipping the criticism is being nice rather than kind, because you seek approval instead of truth.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: He cites Reed Hastings: a company is a pro sports team, not a family. Hormozi says the kindest act is clear feedback and a chance to improve, or a better-fitting place.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: When taking over media and conversion, he removed all meetings, allowed ad hoc stand-ups to solve specific problems, since staff said meetings consumed their days.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: Use what-who-when: state the task, name one owner, and ask how many hours it will take rather than what day. Then prioritize with them and set deadlines.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: Recap every task at the end so earlier ones are repeated more, and ask people to repeat tasks back. He says roughly one in three get it wrong.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: He runs departments like sales teams: daily standup, pay tied to quality, and one strong person paid more over several mediocre ones. He thinks sales structures are already optimized by tight feedback loops.

text: Onboard like sales: listen to gametape, roleplay, start with half calendars that grow with KPIs. In huddles review good and bad work, letting the person self-correct first before the team adds praise.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: If a change will not suit some people, he thinks you owe high performers an environment of only high performers. Removal should come from the team's culture.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: When the only promotion path is managing more people, incentives go perverse: hoarding knowledge, hiring more, pleasing the promoter, and displaying busyness. Hormozi built tracks for top individual contributors.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: He says people have large discretionary effort beyond keeping their job that unlocks with aligned incentives. After changes, one team's output more than doubled, and he expects triple or quadruple.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: Pay for performance costs more math, but worth it if output multiplies. Existing staff keep salary with performance on top; new hires get performance pay. Raises should scale with output.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: He recommends letting low performers go when things are good, since bloat peaks then and it feels like discipline instead of loss. Pre-Covid efficiency helped morale.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: Pay-for-performance can be simple flat bonuses at a few tiers. Back-test the plan on the previous month to check it pays for itself.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: Huddle-style management suits teams doing the same function. Teams with different functions work better as a round table that solves shared problems.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: Problems come from six months earlier and solutions take time. Decide before implementing how long it should take to judge it, then stick to that while enduring the cost.
title: No BS Business Advice to Get Rich in 2026

text: To diagnose a decline, find when growth first stopped and what changed then. Often the cause is a bad person added; his ascension-rate drop traced to a new hire.

text: He argues you make better decisions and learn more by assuming you are less smart than everyone else, because you cannot learn while you are talking; he wasted early meetings bragging to people well ahead of him.

text: Extraordinary accomplishments come from ordinary actions sustained for extraordinary periods; the commitment, not the action, is extraordinary, and he says there is no hidden shortcut beyond doing the basics a lot.

text: If it is worth doing, do it well, but first ask what problem you are solving and whether it merits the time doing it well takes; this lens helps prioritize.

text: He earns far more than when younger because he does fewer, different things; he would spend a year on a book, and says great work takes five to ten times the effort of good work.

title: 14 Life Lessons I Wish I Knew Earlier

title: 14 Life Lessons I Wish I Knew Earlier

text: He defines humility not as thinking less of yourself but as raising your regard for others, citing Clayton Christensen.
title: 14 Life Lessons I Wish I Knew Earlier

title: 14 Life Lessons I Wish I Knew Earlier

text: He reframes people who wronged him as simply wanting to feel better, and says imagined judging voices consumed his attention and energy, leaving little to act.
title: 14 Life Lessons I Wish I Knew Earlier

text: Hormozi says a salesperson has three jobs: maximize opportunities, convert the highest share of them, and do it consistently over a long period.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: In every company he has owned or examined, the person working the most hours sells the most deals, so being available when prospects are available matters, including weekends.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: His software company scheduled 4,000+ appointments a day; data analysts found total available time slots was the strongest lever on throughput and predictor of sales across companies.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: Pull future appointments into open slots today, because same-day appointments show up more and are more interested. If an unconfirmed prospect is near, push them out and fill the slot with a responsive lead.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: A solar rep who outperformed others called each new booking immediately to qualify. If the prospect had time, he closed then; if not, he used the call to fill open slots that day.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: Salespeople should keep two checklists, one for on-call and one for off-call time, since output correlates with opportunities created between calls. Most companies lack an off-call procedure.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: Never end a call without knowing when you next speak. Resolve time obstacles on the spot with calendars open, and address concerns rather than letting the prospect drift.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: Top salespeople do more outreach and follow-up, treat rejection and no-shows as a numbers game, and keep a visible everyday kill list of high-value prospects.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: Ask for referrals with who do you know, which needs a name rather than yes or no, framed as a compliment about who else is as great as them.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: A brand-new rep topped the leaderboard by about 50% by asking every caller who else would want to come. Referrals close at roughly 80-90% even if only one in three or four give one.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: If one in three customers refers someone, acquisition cost falls by a third; he expects referral-driven businesses to win as advertising gets pricier.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: Spend five minutes researching the prospect before the call; feeling known builds liking and trust in the first minute instead of wasting early minutes.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: When new and without reputation, he won through prep: he built profiles of gym owners and arrived with specific solutions. He says small players win through preparation and big ones through reputation.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: The best salespeople listen about twice as much as they talk, per his AI call analysis. Answer questions with questions so the prospect, not you, gets picked apart.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: Ask what prospects did before and liked or disliked rather than critiquing it, and educate only after you know the answer. Do not ask for the sale unless you already know they will buy.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: Use commands like tell me about your day to break automatic responses, and highlight the features they said they liked in past options.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: Scripts bloat because reps add habits like a cough or extra question that coincided with a close. Keep scripts concise, since less time after the sale leaves more time to fill the calendar.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: Managers should run daily role plays focused on one part of the script, repeated until it is second nature; people cannot improve many things at once.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: An obstacle arises before price is mentioned and an objection after; handle obstacles up front because it is far easier before asking for money.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: Objections group into circumstances (time, money, fit), other people, and oneself. People usually start with outside blame, which is easiest to voice.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: When someone blames a spouse, he reframes that they want permission when they need support, then plays out the future; for time or money he uses resourcefulness, not resources.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: Confront hard obstacles before price, asking what are you afraid of and then letting them play it out. If unaddressed, it will come back after price.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: Best case, worst case play-out removes emotion from the decision; he says he has probably closed more sales this way than any other close.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: He defines sales as raising the likelihood the prospect buys; a perfect process would convert everyone, so it is a percentage conversion.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: Sustaining enthusiasm and performance is a skill; salespeople who swing on and off have a skill deficiency, and he says champions differ by sustaining performance.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: Citing Mike Ary: dogs need constant feeding, horses gallop only while whipped, tigers kill for sport. Top salespeople love the hunt.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: Treat unqualified leads as free practice with stakes; sloppy warm-up reps build bad habits. Jacob took the worst leads for reps and then outperformed others.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: Score leads by data, then route best leads to best closers and worst to newest. A timeshare rep got this from the CEO, made 5x income, and the rollout grew the business 5x.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: Big upside for top closers attracts more recruits, and new reps learn on the worst leads so the business loses least.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: The best salespeople never blame circumstances; give feedback privately to a manager, not on group calls, and take full control of outcomes.
title: Sales Was Hard Until I Understood These 9 Concepts

text: He believes information is the best investment because it is the only thing that buys time. People who move faster use the same time as everyone, but put attention where returns are disproportionate.
title: 9 Money Beliefs of the Ultra Wealthy

text: He says the key is having four to five hours daily of uninterrupted time for yourself, and moving big pieces forward every day. It need not be morning; he mentions billionaire friends who are night owls.
title: 9 Money Beliefs of the Ultra Wealthy

text: He believes you should spend all your money acquiring skills until you can no longer find ways to spend on skills, rather than putting it into investments like crypto.
title: 9 Money Beliefs of the Ultra Wealthy

text: Talent stacking means layering one skill on another, such as math, bookkeeping, accounting, tax strategy, then raising capital. Each new skill is worth disproportionately more than earlier ones, producing a hockey stick curve.
title: 9 Money Beliefs of the Ultra Wealthy

text: If your income has not risen for a long time, he says it is because you have avoided finding the next skill to stack. Entrepreneurs who cannot get good salespeople usually lack skill in recruiting, training and managing them.
title: 9 Money Beliefs of the Ultra Wealthy

text: He says everything is 100 percent your fault, and you are fully responsible for your income. If dissatisfied, you are not valuable enough, and the first step is admitting a deficit, since ego blocks improvement.
title: 9 Money Beliefs of the Ultra Wealthy

text: No single course makes you a million dollars; each teaches one skill. The goal is to gather many, and the key is discernment about which skill you are missing now. He says discernment is the one thing he cannot teach.
title: 9 Money Beliefs of the Ultra Wealthy

text: He thinks there is no point saving if your income is below roughly two to five hundred thousand dollars a year. He also thinks it is not worth skipping enjoyment for decades to become a millionaire.
title: 9 Money Beliefs of the Ultra Wealthy

text: In his opinion, consider investments like bitcoin, stocks or real estate only when so much money comes in that even after aggressively funding your next skill there is still excess.
title: 9 Money Beliefs of the Ultra Wealthy

text: Returns per hour shrink as you learn a skill, but absolute payoff from small gains at the top rises. The first 20 hours of sales teach the most, while the last increments separate first from third place.
title: 9 Money Beliefs of the Ultra Wealthy

text: He uses the bamboo parable: it grows underground for years then shoots up fast. Overnight successes are usually people who stacked around 20 skills, with the 21st completing the bridge.
title: 9 Money Beliefs of the Ultra Wealthy

text: Under 100,000 dollars a year, he says everything is about promotion, and he strongly recommends not outsourcing for as long as possible. He still thinks he is his company's best marketer and knows what ad costs should be.
title: 9 Money Beliefs of the Ultra Wealthy

text: Do not hire a salesperson because you are weak at sales; you will lack the confidence to correct them. Being good at the function yourself is needed to manage it.
title: 9 Money Beliefs of the Ultra Wealthy

text: His path to a 100 million dollar company: get so good at one thing that people come to you because of your reputation. If that has not happened, you are not good enough yet.
title: 9 Money Beliefs of the Ultra Wealthy

text: Once you are the most sought-after in your skill, keep raising prices as you fill capacity. You can then sell teaching of that skill as a high-margin business.
title: 9 Money Beliefs of the Ultra Wealthy

text: His 100 million plan has three phases: acquire a skill, monetize it, then reinvest profits into a business with enterprise value that does not need you, like software or a product, and grow it using your stack.
title: 9 Money Beliefs of the Ultra Wealthy

text: He thinks outside funding has disadvantages, because you may skip talent stacks and not know the missing link when you hit a plateau.
title: 9 Money Beliefs of the Ultra Wealthy

text: If you are on a plateau, he says you are not good enough, and accepting that lets you act. Actions must be high volume, such as more consultations per day for weaker sales.
title: 9 Money Beliefs of the Ultra Wealthy

title: 9 Money Beliefs of the Ultra Wealthy

text: For a videographer, he suggests making two commercials daily, running them, deconstructing winners and repeating for years. He says there is no shortcut around the boring volume work.
title: 9 Money Beliefs of the Ultra Wealthy

title: 9 Money Beliefs of the Ultra Wealthy

text: Status comes from controlling a scarce resource others want, and it is situational: a busy-bar bartender has it at work but loses it outside the bar.
title: My Actual Social Media Strategy For 2026

text: Status, power, credibility and likeness can each create influence alone, but stacking all four together gives the most influence.
title: My Actual Social Media Strategy For 2026

text: He defines influence as a high likelihood that people comply with your requests, such as buying a book or attending a webinar. Bigger asks need more influence.
title: My Actual Social Media Strategy For 2026

text: Likeness means relatability: shared values, a vibe or behavior that matches positive people from your past, or simply looking like you. He notes his audience is about 89% male versus roughly 54% female for a colleague.
title: My Actual Social Media Strategy For 2026

text: For likeness in content, he says there is no return in acting differently from who you are; lean into your quirks and be able to defend why you do things.
title: My Actual Social Media Strategy For 2026

text: Status is a continuum, not a yes or no: someone with more money has some status over you, and a billionaire has far more than someone with ten thousand dollars.
title: My Actual Social Media Strategy For 2026

text: Power comes from reinforcement cycles: people give directions, you follow, and something good happens or something bad is avoided. Parents accumulate many of these.
title: My Actual Social Media Strategy For 2026

text: How much your influence works depends on the request and your credibility in that area; he says he would lack credibility giving fashion tips.
title: My Actual Social Media Strategy For 2026

text: He used a third-party verifier to confirm his company's revenue records, which he says gives credibility because the verifier's business rests on trust.
title: My Actual Social Media Strategy For 2026

text: His future media strategy centers on two words: live and interactive.

text: He sees shorts mainly as a way to get people to risk time on long-form content, and long form allows far more reinforcement cycles than 30 seconds does.
title: My Actual Social Media Strategy For 2026

text: He says chasing views is a mistake; aim for prospects more likely to comply with future requests. Meme content shows almost none of the four elements.
title: My Actual Social Media Strategy For 2026

text: He thinks the internet moves toward truth, so raw formats like live streams and long unscripted podcasts unlock the most influence, provided the four elements are included as often as possible.

text: Real estate earns in two ways: the property value rises, and tenants pay rent. Appreciation can be natural over time or forced by fixing and improving the property.
title: How the top 1% make their money

text: Real estate is a good investment only while population growth continues, which he calls a real risk, citing Japan's declining population and shrinking real estate market.
title: How the top 1% make their money

text: In private equity, you can turn a business's risks into pillars of value one by one, such as finding a reliable customer channel or hiring a key person. The negative discount then becomes a plus on the multiple.
title: How the top 1% make their money

text: Real estate has an upside limit because you can't change the neighborhood, while private equity can produce 100x deals. He says the richest people know how to create 10x to 50x returns reliably.
title: How the top 1% make their money

text: The multiple applied to profits corresponds directly to perceived risk: how likely the business is to keep earning if nothing changes, such as the owner leaving. Higher certainty means a higher multiple.
title: How the top 1% make their money

text: A business bought for almost nothing, with profit taken from $1M to $5M via a new CEO, COO, marketing director, sales ops and pricing updates in 12 to 24 months, at an 8x multiple becomes a $40M business.
title: How the top 1% make their money

text: EBITDA means earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization; buyers want earnings before those items so state and equipment choices don't distort value. Two levers: profit amount, and its reliability and growth.
title: How the top 1% make their money

text: Build the business to be valuable to anyone, not just to you. A founder-run, one-channel, declining, non-recurring business has value to the owner but is basically unsellable to outsiders.
title: How the top 1% make their money

text: Two businesses with equal size and profit can differ hugely: a growing, recurring-revenue one might get a 12x multiple ($36M) while the fragile one gets nothing. Value depends on how reliable and how large the profit is.
title: How the top 1% make their money

text: Private equity beats real estate at the top because a business can start for almost nothing and grow to billions, and it requires more skill.
title: How the top 1% make their money

text: There are only three ways to make a business more valuable: more customers, customers worth more (LTV or LTGP), and lower risk. Every use of money or time should clearly tie to one of these.
title: How the top 1% make their money

text: Debt capacity depends on cash flow. Unlike home loans with fixed down payments, a business with tons of cash flow can carry a disproportionate amount of debt, while one with little can carry almost none.
title: How the top 1% make their money

text: Consistent growth raises the multiple. If a buyer believes 20% yearly growth for five years, they expect a doubling, and buying with debt magnifies their return.
title: How the top 1% make their money

text: Categorization affects multiples: tech-enabled services get higher multiples than traditional services, and SaaS higher still. Adding technology to delivery can shift how the business is classified.
title: How the top 1% make their money

text: Example: a $100K technology investment that moves a multiple from 5 to 8 on $1M profit adds $3M of enterprise value, a 30x return.
title: How the top 1% make their money

text: Businesses get a size premium: more profit earns a higher multiple, unlike bulk discounts. Giant funds have minimum check sizes, one bank's reportedly $150M, so they pay operators who aggregate assets.
title: How the top 1% make their money

text: Institutional investors begin to notice around $5M yearly profit, where multiples might be 20 to 40 by his estimate. Crossing $10M adds a further size premium, a double multiplier effect.
title: How the top 1% make their money

text: Waiting one more year, growing profit from $5M to $8M, could turn a $25M sale into a $75M sale, illustrating the reward for patience.
title: How the top 1% make their money

text: An older business is more valuable. He recalls a partner saying a business grows in value every year until it stops growing, then is worth nothing.
title: How the top 1% make their money

text: Wealth here takes years, not weeks. He says sticking with one business for many years beats starting a new venture every six months.
title: How the top 1% make their money

text: A mediocre opportunity pursued consistently beats an inferior one you keep switching to, because switching forfeits the compounding of your current business.
title: How the top 1% make their money

text: Filters added to a funnel raise lead cost, but only good filters raise quality. Bad friction, like a slow page, costs more without improving leads; a video sales letter is good friction.

text: When someone buys a high-ticket item, bundling in low-ticket add-ons, like a year of supplies, is likely to sell to a good share, lifting average cart value.
