text: An entrepreneur should be able to run key business calculations in their head on the back of a napkin rather than depending on systems or finance reports for directional decisions, or they will be weak.
title: 'My business has stopped growing..what should I do?'

text: His analysis equation uses five variables: new sales per month, current revenue, price, churn and lifetime value, with gross profit as a further number. Most owners know the first three but not churn or lifetime value.
title: 'My business has stopped growing..what should I do?'

text: To get monthly churn, count cancellations per month and divide by active clients. Example: about 50 cancellations across 380 active clients gives roughly 13% churn.
title: 'My business has stopped growing..what should I do?'

text: Lifetime value per customer equals price divided by churn. Multiplying that by monthly new sales gives the hypothetical revenue max the business approaches but never reaches, like an asymptote, as churn eats more of new business.
title: 'My business has stopped growing..what should I do?'

text: Multiply lifetime value by gross margin to get lifetime gross profit per customer. While acquisition cost stays below that figure, the business is generally profitable.
title: 'My business has stopped growing..what should I do?'

text: A business grows only by getting more customers or making each customer worth more. Nothing else.
title: 'My business has stopped growing..what should I do?'

text: Cutting churn is often the bigger lever. In his example, dropping churn from 13% to 3% lifts lifetime value to about 33,000 and the cap to about 3.3 million monthly, mostly margin, with nothing else changed.
title: 'My business has stopped growing..what should I do?'

text: He argues that dropping churn from 13% to 3% is easier than multiplying customer acquisition tenfold, and says he has a separate video on eight ways to reduce churn.
title: 'My business has stopped growing..what should I do?'

text: Private equity firms generally want roughly 80% yearly retention for a company to carry enterprise value. He notes 13% monthly churn leaves you with under 20% of customers after a year.
title: 'My business has stopped growing..what should I do?'

text: Buyers weigh three things: growth, stickiness of revenue, and profit. He says you can roughly multiply them, so fast, sticky, profitable companies are very valuable and slow, leaky, low-profit ones are not.
title: 'My business has stopped growing..what should I do?'

text: An owner who does not know their hypothetical max under current numbers is fooling themselves, since they cannot see where they cap out or where the weak points are.
title: 'My business has stopped growing..what should I do?'

text: He follows the theory of constraints: a business grows only up to its nearest constraint, so his job is to find the biggest one and remove it.
title: 'My business has stopped growing..what should I do?'

text: He believes the smartest people find the fewest things that produce the most return, and removing the biggest constraint is the top example.
title: 'My business has stopped growing..what should I do?'

text: He states that portfolio companies at acquisition.com do about 85 million dollars a year in revenue.
title: 'My business has stopped growing..what should I do?'

text: Big life decisions feel scary because the easy ones are already made. What remains is obvious but risky, and involves trading being stuck for a chance of getting better or worse.
title: Why Being Fast Makes You Always Win (thank me later)

text: Spelling out both sides of a trade, including the cost of staying dissatisfied, makes today feel worse so tomorrow looks better. That contrast is what pushes him to make jumps.
title: Why Being Fast Makes You Always Win (thank me later)

text: He says most of his big decisions came from his present becoming so painful that anything seemed better, rather than from a grand passion or vision.
title: Why Being Fast Makes You Always Win (thank me later)

text: Investments and lifting weights both dip before they rise: bank balance falls before it grows, muscles shrink before growing. A step back is usually needed before steps forward.
title: Why Being Fast Makes You Always Win (thank me later)

text: If you never take the step back, you never get the outsized return of the steps forward.
title: Why Being Fast Makes You Always Win (thank me later)

text: When demand exceeds capacity and cash is short to hire, raise price first. This trims incoming volume, adds cash flow, funds higher pay and advertising to attract talent, and ends the supply constraint. Each step carries risk.
title: Why Being Fast Makes You Always Win (thank me later)

text: Relative return on ad spend usually falls as spend rises, but absolute return rises. Spending a million to make two million beats spending ten thousand to make a hundred thousand in profit terms.
title: Why Being Fast Makes You Always Win (thank me later)

text: Small business owners, such as gym owners, often cap ad spend at break-even. He says to spend more, since everything above break-even is gravy.
title: Why Being Fast Makes You Always Win (thank me later)

text: People downgrade goals based on difficulty. He says spelling out the trade has given him outsized returns in his life.
title: Why Being Fast Makes You Always Win (thank me later)

text: Having only make more money as a goal makes focus hard because everything seems to make money. He says the most money comes from focus.
title: Why Being Fast Makes You Always Win (thank me later)

text: The more capable you are, the more things you can do decently at once, yet spreading thin gives up an aggregate upside he says is almost always about ten times bigger.
title: Why Being Fast Makes You Always Win (thank me later)

text: He went from roughly a couple million a year across nine ventures, with agencies, a launch business and gym locations, to about ten times that by consolidating into one business. Numbers are rough.
title: Why Being Fast Makes You Always Win (thank me later)

text: Growth requires pruning: cutting branches so the whole grows. He says people are unwilling to do this.
title: Why Being Fast Makes You Always Win (thank me later)

text: When hiring an agency, state your intent up front: commit to a fixed period, ask them to explain their decisions, and plan to move to a cheaper consulting arrangement once your team can do the work.
title: I Gained 5,000,000+ Followers with this Secret Method

text: Paying both an agency and your own team for a while is worth it, because you are building an asset you own instead of depending on someone who could cut you off or raise prices as they see your profits.
title: I Gained 5,000,000+ Followers with this Secret Method

text: With an agency, document what they do into your internal processes and start co-creating, until what your team makes matches and then beats the agency's output.
title: I Gained 5,000,000+ Followers with this Secret Method

text: An in-house team should eventually outperform an agency because they give you all their time and know your brand better; you only need to close the expertise gap, then you can let the agency go.
title: I Gained 5,000,000+ Followers with this Secret Method

text: Set a clear deadline for the transition. It sets expectations with the agency, lets you talk in terms of their total contract value, and pushes your team to get up to speed faster each month.
title: I Gained 5,000,000+ Followers with this Secret Method

text: If your team is still behind at the deadline, he says either the people are wrong or the agency is not teaching everything. If the platform is just complex, keep going until your team matches theirs.
title: I Gained 5,000,000+ Followers with this Secret Method

text: After your team matches the agency, downgrade to a consulting agreement as insurance. If the calls stop teaching you anything after a month or two, cut it, amicably, since that was the expectation.
title: I Gained 5,000,000+ Followers with this Secret Method

text: Being transparent that you want to learn from an agency and bring the work in-house keeps relationships good. He says this combines the best of agencies with building an enterprise and avoids common agency traps.
title: I Gained 5,000,000+ Followers with this Secret Method

text: On TikTok, an agency approached him offering to repurpose his existing content into shorts. It gained traction, and his director of brand, who came from a premium agency, brought the processes in, scaling short-form output within about six months.
title: I Gained 5,000,000+ Followers with this Secret Method

text: When someone asks him to approve an action, he almost always replies by asking what problem they are trying to solve, since people often act out of emotional discomfort rather than a defined problem.
title: Learn 97% of How to Get Rich in 11 Mins

text: He argues much lack of focus is intellectual laziness: people know roughly what needs doing, but avoid what they cannot do yet and pick tasks they can solve, feeling competent though it changes nothing.
title: Learn 97% of How to Get Rich in 11 Mins

text: Asking someone what problem they are solving reveals how diligently the requester thought the idea through.
title: Learn 97% of How to Get Rich in 11 Mins

text: When he wants something done, he asks what would it take instead of can we, because it assumes success. Can-we questions used to get quick no answers based on incomplete context about his plans.
title: Learn 97% of How to Get Rich in 11 Mins

text: After hearing no, he asks what it would take, walking through extremes like a billion or a million dollars until the real requirement, such as hiring one person, appears and he can judge whether it is worth it.
title: Learn 97% of How to Get Rich in 11 Mins

text: What would it take fits many goals: halving delivery time, delivering in 24 hours instead of 30 days, buying a company, closing a deal, or doubling content output. He calls it one of the most powerful entrepreneurship questions.
title: Learn 97% of How to Get Rich in 11 Mins

text: When someone proposes something and the problem is unclear, his first follow-up is asking what they want to have happen, which cuts past emotional noise to the desired outcome.
title: Learn 97% of How to Get Rich in 11 Mins

text: He follows up with asking what else the same time and energy could do for a higher return to the business.
title: Learn 97% of How to Get Rich in 11 Mins

text: He treats questions like weapons showing how sharp thinking is, on both sides; he expects people to answer these questions when turned on him because he has thought it through.
title: Learn 97% of How to Get Rich in 11 Mins

text: Asking what would it take produces more divergent thinking, as people solve for success and reverse engineer it; imagining unlimited time and money then shows the real, small requirement.
title: Learn 97% of How to Get Rich in 11 Mins

text: Many of these questions end with the conclusion not to do the thing, which he says is usually correct. His joke: do nothing is the undefeated heavyweight champion, so keep funding what earns the highest return.
title: Learn 97% of How to Get Rich in 11 Mins

text: He suggests people often propose new actions because they are uncomfortable with the present moment and want something to do, rather than doing what they know works.
title: Learn 97% of How to Get Rich in 11 Mins

text: Businesses do not need to become AI businesses. Like the internet, AI is one more tool used to deliver what you sell.
title: How to Use AI in Your Business in 2026

text: A common mistake is assuming the tech people will implement AI for you. Hormozi credits his edge to knowing everything from high-level strategy and people down to connecting APIs.
title: How to Use AI in Your Business in 2026

text: Owners know their business best, so they see how pieces combine. A technical person, working from limited context, defaults to commoditized automations. Big gains come from business acumen layered over technical acumen.
title: How to Use AI in Your Business in 2026

text: Take a YouTube tutorial's link and transcript, ask an AI to help you build it, follow its directions, and send screenshots when stuck. Repeat over and over.
title: How to Use AI in Your Business in 2026

text: Owners often install a half-built AI function and compare it to a process refined over years. Compare fairly: apply the same training and SOP effort to the AI.
title: How to Use AI in Your Business in 2026

text: Sales AI agencies will struggle because implementing sales in other businesses takes more than tech and selling skill. Dropping his AI setter into another business is like transplanting a salesperson: expect poor first results.
title: How to Use AI in Your Business in 2026

text: AI makes existing sales work easier and faster, but you still need a sales process. Weak processes are not fixed by having AI call every opt-in.
title: How to Use AI in Your Business in 2026

text: Human psychology will not change, so persuasion rules still apply. He would not advertise using AI; customers care only about faster, cheaper, better and risk-free.
title: How to Use AI in Your Business in 2026

text: For his book launch, five AI agents handled roughly 120,000 support tickets, resolving 90% without human intervention, mostly simple questions like where to find free items.
title: How to Use AI in Your Business in 2026

text: Pick a block of time and fully automate one portion of your day, start to finish. This is his only ask.
title: How to Use AI in Your Business in 2026

text: Automate your own workflow so you gain time for more valuable work. Treat gut feeling as pattern recognition, and ask which observable behaviors produce the outcome.
title: How to Use AI in Your Business in 2026

text: Content idea pipeline: bot reads your calendar, transcribes your calls, then extracts the five most interesting situations or decisions of the week into a document. This yields true stories.
title: How to Use AI in Your Business in 2026

text: He thinks AI avatars without real proof will not work well in B2B, since people ask why they should listen. Consumer settings such as skin care may be more forgiving.
title: How to Use AI in Your Business in 2026

text: Use AI tools for outcomes without advertising them, as he does not talk about his CRM. Customers care about results, and repeat buying reflects your skill.
title: How to Use AI in Your Business in 2026

text: Marketing AI examples: generate ideas, script headlines and thumbnails, auto-test thumbnails and learn what wins, and research trending formats and hooks.
title: How to Use AI in Your Business in 2026

text: Give AI trending formats and hooks plus your brand material, ask for the overlap, get ten ideas, pick one, then generate headline and script.
title: How to Use AI in Your Business in 2026

text: Ad automation: overlay a call to action on content and launch it daily as an ad with yesterday's content. Turn community wins into static ads through proven templates.
title: How to Use AI in Your Business in 2026

text: Sales uses: enrich leads, respond fast with personalized voice notes, images or texts, including Instagram DMs, and hand off between AIs for scheduling, boosting speed to contact.
title: How to Use AI in Your Business in 2026

text: He says about 18 months remain in which people starting with nothing can create huge wealth using AI, and an army of autonomous agents would get much more done.
title: How to Use AI in Your Business in 2026

text: He has eaten dessert nearly every night for 20 years, kept a six-pack throughout, and has eaten essentially the same way for the last 10 years, including business dinners and drinks.
title: The Alex Hormozi Diet (REVEALED)

text: He says this is not the most scientifically researched approach; it is what worked for him, and if something already works for you, keep doing it.
title: The Alex Hormozi Diet (REVEALED)

text: Start by deciding whether you want to get bigger or smaller. Then pick a bodyweight multiplier from 7 to 21, moving in steps of three from extreme loss through moderate loss, maintenance, moderate gain, to extreme gain.
title: The Alex Hormozi Diet (REVEALED)

text: Daily calories equal bodyweight times the multiplier. For a 200 lb person wanting a moderate cut, using 10 gives 2,000 calories. If weight drops too fast, move up to 11 instead of adjusting for exercise or job.
title: The Alex Hormozi Diet (REVEALED)

text: Set protein in grams equal to bodyweight in pounds, so 200 g for a 200 lb person. He dismisses the objection that the body only absorbs a limited amount per meal.
title: The Alex Hormozi Diet (REVEALED)

text: A pound of lean meat such as white fish, ground turkey breast, lean beef or shrimp gives about 100 g of protein, so 200 g needs roughly 2 lb of meat.
title: The Alex Hormozi Diet (REVEALED)

text: Subtract the calories of your protein sources from your daily total; what remains can be spent on anything. Example: 1,120 calories of turkey from 2,000 leaves 880 for cocktails, a dinner out, ice cream or cookies.
title: The Alex Hormozi Diet (REVEALED)

text: At maintenance using a multiplier of 15 for 200 lb, he gets 3,000 calories, leaving about 1,000 extra to spend on flexible food compared with the cut.
title: The Alex Hormozi Diet (REVEALED)

text: He eats the same breakfast and lunch daily: a bar plus a protein shake, then a pound of turkey with some rice. That reaches about 150 g of protein and 1,140 calories before dinner.
title: The Alex Hormozi Diet (REVEALED)

text: Dinner is his flexible meal. If you already hit your protein earlier, dinner can be anything that fits the calorie total. He also eats protein at dinner because it keeps him full, unlike only cookies.
title: The Alex Hormozi Diet (REVEALED)

text: He skips greens and takes a multivitamin instead, and he mostly avoids fitness content because of endless armchair debates.
title: The Alex Hormozi Diet (REVEALED)

text: Work should be defined as output, which is volume (how many times you do something) times leverage (what you get from each time). Effort, hours on the clock or physics definitions are less useful for knowledge workers.
title: You're Not Behind: My System for Outworking Everyone

text: Output per unit of time is volume times leverage divided by time. To do more work you can raise the number of actions or the payoff of each action.
title: You're Not Behind: My System for Outworking Everyone

text: Growing a business comes down to getting more customers or making each worth more. Actions: more traffic, higher conversion, raising prices, cutting costs, and getting people to buy more often.
title: You're Not Behind: My System for Outworking Everyone

text: Time spent on things that do not feed the four levers (advertising, conversion, pricing, retention) has the same effect as doing nothing, and can be worse than resting.
title: You're Not Behind: My System for Outworking Everyone

text: For smaller businesses, effort should be weighted toward getting more traffic and improving conversion, because without customers there is nobody to raise prices on or resell to.
title: You're Not Behind: My System for Outworking Everyone

text: You get better at advertising by doing far more of it. He suggests committing about four hours a day to your main channel: ads, outreach, content or partner and affiliate work.
title: You're Not Behind: My System for Outworking Everyone

text: If your business is stalled and you keep doing the same things, those things are wrong. Learn to let some fires burn and focus on the current constraint for four hours a day until solved.
title: You're Not Behind: My System for Outworking Everyone

text: Once traffic is mastered, conversion becomes the limiter; train someone else on advertising and spend the hours on conversion: track close rate, record calls, review winning sales, practice scripts, get daily feedback, pre-qualify and pre-sell.
title: You're Not Behind: My System for Outworking Everyone

text: All problems are solvable with skills, and skills come from repetition and feedback. Once good, a skill takes less time, and maintaining it is easier than gaining it.
title: You're Not Behind: My System for Outworking Everyone

text: Customers do not care about your excuses, however justified; they care about output and what they get from you.
title: You're Not Behind: My System for Outworking Everyone

text: Maker time is long uninterrupted blocks of four to six hours, about 14 per week, for important low-urgency work; one interruption can ruin the block. Manager time is 5-15 minute slots, 100+ per week. Do not mix them.
title: You're Not Behind: My System for Outworking Everyone

text: His maker habits: pick the one most important project, wake at 4 a.m. and work to 9, notifications off, dark windowless quiet office with earplugs, consistent bedtime including weekends.
title: You're Not Behind: My System for Outworking Everyone

text: He says there are no business emergencies beyond life-threatening ones; the real emergency is a business that fails to grow. He also treats weekends as extra uninterrupted time, about 104 days a year.
title: You're Not Behind: My System for Outworking Everyone

text: You become more productive through elimination than optimization. Removing energy drains is permanent, whereas timer hacks rarely stick.
title: You're Not Behind: My System for Outworking Everyone

text: Someone doing 96 productive hours a month versus 3 hours a week of real work moves roughly 30 times faster, even if both work all day.
title: You're Not Behind: My System for Outworking Everyone

text: He cites average American time: food 50 hours a month (about $800 to replace), cleaning 25 hours ($500), laundry 16 hours ($200). Around $1,500 monthly buys back roughly 96 hours.
title: You're Not Behind: My System for Outworking Everyone

text: Bought time must be used to work and earn more, not for extra entertainment. Owners who readily hire staff but resist spending on their own time are inconsistent, since the owner is the most valuable person.
title: You're Not Behind: My System for Outworking Everyone

text: Watching TV, sports and scrolling need no replacement cost, so you can keep them and still buy back the 96 hours. He also mentions a $700 monthly cost of being driven to work.
title: You're Not Behind: My System for Outworking Everyone

text: Trading money for time means paying for lower-value tasks to free hours for higher-value work, which earns more money, and the cycle never ends.
title: You're Not Behind: My System for Outworking Everyone

text: He thinks sleep alarms matter more than wake alarms; he has not used an alarm in years and finds nine hours of sleep makes him ready for the hardest problems.
title: You're Not Behind: My System for Outworking Everyone

text: Maker versus manager is a continuum. He runs four maker days and one stacked manager day on Mondays, while his wife has the reverse and runs the business day to day.
title: You're Not Behind: My System for Outworking Everyone

text: His fitness advice: get in shape between 18 and 24; after that maintenance takes roughly 10 percent of your time. He trains three or four days weekly in a home gym.
title: You're Not Behind: My System for Outworking Everyone

text: He says that after people have some success and reach what they personally count as making it, they get comfortable and complacent and lose their hunger, even when that bar is as low as ten thousand dollars in the bank.
title: Why entrepreneurs stay broke and sad [trigger warning]

text: He argues that once people are comfortable, tactics stop mattering because they are not hungry, and they skip obvious actions. He asks how you would act if a loved one's life depended on your success.
title: Why entrepreneurs stay broke and sad [trigger warning]

text: He says you usually know what to do; if you coached yourself you would probably have the answer, so attention should go to why you do not do it.
title: Why entrepreneurs stay broke and sad [trigger warning]

text: He says there is no secret or hack; success is repeated boring work, like reaching out, great service, working leads, being enthusiastic, and asking the same questions again since each person hears them fresh.
title: Why entrepreneurs stay broke and sad [trigger warning]

text: He says once owners learn how to build a seven-figure gym, responsibility shifts to them, which he calls both freeing and soul crushing.
title: Why entrepreneurs stay broke and sad [trigger warning]

text: He says tactics are widely available, even free in books, so when someone knows them but does not act, the thing to attack is why they are not hungry or trying.
title: Why entrepreneurs stay broke and sad [trigger warning]

text: He says his own drive is fear and insecurity: fear of failing, of not being good enough, and of people who doubted him being right, and it is not about money.
title: Why entrepreneurs stay broke and sad [trigger warning]

text: He warns that feeling relief after a big-money month means your motivation is not that of a champion; money is just an output of internal effort, so focus on the internal efforts and shortfalls.
title: Why entrepreneurs stay broke and sad [trigger warning]

text: He points out that when you truly need money, like payroll, you tend to produce it fast, so you already know how; the question is why you do not do it otherwise.
title: Why entrepreneurs stay broke and sad [trigger warning]

text: He says if you only want to satisfy yourself or one family, you will stay small; building something bigger requires wanting to serve a community, state, or nation.
title: Why entrepreneurs stay broke and sad [trigger warning]

text: Hormozi says 99.9% of people will never have truly passive income in any material amount. Owning dividend stocks is passive, but actively managing those holdings makes it active income.
title: the brutal truth behind passive income

text: Everyone trades time for money; the difference is only how much leverage they have. Passive just means trading a smaller share of time, so income is better viewed as a spectrum than active versus passive.
title: the brutal truth behind passive income

text: Having watched many 40 to 60 year old wealthy entrepreneurs in his building, he concludes people are not meant to not work, and finds seeing them chase pleasure sad.
title: the brutal truth behind passive income

text: He and his wife earn roughly six million a year, which he rates about eight and a half on a zero-to-ten passive scale. He says it is less fun than when they were actively involved.
title: the brutal truth behind passive income

text: Passive income was the goal he optimized around for years, and having reached it he regrets it. He says he is bored out of his mind, and if you love the game, asks why remove yourself.
title: the brutal truth behind passive income

text: His original aim was freedom to choose, but it morphed into needing everything to be passive. He warns others not to repeat this; running your own business is fine.
title: the brutal truth behind passive income

text: He stepped back to let others grow, but now cannot return to the business without displacing people who have taken over his roles.
title: the brutal truth behind passive income

text: Building a business that merely maintains cash flow without you is different from placing enough talent so it grows without you. He says only the latter is truly a business, and he has now proven he can do it.
title: the brutal truth behind passive income

text: Having proven he can build a business that runs without him, he chooses the challenge and being in the game over watching the team win. He says we have freedom to choose, not freedom to do nothing.
title: the brutal truth behind passive income

text: He describes trading things away to buy back time until you have all your time but nothing to do. He says seeking pleasure is not the game and is boring.
title: the brutal truth behind passive income

text: Hormozi says three levels of talent exist, and they apply to you and your team. Early on you are the individual contributor, spending all your time doing, and you learn what to do.
title: The Talent Grid - How I Recognize Skill in Self & Team

text: He holds that identity is fluid, and people often stay stuck at one level because of beliefs about themselves. Changing how you see yourself is needed to remove the business bottleneck.
title: The Talent Grid - How I Recognize Skill in Self & Team

text: Level two is understanding how: you grasp the sequence of the work so you can teach others to replicate it. That makes you a manager, whose job is ensuring people execute consistently.
title: The Talent Grid - How I Recognize Skill in Self & Team

text: Managers need not out-perform individual contributors at the task, since niche expertise exists, but they should understand how the work functions.
title: The Talent Grid - How I Recognize Skill in Self & Team

text: Level three is the leader, who systematizes. He says this differs from managing and typically arises around a three-million-a-year business, enabling growth toward multiple millions per month.
title: The Talent Grid - How I Recognize Skill in Self & Team

text: The grid can grade yourself, a team member, or each department, by asking what level of involvement you have in that function.
title: The Talent Grid - How I Recognize Skill in Self & Team

text: His definition of a truly delegated portfolio business: he is off its Slack, meets the operator once a week, and the company keeps growing between meetings without his direct involvement.
title: The Talent Grid - How I Recognize Skill in Self & Team

text: He warns that founders claiming their business is systematized often still get constant messages; deferring a reply does not remove the need for their presence and decisions.
title: The Talent Grid - How I Recognize Skill in Self & Team

text: For sales, ask whether you sell, teach selling, or have a machine that trains salespeople so you can bring in one to three hires monthly and run them through it.
title: The Talent Grid - How I Recognize Skill in Self & Team

text: He says it took him a long time to see that the owner's own strengths usually become the bottleneck, because weak areas are more comfortably handed to people with better expertise.
title: The Talent Grid - How I Recognize Skill in Self & Team

text: Each quarter, review every department on a sheet: do people know what to do, is there a taught sequence with accountability, and can someone build the machine that recreates the skill.
title: The Talent Grid - How I Recognize Skill in Self & Team

text: He notes, citing Reid Hoffman, that jumping levels is hard, so fast-growing companies often replace leadership because tenured managers frequently are not leaders.
title: The Talent Grid - How I Recognize Skill in Self & Team

text: Great leaders are sometimes terrible individual contributors and good contributors are often poor leaders, so he assesses each person's level separately.
title: The Talent Grid - How I Recognize Skill in Self & Team

text: He says entrepreneurs must improve their own character to attract higher-level people, since people follow those they aspire to be like.
title: The Talent Grid - How I Recognize Skill in Self & Team

text: He says about 95 percent of entrepreneurs praise their team while telling horror stories, and months later reverse their verdict, so he distrusts their judgment of talent.
title: The Talent Grid - How I Recognize Skill in Self & Team

text: Hard money lending means acting as the bank, so he can set the deal structure, including upside and downside, and the other party chooses whether to accept it. Controlling those variables lets him limit downside risk.
title: Hard Money Lending EXPLAINED [I lent $3,000,000 using this]

text: He protected the $2.5 million loan in layers: two personal guarantors each worth over $2.5 million, a property with three offers between 5 and 5.6 million, and 300K earnest money from one buyer.
title: Hard Money Lending EXPLAINED [I lent $3,000,000 using this]

text: He says making sure you are on the title, first in line with no other liens, is a minor-sounding step that is where many deals get messed up. His cash paid off the prior lien holder.
title: Hard Money Lending EXPLAINED [I lent $3,000,000 using this]

text: Terms: 4% per month on 2.5 million, about 100K monthly, doubling after month four to compensate for added risk. He also required a two-month minimum carry, guaranteeing at least 200K even if the deal closes immediately.
title: Hard Money Lending EXPLAINED [I lent $3,000,000 using this]

text: His lawyers under-billed the repayment. The borrower, whose own lawyer advised paying the lower amount, instead flagged it and fired that lawyer. Hormozi says this was more valuable than the deal itself.
title: Hard Money Lending EXPLAINED [I lent $3,000,000 using this]

text: The more often you lend to someone and they repay as agreed, the more trust builds, especially when they could have exploited a mistake unnoticed.
title: Hard Money Lending EXPLAINED [I lent $3,000,000 using this]

text: He judges vendors on three circles: skill, ethics, and hard work. His lawyer lacked skill and the borrower's lawyer lacked ethics, though both worked hard.
title: Hard Money Lending EXPLAINED [I lent $3,000,000 using this]

text: He says trust is the most valuable currency in business and that people new to business underestimate it. You only get one name and one reputation.
title: Hard Money Lending EXPLAINED [I lent $3,000,000 using this]

text: He owes roughly 50% tax on the interest income as ordinary income, leaving about 175K after tax on this deal. He would still lend again for at least a 10 to 20% return.
title: Hard Money Lending EXPLAINED [I lent $3,000,000 using this]

text: Everyone has some money and some problem, so a seller should look for a way to help everyone to some degree, while still aiming first to sell the primary program.
title: How To Close Everyone Downselling Like A Pro (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Downselling done badly sounds like begging, loses the seller's frame and makes them seem desperate, so even buyers who could pay may refuse. Done well, it raises close rate.
title: How To Close Everyone Downselling Like A Pro (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Handle downsells with a set of cards in your back pocket, played as a step down, where each lower price is traded for something in exchange rather than simply cut.
title: How To Close Everyone Downselling Like A Pro (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Reciprocity is a strong persuader because people judge exchanges poorly: after a small favor, a large ask is still hard to refuse. Whoever sets the terms of an exchange holds the power.
title: How To Close Everyone Downselling Like A Pro (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: When a prospect says they cannot afford it, offer a lower price in return for something, such as a testimonial, then ask if that sounds fair. It is hard to keep declining repeated accommodations.
title: How To Close Everyone Downselling Like A Pro (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Cards for ethical price reduction include longer commitment term, testimonial, reviews, and bringing a friend. He prefers asking for more over removing bonuses.
title: How To Close Everyone Downselling Like A Pro (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Because lower-priced buyers agree to extra terms, you can answer a customer asking why others pay differently: the other person is doing extra things for you, so the terms differ.
title: How To Close Everyone Downselling Like A Pro (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Acknowledge lightly that the repeated offers are getting ridiculous; the light tone keeps the pull toward saying yes. A testimonial ask also implies they will get results, so you sell while downselling.
title: How To Close Everyone Downselling Like A Pro (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Ask fair enough or sound fair as the call to action when downselling, since it lowers the bar to yes. Then move into micro-steps like scheduling before taking the card.
title: How To Close Everyone Downselling Like A Pro (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Tonality matters greatly, especially by phone: ask the fair-enough question as if you truly want a yes. He cites that only 9% of communication is verbal.
title: How To Close Everyone Downselling Like A Pro (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Frame downselling as collaborative, on the same side of the table figuring out how to make it work. This works if you built rapport and dug into pain earlier without getting aggressive.
title: How To Close Everyone Downselling Like A Pro (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: If a prospect refuses even after about six drop-downs, he thinks it is not about money; they disengaged earlier in the sale. Confront disengagement early, asking permission to be real rather than nice.
title: How To Close Everyone Downselling Like A Pro (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: The goal of a downsell is to get a foot in the door, since after 7 to 14 days they trust you and may buy the full-price program later.
title: How To Close Everyone Downselling Like A Pro (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Business runs as inputs, efficiencies and an output, usually money. Many owners are unclear on the inputs. The first step is that people must know you exist, so under-advertising is a common cause of stalled growth.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: For local businesses, he sees content mainly as a way to convert more people who already found you, since platform algorithms reach global audiences. If you make none, one piece a week is a light, high-return start.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: His company makes about 400 pieces of content a week. As a baseline for someone who makes content their main marketing, he suggests starting at two a day.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: Rule of thumb: for whichever main customer-getting activity you use, spend about four hours a day on it. Paid ads work is mostly creative: scripting, hooks, researching working ads, and learning editing.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: Brand is built three ways: what you say, what others say, and what people experience. The first two are approximations; product experience decides whether the promise is reinforced or broken.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: Owners often think their gym is great but pay it no attention. If it were that good, he argues, customers would be sending in more customers.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: Save every ad you like in an album. Before making ads, review your all-time best, look at new ones from the week, merge elements, and remake winners with the same words.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: Bringing in customers is how you find out your service is weak; you cannot imagine your customer success into shape before real members expose broken processes.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: Outreach through the rule of 100 works consistently, but most people skip the work. He says gyms have essentially no emergencies; the real emergency is not doing growth work.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: To win referral partners such as chiropractors or doctors, reach out, give gifts, and send them business first. If one partner sends half your customers, get ten or twenty.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: The only ways to make more money are getting more customers or making each worth more. More customers needs more traffic or better conversion; more value needs higher prices or lower churn.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: Spend the first four hours each day on your biggest current problem, then switch when it is solved. Looking back, only that block shows progress; fires get put out anyway.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: Practice sales by role-play with fast feedback. The person answering questions in a sale is losing, so answer objections by asking what they are trying to get from the question.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: Break conversion into schedule, show and close rates, and spend your hours on whichever is below benchmark. He promises schedule and show rate stop being problems with four hours a day.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: If your gym is full but not profitable, you are underpriced. Raise the price by sending existing customers a letter or email, then deliver well at the new price.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: Reduce churn with exit interviews that can save about half of leavers, check-ins every couple weeks, attendance tracking with follow-up when they miss, and heavy communication in the first 24-72 hours.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: Reverse engineer goals: if 30 posts yield five customers, that is one customer per six posts, so 25 customers needs 150 posts, about five a day. Boil work down to what makes money.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: Raising volume also raises skill. Doing 100 attempts a day gets you good; doing ten a day tends to keep you bad. Rich keep getting richer by doing more.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: Every business has one constraint; until removed it stays stuck, then grows until the next one. Keep your action list to about three items, the right ones.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: He cites about 96 hours a month spent on food, cleaning and laundry, and says paying about 1,500 dollars a month to outsource them is worth it for owners of businesses under 150,000 a month, if used on the constraint.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: Focus on a to-don't list. He credits his speed to avoiding work that does not matter and buying replacements for mental energy sinks, like eating at Chipotle when single.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: When buying education, aim to be the best student, not just a success story. Buying something to prove it does not work is a terrible way to live.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: Toughness is doing what you dislike, such as working leads, follow-ups, ads, reviews, referrals and sales practice. Posting early gym hours while skipping these fools only yourself.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: Fire the consistently weak employee. She sets your standards, repels good people, hurts customers, and drains your time. He says what you see is her best behavior.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: He says he can judge an entrepreneur by their team. Better people will not join a mediocre team, so mediocre staff means a mediocre gym, and tolerating it is the owner's fault.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: He splits his day between today's job and tomorrow's job. He bets that work an underperformer takes 20 hours on, you could do in five, and clean up systems.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: Give people positive feedback when they do things right, not only when they fail; otherwise they may do a task once and stop, and you pay for work not done.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: He has not seen brick-and-mortar service chains scale without an operator on profit share, usually 10 to 20 percent. Test readiness: can the business grow while you are away six months?
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: He believes anyone can be trained to do anything; the question is whether the cost is worth it. Business is reallocating time, money and energy.
title: If you're not unbelievably rich yet, this is why

text: Over a long enough time, the product is what matters. Marketing only speeds up how fast people find it, so it can accelerate growth but cannot create a good business.
title: Building a $3,500,000 Business for Two Strangers in 52 Minutes

text: He prefers to charge full price or give something free, not percentage discounts, especially at food businesses, so you avoid training discount seekers. He treats prepayment or time-limited sales incentives as different from promotions.
title: Building a $3,500,000 Business for Two Strangers in 52 Minutes

text: He prefers giving a free item paired with a clear path to turning that person into a full-paying customer.
title: Building a $3,500,000 Business for Two Strangers in 52 Minutes

text: Expanding before the core model is solid may get you a second location faster but slows you to the tenth. Check cost to open, time to profit, payback, grand opening, and hiring and culture.
title: Building a $3,500,000 Business for Two Strangers in 52 Minutes

text: Adding a card processing fee of about 3% on the menu usually does not change what people order, and for this business it would lift profit around 15%.
title: Building a $3,500,000 Business for Two Strangers in 52 Minutes

text: Moving from round prices to 99-ending prices adds a small amount per item. On a $16 ticket he estimates it lifts profit margin about 30% if sales do not drop, and he doubts it would.
title: Building a $3,500,000 Business for Two Strangers in 52 Minutes

text: Busy days can carry higher menu prices, like surge pricing. A separate weekend menu with roughly $2 more per dish works like a dinner menu costing more than lunch.
title: Building a $3,500,000 Business for Two Strangers in 52 Minutes

text: Menu layout: rank items in each section by gross profit, start with higher prices to anchor, and balance profit with what brings people back. Place a must-try box for first-timers.
title: Building a $3,500,000 Business for Two Strangers in 52 Minutes

text: Printing a drink pairing under each dish makes alcohol purchase easier for customers. He thinks it would move alcohol from 1% of sales toward 6%, which he says adds around 25% profit.
title: Building a $3,500,000 Business for Two Strangers in 52 Minutes

text: Offer one rotating fresh drink special, introduced by staff before taking drink orders, and made seasonal. Staff can pick it through weekly team tastings.
title: Building a $3,500,000 Business for Two Strangers in 52 Minutes

text: Mark first-time guests with a coaster or napkin color so staff know. Because people remember peak and end moments, give them a surprise free item at the end.
title: Building a $3,500,000 Business for Two Strangers in 52 Minutes

text: Hand first-timers a manager card with free dessert written on back for their next visit. It feels like a personal gift, not a coupon, and it creates a reason to return.
title: Building a $3,500,000 Business for Two Strangers in 52 Minutes

text: Ask for reviews at the point of sale with an immediate reward, like removing a drink from the check. A promise for next time does not work as well. An alternative is a server bonus ask.
title: Building a $3,500,000 Business for Two Strangers in 52 Minutes

text: For local businesses, most people search online before choosing. A high rating with a huge review count signals a destination, so volume of reviews matters as well as stars.
title: Building a $3,500,000 Business for Two Strangers in 52 Minutes

text: Add a threshold offer just above the current average order, such as a free extra dish on orders over $80. He thinks it fits takeout best since it feels natural on a phone or order page.
title: Building a $3,500,000 Business for Two Strangers in 52 Minutes

text: He cites a McKinsey study saying one in three strategies succeed and culture, meaning rewards and consequences for behavior, is the big difference. So tactics must come with staff training.
title: Building a $3,500,000 Business for Two Strangers in 52 Minutes

text: Running starts on punch cards: giving two or three punches upfront makes people two to three times more likely to finish than a shorter card. He is split on loyalty programs for restaurants.
title: Building a $3,500,000 Business for Two Strangers in 52 Minutes

text: To improve any product he asks how to lower risk, speed it up, and make it easier. Pairing suggestions for drinks remove friction from ordering.
title: Building a $3,500,000 Business for Two Strangers in 52 Minutes

text: Train staff with behavior rules, when this then that, drilled as short skits with many repetitions before shifts. Start with four rules: greeting, drink special, pairings, review or comeback offer.
title: Building a $3,500,000 Business for Two Strangers in 52 Minutes

text: Servers should add a short nudging phrase after each order, like fast food does, phrased so yes feels normal. Saying what most people do helps first-timers unsure of the process.
title: Building a $3,500,000 Business for Two Strangers in 52 Minutes

text: Give servers a leaderboard for alcohol sales with a small prize like cash or first pick of next month's schedule.
title: Building a $3,500,000 Business for Two Strangers in 52 Minutes

text: Before opening, host a VIP night for local influencers or business owners with big audiences, trading free or discounted food for videos and posts. Their reach launches word of mouth.
title: Building a $3,500,000 Business for Two Strangers in 52 Minutes

text: He says no one works effectively all day; when his output rate for a known task drops noticeably, he stops, since quality falls and he must fix the work later anyway.
title: Answering Juicy Questions About Our Relationship

text: He thinks about a minimum effective dose per goal: an hour of marriage time can yield higher return than the last hour of work, so he weighs that trade within roughly 16 waking hours.
title: Answering Juicy Questions About Our Relationship

text: He argues spouses should not hold conflicting desires: if you want a very ambitious partner, the price is more work and less flexible schedules, so pick what matters more.
title: Answering Juicy Questions About Our Relationship

text: He used to demand she prove her reasoning step by step rather than just stating a conclusion; he says their partnership took years of work and communication.
title: Answering Juicy Questions About Our Relationship

text: He says their relationship is built on respect rather than love, because feelings are fleeting while admiration of someone's character stays steadier through annoying or unromantic stretches.
title: Answering Juicy Questions About Our Relationship

text: When they clash, they step away and write to each other, and often change rooms, giving time to think and lowering emotionality; often the issue fades once tired or hungry states pass.
title: Answering Juicy Questions About Our Relationship

text: He put business ahead of the marriage for the first three years, both were miserable, and after they flipped priorities to marriage first he says their lives improved greatly.
title: Answering Juicy Questions About Our Relationship

text: He describes the most successful marriages as low expectations paired with high commitment: expect the partner may not change or may get worse, yet stay committed as long as core values hold.
title: Answering Juicy Questions About Our Relationship

text: He advises not catastrophizing small annoyances: note it, raise it when there is time, and if you forget by next conversation it likely was not important.
title: Answering Juicy Questions About Our Relationship

text: He picks the one highest-leverage task after long thought and spends his first six hours of each day on it, a habit held for over a decade.
title: Answering Juicy Questions About Our Relationship

text: He says finding the right business partner is among the hardest things, and that poor partnerships often explain why businesses stall; he could not have done it alone.
title: Answering Juicy Questions About Our Relationship

text: He notes that because both work in the same business they are nearly always in different seasons, so they shifted expectations of each other; scarcity of time makes shared time more cherished.
title: Answering Juicy Questions About Our Relationship

title: The Alex Hormozi Cookbook [REVEALED]

text: Greek yogurt is available in nearly any grocery store, so this breakfast works when traveling away from your usual routine.
title: The Alex Hormozi Cookbook [REVEALED]

title: The Alex Hormozi Cookbook [REVEALED]

title: The Alex Hormozi Cookbook [REVEALED]

text: Chop the lox roughly into bite-sized pieces so it does not pull off the bread, and toast bread hot with cold cream cheese so it stays crunchy.
title: The Alex Hormozi Cookbook [REVEALED]

text: He aims for roughly 100g protein per meal, eats mostly protein through the day, and saves carbs for when he eats them on purpose; three open-face sandwiches give about 90g.

text: Peeled cooked frozen shrimp with cocktail sauce is a cutting meal; shrimp is zero carbs and zero fat, and he found it filling due to volume.

text: Ultra-pasteurized carton egg whites give 100g protein with no fat or carbs and need no prep; mix with zero-sugar chocolate syrup and drink.

title: The Alex Hormozi Cookbook [REVEALED]

title: The Alex Hormozi Cookbook [REVEALED]

text: Water-packed tuna with Greek yogurt and yellow mustard makes a bowl of about 84g protein under 400 calories; three a day would keep you under 1,200 calories.
title: The Alex Hormozi Cookbook [REVEALED]

text: Chocolate egg whites can be microwaved without a pan and fluff up; about 90 seconds worked, and salsa on top adds little calories.
title: The Alex Hormozi Cookbook [REVEALED]

text: His daily breakfast is a ready-to-drink protein shake: around 84g protein for 460 calories total.
title: The Alex Hormozi Cookbook [REVEALED]

text: Bro nachos combine protein chips, no-bean chili, Greek yogurt as sour cream, and salsa; two bags of chips plus chili plus yogurt reach about 100g protein.

text: The company's mission is making real business education accessible to everyone. He says few credible people teach business, since the most credible are busy running companies, which left an opening for them.
title: How Acquisition.com Makes Money

text: The core targets are business owners and people one step away from that, such as wantrepreneurs. The latter are mostly helped for free, while owners who ascend are the ones eventually monetized.
title: How Acquisition.com Makes Money

text: Advisory practice has three levels priced around 5,000, 35,000 and 135,000 dollars. People enter at the lowest and a share moves upward; the top level is for those wanting more detailed help from Hormozi.
title: How Acquisition.com Makes Money

text: Small early conversions such as an email list signup, a free trial into a 9 dollar product, or a 30 dollar book give contact information and let them funnel people to higher-value services.
title: How Acquisition.com Makes Money

text: Excess cash goes into real estate, mostly multi-family, partly because it is tax efficient, and into a venture portfolio making small 1 to 5 percent bets or seeding companies sold through their audience.
title: How Acquisition.com Makes Money

text: He sees the best career path for strong advisory staff as launching ventures the company sponsors, since they will have applied the process across around 100 businesses.
title: How Acquisition.com Makes Money

text: A planned network membership for business owners would likely cost roughly 5,000 to 10,000 dollars per year in 2026, with AI consulting, community and industry calls, priced high enough to keep out non-owners.
title: How Acquisition.com Makes Money

text: A large base of owners gives negotiating power with vendors like agencies and credit card providers. He believes the savings could be so large that members would never want to leave.
title: How Acquisition.com Makes Money

text: For some businesses in the ecosystem, they may take stakes of 30 to 100 percent instead of small 1 to 5 percent chunks, letting them run independently.
title: How Acquisition.com Makes Money

text: He compares the structure to Disney: a big media brand at the top, the network as the scalable streaming-like piece, advisory as the in-person parks, and other companies as separate universes.
title: How Acquisition.com Makes Money

text: Going forward, deals especially in private equity are meant only for companies that can directly benefit their distribution base of business owners, rather than just companies they feel comfortable growing.
title: How Acquisition.com Makes Money

text: Almost all of their conversions into the advisory levels happen over the phone, handled by a phone sales team.
title: How Acquisition.com Makes Money

text: He says everything depends on making business education accessible, making free content better than others' paid content, and keeping premium brand credibility that they have done what they claim.
title: How Acquisition.com Makes Money

text: Their monetization sweet spot is business owners at about 500,000 to 50 million dollars in revenue. Below 500,000 it is more distributed, through platform ad revenue, low-ticket products and book sales.
title: How Acquisition.com Makes Money

text: For owners under 500,000 the goal is not direct monetization but helping them build businesses that ascend into the paying tier, opening later options such as investment, acquisition or other services.
title: How Acquisition.com Makes Money

text: He suggests every company should have a video sales letter selling the company itself to potential recruits.
title: How Acquisition.com Makes Money

text: To reach very large success, he believes you must concentrate your energy like a magnifying glass on the sun. Potential, intelligence or work ethic is the lens size, but it does nothing unless focused on one point.
title: Why Doing More Is Actually Making You Less Money

text: Before his breakthrough he ran nine businesses: six gyms, a chiropractor agency, a dental agency and a launch business. Revenue was a few million a year, and he felt spread thin and overwhelmed.
title: Why Doing More Is Actually Making You Less Money

text: Go where the money is. When customers repeatedly ask to buy something, treat it as marketplace feedback and build the business around it.
title: Why Doing More Is Actually Making You Less Money

text: None of his businesses ended up being what he first imagined; the market showed him what people wanted, sometimes forcing big pivots. Be a bloodhound for value by solving problems people pay for.
title: Why Doing More Is Actually Making You Less Money

text: If customers keep coming through one door and ignore the others, crush that one, remove the other doors and go all in on it instead of pushing them toward two or three.
title: Why Doing More Is Actually Making You Less Money

text: You cannot pursue every opportunity; you must say no to nearly all of them to make one worth pursuing. He stayed stuck on multi-year plateaus by chasing everything, and says to trade novelty for loyalty.
title: Why Doing More Is Actually Making You Less Money

text: Once he grasped how much work greatness takes, he felt sad realizing he has maybe two or three entrepreneurial seasons left. He plans to keep swinging with acquisition.com.
title: Why Doing More Is Actually Making You Less Money

text: Direct creative energy into what adds to the business, especially marketing, ads and content. He puts his ADD into content and writing, and the business does well when he is in writing mode because he interferes less.
title: Why Doing More Is Actually Making You Less Money

text: In his own experience, any change to sales, leadership or onboarding processes causes roughly a 20% performance drop at first, even if the change is better. It is anecdotal, not research.
title: Why Doing More Is Actually Making You Less Money

text: He only makes a change if he sees a risk-adjusted 20% improvement, meaning about a 40% improvement with a 50/50 chance. Left alone, people also tend to improve at their jobs.
title: Why Doing More Is Actually Making You Less Money

text: Testing has a cost. Changing several things at once ruins attribution, so you have about 52 tests a year at best, far fewer on the people side, perhaps one a quarter per department.
title: Why Doing More Is Actually Making You Less Money

text: Treat changes like a punch card with only about four per department per year, akin to Buffett's idea of a limited number of investments. Pick the bet with highest upside and likelihood.
title: Why Doing More Is Actually Making You Less Money

text: Keep a big list of ideas with an estimated value and likelihood next to each, rank them, and pull one only when the team has bandwidth.
title: Why Doing More Is Actually Making You Less Money

text: Instead of messaging the team about every idea, write it down. He only brings one forward if it beats the other roughly 50% ideas already pending. He has accepted that some imperfect things stay imperfect.
title: Why Doing More Is Actually Making You Less Money

text: People usually overestimate the payoff of a change, expecting 40% and getting 5%, while ignoring the guaranteed dip. Fast feedback loops across departments taught him this razor.
title: Why Doing More Is Actually Making You Less Money

text: Most entrepreneurs do not see the cost of changes because they lack real-time metrics such as NPS, ascension and churn, and they change so many things they never know what broke.
title: Why Doing More Is Actually Making You Less Money

text: Let ideas season for two to four weeks; if you still think about one after a month, it probably has legs. Buying on impulse is usually a bad decision.
title: Why Doing More Is Actually Making You Less Money

text: When pulling an idea from the list, it must be worth it, because the change will detonate a bomb in the business and it has to justify the aftermath.
title: Why Doing More Is Actually Making You Less Money

text: Vista's approach, as he relays it, is to dig through data to find the most valuable customer buckets, then expand and focus on that high lifetime value vein.
title: Pricing Lessons From a Private Equity God

text: Most companies do not score leads, prospects or customers by value. Scoring uses characteristics and behaviors to place people in buckets.
title: Pricing Lessons From a Private Equity God

text: He says the most advanced operators still do the fundamentals, and the Vista pricing head stressed simple systems and processes.
title: Pricing Lessons From a Private Equity God

text: Vista scores three segments separately: prospects, opportunities and customers, looking at each stage of the pipeline.
title: Pricing Lessons From a Private Equity God

text: Gym Launch reviewed 90 days of exits, escalations and hard-to-serve clients against the top-result, easiest clients to find differing traits.
title: Pricing Lessons From a Private Equity God

text: Gym Launch found worse results from non-gym-owners, part-time owners with outside jobs, those without a signed lease or own building, and those with no employees.
title: Pricing Lessons From a Private Equity God

text: Gym Launch began qualifying in October: at least 25 clients, signed lease, full-time owner, and ideally one employee or more.
title: Pricing Lessons From a Private Equity God

text: After qualifying, monthly gym sales dropped from over a hundred to about 40 to 50, yet escalations fell from 22 in the prior four weeks to zero.
title: Pricing Lessons From a Private Equity God

text: Poor-fit customers consumed most of the team's time and were worth less, which hurts scaling, operational efficiency and profit.
title: Pricing Lessons From a Private Equity God

text: Gym Launch tried signing people up for a year upfront, but a defined-end program worked much better, and the newly qualified customers paid more.
title: Pricing Lessons From a Private Equity God

text: Lowering the bar brings in unqualified people who cost effort, earn less and may blame the product when it is simply a poor fit for them.
title: Pricing Lessons From a Private Equity God

text: To find good and bad customers, review the last three months of departures and gather traits such as age, job, goals, what they signed up for, money down and continuity.
title: Pricing Lessons From a Private Equity God

text: Cutting inflow in half also cut operational overhead and the work spent serving poor-fit customers.
title: Pricing Lessons From a Private Equity God

text: Customers decide whether to stay at two early points: between sale and start, and during onboarding. Treating orientation as an afterthought loses lots of money.
title: Pricing Lessons From a Private Equity God

text: Onboarding should demonstrate the needed skills, do them with the customer, and have them repeat it, so they become self-sufficient. If it is rushed, expand the time.
title: Pricing Lessons From a Private Equity God

text: Between sale and onboarding, communicate deliberately, for example with a personalized video, swag, a letter, and texts.
title: Pricing Lessons From a Private Equity God

text: Expectations are everything: set proper expectations for what happens next and fulfill them, and trust with the prospect rises.
title: Pricing Lessons From a Private Equity God

text: Selling hot means setting expectations so high most customers cannot hit them. Selling toward behavior and long-term change shifts the prospect's time frame.
title: Pricing Lessons From a Private Equity God

text: Gym Launch now shares average results, around 16,000 in the first six weeks, instead of top testimonials, and explains that half of clients get less.
title: Pricing Lessons From a Private Equity God

text: He suggests ideally selling on the bottom 25 percent of results so customers overachieve from a low baseline.
title: Pricing Lessons From a Private Equity God

text: Disappointment with a good start comes from expectations set in the sale and orientation being too high for the average person.
title: Pricing Lessons From a Private Equity God

text: Gym Launch found entrepreneurs a poor demographic; it may serve them with a self-paced info product instead of the intense program.
title: Pricing Lessons From a Private Equity God

text: He thinks the too-small-market excuse mostly protects egos. Hitting an ad spend ceiling usually means poor ads and not knowing awareness levels, since many advertise only to people already aware of the solution.
title: You can make way more money than you think

text: Even in local markets, a city of hundreds of thousands can support a business needing around 200 customers; something else is holding you back.
title: You can make way more money than you think

text: He was startled to learn a gym software company he had never heard of did about 10 million a month, purely via outbound, roughly five times his revenue then; it broke his belief about outbound.
title: You can make way more money than you think

text: Extra competitors do not cut your pie into equal shares. Your current slice is one platform and one medium; content, ads and one-to-one outreach across many platforms are mostly untouched.
title: You can make way more money than you think

text: Within a single platform, check whether you use every format, such as stories, images, carousels, shorts, longer videos and community posts, and how many you produce.

text: Fierce competition often signals the biggest rewards: more fish where the water is bloodiest. Business advice is crowded and he still entered it.
title: You can make way more money than you think

text: Start by constraining your pond to be the biggest fish in a puddle, then grow to pond, lake and ocean as skill and experience grow. He moved from training to nutrition to gyms to business.
title: You can make way more money than you think

text: Niches mean fewer competitors and fewer comparisons, so you can charge niche prices with more profit and pricing power. The upside is capped, but higher than people assume.
title: You can make way more money than you think

text: Small owners often never define their market and accept anyone with a credit card, which confuses customers about what the business stands for.
title: You can make way more money than you think

text: Not getting enough leads and having too small a market are different issues. Fix leads by making content in more places, more of it, better, then adding ads and outreach for omnipresence.
title: You can make way more money than you think

text: Do more in more places, better, for a long time. He says you likely have not capped the market; you lack the skill to capture more of it yet.
title: You can make way more money than you think

text: A single-location business can grow by extracting more from its four walls: knock down walls, add seats, extend hours, and shorten classes. He cut class times from 45 to 30 minutes, fitting about one and a half times more classes.
title: You can make way more money than you think

text: His rule is one avatar, one product, one channel until a million a year. Local businesses are the exception in C or D markets, likely under 50,000 people within about 10 miles, where several channels are needed.
title: You can make way more money than you think

text: When four walls max out, open another location. One store may not be a 100 million opportunity, but duplicating and scaling a proven model can be; he says nearly any business can reach 10 million by opening in new markets.
title: You can make way more money than you think

text: Most goals are achievable in your current vehicle; people are impatient and chase shiny objects. Switching resets your years of head start, and growth is easier when bigger, so a new venture stays behind.
title: You can make way more money than you think

text: Every business has a built-in difficulty, a feature not a bug, and that difficulty is why you are paid. Cleaning struggles with talent; fitness struggles with acquisition and retention.
title: You can make way more money than you think

text: Business models have distinct growth shapes: info starts fast but is hard to scale, software starts slow then scales fast, ecom scales fast but strains cash flow, services are slowest but steady.
title: You can make way more money than you think

text: Info and coaching make money fast but have almost no revenue retention because people learn and leave, so scaling is hard.
title: You can make way more money than you think

text: Industries balance supply and demand: popular fields make talent easy but customers churn, while supply-constrained fields like accounting retain customers but struggle to hire. Being the inverse of your industry means doing something very right or very wrong.
title: You can make way more money than you think

text: Years spent not fully committed lead to frustration at slow growth. He compares constant looking for the next opportunity to a wandering eye in a marriage, and says doubling down usually takes less time.
title: You can make way more money than you think

text: Restate external blame as a personal skill gap, such as lacking the skill to get leads or hire a salesperson. Then you own the outcome and can change it.
title: You can make way more money than you think

text: Winning despite a hard past makes a stronger story that inspires others. When torn at 85 between choices, pick the cooler story, and he thinks you should take the hard option because you would already have taken the easy one.
