text: Hormozi calls his approach the grandfather frame: imagine being 85 and getting to return to your current body and life, then view today through that older self's eyes.
title: How I Hacked My Brain to Feel Gratitude All the Time

text: He says he has struggled to feel gratitude for most of his life despite having plenty to be grateful for, and gratitude journals and daily meditations never stuck for him, though they may work for others.
title: How I Hacked My Brain to Feel Gratitude All the Time

text: He defines nostalgia as gratitude felt in the present for past circumstances, because looking back lets us skip the daily minutiae and moods and see the big picture we appreciate.
title: How I Hacked My Brain to Feel Gratitude All the Time

text: He applies the frame each morning: noticing a body without joint pain or arthritis, coffee with his wife six years into marriage, and Vegas being less developed, all as things his 85-year-old self would treasure.
title: How I Hacked My Brain to Feel Gratitude All the Time

text: He considers the grandfather frame the most powerful frame he has found, because it works through gratitude he can actually feel and lowers his anxiety and stress about outcomes, since they will not matter in the long run.
title: How I Hacked My Brain to Feel Gratitude All the Time

text: He thinks the frame also helps business judgment: viewing decisions within the whole of life stops him chasing short-term dollars, since an 85-year-old has nothing to prove.
title: How I Hacked My Brain to Feel Gratitude All the Time

text: He feels nostalgia for past hardships like sleeping on the floor at his gyms and taking many sales calls for months, and reframes present work as something he gets to do rather than has to do.
title: How I Hacked My Brain to Feel Gratitude All the Time

text: He describes his life as moving from anger, to awareness of the gap from happiness, to giving up on optimizing for happiness, which he believes moved him nearer to joy.
title: How I Hacked My Brain to Feel Gratitude All the Time

text: He distinguishes joy from happiness: joy comes from within and is independent of circumstance, while happiness tends to come from external circumstances. He admires older people who have this internal joy and gratitude.
title: How I Hacked My Brain to Feel Gratitude All the Time

text: He notes that a classmate who was successful and full of plans died recently, reminding him that tomorrow is not guaranteed and that every day is effectively the last time.
title: How I Hacked My Brain to Feel Gratitude All the Time

text: Methods such as DM hacks or viral hashtags expire, while the economics of the business itself endure, so the model is the thing worth learning.
title: How I Would Build a Business in 2026 (If I Had to Start Over)

text: The first rule of business is to avoid going out of business, and cash flow is what prevents that. Bootstrapped owners, about 99% of businesses, must build a business that generates cash.
title: How I Would Build a Business in 2026 (If I Had to Start Over)

text: The business that makes more money per customer than competitors can spend more to acquire customers, so it can outbid everyone in the attention auction and dominate the ad space.
title: How I Would Build a Business in 2026 (If I Had to Start Over)

text: If a business loses money acquiring customers it needs a budget cap, but if it makes about $1,000 from a $100 spend, it should spend as much as it possibly can.
title: How I Would Build a Business in 2026 (If I Had to Start Over)

text: His gym six-week challenge took roughly $600 on day one, about $200 of supplements within 48 hours, and about $2,000 annual prepay at week three, blending to around $1,000 in 30 days versus a $21 offer.
title: How I Would Build a Business in 2026 (If I Had to Start Over)

text: He funded each gym opening by putting $5,000 in the bank, running ads daily, and collecting roughly $100,000 in presales in month one, which paid for equipment and buildout before opening.
title: How I Would Build a Business in 2026 (If I Had to Start Over)

text: Measure what a customer is worth in gross profit within the first 30 days, since most small businesses can only carry cash outlay about that long. Aim to recover acquisition cost within 30 days.
title: How I Would Build a Business in 2026 (If I Had to Start Over)

text: Without knowing your business math, you blame methods like Facebook or outbound when the real issue may be the model.
title: How I Would Build a Business in 2026 (If I Had to Start Over)

text: LTGP, LTV and CLV roughly mean the same thing: what you earn from a customer after delivery costs. CAC is the cost to acquire a customer. The ratio of the two is the key number.
title: How I Would Build a Business in 2026 (If I Had to Start Over)

text: To estimate CAC, add a full year of marketing, ad, labor and commission costs and divide by new customers gained. For lifetime revenue, divide revenue by total customers, then multiply by gross margin.
title: How I Would Build a Business in 2026 (If I Had to Start Over)

text: Napkin math over a long period tends to be most accurate because it smooths out good and bad months. Divide a full year of delivery costs by customers to get cost per customer.
title: How I Would Build a Business in 2026 (If I Had to Start Over)

text: Silicon Valley's 3:1 rule holds only when lead generation, sales and delivery are all automated. He says use about 6:1 if two are automated, 9:1 minimum if one, and over 12:1 if none.
title: How I Would Build a Business in 2026 (If I Had to Start Over)

text: Acquisition costs tend to rise over time through higher CPMs, more competitors and colder audiences, so what you have today is likely your best cost per customer ever.
title: How I Would Build a Business in 2026 (If I Had to Start Over)

text: Scaling adds management layers, later customers are less sold and may be worth less, and new hires are weaker at first, so a higher ratio provides cash padding.
title: How I Would Build a Business in 2026 (If I Had to Start Over)

text: Ways to raise lifetime value: raise price, cut costs, upsell, downsell, add financing, change collection terms, and cross-sell. Downsells must be used carefully because selling cheap to buyers of expensive things loses money.
title: How I Would Build a Business in 2026 (If I Had to Start Over)

text: Ways to lower CAC: improve the offer, produce more and better ad creatives, split test pages, follow-up and phone scripts, and advertise where eyeballs cost less. Cheap leads do not guarantee customers.
title: How I Would Build a Business in 2026 (If I Had to Start Over)

text: Optimize the return between LTV and CAC, not a single cheap number. A $5,000 LTV at $500 CAC beats a 5:1 business even though each customer costs over twice as much.
title: How I Would Build a Business in 2026 (If I Had to Start Over)

text: Broadening ads to get cheaper customers brings more low-quality ones. Higher-caliber customers typically widen the LTV to CAC ratio, so be willing to pay more for them.
title: How I Would Build a Business in 2026 (If I Had to Start Over)

text: A jewelry-industry donor told him that when demand rises, you cut supply. At the charity event, ticket prices went from 10,000 to 25,000 dollars and more people still bought.
title: How To Charge Exorbitant Prices

text: Chanel and Louis Vuitton stimulate demand by making stores uncertain about which bags arrive and when production stops, so shoppers face one-of-a-kind items that are not sold online, supporting higher prices.
title: How To Charge Exorbitant Prices

text: Many buyers would have paid far more than the price they were quoted. Selling five day-slots at 20,000 dollars each may miss the top two buyers, who might have paid 200,000 for that day.
title: How To Charge Exorbitant Prices

text: A common mistake is cutting supply but keeping the lower price. When supply drops, you should move along the demand curve and raise the price accordingly.
title: How To Charge Exorbitant Prices

text: Textbook demand curves assume a static market, but marketing shifts demand outward by telling more people about you, which lets you push prices further up the curve.
title: How To Charge Exorbitant Prices

text: Selling three days at 100,000 dollars earns more than five at 20,000, is easier to deliver, reduces operational drag, adds profit, creates a premium feel, and allows over-delivery.
title: How To Charge Exorbitant Prices

text: He sees many entrepreneurs spend too much effort on supply and too little on generating demand.
title: How To Charge Exorbitant Prices

text: Delay satisfying demand: tease, hint at upcoming things, and keep a waiting list. The point where people feel rejected is much further away than most assume, and a waiting list adds allure.
title: How To Charge Exorbitant Prices

text: Full capacity is your own decision, even zero supply. Holding supply back builds pressure like a pot, and you should release steam only periodically, because that pressure is your pricing power.
title: How To Charge Exorbitant Prices

text: Envy is wanting something another person has that you lack. Jealousy is fear that someone will take something you already have. Naming which one you feel lets you analyze the feeling and choose actions.
title: Negative Emotional Motivation

text: He believes envy does not make you happy but does make you successful. He sees it as an adaptive trait from our old brain, seen in animals too, pushing a group to match its top contributor.
title: Negative Emotional Motivation

text: Naming an emotion precisely, such as envy, instead of vaguely disliking or being angry at someone, brought him relief and lets him tell people directly that he is envious of them.
title: Negative Emotional Motivation

text: He says admitting envy tends to create candor, and people usually respond by offering help rather than getting defensive. Faking happiness for someone is detectable through tone and looks.
title: Negative Emotional Motivation

text: He would rather deal with people who do right things for wrong reasons than wrong things for right reasons, valuing the outcome over the motive.
title: Negative Emotional Motivation

text: He relays a story of a top Navy Seal who as an EMT cared little about patients but wanted the best stats and survival rates for status. Hormozi would choose that EMT if he were the patient.
title: Negative Emotional Motivation

text: Naming an emotion and asking whether it is pushing you toward something helpful or harmful increases the time between emotion and action. He says a longer gap generally means better, more rational decisions.
title: Negative Emotional Motivation

text: His big picture: name the emotion, use the space to decide better, then judge whether the resulting action helps or hurts you, so you judge what you do rather than why you do it.
title: Negative Emotional Motivation

text: Citing Dan Sullivan, he says wanting something is reason enough, since asking why you want it rarely changes the desire.
title: Negative Emotional Motivation

text: Allowing himself to desire things freed up attention once spent judging his wants. He thinks wanting is fine as long as it hurts neither others nor himself.
title: Negative Emotional Motivation

text: Every sale ends with either the buyer selling you or you selling them, and the person who cares most about the buyer is the one who makes the sale.
title: How To Win Sales Without Being Skilled (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Approach each sale believing you care more about the buyer's best interest than they do. He calls the way people sense whether you serve your agenda or theirs commission breath.
title: How To Win Sales Without Being Skilled (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: People bring emotional baggage, shame and guilt to a sale, so building rapport enough for them to be real with you is hard. Once they are real, he says you have effectively already won.
title: How To Win Sales Without Being Skilled (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Some gym owners who are not the most skilled sellers still close well because they visibly love fitness and helping people. Buyers believe they act in their interest, which is why conviction in your product matters.
title: How To Win Sales Without Being Skilled (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: If you truly hold that care, you can force buyers to confront limiting beliefs, such as asking whose responsibility it is that they fell off track, while making clear you are helping, not being mean.
title: How To Win Sales Without Being Skilled (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Sales is coaching with an outcome defined over a period of time.
title: How To Win Sales Without Being Skilled (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: The gym owner used the same script from his first 25 reps through his last nine. He realized at rep 25 he had been selling on his own agenda, not the buyer's.
title: How To Win Sales Without Being Skilled (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Advanced people are defined by outcomes, not tactics. Advanced lifters use the same tactics as novices; they never skip the basics, and top salespeople are consistent the same way.
title: How To Win Sales Without Being Skilled (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: He sees three breaking points in an entrepreneur's development, starting with skills. Getting customers alone bundles many skills: copy, creative, landing pages, buying traffic, nurturing leads, choosing a sales format, scripting, closing and payments.
title: How To Win Sales Without Being Skilled (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: The second block is character traits such as patience, endurance and discipline. They separate the very successful from the moderately successful, because they let you execute your skills consistently.
title: How To Win Sales Without Being Skilled (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: The third block is beliefs about the world, the market, what is possible, and acceptable speed and excellence in the organization. These come top down from the founder.
title: How To Win Sales Without Being Skilled (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: He thinks the three blocks cycle at every level: you must maintain the old skills, traits and beliefs while building new ones for the next level, which is why entrepreneurship forces growth.
title: How To Win Sales Without Being Skilled (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Hormozi learned from a Baltimore fur retailer owner, whom he observed as a teenager, a method for getting people to say no in order to end up saying yes on additional purchases.
title: How To Close Prospects By Saying 'No' First (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: He says the technique fits simple bolt-on upsells rather than complex core offers, such as supplements, scarves, orthotics, dental extras or night serums. Typical upsell uptake is about 20-30%, while this approach reportedly reaches 90% or more.
title: How To Close Prospects By Saying 'No' First (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: At the furrier, customers who came for free earmuffs with coat storage were asked whether they wanted anything else. Most said no, which quietly locked in the conditioning service, adding a couple hundred dollars per coat across thousands of coats.
title: How To Close Prospects By Saying 'No' First (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: After recommending a set of products, ask a negative question such as whether they want to buy anything else. Their reflexive no counts as agreement to the recommendation you just made.
title: How To Close Prospects By Saying 'No' First (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Another version: tell the customer they surely do not want to pay full retail, then offer to ship with a discount to the address on file. Their no leads to a yes.
title: How To Close Prospects By Saying 'No' First (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: He explains it as customers being so conditioned to avoid buying that they agree to purchases while refusing to be sold. He calls it one of the strongest sales techniques he has seen.
title: How To Close Prospects By Saying 'No' First (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: The furrier repeated the pattern during the visit: after the earmuffs, he asked about anything else beyond storage, then suggested fixing a loose button or seam. Customers kept saying no and kept buying.
title: How To Close Prospects By Saying 'No' First (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: He thinks the method works best for hand-to-hand small upsells, which can drive big profits. Like fries and a coke, the money is in high-margin extras rather than the core offer, and small business owners often miss this.
title: How To Close Prospects By Saying 'No' First (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: He says winners ask how a tactic could work in their business, while losers insist their business is different. He urges creativity in applying it.
title: How To Close Prospects By Saying 'No' First (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: He spends only about 5 to maybe 10 percent of a launch budget in week one for creative testing, keeps the next two weeks roughly flat, and puts 60 to 70 percent into the final week.
title: Building a $3,000,000 Business for a Stranger in 31 Minutes | Scale or Fail

text: Static ads take seconds to make, so he wants creative counted in hundreds; screenshots from a customer group can serve as ads.
title: Building a $3,000,000 Business for a Stranger in 31 Minutes | Scale or Fail

text: Have every new customer make a sticker in their first seven days, which onboards them and yields an ad each; 200 customers per launch means 200 ads.
title: Building a $3,000,000 Business for a Stranger in 31 Minutes | Scale or Fail

text: If ad performance collapses when spend rises, the ads probably target only product or offer aware people; add pain-driven hooks to reach more pain-aware audiences.
title: Building a $3,000,000 Business for a Stranger in 31 Minutes | Scale or Fail

text: He suggests a physical product premium for annual buyers and selling only annual during the launch, then sending everyone to monthly after the cart closes.
title: Building a $3,000,000 Business for a Stranger in 31 Minutes | Scale or Fail

text: Positioning the launch event as a trial of the membership could convert all traffic to continuity instead of about 20 percent, then push everyone toward annual.
title: Building a $3,000,000 Business for a Stranger in 31 Minutes | Scale or Fail

text: He advises optimizing campaigns around purchases and tracking earnings per click.
title: Building a $3,000,000 Business for a Stranger in 31 Minutes | Scale or Fail

text: To scale, go sub-specific with avatar callouts: drain many small ponds rather than advertising to the whole ocean with two ads.
title: Building a $3,000,000 Business for a Stranger in 31 Minutes | Scale or Fail

text: He describes her business as media arbitrage: whether you can buy clicks for less than they earn, which he calls very scalable once the math works.
title: Building a $3,000,000 Business for a Stranger in 31 Minutes | Scale or Fail

text: He says the events we go through shape us more than we shape them, and how we view a traumatic event changes how much it affects and forms us.
title: Want to be rich? Stop letting THIS affect you...

text: He argues trauma is partly a label: identical facts are treated as traumatic in one culture or era and normal in another, so the meaning attached to an event is what makes it matter.
title: Want to be rich? Stop letting THIS affect you...

text: Beliefs like needing to mourn to prove you cared are inherited statements we choose to accept; he suggests monitoring what those statements are, since the opposite belief could just as easily be held.
title: Want to be rich? Stop letting THIS affect you...

text: He says a brain essentially creates and destroys meaning, deciding what is a threat or worth reinforcing. Controlling what you deem meaningful, he argues, shifts the odds in your favor.
title: Want to be rich? Stop letting THIS affect you...

text: He cites the idea that nobody yells at a rock: if you control your response to stimulus, treating things as unimportant, others eventually leave you alone. He applies it to labeling events good or bad.
title: Want to be rich? Stop letting THIS affect you...

text: Before discussing a word like trauma, define it, because each person's meaning differs. He compares this to academic writing that defines terms up front, since words are buckets for thoughts.
title: Want to be rich? Stop letting THIS affect you...

text: At about 19 or 20 he became a born-again Christian, then drifted away and spent roughly five years studying apologetics before ending up not believing.
title: Want to be rich? Stop letting THIS affect you...

text: He says both good-person and faith-based salvation systems create a false binary with an arbitrary 50 percent line, which is his simplest reason for not believing.
title: Want to be rich? Stop letting THIS affect you...

text: After becoming sad, he adopted a slogan of rejecting happiness as a goal and doing what he thinks is cool. He calls this the first break in the chain and wildly freeing.
title: Want to be rich? Stop letting THIS affect you...

text: Stopping judging himself for being unhappy made it stop mattering. He now does what he wants while keeping a long-term view, like writing books and building courses he enjoys.
title: Want to be rich? Stop letting THIS affect you...

text: He says being in the 1% means not doing what 99% do, which requires uncomfortable conversations. Stating your beliefs well can make people feel attacked, so he talks about this less publicly.
title: Want to be rich? Stop letting THIS affect you...

text: He doesn't complain when a restaurant order comes back wrong. For a flawed ad campaign he'd be annoyed but would simply say to fix it and try again.
title: Want to be rich? Stop letting THIS affect you...

text: His analogy: life is a casino where everyone plays dealt cards and accumulates chips, but death pushes all the chips back to the table, so accumulated wealth is a fake game that ends empty-handed.
title: Want to be rich? Stop letting THIS affect you...

text: Buying land in Austin made the analogy real: prior owners each thought it was theirs, then died or sold. He sees assets as chips that get amassed and redistributed.
title: Want to be rich? Stop letting THIS affect you...

text: He argues estate planning matters little: after many generations heirs are diluted to ordinary humans, and giving unmanaged resources to family can destroy them. So build something you think is cool.
title: Want to be rich? Stop letting THIS affect you...

text: He says his views are simply how he sees the world and beliefs that served him well, not a projection onto others, and that he did not intend to offend.
title: Want to be rich? Stop letting THIS affect you...

text: Hormozi says being a recurring revenue business is not a yes-or-no matter; the better question is how recurring a business is, and any business can become more recurring.
title: Netflix's Recurring Revenue Tactics Can Scale Any Business

text: He states that for most businesses, small or large, adding recurring revenue is the single greatest way to increase enterprise value.
title: Netflix's Recurring Revenue Tactics Can Scale Any Business

text: He says his physical products business raised customer lifetime value two and a half times by adding recurring revenue.
title: Netflix's Recurring Revenue Tactics Can Scale Any Business

text: Consumption drives stickiness: if people keep using and enjoying a product, as with Netflix or Spotify, they keep paying even without contracts.
title: Netflix's Recurring Revenue Tactics Can Scale Any Business

text: Raise consumption through better onboarding, improving the product's actual value and making it more habit-forming, so people want to keep using it.
title: Netflix's Recurring Revenue Tactics Can Scale Any Business

text: Collateral: secure the recurring fee against something the customer needs kept, such as stored goods, files in Dropbox or contacts in a CRM, so they stay and pay.
title: Netflix's Recurring Revenue Tactics Can Scale Any Business

text: Switching cost, both time and money, boosts retention, and sunk cost adds to it. Example: a required one-time 5,000 dollar start fee before a 100 dollar monthly plan would lower cancellations.
title: Netflix's Recurring Revenue Tactics Can Scale Any Business

text: The harder something is to get into, the harder it is psychologically to leave; a big head makes the recurring tail stickier.
title: Netflix's Recurring Revenue Tactics Can Scale Any Business

text: Fewer alternatives make revenue stickier. Patents, trade secrets, being the best, or niching down all reduce the choices a customer has.
title: Netflix's Recurring Revenue Tactics Can Scale Any Business

text: Control of money flow: the less visible a fee is to the payer, such as one taken off the top before payment, the stickier it is. He frames this as economics, not ethics.
title: Netflix's Recurring Revenue Tactics Can Scale Any Business

text: When customers tie their identity to a cause, as with churches, charities, political donations or brands, they keep paying. Building a movement inside a business makes revenue stickier.
title: Netflix's Recurring Revenue Tactics Can Scale Any Business

text: Community keeps people paying because they want to stay consistent with an identity they hold and avoid giving it up.
title: Netflix's Recurring Revenue Tactics Can Scale Any Business

text: Contracts add stickiness. Example: selling a 12,000 dollar six-payment package instead of 2,000 monthly, when month-to-month lasts about four months, likely gains an extra month or two.
title: Netflix's Recurring Revenue Tactics Can Scale Any Business

text: People tend to honor stated commitments, so getting them to say they will stay six months keeps more of them, though it may make the sale harder and requires balance.
title: Netflix's Recurring Revenue Tactics Can Scale Any Business

text: He says he felt wealthiest when he had $100,000 in the bank, more than at his later big exits, because it ended worry about rent, bills and groceries and let him think long-term.
title: If I Wanted to Make My First $100K in 2026, I’d Do This

text: Step one is cutting every cost, food, housing and car, so surplus cash flow exists to reinvest in skills and take more risk. Ideal car is a paid-off clunker.
title: If I Wanted to Make My First $100K in 2026, I’d Do This

text: Step two is reclaiming time. For a nine-to-five worker, the hours before and after work are the two four-hour blocks to use rather than scrolling.
title: If I Wanted to Make My First $100K in 2026, I’d Do This

text: He says focus comes from subtraction: remove everything that does not matter and what remains is focus.
title: If I Wanted to Make My First $100K in 2026, I’d Do This

text: Without a day job, he splits time into three four-hour blocks: promotion, delivery to paying customers, and building the future by finding and prioritizing opportunities.
title: If I Wanted to Make My First $100K in 2026, I’d Do This

text: Makers do best with empty calendars; managers thrive on many short touchpoints. Keep the modes separated because task switching kills productivity. He keeps Mondays for manager work and protects the first hours of his day.
title: If I Wanted to Make My First $100K in 2026, I’d Do This

text: Choose a skill people already pay for. For consumers, review your own card or bank statement; businesses pay for things like ads, content, outreach and funnels. Each could support a large business.
title: If I Wanted to Make My First $100K in 2026, I’d Do This

text: Learning means same condition, new behavior. If content you consume does not tell you what to do differently, it is not helping.
title: If I Wanted to Make My First $100K in 2026, I’d Do This

text: He prefers the framing of 10,000 iterations over 10,000 hours, since it assumes failure and improvement, and feedback loops are required; even a post that flops is feedback.
title: If I Wanted to Make My First $100K in 2026, I’d Do This

text: The fastest way to learn a skill is to hire someone very good one-on-one, which he did even when he could barely afford it.
title: If I Wanted to Make My First $100K in 2026, I’d Do This

text: Learning loop: gather high volume of examples, study the top ten percent, find what they share that the rest lack, test differences one at a time, avoid the bottom ninety percent's mistakes, repeat over new batches.
title: If I Wanted to Make My First $100K in 2026, I’d Do This

text: Spend money in three buckets: tools, implementation help such as courses, communities and tutoring, and trial attempts like ads or editing software. Saving alone will not reach 100K.
title: If I Wanted to Make My First $100K in 2026, I’d Do This

text: He notes self-made billionaires mostly built wealth from active income they could put at risk, and you cannot take risk without time and money.
title: If I Wanted to Make My First $100K in 2026, I’d Do This

text: Step six: do not raise your lifestyle. Aim to be rich, not look rich; 100K in the bank matters, not revenue. He knows people earning $40,000 monthly who spent it all.
title: If I Wanted to Make My First $100K in 2026, I’d Do This

text: When his first gym paid him about $20,000 monthly, he still paid $400 rent in a shared room, keeping cash for a new location, learning and conferences.
title: If I Wanted to Make My First $100K in 2026, I’d Do This

text: He recalls an economics class graph showing a 71 correlation between subjective well-being and the strength of the relationship with your significant other.

text: He says a spouse marries two people: who you are now and who you want to become, so make sure they love both.

text: He distinguishes growth from change: growth is more of what you are in your current direction, while change is being made into someone different. He calls treating a partner as a project a terrible way to live.

text: He argues not knowing what you want from life is your problem to solve. He thinks wanting different things is a fine reason not to be with someone, even if the couple is married.
title: If I Were Single and Starting Over, This Is What I Would Do

text: He says a spouse is an asset or liability, and liabilities lose value over time. He prefers a partner who keeps growing over one relying on a genetic lottery of looks.

text: Every business must define the core actions that increase its revenue. If the owner cannot define them, employees certainly cannot know them either.
title: Watch This If You Have a Service Business

text: If a business is not supply constrained but demand constrained, lead generation is the issue, and the activity is content, affiliates or paid ads, or people doing those for you.
title: Watch This If You Have a Service Business

text: For local businesses, existing local trust means funnels need less complexity, and one or two conversation closes work even at high ticket prices. The downside is a small market, so you must dominate it.
title: Watch This If You Have a Service Business

text: Building a brand long-term expands the radius people will travel to reach you and the premium they will pay, as with a clinic that has a national reputation.
title: Watch This If You Have a Service Business

text: When stuck in the swamp, cash flow is the biggest need. His order of operations is pricing and packaging first, then feed freed cash into ads with attribution, then raise content cadence for thought leadership.
title: Watch This If You Have a Service Business

text: Serving SMBs means their volatility becomes yours. He says CAC only rises, churn eats the business, and margins compress even as revenue grows.
title: Watch This If You Have a Service Business

text: For SMB customers paying roughly 1,500 to 3K a month, average stick is 4 to 6 months, which makes that the churn sweet spot to avoid.
title: Watch This If You Have a Service Business

text: SMB services work only at the cheap end, around 400 a month or less, with almost nothing to deliver, where he says sticks reach 30 to 40 months. Otherwise go upmarket to customers who know their metrics.
title: Watch This If You Have a Service Business

text: He says the middle price zone for SMB services is a dead zone: either go low with near-zero delivery or go high with a sophisticated avatar.
title: Watch This If You Have a Service Business

text: Do not solve problems that do not exist. If AI is not showing up in churn or other metrics, he would not rebuild the product because of a narrative.
title: Watch This If You Have a Service Business

text: He suggests prepaying for the quarter to offset CAC when adding paid inbound, since media spend adds to sales commission cost.
title: Watch This If You Have a Service Business

text: Use AI workflows to cut headcount and lift margin, so cash flow lets you accept a negative quarter on acquisition, knowing a long stick will repay it.
title: Watch This If You Have a Service Business

text: He says hard things stay hard: courses have sticky-less customers who expect you to do everything, so a new business will not be easier.
title: Watch This If You Have a Service Business

text: If supply constrained, create operating leverage: offshore talent giving each person two to three times capacity, so external headcount grows without internal headcount.
title: Watch This If You Have a Service Business

text: An AI-first company must first be data-first, because AI works on data. Build the data architecture, then layer AI on top.
title: Watch This If You Have a Service Business

text: He sees the current AI wave as the next once-in-a-generation boom, comparable to the move from CDs to cloud software over the past 25 years.
title: Watch This If You Have a Service Business

text: Work-life balance has no right answer, only preference. Dissatisfaction comes from wanting both outcomes, so either want less or trade more.
title: Watch This If You Have a Service Business

text: To grow bigger without working more, you may accept a short-term profit hit to hire better talent, and you need a vision big enough for their aspirations.
title: Watch This If You Have a Service Business

text: He believes he has only four or five big seasons left, and compares entrepreneurs to Buffett's punch card idea: fewer chances mean better choices.
title: Watch This If You Have a Service Business

text: Keep passive investments passive and active work active, since active income likely gives far better returns than squeezing passive returns with more time.
title: Watch This If You Have a Service Business

text: At a certain home-services scale you need an internal sales academy: recruiting, nurture, onboarding and retention for salespeople, parallel to demand generation.
title: Watch This If You Have a Service Business

text: Track the recruiting funnel stats as reliably as ad stats, and spend reliably on supply generation just as on demand generation.
title: Watch This If You Have a Service Business
