text: Hormozi's company holds the belief that the only people who ever hate you are people who are not ahead of you.
title: How to Get Rich [Full Interview with Dave Ramsey]

text: Hormozi tries to be as trustworthy as possible because reputation compounds on trust. Even though nearly all of his audience will never do business with him, he wants to do deals over the long term.
title: How to Get Rich [Full Interview with Dave Ramsey]

text: After a liquidity event, Hormozi had taken about 40 million home and asked many richer people where to invest. Their answers varied widely, and advice tailored to his own knowledge was what helped him.
title: How to Get Rich [Full Interview with Dave Ramsey]

text: Hormozi and his wife decided to stick to business and buy and grow businesses, since his knowledge and income came from business. He felt uneasy writing multi-million checks into buildings he did not understand.
title: How to Get Rich [Full Interview with Dave Ramsey]

text: Hormozi observes that most billionaires he has studied made their money in one or two vehicles they know exceedingly well, giving them an information advantage rather than a market advantage.
title: How to Get Rich [Full Interview with Dave Ramsey]

text: Hormozi says he has no debt and has paid cash for everything so far, including his acquisitions. He is not against debt, but tends to back away from loans near the edge.
title: How to Get Rich [Full Interview with Dave Ramsey]

text: Hormozi says many small business owners suffer from shiny object syndrome: when something gets hard, something new looks easy, and they swap the hard thing for it. He calls it uninformed optimism followed by informed pessimism.
title: How to Get Rich [Full Interview with Dave Ramsey]

text: Hormozi says one ratio, lifetime gross profit to acquisition cost, lets you decide better, predict how far ads can scale, and estimate profit and customer count. He says his biggest wealth growth came when it was maximized.
title: Business Owners: You NEED to Know This Number

text: Lifetime value should really mean lifetime gross profit: revenue over the customer's life minus the cost of delivering the product or service, since that is the profit you can reinvest or take out.
title: Business Owners: You NEED to Know This Number

text: With a 100 to 1 ratio and a reliable way to get customers, he says a business can scale enormously, since ad efficiency can drop to a tenth and still return ten to one.
title: Business Owners: You NEED to Know This Number

text: Lifetime value can be computed as price divided by churn rate, or price times average months retained. Twenty percent churn on a 2,000 monthly price gives 10,000.
title: Business Owners: You NEED to Know This Number

text: Fixed costs unrelated to delivery, like rent, are left out of gross profit, because an extra unit sold adds its gross profit straight to you to reinvest or keep.
title: Business Owners: You NEED to Know This Number

text: CAC is total marketing spend, ad spend, and sales payroll or commissions over a period, divided by customers acquired. Example: 20,000 total over 20 customers is 1,000 each.
title: Business Owners: You NEED to Know This Number

text: As you grow, customers get costlier because audiences get colder. A large ratio lets you afford higher CAC, enter new channels, and outspend competitors, which he calls an ethical competitive moat.
title: Business Owners: You NEED to Know This Number

text: He says owners who do not know these metrics may reach a few million a year but struggle to scale, since they cannot spend confidently up front or know when it pays back.
title: Business Owners: You NEED to Know This Number

text: For a more accurate CAC, use a full year of marketing payroll and ad spend divided by customers, which smooths out swings from campaigns and sales days.
title: Business Owners: You NEED to Know This Number

text: Service businesses often miss that delivery payroll is a cost of goods. Divide delivery payroll by customers to get delivery cost per customer, and model how it changes as you hire per set number of customers.
title: Business Owners: You NEED to Know This Number

text: A young business can estimate lifetime value: check how many of ten customers remain after 30 days. If nine stay, churn is 10 percent, so divide price by 10 percent, meaning about ten months.
title: Business Owners: You NEED to Know This Number

text: If several offers exist, advertise the one with the best ratio as the front end and ascend buyers into the others. Adding the expected back-end value to a front end raises its ratio.
title: Business Owners: You NEED to Know This Number

text: Which offer to advertise is a math question, not an opinion one. The exception is a tiny addressable market, but he says most listeners are nowhere near saturating theirs.
title: Business Owners: You NEED to Know This Number

text: A productized, easy-to-deliver, widely wanted offer can have a better ratio than a higher-ticket custom one, even with a lower ticket, because it repeats faster and scales as a machine.
title: Business Owners: You NEED to Know This Number

text: He believes business at the highest level looks the same across industries, so start with the one most likely to succeed rather than following passion, to avoid your passion becoming work.
title: Business Owners: You NEED to Know This Number

text: In the first year of Gym Launch his ratio was 100 to 1: he says 100,000 spent returned 10 million. He advises pushing hard through such a machine when you find one.
title: Business Owners: You NEED to Know This Number

text: Ways to raise lifetime gross profit: raise price, cut delivery cost, get repeat purchases, cross-sell, upsell, sell more quantity, or downsell to convert a no into a sale.
title: Business Owners: You NEED to Know This Number

text: The ratio also improves by cutting CAC without changing lifetime value. Advertising always reaches people, so the question is efficiency: cheaper eyeballs, or better conversion after paying for them.
title: Business Owners: You NEED to Know This Number

text: He builds lifetime value back to front, from the priciest offering, but improves CAC front to back, since early funnel steps affect larger percentages. Exception: a clear outlier stage well below industry average.
title: Business Owners: You NEED to Know This Number

text: The closest thing to a silver bullet for lowering CAC is nailing the offer, meaning what you package that everybody wants.
title: Business Owners: You NEED to Know This Number

text: He says CAC among the biggest businesses is often similar, since they sell to the same avatars, so the long-term difference is how much lifetime value they have stacked.
title: Business Owners: You NEED to Know This Number

text: Activities that do not bring customers cheaper or make customers worth more are probably a waste of time. The ratio also applies to investing, like buying a company and asking what it returns over its life.
title: Business Owners: You NEED to Know This Number

text: Hormozi says you cannot price out of your own wallet; you must charge based on the value you create for the buyer. He credits this for charging what others in his space charged a tenth of.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: The Value Equation has four parts: dream outcome, perceived likelihood of achievement (the opposite of risk), time delay, and effort and sacrifice. Longer time makes the offer less valuable.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: He built the value equation because advice to create value was vague. He asked what makes him buy, and concluded the most valuable thing is immediate, effortless, guaranteed and exactly what the buyer wants.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: For consumer sales, translate the dream outcome into something like status, and show how painful lacking it is. For business buyers the outcome is simply money, so effort goes into making it easier, faster and less risky.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: He found that customer acquisition cost across similar businesses in an industry is not that different if they are proficient at marketing. A rival with equal ad spend and sales staff earned about eight times less per customer than he did.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: He cites a survey where 85% of companies competed on price and only 1% won on it, calling low price the worst strategy. Being the second cheapest brings no reward.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: Buyers pay more when delivery is faster, when the product is guaranteed, risk-free or well proven, and when it needs little work from them. This turns the value equation into operational tasks for owners.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: Client financed acquisition means using customer payments as a loan to buy the next customer. Collect enough on the first sale to cover that customer's acquisition, the next customer's acquisition and product cost, then repeat.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: Hormozi calls the most significant arbitrage the gap between what it costs to acquire a customer and what a well-designed business earns from them. He says the richest people concentrate in businesses they understand.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: He says his big income jumps came in short bursts followed by plateaus. If you are stuck, find the constraint; for him it was capital, which client financed acquisition solved, though not hiring or key-person issues.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: For United Fitness he put about $5,000 down, signed a lease, and spent around $100 a day on ads, opening a new gym every six months without personal cash. Roughly $100,000 came in by week four.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: His gym economics: about $5 per lead, closing one in five on a $500 offer, so roughly $25 to acquire a customer paying $500. That reached six locations by age 25, after which trainers, managers and salespeople limited growth.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: His target: 30-day cash collected should equal two times CAC plus COGS. With $100 CAC and $50 COGS, that means collecting $300 from a new customer within 30 days.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: He fixates on 30 days because that is the window for interest-free credit card cash. A faster cash cycle allows repeating the loop more often per month, accelerating growth.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: Hormozi thinks many businesses stay poor because they believe industry norms, like billing after service on net terms, bind them. His fix is offering prepay incentives, such as a quarterly discount built into the price.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: He advises asking to get paid sooner, noting different workers and firms are paid before or after work depending on leverage. Get more cash by raising price or getting customers to buy more immediately.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: Customers dislike being sold but love buying, so make offers at convenient moments. In his gyms, prospects who declined membership were invited to a nutrition seminar and bought more on average than those who joined.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: Offering multiple offers helps customers solve the problem in more ways and brings the business more upfront cash. He notes people who make a new decision enter a hyper buying cycle.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: Sellers fear pushiness, but a purchase opens the next problem, like shoes then socks then shorts for a marathon runner. Just make the follow-on offer available; those uninterested can decline.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: Each upsell should still run through the value equation: identify the dream outcome, make it risk-free, faster and easier. Structure upsells and downsells to gather enough cash in 30 days to fund customers.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: Free trial example: a $100 trial cost, one in three converting, and one in three of those staying permanently gives about $900 permanent CAC against $1,200 annual revenue per customer.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: Hormozi calls wealth alchemy the gap between permanent CAC, annual revenue per customer and the enterprise value multiple. His example spends $9 million to add $12 million revenue and $120 million of value, untaxed.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: Leverage means getting more out than you put in. The same $900 CAC and $1,200 revenue is worth less in a business valued on profit at 7x than one valued at 10x revenue, so opportunity choice matters.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: Prefer a business that keeps customers over one that churns. Two firms with 300 customers differ hugely if one keeps prior cohorts while the other must reacquire, since time works for the retainer.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: He says investors value businesses using the same logic as the value equation: likelihood, effort and time delay. Retention is unglamorous, but he says it is where the real leverage occurs.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: He cites Starbucks as making about $14,000 lifetime value per customer while acquisition cost is similar to competitors, because its model keeps people returning. He distinguishes recurring subscriptions from reoccurring repeat buying.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: To find permanent customer cost, define permanent as staying two-plus years, find what share of customers qualify, and multiply CAC. Then target the type who stay; even doubled CAC wins if the hit rate improves.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: He says growth in business value is untaxed until you sell. His example: taxed profit of $3 million to $1.5 million, versus $120 million of value added, makes the effective tax rate tiny.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: He says he used to obsess over tax loopholes, but the biggest one is building something valuable and not cashing out, letting growth compound.
title: How to Make Money So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL

text: Trust means making yourself punishable by someone. Sharing a secret gives the other person something they could use against you, and you are betting they will not. Trust is defined by who takes the risk and who does the punishing.
title: How The Top 1% Actually Think About Trust

text: Four types of trust exist. You can be the one at risk or the one trusted with someone's risk, and the punisher can be the other person or the environment, as when someone fails to keep their word.
title: How The Top 1% Actually Think About Trust

text: The ceiling of a relationship depends on shared context each person has about the other. Volunteering things about yourself gives context, though it also gives them more ability to hurt you.
title: How The Top 1% Actually Think About Trust

text: Trust rests on zero punishment: you give a little, nothing bad happens, you give more. One betrayal can undo all earlier reinforcement, like a marriage of twenty years ending over one act.
title: How The Top 1% Actually Think About Trust

text: To be trustworthy, avoid punishing at two moments: when they disclose something, respond neutrally and reassuringly, and later never use it against them, including via sharing it with others who then hurt them.
title: How The Top 1% Actually Think About Trust

text: He recommends deliberately weighing what you gain versus risk each time you share something material. He rejects calling this merely transactional, saying everyone appraises this anyway, and naming it lets you pinpoint why you distrust someone.
title: How The Top 1% Actually Think About Trust

text: Being trustworthy makes you more influential, since people who trust you share more. When they trust your advice and good things follow, they are likelier to follow later advice.
title: How The Top 1% Actually Think About Trust

text: Breaking your word for a short-term benefit likely ends the relationship, though it may not die immediately. He compares it to a tree that looks alive but is dead inside.
title: How The Top 1% Actually Think About Trust

text: Hormozi argues that advice gains credibility when its seller demonstrates the advertised capability; he uses his own book marketing as a test of the methods he teaches.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: He presents $100M Offers as a Grand Slam Offer itself: useful material and a course requiring no registration, offered at a price far below its perceived value.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: With other business conditions unchanged, he says doubling the number of leads doubles the business.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: Knowing how to acquire additional leads gives entrepreneurs repeated opportunities to improve their business rather than depending on a single attempt succeeding.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: Making money requires an offer, prospective buyers, and a process that converts those prospects into customers.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: Warm outreach means communicating individually with people who already know you. He says it remains useful for both initial customers and new launches inside established companies.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: He describes free content as communicating publicly to multiple people who know you, rather than contacting each person separately.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: When promoting to an existing audience, maintain the content they originally followed you for and add promotional material to it. This requires producing more during the promotion.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: His launch content reportedly produced more than 400 million impressions and 194,000 registrations, using over 300 pieces weekly.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: He defines paid advertising as reaching unfamiliar people through one-to-many communication.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: For the book launch, he reports spending $275,000 to attract 137,000 people at approximately $2 per lead; the destination page converted 55% of visitors into opt-ins.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: He says paid advertising can generate leads without an existing following, begin with a few dollars daily, and expand through larger spending.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: Cold outreach means contacting unfamiliar people individually and privately to introduce what the business offers.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: Cold outreach requires obtaining contact details, deciding what to communicate, and reaching people when they can engage. It can begin with personal effort and later expand through staff and automation.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: Cold outreach lets a business select its prospects directly, allowing attention to focus on people who fit its desired customer profile.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: The Core Four comprises warm outreach, free content, paid advertising, and cold outreach. He distinguishes these communication methods from the people who perform them.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: Customers, employees, agencies, and affiliates are the four lead-getter categories: other people who use the Core Four to attract prospects for a business.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: Recruiting people who generate leads creates leverage because lead production can increase without requiring the owner to perform all the advertising personally.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: Use the Core Four to recruit lead getters; those people then apply the same advertising methods for your business.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: He reports that his previous book sold 467,000 copies without paid advertising, illustrating customers bringing in further customers.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: He reports that 23,722 affiliates promoted the launch through content, advertising, and email, bringing 104,361 people to the event.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: A lead magnet fully addresses a small, specific problem for free before introducing a paid solution to a subsequent problem.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: He says a well-designed lead magnet can multiply leads by 2, 5, or sometimes 10 while creating goodwill among the 99% he says will never purchase.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: Choose a lead-magnet problem whose solution encourages an eventual purchase; solving an unrelated problem can consume effort without helping sales.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: For a lead magnet, select the problem, design its solution and delivery, test its name, simplify consumption, improve quality, and provide an easy way to request additional help.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: He identifies the missing next step as a frequent lead-magnet mistake: people receive the free resource but are not clearly shown how to request more.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: For a new venture with no advertising budget, he recommends warm outreach as a dependable, inexpensive, low-risk way to obtain the first five customers.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: Begin warm outreach by assembling contacts, choosing a communication platform, tailoring the message, and initiating conversations. He also recommends encouraging introductions to friends.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: Content can improve other acquisition channels because prospects may inspect a business's profile and material after seeing an ad, then return to purchase once they trust it.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: Hook, Retain, Reward means attracting attention, sustaining consumption, and delivering the benefit that motivated someone to engage. He recommends lists, sequential explanations, and stories for retention.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: He says content should fulfill its initial promise at an appropriate moment; delivering too soon, delivering something different, or never delivering can reduce sharing.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: He argues that cold outreach suits operators who dislike appearing on camera or producing large amounts of content, and that sufficient outreach volume makes results more dependable.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: Cold-outreach contact lists can be purchased, gathered with software, or built manually when the business lacks money.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: His cold-outreach process includes personalization at scale, prepared responses to replies, automated message delivery, and follow-up intended to reach prospects when they can respond.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: He presents paid advertising as suitable for operators seeking rapid lead growth, accepting greater risk, and wanting to scale with relatively few employees.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: His paid-ad process has four stages: choose the advertising venue, reach appropriate prospects, create the advertisement, and obtain permission for subsequent contact.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: He argues that audience selection matters so much that an advertisement can succeed despite mediocre creative when the appropriate people see it.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: A referral occurs when someone directs an interested prospect to a business. He says anyone can refer, but considers existing customers the strongest source.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: In his simplified example, a 4:1 advertising return becomes 8:1 when every acquired customer brings one additional customer; subsequent referrals can extend that effect.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: He says referral-driven growth can continue when customers acquired through recommendations outnumber those leaving, and recommends comparing the referral percentage with the churn percentage.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: Earn more unprompted referrals by selecting suitable customers, setting expectations, improving outcomes, accelerating actual and perceived progress, continually improving the product, and explaining the next purchase.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: Affiliates are independent businesses that promote another business's products to their own prospects in return for money, free products, or a combination.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: His affiliate illustration compares 10 monthly customers worth $10,000 each with recruiting 10 monthly affiliates who each supply one customer monthly: annual revenue totals $1.2 million versus $7.8 million, assuming affiliates continue producing.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: His affiliate process is to identify suitable partners, propose mutual benefits, teach them to sell, establish compensation, activate their promotion, and sustain their participation.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: For launch affiliates, he preferred rewards that benefited their audiences, such as providing educational value, rather than prizes that benefited only the affiliate.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: He describes the advertising roadmap as seven stages that help a business decide which acquisition playbook to use at its current level.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: His picture of a scaled acquisition business includes specialized content, advertising, outbound, affiliate, and recruiting teams, with executives directing growth independently of the owner.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: He believes examining how a framework was developed helps people understand its logic rather than merely remember the finished model.
title: $100M Leads Launch

text: His fitness headline formula has three parts in order: a duration, then a benefit or result, then a power word. He used it for all the fitness ads he ran at his gyms.
title: How To Make Ad Headlines That Get Clicks [ALEX HORMOZI]

text: The duration goes first because it tells prospects the commitment and when they could reach the result. It is only an ad title, not a guarantee. Examples: 28 days, 6 weeks, 42 days.
title: How To Make Ad Headlines That Get Clicks [ALEX HORMOZI]

text: The benefit part should show what the result looks like, such as a small dress, a little black dress, or two notches down on a belt. He also suggests creative angles like the skinny friend, which taps status among friends.
title: How To Make Ad Headlines That Get Clicks [ALEX HORMOZI]

text: The third headline piece is a power word like challenge, blueprint, accelerator, intensive, program or transformation, which acts like the period ending the sentence.
title: How To Make Ad Headlines That Get Clicks [ALEX HORMOZI]

text: The three-part headline goes in the ad banner. He says an ad lacking it is much less likely to convert, and notes many gym owners skip this basic step and then wonder why results are poor.
title: How To Make Ad Headlines That Get Clicks [ALEX HORMOZI]

text: For creative he points to the lead gen scrambler: group workouts, a pitch explaining the program, images of people sweating together, testimonials.
title: How To Make Ad Headlines That Get Clicks [ALEX HORMOZI]

text: Headline and creative do not need to be connected. He calls this one of the biggest things he has learned as a marketer.
title: How To Make Ad Headlines That Get Clicks [ALEX HORMOZI]

text: For Facebook ad copy, the first lines should call out who you want and, arguably more important, who you do not want. Compliance rules stop you addressing the reader directly, so describe the audience indirectly.
title: How To Make Ad Headlines That Get Clicks [ALEX HORMOZI]

text: After the callout, write a subhead that ties back to the headline as a lead-in, then add implied authority such as number of locals helped, then announce the spot opening and give the call to action.
title: How To Make Ad Headlines That Get Clicks [ALEX HORMOZI]

text: Colors and fonts can matter even more than words. Avoid hardcore combos like black with yellow or red, or stencil lettering, for women; male-oriented colors like black with green or blue suit ads for men.
title: How To Make Ad Headlines That Get Clicks [ALEX HORMOZI]

text: Some fonts, such as Permanent Marker from Google Fonts, work for both men and women. The point is to match colors and fonts to the prospect you want to attract.
title: How To Make Ad Headlines That Get Clicks [ALEX HORMOZI]

text: Creative types he knows convert for fitness: people working out together, food pictures, sweaty selfies, images of someone staring at the camera, and selfie pitch videos.
title: How To Make Ad Headlines That Get Clicks [ALEX HORMOZI]

text: Saying who an offer is not for is as powerful as, or more than, saying who it is for, because it signals selectivity and makes the ad more magnetic. Gym Launch ads exclude personal trainers and require over 25 clients or a signed lease.
title: How To Make Ad Headlines That Get Clicks [ALEX HORMOZI]

text: Analyze your own clients to find which are worth the most, then put that profile in your copy to ward off poor fits. Those who see themselves in it are more likely to click, raising click quality.
title: How To Make Ad Headlines That Get Clicks [ALEX HORMOZI]

text: The subhead lead-in should tie to the benefit word in the headline. For a two-notches headline, use a belt or jeans image and open by asking if they have noticed going up notches, then say it is fixable.
title: How To Make Ad Headlines That Get Clicks [ALEX HORMOZI]

text: The subhead is kept out of the banner because it has too many words, but it should still sit in the copy so readers who want more find it relevant to what they just read.
title: How To Make Ad Headlines That Get Clicks [ALEX HORMOZI]

text: After the click, the landing page must match the ad's offer, benefits and results. He says good marketers beat mediocre ones simply by not being lazy on this.
title: How To Make Ad Headlines That Get Clicks [ALEX HORMOZI]

text: You can run separate funnels for the same campaign, such as one for men and one for women, or split further by age, since the messaging and page would differ, for example older versus younger women.
title: How To Make Ad Headlines That Get Clicks [ALEX HORMOZI]

text: Hormozi calls the belief that a business is not scalable one of the most damaging myths, and says it may end more businesses than anything else, because it is about how owners treat the business, not the business itself.
title: The Biggest MYTH You Probably Still Believe

text: Service businesses are easy to start but harder to scale as quality slips with untrained hires; e-commerce sits in the middle with supply chain issues; software costs most to start but is easiest once scaled. He says all have limits.
title: The Biggest MYTH You Probably Still Believe

text: He says switching from one service business to another rarely changes growth, since you are still constrained by humans, and he states 78% of US businesses are service based.
title: The Biggest MYTH You Probably Still Believe

text: Demand-constrained and supply-constrained service businesses have similar problems; in both cases the fix is promotion, either to get customers or to get staff such as accountants.
title: The Biggest MYTH You Probably Still Believe

text: Saying a business is not scalable really means it is hard and you want it easy. Difficulty is a feature of scaling, not a bug, and some problems must be endured for many quarters.
title: The Biggest MYTH You Probably Still Believe

text: During the wait for a fix to work, most entrepreneurs change model, price or deliverable, such as more clients per account, which drops delivery and raises churn. He calls this the real pain tolerance, sometimes lasting years.
title: The Biggest MYTH You Probably Still Believe

text: Citing Sam Altman, he says execution cannot be delegated: the idea is about 10% of the business and execution the other 90%, so resist breaking what works.
title: The Biggest MYTH You Probably Still Believe

text: Using a brick analogy, he says a change to something that works is unlikely to improve it, since only one placement of a brick holds up the building.
title: The Biggest MYTH You Probably Still Believe

text: Founders mistake features for bugs. In a service business people are the business, and software firms struggle to find good developers; some problems are managed continually rather than solved.
title: The Biggest MYTH You Probably Still Believe

text: Fixes are fast or slow, and slow ones fill most of a career. You must tolerate flaws and tell the team you are already working on it, instead of changing course.
title: The Biggest MYTH You Probably Still Believe

text: Before leaving for another path, ask what problems that path has and whether you are better equipped to solve them. He says the longer in an industry, the better you know its terrain.
title: The Biggest MYTH You Probably Still Believe

text: Wishing problems would stop is the biggest business problem, since it makes you break what works. No successful entrepreneur has ever said they solved all problems; give solutions time to work.
title: The Biggest MYTH You Probably Still Believe

text: Solving one constraint creates the next: with plenty of accountants you need customers, and filling slots may lower quality, raise churn and squeeze margins as fixed costs rise.
title: The Biggest MYTH You Probably Still Believe

text: He works in decades, noting big companies can go from idea to large scale in roughly ten years. He thinks the rush is imaginary, and arbitrary deadlines lead to cutting corners and wrong hires.
title: The Biggest MYTH You Probably Still Believe

text: Change your timelines, not your dreams. Every business is scalable; the question is how hard, and the alternative path has equally hard problems you are less equipped to solve.
title: The Biggest MYTH You Probably Still Believe

text: Changing things adds a new problem plus the cost of change. If urgent, speed up the current solution yourself, like doing interviews, but you will not eliminate the problem.
title: The Biggest MYTH You Probably Still Believe

text: Big businesses take decades, so you must say no to every opportunity besides your current one; chasing all of them means getting none.
title: The Biggest MYTH You Probably Still Believe

text: Sticking with the plan is the hard part, not making or executing it. Saying no is a muscle that gets a little easier; he thinks no FOMO signals it is trained.
title: The Biggest MYTH You Probably Still Believe

text: He says he sees more businesses ruined by moving expectations and calling the gap a problem than by almost anything else; stick with it and question your expectations.
title: The Biggest MYTH You Probably Still Believe

text: Hormozi argues that a course can teach a necessary business skill without generating income, because earning money requires other capabilities as well.
title: I SPENT $100,000 on courses, so you don't have to...

text: He recommends identifying the skill currently restricting business results. Repeatedly studying an existing strength will not resolve a different missing capability.
title: I SPENT $100,000 on courses, so you don't have to...

text: He suggests that the course credited with a breakthrough may simply complete a set of capabilities developed through earlier courses, rather than prove those earlier courses were useless.
title: I SPENT $100,000 on courses, so you don't have to...

text: For solo founders and businesses with teams of 5 or 10, he says every essential function still needs coverage. Founders should understand unfamiliar functions sufficiently to judge potential hires, even without specializing in them.
title: I SPENT $100,000 on courses, so you don't have to...

text: He attributes disappointment with courses partly to expecting purchase alone to produce success. He acknowledges that sellers can encourage those expectations, while maintaining that students must contribute effort.
title: I SPENT $100,000 on courses, so you don't have to...

text: Hormozi favors vocational training that teaches people how to operate particular businesses. He believes conventional education is overpriced and has failed to adapt to practical earning needs.
title: I SPENT $100,000 on courses, so you don't have to...

text: He believes spending $100,000 on carefully vetted online training and allowing 4 years for application would produce stronger earning capabilities than spending the same amount and time on a university degree.
title: I SPENT $100,000 on courses, so you don't have to...

text: He says he has learned even from poor courses by identifying practices he would avoid when creating his own training.
title: I SPENT $100,000 on courses, so you don't have to...

text: He and his partner simplify recurring decisions with predetermined conditions. For investments, they require due diligence and agreement from both partners before proceeding.
title: I SPENT $100,000 on courses, so you don't have to...

text: His personal rule is to withhold judgments about people he does not know firsthand, partly because recognizing errors in his past thinking makes him question his current judgment.
title: I SPENT $100,000 on courses, so you don't have to...

text: He says sellers should aim for 100% of customers to receive enough surplus value to recommend them. Blaming customers does not improve the business, even though customers also bear responsibility for their outcomes.
title: I SPENT $100,000 on courses, so you don't have to...

text: He says secondhand criticism kept him from relationships he later valued, including a connection delayed by 5 years. He also reports spending $120,000 for 4 hours with Grant, equivalent to $30,000 per hour.
title: I SPENT $100,000 on courses, so you don't have to...

text: He recommends evaluating whether someone offers useful knowledge rather than assigning the whole person a positive or negative label. Disliking someone need not prevent learning from their stronger capabilities.
title: I SPENT $100,000 on courses, so you don't have to...

text: He says becoming more aware of his expectations has made him happier by reducing disappointment and allowing unexpected experiences to feel positive.
title: I SPENT $100,000 on courses, so you don't have to...

text: Hormozi argues that shared belief can enable the same people to produce 2, 4, or 8 times as much, without fundamentally changing the team's strategy.
title: $100M CEO: How I know who to trust...

text: Company values should describe existing, essential commitments rather than desired future traits. They must govern both hiring and dismissal.
title: $100M CEO: How I know who to trust...

text: Useful values distinguish acceptable behavior from unacceptable behavior and exclude some people. Hormozi considers statements that accommodate everyone too vague to function as values.
title: $100M CEO: How I know who to trust...

text: Express company values in language the team naturally uses; familiar internal sayings can communicate standards more authentically than generic corporate terms.
title: $100M CEO: How I know who to trust...

text: Hormozi thinks 3 core values work best because people can remember and apply them when making decisions without the founder. His standard requires alignment with all 3.
title: $100M CEO: How I know who to trust...

text: Use a decade-long relationship as a screening test for clients, employees, and business partners. If that prospect is unacceptable, Hormozi advises against starting even a day's relationship.
title: $100M CEO: How I know who to trust...

text: When existing employees or clients violate genuine company non-negotiables, enforce those standards despite the immediate discomfort; Hormozi sees this pruning as necessary for longer-term organizational health.
title: $100M CEO: How I know who to trust...

text: An employee's strong performance does not cancel out an oversized ego. Hormozi warns that such people resist feedback, blame others, and damage the culture in ways that hurt overall performance.
title: $100M CEO: How I know who to trust...

text: To assess character, Hormozi considers whether someone would respect his marriage during a month away and safeguard an unusually large sum for a month, year, or decade.
title: $100M CEO: How I know who to trust...

text: Constructive feedback requires accurate awareness and useful delivery from the giver, plus humility and willingness to improve from the recipient. Hormozi argues that progress depends on both abilities.
title: $100M CEO: How I know who to trust...

text: Unaddressed grievances create distance between people and weaken communication. Hormozi considers clear communication fundamental to running a company.
title: $100M CEO: How I know who to trust...

text: Do not accept a candidate who satisfies only 2 of 3 required values. Strong ambition and feedback skills cannot compensate for questionable character, particularly because business difficulties will eventually test it.
title: $100M CEO: How I know who to trust...

text: He argues that expressing a desire can make present contentment conditional on obtaining something, including money, happiness, or meaning.
title: If you think like this, you will stay poor and unhappy...

text: He believes rigid expectations about how work, marriage, or life ought to function eventually conflict with experience. He favors accepting each situation without automatically assigning a positive or negative judgment.
title: If you think like this, you will stay poor and unhappy...

text: He distinguishes doing an activity for itself from following a process to obtain results. In his view, genuinely pursuing the activity itself requires removing happiness, meaning, or relationship outcomes as its justification.
title: If you think like this, you will stay poor and unhappy...

text: Hormozi says becoming wealthy left his feelings unchanged from when he had nothing; receiving the money produced no emotional lift for him.
title: If you think like this, you will stay poor and unhappy...

text: He believes language shapes thought and that people restrict themselves through their own descriptions and conditions for success. He describes first dropping his judgment about feeling unhappy, then ceasing to dwell on it.
title: If you think like this, you will stay poor and unhappy...

text: When asked whether positive affirmations help counter feelings of worthlessness, he proposes dropping worthiness as a criterion altogether instead of replacing a negative assessment with a positive one.
title: If you think like this, you will stay poor and unhappy...

text: He thinks many unhappy people he has observed avoid activities they want to pursue because they fear disapproval from family, friends, or others whose judgments they value.
title: If you think like this, you will stay poor and unhappy...

text: He argues that material success does not depend on deserving it: even someone with poor character can perform the actions that produce it. Personal worth need not be settled before taking action.
title: If you think like this, you will stay poor and unhappy...

text: Four levers drive business growth: traffic, conversion, price, and churn. Everything you do should map to one of them; if it does not, question why you are doing it.
title: 4 Steps to Unf*** Your Business

text: His approach is to scale as far as possible until something breaks, fix that, then return to scaling.
title: 4 Steps to Unf*** Your Business

text: Pick the lever that is the biggest constraint and compare options by effort against payoff; a poor landing page may deserve a day of work before chasing more traffic.
title: 4 Steps to Unf*** Your Business

text: He asks in order: can we do more of what works, then do it better, and only then try something new. He rarely does new things once something works.
title: 4 Steps to Unf*** Your Business

text: He thinks small entrepreneurs get stuck because they find something that works, stop, and get spread thin chasing new things.
title: 4 Steps to Unf*** Your Business

text: For a solo operator, start with traffic, since acquiring customers is the lifeblood; once it is relatively consistent even at a low level, shift attention to other levers.
title: 4 Steps to Unf*** Your Business

text: Consumption should be the top priority: customers must consume value to get it, so he removes things and simplifies rather than adding.
title: 4 Steps to Unf*** Your Business

text: To cut churn, talk to customers who cancelled and who stayed, find the differences, emphasize what stayers did and remove what leavers did.
title: 4 Steps to Unf*** Your Business

text: Overwhelm is the main cause of churn in communities; people keep adding content thinking it helps, but it does not.
title: 4 Steps to Unf*** Your Business

text: Solving business problems takes far more effort than people expect, and there is no silver bullet; his sense of required effort has risen about 100x as he grew.
title: 4 Steps to Unf*** Your Business

text: He tested price points of 50, 35, 25, and 15 in a portfolio business and results were the same, so he picked the business he preferred.
title: 4 Steps to Unf*** Your Business

text: His School Games funnel problem was that an outsider could not tell what it was; using extreme cases as a test helps clarify a message.
title: 4 Steps to Unf*** Your Business

text: Spend most time listening to what people struggle with, validate problems, prioritize the most pressing one, fix it, then tell the community you fixed it.
title: 4 Steps to Unf*** Your Business

text: A good community understands members' pain; it is not a fast production line of posts.
title: 4 Steps to Unf*** Your Business

text: Widening his content beyond business grew his audience with the wrong people; returning to business-only content raised opt-ins, book sales and applications even as views per video fell.
title: 4 Steps to Unf*** Your Business

text: To attract talented people the vision must be big enough for them to fit their dreams inside it; the best people have many opportunities.
title: 4 Steps to Unf*** Your Business

text: He delayed starting School by a year to find the right software co-founder, and networked in the software world to do it.
title: 4 Steps to Unf*** Your Business

text: Every skill is trainable, but the question is whether it is worth the effort; he prefers to nudge people with existing skills.
title: 4 Steps to Unf*** Your Business

text: He capped at $3 million a year until Leila joined, and 24 months later he took home 17 million net; she likes people while he avoided them.
title: 4 Steps to Unf*** Your Business

text: The direction someone needs is inversely proportional to their skill: less skilled people need more specific instructions.
title: 4 Steps to Unf*** Your Business

text: Meeting private equity teams reset his bar for talent; he believes someone 10 times better than your best person exists.
title: 4 Steps to Unf*** Your Business

text: Bad hires teach what good looks like for each role; the faster you learn that pattern, the faster you move. He calls this pattern recognition the highest-value entrepreneurial skill.
title: 4 Steps to Unf*** Your Business

text: Hormozi describes a persuasion tactic: assign someone a desirable identity, obtain their agreement, then present a purchase as consistent with that identity. He says people feel pressure to behave consistently with the label they accepted.
title: How the best entrepreneurs REDEFINE reality..

text: He believes judging ordinary fluctuations such as sadness or fatigue as bad can turn a passing emotional state into an enduring disturbance by making the feeling itself seem like a problem.
title: How the best entrepreneurs REDEFINE reality..

text: He recommends noticing language that turns preferences into necessities or obligations. He argues that treating something like morning coffee as indispensable creates an implied threat about what happens without it.
title: How the best entrepreneurs REDEFINE reality..

text: He believes uncomfortable emotions provide contrast for pleasant ones, and that trying to eliminate one end of an emotional range can leave people numb to both.
title: How the best entrepreneurs REDEFINE reality..

text: Drawing on his interpretation of Viktor Frankl, Hormozi argues that people retain a choice about their response to circumstances, even when external conditions severely restrict their freedom.
title: How the best entrepreneurs REDEFINE reality..

text: Hormozi says his fixation on happiness led him to judge every other emotional state negatively. He thinks that pursuit made him more unhappy.
title: How the best entrepreneurs REDEFINE reality..

text: His personal practice is to acknowledge an uncomfortable emotion and mentally accept its presence. He distinguishes the feeling, which may be involuntary, from the judgment and response a person applies to it.
title: How the best entrepreneurs REDEFINE reality..

text: He argues that disagreements often reflect different or missing definitions of terms such as health, wealth, and success. Agreeing on meanings can resolve disputes, while defining desired outcomes can help people pursue them.
title: How the best entrepreneurs REDEFINE reality..

text: Hormozi recalls selling three companies the previous year to different buyers. He says definitions occupied roughly the first half of contracts exceeding 50 pages, illustrating how much agreement depends on specifying meanings.
title: How the best entrepreneurs REDEFINE reality..

text: He proposes defining a fulfilling life as experiencing a broad emotional range. Under that definition, periods of sadness or stress can count as part of living fully instead of evidence that life is going wrong.
title: How the best entrepreneurs REDEFINE reality..

text: Hormozi says a 90-day experiment with broader topics increased views but reduced qualified applications and book sales, prompting a return to predominantly business content.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: His data did not support assuming short video viewers become long video viewers. He allows that someone discovering him through shorts elsewhere might already prefer long videos on YouTube.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: When advertising carries the sales requests, he thinks organic content can concentrate on helping. He evaluates the balance of giving and asking across everything the audience encounters.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: He treats relevant calls to action for free resources as additional help. Their fit and presentation matter; he reports that his leading YouTube video ends with a 14-minute call to action.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: He sees familiarity progressing from recognizing his face, to remembering a helpful encounter, to knowing his name, to watching regularly. He believes recognition improves advertising clicks, conversions, and achievable prices.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: He thinks short videos produce more return alongside advertising than through direct calls to action. He places next steps in descriptions, an initial comment, and his profile to preserve viewing attention.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: On his Instagram account, he sees reels primarily reaching new people and photos or carousels reaching existing followers. He suggests using images to nurture followers and present calls to action.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: To attract business owners, he recommends business subjects and nearby topics such as productivity. He considers relationship content too distant because those viewers generally want more relationship content.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: Credibility should rest on accurate facts and evidence distinctive to the business. He encourages marketers to surface accomplishments and demonstrations that competitors cannot reproduce.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: Useful content can prompt a profile visit. He recommends using the profile to quickly establish identity and credibility, then provide a link, messaging option, or other next step.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: He recommends explaining what someone personally did or achieved with clients instead of publishing interchangeable instructional lists. Personal case studies give creators material others cannot authentically duplicate.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: He ranks proof from helping similar customers achieve results, to achieving the result personally, to doing substantial work and reporting its lessons. Action supplies credibility when an established reputation is absent.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: He sees education as compressing learning time. Showing the effort and expense behind a lesson helps audiences understand how much learning they can obtain without repeating that investment.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: He recommends continuing to earn attention even after building an audience. He reports his strongest percentage growth came when he treated viewers as strangers whose attention required constant justification.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: He is moving away from content framed around his name. For discovery, he prefers framing topics around accomplishments, since unfamiliar viewers have little reason to care about his identity alone.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: He speculates that asking live viewers to comment for a resource could generate many responses. He also thinks comment triggers may improve post distribution and require less effort than sending a direct message.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: His content system tests writing on X, turns successful tweets into Instagram reels and recorded clips, and combines 20 proven pieces into a YouTube video. Other successful tweets supply captions.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: Starting a Twitter account, he would establish evidence in the profile description and a substantial pinned introduction. Someone without accomplishments should document work underway rather than assert expertise they cannot demonstrate.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: He reports publishing 5–7 YouTube shorts, 5–7 tweets, 2–3 Instagram reels, and about 4 TikToks daily on his account, alongside a couple of long YouTube videos weekly.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: His team found Instagram output reached its useful limit around 2–3 daily posts. He says increasing to 11 would not deliver equivalent gains and cautions against treating Instagram like unlimited publishing inventory.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: When a tweet performs well, he treats its subject or wording as evidence of interest and adapts it into camera recordings, emails, and captions across platforms.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: He supports repeating successful older material but says his team has underused that approach. At the time of the discussion, most of their production had been newly created.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: He thinks reuse timing depends on platform memory and audience growth. He says a tweet can succeed again after 6 months, while Instagram tolerates less repetition and YouTube videos remain available much longer.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: He describes four repurposing options: moving material between platforms, changing its format, recording it again, and publishing an existing clip again.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: He hired content agencies immediately, disclosed his intention to move production internally, and learned from their experience to avoid beginner errors. He notes that available capital made this approach possible for him.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: His topics follow current interests and operating problems rather than predetermined categories. He says recurring themes emerge naturally, including periods focused on customer lifetime value or sales.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: He urges beginners to make content useful enough that a single viewer would want to share it, while recognizing that their early work may still seem poor as their skills improve.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: He recommends sharing knowledge without withholding the valuable parts. Audiences can learn from free material and still pay for help putting it into practice.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: He identifies broad recruiting access as fame’s biggest benefit and lost privacy as its biggest cost. Public interruptions and the possibility of being recorded affect how he behaves.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: He regards fame as an irreversible choice. For skilled operators uninterested in public attention, he suggests acquiring business through methods they already know and focusing on their existing work.
title: More Followers Won't Make You Rich, But This Will

text: When an employee fails to execute, Hormozi first examines his own management: whether the employee understands the assignment, has the skills to perform it, and feels motivated to act.
title: How To Scale Yourself: The What-Why-How Framework

text: Managers should follow spoken assignments with a written digital record specifying the expected work and deadline. Hormozi treats undocumented instructions as insufficient evidence that expectations were communicated.
title: How To Scale Yourself: The What-Why-How Framework

text: To address weak motivation, explain how an employee's role affects business results, what would fail without that function, and what successful performance contributes.
title: How To Scale Yourself: The What-Why-How Framework

text: Beyond understanding their role's contribution, employees need commitment to the company's mission, including whom it serves and which problem it aims to solve.
title: How To Scale Yourself: The What-Why-How Framework

text: Hormozi argues that scaling decision-making, especially in service businesses, depends on culture and training: culture communicates expectations and purpose, while training prepares employees to perform.
title: How To Scale Yourself: The What-Why-How Framework

text: Motivated, capable employees who lack clear assignments may freeze or spend effort on work outside company priorities. Their activity can appear useful while failing to advance the company's direction.
title: How To Scale Yourself: The What-Why-How Framework

title: How to get rich this Black Friday

title: How to get rich this Black Friday

text: Hormozi believes repeatedly defining oneself through an addiction or anxiety reinforces that difficulty as part of one’s identity.
title: $100M CEO: 'Why therapists failed me...' [language warning]

text: Hormozi recalls studying happiness extensively without feeling happier. He decided to stop investing effort in that pursuit because remaining unhappy without the extra work seemed less costly.
title: $100M CEO: 'Why therapists failed me...' [language warning]

text: For his own recurring unhappiness, he used a blunt mental dismissal to stop evaluating his happiness and continue his activities. He describes this as removing significance rather than substituting a positive interpretation.
title: $100M CEO: 'Why therapists failed me...' [language warning]

text: Hormozi believes anticipating a feared recurrence can reinforce distress, with shame about the experience contributing to its psychological influence.
title: $100M CEO: 'Why therapists failed me...' [language warning]

text: For recurring distressing thoughts, he advocates regarding them as unimportant background activity. He distinguishes this from fearfully attempting to suppress them, which he believes preserves their influence.
title: $100M CEO: 'Why therapists failed me...' [language warning]

text: A few years after abandoning constant happiness evaluation, Hormozi noticed that he felt considerably less unhappy.
title: $100M CEO: 'Why therapists failed me...' [language warning]

text: Hormozi believes much fear and shame comes from imagined social judgment. While growing his licensing business, he openly acknowledged his financial motives to reduce his own shame about earning money.
title: $100M CEO: 'Why therapists failed me...' [language warning]

text: When facing repetitive internal accusations, he suggests accepting the characterization without arguing. He believes denying it or reinterpreting it preserves its significance, whereas agreement can interrupt the mental conflict.
title: $100M CEO: 'Why therapists failed me...' [language warning]

text: He presents his approach as something that helped him personally and addresses people who found therapy unhelpful. He explicitly supports continuing therapy when someone finds it beneficial.
title: $100M CEO: 'Why therapists failed me...' [language warning]

text: Hormozi believes openly acknowledging a source of shame reduces its influence, and that declining to treat an internal struggle as significant can make it fade.
title: $100M CEO: 'Why therapists failed me...' [language warning]

text: Hormozi finds a day spent performing onstage or on camera more exhausting than working alone because the audience and production team require continuous performance.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Productivity itself improves through practice: spending many hours at work does not initially mean producing much, but repeated work can increase both output and quality.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Hormozi describes improving his concentration as becoming quicker at returning to the task when he feels an urge to stop.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Hormozi recalls encountering people much further ahead who appeared to work five to ten times as much as he did, repeatedly exposing how much he underestimated entrepreneurial effort.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Work ethic is demonstrated when someone continues through fatigue, distraction, or unpleasant tasks; favorable conditions do not meaningfully test that commitment.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Hormozi says wanting to turn an idea into something real has sustained him through difficult periods more than enthusiasm for the work itself.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Entrepreneurs can increase their effectiveness by shortening the interval between choosing an action and carrying it out.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Once there is no further information to gather for a decision, make the choice and eliminate the alternatives.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: When assigning a deadline for the week, ask whether completion is possible today. Hormozi describes this compression as a sevenfold increase in pace.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: What appears to be natural ability can reflect earlier practice that transfers to a new skill. Hormozi uses his bilingual upbringing to explain why learning languages felt easier.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Hormozi frames difficulty as having three possible endings: abandoning the pursuit, circumstances becoming easier, or personal capability increasing enough to handle them.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Compare today's ability with business problems that caused stress five years earlier. Problems that now seem straightforward can reveal how much personal capability has increased.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Hormozi tries to appreciate difficult periods while living through them because experiences that once felt stressful can later become cherished memories.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Growth, stagnation, and decline can all produce stress. Hormozi argues that having problems does not itself mean something has gone wrong.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Hormozi believes a worthwhile life develops character through challenges rather than being defined by ease.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: After selling Gym Launch, Hormozi largely stopped working for a year and felt miserable. He concluded that demanding work had been a major source of enjoyment and fulfillment.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Hormozi treats fully using his daily capacity as a personal aim because his most demanding days tend to feel most fulfilling in retrospect.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Pursuing exceptional results can require actions that others disapprove of. Hormozi describes widespread opposition when he left consulting and later moved from operating gyms into gym turnarounds.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Choose guidance from people nearer the outcome being pursued rather than giving priority to people merely because they are personally close.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Experts recognize multiple intermediate signs of progress, while beginners may recognize only the final result. Developing more ways to measure progress creates more rewarding moments during the work.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Evaluate education as an investment in personal capability by comparing its cost with the expected return, rather than judging the price in isolation.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Hormozi says he reinvested his spare money in skills, courses, workshops, seminars, coaching, networks, and surroundings rather than raising his living expenses.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Even disappointing educational experiences can provide lessons about conduct to avoid. Hormozi says he learned both useful practices and ways he would refuse to treat others.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: A person's starting position is outside their control, but Hormozi argues that their pace of progress can change through learning and subsequent action.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Hormozi defines education through changed behavior after learning and intelligence through the speed of learning.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Hormozi presents desirable outcomes as exchanges: fame sacrifices privacy, ambition can require loneliness, discipline sacrifices immediate pleasure, loyalty limits romantic novelty, and earning trust requires discretion.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Feeling maximally challenged does not establish that effort matches the goal. Hormozi illustrates this with effort rated ten out of ten for a $100,000 goal but only one out of ten for a $1 million goal.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: An outcome may require several conditions together. Meeting three of four can produce no visible result even when those three improvements worked; investigate the remaining requirement.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Hormozi attributes unsuccessful exchanges either to refusing a required sacrifice or to underestimating its size. Willingness to contribute something does not establish that the contribution is sufficient.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: When an initial commitment proves insufficient, repeatedly revise expectations and increase the commitment until it meets the outcome's requirements.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Hormozi describes four tradeoff levels: expecting an outcome free, rejecting its cost, progressively increasing commitment, and source, where personal standards determine what is sufficient.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Hormozi says his early gym videos were made thirteen years earlier and that he drank alcohol before recording because he feared looking foolish, challenging the impression that his camera confidence was innate.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: At the source level, internal standards exceed what outsiders will accept. The creator evaluates whether the work meets their own expectations rather than whether others will approve.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Hormozi believes decision authority within a function should belong to whoever demands the highest quality, regardless of seniority, ownership stake, or tenure.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Hormozi estimates that becoming the world's best author would require him to spend at least a decade practicing hard every day; expecting immediate excellence ignores the development involved.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Continually sampling pursuits can obscure the need to commit and iterate. Hormozi argues that many pursuits could succeed, but selecting one and doing enough revisions is essential.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Hormozi illustrates underestimated repetition with nineteen drafts versus two, 500 editing minutes versus fifty, and 1,000 calls weekly for two years versus two months.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich Like the 1%

text: Express appreciation or give a thoughtful gift when the impulse arises. Hormozi says communicating mainly to correct mistakes teaches employees to avoid the boss and withhold information.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Discretionary effort is the gap between doing enough to remain employed and doing one's best. Hormozi credits supportive coaching and frequent positive feedback with encouraging employees to contribute that additional effort.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Leila records employees' preferences when they join and uses those profiles to choose gifts after strong work. Hormozi presents personalized recognition as evidence that leadership pays attention.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Sleep before responding to upsetting news. Hormozi says his anger subsided by morning 9 times out of 10, allowing him to address prevention instead of attacking someone's character.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Hormozi treats business stress as evidence of caring rather than proof that something is wrong. He says dropping self-criticism about being stressed freed attention for productive work.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Feeling uncomfortable does not require corrective action. When acting merely to relieve discomfort would move someone away from their goals, Hormozi recommends accepting the feeling while continuing the necessary work.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Protect long-term goals when considering immediate opportunities. Hormozi particularly emphasizes verifying product promises because exaggerated marketing can damage the reputation needed for future success.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Hormozi links business quality to employee quality, and recruiting ability to the leader's character and vision. A mission centered only on enriching the owner gives others little reason to join.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Talented employees discuss their employers with peers at other companies. Hormozi says a reputation for treating staff well helps attract people when they become dissatisfied elsewhere.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Being a likable leader is insufficient to retain ambitious people. The company's direction must also provide room for employees to pursue their own aspirations.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Hormozi recommends The Motive to owners and operators. He says reading it exposed how poorly his previous approach matched the responsibilities of effective business leadership.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Trust teammates once they have passed hiring scrutiny, but withdraw that trust promptly when their actions warrant it. Hormozi distinguishes this approach from Leila's greater caution toward outside vendors and partners.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: A prospective partner's record of misconduct is sufficient reason to decline involvement. Hormozi prefers working with people who have demonstrated reliability rather than betting on someone's rehabilitation.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Hormozi argues that punishment produces quick compliance but requires continuing pressure, whereas rewarding desired behavior takes longer initially and builds greater employee independence.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Demonstrate patience, forgiveness, and trust before expecting them from employees. Hormozi says leaders influence team behavior through their own conduct more effectively than through requests alone.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Competing only to outperform nearby rivals can set an unnecessarily low ceiling. Hormozi credits Leila with redirecting him toward improving against his own potential.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Reacting angrily to bad news makes employees stop sharing it, depriving leaders of reliable information. Hormozi says useful feedback should prompt improvement as soon as it is received, even when it hurts.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Invite people to share what they would say if they knew the feedback would not provoke anger. Keep encouraging honesty even when the first responses are uncomfortable.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Effective operators rapidly delegate work and maintain accountability. Hormozi emphasizes developing employees' judgment rather than trying to prescribe every action through procedures.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Help employees make independent decisions by demonstrating shared values under difficult circumstances and publicly recognizing employees who uphold those values without managerial intervention.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Judge a process by its benefit to the whole organization relative to the work it adds locally. Collecting information that nobody uses creates extra effort without a corresponding organizational gain.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Hormozi credits Leila's operating success to hiring capable people, delegating authority promptly, and allowing flexibility in how they achieve the required outcome.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Prioritizing employees as people can mean supporting a better opportunity elsewhere, even after substantial investment in their development. Hormozi describes this as separating the person's interests from the company's role for them.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Hormozi says employees who left his companies on good terms have referred customers, helped train replacements, supported recruiting, and later become business collaborators.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Ask which action feels most frightening and what the business would attempt if failure seemed impossible. Hormozi says these questions often expose necessary conversations, product changes, or strategic moves being postponed.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Do not sacrifice meaningful accomplishments to spend more time networking. Hormozi argues that achieving goals increases what someone can offer others and creates access that networking alone cannot sustain.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Another person's request for time or a reply does not create an obligation. Hormozi describes becoming more selective about meetings, messages, and social invitations.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Holding equity in several companies differs from operating them. Hormozi believes a person can run only one business exceptionally well because divided attention prevents the detailed improvements that produce disproportionate gains.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: When leaving business commitments, honor obligations to employees, customers, partners, landlords, and vendors. Hormozi recounts accepting costly settlements and refunds to exit without mistreating stakeholders.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Hormozi reports that before meeting Leila he had not exceeded $3 million in annual revenue; 24 months later, he received $17 million in personal income. He attributes the change to lessons from working with her.
title: Money Lessons I Learned In Marriage.

text: Hormozi says deciding to leave his job took six months because fear of appearing unsuccessful made the decision especially difficult.

title: Never start a business until you hear this..(3 THINGS THAT MAY CHANGE YOUR MIND)

title: Never start a business until you hear this..(3 THINGS THAT MAY CHANGE YOUR MIND)

text: Successful business ownership requires skills beyond a single employee function, including generating demand, handling leads, selling, delivering, managing people, communicating expectations, recruiting, interviewing, and hiring.

text: If dissatisfaction comes from the employer or the work itself, he recommends considering another company or role, where employment can provide income while teaching useful business skills.
