text: Employees who like their employer and work but want higher pay should ask how they can contribute more value, giving the owner an opportunity to explain a path toward greater compensation.
title: Never start a business until you hear this..(3 THINGS THAT MAY CHANGE YOUR MIND)

text: Before resigning, use spare time to build missing skills and generate business demand through marketing or outreach. He suggests letting the side business exceed employment earnings before making the transition.
title: Never start a business until you hear this..(3 THINGS THAT MAY CHANGE YOUR MIND)

text: He recommends maintaining inexpensive living habits so a decline in income does not force spending beyond earnings and continued investment in personal development remains possible.
title: Never start a business until you hear this..(3 THINGS THAT MAY CHANGE YOUR MIND)

text: If employment changes and a side business still leave someone dissatisfied, he considers quitting reasonable when they have savings and a tested business approach that others are already using and they can execute.
title: Never start a business until you hear this..(3 THINGS THAT MAY CHANGE YOUR MIND)

text: He recommends listing an offer priced 10 or 100 times above other options, with delivery terms worth honoring if purchased. The high anchor can support core-offer conversion and higher core pricing.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: He estimates that 10% of customers prefer the highest-priced option, so a business offering only inexpensive choices can miss spending from customers with larger budgets.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: Creators tire of their promotions before prospective customers remember them. He recommends repeating useful messages because audiences often need reminders rather than constant novelty.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: For beginners, he recommends four daily hours of Core Four activity. His Rule of 100 targets are 100 minutes of content, 100 warm or cold outreach attempts, or at least $100 in daily advertising.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: Below $100,000 monthly revenue, he prioritizes advertising to generate customers and product feedback. At that level, he recommends shifting attention toward delivery, repeat purchases, and referrals before further acquisition expansion.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: Scaling acquisition before repairing delivery can leave a business supporting large overhead while additional sales damage its reputation, making both continued growth and reduced advertising difficult.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: Below $1 million annual revenue, he recommends concentrating on one acquisition channel, one customer profile, and one product so limited customer volume produces focused improvements.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: He suggests considering additional acquisition channels around $1 million monthly revenue, after other people can sustain or exceed the founder's results in the original channel.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: He advocates beginning every new offer with free delivery to establish results and confidence before charging, including new products within established companies.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: A product's biggest customer cost may be the time, inconvenience, unwanted activities, or sacrificed pleasures it requires. Reducing those burdens can support higher monetary prices.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: Free customers can create future revenue by providing testimonials, referring buyers, or continuing as paying customers after the free period.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: He argues that demonstrated customer results sell more effectively than elaborate promises. Recent evidence and visual demonstrations make that proof more convincing.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: Businesses can make existing evidence more persuasive by collecting individual reviews from multiple platforms and displaying many of them together, including on physical premises.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: He reports stronger conversion from testimonials that begin with the customer's earlier pain. He suspects this works because prospects recognize their current situation before hearing about a result that otherwise feels distant.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: Request testimonials when customers feel most satisfied; present a sale when their unmet need is strongest. He treats these as different moments requiring different requests.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: He tests price differences as large as 4x or 5x and expects more rejections at higher prices. The relevant question is whether increased revenue and profit offset lower conversion.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: With a $500 delivery cost, increasing price from $1,000 to $2,000 raises per-sale profit from $500 to $1,500. In his illustration, losing one-third of sales still doubles total profit.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: He recommends annual price increases of at least 3–6% to counter inflation, warning that unchanged prices can progressively compress margins.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: For existing recurring customers, explain the investments and service quality a price increase supports, give an effective date, and temporarily preserve their old rate to recognize loyalty.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: Record conversion before changing prices and evaluate a statistically meaningful sample afterward. Two or three rejections are insufficient evidence because some refusals would also occur at the previous price.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: Direct sales conversations reveal customers' actual language and purchase motivations. Use those discoveries to adjust sales scripts, headlines, and product priorities, even when the immediate sale is small.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: Ask buyers why they purchased and nonbuyers why they declined. He considers both groups valuable sources of information for improving the business.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: When customers request cancellation or refunds, speak with them to understand the failure, acknowledge their experience without minimizing it, and ask what would resolve the situation.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: Use feedback from nonbuyers and departed customers to identify acquisition and early-experience friction. Ask highly engaged customers what improvements would increase ongoing value and retention.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: CLOSER starts by asking what prompted an engaged prospect's action, confirming their unmet objective, and reviewing previous attempts and consequences to increase the problem's importance during the conversation.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: In CLOSER, describe the desired outcome rather than dwelling on delivery mechanics. He recommends organizing the pitch into three elements the prospect believes would enable success.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: CLOSER addresses five kinds of purchase concerns: program specifics, time, money, another decision-maker's authority, and fear of choosing incorrectly.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: Reinforce a purchase during the first 24 hours by specifying immediate next steps and fulfilling those promises, ideally early. He says customers strongly judge the business during that initial period.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: Before pursuing something new, ask what prevents doing 10 times more of an existing successful activity. If a specific obstacle prevents expansion, make resolving it the growth priority.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: He describes five stages: uninformed optimism, informed pessimism, despair, informed optimism, and achievement. Repeatedly switching opportunities during despair prevents reaching the informed, successful stages.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: He believes a new opportunity often looks easier because its problems remain unfamiliar. Scaling a proven activity usually introduces fewer unknowns than starting another one.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: He regards stress as common to business growth, stagnation, and decline. Experience can make earlier difficulties feel routine, so stress alone does not establish that the business should be abandoned.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: His look-back-window theory holds that customers assess value against their most recent purchase period. Longer prepaid billing periods let them evaluate uneven results across more time.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: He recommends longer upfront payment periods rather than merely longer contracts. Encourage prepayment through discounts, bonuses, service benefits, or guarantees that offset the customer's additional risk.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: Across his portfolio, he reports 10–15% uptake when annual prepayment is optional rather than the default. At roughly 10% uptake and a 12x upfront payment, he says initial cash collection approximately doubles.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: Collecting enough cash early to cover acquisition and delivery, plus acquiring and serving another customer, allows customer receipts to finance growth until a different constraint emerges.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: Look for additional products or services assembled from resources the business already pays for. His sawdust approach depends on avoiding substantial new infrastructure or operational burden.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: Inventory staff capabilities and digital and physical assets in detail. Search for combinations or unused capacity that can generate additional revenue from existing resources.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: A single business activity can generate several benefits when reused: workshops, for example, can produce revenue, content, investment prospects, and learning opportunities for staff.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: Create content answering each major purchase concern and organize effective pieces in a spreadsheet. Salespeople can send the relevant material before or after calls and arrange follow-up conversations.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: Put advertising and sales under a shared acquisition leader. He views both as buyer education, with sales supplying information that advertising did not successfully communicate.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: Assign clear leaders to customer acquisition, delivery, and internal operations. He links these functions to gaining customers, increasing customer value, and reducing business risk respectively.
title: 13 Years of No BS Business Advice in 79 Mins

text: As the business develops, identify which leadership function best matches the founder's strengths and recruit complementary specialists whose expertise exceeds the founder's in their own areas.

text: Hormozi identifies four audience monetization arrangements: affiliates receive compensation after sales, sponsors pay before promotion, equity partners earn ownership in an existing business, and creators launch brands they own.
title: If I Wanted to Monetize An Audience in 2026, This is What I Would Do

text: Hormozi considers affiliate programs the quickest monetization option: many offer automatic enrollment and preset terms. Businesses pay only after a sale, while creators can demonstrate their selling ability without a fixed earnings ceiling.
title: If I Wanted to Monetize An Audience in 2026, This is What I Would Do

text: Hormozi thinks affiliate income generally creates limited resale value. Its contribution to a company's valuation depends on the cash flow it produces and the reliability of the business paying the commissions.
title: If I Wanted to Monetize An Audience in 2026, This is What I Would Do

text: Creators can let a partner business run their endorsement as paid advertising beyond their existing audience. Hormozi likes this arrangement because the business funds creator exposure while benefiting from the creator's presentation skills and audience recognition.
title: If I Wanted to Monetize An Audience in 2026, This is What I Would Do

text: Hormozi says sponsorships are harder to secure than standard affiliate agreements because terms require individual negotiation. The creator's size relative to the sponsoring company affects negotiating power.
title: If I Wanted to Monetize An Audience in 2026, This is What I Would Do

text: An equity partnership can reward measurable customer acquisition. Hormozi illustrates granting 1% ownership for every 1,000 additional customers, with total earned ownership capped at 10%.
title: If I Wanted to Monetize An Audience in 2026, This is What I Would Do

text: Hormozi recommends that creators negotiating equity partnerships receive some ownership immediately and earn another portion through performance, because publicly endorsing a business creates a lasting association and transfers goodwill.
title: If I Wanted to Monetize An Audience in 2026, This is What I Would Do

text: For creators launching products, white labeling an existing manufacturer's product is faster, easier, and usually cheaper than developing a custom version, which adds development and tooling costs.
title: If I Wanted to Monetize An Audience in 2026, This is What I Would Do

text: Hormozi personally favors custom products because competitors cannot offer an identical item and undermine his pricing power. He also thinks customers discovering a generic product beneath a creator's label can hurt their impression of the brand.
title: If I Wanted to Monetize An Audience in 2026, This is What I Would Do

text: Education providers should screen applicants for their likelihood of succeeding. Hormozi warns that accepting anyone who can pay increases the likelihood of dissatisfied customers, poor reviews, and accusations of being a scam.

title: How to Build a LEGIT Online Course (Works in 2026)

text: An education provider should allow paying students to finish without earning its endorsement when they fall short of its standards. Hormozi argues that withholding endorsement protects the brand over time.
title: How to Build a LEGIT Online Course (Works in 2026)

text: Hormozi argues that publishing free material better than competitors’ paid offerings can create demand beyond available capacity and sustain high prices. He believes buyers infer paid quality from the quality of free material.

text: Hormozi describes entrepreneurial power as the ability to shorten the delay between forming an intention and making it real.
title: A DOER's approach to PROCRASTINATION

text: Entrepreneurs who repeat the observe, orient, decide, act cycle more quickly can respond sooner to opportunities and discover failures sooner.
title: A DOER's approach to PROCRASTINATION

text: Business owners establish their team's execution pace. When an important task requires an hour, challenge a proposed end-of-week deadline and ask whether the competing commitments actually deserve priority.
title: A DOER's approach to PROCRASTINATION

text: For a task raised at 10 a.m., Hormozi suggests asking for completion by noon. He argues this cadence can allow three improvement cycles within one day instead of spreading them across three weeks.
title: A DOER's approach to PROCRASTINATION

text: A competitor that implements and improves faster can overcome another business's first-mover advantage by completing more learning cycles.
title: A DOER's approach to PROCRASTINATION

text: After identifying a business problem, estimate the actual work hours required, compare it with today's priorities, and look for time starting immediately. If implementation needs two hours, identify where those hours fit.
title: A DOER's approach to PROCRASTINATION

text: Hormozi claims that replacing end-of-week implementation with same-day implementation can multiply business growth speed by seven, because successive bottlenecks get addressed sooner.
title: A DOER's approach to PROCRASTINATION

text: When employees resist an urgent deadline, ask them to explain why their competing task matters more. If they cannot justify it, help them prioritize the work that drives revenue, retention, or business progress.
title: A DOER's approach to PROCRASTINATION

text: Before a discretionary purchase, translate its price into the working hours required to earn that amount after tax. He says this comparison changed what he was willing to buy.

text: He distinguishes saving from earning: retained money lets someone plan further ahead and consider larger risks that he believes can increase earnings.

title: No BS Advice to Get Rich in the Next 10 Years

text: He argues that people expect too much progress within one year and too little across a decade, encouraging employees to consider multiplying their net worth by 10 or 100 over 10 years.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich in the Next 10 Years

title: No BS Advice to Get Rich in the Next 10 Years

text: Taking immediate income from an existing skill can sacrifice opportunities to expand future earning capacity. He favors environments where time and effort produce experience and increasingly valuable skills.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich in the Next 10 Years

title: No BS Advice to Get Rich in the Next 10 Years

title: No BS Advice to Get Rich in the Next 10 Years

text: He views money as stored time because people exchange time for earnings, and argues that learning to allocate time effectively underpins effective money management.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich in the Next 10 Years

title: No BS Advice to Get Rich in the Next 10 Years

title: No BS Advice to Get Rich in the Next 10 Years

text: He prioritizes closing knowledge gaps through relationships, favors, or money, although he considers paying cash the least efficient route. He recommends learning before entering an unfamiliar business rather than correcting avoidable mistakes afterward.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich in the Next 10 Years

title: No BS Advice to Get Rich in the Next 10 Years

text: He says he devoted his twenties to developing skills and would not exchange that period for more leisure. Looking back, some difficult periods became especially meaningful because they involved substantial personal growth.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich in the Next 10 Years

title: No BS Advice to Get Rich in the Next 10 Years

title: No BS Advice to Get Rich in the Next 10 Years

text: He regards money as morally neutral capacity: it can finance harm or useful work. He argues that acquiring it can expand a person's ability to pursue a beneficial mission.
title: No BS Advice to Get Rich in the Next 10 Years

text: He closes by associating income generation with prompt action, lasting wealth with patience, and poverty with prolonged indecision, while emphasizing the skills accumulated through wisely invested time.

text: Hormozi says his strongest sales scripts use questions within a repeatable framework. He applies this approach to consumer and business sales, including purchases of $500 and $100,000.
title: 30 Minutes of sales training that will explode your business in 2022

text: Begin sales discovery by establishing why the prospect contacted you, what outcome they want, which problem they acknowledge, and what previous attempts failed.
title: 30 Minutes of sales training that will explode your business in 2022

text: Hormozi keeps his sales pitch below 3 minutes, or 180 seconds, and generally organizes it around three benefits. He emphasizes the experience customers want rather than delivery details.
title: 30 Minutes of sales training that will explode your business in 2022

text: For each pitch component, ask whether the prospect can make the required commitment. If they hesitate, use a memorized 30-second story to address the concern.
title: 30 Minutes of sales training that will explode your business in 2022

text: A question-led script helps salespeople recover their place during a call. Long blocks of scripted prose can leave them lost and improvising.
title: 30 Minutes of sales training that will explode your business in 2022

text: Train salespeople to explain each main benefit through a familiar anecdote. Hormozi illustrates this by comparing enjoyable exercise with looking forward to a favorite television show instead of describing workout mechanics.
title: 30 Minutes of sales training that will explode your business in 2022

text: When a prospect invokes an absent decision maker, ask what that person would object to. This can reveal a specific concern to address even without the other person on the call.
title: 30 Minutes of sales training that will explode your business in 2022

text: For objections involving a business partner, establish whether that partner already recognizes the problem and wants it resolved. Hormozi uses those previous agreements to support taking action now.
title: 30 Minutes of sales training that will explode your business in 2022

text: Hormozi addresses price objections through value. When prospects delay because they fear choosing incorrectly, he walks them through decision criteria, including whether the product meets their needs and whether they want to work together.
title: 30 Minutes of sales training that will explode your business in 2022

text: Words carry logical meaning while vocal delivery carries emotional meaning. Salespeople need both, and experienced representatives can deliberately change their tone to influence how a statement is understood.
title: 30 Minutes of sales training that will explode your business in 2022

text: Hormozi believes strong conviction in the product helps salespeople naturally use an effective tone, providing a shortcut while deliberate vocal mastery takes time to develop.
title: 30 Minutes of sales training that will explode your business in 2022

text: Study recordings from a salesperson’s strong closing streak. Examine their question delivery, timing, and closing approach to help reproduce those successful performances.
title: 30 Minutes of sales training that will explode your business in 2022

text: Read customer testimonials aloud to the sales team daily, using fresh examples when available. Hormozi uses this practice to remind representatives of their impact amid frequent rejection.
title: 30 Minutes of sales training that will explode your business in 2022

text: Take responsibility for customer failures where the product can improve, rather than blaming customers. Keep improving the product and ensure salespeople understand its current delivery.
title: 30 Minutes of sales training that will explode your business in 2022

text: If sales decline, invite the customer support leader into a sales meeting to explain what the company does for customers.
title: 30 Minutes of sales training that will explode your business in 2022

text: Hormozi’s team spends 25 minutes practicing script questions aloud with appropriate tone, restarting after mistakes, then 5 minutes rehearsing objection responses. The memorized material consists of 30-second anecdotes and objection responses.
title: 30 Minutes of sales training that will explode your business in 2022

text: Review a 30-minute sales recording daily as a team. Identify what worked, what failed, and what the salesperson will change on the next call.
title: 30 Minutes of sales training that will explode your business in 2022

text: Record sales calls so the team can study actual performance, much as athletes review game footage.
title: 30 Minutes of sales training that will explode your business in 2022

text: After reviewing a call, give the salesperson one specific improvement to practice. Hormozi argues that multiple simultaneous corrections make execution harder.
title: 30 Minutes of sales training that will explode your business in 2022

text: Hormozi describes weekly team communication, daily training, and a daily closing check-in focused on encouragement after the rejection salespeople experience.
title: 30 Minutes of sales training that will explode your business in 2022

text: Hormozi reports that six-week sales competitions work best for his team: participants see enough time to achieve something while still feeling the finish is near.
title: 30 Minutes of sales training that will explode your business in 2022

text: Use small teams for sales competitions to combine rivalry with camaraderie. Hormozi describes four teams of four and pairing stronger sellers with weaker sellers so they help develop one another.
title: 30 Minutes of sales training that will explode your business in 2022

text: Create visible sales career milestones, such as 50, 100, and 150 closed deals, with commission steps from $500 to $525 to $550 per deal. Hormozi thinks visible progression reduces anxiety in repetitive sales work.
title: 30 Minutes of sales training that will explode your business in 2022

text: He describes a large-company owner using four advertising agencies simultaneously to gain more creative attention and expertise, while accepting some audience overlap.
title: He Makes $600,000,000/Yr Selling Bacon

text: He endorses a rough heuristic that the square root of a company’s headcount produces half its value: with 100 employees, around 10 would account for 50%.

text: Hormozi thinks business becomes easier when owners identify the fundamentals that matter and concentrate on them.

text: Hormozi thinks treating continued commitment to a business as a fixed premise helps owners approach difficulties as problems to solve individually.

text: Arbitrage means exploiting a price difference for the same asset across markets. He extends the idea to earning service income from expensive markets while living somewhere cheaper.
title: The 3 Fastest Ways I Know To Grow Any Business

text: He frames wealth as income relative to spending: someone spending beyond monthly earnings of $50,000 or $500,000 can feel poor, while someone earning $5,000 and spending $500 can feel rich.
title: The 3 Fastest Ways I Know To Grow Any Business

text: To improve the gap between earnings and expenses, keep income while moving somewhere cheaper, or remain where you are and sell into a more expensive geography.
title: The 3 Fastest Ways I Know To Grow Any Business

text: He considers paying beyond one's means for access to wealthy contacts risky, even though a founder in his building successfully financed company growth that way.
title: The 3 Fastest Ways I Know To Grow Any Business

text: Personal spending affects how much capital an owner can reinvest in growth. If increasing income is unclear, he recommends cutting spending substantially, including sharing living costs.
title: The 3 Fastest Ways I Know To Grow Any Business

text: A skill advantage can create an economic opportunity because someone pays you to perform work that would cost them more to accomplish themselves; your profit comes from charging above your own cost.
title: The 3 Fastest Ways I Know To Grow Any Business

text: To increase the number of people who know about a business, he recommends giving away something exceptionally valuable.
title: The 3 Fastest Ways I Know To Grow Any Business

text: He treats writing a book before entering a market as a learning exercise: researching, combining information, and organizing it clearly helps him improve his thinking.
title: The 3 Fastest Ways I Know To Grow Any Business

text: Sharing detailed methods can create demand for paid implementation assistance, rather than eliminate the need for the business.
title: The 3 Fastest Ways I Know To Grow Any Business

text: A sustainable free offer needs a connected paid product. Its delivery costs must be supported by the customers it attracts and the revenue generated afterward.
title: The 3 Fastest Ways I Know To Grow Any Business

text: His preferred business approach is to identify something people already purchase, improve it, offer it without charge, and earn revenue through a different connected product.
title: The 3 Fastest Ways I Know To Grow Any Business

text: He argues that a giveaway needs recognizable, substantial value to generate reciprocity, and the business must be willing to wait before receiving money in return.
title: The 3 Fastest Ways I Know To Grow Any Business

text: A lead magnet can expose a problem, offer a trial, or complete one part of a larger process. The paid offer should address the need that becomes apparent next.
title: The 3 Fastest Ways I Know To Grow Any Business

text: He identifies pricing as the fastest way to increase customer value and regards it as the strongest profit lever.
title: The 3 Fastest Ways I Know To Grow Any Business

text: Employees can accept more risk by tying part or all of their compensation to a metric they influence and can connect to company revenue or profit.
title: The 3 Fastest Ways I Know To Grow Any Business

text: He thinks changing roles, including within the same company, can produce a larger pay increase than simply requesting a raise, because a different title or responsibility allows a different compensation level.
title: The 3 Fastest Ways I Know To Grow Any Business

text: Add an offer priced far above the regular menu to influence how customers judge the other prices. The expensive option makes the remaining choices appear cheaper by comparison.
title: The 3 Fastest Ways I Know To Grow Any Business

text: He distinguishes luxury from premium: luxury derives value from a publicly recognizable high price and associated status, while premium derives value from better results or a better experience.
title: The 3 Fastest Ways I Know To Grow Any Business

text: The item a business sells most often need not generate most of its profit. He recommends considering a separate profit-maximizing offer alongside the main product or free offer.
title: The 3 Fastest Ways I Know To Grow Any Business

text: An expensive service tier can provide more personal support or more work completed for the customer. For physical products, he points to newer designs or different materials that improve the experience.
title: The 3 Fastest Ways I Know To Grow Any Business

text: Promote a valuable free offer to phone contacts, email contacts, and social audiences, then provide a natural progression into the paid solution.
title: The 3 Fastest Ways I Know To Grow Any Business

text: He argues that selling to an existing audience can generate revenue with little additional acquisition expense because the business has already paid to obtain those customer relationships.
title: The 3 Fastest Ways I Know To Grow Any Business

text: When customers insulted him or their children damaged his gym, he prioritized staying composed and completing the sale over defending his pride, because he needed the income.
title: Advice I Wish Someone Gave Me When I Was Broke

text: For people with few resources, he argues that time is their available asset and progress requires substantial extra work alongside ordinary employment and daily responsibilities.
title: Advice I Wish Someone Gave Me When I Was Broke

text: He describes anger and fear of failure as the motivation he had available when starting. He presents his sacrifices as his own route forward, rather than claiming that everyone must follow the same path.
title: Advice I Wish Someone Gave Me When I Was Broke

text: Despite earning well in consulting and receiving approval from peers, he recalls being so dissatisfied that he felt indifferent about waking up the following morning.
title: Advice I Wish Someone Gave Me When I Was Broke

text: For people trying to escape low earnings, he recommends accepting responsibility, keeping spending below income, and directing the entire surplus toward increasing future earnings.
title: Advice I Wish Someone Gave Me When I Was Broke

text: He argues that saving from minimum-wage work alone is insufficient for getting ahead and urges people to develop skills, even while others interpret their temporary circumstances as evidence of failure.
title: Advice I Wish Someone Gave Me When I Was Broke

text: He says requests for gym-business advice followed his operation of six gyms by age 26, funded through cash flow. He uses this history to recommend becoming demonstrably capable before teaching others.
title: Advice I Wish Someone Gave Me When I Was Broke

text: When his licensing business reached $4 million monthly, owners of businesses generating $1 million or $500,000 monthly asked how he had reached that level.
title: Advice I Wish Someone Gave Me When I Was Broke

text: He believes beginners cannot determine their entire route in advance; his own opportunities became apparent as he acted.
title: Advice I Wish Someone Gave Me When I Was Broke

text: Before earning an initial dollar, he emphasizes accepting responsibility and applying resources already available toward the next attainable step, instead of planning 100 steps ahead.
title: Advice I Wish Someone Gave Me When I Was Broke

text: He argues that positive feelings are unnecessary for starting. His early motivation was escaping poverty and Baltimore, and earning more subsequently helped him handle inconveniences and family health expenses.
title: Advice I Wish Someone Gave Me When I Was Broke

text: He defines patience through the actions taken while waiting, and courage through behaving as someone would without fear. His emphasis is on observable behavior rather than emotional state.
title: Advice I Wish Someone Gave Me When I Was Broke

text: To motivate change, he recommends vividly considering the future pain of continuing current behavior until remaining comfortable feels more costly than acting.
title: Advice I Wish Someone Gave Me When I Was Broke

text: He defines a supportive friend as someone whose deliberate actions reduce the likelihood of failing at a goal, and recommends evaluating friendships by that standard.
title: Advice I Wish Someone Gave Me When I Was Broke

text: He recommends assessing advice against the adviser's life: disregard guidance from people whose outcomes you do not want, and consider guidance relevant to outcomes you admire.
title: Advice I Wish Someone Gave Me When I Was Broke

text: He describes a potentially lonely transition between old friendships and new circles. For people short on money, he recommends spending that available time developing skills that can command higher earnings.

text: Businesses should expect mistakes from owners and employees, as well as complaints about perceived mistakes; treating each incident as unprecedented can worsen the response.
title: You Made Your Customers ANGRY... Now What?

text: Hormozi attributes to Disney a guideline of 37 positive experiences to offset one negative experience, using it to emphasize both preventing failures and investing heavily in recovery.
title: You Made Your Customers ANGRY... Now What?

text: A refund alone does not restore a wronged customer: customers also spend time and incur other costs, so adequate recovery can require the business to lose money.
title: You Made Your Customers ANGRY... Now What?

text: Downplaying a customer's complaint communicates that their experience does not matter, which can push them to escalate and seek punishment.
title: You Made Your Customers ANGRY... Now What?

text: Hormozi views some one-star reviews as customers imposing a penalty when they believe a refund did not sufficiently address the harm.
title: You Made Your Customers ANGRY... Now What?

text: In the Angry Boat approach, businesses immediately accept responsibility and express stronger concern about a failure than the customer does, validating the customer's frustration.
title: You Made Your Customers ANGRY... Now What?

text: Business owners should accept responsibility for team failures even when they did not personally cause them; ownership includes the downside as well as the upside.
title: You Made Your Customers ANGRY... Now What?

text: Someone with the power to resolve a customer failure should take responsibility for the remedy, even if the original failure occurred outside their department.
title: You Made Your Customers ANGRY... Now What?

text: Only customers can decide that their grievance has become less serious. Hormozi argues that strongly validating their distress allows them to initiate de-escalation themselves.
title: You Made Your Customers ANGRY... Now What?

text: Employees reporting their own mistakes should acknowledge the seriousness instead of presenting the error casually or trying to minimize its impact.
title: You Made Your Customers ANGRY... Now What?

text: After an employee makes a mistake, privately feeling guilty earns little credit; the useful work is repairing the damage and preventing recurrence.
title: You Made Your Customers ANGRY... Now What?

text: Paying refunds plus additional recovery expenses makes the real cost of mistakes visible and gives businesses a stronger incentive to prevent them.
title: You Made Your Customers ANGRY... Now What?

text: If many customers request refunds, the business should correct unrealistic sales expectations or poor delivery, or stop selling the offering; inability to afford refunds does not resolve the underlying failure.
title: You Made Your Customers ANGRY... Now What?

text: Hormozi believes that owning a failure and delivering an exceptional recovery can increase the chance of turning the affected customer into a lasting advocate.
title: You Made Your Customers ANGRY... Now What?

text: High-volume businesses should authorize frontline staff to use two or three specific remedies, such as complimentary drinks, meals, or upgrades, matched to the severity of the customer's problem.
title: You Made Your Customers ANGRY... Now What?

text: Budget customer recovery benefits into business margins. As an example monitoring threshold, Hormozi suggests investigating the process when an employee uses more than five such remedies in a month.
title: You Made Your Customers ANGRY... Now What?

text: Email follow-up can be inexpensive because acquiring the contact has already been paid for; Hormozi identifies software and writing as the main remaining costs.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: Hormozi says email has two commercial purposes: encouraging a purchase now or making a later purchase more likely.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: Segment subscribers using relevant signup information, such as business ownership or revenue, so beginners and experienced operators receive material suited to their situations.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: Hormozi uses a recurring newsletter name in subject lines because he wants readers' previous positive experiences to motivate future opens, even when individual topics change.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: Place something immediately useful near the beginning of an email so opening it produces a quick reward before the reader reaches the main lesson.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: For his minute-long newsletter, Hormozi aims for roughly 200 words covering one actionable concept. He presents this as a format choice, acknowledging that longer, story-driven emails can also work.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: Physical businesses can make existing proof more visible by printing five-star reviews from review platforms, placing them in $1 frames, and filling their lobby walls with them.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: Hormozi recommends including a postscript because he says it attracts more reading than any email component except the headline.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: For blog promotion, put a compelling takeaway in the email and link to the full article. Hormozi wants useful destinations to reinforce subscribers' willingness to click again.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: Hormozi would rather leave a longer gap between emails than send weak material, because disappointing readers can reduce their willingness to open subsequent messages.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: Check email presentation on both desktop and mobile, particularly when using images; Hormozi warns that poor rendering can make messages look unprofessional and reduce clicks.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: Experiment with email layouts initially, then reuse a format that produces stronger replies or clicks so readers know what experience to expect.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: Hormozi recommends contacting newly opted-in leads within 60 seconds, citing research he attributes to Harvard Business Review reporting an average 391% sales increase.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: Write preview text deliberately instead of accepting the first 150 characters automatically. Lead with valuable or curiosity-provoking information rather than routine greetings.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: Hormozi considers one or two calls to action reasonable when each serves a distinct audience or objective, such as further exploration versus purchasing. He warns that five can become excessive.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: For recurring businesses retaining customers beyond a year, Hormozi proposes an annual renewal charge equal to 1–3 monthly payments. He says this can add approximately 8–24% in revenue without additional costs.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: Based on conversations with email marketers, Hormozi suggests roughly three emails weekly as a useful cadence, while stressing that it is not mandatory and that tolerance depends on content quality.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: Hormozi prefers making each newsletter useful and keeping a relevant next-step link available, rather than separating newsletters into educational messages and dedicated promotions.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: To start emailing with a manageable commitment, batch-write 12 messages for monthly distribution across a year, then add extra emails when useful ideas arise.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: Hormozi prefers a quality threshold over a public publishing commitment: send two or four emails when that many are good enough, and none when nothing meets the threshold.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: Hormozi favors ordinary-looking, text-heavy emails without images and with at most one or two links. He also reports that stronger money-related language has correlated with more promotional-tab placement in his emails.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: Hormozi argues that deliverability improves through consistently engaging emails and alignment with providers' goal of a useful inbox, rather than reliance on a single workaround.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: Hormozi suspects links to Google-hosted destinations, including YouTube and Drive, may improve delivery and clicks. He recommends testing them rather than assuming polished standalone assets always perform better.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: Test two subject lines on a small portion of the list, then distribute the better-performing version to the remaining subscribers.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: A lead magnet should repay the effort required to obtain it; Hormozi worries that subscribers will disengage if the content fails to justify those steps.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: Distinguish clicks divided by total recipients from clicks divided by opens. With 100,000 recipients, 30,000 opens, and 10,000 clicks, the respective rates are 10% and approximately 33%.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: Hormozi prioritizes click performance across multiple emails over maximizing the immediate click request in every message, allowing some emails to build value before others ask for action.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: Citing figures shared by Neil Patel, Hormozi suggests Monday or Tuesday for consumer emails, with an approximately 18% open-rate lift, and Wednesday for business emails, with a comparable lift.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: Hormozi suggests testing sending windows of 10 a.m.–noon and 1–3 p.m. He considers these more relevant to businesses serving one time zone than to internationally distributed audiences.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: When collecting testimonials, ask customers about their lowest point rather than requesting a broad account of life before buying. Hormozi says specific painful moments produce stronger openings than vague descriptions of difficulty.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: Match both the offer and the transition into a call to action to the content's subject and audience, rather than repeatedly inserting identical promotional copy.
title: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!

text: Hormozi places the lower boundary of institutional acquisition interest at roughly $5 million per transaction, distinguishing those deals from smaller purchases by individual investors.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: A business can attract a lower valuation or no offer when revenue depends on too few customers, particularly when the owner personally holds those relationships.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: Businesses seeking a strong sale valuation need a dependable, repeatable method for obtaining customers; he prefers having several acquisition channels.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: He believes owners more often wait too long to sell than sell prematurely; once a small business starts deteriorating, finding a buyer can become difficult.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: He recommends maintaining growth for 12–18 months before a sale because buyers interpret decline as a warning and project positive growth forward.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: Buyers value what a business could become. A credible explanation of expansion opportunities and sufficient market size can make the business more valuable.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: When customers depend on the founder for selling or delivery, the founder's departure threatens business value. Dependence on a single acquisition channel creates another major risk for buyers.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: Hormozi describes enterprise value through the scale of future revenue and the risk that it will not materialize: larger, more dependable future sales support greater value.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: He distinguishes investment bankers serving institutional transactions from brokers typically handling sales below $5 million.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: Find advisers through introductions, then use a one-page business overview to obtain a conversation. Suitable advisers need experience with both the company's industry and its transaction size.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: Evaluate bankers by recent sales of comparable businesses in the same market and size range, rather than relying on their assurances about knowing buyers.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: When negotiating banker compensation, examine upfront charges, termination fees, minimum acceptable offers, and whether commissions apply to seller cash receipts or the company's overall valuation. He favors the cash-receipts basis.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: Before advisers influence expectations, record the amount you would accept and why. He considers selling emotionally difficult because the business can be part of the owner's identity.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: Owners should actively supply the strongest reasons to buy their business. Bankers understand the transaction process but do not know the company as deeply as its owner.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: He warns that bankers primarily want a transaction completed, so their efforts to bring both parties together may conflict with obtaining the seller's preferred outcome.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: Negotiating power improves when the owner has alternatives and can credibly reject a deal. In his experience, bankers took disputed requirements seriously only when he made them conditions of continuing.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: His illustrative sale funnel contacts 500 buyers, receives 98 confidentiality agreements and about 14–15 indications of interest, gives management presentations to roughly half, obtains 2–4 letters of intent, and completes one transaction.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: Use an anonymous initial teaser so early outreach does not reveal the company's identity and alarm employees.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: Push bankers to revisit prospective buyers. His eventual acquirer emerged after his finance chief pressed the bankers to contact that prospect again.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: He estimates 12–18 months between starting the sale process and receiving proceeds, despite a presentation showing roughly 20 weeks for the central process and about three additional months spent finding bankers.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: Organize diligence materials in a shared data room so prospective buyers can review them and develop questions without requiring repeated individual exchanges.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: Compare competing offers on both price and payment conditions. He considers favorable terms valuable enough to justify accepting a lower headline valuation.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: A headline exit price can substantially exceed immediate personal proceeds because earnouts, seller loans, retained equity, partner distributions, bonuses, taxes, and transaction charges affect what the seller receives.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: He favors strategic acquirers for higher multiples because existing systems can let them earn more from the acquired business, while noting that financial buyers are more numerous.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: Evaluate the buyer's relevant experience and compatibility with the team alongside price. He says some sellers regret choosing the highest bidder over accepting 10% less for a better working relationship.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: He says letters of intent commonly give one buyer exclusivity during diligence, preventing the seller from continuing to market the business during that period.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: He advises against conceding terms for a promised quick closing. In one sale, he accepted worse conditions for a projected 30-day completion that actually took 112 days.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: Buyer diligence examines earnings quality, ownership, litigation, and legal compliance. He reports knowing someone whose compliance problems prevented two separate nine-figure transactions, years apart.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: Expect buyers to interview customers and informed employees, investigate management backgrounds, and examine employment agreements to assess whether the business can continue after the owner leaves.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: A lengthy sale absorbs the owner's attention, making a management team that can sustain growth essential. He argues that strong ongoing growth also increases the seller's negotiating leverage.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: He recommends accepting reasonable assurances about ownership while negotiating hard against indemnities that expose the seller to matters beyond their control.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: Examine noncompetes in both the purchase documents and documents governing retained equity. He warns that ownership-related restrictions may continue beyond the sale agreement's noncompete.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: Decide what business activity you intend to pursue after selling, disclose it honestly, and negotiate specific noncompete language that accommodates those plans.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: Ensure supporting disclosures discussed during negotiations appear in the agreement's schedules. He recommends using a capable lawyer for this documentation work.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: Read contractual definitions carefully: narrowing a term can change the effect of provisions throughout an agreement and sometimes resolve an issue more effectively than disputing individual clauses.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: Negotiate the working capital that must remain available for normal operations after the sale. A lower agreed requirement allows the seller to withdraw more cash alongside the sale proceeds.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: Negotiate both the escrow amount and release schedule. He considers holding back less than 10% favorable; his own arrangement had releases around 90 days and one year.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: Trust the people involved in the transaction, but verify that the written agreement actually expresses what they say it does.
title: I sold 8 businesses by age 32 [here’s how]

text: Hormozi argues that larger monetary reference units encourage pursuing larger opportunities. Someone thinking in $10,000 or $100,000 increments becomes less interested in activities producing $100 or $1,000 because those returns fall below a single mental unit.
title: 2 Signs That You Will Become Wealthy One Day..

text: Hormozi illustrates how response speed changes project duration: five exchanges with each person taking a day to reply consume 10 days, whereas responsive collaborators could finish the same exchange in 30 minutes.
title: 2 Signs That You Will Become Wealthy One Day..

text: For routine company work, Hormozi recommends replacing an assumed end-of-week deadline with an end-of-day deadline, immediate action, or completion within four hours, making faster execution the default.
title: 2 Signs That You Will Become Wealthy One Day..

text: Hormozi considers willingness to pursue goals over decades, rather than days, a sign of future wealth. He pairs that long horizon with rapid action on everyday tasks.
title: 2 Signs That You Will Become Wealthy One Day..

text: Hormozi argues that resisting immediate rewards supports success because substantial achievements take time. He uses the marshmallow experiment to support his belief that greater willingness to wait predicts greater eventual success.

text: He viewed leaving employment to start a business as a recoverable experiment because he believed he could return to a job if it failed.

text: Hormozi says nine of his businesses produced little before his first major success, illustrating his experience of repeated attempts preceding a substantial win.

text: For businesses acquiring customers inconsistently, he attributes the volatility to insufficient advertising activity and recommends increasing volume to make results more consistent.

text: A small competitor can focus on outperforming the particular employee or operation serving its target customer, rather than imagining it must defeat the entire leading company.

text: He says learning to advertise and sell is insufficient for sustained growth unless the business also develops a mechanism that allows results to accumulate.

text: Retaining existing customers lets new acquisitions add to the customer base; replacing departing customers repeatedly consumes acquisition spending that could otherwise contribute to profit.

text: He argues that expanding acquisition becomes more expensive as a business reaches colder, less suitable prospects who are harder to sell and more sensitive to price.
title: Your biggest advantage is no one knows who you are

text: Acquire enough customers to learn how to retain them, satisfy them, generate referrals, and sustain payments before expanding aggressively; otherwise, he warns, acquisition costs rise and margins weaken.
title: Your biggest advantage is no one knows who you are

text: He recommends designing around a specific, clearly described customer and evaluating product and brand decisions from that customer's perspective, rather than trying to satisfy an indistinct mass audience.

text: Begin offer development by defining the customer's desired outcome precisely, then enumerate the specific obstacles preventing it; customers' explanations for not succeeding can reveal those obstacles.

text: Convert each customer obstacle into a named solution, then brainstorm possible delivery methods without initially restricting cost. He recommends extending ideas rather than rejecting them during this stage.
title: Your biggest advantage is no one knows who you are

text: Prioritize delivery options offering substantial customer value at low cost, but also consider exceptionally valuable options with meaningful costs; he says restricting everything to free delivery overlooks less crowded opportunities.
title: Your biggest advantage is no one knows who you are

text: Assemble the most valuable combination of solutions before setting a price appropriate to that package, rather than eliminating expensive delivery ideas before considering what the offer could command.
title: Your biggest advantage is no one knows who you are

text: A persuasive offer should not be scaled until the business can fulfill it. He cautions that work expected to take six weeks can instead require six months or a year.

text: In his experience, changes often initially reduce performance by about 20%, particularly in operations. He therefore seeks changes with an expected improvement of at least 20% to justify the disruption.
title: Your biggest advantage is no one knows who you are

text: Repeated process changes can prevent employees from becoming proficient. He now favors stability in service businesses and accepts leaving minor imperfections unresolved when changing them would create more disruption than benefit.
title: Your biggest advantage is no one knows who you are

text: Small businesses can refine delivery more easily because changes require less coordination; he contrasts acting alone with communicating a change across a 50-person team.

text: He describes entrepreneurial challenges as accumulating: managing oneself, handling expectations from friends and family, and persuading capable employees to join. Earlier challenges remain as new ones appear.
title: Your biggest advantage is no one knows who you are

text: Building something substantial requires varied expertise and time; hiring experienced specialists allows an entrepreneur to benefit from skills that would take many years to acquire personally.
title: Your biggest advantage is no one knows who you are

text: He argues that larger businesses face greater exposure to market shifts and regulatory attention, while smaller entrepreneurs can concentrate on the immediate problems in front of them.
title: Your biggest advantage is no one knows who you are

text: From his experience as a gym owner, he came to believe that some people encourage ambition but resent its success; he recommends valuing friends who continue to support achievement.

text: He says accepting that both entrepreneurship and alternative paths contain difficulties helps him manage stress, especially when he notices himself expecting business to become easy or free of interpersonal problems.

text: An exceptional core offer can reduce how much a business depends on forceful selling, polished copy, or outstanding advertising creative.
title: The Offer Is King (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: An attractive offer must also seem credible. Explaining a genuine reason for a steep discount, such as excess inventory or spoilage, can make the offer believable.
title: The Offer Is King (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: An offer needs customer-perceived value that can be communicated briefly, alongside a business model that makes the offer financially workable.
title: The Offer Is King (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Hormozi believes free offers can produce the most leads and typically lower customer acquisition costs. He sees an easily understood free offer that spreads through recommendations as a major growth tool.
title: The Offer Is King (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: A valuable program offered as a purchase bonus can attract attention, establish a price anchor, and encourage customers to enter a recurring membership.
title: The Offer Is King (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Use a limited free trial to attract prospects, then offer a paid version with additional access and support. Hormozi says this structure can upgrade three out of four prospects.
title: The Offer Is King (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: For prospects declining the paid upgrade, offer a free trial requiring a payment card and participation commitments. His example charges $50 for missing required sessions, aiming to increase participation and eventual conversion.
title: The Offer Is King (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: A deposit-based free offer can return the deposit or apply it toward another program when customers meet stated conditions. Advertising should disclose those conditions, and applicable requirements can differ by state.
title: The Offer Is King (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: A service can remain free when another revenue stream funds the customer relationship. His example requires customers receiving free training to purchase supplements as part of the program.
title: The Offer Is King (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: A valuable giveaway related to the main offer can attract inexpensive prospects who demonstrate demand for that service. After selecting a winner, offer other entrants a discount on the paid program.
title: The Offer Is King (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Offer the initial 28 days or first month free in exchange for a longer commitment, such as a nine-month contract. Disclose the conditions and continue persuading customers to stay during the introductory period.
title: The Offer Is King (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Automatic billing does not replace selling continued participation. Ensure customers expect the charge; Hormozi says he would prefer billing customers whose willingness to continue he had confirmed, at least verbally, even with a signed contract.
title: The Offer Is King (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Before scaling free-offer acquisition, understand conversion, retention, average customer spending, and lifetime value. Hormozi argues these figures reveal whether the business can profitably compete for customers.
title: The Offer Is King (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: A prospect should be able to describe an offer to someone else in one or two sentences. If that is difficult, Hormozi considers the offer insufficiently clear.
title: The Offer Is King (ALEX HORMOZI)

text: Across his experience with different sales formats, Hormozi considers simplicity essential to making a sales process scalable.
title: I Taught 116+ Salesmen My Closing Framework

text: Hormozi attributes his customer monetization advantage to efficient phone conversion attached to a marketing funnel.
title: I Taught 116+ Salesmen My Closing Framework

text: He presents $100,000 in monthly revenue as the dividing point between selling individually and needing other people to scale sales.
title: I Taught 116+ Salesmen My Closing Framework

text: Teaching others to sell is more valuable than selling personally because it removes the constraint of the seller’s own time; he describes potential earnings increases of 10 or 100 times.
title: I Taught 116+ Salesmen My Closing Framework

text: He says the same underlying sales milestones apply to consumer and business sales, including transactions priced at $500 and $100,000.
title: I Taught 116+ Salesmen My Closing Framework

text: His CLOSER sequence establishes the prospect’s reason for engaging, confirms the problem, examines previous attempts, presents the desired outcome, addresses concerns, and strengthens commitment after purchase.
title: I Taught 116+ Salesmen My Closing Framework

text: Reinforcing a purchase continues through onboarding and the first weekly check-in: customers repeatedly need reasons to act despite discomfort and possible failure.
title: I Taught 116+ Salesmen My Closing Framework

text: When prospects say they only want information, ask what problem that information would help solve, then summarize their goal and get their acknowledgment.
title: I Taught 116+ Salesmen My Closing Framework

text: Explore previous solutions by asking what prospects tried, for how long, when, and with what results. Repeat until their attempts are covered; he calls this the pain cycle.
title: I Taught 116+ Salesmen My Closing Framework

text: Position previous unsuccessful attempts as incomplete solutions, identifying the missing component that the offered program supplies rather than attributing failure to the prospect.
title: I Taught 116+ Salesmen My Closing Framework

text: He favors organizing a pitch around three main components, based on his belief that people struggle to absorb more than three.
title: I Taught 116+ Salesmen My Closing Framework

text: Present the result customers want and how painless reaching it can be, instead of centering the pitch on modules, technical methods, or implementation tasks.
title: I Taught 116+ Salesmen My Closing Framework

text: For multiple service levels, he describes selling the same destination while distinguishing the ways customers can reach it.
title: I Taught 116+ Salesmen My Closing Framework

text: He considers the product the most important element of selling: genuine belief in its usefulness enables an ethical salesperson to sell forcefully and communicate with conviction.
title: I Taught 116+ Salesmen My Closing Framework

text: Read customer testimonials aloud to the sales team every day to strengthen product conviction. He advises salespeople working for businesses without testimonials to find another business.
title: I Taught 116+ Salesmen My Closing Framework

text: Business owners should improve every product weakness they can identify. When customers fail, ask what could help the next similar customer succeed instead of blaming the customer.
title: I Taught 116+ Salesmen My Closing Framework

text: His team trains for 60 minutes daily, five days weekly: 25 minutes reading scripts aloud, five minutes practicing objections, and the second half developing listening through recorded-call review.
title: I Taught 116+ Salesmen My Closing Framework

text: Train speaking through tone, wording, and sequence until delivery becomes automatic. Train listening by reviewing recordings, identifying successes and mistakes, and rehearsing what to do differently next time.
title: I Taught 116+ Salesmen My Closing Framework

text: Hormozi argues that people in their twenties should direct money toward education and earning ability instead of status purchases intended to impress peers.
title: 14 Money Mistakes to AVOID in Your 20's

text: He advises young workers to choose jobs for skill development rather than immediate pay increases; an additional $10,000 or $25,000 annually in their twenties matters less, in his view, than their longer-term learning.
title: 14 Money Mistakes to AVOID in Your 20's

text: For young people pursuing substantial wealth, he favors investing savings in earning ability. He illustrates this with spending $10,000 on development that could double or triple earning capacity.
title: 14 Money Mistakes to AVOID in Your 20's

text: He recommends allocating money for education before discretionary spending and accumulating it in a separate account until a worthwhile learning opportunity appears.
title: 14 Money Mistakes to AVOID in Your 20's

text: He recommends making allocations for personal investment automatic while making discretionary purchases require deliberate effort, so investing becomes easier and spending becomes harder.
title: 14 Money Mistakes to AVOID in Your 20's

text: He recommends living with people pursuing similar goals, because even responsible roommates can discourage an unfamiliar ambition; aligned housemates can encourage one another.
title: 14 Money Mistakes to AVOID in Your 20's

text: He advises people to study what a successful person did at a comparable stage, rather than copying that person's current lifestyle before developing a similar record of achievement.
title: 14 Money Mistakes to AVOID in Your 20's

text: He recommends checking bank balances each morning to confront financial reality and recognize payment patterns. He says avoiding his own balance because it felt discouraging kept him unaware of money leaving.
title: 14 Money Mistakes to AVOID in Your 20's

text: He supports limited spending on meaningful experiences especially suited to one's twenties, even without a financial payoff, because opportunities for those experiences can close. He cautions against exhausting the money reserved for personal investment.
title: 14 Money Mistakes to AVOID in Your 20's

text: When a business stalls, Hormozi suggests its owner may still be solving an earlier-stage problem whose importance has diminished.

text: To understand what drives an industry, examine its leading businesses; operators only slightly ahead may still misunderstand the same challenges.

title: The Top 1% of Business Owners Aren't Smarter Than You

title: The Top 1% of Business Owners Aren't Smarter Than You

text: Hormozi argues that supplement suppliers largely share ingredient access, making brand, taste, and the customer's desired identity important purchase differentiators.
title: The Top 1% of Business Owners Aren't Smarter Than You

text: Software can be easy to sell when its promised benefit is clear, but users quickly become dissatisfied if it fails to solve their problem or creates additional work.

title: The Top 1% of Business Owners Aren't Smarter Than You

title: The Top 1% of Business Owners Aren't Smarter Than You

text: Evaluate spending to acquire employees against the gross profit they can generate throughout their employment.
title: The Top 1% of Business Owners Aren't Smarter Than You

text: Owners often keep addressing problems they enjoy instead of the problem their business currently needs resolved.
title: The Top 1% of Business Owners Aren't Smarter Than You

text: Before entering an industry, ask existing operators which part of running their businesses is hardest.
title: The Top 1% of Business Owners Aren't Smarter Than You

text: He describes major consulting firms as talent-recruitment operations: sustained service growth requires excellent people who give customers reasons to keep buying.
title: The Top 1% of Business Owners Aren't Smarter Than You

text: Education businesses can lose momentum when an exceptional founder delegates delivery to less capable employees and service quality deteriorates.

text: Recast claims that a business problem is impossible as a capability you have not learned yet, making the obstacle a question you can investigate.
title: The Top 1% of Business Owners Aren't Smarter Than You

title: The Top 1% of Business Owners Aren't Smarter Than You

text: Starting another business to escape an unfamiliar growth problem can simply postpone learning the skill that caused the original plateau.
title: The Top 1% of Business Owners Aren't Smarter Than You

title: The Top 1% of Business Owners Aren't Smarter Than You

title: The Top 1% of Business Owners Aren't Smarter Than You

text: Moving rapidly through familiar stages in a new business can resemble progress while leaving the same unlearned skill as the next barrier.

text: When comparing strategic paths, specify the desired outcome and timeline, identify each path's hardest problem, and consider which problem you prefer and are currently equipped to solve.
title: The Top 1% of Business Owners Aren't Smarter Than You

text: Owners tend to receive problems that are both difficult and unwanted because easier problems, or difficult ones others enjoy, can be handled elsewhere in the company.
title: The Top 1% of Business Owners Aren't Smarter Than You

text: He considers choosing greater comfort over additional business potential acceptable, provided the owner recognizes it as a tradeoff.
title: The Top 1% of Business Owners Aren't Smarter Than You

text: Productive difficulty involves iterating toward an outcome while the assumptions supporting its feasibility remain credible.

title: The Top 1% of Business Owners Aren't Smarter Than You

text: He explains frustration tolerance partly through reinforcement history: receiving rewards after repeated attempts can increase willingness to persist through future unsuccessful attempts.
title: The Top 1% of Business Owners Aren't Smarter Than You

title: The Top 1% of Business Owners Aren't Smarter Than You

text: Hormozi defines learning as responding differently when a previously encountered situation occurs again.
title: how to outlearn everyone

text: To learn a skill, identify its component actions and describe observable signs of competence for each part. Make the description specific enough to measure performance.
title: how to outlearn everyone

text: He argues that learning capacity declines with age, but learning technique can improve through greater precision about what needs practice.
title: how to outlearn everyone

text: Quantify skill performance as thoroughly as possible and refine the measures over time. He treats tracking as evidence of commitment because it lets learners judge whether they are improving.
title: how to outlearn everyone

text: Early in learning, prioritize repeated attempts and adjustments over obtaining a complete explanation of why the skill works. He argues that practice supplies feedback that helps learners improve.
title: how to outlearn everyone

text: When learning a skill, he first studies performers in the top 10% or top 1%, identifying actions he can reproduce instead of relying on their explanations.
title: how to outlearn everyone

text: Skill execution and skill instruction are separate abilities. He argues that many excellent performers cannot accurately explain what makes them effective.
title: how to outlearn everyone

text: When imitating strong performers produces poor results, he suggests the learner probably missed details of their behavior. Replication requires observing the smaller actions that contribute to the outcome.
title: how to outlearn everyone

text: Repeatedly comparing actual performance with a desired example reveals additional differences. He considers this growing ability to observe differences central to learning.
title: how to outlearn everyone

text: He interprets natural talent as learning through observation without necessarily being conscious of that learning.
title: how to outlearn everyone

text: Most of his current learning comes from his own business activity: trying things, examining results, repeating effective actions, and then sharing what happened.
title: how to outlearn everyone

text: In an unfamiliar field, he hires experts to make his first attempt comparable to a ninth iteration. He then aims to surpass them through faster cycles of feedback and improvement.
title: how to outlearn everyone

text: He considers the pace of improvement across iterations decisive over a sufficiently long period. Simply making changes does not count unless those changes improve performance.
title: how to outlearn everyone

text: Successful people may repeat explanations that receive approval without those explanations accurately describing their actions or the causes of success.
title: how to outlearn everyone

text: He endorses understanding a failure over achieving an unexplained success: knowing the cause of failure allows correction, while unexplained success cannot reliably be reproduced.
title: how to outlearn everyone

text: He values the person developed through pursuing success more than the rewards obtained, and believes a lucky outcome can deprive someone of opportunities to develop their abilities.
title: how to outlearn everyone

text: After buying a Powerball ticket with his then-girlfriend, he recalls fearing that winning would prevent him from proving his ability to succeed. He feels grateful that he lost.
title: how to outlearn everyone

text: Hormozi identifies three paths: concentrate on a craft, make business building the craft, or retain a preferred specialty while others grow the company. The appropriate choice depends on current preferences and can change later.
title: 3 Ways to Do What You Love (and get wealthy too)

text: Craft specialists can increase earnings without expanding output: improve their work, earn trust and recommendations, and raise prices as demand grows, progressing from ordinary market rates toward premium and luxury positioning.
title: 3 Ways to Do What You Love (and get wealthy too)

text: For founders choosing company leadership, Hormozi ranks advisors highest when they have achieved the desired outcome themselves and repeatedly helped comparable people achieve it. Experienced outside advisors can help assess leadership candidates.
title: 3 Ways to Do What You Love (and get wealthy too)

text: People who enjoy entrepreneurship regardless of the product can identify market needs, connect them with purchases, build an organization, and install an operator to run it and generate cash flow.
title: 3 Ways to Do What You Love (and get wealthy too)

text: The hybrid path can center on marketing, finance, or fundraising as well as product development. A founder can keep responsibility for a favored function while assembling people to operate the rest.
title: 3 Ways to Do What You Love (and get wealthy too)

text: Hormozi ranks product capability above marketing, and marketing above sales. He argues that marketing eventually faces rising acquisition costs; without customer recommendations, growth becomes unsustainable and the company levels off.
title: 3 Ways to Do What You Love (and get wealthy too)

text: Hormozi says entrepreneurs commonly learn sales first because it can be learned in a couple of weeks; marketing takes longer. He describes marketing as adapting sales persuasion across media to reach many people simultaneously.
title: 3 Ways to Do What You Love (and get wealthy too)
