text: Hormozi says referred customers convert more readily, accept higher prices, purchase more frequently, and are more likely to send additional customers.
title: 7 Ways To Get Customers for Free

text: After completing a sale, ask customers to identify specific people who could benefit or participate with them. He favors an open-ended question over a yes-or-no referral request.
title: 7 Ways To Get Customers for Free

text: For a membership business losing 10% of customers monthly, referrals producing new customers equal to 10% of the base would replace those losses. His illustration uses 1,000 customers and 100 monthly replacements.
title: 7 Ways To Get Customers for Free

text: Tie a gift card campaign to a holiday or business milestone. Set the card’s face value around a basic service unit the business would otherwise be comfortable providing free to attract customers.
title: 7 Ways To Get Customers for Free

text: Offer existing customers gift cards discounted by at least 90%, limited to two per buyer and usable only by other people. Ask buyers to identify recipients when purchasing so the business captures referral leads.
title: 7 Ways To Get Customers for Free

text: For the referral gift card promotion, he recommends a 30-day expiration and direct follow-up with recipients to encourage prompt redemption.
title: 7 Ways To Get Customers for Free

text: A referral gift card can cover the basic service or become credit toward a larger package. His example applies $200 toward a $2,000 purchase, creating a 10% reduction on that package.
title: 7 Ways To Get Customers for Free

text: When a prospect requests a discount, offer it in exchange for introductions to three friends, completed immediately. He says he discounts only when the offer or the customer’s obligations also change.
title: 7 Ways To Get Customers for Free

text: If three referral introductions are expected to produce one customer, he would allow a discount equal to his usual cost of acquiring one customer. He recommends refining the incentive as conversion data becomes predictable.
title: 7 Ways To Get Customers for Free

text: Exchange referrals for additional service instead of reducing price when delivery costs are low. His example replaces a $200 discount with $400 of service costing $80 to deliver, based on $40 cost per $200 sold.
title: 7 Ways To Get Customers for Free

text: Once a customer has signed and paid, explain how referral rewards could cover their purchase. His example pays $100 for each referred customer who buys against an original $500 purchase; introductions alone do not qualify.
title: 7 Ways To Get Customers for Free

text: Build referral attribution into the sales workflow: record referred people beneath the contract or obtain a digital introduction immediately. He used the contract fields to remind salespeople to ask and connect referrals to their source.
title: 7 Ways To Get Customers for Free

text: After a customer achieves a visible result, collect a testimonial and request a referral. With established rapport and customer agreement, take a shared photo and use their phone to initiate an introduction showing the outcome.
title: 7 Ways To Get Customers for Free

text: For local businesses, he recommends customer appreciation events at least quarterly. Send handwritten invitations with a postscript allowing customers to share a photo of the invitation so a friend can attend and enjoy the refreshments.
title: 7 Ways To Get Customers for Free

text: Ask customers to introduce event guests through a group text before arrival. At the event, arrange follow-up appointments rather than selling; schedule them promptly while interest is high, then use normal lead reminders.
title: 7 Ways To Get Customers for Free

text: For services couples can use together, encourage spouse participation and explain the support benefits. He recommends using an outcome statistic to strengthen the invitation, illustrating this with a claim of threefold success rather than presenting verified data.
title: 7 Ways To Get Customers for Free

text: Repeat invitations to participate with a friend across campaign content, advertisements, and messages. He recommends emphasizing shared support, better experiences, and improved results rather than relying only on occasional referral requests.
title: 7 Ways To Get Customers for Free

text: Based on his businesses, Hormozi estimates these referral practices can generate roughly 30% of leads. He also describes the benefit as 30% more customers, without reconciling those different measures.
title: 7 Ways To Get Customers for Free

text: Hormozi argues that protecting your reputation from embarrassment can prevent progress; the practical goal is continuing necessary work even when other people's opinions still hurt.
title: Stop Caring What Others Think of You So Much

text: When making consequential decisions, seek guidance from people approaching or achieving your desired outcomes. If nobody nearby qualifies, learn from people outside your immediate environment.
title: Stop Caring What Others Think of You So Much

title: Stop Caring What Others Think of You So Much

title: Stop Caring What Others Think of You So Much

text: Hormozi groups businesses into four models: e-commerce, services, education, and software. Each has recurring constraints that owners should understand rather than interpret as evidence that their business is broken.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: E-commerce often expands in bursts separated by plateaus when inventory funding, advertising reach, retail access, or production capacity becomes the limiting factor.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: Online product sales can expand quickly when inventory and fulfillment have spare capacity, because purchasing does not require a matching increase in customer-facing staff.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: A growing e-commerce company may show accounting profits while leaving little cash for its owner, because purchasing the next round of inventory consumes the money.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: E-commerce operators should develop backup sources for materials, manufacturing, fulfillment, and financing because failures among these outside partners can interrupt their own business.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: Inventory forecasting must match supplier lead times: with a 12-week replenishment delay, an e-commerce owner needs to estimate sales 12 weeks ahead.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: Hormozi considers brand the strongest protection against physical-product imitation; competitors may reproduce the item without reproducing its established meaning to customers.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: Brand can improve advertising response, encourage repeat purchases, and support higher prices, improving acquisition costs, customer lifetime value, and gross profit.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: E-commerce brands should choose affiliates, influencers, and discount policies according to the associations they want customers to form, even when rejecting a partnership means sacrificing immediate sales.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: Hormozi says enduring e-commerce companies tend to allocate 70% of marketing spending to awareness and brand associations, with 30% directed toward immediate purchasing.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: At broad brand awareness, physical stores can make purchasing easier, reduce individual shipping needs, and increase order size, although expanding a retail footprint requires substantial capital.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: As e-commerce acquisition costs increase, exceptional products support a compounding source of demand through returning customers and customers who introduce other buyers.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: Hormozi suggests that 60%–70% repurchasing within a first-purchase cohort likely indicates a strong product. The overall share of returning buyers is harder to interpret because it depends on the company's growth rate.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: Service businesses need gross-margin room for new employees' learning periods, because hiring can temporarily reduce sales effectiveness or delivery quality.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: Hormozi argues that competent businesses performing work for customers usually find capable delivery staff harder to obtain than customers, unlike coaching offers that require customers to do difficult work themselves.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: For primarily labor-based services, Hormozi argues that appropriate pricing and adjustable staffing can preserve profitability during declining revenue, potentially by shrinking back to the owner's own labor.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: Service businesses can generate substantial distributable cash because repeating paid work generally does not require the inventory purchases or development spending associated with other models.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: A service company should treat recruiting, onboarding, and training as core capabilities: developing less-skilled recruits into valuable practitioners creates the difference between labor cost and what customers will pay.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: Service founders must learn to transfer their expertise through substantial training. Expecting a weekend of instruction to reproduce skills developed over 10 years is unrealistic.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: Hormozi says service businesses commonly need to narrow their customer focus around $1–$3 million in revenue, moving beyond accepting every type of customer and project.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: For a focused service customer group, offer one to three repeatable deliverables. Standardized delivery allows more efficient operations and clearer employee training.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: Service companies need defined employee advancement paths so that hard-to-recruit talent has a reason to remain with the business.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: Hormozi recommends reinvesting service-company cash into recruiting stronger people and building brand; brand can support premium prices and attract candidates who value the affiliation.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: When a service company's reputation produces more demand than it can fulfill, raising prices can expand margins. Maintaining delivery quality allows that process to continue as the company attracts customers with larger budgets.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: A low-price service strategy requires designing the company around cost efficiency from inception, including automation and lower-cost staffing; simply cutting prices after sales resistance does not constitute that strategy.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: Education businesses can generate revenue rapidly, but successful instruction naturally reduces retention when students learn the skill and finish the program.

text: Education businesses face easy market entry and can train future competitors, because students may resell the skills they have learned.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: Hormozi generally favors giving customers less access to a strong educator over selling equivalent access to poorly prepared substitutes, because weaker instruction can damage reputation and referrals.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: Education businesses can add recurring value through resources customers repeatedly need, such as fresh advertising creative, community access, or regularly researched opportunities.

text: Separate the substantial initial price of learning a skill from the potentially much smaller ongoing price of maintaining it or accessing recurring benefits. Hormozi calls this structure Big Head, Long Tail.

text: Before expanding software marketing, founders must survive the early development period and establish that customers both want the product initially and continue using and paying for it.

title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: Revenue retention tracks spending from an original customer group. Ten customers paying $10 monthly produce $100; retaining that $100 a year later equals 100%, even if some customers leave and others increase spending.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: Customer feedback should inform software decisions without automatically becoming new features. Each addition must justify the complexity it introduces into the user experience.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: Especially for lower-priced software, Hormozi recommends customer-driven referral loops alongside paid acquisition so that additional customers reduce the effective acquisition cost over time.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: Software founders need enough technical judgment to assess engineering talent, either personally or through a strong technical cofounder, and should establish scalable code and documentation from the beginning.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: Hormozi defines effective software design as identifying an outcome people want and systematically removing the effort and obstacles between the user and that outcome.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: Estimate the enterprise value unlocked by solving a business model's central constraint, then use that value to judge how much time and money the solution deserves.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: Hormozi suggests matching model choice to temperament: patient technical builders may suit software, promoters may suit e-commerce or education, and people who enjoy teaching and developing teams may suit services.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: Strong marketing should be paired with exceptional products because satisfaction with an earlier purchase influences whether customers participate in the next launch.
title: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)

text: Hormozi presents employment as the most dependable, lowest-risk payment arrangement: workers receive compensation after doing their work, provided they retain the job.
title: The 6 Levels of Making Money

text: Staged contractor payments bring some cash forward, but Hormozi warns that customers dismiss vendors more readily than employers dismiss employees.
title: The 6 Levels of Making Money

text: Hormozi cites average employee tenure of 3.9 years, contractor engagements of 3–12 months, and temporary gigs of 1–3 months, describing vendor turnover as five times higher annually.
title: The 6 Levels of Making Money

text: Businesses with stronger bargaining power can require complete payment before starting delivery. Hormozi treats this as more favorable payment terms, conditional on knowing how to deliver.
title: The 6 Levels of Making Money

text: Business owner layaway lets customers choose installments while postponing delivery until payment is complete. Hormozi says this often motivates customers to pay faster because they want the service sooner.
title: The 6 Levels of Making Money

text: A prepaid retainer allows a service provider to deduct fees as work proceeds and request replenishment, keeping payment ahead of labor.
title: The 6 Levels of Making Money

text: Compensation triggered by results, milestones, revenue, profit, or ownership performance separates earnings from hours worked. Hormozi argues that delivery skill can make these arrangements less risky for the provider.
title: The 6 Levels of Making Money

text: Hormozi argues that attractive opportunities arise when others perceive substantial risk but a skilled operator faces much less of it; compensation can reflect the market's fear rather than the operator's actual exposure.
title: The 6 Levels of Making Money

text: A capable employee can negotiate lower guaranteed pay for greater performance upside. Hormozi illustrates a $100,000 advertised role with a $60,000 base and potential compensation of $180,000 if agreed outcomes occur.
title: The 6 Levels of Making Money

text: Hormozi describes insurance as earning payment for assuming risk: customers contribute premiums, and the pooled funds cover those who experience the insured loss.
title: The 6 Levels of Making Money

text: Hormozi places government taxation at the highest tier of his payment hierarchy, arguing that government supplies physical protection and possesses the force needed to enforce collection.
title: The 6 Levels of Making Money

text: Hormozi prefers revenue participation over profit participation because a counterparty's spending can reduce reported profit. He presents royalties and licensing as ways to collect from revenue before those expenses.
title: The 6 Levels of Making Money

text: Subject to applicable law, businesses can charge for warranties or guarantees. Service providers can similarly charge a premium for accepting the risk of problems, delays, or unexpectedly difficult work.
title: The 6 Levels of Making Money

text: Controlling customer collections lets a business deduct its share before forwarding the balance. Hormozi points to payment processors and certain franchise arrangements as examples of this payment priority.
title: The 6 Levels of Making Money

text: Hormozi argues that counting unsuccessful attempts can misrepresent risk; the total payoff matters because a sufficiently large success can cover many failed experiments.
title: The 6 Levels of Making Money

text: Endorsing an example attributed to Bezos, Hormozi says a 10% chance of a 100-fold payoff warrants taking the bet, despite expecting failure in nine of ten attempts.
title: The 6 Levels of Making Money

text: He defines focus as declining activities that fall outside the work someone has already committed to doing.

text: Focus has degrees: protecting a goal can involve declining business proposals, new friendships, and networking invitations. Each refusal preserves resources for the existing commitment.
title: Business Owners, We Have a Problem

text: Entrepreneurs can become excited about a second financial milestone before securing their first. He recommends protecting the current target from competing opportunities.
title: Business Owners, We Have a Problem

text: Meaningful focus requires rejecting opportunities someone actually wants. Turning down obviously unsuitable options does not involve the same sacrifice.
title: Business Owners, We Have a Problem

text: He describes business output as activity volume multiplied by leverage: how many repetitions someone performs and what each repetition produces.
title: Business Owners, We Have a Problem

text: Doing more repetitions can improve skill as well as increase production. Practice can therefore raise both output quantity and quality.
title: Business Owners, We Have a Problem

text: Repeatedly starting different businesses means repeatedly practicing beginner tasks instead of developing deeper competence in one business.
title: Business Owners, We Have a Problem

text: He thinks entrepreneurs who divide attention overestimate their ability to beat equally capable competitors who concentrate on one business.
title: Business Owners, We Have a Problem

text: Accepting a commitment can feel rewarding immediately but impose costs later. Declining can create immediate discomfort while preserving future time and freedom.
title: Business Owners, We Have a Problem

title: Business Owners, We Have a Problem

title: Business Owners, We Have a Problem

title: Business Owners, We Have a Problem

text: Hormozi argues that protecting reputation matters more than a short-term payout because reputation compounds, enabling larger and faster deals; sacrificing it interrupts those benefits.
title: 42 Recession Proof Money Hacks

text: Hormozi distinguishes building a fortune from preserving one: someone starting with little can risk that small base, but continuing the same behavior after accumulating wealth can destroy it.
title: 42 Recession Proof Money Hacks

text: When buying an investment or business, take time to evaluate it because entering a purchase is easier than selling afterward.
title: 42 Recession Proof Money Hacks

text: Hormozi thinks deliberately limiting time and money can encourage creative problem-solving, including for people who already have ample resources.
title: 42 Recession Proof Money Hacks

text: An opportunity can be attractive without fitting your priorities. Hormozi says learning to decline becomes important once initial hesitation gives way to accepting too many projects.
title: 42 Recession Proof Money Hacks

text: Build a financial cushion as soon as possible, even if it covers only 3 or 6 months. Hormozi says having protection gives him peace of mind and supports more aggressive action.
title: 42 Recession Proof Money Hacks

text: Compensation depends on the value delivered, negotiating ability, and difficulty of replacement. A cheaper substitute weakens bargaining power even when the work is valuable and the provider negotiates well.
title: 42 Recession Proof Money Hacks

text: Hormozi treats fear of missing out as a signal to pause a financial decision; he says slowing down in that state has prevented expensive mistakes.
title: 42 Recession Proof Money Hacks

text: Make the initial transaction with an unfamiliar business partner small, even when the economics and the person's character appear sound, so you can observe how they operate while limiting exposure.
title: 42 Recession Proof Money Hacks

text: Hormozi values durable trust above extracting the largest immediate return from a partner because trust accelerates transactions and allows relationships to compound.
title: 42 Recession Proof Money Hacks

text: Hormozi prefers evaluating an investment by its doubling or tripling time rather than its internal rate of return; he finds doubling over 3 years easier to reason about than 25% annual growth.
title: 42 Recession Proof Money Hacks

text: Before committing money, require a concrete, step-by-step explanation of how you could recover it. Vague assurances are insufficient, and an inability to explain the process can reveal a problem.
title: 42 Recession Proof Money Hacks

text: Track the amount retained each month after expenses rather than focusing only on earnings. Hormozi presents this cash surplus as a central measure for both personal and business finances.
title: 42 Recession Proof Money Hacks

text: Consider diversification by repayment priority as well as industry or asset category. Hormozi emphasizes that a creditor's position in the capital structure affects who recovers money first when conditions deteriorate.
title: 42 Recession Proof Money Hacks

text: Hormozi warns that entrepreneurs can turn passive investments into active work by pursuing additional returns. For someone seeking freedom, recovering time needs to remain a priority.
title: I stepped down as CEO...and created a PASSIVE INCOME machine..

text: Hormozi thinks entrepreneurs often leave the chief executive role prematurely. He explains his own decision through having reached his desired wealth and shifting his success measures toward how he spends his time.
title: I stepped down as CEO...and created a PASSIVE INCOME machine..

text: For entrepreneurs pursuing growth, delegation should free hours for more valuable work and skill development. Hiring someone at $10 or $15 per hour to handle 10 weekly hours creates time to reinvest; leisure is a different objective.
title: I stepped down as CEO...and created a PASSIVE INCOME machine..

text: Owner income includes payment for labor and ownership returns. In his hypothetical $3 million annual profit example, replacing the owner's work could require four or five senior leaders costing $1.5 million, leaving $1.5 million attributable to ownership.
title: I stepped down as CEO...and created a PASSIVE INCOME machine..

text: To move into ownership, arrange coverage for both your current responsibilities and the work you would otherwise take on next. Replacing only today's duties leaves you responsible for the next stage.
title: I stepped down as CEO...and created a PASSIVE INCOME machine..

text: He describes the owner's oversight role as helping the chief executive develop leadership, manage direct reports, and clarify company direction. Once that direction is chosen, the emphasis becomes consistent execution because the vision changes infrequently.
title: I stepped down as CEO...and created a PASSIVE INCOME machine..

text: His illustration splits $2 million of annual owner income into $1 million from work and $1 million from ownership. Replacing that work halves income, but he argues hourly earnings and enterprise value rise when the business operates independently.
title: I stepped down as CEO...and created a PASSIVE INCOME machine..

text: For owners considering another business because their current one has stalled, Hormozi recommends continuing proven activities and solving the growth problem instead of treating a fresh venture as the solution.
title: Entrepreneurs, stop starting new businesses. Fix the one you've got.

text: Hormozi argues that market saturation or contraction can explain a plateau outside an owner's control; otherwise, he attributes stalled growth to the owner not knowing how to expand.
title: Entrepreneurs, stop starting new businesses. Fix the one you've got.

text: Under the theory of constraints, a system expands until a bottleneck limits it. Removing that bottleneck allows further expansion until another limitation becomes decisive.

text: Hormozi considers speed the most important competitive dimension because shortening the delay before a rewarding outcome strengthens behavior.

text: Speed can mean reducing the wait between purchase and delivery or reducing the time customers spend on each recurring use while preserving the result.
title: 4 Ways To Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Serving a narrower customer group makes delivery easier to standardize, which helps a business fulfill orders faster.
title: 4 Ways To Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Turn recurring work into reusable templates or predetermined steps so employees spend less time deciding how to complete it.
title: 4 Ways To Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Preparing predictable orders before customers arrive can shorten service times; increased throughput may outweigh the cost of some unused inventory.
title: 4 Ways To Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: For appointment businesses, earlier booking availability can improve conversion and willingness to pay. Increasing availability may require higher compensation, longer hours, or additional employees.
title: 4 Ways To Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: For recurring services, dependable attendance and consistent results reduce customer risk and can make switching to a cheaper provider unattractive.
title: 4 Ways To Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Reputation reduces uncertainty before purchase by showing prospective customers that a business has delivered satisfactory results for others.
title: 4 Ways To Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Rising customer acquisition costs can reflect negative reputation rather than higher advertising rates: prospects may decide against buying because of what they hear or read.
title: 4 Ways To Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: A guarantee needs meaningful seller stakes. Performance-based compensation is another way for a capable provider to accept part of the customer's risk.
title: 4 Ways To Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Improve delivery consistency by identifying as many outcome-affecting variables as possible, controlling them, and adding newly discovered conditions to the operating checklist.

title: 4 Ways To Get Ahead of 99% of People

title: 4 Ways To Get Ahead of 99% of People

title: 4 Ways To Get Ahead of 99% of People

title: 4 Ways To Get Ahead of 99% of People

text: Hormozi distinguishes a sales script's wording from its delivery: changing vocal emphasis can change the meaning a prospect hears even when the words stay identical.

text: For sales conversations, Hormozi recommends a speaking rate above 135 and below 185 words per minute. He says excessive speed reduces trust, while an overly slow delivery can make the salesperson seem unintelligent.

text: Hormozi's three sales-delivery constants are sufficient volume, an understandable pace, and clear pronunciation. Their shared purpose is to help the prospect comprehend the message.

text: To memorize a sales script, keep an intact reference copy and a practice copy. Read the entire script aloud, obscure one additional word after each repetition, and continue until every word is hidden.

text: Knowing the script thoroughly lets a salesperson focus on what the prospect says instead of planning the next line. Hormozi wants prospects to provide more information while the salesperson listens.
title: How to Speak So Well People Give You Money

text: Hormozi says every salesperson should follow the team's established script. Shared wording provides the foundation for a consistent sales process; individual improvisation undermines that foundation.
title: How to Speak So Well People Give You Money

text: Use brief pauses to emphasize points and longer pauses to invite responses. Hormozi marks shorter pauses with ellipses and full stops with periods in sales scripts.
title: How to Speak So Well People Give You Money

text: At the purchase invitation, combine rising vocal pitch with an extended pause to indicate that the prospect should answer. Hormozi uses question marks to mark rising pitch in scripts.
title: How to Speak So Well People Give You Money

text: Coach observable vocal behaviors instead of vague emotional impressions. Hormozi recommends specifying increased volume or reduced speed rather than telling a salesperson to sound confident or stop sounding nervous.
title: How to Speak So Well People Give You Money

text: For salespeople who accelerate when nervous, fully pronouncing each word helps reduce speed. Hormozi says delivery requires particular attention during the close, when emotions rise and rapid, loud speech can sound aggressive.
title: How to Speak So Well People Give You Money

text: Hormozi cites three meta-analyses, without identifying them precisely, for a reported 30% increase in sales closed when sellers wait up to eight seconds after requesting a purchase.

text: Hormozi argues that prospects trust their own statements more than a seller's assertions. Questions can therefore help prospects articulate the reasons they would buy, especially during objection handling.
title: How to Speak So Well People Give You Money

text: Hormozi believes objection responses chiefly provide a reasonable opportunity to request the purchase again. The skill is creating additional opportunities without irritating the prospect; he separates genuine logistical mismatches from objections that can be reframed.
title: How to Speak So Well People Give You Money

text: As one of seven universal closes, Hormozi suggests reframing an objection as a reason to act. For a business product, connect the stated obstacle to the problem the product addresses, then renew the purchase invitation.

text: Hormozi considers discovery the stage where sellers most often lose a sale. Its purpose is to identify the prospect's problems and determine how they relate to available products or solutions.

text: When discovery answers are vague, repeatedly request examples and greater specificity. Once a concrete issue emerges, summarize it, confirm the interpretation, and continue until two or three key problems relevant to the offer are established.

text: Hormozi organizes wealth creation into four paths: personal capital in one's business, outside capital in one's business, personal capital in others' businesses, and outside capital in others' businesses.
title: If You Want To Create Wealth In 2026, Watch This (4 Paths)

text: Bootstrapping means financing a company through personal savings and business cash flow, then reinvesting profits without outside investors. He identifies inexpensive service businesses as common starting points.
title: If You Want To Create Wealth In 2026, Watch This (4 Paths)

text: He recommends bootstrapping a first business so beginners can learn without putting friends', relatives', or outside investors' money at risk through their own inexperience.
title: If You Want To Create Wealth In 2026, Watch This (4 Paths)

text: Bootstrapping preserves ownership and decision-making authority, including growth pace, strategy, and whether or when to sell. He favors building repeat purchasing or recurring revenue that can compound over time.
title: If You Want To Create Wealth In 2026, Watch This (4 Paths)

text: Self-funded companies can accumulate management, leadership, technology, and data shortcomings because they cannot afford stronger resources. He argues these accumulated problems can be harder to resolve than financial debt.
title: If You Want To Create Wealth In 2026, Watch This (4 Paths)

text: Bootstrapping often supports longer survival through lower operating costs, but limited capital slows expansion and restricts which opportunities a founder can pursue initially.
title: If You Want To Create Wealth In 2026, Watch This (4 Paths)

text: Raising capital involves selling investors ownership in a company the founder operates. He considers this necessary when substantial upfront spending or prolonged losses prevent the business from financing its own development.
title: If You Want To Create Wealth In 2026, Watch This (4 Paths)

text: Outside funding lets founders recruit stronger teams, build infrastructure sooner, outspend competitors, and accept losses when acquiring customers. Expensive opportunities can also have fewer adequately funded competitors.
title: If You Want To Create Wealth In 2026, Watch This (4 Paths)

text: An externally funded founder must satisfy both customers and investors, whose interests can conflict. Funding also dilutes ownership, and payout preferences can leave founders with less exit money than the headline sale price suggests.
title: If You Want To Create Wealth In 2026, Watch This (4 Paths)

text: Successive funding rounds can give investors board representation and enough authority to remove the founder. He emphasizes that the specific financing terms determine how much control and economic value the founder retains.
title: If You Want To Create Wealth In 2026, Watch This (4 Paths)

text: Fundraising prospects depend on the founder's ability and history, the perceived scale of the opportunity, and investors' confidence that the founder can deliver.
title: If You Want To Create Wealth In 2026, Watch This (4 Paths)

text: Venture investors can tolerate numerous failures while pursuing exceptional winners. A founder bears a concentrated personal cost: a failed venture may consume 5 to 10 or more years without producing wealth.
title: If You Want To Create Wealth In 2026, Watch This (4 Paths)

text: Investing uses money earned elsewhere to purchase interests in assets or other businesses. The investor supplies capital rather than taking responsibility for daily operations.
title: If You Want To Create Wealth In 2026, Watch This (4 Paths)

text: He considers investing suitable for people with substantial surplus cash who want financial upside without daily operating duties. Spreading investments reduces dependence on one business, although he says it also reduces upside.
title: If You Want To Create Wealth In 2026, Watch This (4 Paths)

text: He thinks investing offers the easiest lifestyle among the four paths, but describes it as the slowest wealth-building route. In his view, most investors first establish strong active earnings and then invest the surplus.
title: If You Want To Create Wealth In 2026, Watch This (4 Paths)

text: For investors, he cautions against expecting annual gains of 50%, 100%, or more. He presents investing as a way to accumulate and preserve wealth whose largest outcomes usually require an exceptionally long horizon.
title: If You Want To Create Wealth In 2026, Watch This (4 Paths)

text: Fund management means collecting capital from limited partners and deploying it into other businesses. Managers may combine investor money with their own contribution and borrowing to control substantially more assets.
title: If You Want To Create Wealth In 2026, Watch This (4 Paths)

text: He describes a manager contribution of roughly 5% as typical in his fund example: the manager supplies $5 million and limited partners supply $95 million toward a $100 million pool.
title: If You Want To Create Wealth In 2026, Watch This (4 Paths)

text: He says private equity arrangements may require investors to receive a minimum return before managers participate in profits, describing 6% to 8% as a typical hurdle range.
title: If You Want To Create Wealth In 2026, Watch This (4 Paths)

text: He believes compelling deals attract funding when projected gains and risk mitigation are credible. More specialized opportunities with higher expected returns can help managers negotiate a larger share of profits.
title: If You Want To Create Wealth In 2026, Watch This (4 Paths)

text: He considers fund management best suited to people with demonstrated results, exclusive access to opportunities, and a meaningful advantage in selecting and improving businesses.
title: If You Want To Create Wealth In 2026, Watch This (4 Paths)

text: He says newer fund managers often charge fewer fees to attract investors and demonstrate aligned incentives. A stronger history of results can support charging more fees.
title: If You Want To Create Wealth In 2026, Watch This (4 Paths)

text: Fund managers face delayed feedback and obligations to investors, regulators, operators, and indirectly customers. Their work expands into managing portfolio risk, reputation, and people, potentially leaving them wealthy on paper but heavily constrained.
title: If You Want To Create Wealth In 2026, Watch This (4 Paths)

text: A business can double its size either by doubling monthly customer acquisition or by doubling the lifetime value of existing customers.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: During customer onboarding, establish that cancellation requires an exit interview so the company can identify and repair weaknesses in the offering.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: When an upset customer complains, de-escalate tension by displaying greater frustration with the underlying problem than they feel, prompting them to calm down.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: During cancellation save discussions, offer to apply all prior subscription payments toward remaining for an additional trial period.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: When canceling clients express a need for additional hand-holding, credit their previous payments toward upgrading them into an advanced, higher-priced service level.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Upgrading a portion of dissatisfied clients into premium tiers eliminates net revenue loss even if the remaining churners depart.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Service companies frequently plateau near one hundred fifty accounts because individuals cannot sustain more personal relationships without standardized management systems.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Schedule non-commercial check-in messages every fourteen to twenty-one days to ask clients about personal milestones rather than product performance.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Building authentic interpersonal connections curbs churn because people hesitate far more to abandon relationships than transactional subscriptions.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Exclude recurring personal check-ins from the initial marketing offer so they arrive post-purchase as unexpected surprise and delight.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Assign each staff member responsibility for roughly forty accounts, requiring ten to fifteen brief check-ins per week to maintain human connections.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Routine personal outreach gives customers a familiar contact, creating an early warning detection network for service friction.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Organize client gatherings where members may invite acquaintances, turning community retention events into self-funding lead generation channels.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Referred leads typically yield two to three times greater value than standard cold prospects, justifying higher acquisition expenditure.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Hosting member gatherings without announcing the next date triggers post-event cancellations because participants feel they extracted full value.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Create an open loop by publicizing the upcoming gathering before the current one finishes, giving attendees a continuing milestone to anticipate.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Mail handwritten appreciation cards every six weeks with a postscript asking recipients to photograph the note and text it into a three-way friend invite.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Customer retention depends directly on consumption; subscribers will eventually drop any unused membership regardless of low pricing.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Subscribers almost never contest service pricing when they actively utilize the offering on a daily basis.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Customer cancellations are lagging indicators of past dissatisfaction, while drops in daily or weekly usage provide leading indicators for proactive intervention.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Unlike sales outreach which reduces contact attempts over time, follow-up for disengaged customers should escalate in daily frequency until contact is re-established.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Design a step-by-step onboarding sequence across the initial thirty days to establish explicit expectations and counteract buyer remorse within twenty-four hours.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Reinforce the initial buying choice during onboarding by restating the original motivations of the buyer and highlighting additional unannounced benefits.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Deliver multiple small cycles of setting and fulfilling expectations on a daily rhythm rather than batching updates into infrequent reports.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Continuously repeat basic service walkthrough instructions because distracted clients rarely internalize procedures after a single orientation.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Pinpoint the single early action strongly correlated with long-term retention, then steer all onboarding energy toward achieving that milestone immediately.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Prompt satisfied clients to submit reviews, social media posts, or video testimonials right after they reach their initial activation win.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Secure warm referrals by taking a selfie with the client and sending a joint introduction text to their friend.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Offering existing customers higher-tier solutions aids retention because clients wanting further progress will look to outside competitors if unaddressed internally.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Award valuable bonus training or perks when clients accomplish critical actions such as activation milestones, testimonials, or referrals.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Incentivize subscription longevity by granting unlockable rewards at expanding tenure intervals, such as months three, eight, and fifteen.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Reducing monthly churn from ten percent to five percent on a one-hundred-dollar subscription doubles customer lifetime value from one thousand to two thousand dollars.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Doubling customer lifetime value produces outsized profit expansion because the additional retained revenue requires no incremental acquisition expense.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Doubling customer lifetime value allows a business to double acceptable acquisition costs, dramatically lifting daily paid advertising capacity.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Prioritize retention rollouts by cost and speed of return: begin with onboarding, introduce unlockables near typical drop-off months, then launch exit interviews.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Automated check-in texts fail because customers recognize impersonal outreach; relationship nurturing must be human-delivered through systematized workflows.
title: 7 Ways to Get People to Buy More Times

text: Hormozi recounts learning from his father that repairing his reputation required changing his conduct; trying to manage other people's opinions could not substitute for behaving differently.
title: The biggest mistake in your 20's that will make you poor in your 30's

text: He says reversing the negative reputation he established during his first 3 months of college took approximately 2 years, teaching him how difficult an unfavorable initial impression can be to undo.
title: The biggest mistake in your 20's that will make you poor in your 30's

text: He distinguishes isolated criticism from consistent negative feedback: when everyone someone knows raises the same criticism and the evidence seems overwhelming, he thinks the person probably needs to examine their own behavior.
title: The biggest mistake in your 20's that will make you poor in your 30's

text: He describes shifting his attention toward becoming someone he could respect despite others' disapproval, then identifying that person's behaviors: diligent study, hard training, dependable friendship, respectful conduct, and humility.
title: The biggest mistake in your 20's that will make you poor in your 30's

text: He believes improving a reputation begins with meeting one's own standards, because people can judge their own conduct without outside validation; public perceptions can follow that internal change.
title: The biggest mistake in your 20's that will make you poor in your 30's

text: Essential-person risk exists when losing one individual would substantially reduce business earnings or stop operations. Redundancy means other people can keep the affected function running.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: An essential owner who intends to leave after a sale creates a particular problem for buyers: they would acquire earnings while losing the person responsible for producing them.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: Individual dependency can exist in marketing, sales, or delivery, including several functions simultaneously. Concentrating more essential functions in one person increases the business's exposure.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: After acquiring a valuable skill, he considers teaching someone else that skill the most valuable next step. This reduces bottlenecks caused by too few capable people.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: Making a business transferable can improve ownership even without a sale: removing the owner's essential role in marketing, sales, and delivery makes the business less dependent on their daily work.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: Operational leaders can be essential because they coordinate people across functions. Essential-person exposure therefore includes employees, not just founders or frontline specialists.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: Processes and trained replacements address dependence on an owner. For essential employees, retention incentives are another option; he gives equity vesting over three or five years as an example.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: Recruiting can use network outreach, direct prospecting, job content, paid listings, employee referrals, relevant associations, and staffing firms.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: Document, Demonstrate, Duplicate means creating a task checklist, performing it while the trainee watches, then observing the trainee perform it. Any necessary action missing from the checklist should be added.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: Training instructions should reflect the learner's existing ability. Less experienced learners need tasks divided into more explicit steps; experienced learners can start with assumed prerequisites.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: Delegation succeeds when the transferred function maintains or improves its performance. Assigning responsibility without checking results does not establish successful delegation, and training may need repetition.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: For service businesses with demand exceeding capacity, he recommends first raising prices, then serving more customers per provider while preserving sufficient value, and finally transferring delivery to trained people.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: Some businesses depend on uniquely valuable talent that cannot realistically be substituted. In those situations, he favors strong incentive alignment and recognizes that earning substantial income may remain the objective.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: He defines single-channel exposure as receiving more than half of customers or leads from one source, whose interruption would materially damage the business over time.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: Multiple acquisition channels allow customer flow to continue when one source fails. Depending on both one operator and one channel compounds the business's vulnerability.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: Channel volatility becomes harder to manage at scale: a 20% decline leaves one salesperson's calendar 80% occupied, but across 100 salespeople it represents the equivalent of 20 empty calendars.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: For small businesses, he recommends one main acquisition method from outbound, affiliates, or advertising, supported by basic organic content. Even one weekly post can help prospects verify that the business is active.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: Before larger businesses expand acquisition channels, he strengthens ongoing nurture through content and scheduled email follow-up, providing useful material and periodically presenting offers to existing contacts.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: After strengthening nurture, he installs a referral system with repeated requests at different customer stages. The resulting cash flow provides room to invest in another acquisition channel.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: A new acquisition channel may produce little for an extended period before working. He argues its potential value includes additional earnings and reduced dependence on the original channel.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: When testing an unfamiliar channel, use an operator whose ability is already established. Combining an unproven person with an unfamiliar channel makes disappointing results harder to diagnose.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: He believes founders should deeply understand customer acquisition, sales, and value delivery. He is more comfortable outsourcing supporting activities such as accounting, human resources, or payroll.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: Before an established operator develops another channel, transfer the existing channel to someone who can maintain or improve results. Only then move the proven operator into the new experiment.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: An outside channel specialist can work alongside the founder: the specialist contributes method expertise while the founder contributes business context, allowing both to learn.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: He flags customer concentration when losing one customer or connected customer group would reduce revenue by at least 20%. His rationale references margins of 10%, 20%, 30%, or 40% and potentially severe profit loss.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: He prefers addressing dependence on one large customer by acquiring additional large accounts, when feasible, so the original account represents a smaller share of the business.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: He cautions against redesigning a business around a large customer acquired through an unpredictable opportunity. A repeatable way to obtain similar customers changes whether that strategic shift makes sense.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: Critical-vendor exposure occurs when an outside business controls an essential function, including lead generation, manufacturing, or other services necessary to operate.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: For a software business, he advocates having technical capability internally. Otherwise, the external team building the product can gain substantial leverage over the company.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: He keeps multiple payment processors approved and ready, each capable of handling his entire monthly volume immediately. He says these alternatives also improve negotiating leverage over fees and service.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: He recommends backups for essential acquisition, sales, delivery, payment, and banking functions. He treats seemingly unused redundancy as insurance against events that could threaten the company's survival.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: Knowing how much of a supplier's business your account represents helps assess negotiating leverage. As your importance increases, the supplier has more to lose by ending or damaging the relationship.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: For important vendors, he suggests negotiating six or twelve months of termination notice, exit charges, and financial penalties tied to service commitments.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: Vendor service commitments can specify response deadlines, shipment schedules, or advertising activity. He presents associated financial penalties as a way to offset losses when agreed work is not performed.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: If a capable supplier remains essential and your company is much larger or provides substantial business, he suggests exploring acquisition or bringing its team inside to align incentives more permanently.
title: Give Me 47 minutes, And I'll Fix Your Small Business

text: He considers self-awareness especially valuable for choosing advice that fits a person's existing abilities, resources, and current constraint.

title: Watch This To Get Ahead In 2026

text: New initiatives must enter the business at a pace its people can handle. Hormozi thinks talent availability becomes a frequent limit as a company grows.
title: Watch This To Get Ahead In 2026

text: Entrepreneurs must build something that attracts excellent people. Treating those people well can create a growing group of strong colleagues willing to join later ventures.
title: Watch This To Get Ahead In 2026

text: Hormozi believes subsequent businesses often scale faster because prior hiring experience helps founders recognize effective people and understand what different organizational roles require.
title: Watch This To Get Ahead In 2026

text: Liking an employee personally does not resolve inadequate performance. Avoiding difficult conversations can prolong a staffing gap that blocks business growth.
title: Watch This To Get Ahead In 2026

text: He believes longer planning horizons offer an advantage when grounded in realistic steps, but financial stability must first provide enough breathing room to think further ahead.
title: Watch This To Get Ahead In 2026

text: Hormozi expects AI to increase the output businesses obtain from their inputs without changing business fundamentals. He frames current competition as people using increasingly capable tools.
title: Watch This To Get Ahead In 2026

text: For services constrained by human labor, Hormozi favors affluent customers and high gross margins. Serving a mass audience at low prices requires a product with very low costs for each additional customer.
title: Watch This To Get Ahead In 2026

text: He warns that buyers spending a large share of their available money may expect more than a provider can deliver, damaging team morale and the provider's reputation.
title: Watch This To Get Ahead In 2026

text: Time offers around strong unmet demand. A satisfied customer may reject more of the same product even after receiving excellent value.

text: Delivering value supports another sale when it exposes a further unmet need; satisfaction alone does not necessarily create motivation to purchase again.

text: Hormozi says 99% of an audience will never purchase but will assess a business through its free material. His approach is to share information freely and charge for implementation.

text: For educational selling, he recommends emphasizing concepts, possibilities, and outcomes. Detailed procedures create tasks whose value requires later execution, which he says can weaken the desire to buy immediately.

text: To memorize a sales script, repeatedly read it aloud while hiding one additional word each time. Continue until the entire page is obscured and the script can be delivered from memory.
title: Watch This To Get Ahead In 2026

text: During sales practice, correct mistakes immediately, demonstrate the replacement, and repeat the successful version before proceeding. Waiting until the entire exercise ends makes the feedback harder to retain.
title: Watch This To Get Ahead In 2026

text: Build sales training from observation: record the successful salesperson's language and actions, use that record for memorization, then practice faithful execution.

title: Watch This To Get Ahead In 2026

text: The SPCL components can influence people independently, but combining them strengthens influence. Evidence supporting expertise in one field does not automatically establish credibility in another.

text: Branding builds associations by repeatedly connecting something unfamiliar with something already understood, until the unfamiliar thing carries those associations independently.

text: For service businesses, Hormozi uses the Delivery Cube to explore new offers that repurpose existing resources and unused capacity, aiming to increase customer value, revenue, and profit without adding expenses or liabilities.
title: I Broke Down Every High Margin Service Into 6 Buckets [Delivery Cube]

text: When designing a service, consider changing how many customers receive attention together: individual delivery, a small group, or one provider serving many customers without a fixed upper limit.
title: I Broke Down Every High Margin Service Into 6 Buckets [Delivery Cube]

text: Hormozi says customer-led implementation tends to simplify fulfillment but complicate selling because customers do the work. Provider-led implementation tends to sell more easily but creates greater operational complexity; shared implementation occupies the middle.
title: I Broke Down Every High Margin Service Into 6 Buckets [Delivery Cube]

text: Support access is an offer-design variable: decide which channels customers can use to reach the business, such as text, chat, email, phone, or Zoom.
title: I Broke Down Every High Margin Service Into 6 Buckets [Delivery Cube]

text: For information delivered within a service, consider both timing and medium: live versus recorded delivery, and written, audio, or video formats.
title: I Broke Down Every High Margin Service Into 6 Buckets [Delivery Cube]

text: Customers may pay for faster results or support. Hormozi suggests exploring delivery in half the time, or differentiating standard support with a 24-hour reply from VIP support responding within 60 minutes.
title: I Broke Down Every High Margin Service Into 6 Buckets [Delivery Cube]

text: Using his estimated 20% disruption cost, he considers a possible 5% improvement insufficient justification for changing a process. He prefers opportunities with substantially larger potential gains.
