text: He thinks overlapping operational changes can keep a business roughly 20% below its potential. He also claims unchanged operations improve about 5% as people become more proficient through repetition.
title: I Just Learned This After 14 Years of Business

text: He uses the borrowed ICE framework to prioritize changes: estimate their impact, confidence of success, and ease of execution. Ease includes both required resources and implementation time.
title: I Just Learned This After 14 Years of Business

text: He records potential improvements in a growth spreadsheet instead of immediately assigning every idea. When the team has capacity, he revisits the list and ranks opportunities using ICE.
title: I Just Learned This After 14 Years of Business

text: Repeat purchases and subscriptions represent retention, while customers introducing others represent virality. A product can retain customers without spreading through referrals.
title: I Just Learned This After 14 Years of Business

text: Referrals face two obstacles: customers may avoid helping competitors, and they may rarely communicate with other prospective buyers. He no longer believes every business can grow through customer recommendations.
title: I Just Learned This After 14 Years of Business

text: He considers retaining customer revenue a priority for every business. He expects referrals to matter more where customers willingly share and frequently interact with people who could buy.
title: I Just Learned This After 14 Years of Business

text: Customer retention counts remaining buyers; revenue retention tracks their spending. His example contrasts retaining 50 of 100 customers with retaining 25 who spend twice as much. His investment decisions emphasize the retained revenue.
title: I Just Learned This After 14 Years of Business

text: Customer acquisition economics should use lifetime gross profit rather than lifetime revenue. His example of $100 monthly payments for 10 months, with $20 fulfillment costs per payment, yields $800 gross profit rather than $1,000.
title: I Just Learned This After 14 Years of Business

text: He thinks the necessary lifetime-gross-profit-to-acquisition-cost ratio depends on how labor-intensive three functions are: attracting customers, converting them, and delivering the purchase.
title: I Just Learned This After 14 Years of Business

text: For highly automated acquisition, checkout, and delivery, he considers a 3:1 lifetime-gross-profit-to-CAC ratio workable. He says even 1.5:1 can produce profit at some scales, though he considers it undesirable.
title: I Just Learned This After 14 Years of Business

text: For businesses requiring manual outreach, salespeople, and labor-intensive delivery, he wants lifetime gross profit at least 20 times CAC and targets above 30 times CAC. These are his preferred economics, not universal requirements.
title: I Just Learned This After 14 Years of Business

text: He attributes most of his accumulated wealth to periods when his businesses achieved ratios of at least 30:1. At 5:1 or 8:1, he prefers refining one location's economics before expanding.
title: I Just Learned This After 14 Years of Business

text: Expanding into colder audiences lowers conversion and raises acquisition costs. Growth also adds management overhead. He argues that labor-intensive businesses need substantial initial acquisition margins to absorb both pressures.
title: I Just Learned This After 14 Years of Business

text: Manual businesses incur uneven expansion costs because new prospectors, salespeople, and delivery staff need training and may fail. He says faster expansion increases inefficiency, making strong acquisition economics a buffer.
title: I Just Learned This After 14 Years of Business

text: He explains the $1–3 million revenue swamp with a hypothetical $2 million business earning 20%, or $400,000. A strong hire costing at least $250,000 annually risks more than half its profit without assuring additional capacity.
title: I Just Learned This After 14 Years of Business

text: When a growing owner lacks both time and hiring funds, he recommends combining extra personal effort with hiring. His approach uses profitable, less scalable work to finance two or three hiring attempts rather than depending on one.
title: I Just Learned This After 14 Years of Business

text: His team's scaling roadmap categorizes business stages by headcount rather than revenue. Businesses generating $1–3 million can occupy different stages because their operating models differ.
title: I Just Learned This After 14 Years of Business

text: He attributes his reduced fear of missing out in 2024 to questioning deadlines he had invented for himself. Measuring success against those arbitrary timelines had created a persistent sense of urgency.
title: I Just Learned This After 14 Years of Business

text: He considers much entrepreneurial urgency self-imposed, with an exception for platforms competing to capture a network where network effects could produce a dominant winner.
title: I Just Learned This After 14 Years of Business

text: To resist rushing into additional ventures, he studies people roughly 20 years ahead with the business he ultimately wants. He observes that most built one substantial business and uses that endpoint to guide focus.
title: I Just Learned This After 14 Years of Business

text: He argues that unstable customers create unstable businesses, reducing their ability to survive difficult periods and become large. He uses agencies moving toward enterprise customers to illustrate the value of customer stability.
title: I Just Learned This After 14 Years of Business

text: When owners know how to build a $3 million business, starting more such businesses can avoid the harder question of reaching $10 million. He advises confronting the existing business's growth problem.
title: I Just Learned This After 14 Years of Business

text: He believes owners become stuck when they master one difficulty but avoid the next. Progress may require rejecting attractive opportunities and accepting that some possible futures will remain unexplored.
title: I Just Learned This After 14 Years of Business

text: Hormozi says businesses exhibit recurring patterns across sizes and industries, making many operating principles transferable between businesses.
title: This Video Should Be Required Viewing for Business Owners

text: Hormozi thinks founders can resist delegation because being indispensable feels rewarding, even though other people can learn the work.
title: This Video Should Be Required Viewing for Business Owners

text: Higher prices can support a reinforcing cycle: attracting better customers, improving service, increasing profit, hiring stronger talent, and further improving delivery.
title: This Video Should Be Required Viewing for Business Owners

text: Hormozi describes Veblen goods as products whose demand increases with price. He thinks cosmetic health services often exhibit this relationship because buyers associate higher prices with reduced risk.
title: This Video Should Be Required Viewing for Business Owners

text: Sales qualification determines whether suitable prospects arrive; sales education prepares them to be more willing to purchase.
title: This Video Should Be Required Viewing for Business Owners

text: When selling requires too many conversations or takes too long, Hormozi says prospects usually need more education before the sales conversation.
title: This Video Should Be Required Viewing for Business Owners

text: Educating prospects can cause drop-off before a meeting. Hormozi argues that educating people already waiting at an office can shorten sales conversations and improve purchasing readiness without that same attrition.
title: This Video Should Be Required Viewing for Business Owners

text: For physical businesses seeking greater earnings, Hormozi generally favors improving existing locations’ profitability before opening additional ones.
title: This Video Should Be Required Viewing for Business Owners

text: For paid-search leads, Hormozi recommends responding within about 60 seconds because these prospects have strong intent but are comparing providers.
title: This Video Should Be Required Viewing for Business Owners

text: Hormozi argues that faster service availability usually improves sales and profitability through better attendance, higher conversion, lower acquisition costs, and customers’ willingness to pay for speed.
title: This Video Should Be Required Viewing for Business Owners

text: Businesses that make customers wait several weeks expose themselves to competitors who can serve those customers sooner.
title: This Video Should Be Required Viewing for Business Owners

text: Evaluate price increases using conversion multiplied by price, rather than conversion alone. A 50% increase in price can remain worthwhile even if sales volume falls 10%.
title: This Video Should Be Required Viewing for Business Owners

text: When delivery capacity limits a business, additional marketing does not increase throughput. Fixing that bottleneck takes priority over adding another marketing channel.
title: This Video Should Be Required Viewing for Business Owners

text: A business can occupy different development stages across its functions, so its marketing, sales, and delivery needs may differ.
title: This Video Should Be Required Viewing for Business Owners

text: Hormozi suspects public accountability increases entrepreneurial effort and wonders how to reproduce the execution pressure created by a competition.
title: This Video Should Be Required Viewing for Business Owners

text: In his weight-loss business, Hormozi says challenges improved participants’ results by offering successful participants their payment back as credit toward additional services.
title: This Video Should Be Required Viewing for Business Owners

text: For career selection, he recommends starting with an existing strength that customers already pay for. Enjoyment alone establishes neither competence nor earning potential, and interests can change with age.
title: If you're ambitious and in your 20s or 30s, please watch this.

text: Liking an activity differs from enjoying its training. His table-tennis example involves 500 forehands and 500 backhands each morning and evening; developing competence requires tolerating monotonous repetition.
title: If you're ambitious and in your 20s or 30s, please watch this.

text: He recounts closing every business except one to concentrate on his strongest capability. Ending partnerships with people he liked made the decision personally difficult.
title: If you're ambitious and in your 20s or 30s, please watch this.

text: He argues that experienced, successful people assess demonstrated excellence in a single area more than the number of activities someone claims to pursue.
title: If you're ambitious and in your 20s or 30s, please watch this.

text: He attributes impostor feelings to presenting an inflated impression of success. His prescription is to describe actual accomplishments honestly and improve those accomplishments until they become persuasive.
title: If you're ambitious and in your 20s or 30s, please watch this.

text: He recommends evaluating advisers by whether they have lives you want. Changing your peer group changes your comparison standard and can expose the distance between your current position and your aspirations.
title: If you're ambitious and in your 20s or 30s, please watch this.

text: He believes demonstrated effort earns access to more accomplished people because they expect their guidance to be implemented. He credits that expectation with helping him build relationships beyond his own level of achievement.
title: If you're ambitious and in your 20s or 30s, please watch this.

text: When important variables are unknown, he favors testing and learning over extended deliberation. He says this approach has served him on increasingly large decisions despite substantial mistakes.
title: If you're ambitious and in your 20s or 30s, please watch this.

text: He claims replacing a week-end decision deadline with a same-day deadline permits sevenfold faster progress. He suggests shortening the deadline further to an hour or deciding immediately.
title: If you're ambitious and in your 20s or 30s, please watch this.

text: He calls the cost of missing necessary skills and knowledge ignorance debt. He considers it more expensive than financial debt and views failed attempts as a way to reduce it.
title: If you're ambitious and in your 20s or 30s, please watch this.

text: For repeatedly postponed decisions, he recommends examining the cost of inaction: count how often you approached the decision without acting and assess whether the resulting life is the one you want.
title: If you're ambitious and in your 20s or 30s, please watch this.

text: If you already intend to act eventually, he argues that acting sooner brings the benefits forward. He attributes postponement to wanting to delay the possible costs of failure.
title: If you're ambitious and in your 20s or 30s, please watch this.

text: When anticipated judgment blocks action, identify the person whose imagined criticism you hear and decide whether that person should influence your life choices.
title: If you're ambitious and in your 20s or 30s, please watch this.

text: He argues that earning $1 million requires accepting a corresponding $1 million of difficulty, and $10 million requires $10 million of difficulty. These are metaphors for the burden of solving larger problems.
title: If you're ambitious and in your 20s or 30s, please watch this.

text: He says uncertainty persists at every business stage, even as difficulties change from unfamiliar tasks to criticism or lawsuits. He recommends becoming comfortable acting without complete knowledge.
title: If you're ambitious and in your 20s or 30s, please watch this.

text: Drawing on Stephen Schwarzman, he argues that smaller and larger ambitions can demand similar effort. His example contrasts an 80-hour restaurant workweek with the management demands of building a billion-dollar company.
title: If you're ambitious and in your 20s or 30s, please watch this.

text: He experiences discomfort during growth, stagnation, and decline. Because he regards it as present in all three conditions, he does not consider discomfort alone a useful basis for choosing a direction.
title: If you're ambitious and in your 20s or 30s, please watch this.

text: He believes exceptionally ambitious goals attract fewer competitors because many people dismiss them as unattainable. He also argues that extraordinary outcomes require habits unlike those of ordinary peers.
title: If you're ambitious and in your 20s or 30s, please watch this.

text: He regards work-life balance as a legitimate preference but incompatible with becoming the best. Against equally capable competitors, he argues that effective methods must be accompanied by greater effort.
title: If you're ambitious and in your 20s or 30s, please watch this.

text: He frames your 20s and 30s as a trade-off between experiences and skill development: prioritizing enjoyment risks reaching 30 or 40 with fewer skills, while prioritizing work risks reaching those ages with fewer life experiences.
title: If you're ambitious and in your 20s or 30s, please watch this.

text: With only 24 hours available daily, he treats actual time allocation as evidence of priorities. He recommends examining whether entertainment and idle browsing deserve the time they take from a stated goal.
title: If you're ambitious and in your 20s or 30s, please watch this.

text: His condensed advice for people in their 20s and 30s is to select a desired outcome, disregard outside judgment, and perform enough repetitions that failure becomes increasingly unlikely.
title: If you're ambitious and in your 20s or 30s, please watch this.

text: For people struggling with productivity, Hormozi recommends a season of no: temporarily declining competing commitments to prioritize a major goal. He says this can last three months or three years; his longest lasted three years.
title: The SEASON OF NO (What it Takes to Win)

text: Hormozi treats declining requests as choosing his main goal. He believes achieving that goal can preserve or create future opportunities, even when some relationships or opportunities disappear after a refusal.
title: The SEASON OF NO (What it Takes to Win)

text: Using an exercise he attributes to Buffett, Hormozi describes ranking 25 goals and retaining five. During a season of no, he prioritizes one of those five and defines minimum maintenance work for the others.
title: The SEASON OF NO (What it Takes to Win)

text: As a business improves, attractive side deals can introduce inefficiencies that weaken its main operation. Hormozi says an investor may interpret an assortment of unrelated arrangements as evidence that the entrepreneur lacks focus.
title: The SEASON OF NO (What it Takes to Win)

text: Hormozi argues that family expectations can conflict with personal ambitions without malicious intent. He recommends accepting short-term disapproval when necessary to pursue one's own goal, rather than dividing effort and accomplishing neither side's aims.
title: The SEASON OF NO (What it Takes to Win)

text: Hormozi says business calls consume attention before and afterward. Citing unspecified research, he claims alternating between two tasks takes four times as long as completing them sequentially, and uses this to argue against interruptions.
title: The SEASON OF NO (What it Takes to Win)

text: For people working all day without their desired progress, Hormozi recommends listing activities they will sacrifice for their goal. He argues that faster progress can depend on eliminating activities rather than adding more work.
title: The SEASON OF NO (What it Takes to Win)

text: Hormozi recommends removing alternative activities during focused work so boredom can give way to productivity. When changing his own behavior, he prefers adjusting his surroundings because he finds that easier than changing himself directly.
title: The SEASON OF NO (What it Takes to Win)

text: For entrepreneurs bored with a successful business, Hormozi suggests treating persistence and tolerance for repetition as personal growth rather than assuming growth requires a new venture.
title: How I'm building a BILLION DOLLAR empire working 2-3 days per week..

text: A business should address customers' needs. Hormozi warns that making it satisfy the owner's desire for connection, status, or stimulation can lead to decisions that damage it.
title: How I'm building a BILLION DOLLAR empire working 2-3 days per week..

text: Hormozi warns that accomplished entrepreneurs who switch industries out of boredom must start learning again while competing against established operators.
title: How I'm building a BILLION DOLLAR empire working 2-3 days per week..

text: Entrepreneurs seeking novelty can experiment with hooks, advertising creative, and acquisition approaches inside their existing business. He says this variety can attract different customer groups and support growth.
title: How I'm building a BILLION DOLLAR empire working 2-3 days per week..

text: Hormozi proposes measuring success through several outcomes together, such as increasing wealth while maintaining a strong marriage or physical fitness, instead of judging progress only by money.
title: How I'm building a BILLION DOLLAR empire working 2-3 days per week..

text: Owners bored with their business can make the existing goal harder by limiting the time available to achieve it, creating a fresh challenge without disrupting what already works.
title: How I'm building a BILLION DOLLAR empire working 2-3 days per week..

text: During college fraternity pledging, he had 3 required study hours daily. He found that continuing to study when immediate assignments were finished let him complete future work early.
title: How I'm building a BILLION DOLLAR empire working 2-3 days per week..

text: Hormozi believes people must first learn to sacrifice for achievement before learning to succeed with fewer sacrifices. He says he does not know successful people who avoided that earlier stage.
title: How I'm building a BILLION DOLLAR empire working 2-3 days per week..

text: When cash is scarce, exchange services with low additional delivery costs for needed work or resources. Review existing expenses and find customers who can supply those needs.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Beginners can attract help by admitting what they need. Pretending to have everything handled discourages people from offering useful support.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Access to experienced operators can prevent expensive startup mistakes. He favors paying for that access when affordable, observing their operations, and testing their suggestions rather than assuming every suggestion will work.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: For new locations, begin marketing and collecting presales before delivery expenses start. After his first gym, he used 3 months of preselling, including advance payments covering 3 months, 6 months, or a year.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Test prospective locations with advertising before committing to leases and construction. He describes spending $500–$1,000 per market across 5–10 markets and comparing lead costs.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Do not accept presale payments for services you expect you cannot deliver.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Refresh promotion names and presentation without changing the underlying service. Small local audiences pushed him to develop frequent creative variations, a capability he later used in national advertising.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: He says advertising creative now helps determine targeting: featuring people resembling the desired customer can attract that audience, particularly in national campaigns.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: A meaningful guarantee specifies the promised outcome, deadline, conditions, and remedy if the promise fails. Merely labeling something guaranteed does not communicate what the seller risks.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: A continued-service guarantee is more compelling when fulfilling it requires meaningful delivery effort. Extending access to existing digital material may offer little additional value to someone who has not achieved the result.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: A short challenge can lead into an ongoing membership when customers make progress but still have a larger goal. The longer commitment becomes a continuation of work they already want to pursue.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Collecting substantial cash at the first purchase can create more advertising capacity than low-priced introductory offers whose revenue arrives over several months.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: His Best Case Worst Case Close contrasts the customer's desired transformation with the downside covered by the refund guarantee, then asks for a decision.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: He regrets reinvesting so aggressively that personal financial pressure impaired his decisions. He would now allow himself financial breathing room instead of rushing expansion to prove himself.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: When customers must act to achieve results, make the required behavior easier for beginners rather than designing instructions around the provider's advanced expertise.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Ask about specific actions and their frequency instead of asking whether customers followed everything. Detailed questions can expose large gaps hidden by broad assurances of compliance.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: In sales, explore the customer's present frustrations and describe the experience of the desired result. Dwelling on the effort and procedural steps can make buying less appealing.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Prefer additional value over a lower core-service price. If offering a discount, change the exchange: his example grants $100 off a $500 purchase for referring 3 friends.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Turn recurring purchase objections into reusable resources. During individual sales conversations, introduce the resource that resolves the prospect's stated obstacle rather than presenting every bonus automatically.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Use open, nonleading customer questions to discover what the service contributes to their lives. Prioritize improvements they value instead of assuming the owner's technical interests define a better product.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Display existing reviews and customer results in the sales area, with appropriate permissions. If credibility objections persist despite extensive proof, ask what the prospect actually fears.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Build a repeating process that attracts customers, produces results, and uses those results to attract more customers. Capture reactions at meaningful milestones and deliberately display the resulting proof.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Evaluate potential partners using TEAM: time, expertise, assets, and money. Partners should contribute something complementary; friendship and matching skills alone are weak reasons to share a business.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: A working partner should clarify compensation for managing the business separately from ownership. That management work has a cost even when the owner currently performs it.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Avoid giving away early equity unnecessarily. Ownership need not be divided equally; contributions, experience, compensation, and especially the risks each partner bears should inform the allocation.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: He favors location operators sharing in profits. Set expected total compensation for the required skill level, allocate half to salary, and size the profit percentage so typical performance supplies the other half.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Operating a future location can become an employee career path. He suggests requiring 3–5 years of demonstrated performance so candidates understand the business before receiving that opportunity.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: His expansion rule is to wait until the existing location grows for 6 consecutive months without the owner's involvement. Independence includes someone else handling decisions and customer problems, not merely delivering sessions.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Match delegated responsibility with authority. Give operators explicit spending discretion so they can resolve routine problems without repeatedly seeking the owner's permission.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: For customer recovery, he suggests allowing staff to spend up to 100% of what that customer paid during the previous month to resolve the problem or improve the experience.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Fix customer losses before scaling acquisition. Retention problems are easier to resolve while a business is small, and expansion can worsen delivery weaknesses.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: A 1-month vacation can test whether a business operates independently and reveal what still breaks without the owner.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Early owners may fund their living costs with expensive personal services while building a business independent of their time. Keep that work limited and separate from judging whether the core operation can scale.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Owners seeking independence should measure themselves by how well they teach others, rather than by their ability to outperform or rescue the team personally.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: His CLOSER Framework organizes selling around understanding the visit, identifying the problem, reviewing previous attempts, presenting the desired outcome, addressing concerns, and affirming the customer's purchase decision.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Training should teach the minimum actions required for successful performance. He argues that removing unnecessary complexity makes processes easier for inexperienced employees to learn and use.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Service businesses can add complementary product sales requiring little extra delivery time. Aim for the product margin to recover customer acquisition costs upfront.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: A guarantee can be a paid addition rather than a free inclusion. He suggests a 10% surcharge as an example and says the price can be higher.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Offer existing customers a focused additional program roughly quarterly, or every 12 weeks. These promotions can produce high incremental margins because acquisition costs and existing fixed expenses are already covered.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: He prefers collecting tactics he has observed working over asserting untested explanations for why they work. He describes causal explanations without research or comparison tests as hypotheses.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Customer acquisition and delivery are core business capabilities. He recommends using agencies as a way to learn acquisition methods, openly stating the intention to eventually replace their execution.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: When learning from an expert, perform the computer work yourself while they guide you. Ask them to explain their decisions so you learn judgment as well as procedural steps.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Evaluate advertising expansion by total earnings rather than return ratios alone. A lower return multiple on a larger budget can generate more money than a high multiple on a small budget.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Once customers love a profitable product, expand its availability instead of altering the experience to squeeze in more buyers. If the beloved product is unprofitable, he recommends addressing pricing.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Improving lead attendance from 10% to 50% multiplies that stage's output by 5. He argues lead nurturing can offer greater improvement potential than increasing an already respectable closing rate.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Compare the additional revenue from immediate lead response with the cost of dedicated staffing. If the improvement is worth more than the employee's cost, he recommends funding that availability.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: He distinguishes starting with one reliable acquisition channel from depending on another business that can terminate lead supply. He prefers adding acquisition methods as the company grows.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Higher compensation can make strong candidates easier to attract. With limited pay, he says finding exceptional employees can require interviewing approximately 10 times as many people.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: His Platinum Rule is to accommodate how other people want to be treated. Learn employees' actual motivations when designing roles, incentives, and career paths rather than assuming they share the owner's priorities.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: He believes friendship with employees can work when professional expectations remain clear. Explicitly signaling whether a conversation is personal or managerial helps maintain that boundary.
title: How to Start a Business From Nothing (Thank Me Later)

text: Hormozi argues that total money earned matters more than advertising efficiency or lead conversion percentages; he says advertising spend will become less efficient as it scales.
title: The Mind-Blowing Reason A Competitor Made Twice As Much As Me

text: For six annual round trips with two-hour flights each way, he estimates 24 private flying hours. At roughly $4,000 hourly, he rounds the annual cost to $100,000, versus approximately $6,000–$10,000 for first class.
title: I Spent $312,900 Living Like The 1% (Here's What I Learned)

text: He estimates roughly $300,000 in annual spending for a lifestyle combining private flights, an exotic car, a penthouse, designer clothes, and expensive dining.
title: I Spent $312,900 Living Like The 1% (Here's What I Learned)

text: He owns two exotic cars and regrets buying them. Compared with an older Prius or pickup, he finds the added enjoyment negligible and says the novelty fades within one or two weeks.
title: I Spent $312,900 Living Like The 1% (Here's What I Learned)

text: Visible luxury is a poor basis for choosing financial advisers: he warns that some people spend their entire income maintaining that appearance.
title: I Spent $312,900 Living Like The 1% (Here's What I Learned)

text: In his opinion, a luxury lifestyle should consume less than 10% of earnings, with 90% saved.
title: I Spent $312,900 Living Like The 1% (Here's What I Learned)

text: He values dates with his wife but enjoys inexpensive restaurants just as much as costly ones. He thinks dressing up contributes more to fancy dining's appeal than the food or experience.
title: I Spent $312,900 Living Like The 1% (Here's What I Learned)

text: He thinks mass-market products often provide better quality because they undergo more product testing. He found a rented Chevrolet Suburban's interface easier to use than the interface in his $350,000 Bentley.
title: I Spent $312,900 Living Like The 1% (Here's What I Learned)

text: He favors treating a primary residence as an income-producing investment where possible; his example is occupying one side of a duplex while renting the other to cover living costs.
title: I Spent $312,900 Living Like The 1% (Here's What I Learned)

text: He describes wealth as income relative to expenses. His example is someone earning $300,000 annually while spending $30,000: a 10:1 ratio that he considers very wealthy.
title: I Spent $312,900 Living Like The 1% (Here's What I Learned)

text: He presents happiness as what someone has divided by what they want. He argues that reducing desire increases perceived abundance and improves the relationship between income and expenses.
title: I Spent $312,900 Living Like The 1% (Here's What I Learned)

text: Hormozi argues that wanting an outcome does not distinguish someone from others who want it; accepting the necessary sacrifices does.
title: Why old friends keep you poor...

text: He believes longtime acquaintances can reinforce an outdated identity by repeatedly describing someone as they used to be, even while that person is trying to behave differently.
title: Why old friends keep you poor...

text: He evaluates which friendships matter most to him by considering how much he would sacrifice to preserve each relationship.
title: Why old friends keep you poor...

text: He believes a history of rewarding interactions increases someone's willingness to support a friend through difficult periods, but that even a friendship lasting 10 years can end if positive experiences stop.
title: Why old friends keep you poor...

text: Hormozi declined a former teacher's request for a weekly two-hour call, described as 100 hours annually for life. Although the teacher helped launch his interest in fitness, he would not commit that time to repay past help.
title: Why old friends keep you poor...

text: For relationships he no longer finds rewarding, he suggests gradually reducing contact. When the relationship is close enough to require an explanation, he recommends directly discussing concerns that would otherwise be expressed behind the person's back.
title: Why old friends keep you poor...

text: After leaving friendships, he recommends joining communities organized around shared goals. He argues that sustained effort and achievement can raise someone's standing there and create access to other communities.
title: Why old friends keep you poor...

text: He believes a friendship can have been valuable even if it ends, and considers reaching life's end with one or two close friends a good outcome.
title: Why old friends keep you poor...

text: When customers complain, acknowledge their frustration and take responsibility. Minimizing the problem can make them escalate because they do not feel understood; treating it seriously also holds the business accountable.
title: Hardcore Business Lessons I Learned From A Dealer

text: Businesses can sell services that protect a purchase's usefulness over time. Hormozi describes this as an insurance-like offer, even when the service is maintenance or storage rather than actual insurance.
title: Hardcore Business Lessons I Learned From A Dealer

text: Present the intended service bundle as the default, then ask whether customers want anything additional. Hormozi says their habitual refusal of extras can become acceptance of the proposed bundle.
title: Hardcore Business Lessons I Learned From A Dealer

text: Hormozi calls normally discarded business byproducts sawdust. These leftovers can become bonuses customers value, giving them a reason to visit and consider an upsell.

text: Hormozi attributes national productivity gains largely to investment in education and technology: education improves workers' capabilities, while technology increases what those capabilities can produce.
title: How the Top 1% ACTUALLY Make Their Money

text: Technology can increase output, improve quality, and reduce the skill needed for a task. Hormozi evaluates these advantages relative to the time required to produce a result.
title: How the Top 1% ACTUALLY Make Their Money

text: Hormozi groups economically productive skills into building, selling, and leading. These are graduated capabilities: their value depends on proficiency, rather than simply whether someone possesses them.
title: How the Top 1% ACTUALLY Make Their Money

text: Building creates things others can repeatedly use; selling can reach multiple buyers simultaneously; leadership coordinates other people's work. Each can increase the output attributable to one person's time.
title: How the Top 1% ACTUALLY Make Their Money

text: When designing a customer solution, vary personal attention, customer effort, delivery setting, consumption format, and response speed. Also imagine versions priced 10 times higher and one-tenth as high that preserve the outcome.
title: How the Top 1% ACTUALLY Make Their Money

text: A customer's problem can sometimes be resolved by changing their experience rather than the underlying physical process. Hormozi uses mirrors distracting elevator passengers as an example of a psychological solution.
title: How the Top 1% ACTUALLY Make Their Money

text: Solving one customer problem often exposes another. Over time, a capable builder can develop related products that address successive needs.
title: How the Top 1% ACTUALLY Make Their Money

text: Product quality alone cannot generate purchases if prospects are unaware of the product or do not perceive its value. Selling communicates that value, ideally to many prospects simultaneously.
title: How the Top 1% ACTUALLY Make Their Money

text: Hormozi uses selling to encompass the entire journey from initial unawareness to payment, including advertising, marketing, branding, promotion, and purchase conversion.
title: How the Top 1% ACTUALLY Make Their Money

title: How the Top 1% ACTUALLY Make Their Money

text: Businesses should initially target a narrow market where they can compete, then broaden their audience as their capabilities and size increase.
title: How the Top 1% ACTUALLY Make Their Money

title: How the Top 1% ACTUALLY Make Their Money

text: Hormozi considers leadership a particularly powerful capability because it provides access to other people's expertise, including builders and sellers who can work toward a shared objective.
title: How the Top 1% ACTUALLY Make Their Money

text: A business needs building, selling, and leadership capabilities. Strong sales cannot compensate for a poor product, and a strong product cannot attract purchases when nobody discovers it.
title: How the Top 1% ACTUALLY Make Their Money

title: How the Top 1% ACTUALLY Make Their Money

title: How the Top 1% ACTUALLY Make Their Money

title: How the Top 1% ACTUALLY Make Their Money

title: How the Top 1% ACTUALLY Make Their Money

text: Hormozi reports nine failed partnerships and acknowledges that his own involvement may have contributed to those failures.

text: He generally favors starting without partners when the motivation is companionship. In his view, a partner should contribute capital or abilities the founder lacks.
title: Top Signs You Have The Wrong Business Partner

text: Negotiate a partnership agreement before committing. He treats disagreements during negotiations as a preview of behavior under stress and recommends addressing departures, unequal willingness to work, and either partner wanting to stop.
title: Top Signs You Have The Wrong Business Partner

text: He prefers separate legal representation for partners. If that is unaffordable, he suggests a free agreement template and one hour of legal guidance to identify issues before partners settle the terms themselves.
title: Top Signs You Have The Wrong Business Partner

text: His three business pillars are acquisition, covering marketing and selling; product, covering delivery of the offering; and operations, covering supporting responsibilities such as payroll, taxes, legal work, technology, accounting, and HR.
title: Top Signs You Have The Wrong Business Partner

text: Every business needs acquisition, product, and operations covered, but each function does not require an equity partner. One person can cover several functions, and he says operators can often be hired without granting ownership.
title: Top Signs You Have The Wrong Business Partner

text: Partners should divide responsibility into distinct areas based on their strengths. He warns that sharing responsibility for everything undermines accountability and makes it unclear who owns unfinished work.
title: Top Signs You Have The Wrong Business Partner

text: To divide partnership duties, list every business activity and assign an owner according to skills. If activities are unclear, each partner should record their work every 15 minutes for one week before comparing lists.
title: Top Signs You Have The Wrong Business Partner

text: When partners have identical abilities, he suggests developing different specialties or operating separate businesses. He warns that giving away half the ownership at formation can become the largest reduction in a founder's eventual earnings if the business grows.
title: Top Signs You Have The Wrong Business Partner

text: Partners should explicitly agree on schedules, vacation, weekend work, preferred working hours, and responsiveness. He warns that resolving these expectations becomes harder once disappointments and money are involved.
title: Top Signs You Have The Wrong Business Partner

text: He believes married couples often work well as business partners because they already divide responsibilities, frequently bring complementary commercial and organizational abilities, and provide emotional support during business stress.

text: Before choosing a goal, identify its business problem. Hormozi says it should contribute to acquiring customers, increasing customer value, or increasing enterprise value; otherwise, it should not be pursued.

text: Frame a goal as a hypothesis linking an action to an expected result. Specify baseline and target measures for both, because completing an activity does not guarantee the business outcome.
title: How I Set Goals That ACTUALLY MAKE MONEY

text: At quarter-end or year-end, evaluate execution and results separately: determine whether the planned action happened, then whether its predicted effect occurred. Completing the action can count as successful execution even when the hypothesis fails.
title: How I Set Goals That ACTUALLY MAKE MONEY

text: Large businesses often grow through repeated 1% improvements. Hormozi says companies around $5 million, $10 million, $15 million, or $20 million in revenue often need systems for improving existing operations rather than continually inventing new initiatives.

text: For an early-stage business, establishing metric tracking can itself be a worthwhile quarterly goal, providing measurements the company can subsequently improve.
title: How I Set Goals That ACTUALLY MAKE MONEY

title: How I Set Goals That ACTUALLY MAKE MONEY

text: He defines strategy as choosing how to distribute finite resources among an unlimited set of possible activities, and thinks existing problems should receive priority.

text: Only report metrics whose movement could change an action. The leader and team should understand which behavior each reported metric informs.

text: Use four checks when testing a solution: define the problem or desired condition, propose an action and predicted effect, verify execution, and compare the actual result with the prediction.

text: An unimplemented action leaves its hypothesis untested. An implemented action can still fail to improve the target metric, consuming resources while leaving the problem unresolved.

text: He argues that founders sometimes avoid unfamiliar, unpleasant problems by pursuing more opportunities in areas they understand, eventually allowing unresolved problems to restrict growth.

text: Separate expansion ideas from the active problem list and store them for later. His own company implements approximately one idea out of every 10 or 20 he proposes.

text: He thinks limited resources make current business problems more dependable priorities than speculative opportunities. Once operations are running smoothly, revisit the stored opportunities and choose a bet.
